body:
## What

`DhcpLFC` and the `kea-dhcp6` Lease File Cleanup lines are the single largest source of unparsed
syslog volume on the live box — **720 of 1956 capture entries (36.8%)**. `kea-dhcp6` has a parser
(`parseDHCP`, `internal/logship/syslog/dhcp.go:35`) but it does not match the LFC message family;
`DhcpLFC` has no parser and **no subsystem at all**.

Triaged from the <host-1> debug-capture archive (`/opt/opnsense2otel/capture/syslog/*.ndjson`,
2026-08-04 08:46 → 2026-08-07 16:33 UTC). Context: #659, which owns the unbound half of the same
archive triage.

> **Read the counts as shape samples, not frequencies.** The syslog capture lane goes through
> `Capturer.CaptureShape` (`internal/logship/syslog/source.go:287`), which keeps one example per
> `(program, NormaliseShape(message))` per 15-minute window, bounded at 256 process-wide keys
> (`internal/logship/capture/dedupe.go`). 80 entries for a shape means "seen in 80 distinct
> 15-minute windows", not "80 lines".

## Counts

| program | capture entries | distinct shapes | subsystem assigned |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DhcpLFC` | 560 | 7 | **none (empty)** |
| `kea-dhcp6` (LFC lines only) | 160 | 2 | `dhcp` |

## Shapes

All seven `DhcpLFC` shapes, verbatim:

```
INFO  [DhcpLFC.0x10b74225f010] LFC_START Starting lease file cleanup
INFO  [DhcpLFC.0x10b74225f010] LFC_PROCESSING Previous file: /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.2, copy file: /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.1
INFO  [DhcpLFC.dhcpsrv.0x378a5665f010] DHCPSRV_MEMFILE_LEASE_FILE_LOAD loading leases from file /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.1
INFO  [DhcpLFC.0x10b74225f010] LFC_READ_STATS Leases: 162, attempts: 164, errors: 0.
INFO  [DhcpLFC.0x10b74225f010] LFC_WRITE_STATS Leases: 21, attempts: 21, errors: 0.
INFO  [DhcpLFC.0x10b74225f010] LFC_ROTATING LFC rotating files
INFO  [DhcpLFC.0x10b74225f010] LFC_TERMINATE LFC finished processing
```

Both `kea-dhcp6` LFC shapes, verbatim:

```
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.dhcpsrv.0x3fa9c3469010] DHCPSRV_MEMFILE_LFC_START starting Lease File Cleanup
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.dhcpsrv.0x3fa9c3469010] DHCPSRV_MEMFILE_LFC_EXECUTE executing Lease File Cleanup using: /usr/local/sbin/kea-lfc -6 -x /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.2 -i /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.1 -o /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.output -f /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.completed -p /var/db/kea/kea-leases6.csv.pid -c ignored-path
```

Every line shares one Kea-wide envelope:

```
<SEVERITY>  [<logger-hierarchy>.<0xADDR>] <MESSAGE_ID> <free text>
```

`<MESSAGE_ID>` is a **closed, upstream-defined vocabulary** (`SCREAMING_SNAKE`, generated into Kea's
`*_messages.h`), which is what makes this cheap to parse and stable across Kea releases. The
`0x...` component is a thread/context pointer and carries no operational meaning — it must not be
captured (same reasoning as the deliberately-dropped unbound pid at
`internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go:112`).

## Verdict: worth structuring

Three reasons, in order of weight.

1. **`LFC_READ_STATS` / `LFC_WRITE_STATS` carry `errors:`, and nothing else on the box reports it.**
   The Kea collector polls lease counts; it has no visibility into whether the lease database is
   being rewritten cleanly. A non-zero `errors` here is silent lease-file corruption. It reads `0`
   on every one of the 80 captured cycles, so today it is a healthy baseline with no alarm attached.
2. **`Leases: 162, attempts: 164` is a read-integrity ratio.** `attempts - leases` is the count of
   records read but not retained. Structuring both numbers makes that derivable.
3. **`DhcpLFC` currently ships with an empty `opnsense_subsystem`.** `subsystemFor`
   (`internal/logship/syslog/registry.go:279`) maps `kea-*` by prefix and lists `kea-dhcp4`,
   `kea-dhcp6`, `kea-ctrl-agent`, `kea-dhcp-ddns` explicitly — but `DhcpLFC` matches neither, so 36.8%
   of the archive lands under no subsystem. That is a one-line fix worth making regardless of whether
   the rest of this issue is done.

The `LFC_PROCESSING` / `DHCPSRV_MEMFILE_LEASE_FILE_LOAD` / `DHCPSRV_MEMFILE_LFC_EXECUTE` lines carry
only file paths that are fixed by Kea's own layout. Structure the message ID and let the free text
stay in the body; do not parse the paths or the `kea-lfc` argv.

Prefer one generic Kea-envelope parser over seven per-message regexes: the envelope is uniform across
`kea-dhcp4`, `kea-dhcp6`, `kea-ctrl-agent`, `kea-dhcp-ddns` and `DhcpLFC`, so one branch covers the
whole family and any future message ID degrades to "ID captured, text in the body" rather than to an
unparsed line.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `DhcpLFC` added to the `subsystems` map in `internal/logship/syslog/registry.go` as `dhcp`
      (explicit entry — it does not match the `kea-` prefix rule)
- [x] A Kea-envelope branch parses `<SEV>  [<hierarchy>.<0xaddr>] <MSG_ID> <text>` into
      `kea.msg_id` and `kea.component` (the hierarchy with the `0x` context stripped), registered for
      `DhcpLFC` in addition to the existing `kea-dhcp*` programs
- [x] `LFC_READ_STATS` / `LFC_WRITE_STATS` additionally emit `kea.lfc_leases`, `kea.lfc_attempts`,
      `kea.lfc_errors` as integers, and `kea.lfc_phase` (`read`/`write`)
- [x] The `0x...` context pointer is never emitted as an attribute
- [x] Table-driven tests over all nine verbatim lines above (every one is a real captured line; none
      synthetic)
- [x] An unrecognised Kea message ID still parses the envelope and does not regress to unparsed
- [x] `make test` / `make docs` green

comments.body:
Landed in `e85af857` (pushed to `main`).

Kea-wide envelope fallback registered as parseKeaDHCP's **last** branch, so it can never override an already-modelled lease/packet/alloc-fail message. Emits `kea.msg_id` + `kea.component`, with the per-thread `0x` context pointer stripped — that is a heap address, so promoting it would put an unbounded value on every record.

`LFC_READ_STATS`/`LFC_WRITE_STATS` additionally yield `kea.lfc_leases`, `kea.lfc_attempts`, `kea.lfc_errors`, `kea.lfc_phase`. The errors count was the genuinely unobservable-elsewhere signal: a compaction pass failing is silent in every other source.

`DhcpLFC` needed its own `subsystems` entry despite being Kea — the `kea-` prefix fallback does not match the CamelCase name.

One pre-existing test changed on purpose: `TestKeaDHCP6LFCLinesStayUnmodelled` asserted the pre-#664 contract. Renamed to `TestKeaDHCP6LFCLinesDoNotCountAsAllocFail`, now pinning the narrower invariant that still matters — these lines are claimed, but must never set `dhcp.alloc_fail_reason` or reach the alloc-fail counter.

Gate green on the committed tree: `make test` 28 packages ok / 0 failures, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `make docs-check` and `make grafana-check` both exit 0. Shared seams (`registry.go` subsystem attribution, `derive.go` family decisions, the `docs/syslog-receiver.md` parser table) landed together in `0ad3d468` rather than being contended six ways.

title: logship: structure the Kea Lease File Cleanup syslog family (DhcpLFC + kea-dhcp6), 37% of all unparsed volume

body:
## What

Under a sustained burst of log volume, the log shipper builds batches far larger than a Loki
tenant's **ingestion rate limit** can ever accept in one push, then retries the identical oversized
batch until it exhausts `--logs.ship-max-attempts` and drops every record in it. Because the emitter
is a single goroutine, the whole log pipeline head-of-line blocks for the duration.

Batch sizing is currently derived from the **OTLP transport ceiling** and takes no account of any
receiver-side bytes/sec budget. Those are different constraints and the code only models one.

## Observed

Logged repeatedly during a synthetic DNS load test that raised syslog volume sharply (tenant id and
limit value redacted):

```
level=WARN source=pipeline.go:404 msg="log sink export failed; retrying" attempt=3 count=2777
  err="max retry time elapsed: retry-able request failure: body: ingestion rate limit exceeded
  for user <REDACTED> (limit: <REDACTED> bytes/sec) while attempting to ingest '2777' lines
  totaling '7513325' bytes, reduce log volume or contact your Loki administrator..."
```

Identical message at `attempt=3` through `attempt=9`, same `count=2777`, same byte total, spanning
roughly **eight minutes of wall clock on one batch**.

The tenant was nowhere near its limits in aggregate — steady-state volume is a small fraction of the
budget. This is a burst-shape and batch-shape problem in the shipper, not a genuinely over-quota
tenant.

## Analysis

**1. Batch byte cap is sized to the wire, not to ingest rate.**
`maxExportBytes = 32 << 20` (`internal/logship/sink_otlp.go:81`) is deliberately half of
`otlpMaxRequestBytes = 64 << 20`, i.e. it answers "what will the OTLP exporter agree to send". A
Loki ingestion rate limit is a **bytes per second** budget. A single 7.5 MB push is worth many
seconds of that budget, so it is rejected atomically no matter how long we wait — and 7.5 MB is
itself well under the 32 MB cap, so nothing in our code considered it large.

`--logs.batch-max` defaults to **5000** records (`internal/options/logs.go:42`), so the count cap
did not bind either; the batch was 2777 records.

**2. A rate-limit rejection is treated as a generic transient failure.**
`shipBatch` sets `pending = res.Retry` and re-sends the **same batch unchanged**
(`internal/logship/pipeline.go:366-415`). For a network blip that is correct. For a rate limit it is
guaranteed to fail forever: the request is rejected *because of its size against a rate*, so
resending it identically cannot succeed. The correct responses are to **split the batch** and/or
**pace to the advertised limit** — neither of which the retry path can currently express.

**3. Two nested retry layers, and the outer one is not what governs.**
`shipBackoff` caps at `shipRetryMax = 5s` (`internal/logship/pipeline.go:325`), yet observed spacing
between attempts was ~75-90s. The gap is spent *inside* `Emit`: the OTLP SDK runs its own
retry/backoff and `"max retry time elapsed"` is it giving up. So worst-case time on one undeliverable
batch is `ship-max-attempts × SDK max-elapsed`, which is what produced the ~8-minute observation and
would be ~10+ minutes at the default of 10 attempts. Neither layer knows about the other.

**4. Head-of-line blocking is the real operational damage.**
`runEmitter` (`internal/logship/pipeline.go:329-339`) loops `drainUpTo` → `shipBatch`
**synchronously**. While one batch is stuck for minutes, no other batch ships, the bounded queue
behind it fills, and it oldest-drops as `logs_dropped_total{reason="overflow"}` — so a single
undeliverable batch causes collateral loss of unrelated, perfectly deliverable records from every
other source. The final drop of the stuck batch itself is counted separately as
`reason="ship_failed_permanent"`.

**5. Secondary question — 2705 bytes per record.**
`7513325 / 2777 = 2705` bytes per line as **Loki measured it**. The bodies in question are syslog DNS
lines of roughly 100-150 bytes. Structured metadata explains some of the gap, but a ~20x multiplier
deserves its own look: either the per-record structured-metadata set is far heavier than intended, or
resource attributes are being repeated per partition in a way that multiplies cost (the sink creates
one resource, and one LoggerProvider, per distinct `(source, subsystem)` pair — see the LABELS VS
STRUCTURED METADATA note at `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go:88`). Worth confirming against a real
payload before assuming it is fine. If this multiplier is wrong, every byte-budget constant in the
pipeline is calibrated against a bad estimate, including `recordBytes` in `queue.go`, which
`maxExportBytes` explicitly documents itself as trusting only to within 2x.

## Suggested direction

Not prescriptive — the implementer should weigh these.

- Add an ingest-rate-aware batch bound: a `--logs.max-export-bytes` (or bytes/sec pacing) that is
  independent of the transport ceiling, defaulting to something a rate-limited tenant can accept.
- Detect rate-limit rejections distinctly (HTTP 429 and `Retry-After` rather than matching on the
  error string, which is fragile and Loki-specific) and respond by **splitting the batch** and
  honouring the advertised delay, instead of resending unchanged.
- Reconcile the two retry layers so the SDK's max-elapsed and `--logs.ship-max-attempts` compose to a
  bounded, documented worst case rather than multiplying.
- Consider whether a stuck batch should block the emitter at all, or be set aside so unrelated
  batches keep flowing.
- Whatever changes, `logs_dropped_total` must keep distinguishing "this batch was undeliverable" from
  "unrelated records were evicted because the emitter was blocked" — the current reason labels do
  make that distinction and it should survive.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] A batch is bounded by something derived from the receiver's accept rate, not only the OTLP wire
      ceiling
- [x] A rate-limit rejection causes a split and/or paced retry, not an identical resend
- [x] Worst-case time spent on one undeliverable batch is bounded and documented, accounting for BOTH
      retry layers
- [x] A sustained burst above the tenant's rate limit degrades by pacing, not by dropping whole
      batches plus collateral queue overflow
- [x] Test covering a simulated 429 with `Retry-After`, asserting split/pacing rather than resend
- [x] The 2705 bytes/record multiplier is explained, and `recordBytes`' estimate confirmed or
      corrected against a real measured payload
- [x] Drop accounting still distinguishes the stuck batch from collateral overflow

comments.body:
Landed in a32463da (pushed to `main`).

Gate green: `make test` 28 packages ok / 0 failures, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `make docs-check` and `make grafana-check` both exit 0.

All seven acceptance criteria met. Two things worth reading rather than assuming:

**The 2705 bytes/record is a mix effect, not a multiplier, and both hypotheses in the issue are negative results.** Measured by driving the real `otlpSink` over a real socket and weighing the uncompressed protobuf: a syslog DNS record bills ~589 B, a Zenarmor conn document ~2549 B. The batch was Zenarmor documents, not the 100-150 byte syslog lines the burst was named after — `parse.go` sets `Body` to the raw NDJSON document (~1.75 kB) and derives ~32 attributes from that same JSON. There is no runaway structured-metadata set, and resource attributes are **not** repeated per partition; they travel once per `ResourceLogs`. Caveat: the wire numbers are measured, the Loki-billable column is computed from Loki's formula, not observed against a Loki instance.

**`recordBytes` is corrected, not confirmed.** It never under-counts the wire — the only direction that breaks a byte budget — but over-counts by 1.6x (Zenarmor) to 2.6x (attribute-heavy syslog), because `recordAttrOverheadBytes = 48` charges Go map/string-header cost protobuf does not pay. That is correct for its primary job, retained heap, so the constants stand and the test pins an asymmetric contract (`est >= wire`, `est <= 3x wire`) instead. `maxExportBytes`' "within 2x" claim is right in the under direction and wrong in the over direction.

Worst case on one undeliverable batch, both layers composed: **195s** with nothing advertised, **420s** if max `Retry-After` is advertised every attempt — down from 700s. Attempts are counted globally per `shipBatch`, so splitting never buys extra attempts.

Known gap: gRPC `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` is detected but carries no advertised delay — `google.rpc.RetryInfo` needs a direct import of `genproto/.../errdetails`, currently indirect, and promoting it changes `go.mod`/`vendor` for an optional hint. The 2s pacing floor covers it.

Method note: implementation was written before tests here rather than test-first. `TestShipBatch_RateLimitSplitsInsteadOfResending` does fail against the old behaviour by construction, but it was not watched failing first.

title: logship: batches sized to the OTLP wire ceiling ignore Loki ingest rate limits; identical oversized batch retried until dropped, blocking the emitter

body:
## What

Every instant Prometheus query in the generated dashboard is emitted with `"format": "table"`
(`grafana/builder.py:278`). For `table()` panels that is correct — they carry transformations that
consume the table shape. For **bargauge and piechart** panels it collapses every series into a single
unlabelled `Value`, so the panel displays one arbitrary number instead of the distribution it exists
to show.

**53 bargauge/piechart panels** across the dashboard are built this way.

## Symptom

On the "DNS - Unbound" tab, with the underlying metrics completely healthy:

| panel | rendered | actual data |
|---|---|---|
| Queries by Type | `Value 0 req/s` — empty donut | A=1.68, AAAA=1.96, PTR=0.13, SRV=0.25, HTTPS=0.26, SVCB=0.004, + 9 zero types |
| Answers by RCode | `Value 1.45 req/s 100%` — single slice | NOERROR=3.82, NXDOMAIN=0.45, nodata=0.90, SERVFAIL=0.008, + 3 zero rcodes |
| Query Flags | `0 req/s` — one empty bar | RD=4.28, AD=0.94, + 6 zero flags |
| Memory Usage | `0 B` — one empty bar | message_cache=9,325,361; rrset_cache=6,550,136; iterator=16,716; + 3 zeros |
| Cache Entries | one bar, `21.5 K` | four caches (rrset, msg, infra, key) |

The pattern is diagnostic: the number shown is whichever series happens to sort last, which is why
panels whose last series is a zero-valued member ("Queries by Type" → a zero qtype, "Memory Usage" →
`validator=0`) look like no-data, while panels whose last series is non-zero ("Answers by RCode")
look like a working single-slice donut. **Neither is right**, and the second is the more dangerous
one because it reads as a legitimate 100% reading.

("TCP Usage Ratio" showing 0% in the same screenshot is NOT this bug — that metric is genuinely 0.)

## Cause

`builder.py:278`:

```python
if instant:
    spec.update({"instant": True, "range": False, "format": "table"})
```

A Prometheus instant query with `format: table` returns **one dataframe**: a Time column, one column
per label, and a single numeric `Value` column — one row per series. Bargauge and piechart reduce
each *numeric field* to one displayed item (`reduceOptions: {calcs: ["lastNotNull"], values: false}`),
and there is exactly one numeric field, so exactly one item is displayed. `legendFormat: "{{type}}"`
is also inert in table format, which is why the legend reads a bare `Value` rather than a type name.

Deployed panel spec confirming it (`Queries by Type`, panel id 239):

```json
"expr": "max without (job, service_instance_id, service_name, service_version) (topk by (opnsense_instance) (15, sum by (opnsense_instance, type) (rate(opnsense_unbound_dns_queries_by_type_total{...}[$__rate_interval]))))",
"format": "table", "instant": true, "range": false, "legendFormat": "{{type}}"
```

## Fix

Instant queries feeding a **multi-series** viz need `format: "time_series"` — each series becomes its
own frame, `legendFormat` names it, and the reducer runs per frame. `format: "table"` should stay only
where a transformation consumes it (the `table()` panels).

`_query()` doesn't currently know what viz it is feeding, so the format has to become a parameter
rather than an unconditional consequence of `instant`. Cheapest correct shape is a `fmt` argument on
`_query()`, defaulted so `table()` keeps `"table"` and `bargauge()`/`piechart()` pass
`"time_series"`.

**Do not just flip the default.** `table()` panels' transformations (`excludes`/`renames` operate on
field names) depend on the table shape; changing it breaks them the other way. Whatever the fix, both
shapes must stay reachable.

## Blast radius

- 53 bargauge/piechart panels — broken, this is the fix target.
- 7 `stat` and 1 `gauge` panel share the pattern but aggregate to a single series, so they render
  correctly today. They are latent: any of them growing a second series starts silently showing one
  arbitrary member. Worth converting for consistency, but they are not the reported breakage.

Affected panels are spread across the whole dashboard, not one tab — examples outside DNS include
"Jumbo Pool Utilization %", "PF Memory Limits by Pool", "ARP Entries by Interface",
"Configured Rules (enabled vs disabled)", "Bytes by Transport", "Events by Family".

## Why no test caught it

The dashboard gates (`make grafana-check`) verify catalogue coverage, regeneration staleness and
manifest validity — that every metric appears on *some* panel, and that the JSON is current. Nothing
asserts that a panel's query shape can actually **render** the viz it is attached to. A gate pairing
viz type against query format would have caught all 53 at authoring time, and is the thing that stops
this class recurring.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `_query()` can emit `time_series` or `table`, chosen by the calling viz rather than by `instant`
- [x] `bargauge()` and `piechart()` emit `time_series`; `table()` keeps `table`
- [x] Regenerated `dashboard.json` shows all 53 panels changed, and `table()` panels unchanged
- [x] A builder test asserts multi-series viz types never emit `format: "table"`
- [ ] Verified against the live stack: Queries by Type shows its qtype split, Memory Usage shows all
      six components, Answers by RCode shows all rcodes
- [x] `make grafana-check` / `make docs-check` / `make test` green
- [x] Decision recorded here on whether the 8 single-series stat/gauge panels are converted too

comments.body:
Landed in 287d0193 (pushed to `main`).

Gate green: `make grafana-check` exit 0 (1200 Prometheus targets validated, 80 manifests OK), `make docs-check` exit 0, `make test` 28 packages ok, 420 grafana tests OK.

**The 53 is confirmed exactly.** Counted from the regenerated `dashboard.json` by diffing every instant panel's format against `HEAD`, grouped by viz type:

| viz | instant panels changed |
|---|---|
| bargauge | 43 |
| piechart | 10 |
| **subtotal (the reported breakage)** | **53** |
| stat | 30 |
| gauge | 15 |
| **table** | **0** |

`table()` panels changed: **0**. bargauge/piechart still emitting `format: "table"`: **0**.

(A raw `grep` of call sites gives 45 + 10 = 55, but two are in conditional or unreached paths, so the panel count is 53 as the issue said.)

**Decision on the single-series stat/gauge panels: converted.** The issue identified 7 stat + 1 gauge as latent; the fix is uniform across the helpers, so 45 instant stat/gauge panels moved to `time_series`. They render identically today — a single-series response is one frame either way, since `format` only changes how a response with multiple series is shaped into frames. Converting closes the latent bug where adding a second series later would silently start displaying one arbitrary member.

Not verified against the live stack — the acceptance criterion asking for a visual check of Queries by Type / Memory Usage / Answers by RCode on Grafana is the one item not personally confirmed. The structural guarantee is pinned instead by a builder test that sweeps every panel `build_family()` produces and fails if any multi-series viz emits a table format, which is also the gate that stops this class recurring.

## Live-stack check: the data is confirmed multi-series, the render is not mine to confirm

Queried the live Prometheus for all three panels the acceptance criterion names. Every one carries exactly the series the issue predicted:

**Queries by Type — 10 series**
`A`=2.042, `AAAA`=1.942, `SRV`=0.450, `HTTPS`=0.317, `PTR`=0.104, `SVCB`=0.0083, `TXT`=0.0042, and `NAPTR`/`NS`/`SOA` at 0.

**Answers by RCode — 7 series**
`NOERROR`=4.375, `nodata`=0.829, `NXDOMAIN`=0.642, `SERVFAIL`=0.0167, and `NOTIMPL`/`FORMERR`/`REFUSED` at 0.

**Memory Usage — 6 components**, exactly as the issue stated: `iterator`, `message_cache`, `respip`, `rrset_cache`, `streamwait`, `validator`.

**This also corroborates the diagnosed mechanism, not just the fix.** The issue argued the displayed number is whichever series sorts last, which is why "Queries by Type" read `Value 0 req/s` while "Answers by RCode" read a plausible single-slice 100%. In the live response the last `type` series is `SOA=0` and the last `rcode` series is a non-zero one — precisely the asymmetry that made one panel look like no-data and the other look like it was working. That was inference in the issue; it is now observed.

**What I did NOT verify, and cannot.** The rendered panels. `gcx dashboards list` shows no opnsense dashboard in the stack, so the regenerated `dashboard.json` is not deployed there — the render check needs a deploy first and then an eyeball. What is established is that the underlying data is multi-series (precondition), the queries now emit `format: "time_series"` (verified in the regenerated JSON: 43 bargauge + 10 piechart changed, 0 `table()` panels changed), and a builder test sweeps every generated panel so a regression fails the build.

Leaving that criterion unticked rather than claiming it — it is a genuine remaining step, just a very short one once the dashboard is deployed.

title: grafana: instant queries emit format=table, collapsing 53 bargauge/piechart panels to a single unlabelled value

body:
## What

The `unbound` per-query log lane (#233) ships a `client` field that is **sometimes an IP and
sometimes a hostname**, decided upstream by whether a PTR happened to resolve. Normalise it: always
emit the raw client IP, and add the hostname as a separate enriched attribute using the enrichment
layer we already have.

## The problem

`stats.py handle_details()` on the firewall does:

```python
details['client'] = np.where(details['hostname'].isnull(), details['client'], details['hostname'])
```

So the `client` column we receive from `api/unbound/overview/search_queries` is the resolved hostname
whenever OPNsense's own client table has one, and the IP otherwise. Verified live 2026-08-07 — <host-1>
arrives as `<host-3>`, not `<lan-ip-1>`:

```json
{"time":1786114502,"client":"<host-3>","family":"ip4","type":"AAAA",
 "domain":"profiles-prod-023.grafana.net.","action":"Pass","source":"Cache",
 "rcode":"NOERROR","dnssec_status":"Unchecked","ttl":737}
```

`internal/logship/unbound.go` passes this straight through to the `client` attribute.

## Why it matters

1. **Correlation breaks.** Every other per-flow lane keys on IP — netflow records, Zenarmor conn
   documents, the syslog lanes' `src.ip`. A DNS record keyed on `<host-3>` cannot be
   joined to a flow record keyed on `<lan-ip-1>` without a reverse map the consumer does not have.
2. **The field is not one type.** A Loki consumer filtering `client="<lan-ip-1>"` silently misses every
   query from a host with a PTR, and gets no error saying so. Mixed-type fields are worse than either
   type consistently.
3. **It is unstable over time.** A host gains or loses a PTR (DHCP lease change, a static mapping
   added) and its `client` value changes identity mid-series. Panels ranking "top blocked clients"
   then split one device across two rows.
4. **It disagrees with our own attribute conventions.** Everywhere else the exporter emits `src.ip`
   plus separately-enriched `src.hostname` — see the syslog lanes, where `internal/logship/enrich/`
   already resolves hostname, MAC and scope from an IP. This lane is the odd one out.

## Proposed fix

- Emit the raw IP as the primary client attribute, matching the naming the other lanes use.
- Feed it through the existing `internal/logship/enrich/` path so hostname/MAC/scope come from **our**
  enrichment (ARP/NDP/DHCP-lease backed), consistent with every other lane, rather than from
  OPNsense's DNS-derived client table.
- Keep whatever upstream sent as a distinct attribute if it carries anything our enrichment does not,
  rather than discarding it silently.

## The catch — read before implementing

**The API may not give us the IP at all.** The `SELECT * FROM query q LEFT JOIN client resolved`
returns both `client` (IP) and `hostname`, but the script drops `hostname` and `ipaddr` after the
`np.where` collapse (`details.drop(['hostname','ipaddr'], axis=1)`), so by the time it is serialised
there is one column. Confirm against a live payload whether the raw IP survives anywhere in the JSON
before designing around it.

If it does not, the options are:

- **Reverse the substitution locally.** We already know the hostname→IP mapping from our own
  enrichment tables; a hostname-shaped `client` can be mapped back. Lossy when two hosts share a name
  or the PTR is stale, and it inverts a transformation rather than avoiding it — call it a fallback,
  not the design.
- **Use the per-client query form.** `search_queries` accepts `client`+`timeStart`+`timeEnd`, which is
  the only mode with a real time range. Does not scale to a whole-resolver log (see #233).
- **Take the IP from the syslog route instead**, which logs the raw client address and never
  substitutes — see #659. That route has its own costs, and this issue should not silently become a
  reason to prefer it; but if the IP genuinely is unavailable from the API, it is the honest answer
  and belongs in the docs comparison.

Decide which of these applies and record the verdict on this issue before writing code.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Confirmed against a live payload whether the raw client IP is recoverable from
      `search_queries` at all, verdict recorded here
- [x] `client` (or its replacement attribute) is a single consistent type across all records
- [x] Hostname enrichment comes from `internal/logship/enrich/`, consistent with the other lanes
- [x] Attribute naming matches the conventions the syslog lanes already use
- [x] Tests cover a client with a PTR and one without
- [x] Dashboard "Top Blocked Clients" (`grafana/tabs/dns_unbound.py`) still renders. (The
      "no longer splits one device across two rows when its PTR changes" half is STRUCK — with no
      IP anywhere in the payload it is unfixable in this lane; it moves to #659. See the decision
      comment.)
- [x] Any residual limitation documented in `docs/` rather than left as a surprise

## Related

- #233 — the lane itself
- #659 — the syslog per-query route, which does not have this problem

comments.body:
## Verdict: the raw client IP is NOT recoverable from the whole-resolver `search_queries` payload

Confirmed live against the production firewall (OPNsense at `<lan-ip-2>`, fetched from the <host-1>
deployment, 2026-08-07) and cross-checked against upstream source. **The catch in the issue body is
real.** Do not design around the IP being present.

### Evidence 1 — the live payload has exactly 15 keys, none of them an IP column

`POST api/unbound/overview/search_queries` with `current=1&rowCount=1000` returned 1000 rows. Every
one of the 1000 rows has the identical key set:

```
action, blocklist, client, dnssec_status, domain, family, policy, rcode,
resolve_time_ms, source, status, time, ttl, type, uuid
```

No `ipaddr`, no `hostname`, no alternate spelling, no nested object. A representative row:

```json
{"uuid":null,"time":1786120703,"client":"<host-4>","family":"ip4","type":"A",
 "domain":"gbl.his.arc.azure.com.","action":"Pass","source":"Cache","blocklist":"",
 "rcode":"NOERROR","resolve_time_ms":0,"dnssec_status":"Unchecked","ttl":616,"policy":"","status":1}
```

The mixed-type problem is visible **inside a single page** — 28 distinct `client` values in those
1000 rows include FQDNs (`<host-3>`), bare IPv6 literals (`<pub-ip-4>105b`), a
non-FQDN name (`<host-5>`), the literal `localhost`, and 22 rows with `client` empty entirely.

### Evidence 2 — upstream source, both query branches drop the IP

`src/opnsense/scripts/unbound/stats.py`, `handle_details()` (master, fetched today). Both branches —
the whole-resolver one *and* the per-client one — feed the same collapse:

```python
details['client'] = np.where(details['hostname'].isnull(), details['client'], details['hostname'])
details['blocklist'] = details['blocklist'].replace(np.nan, None)
details = details.drop(['hostname', 'ipaddr'], axis=1)
```

So the IP is destroyed before serialisation on every code path. `api/unbound/overview/export` and the
rolling/top endpoints are separate aggregations, not a per-query alternative.

### Evidence 3 — the per-client form works, but only over JSON, and still returns no IP column

Worth recording because it is not what the controller looks like it does.
`OverviewController::searchQueriesAction()` gates the per-client branch on:

```php
$client = Util::isIpAddress($client) ? $client : null;
$time_start = is_int($time_start) ? $time_start : null;
```

`is_int()` on a form-encoded POST value is **always false** (they are strings), so a
`Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request with `client=…&timeStart=…&timeEnd=…`
**silently ignores the filter and returns the unfiltered 1000-row page**. Verified live: filtering on
`client=<host-6>` and on `client=<lan-ip-1>` returned byte-for-byte the same client
distribution as no filter at all (`<host-1> 500, winsrv 143, <host-7> 93, iPhone 63, <host-8> 40`).

With a JSON body and real JSON integers it does work:

```
POST api/unbound/overview/search_queries
Content-Type: application/json
{"client":"<lan-ip-1>","timeStart":1786117190,"timeEnd":1786120790}
-> 500 rows, all client="<host-3>"
```

Note the filter matches on `q.client = ?` — the **raw IP** — while the returned `client` column is
still the substituted hostname. So the IP is known only because we supplied it, and the key set is
unchanged (same 15 keys, no `ipaddr`).

### Evidence 4 — reverse-mapping from our enrichment tables measured on real data

Fallback 1 quantified rather than guessed. Built an IP→hostname table from the same sources
`enrich.doRefreshLeases()` uses (`search_arp` hostname + `kea/leases4/search` + `dnsmasq/leases/search`
— 92 IPs with a hostname), inverted it, and matched it against the 28 distinct clients in the live
1000-row page:

| outcome | distinct clients | rows (of 1000) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| already an IP (no PTR upstream) | 5 | 27 |
| reverse-maps to exactly one IP | 11 | 212 |
| reverse-maps to **multiple** IPs (ambiguous) | 1 (`winsrv` → 4 IPs) | 135 |
| **no match at all** | 11 | 626 |

**64% of queries would still have no IP**, dominated by `<host-3>` at 470 rows — a
static-IP host with no DHCP lease and no ARP hostname, i.e. exactly the class of host the ARP/lease
tables cannot name. `<host-6>` resolves to four addresses
(`<lan-ip-3>`, `<lan-ip-4>`, `<lan-ip-5>`, `<lan-ip-6>`) with nothing in the row to pick between
them beyond `family`. Also unmappable: `localhost`, the 22 empty-`client` rows, and every
`*.mgmt` / `*.cam` device.

A reverse map that covers ~36% of traffic and silently guesses on the second-largest client is worse
than no IP: it produces a field that *looks* authoritative and is wrong for one host in the top three.

### Which fallback applies

- **Per-client form (option 2): rejected.** It would need one call per client per poll (28 clients on
  this box), each spawning python+pandas+DuckDB on the firewall (~1s CPU) — the exact cost #233 sized
  the 15s floor around — and the client-IP list would have to come from the same ARP/lease tables that
  miss `<host-1>`. It does not scale to a whole-resolver log.
- **Reverse the substitution (option 1): rejected as a primary design** on the numbers above.
- **The syslog route (#659) is the honest answer for IP-keyed correlation.** It logs the raw client
  address and never substitutes; `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go` already sets `src.ip`.

### Recommendation for this lane (not yet implemented — awaiting a call)

Do not synthesise an IP. Stop the field from being mixed-*meaning* instead:

1. Rename the attribute so it stops claiming to be a client address — it is "whatever label the
   resolver's own client table applied". It is still not one *type*, but it is one *thing*, and no
   consumer is misled into `client="<lan-ip-1>"` filters that silently miss most traffic.
2. Set `src.ip` **only** when the upstream value already parses as an IP (the no-PTR case, 27/1000
   rows here), so `src.ip` on this lane is always a real address when present — consistent with every
   other lane — and absent otherwise. No reverse-map guessing.
3. Run that `src.ip` through `internal/logship/enrich/` for hostname/MAC/scope like the other lanes,
   which is a no-op on rows without one.
4. Document in `docs/` that this lane cannot be joined to flow records by IP, and that #659 is the
   route to use when IP correlation matters.

Open question for the acceptance criterion *"no longer splits one device across two rows when its PTR
changes"*: with no IP available, that criterion **cannot be fully met by this lane**. A device whose
PTR appears or disappears still changes identity in the upstream `client` value. The dashboard panel
becomes stable only if it groups on a field we control, which we cannot construct here.

## Decision: minimal de-mix, IP correlation deferred to #659

Following the verdict in the comment above — the raw client IP is destroyed on the firewall before
serialisation, on every code path — this is the route taken. Recorded before code is written, per
the issue's own gate.

**Rejected: reverse-mapping from our enrichment tables.** Measured against 1000 live rows, not
estimated:

| outcome | distinct clients | rows of 1000 |
|---|---|---|
| already an IP | 5 | 27 |
| maps to exactly one IP | 11 | 212 |
| maps to **multiple** IPs | 1 (`winsrv` → 4 IPs) | 135 |
| no match | 11 | 626 |

35% coverage, and the two failures are the damaging kind: `<host-1>` is absent entirely (470 rows, the
single biggest client — static IP, so no DHCP lease and no ARP hostname), and `winsrv` is ambiguous
across `<lan-ip-3>` / `<lan-ip-4>` / `<lan-ip-5>` / `<lan-ip-6>`. A field that is authoritative-
looking and silently wrong for the number-two client is worse than an absent field.

**Rejected: the per-client `search_queries` form.** One configd/python/pandas/DuckDB call per client
per poll — 28 clients on this box at ~1s CPU each, which is exactly the cost #233's 15s floor was
sized against. It also needs a client list, which would come from the same ARP/lease tables that
miss `<host-1>`.

Worth recording separately: **that form is unreachable over a form-encoded POST at all.**
`OverviewController::searchQueriesAction()` gates it on `is_int($time_start)`, always false for
form values (they are strings), so the filter is **silently ignored** and you get the unfiltered
1000-row page. Proven live — `client=<host-6>` and `client=<lan-ip-1>` both returned the
unfiltered client distribution. With a JSON body and real JSON ints it does filter, but the match is
on `q.client` (the raw IP), so the IP is known only because you supplied it. Still no `ipaddr` in the
response.

### What gets built

- The upstream value keeps its own attribute, named so it stops claiming to be a client address.
  It is always set, and remains what the dashboard groups on.
- `src.ip` is set **only** when the upstream value already parses as an IP (~27/1000 rows). So
  `src.ip` is either a real address or absent — never a hostname. That is the mixed-type defect
  fixed, which is a real problem independent of the IP question.
- When `src.ip` is set, it feeds `internal/logship/enrich/` for hostname/MAC/scope, consistent with
  every other lane.
- `docs/` states that this lane cannot be joined to flow records by IP, and points at #659.

### Acceptance criteria amended

> - [ ] Dashboard "Top Blocked Clients" still renders, and no longer splits one device across two
>       rows when its PTR changes

**The second half of that cannot be met by this lane and is struck.** With no IP available anywhere
in the payload, a device gaining or losing a PTR still changes identity in the upstream value, and
there is no field we control to group on instead. Split-on-PTR-change is only fixable via the syslog
route, so it moves to #659. "Still renders" stands.

Landed in 3726ca97 (pushed to `main`), implementing the minimal de-mix decided above.

Gate green: `make test` 28 packages ok / 0 failures, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `make docs-check` and `make grafana-check` exit 0.

**Attribute chosen: `dns.client_label`.** Dotted namespaces are the house convention for anything a lane derives per-record (`dns.query_name`, `dns.local_zone`, `src.*`, `dnsbl.*`); the poll lane's flat `client`/`domain`/`qtype` keys are the outlier, and since dotted `src.*` is being added here anyway the replacement joins the convention. `_label` rather than `_name`/`_ip`: it says what it is — whatever identity string OPNsense's own client table applied — without claiming to be either. No duplicate bare `client` was kept, and a test asserts it is gone so no consumer can keep filtering the mixed-type key by accident.

Emitted attributes:

- client parses as an address → `dns.client_label`, `src.ip`, plus `src.hostname`/`src.mac`/`src.scope` where our snapshot resolves them
- client is a hostname → `dns.client_label` only, no `src.*` at all
- client empty → neither; the attribute is absent, not empty

The lane also now takes the `enrich.Cache` it was previously ignoring — it was the only lane not wired to it. The JSON **body** still carries `client` verbatim, since the body is a full-fidelity encoding of the row and renaming a field there would misrepresent the payload.

Dashboard: "Top Blocked Clients" now groups on `dns_client_label` (dots become underscores on Loki OTLP ingest). Deliberately **not** `src_ip`, which is null on ~97% of rows.

Docs: `docs/log-shipping.md` gains the limitation in full — why the IP is unavailable, that `src.ip` is present-or-absent but never a hostname, and the measured reason reverse-mapping was rejected.

Acceptance criteria: all met except the struck half of the dashboard item. To restate why, since it is the one thing this issue could not deliver — a device gaining or losing a PTR still changes identity in `dns_client_label`, because there is no address anywhere in the payload to group on instead. That is only fixable via the syslog route and now works there: #659 landed in the same push and ships a raw, never-substituted client IP.

title: logs(unbound): client field is a hostname when a PTR exists — normalise to raw IP and enrich hostname ourselves

body:
## What

Add a second, opt-in route for per-query DNS logs: parse Unbound's own `log-queries` / `log-replies`
syslog output in `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go`, alongside the existing poll-based `unbound`
lane from #233.

The two routes are **complementary, not competing** — they carry different fields, and neither is a
superset of the other. Which one an operator should pick depends on what they need and what their
resolver can afford. Today only the poll route exists, so an operator who needs the raw client IP,
complete coverage, or resolve latency has no option at all.

## Why — what each route can and cannot give you

| | poll (`--logs.unbound.enabled`, #233) | syslog (`log-queries`/`log-replies`, this issue) |
|---|---|---|
| completeness | newest 1000 rows resolver-wide per poll; loss counted via `logs_possible_gap_total{source="unbound"}` | complete, every query |
| client identity | **hostname substituted when a PTR exists** (see below) | raw client IP |
| resolve time / cache-hit flag | no | yes, from `log-replies` |
| action / blocklist / policy | **yes** — the DNSBL disposition | no (only local-zone actions, via `log-local-actions`) |
| dnssec_status, rcode, ttl | yes | rcode only (`log-replies`) |
| cost model | firewall API + DuckDB lock contention | inline printf per query in the resolution hot path |
| transport | poll | push |

The client-identity row is the sharp edge. `stats.py handle_details()` does
`details['client'] = np.where(details['hostname'].isnull(), details['client'], details['hostname'])`,
so the poll route returns `<host-3>` where the syslog route would return `<lan-ip-1>`.
That makes poll records hard to join to netflow/Zenarmor records by IP. Verified live 2026-08-07.

## Measurements (live box, OPNsense 26.7 / FreeBSD 15.1, 12 cores, resolver at 4.2–7.5 qps)

Recorded here so nobody re-derives them.

**Poll route, for comparison:**

- 0.55s wall, 282 KB, 1000 rows per call; ~0.4s python+pandas+DuckDB CPU. Five timed calls: 0.544,
  0.545, 0.562, 0.605, 0.534s.
- `LIMIT 1000` is **hard-coded in the controller** (`OverviewController.php:98`,
  `configdpRun('unbound qstats details', [1000])`) — the `rowCount` form param we send does not
  affect it. At 7.5 qps and the 15s floor that is ~112 rows/window, ~11% of the cap.
- The real cost is **lock contention, not CPU**. DuckDB has no concurrent reader+writer, so
  `site-python/duckdb_helper.py` serialises readers against the writer with an `flock`. Each poll
  blocks `logger.py` — the process draining Unbound's `dns_logger` FIFO — for ~0.5s. Upstream's own
  comment at `logger.py:155` states the consequence: the FIFO can fill while blocked, `dnsbl_module`
  catches `BlockingIOError` and re-buffers, "making the process eventually consistent". Duty cycle at
  a 15s poll is 3.7%.
- Once a day the DuckDB export/import holds the lock for **10–15s** (`Database auto restore from
  /var/cache/unbound.duckdb for cleanup reasons in 14.99 seconds`, observed 3 days running in the
  debug-capture archive). Polls stall through it. Not data loss: 15s at 7.5 qps is ~112 rows, far
  under the 1000 cap.
- Enabled on the live box 2026-08-07; gap counter held at 0, and the ingested breakdown by
  `query_source` over 5m was Cache 1147 / Recursion 568 / Local 10 / Local-data 8. **The poll route
  sees the whole resolver stream, not just local-zone traffic.**

**Syslog route:**

- Upstream warns against it in `man unbound.conf`: `log-queries` *"Prints one line per query to the
  log ... Note that it takes time to print these lines which makes the server (significantly)
  slower."* Same wording on `log-replies`. This is a synchronous write in the resolution hot path,
  per query, per worker thread — structurally worse than the poll's 3.7% duty cycle, which is
  amortised and off the hot path.
- Volume is not the constraint: +648k lines/day at 7.5 qps for `log-queries`, doubling with
  `log-replies`. Against the box's current ~120 lines/s of total syslog that is +6% / +12%.
- Current box state: `log-queries: no`, `log-replies: no`, `log-local-actions: yes`,
  `log-servfail: yes` (`/var/unbound/advanced.conf`). So the local-zone lane already flows at ~3.5/s.
- Unbound is essentially fully parsed today — across the entire syslog debug-capture archive there
  are **3 unparsed unbound lines**, all the daily DB-restore message.

## The parser gap

`reUnboundQuery` (`internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go:46`) requires `(\S+)@(\d+)` — the
`log-local-actions` form. Neither new shape matches it:

- `log-queries` emits `[pid:thread] info: <client-ip> <qname> <qtype> <qclass>` — four tokens, no
  `@port`.
- `log-replies` appends rcode, secure flag, resolve time, cached flag and response size.

Both currently fall through to a generic record carrying the raw body. Nothing is dropped, but
nothing is structured either.

**The exact line shapes must come from a real capture, not from the man page.** Per the repo's
fixture rule, a fixture must never encode a shape upstream cannot produce. `log-queries: yes` needs
setting on the testbed briefly with `OPN2OTEL_LOGS_SYSLOG_DEBUG_CAPTURE=true`, and the captured
lines pasted into this issue before any regex is written.

## Double-count hazard

Running both routes at once ships **two Loki records per DNS query** under different
`opnsense_source` values. Every per-query panel would then depend on which lane the operator enabled,
and the "Query Dispositions/s" panel would silently double. Startup should refuse or warn.

## Scope

- Parser branches in `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go` for `log-queries` and `log-replies`, with
  table-driven tests over captured lines.
- Attribute vocabulary consistent with the poll lane where the fields genuinely coincide
  (`dns.query_name`, `dns.query_type`, `dns.query_class`, `src.ip`, `dns.rcode`), plus the fields
  only this route has (resolve time, cache-hit).
- A decision, recorded here, on whether these records join `opnsense_source="syslog"` under
  `opnsense_subsystem="dns"` (where they naturally land) or get promoted so the dashboard's
  Per-Query Log row can read either lane from one selector. This is the main design fork.
- Guard against both lanes being enabled together.
- Docs: `docs/configuration.md` gains the firewall-side prerequisite and the upstream
  "(significantly) slower" warning verbatim, plus a short "which route should I pick" table.
- Dashboard: the Per-Query Log row (`grafana/tabs/dns_unbound.py`, tab "DNS - Unbound Lists") reads
  `opnsense_source="unbound"` only. It needs to work for whichever lane is on.

## Out of scope

- Changing the poll lane's accepted-loss design (#233). It stays as-is.
- Enabling either route by default. Both stay opt-in.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Real `log-queries` and `log-replies` lines captured from a live box and pasted into this issue
- [x] Parser branches added, driven by those captures, with tests
- [x] Unparsed-line count for `program=unbound` stays at its current floor (the deliberate
      fall-through set only) with both settings on
      — **VERIFIED offline** against the capture window when both settings were on: 766 records,
      730 claimed (= 418 `query:` + 312 `reply:` exactly), 36 unclaimed and every one of them in
      the documented deliberate fall-through set. The archive is shape-deduped, so it holds one
      example of every distinct shape — if every shape parses, every line parses. See the
      verification comment for the full breakdown.
- [x] Both-lanes-enabled produces a startup refusal or warning, with a test
- [x] Per-Query Log dashboard row renders from the syslog lane alone
- [x] `make docs` / `make grafana-check` / `make test` green
- [x] `docs/configuration.md` documents the firewall prerequisite, the performance warning, and the
      route-selection guidance

> **NOTE (2026-08-07):** this body was accidentally blanked by tooling during the implementation run
> and restored verbatim from the pre-edit copy, with only the checkboxes above updated. The four
> comments below were unaffected. The last comment supersedes the earlier ones wherever they
> disagree — in particular the query:reply ratio evidence in the first and third comments is void
> (the capture archive is shape-deduped, so its counts are not frequencies).

comments.body:
## Captured line shapes (live box, OPNsense 26.7, unbound 1.25.1, 2026-08-07)

`log-queries: yes` + `log-replies: yes` enabled on the testbed and the lines pulled out of the
exporter's own syslog debug capture (`OPN2OTEL_LOGS_SYSLOG_DEBUG_CAPTURE=true`). These are verbatim,
not derived from the man page.

**The prefix is `query:` / `reply:`, NOT `info:`.** That is the single most important detail here —
the existing local-actions parser (`reUnboundQuery`, `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go:46`) anchors
on `info:`, so these are a separate discriminator and cannot be folded into a loosened version of it.

### `log-queries`

```
[pid:thread] query: <client> <qname> <qtype> <qclass>
```

```
[96463:4] query: 127.0.0.1 www.tleechreload.org. A IN
[96463:8] query: <lan-ip-7> unitedkingdom.smartscreen.microsoft.com. A IN
[96463:9] query: <lan-ip-1> profiles-prod-023.grafana.net. AAAA IN
[96463:0] query: <ula-ip-1> www.msftconnecttest.com. A IN
```

### `log-replies`

```
[pid:thread] reply: <client> <qname> <qtype> <qclass> <rcode> <resolve_time> <from_cache> <size>
```

```
[96463:8] reply: 127.0.0.1 tvchaosuk.com. AAAA IN NOERROR 0.012482 0 90
[96463:8] reply: <lan-ip-7> unitedkingdom.smartscreen.microsoft.com. A IN NOERROR 0.062836 0 186
[96463:0] reply: <ula-ip-1> www.msftconnecttest.com. A IN NOERROR 0.010623 0 151
[96463:10] reply: <lan-ip-7> safebrowsing-proxy.g.aaplimg.com. HTTPS IN NOERROR 0.000000 1 110
[96463:5] reply: <lan-ip-3> _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<host-9>. SRV IN NXDOMAIN 0.000981 0 58
```

Trailing fields, left to right: rcode, resolve time in seconds (6dp), from-cache flag (`0`/`1`),
response size in bytes.

### Notes for the implementation

- **The client is a raw IP, always** — no PTR substitution, unlike the poll lane (#660). IPv6 clients
  appear bare: no brackets, no `@port`. A single `(\S+)` captures either family whole.
- **A cache hit is `0.000000` + flag `1`**, and both appear together. `resolve_time` alone is not a
  cache discriminator — an uncached-but-fast reply is not 0.000000, but do not rely on that; read the
  flag.
- **`query` and `reply` counts do not match**: 120 query lines to 95 reply lines in the same capture
  window. Do not build anything that assumes a 1:1 pairing, and do not try to correlate the two into a
  single record — there is no request id, only (client, qname, qtype, qclass), which repeats.
  `log-replies` alone carries every field `log-queries` has plus four more, so **`log-replies` on its
  own is probably the better recommendation** and `log-queries` is close to redundant. That belongs in
  the docs comparison.
- The `.` terminator is present on every qname, matching the existing local-actions parser's capture.
- Residual unbound chatter in the same capture is unchanged and still correctly falls through:
  `Database auto restore`, `info: server stats`, `info: histogram`, `info: average`,
  `notice: init module`, `Closing logger`. 14 lines against 215 query/reply lines.

Performance impact of running with both settings on is being measured separately and will be posted
here and in `docs/`.

## Instructions for whoever picks this up — do the capture analysis yourself

The line shapes in the comment above are a **starting sample, not the analysis**. They were pulled
opportunistically to prove the parser gap is real and to pin the `query:`/`reply:` discriminator. Do
not treat them as the complete shape inventory and do not write regexes against that comment alone.

**Pull the full capture set from <host-1> and analyse it yourself.**

```
host:  <host-1>
path:  /opt/opnsense2otel/capture/syslog/*.ndjson
note:  files are 0600 owned by uid 65532 (the container's nonroot user), so read them with sudo
```

`OPN2OTEL_LOGS_SYSLOG_DEBUG_CAPTURE=true` and `OPN2OTEL_LOGS_DEBUG_CAPTURE_DIR=/capture` are set on
that box, so every syslog line the exporter could **not** parse is written there as NDJSON with
`kind`, `program`, `message` and the original `raw` envelope. The archive rolls at ~64 files under a
256 MiB cap, so pull the whole directory rather than the newest file — older shapes may have aged out
of the newest one but still be in the set.

`log-queries: yes` and `log-replies: yes` were enabled on the firewall on 2026-08-07 at 16:24 local
specifically so these shapes would land in that capture. Confirm they are still on before drawing
conclusions from line counts (`/var/unbound/advanced.conf`, or `api/unbound/settings/get` →
`unbound.advanced.logqueries`/`logreplies`); if they have been reverted, the capture is a fixed
historical window rather than a live feed and the volume ratios still hold but nothing new is
arriving.

### What the analysis must cover

- Every distinct `query:` and `reply:` shape, not just the common ones. Group by structure, not by
  frequency, so a rare shape is not lost behind a common one.
- Edge cases that break naive regexes: IPv6 clients, qnames with escaped or non-printable characters
  (unbound prints them as `?`), unusual qtypes, every rcode present, the from-cache flag in both
  states, and any line where field count deviates from the norm.
- The `query:`-to-`reply:` ratio, and whether it is stable. The earlier sample showed 120:95, which is
  why the comment above suggests `log-replies` may make `log-queries` redundant — **verify that
  against the full set before it becomes a docs recommendation.**
- Whatever the daily DuckDB export/import window does to these lines, if anything.

### There is other unrecognised data in there — file issues for it

The capture directory is **not** unbound-only. A quick count by program across the archive showed
unparsed lines from `DhcpLFC` (546), `syslog-ng` (280), `kea-dhcp6` (156), `rule-updater.py` (39),
`opnsense` (27), `configd.py` (24), `dpinger` (9), `kernel` (4), `php` (3) and `config` (3), alongside
the 3 unbound ones.

**Triage all of it and open a separate issue per coherent group of shapes** — one issue per program,
or per subsystem where that groups more naturally. Do not fold them into this issue; this one is
scoped to the unbound per-query route only. For each group decide and record whether the shape is
worth structuring, worth dropping, or correctly left as a generic record, and say why. The
`Database auto restore` / `info: histogram` / `info: server stats` unbound lines are already known to
be deliberate fall-through (multi-line statistics dumps, see the comment block at the top of
`internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go`) — do not "fix" those.

Apply the repo's own rules while doing this: a fixture must never encode a shape upstream cannot
produce, so derive every test case from a real captured line or from the upstream source's own
branches, and say so in the case comment when one is deliberately synthetic.

## Performance impact of `log-queries` + `log-replies` — measured 2026-08-07

Run on the live testbed (OPNsense 26.7 / FreeBSD 15.1, 12 cores, 32 GB). The poll lane
(`--logs.unbound.enabled`) was **disabled** first so the two routes could not confound each other.
Config applied 16:24:26 local, measurement window 16:30–16:46.

### Headline

**At this box's query rate there is no detectable performance impact.** But read the caveat section
before using that to size a busy resolver — this test cannot refute upstream's warning, it operates
nowhere near where that warning bites.

### Resolver metrics

| metric | OFF (2h) | OFF (clean 8m) | ON (16m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| queries/s | 4.881 | 5.264 | **6.466** |
| cache hit ratio | 0.724 | 0.660 | 0.797 |
| recursion time avg (s) | 0.02729 | 0.02728 | 0.02860 |
| recursion time median (s) | 0.01718 | 0.01718 | 0.01804 |
| recursion p95 (s) | 0.07873 | 0.09076 | 0.10258 |
| request list avg | 0.2049 | 0.2041 | 0.1791 |
| req list exceeded /s | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| req list overwritten /s | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| queries timed out /s | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| discard timeout /s | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| wait limit /s | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| recursive replies /s | 1.349 | 1.790 | 1.310 |
| box CPU busy | 6.00% | 6.59% | 6.11% |
| box load1 | 0.749 | 0.903 | 0.826 |

**The saturation counters are the ones that matter, and every one of them is flat zero.**
`request_list_exceeded`, `request_list_overwritten`, `queries_timed_out`, `discard_timeout` and
`wait_limit` are exactly what would move first if a synchronous per-query write were making the
server fall behind. None of them moved off zero. `request_list_avg` went *down*.

Recursion latency rose 5% on avg/median and 30% on p95, but this is **not** attributable to logging:
recursion time measures cache-miss resolutions only, which are upstream-network-bound, the recursive
reply rate fell 2.9% over the same window, and a 16-minute window against a 2-hour baseline is well
inside normal variance for that signal.

### unbound process CPU

Cumulative CPU from `api/diagnostics/activity/getActivity`, summed across all 37 unbound threads.

- **Baseline: 0.0086 cores** (4370 CPU-seconds over 508,903s uptime — a 141-hour average with
  logging off).
- **Logging on, steady state: 0.0049 cores** (3 CPU-seconds over 615s, 16:29:34 → 16:39:49).

No increase. The apparent *decrease* is not real — `top`'s TIME column has 1-second-per-thread
resolution, which across 37 threads puts the noise floor at roughly the size of the entire signal.
The honest reading is "unchanged, and too small to measure precisely at this query rate".

A separate 11-CPU-second spike at 16:39:49 → 16:43:54 is the **DNSBL blocklist reload**, not query
logging — `dnsbl_module.py` runs inside unbound, so the 20-minute blocklist rebuild is charged to
unbound's own CPU.

### Log volume — the cost that IS measurable

| | OFF | ON | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| dns lines/min | 67 | **795** | **11.9x** |
| dns bytes/min | 6.8 KB | 61.8 KB | 9.1x |
| projected/day | 97k lines | **1.14M lines** | |
| dns share of ALL syslog | 5.6% | **41.1%** | |
| total syslog lines/min | 1206 | 1932 | +60% |

795 lines/min against 6.466 qps is 2.05 lines per query — exactly the expected one `query:` plus one
`reply:`. This is the real cost of the syslog route at any query rate: **~2 log lines per DNS query,
forever.** Byte volume is modest (0.09 GB/day) but line count is what most ingest pricing counts.

### Caveats — read before extrapolating

1. **This box runs at ~5–6.5 qps.** `man unbound.conf` warns that `log-queries` "makes the server
   (significantly) slower" because it is a synchronous write in the resolution hot path, per query,
   per worker thread. That cost is *per query*, so it is invisible at 6 qps and would be roughly two
   orders of magnitude larger at a rate where it matters. **A null result here is not evidence the
   warning is wrong** — it is evidence this box is too quiet to test it. Do not cite these numbers to
   justify enabling it on a busy resolver.
2. **The windows are not perfectly matched.** Workload was 32.5% higher during the ON window and
   cache hit ratio 10% higher. Both differences are in the direction that would *mask* a small
   regression in the rate-based signals, though not in the flat-zero saturation counters.
3. **unbound restarted at 16:24:26** to apply the config, so every counter and the request-list
   high-water mark reset. `request_list_max` reading 101 (OFF) versus 8 (ON) is that reset, **not** an
   improvement — ignore that row.
4. `tcp_usage_ratio` moved 0 → 0.125 across the restart. Cause not established; noted rather than
   attributed.

### What this means for the route decision

For a homelab / small-office resolver at single-digit qps, the syslog route's CPU cost is not a
reason to avoid it. The deciding factors are the ones in the comparison table in the issue body —
complete coverage and raw client IP versus DNSBL action/blocklist attribution — plus the ~2 lines per
query of ingest.

`log-replies` alone carries every field `log-queries` has plus four more, so if line volume matters,
enabling only `log-replies` halves the ingest for strictly more data. Verify that against the full
capture set before it becomes a docs recommendation.

### Method note worth keeping

`api/unbound/settings/set` followed by `service/reconfigure` returned `{"status":"ok"}` and unbound
restarted 2–6 seconds later. The config change is **not** queued behind the 20-minute DNSBL cycle —
an earlier reading of this run claimed a 20-minute delay and that was a timestamp-conversion error,
not a real observation. The DNSBL rebuild itself runs every 20 min and completes in 5–62s
(median 36s) across 72 cycles in 24h, so it never blocks a reconfigure for long.

## Load test: does `log-queries`/`log-replies` cost anything at sustained rate?

The earlier measurement ran at the box's natural ~6 qps, which is far too quiet to exercise upstream's
"(significantly) slower" warning. This is the follow-up at 15-150x that rate.

**Method.** Purpose-built open-loop UDP DNS generator (closed-loop self-throttles when the server
slows, which hides the exact signal we want). 8 sockets, 10 pre-warmed names so answers come from
cache and the variable under test is the per-query path rather than upstream recursion. Each config
applied via `settings/set` + `service/reconfigure`, verified in `/var/unbound/advanced.conf` before
measuring. Client is a LAN host, one hop, 5-6 ms baseline RTT.

### Ramp, 30s per rate, runs back-to-back

| offered qps | OFF loss | ON loss | OFF p50 ms | ON p50 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.000% | 0.000% | 5.53 | 5.83 |
| 200 | 0.000% | 0.000% | 5.31 | 5.33 |
| 300 | 0.000% | 0.101% | 5.59 | 5.42 |
| 400 | 58.03% | 59.13% | 581.68 | 584.49 |
| 500 | 67.48% | 67.53% | 590.83 | 593.37 |

### Standalone, 30s per rate, 45s rest between runs

| offered qps | OFF loss | ON loss | OFF replies | ON replies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 600 | 44.11% | 44.29% | 9976 | 10005 |
| 800 | 58.12% | 58.13% | 10018 | 10008 |
| 1000 | 66.52% | 63.38% | 10010 | 10004 |

### unbound CPU

| run | OFF | ON |
|---|---|---|
| ramp 100-500 (165s) | 14 CPU-s | 19 CPU-s |
| standalone 600-1000 (225s) | 22 CPU-s | 22 CPU-s |

## Conclusion

**At every offered rate tested, up to 1000 qps, query logging on versus off is indistinguishable.**
Loss matches within 1 percentage point at every step, p50 latency within a few ms, and delivered
throughput within 0.3%. No knee moved. Nothing degraded.

The CPU comparison is inconclusive rather than supportive: the ramp suggested +36% (14 vs 19
CPU-seconds) but the standalone runs showed no difference at all (22 vs 22). At 1-second-per-thread
`top` resolution across 37 threads, both readings sit inside the noise floor. The standalone pair is
also the weaker test of the two, because delivered throughput was capped identically in both arms, so
unbound did the same amount of real work either way.

## What this test did NOT establish — read before citing it

**The offered rates above are not delivered rates.** Every high-rate run plateaued at almost exactly
10,000 replies per 30 s (~333/s) regardless of whether 600, 800 or 1000 qps was offered, and
regardless of logging. **I did not identify what imposes that plateau**, and it is very likely the
test harness or the client host rather than the resolver:

- 400 qps in the ramp showed 58% loss, but 400 qps standalone showed **0.4%** loss. The cliff is not
  reproducible, so it is an artifact of back-to-back runs, not a capacity limit.
- Raising the generator to 64 sockets made throughput *worse* (3377 replies vs 8528), which is not
  how a server-side bottleneck behaves.
- Every layer I could measure denies dropping: unbound's `queries_ip_ratelimited_total`,
  `request_list_exceeded_total`, `request_list_overwritten_total`, `queries_timed_out_total`,
  `queries_discard_timeout_total` and `queries_wait_limit_total` are all **zero**, and
  `request_list_max` peaked at **14**. The firewall's cumulative `netstat -sp udp` "dropped due to
  full socket buffers" is **6** over five days' uptime. The client host recorded **4** buffer drops
  across a full run.

So the honest ceiling of this experiment is the **~400 qps clean sustained rate**, about **60x** the
box's baseline — not the 100x+ delivered load that was the goal. Anyone re-running this should fix
the harness first (a generator on a Linux host with proper socket handling, or `dnsperf`), and should
not treat the ~333/s plateau as a property of the resolver.

An earlier note in this run claimed "the firewall saturates at ~350 qps". That was wrong — it was
based on the non-reproducible ramp cliff and on a control comparison that did not isolate the client.

## Bottom line for the route decision

Up to ~60x this box's baseline query rate, enabling `log-queries` + `log-replies` has **no measurable
effect on resolver loss, latency or throughput**. Upstream's warning is real in principle — it is a
synchronous write in the resolution hot path — but it does not bite anywhere near the volumes a
homelab or small-office resolver sees. For a genuinely busy resolver the question remains open, and
this test should not be cited as having answered it.

### 4. Upstream source — the shapes the capture CANNOT show

Read out of unbound master; these bound the regex and none can be derived from this archive.

`dname_str` (`util/data/dname.c:639`) is used by **both** lanes and has four branches:

- root/empty dname → **`.`** (bare single dot);
- any byte not `[a-zA-Z0-9]`, `-`, `_`, `*` → **`?`**, one char. **The issue body's `\DDD` escape form
  is WRONG for this code path** — it is `?` only, and the qname can therefore never contain
  whitespace, which is what makes `(\S+)` safe;
- name ≥ `LDNS_MAX_DOMAINLEN` → truncated + **`&`**, *no trailing dot*;
- label > 63 bytes → **`#`** alone, *no trailing dot*.

So **a regex requiring a trailing `.` on the qname is wrong** and will drop the truncation branches.

`log_query_in` (`util/net_help.c:586`) falls back to **`TYPE%d`** for an unknown qtype and
**`CLASS%d`** for an unknown qclass. `log_reply_info` (`util/data/msgreply.c:996`) uses
`sldns_wire2str_rcode_buf`, which falls back to **`RCODE%d`**.

Two `reply:` shapes exist that this capture does not contain:

- **FORMERR**: `log_reply("%s - - - %s - - -%s", ...)` → `client - - - FORMERR - - -`. Still exactly
  8 tokens, but qname/qtype/qclass/time/cache/size are all literal `-`. A naive numeric parse of
  slots 6–8 breaks here.
- **null qname**: `qname_buf` is set to the literal string `null` when `qinf->qname` is NULL.

And an optional **trailing destination clause**, appended when `log-destaddr: yes`:
` on <udp|tcp|dot|doh|unix|raw> <ip> <port>` — 3 extra tokens, 11 total. OPNsense's
`advanced.conf` template does not emit `log-destaddr`, so it is off by default, but the GUI's custom
options box can set it. Tolerate it.

### 5. NEW PREREQUISITE: `log-tag-queryreply` is what produces the `query:`/`reply:` tag

`log_query()`/`log_reply()` are only used when the runtime global `LOG_TAG_QUERYREPLY` is set; the
`else` branch calls `log_info()`, which tags the line **`info:`** instead. That global comes from
`log-tag-queryreply`, and **upstream's default is 0** (`util/config_file.c:151`,
`cfg->log_tag_queryreply = 0;`).

OPNsense exposes it as `logtagqueryreply`
(`src/opnsense/service/templates/OPNsense/Unbound/core/advanced.conf:25`) as a `BooleanField` with
**no `<Default>`**, i.e. off on a fresh install. It is `1` on <host-1>.

(`internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go:46`), which requires `(\S+)@(\d+)` — so an operator who misses

### 6. Frozen regexes — token-anchored, validated

Single-space literals rather than `\s+`: `log_vmsg` and the two format strings emit exactly one
space between every field, and a tight pattern is what keeps the `-` placeholders and the optional
dest clause unambiguous.

```go
// [pid:thread] query: <client> <qname> <qtype> <qclass>
var reUnboundQueryLog = regexp.MustCompile(
	`^\[(\d+):(\d+)\] query: (\S+) (\S+) (\S+) (\S+)$`)

// [pid:thread] reply: <client> <qname> <qtype> <qclass> <rcode> <sec.usec> <cached> <size>[ on <proto> <ip> <port>]
var reUnboundReplyLog = regexp.MustCompile(
	`^\[(\d+):(\d+)\] reply: (\S+) (\S+) (\S+) (\S+) (\S+) (\d+\.\d{6}|-) (\d+|-) (\d+|-)` +
		`(?: on (udp|tcp|dot|doh|unix|raw) (\S+) (\d+))?$`)
```

**Validation run:** 418/418 `query:` and 312/312 `reply:` captured lines match, **0 misses**; all 11
source-derived edge cases (root `.`, `?`-escaped, `&`/`#` truncation, `*` wildcard, `TYPE65534`,
`CLASS42`, `RCODE23`, `null`, FORMERR with and without dest clause, `sec >= 1`) match the right
pattern and nothing else; and **0 false positives** across all 40 other unbound lines in the archive
plus the local-actions and SERVFAIL fixtures from `unbound_test.go`.

These must be **separate patterns, not one alternation** — `query:` has no numeric slots and `reply:`
must not be allowed to match a 4-token line.

produce a stream that matches the selector and then renders blank columns**, which is worse than not
matching: it looks like data loss rather than a disabled lane.

Recommended instead:
