**Why the archive is sufficient here.** It is shape-deduped (`CaptureShape`, one example per `(program, shape)` per 15-minute window), which is fatal for counting frequencies — and exactly right for this question. It contains one example of **every distinct shape** the box produced in that window, so if every shape parses, every line parses.

Replayed all 766 captured `unbound` records through the real `parseUnbound` with the route enabled:

```
TOTAL=766  CLAIMED=730  UNCLAIMED=36  DISTINCT_UNCLAIMED_SHAPES=32
```

**730 claimed is exactly 418 `query:` + 312 `reply:`** — the full per-query population from the frozen spec, with nothing left over.

All 36 unclaimed lines are in the documented deliberate fall-through set (`unbound.go`, the comment block above the DNSBL regexes) and nothing else:

| shape | lines |
|---|---|
| `info: server stats for thread N: ...` (both forms) | 6 |
| `notice: init module N: ...` | 6 |
| `info: histogram of recursion processing times` | 3 |
| `info: lower(secs) upper(secs) recursions` | 3 |
| `info: [25%]=... median[50%]=... [75%]=...` | 3 |
| `info: average recursion processing time ... sec` | 3 |
| `info:  <lower> <upper> <count>` (histogram rows) | 3 |
| `Backgrounding unbound logging backend.` | 3 |
| `Closing logger` | 3 |
| `Database auto restore from /var/cache/unbound.duckdb ...` | 3 |

That is the multi-line statistics dump plus lifecycle chatter — the set the file deliberately declines to half-parse, because parsing one line of a multi-line report produces a record that looks complete and is not. **Zero `query:`/`reply:` lines went unclaimed.**

The verification harness was a throwaway test, run and deleted rather than committed — it depends on a machine-local capture path, so it would only ever be a broken test for anyone else.

Criterion ticked. All seven acceptance criteria on this issue are now met.

title: logship: second per-query DNS route via Unbound's own log-queries/log-replies syslog output (opt-in, complements #233)

body:
## What happened

`OPNsenseGatewayAlarmFlapping` fired on prod (`opnsense`, gateway `WAN_DHCP`) and kept re-firing.
193 `alarm_started` transitions in 7 days, essentially all of them inside a single ~17h window
starting 2026-08-05T21:00Z. `AAISP_PPPOE` produced zero over the same period.

The underlying syslog:

```
12:02:11  WAN_DHCP  Alarm: none  -> delay  RTT: 200.8 ms  Loss: 0.0 %
12:02:32  WAN_DHCP  Alarm: delay -> none   RTT: 199.5 ms  Loss: 0.0 %
12:03:19  WAN_DHCP  Alarm: none  -> delay  RTT: 201.2 ms  Loss: 0.0 %
12:03:50  WAN_DHCP  Alarm: delay -> none   RTT: 198.6 ms  Loss: 0.0 %
```

The link's mean RTT was sitting on 200.0 ms and the gateway's effective `latencylow` was
200 ms (the OPNsense model default, `Routing/FieldTypes/GatewayField.php:43`, applied because
the field was left blank). OPNsense evaluates that threshold itself once per second on a bare
`>` with no hysteresis (`plugins.inc.d/dpinger.inc:365` — note it is `latencylow`, not
`latencyhigh`, that produces the `delay` status; dpinger is started with `latency_alarm 0ms`
and does no threshold work of its own). So the status flipped `none ⇄ delay` roughly every
45 seconds, and each flip is a transition event we ship and count.

The firewall-side cause has been fixed out of band: `WAN_DHCP` now has `latencylow=400`,
`latencyhigh=800` and the flapping stopped immediately. This issue is about the two things
that made our alerting behave badly around it.

## Problem 1 — the flapping rule has no hysteresis

`opnsense-gateway-alarm-flapping` is `> 2` over a fixed `increase(...[15m])` with `for_min=0`.
It fires the instant a third transition lands in the window, so a single brief wobble on a
healthy link pages immediately, and a boundary-sitting threshold like the one above pages
continuously.

The rule's own runbook already lists "a misconfigured latency/loss threshold making dpinger
over-sensitive" as a likely cause, which is exactly what happened — but it fires so eagerly
that the operator gets the page before that's a useful hint.

## Problem 2 — no rule could see the actual degradation

There was a real fault underneath the noise. Measured from the box during the incident:

```
modem   <lan-ip-18>   avg   0.883 ms
CMTS    <pub-ip-5>       avg 211.769 ms
<pub-ip-6>                 avg 204.534 ms
<pub-ip-7>                 avg 207.089 ms
<pub-ip-8>           avg 206.030 ms   (the ISP's own resolver)
AAISP → <pub-ip-9>         avg   5.614 ms
```

Zero loss throughout. The link's 14-day baseline was ~10-14 ms, so this is a sustained ~20x
step change confined to the ISP access network. Nothing in the ruleset fired on it:

- `OPNsenseGatewayHighLoss` — loss was 0%.
- `OPNsenseGatewayDown` / `...DownFailover` — status stayed 1.
- `OPNsenseGatewayHighRTT` — compares against `opnsense_gateways_rtt_high_milliseconds`, which
  is the operator's configured `latencyhigh`. It was 1000 ms, so a 205 ms link was nowhere near
  it and the rule was structurally incapable of firing.

`OPNsenseGatewayHighRTT` is doing what it was designed to do and the design is right: it
deliberately defers to the operator's own threshold rather than a fixed global one. The gap is
that there is nothing watching a link against *its own history*, so any degradation that stays
under the configured ceiling is invisible. The only thing that surfaced a 20x latency
regression was a flapping-transition-count alert, by accident.

## Proposed changes

1. **`opnsense-gateway-alarm-flapping`: `for_min=0` → `for_min=15`.** Require the flapping to
   persist across the pending period rather than paging on the first qualifying window. Update
   the runbook `threshold` text to match.

2. **New rule `opnsense-gateway-rtt-baseline-deviation`** (warning): fire when a gateway's
   recent mean RTT is a large multiple of its own trailing baseline, with an absolute floor so
   low-RTT links don't page on meaningless millisecond ratios.

   Sketch, to be settled during implementation:

   ```promql
   avg_over_time(opnsense_gateways_rtt_milliseconds[30m])
     / (avg_over_time(opnsense_gateways_rtt_milliseconds[7d] offset 30m) > 10)
   ```

   `> 4` for 30m. The `> 10` guard on the denominator drops gateways whose baseline is under
   10 ms, where a 4x ratio is noise.

   Known property to document in the runbook, not a defect: this is a **step-change** detector.
   Once the degraded level has been in place long enough to dominate the trailing baseline it
   stops firing, even though the link is still slow. That is the intended division of labour —
   a new sustained normal is what the operator's own `latencyhigh` and `OPNsenseGatewayHighRTT`
   are for. The runbook must say so plainly, because an alert that resolves while the fault
   persists is otherwise read as a bug.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `opnsense-gateway-alarm-flapping` carries `for_min=15`; runbook threshold text updated
- [ ] New `opnsense-gateway-rtt-baseline-deviation` rule in `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py` with
      a full runbook entry (measures / threshold / absent / checks / causes / verify)
- [ ] The new rule is mapped to a dashboard panel in the title→panel table
- [ ] `make rules` regenerates `grafana-managed/*.json` and `runbooks.md` cleanly
- [ ] `make grafana-check` passes (regeneration staleness + manifest validity)
- [ ] `tests/test_rule_behaviour.py` passes against the regenerated manifests
- [ ] Rules pushed to Grafana and both verified present

## Reference

Firewall-side fix (already applied, no repo change needed): `WAN_DHCP` `latencylow` set to 400
and `latencyhigh` lowered 1000 → 800. `latencyhigh` also drives the `down` status and therefore
failover, so it was deliberately *not* set low enough to alert on the 205 ms fault — a 205 ms
link at 0% loss is still a usable failover path, and pulling it from the pool would be worse
than the noise. Detection of that class of fault belongs in this repo, which is what change 2 is.

comments.body:
Done in `b64d34b6`, pushed to `main`.

## Changes

**`OPNsenseGatewayAlarmFlapping`: `for_min` 0 → 15.** Threshold and expression unchanged.

**New `OPNsenseGatewayRTTBaselineDeviation`** (warning, `gt 4`, `for_min=30`):

```promql
avg_over_time(opnsense_gateways_rtt_milliseconds[30m])
  / (avg_over_time(opnsense_gateways_rtt_milliseconds[7d] offset 30m) > 10)
```

Panel-mapped to `Gateway RTT` on `Gateways & WAN`, same panel as `OPNsenseGatewayHighRTT`.

## Verified against live prod before committing

The expression was run against the real datasource rather than only being schema-validated:

| gateway | 30m mean | 7d baseline | ratio | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `WAN_DHCP` | 196.29 ms | 30.51 ms | **6.43** | over `gt 4` — fires, correctly catching the fault this issue is about |
| `AAISP_PPPOE` | 5.95 ms | 6.07 ms | — | no series, dropped by the `> 10` denominator guard as designed |

The `> 10` guard is doing real work: without it the healthy PPPoE gateway would be in scope at a
6 ms baseline, where a 4x ratio is 24 ms and means nothing.

## One thing the live run turned up

`opnsense_gateways_rtt_milliseconds` carries an `address` label, and `WAN_DHCP` had **two**
baseline series — its address changed on a DHCP lease renewal on 5 Aug. The expression still
returned exactly one result: the stale pre-change series has no counterpart in the 30m window and
is dropped by the join, rather than producing a bogus ratio or a many-to-many error. That was luck
of the design rather than something I'd planned for, so it is now recorded in the runbook's
absent/no-data section along with the consequence — a WAN address change starts a fresh baseline
and the rule is quiet about that gateway until the new address has history.

## Gates

- `make rules` — 80 manifests, 64 alerts, 14 recording rules
- `make grafana-check` — 1200 Prometheus targets, 121 variable queries, 22 annotation queries,
  78 rule expressions; 80 manifests valid
- `grafana/tests/` — 415 passed, 2894 subtests

Two tests pinned the old values and were updated with the reasoning rather than just the numbers:
`test_build_rules.py` (`for_min` 0 → 15) and `test_runbooks.py` (alert count 63 → 64, method
renamed to match).

## Pushed to Grafana

`gcx resources push -p alerts/grafana-managed/` — 80 succeeded, 0 failed. Both confirmed live via
the provisioning API:

- `opnsense-gateway-alarm-flapping` → `for: 15m`
- `opnsense-gateway-rtt-baseline-deviation` → `for: 30m`, expression as above

All acceptance criteria met. `WAN_DHCP` is currently still degraded (~196 ms against a ~10-30 ms
baseline), so the new rule should go pending and then fire on it within the hour — which is the
outcome this issue wanted and is worth watching as the real end-to-end confirmation.

21 endpoints have paths that could not be verified (empty lists/maps or nulls on the box) — see the per-path sections above.

2 endpoints have no schema (see `schemaExemptEndpoints` in `opnsense/schema_registry.go`).

## The one finding is fixed at the root, not exempted — 99b78147

`unboundDNSStatus` `data.num.query.class.ANY` was flagged as an unmodelled nested key, and the issue suggested exempting it under `knownExtraPaths`. **That would have been the wrong verdict.**

Checking upstream before assigning one, as the triage rules require: `unbound-control` emits `num.query.class.<CLASS>` only for classes actually queried. The shape is dynamic — exactly like `num.query.type` sitting directly beside it in the same struct, which #138 already converted to a map for precisely this reason. The `class` field never got the same treatment and still held a fixed struct with a single `IN` member, so **every class other than IN was silently dropped**: `ANY` today, and `CH`, `HS` and `NONE` each returning later as a fresh canary finding.

So this is not `opportunity` (new data we do not model) — it is the #138 defect one field over, and the canary was right. Exempting would have preserved the bug and blinded us to the rest of the class space.

Fixed by decoding `Class` as `map[string]string`. Cardinality is safe for the same reason as `type`: the DNS CLASS space is tiny and IANA-bounded. The golden schema now records `data.num.query.class.*` in place of the single `.IN` path.

Two notes worth keeping:

- **Nothing consumed the old field.** It was carried in `cmd/fieldaudit`'s ledger as "modelled for schema fidelity ... not exported", which is how I could be confident the change breaks no metric. That exemption is now deleted — a map has no per-key field for the audit to call unread — and `TestExemptionLedgerIsCurrent` caught it as stale, which is the gate working as designed.
- **The decode is fixed; no metric is added.** Wiring a query-class metric would need its own catalogue entry and dashboard panels, so it is deliberately separate scope. The point of this change is that the data is no longer lost on the way in.

This issue closes on a clean canary run rather than on a commit, and **there are no runs** — #654 removed the GitHub cron and its replacement is blocked on a token. So this will sit until that lands, even though the finding itself is resolved.
Live-box canary clean on the latest prod run (release 26.7.1_1). Closing.

body:
## The trace

`Race detector` failed on #652's CI run (job 92398992886, 2026-08-05 18:08 UTC). #652 only bumps
`step-security/harden-runner`, so this is **pre-existing on `main`**, not something that PR caused.

```
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c000204f68 by goroutine 1084:
  sync.(*Once).doSlow()
      /opt/hostedtoolcache/go/1.26.5/x64/src/sync/once.go:78 +0xa1
  ...syslog.(*Listener).Run.func1()
      internal/logship/syslog/listener.go:268 +0x176

Previous read at 0x00c000204f68 by goroutine 1085:
  ...syslog.(*Listener).Run.func4()
      internal/logship/syslog/listener.go:284 +0x7b

Goroutine 1084 (running) created at:
  ...syslog.(*Listener).Run()  internal/logship/syslog/listener.go:264 +0x124
  ...TestListenerTLSShutdownCancellationDoesNotCountRejection.func2()
      internal/logship/syslog/listener_tls_test.go:483 +0x9c

Goroutine 1085 (running) created at:
  ...syslog.(*Listener).Run()  internal/logship/syslog/listener.go:284 +0x3f9
  ...TestListenerTLSShutdownCancellationDoesNotCountRejection.func2()
      internal/logship/syslog/listener_tls_test.go:483 +0x9c

--- FAIL: TestListenerTLSShutdownCancellationDoesNotCountRejection (0.00s)
    testing.go:1712: race detected during execution of test
```

Both goroutines belong to the **same** `Run` call: `func1` is the ctx watchdog (`listener.go:268`
= `_ = l.Close()`), `func4` is the TLS accept goroutine. `f()` is inlined into `doSlow`, so the
instrumented write is inside `Close`'s `once.Do` closure body.

## Not reproduced — read this before assuming it is easy

**270 local runs on darwin/arm64, Go 1.26.5, zero races:**

| run | result |
|---|---|
| whole package, `-race -count=30`, `-cpu=1,2,4,8` (120 runs) | clean |
| `-race -count=150 -run TestListenerTLS` | clean |

`main`'s own CI is green on 18 of the last 20 runs, so it is rare there too. Static reading did not
settle it either: every `Listener` field the two goroutines share is either channel-synchronised
(`closing`, `tcpSem`/`tlsSem`), mutex-guarded (`closeCh` under `closeMu`, `refusalLast` under
`refusalMu`) or immutable after `NewListener`. The reported read offset sits in `Run.func4`, a
closure whose only body is `defer wg.Done(); l.serveTLS()` — `serveTLS` is far too large to inline,
so what is actually being read at `+0x7b` is not obvious from the source. **Do not accept a fix that
cannot demonstrate the race first** — the fix would be unfalsifiable.

## Reproduction ideas not yet tried

- linux/amd64 specifically (the trace is amd64; the local runs were arm64, and the race detector's
  scheduling differs)
- whole-suite `go test -race ./...` under CPU contention, which is what CI actually does — the
  failure appeared in a run of every package, not a single-package run
- `GORACE="halt_on_error=1 history_size=7"` for a deeper stack on the read side
- disassembling `Run.func4` on amd64 to identify the `+0x7b` read precisely

## Impact

Shutdown-path only, and `Close` is `sync.Once`-guarded so the observable behaviour (sockets closed,
connection goroutines waited on) is not obviously wrong. The cost today is a flaky required check
that blocks unrelated PRs — #652 went green on a plain re-run with no code change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Race reproduced deterministically (or under a documented flag/platform combination)
- [ ] Root cause identified — the exact field, and which access is unsynchronised
- [ ] Fix verified by the reproduction failing before and passing after

comments.body:
## Reproduction attempt: the top-listed idea does NOT reproduce it

Ran the issue's first two "not yet tried" ideas together — **linux/amd64 specifically**, and **whole-suite `go test -race ./...` under CPU contention**, which is what CI actually does.

| | |
|---|---|
| host | <host-1>, native `x86_64`, 24 cores (not QEMU — emulated amd64 makes the race detector unreliable, so it was ruled out) |
| Go | `go1.26.5 linux/amd64` — the exact version and platform in the trace |
| commit | `8928d155` |
| command | `go test -race -count=1 ./...` (whole suite, every package, all 24 cores contending) |
| env | `GORACE="halt_on_error=1 history_size=7"` — the third listed idea, for a deeper read-side stack |
| passes | **20** |
| result | **no data race, no failure** |

So the count now stands at roughly **290 runs across both platforms without a reproduction** — 270 on darwin/arm64 per the issue, plus these 20 on the native amd64 whole suite.

**What this eliminates.** The most plausible remaining hypothesis was that the failure needed amd64 plus whole-suite scheduling pressure rather than a single-package run. It does not, at least not at this rate — 20 consecutive whole-suite runs on a 24-core amd64 box is a materially harder test than the 150 single-package runs already recorded, and it is still clean. Whatever the trigger is, it is rarer than 1-in-20 whole-suite runs even on the platform that produced it.

**What is still untried**, and now the highest-value next step, is the fourth idea: disassembling `Run.func4` on amd64 to identify what is actually read at `+0x7b`. That is the one line of attack that does not depend on catching a rare interleaving. `serveTLS` is far too large to inline, so the read is not obvious from source, and static reading has already failed to settle it twice.

Leaving this open and unfixed, per the issue's own instruction: **do not accept a fix that cannot demonstrate the race first**, since an unfalsifiable fix here is worse than the flake. Recording the negative result so the next attempt does not spend its budget re-running the same configuration.

Not re-run since: `main` has moved on (#664-#669 landed), but none of those commits touch `listener.go` or the TLS accept path, so this result still stands for current `main`.

## Migrated to the in-repo tracker as `OPN-0001`

Issue tracking for this project has moved to [`backlog/`](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense2otel/tree/main/backlog), managed by the `backlog` CLI (commit f72a9411). This issue is carried over in full, not summarised:

```bash
backlog task view OPN-0001 --plain
```

Everything expensive survives the move — the trace, the ~290 negative reproduction runs across darwin/arm64 and native linux/amd64, what the amd64 whole-suite run eliminated, and the standing constraint that **a fix which cannot demonstrate the race first is not acceptable**, because an unfalsifiable fix here is worse than the flake.

The three acceptance criteria are unchanged. The remaining line of attack — disassembling `Run.func4` on amd64 to identify what is actually read at `+0x7b` — is recorded on the task as the highest-value next step, along with an explicit note not to spend budget re-running the configurations already proven clean.

Closing here rather than leaving two live trackers.

GitHub Issues stays enabled on this repo. External bug reports are still welcome.

body:
## The failure

Every scheduled `live-canary.yml` run since 2026-08-02 has failed:

```
apidrift: transport error on GET api/core/system/status: context deadline exceeded — retrying once in 2s
pre-flight probe failed — box unreachable from here
```

Not a box fault and not drift. #625 put the six testbed guests on a **06:00–08:30 UTC**
window, sized against the workflow's `cron: '47 6 * * *'`. GitHub does not honour that time:

| run | cron | actually started | delay |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-02 | 06:47 UTC | 08:58 UTC | 2h11 |
| 2026-08-03 | 06:47 UTC | 10:26 UTC | 3h39 |
| 2026-08-04 | 06:47 UTC | 09:27 UTC | 2h40 |
| 2026-08-05 | 06:47 UTC | 09:23 UTC | 2h36 |

The lab is already shut down by the time the runner dials it. The delay predates #625
(2026-08-01's scheduled run started 08:55) — it just did not matter while the guests ran 24/7.

This also holds the drift issues open indefinitely: they close only on a clean run, and
there are no runs.

## Why no cron time fixes it

GitHub documents scheduled workflows as best-effort with **no upper bound** on the delay.
Any window wide enough to reliably contain a 2–3.5h+ delay is most of the day, which is the
idle draw #625 exists to reclaim. Moving the cron earlier just moves the miss.

## Fix — invert the trigger

`<host-8>` already knows the exact moment the lab is ready: `opnsense-testbed-power.sh up` returns
only after both firewalls serve `:443`. So `<host-8>` starts the run instead of GitHub.

- `scripts/testbed/opnsense-testbed-canary-dispatch.sh` — POSTs `workflow_dispatch`, finds the
  run it created, polls to completion, and holds the lab up for the duration (releasing only a
  hold it took itself, so an ad-hoc `testbed up 28800` is left alone).
- `scripts/testbed/opnsense-testbed-canary.{service,timer}` — 06:05 UTC, `Requires=`/`After=`
  the up unit, so it starts when the lab is genuinely ready rather than at a hoped-for time.
- `live-canary.yml` loses its `schedule:` block and becomes dispatch-only.

The probe, the tailnet OAuth credentials and the issue machinery all stay in Actions — only the
trigger moves. That is the difference from <host-1>'s `prod` canary, which runs locally: the
nightly/release-vm targets also run the end-to-end exporter smoke and hold the `tailnet`
environment secrets, and moving those onto `<host-8>` would move the credentials with them.

## Blocked on: a token with `actions: write`

`<host-8>` needs a fine-grained PAT that can create a workflow dispatch on this repo, at
`/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token` (mode 0600). Verified 2026-08-05 that <host-1>'s existing
`/root/.opnsense-canary-gh-token` is **not** sufficient — it has `Actions: read` (200 on
`GET /actions/workflows`) but the dispatch POST returns:

```
403 {"message": "Resource not accessible by personal access token"}
```

Two ways to resolve, Rob's call:
1. Add `Actions: Read and write` to the existing canary PAT and copy it to `<host-8>`. One token,
   already scoped to this repo.
2. Mint a separate PAT scoped to `rknightion/opnsense2otel` with `Actions: Read and write`.
   Smaller blast radius per host.

Until then the unit fails fast and loudly with `no dispatch token at ...` — deliberately, since
a silent no-op would look exactly like the bug this issue is about.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `live-canary.yml` is dispatch-only; no `schedule:` block
- [x] Dispatch script + units in `scripts/testbed/`, deployed and enabled on `<host-8>`
- [x] Script holds the lab across the run and releases only a hold it took itself
- [x] Every stale `06:47` / "47-minute lead" comment across `scripts/` updated
- [x] Token provisioned at `/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token` on `<host-8>`
- [ ] One unattended 06:05 UTC run completes green end-to-end

comments.body:
Repo side is done and deployed in e9c8c1b7. `live-canary.yml` is dispatch-only, the script and both units are on `<host-8>`, and `opnsense-testbed-canary.timer` is enabled — next fire Thu 2026-08-06 07:05 BST (06:05 UTC).

Verified the failure path end to end: with no token present the unit exits 1 with `ERROR: no dispatch token at /root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token` and leaves `hold: none`, so a missing token cannot silently strand the lab powered on.

Still blocked on the token — that is the only remaining step. Until it lands there is **no daily canary at all** (the cron is gone), so this should not sit long.

## Four of six criteria verified; still blocked on the token, and the gap is live

Re-verified the deployed state rather than trusting the previous comment:

| criterion | state |
|---|---|
| `live-canary.yml` dispatch-only, no `schedule:` | ✅ `workflow_dispatch: {}` only; the removed cron is documented in a comment that also warns against re-adding it as a second trigger |
| Script + units in `scripts/testbed/`, deployed and enabled on `<host-8>` | ✅ `opnsense-testbed-canary.timer` is `enabled`, next fire **Sat 2026-08-08 07:05 BST**; script present at `/usr/local/bin/opnsense-testbed-canary-dispatch.sh` |
| Holds the lab across the run, releases only its own hold | ✅ `took_hold` guard + `trap release_hold EXIT`; an existing hold is left alone ("a hold is already live — leaving it alone"), so an ad-hoc `testbed up 28800` is untouched |
| Stale `06:47` / 47-minute-lead comments updated | ✅ now genuinely clean — one live-sounding reference survived the original sweep in `opnsense-testbed-power.sh` and is fixed in `0ad3d468`. The remaining `47`-matches are all historical ("used to carry", "that cron is gone", "REPLACES ... which was removed"), which are correct as written |
| Token at `/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token` on `<host-8>` | ❌ **absent** — `ls` returns `No such file or directory` |
| One unattended 06:05 UTC run green end-to-end | ❌ pending the token |

The timer **did** fire on schedule (Fri 2026-08-07 07:05 BST) and failed as designed on the missing token, which is the intended loud failure rather than a silent no-op.

### The stale comment that was fixed

`opnsense-testbed-power.sh` justified not fixing a keepalive race with "On a 47-minute lead that margin is ample either way". There is no lead any more — the dispatch fires the moment `up` returns — so that reasoning had quietly inverted: the ordering it dismissed as a nicety is now load-bearing. Comment rewritten to say so.

### Remaining step is yours

Decision taken: **widen the existing canary PAT** with `Actions: Read and write` and copy it to `<host-8>` at `/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token` (mode 0600). I have not touched it — I do not create or modify GitHub credentials.

**Worth not letting this sit.** The cron is already gone, so there is currently **no daily canary at all** — not a delayed one, none. That also holds #656 open indefinitely: it closes only on a clean canary run, and its actual finding is already fixed (`99b78147`), so it is now waiting purely on a run happening.

## Token pre-positioned on `<host-8>`; the permission edit is the only step left, and it is UI-only

Did the parts that are doable programmatically.

**Copied the existing canary PAT to `<host-8>`**, byte-for-byte:

```
<host-8>:/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token   -rw------- root root   93 bytes
md5 <host-1>:/root/.opnsense-canary-gh-token  = <hash-1>
md5 <host-8>:/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token = <hash-1>
```

Verified end to end from `<host-8>` itself: the token reads, and `GET .../actions/workflows` returns **200**. The dispatch script's two preconditions (`[ -r "$TOKEN_FILE" ]` and non-empty) now both pass, so it no longer dies at `no dispatch token at ...`.

**This is safe to do before the permission edit**, because editing a fine-grained PAT's permissions does not change the token string. The value already in place will simply start working the moment the box is ticked — no second copy, no redeploy.

### The remaining step, and why I could not do it

`POST .../actions/workflows/live-canary.yml/dispatches` still returns **403 `Resource not accessible by personal access token`** — probed from both hosts against a deliberately nonexistent ref, so the probe could not trigger a real run either way (a permitted token would have answered 422 for the bad ref, not 204).

**There is no REST API to change an existing fine-grained PAT's permissions.** Creation and editing are both browser-only for fine-grained tokens (the old classic-token Authorizations API was removed in 2020). So this one action genuinely cannot be automated.

The token is fine-grained (`github_pat_` prefix), so:

1. https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens
2. Open the token that has access to `rknightion/opnsense2otel` with **Actions: Read-only**
3. Repository permissions → **Actions** → change to **Read and write**
4. Update

Nothing else changes — same token string, same repo scope, and `<host-1>`'s copy keeps working exactly as it does now.

### Once that is done

The timer fires **06:05 UTC** daily and will just work. To confirm without waiting, re-run the probe — it should return `422` for the nonexistent ref:

```
ssh <host-8> 'T=$(cat /root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token); curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  https://api.github.com/repos/rknightion/opnsense2otel/actions/workflows/live-canary.yml/dispatches \
  -d "{\"ref\":\"refs/heads/__perm_probe_nonexistent__\"}"'
```

Happy to trigger the first real run and watch it through to green for the last acceptance criterion — say the word once the permission is in.

Reminder on urgency: the cron is already removed, so there is **no daily canary at all** until this lands, and #656 (whose finding is already fixed in `99b78147`) closes only on a clean run.

## STOP — the decision to widen "the existing canary PAT" was made on a false premise

**`<host-1>:/root/.opnsense-canary-gh-token` is not a canary-specific token. It is byte-identical to `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`.**

```
md5 <host-1>:/root/.opnsense-canary-gh-token   <hash-1>
md5 RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN (secrets store)     <hash-1>
```

This is why the token could not be found in the UI as "a token with Actions: read-only" — it is not one. Fingerprinting it live:

| probe | result |
|---|---|
| `GET /user` | `rknightion` |
| repo reach | **multiple** repos, not just this one (`opnsense2otel`, `meraki-dashboard-exporter`, `m7kni-net-site` all 200) |
| contents **write** | **yes** — `POST /git/refs` returns 422 (bad sha), not 403 |
| contents / issues / pulls / releases read | 200 |
| actions read | 200 |
| actions write | **403** — the gap this issue is about |
| actions secrets | 403 |
| expiry | **none set** (no `github-authentication-token-expiration` header) |

And it is provisioned as the repo secret `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` here, consumed by `.github/workflows/release-please.yml` — and per the standing setup, in **every** rknightion repo that uses release-please.

### Why this reverses the choice

The option selected was "widen the existing canary PAT — one token, already scoped to this repo, blast radius: it sits on two hosts". None of that holds. Widening this token actually means:

- granting **`Actions: write`** to a credential that already has **`Contents: write`** across multiple repos;
- to a credential stored as an **Actions secret in every release-please repo**, so anything that can read that secret gains workflow-dispatch;
- with **no expiry**;
- on a third location (`<host-8>`), in addition to <host-1> and every repo secret store.

That is a materially larger blast radius than either option in the original choice, and it couples the release pipeline to the canary: rotating or scoping one now affects the other.

### What I did, and undid

I had copied this token to `<host-8>:/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token` before identifying it. **It has been removed** (`shred -u`, confirmed absent). Nothing else was changed — <host-1>'s copy and the repo secret are untouched, and no permission was modified anywhere.

### Recommendation: mint a separate PAT after all

The original option 1, now with a much stronger reason than "smaller blast radius per host":

- fine-grained PAT, **`rknightion/opnsense2otel` only**, single permission **`Actions: Read and write`**;
- drop at `<host-8>:/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token`, mode 0600;
- leaves `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` completely alone, so the release pipeline and the canary stay independently rotatable;
- worst case on leak is "can dispatch workflows on one repo", instead of "can push to several repos and dispatch workflows on all of them".

Separate, and worth its own look: **<host-1>'s canary is currently authenticating with the release-please token.** That is a pre-existing reuse this issue did not create, but it means the drift canary and the release pipeline already share one credential. Worth splitting while you are in the token UI anyway.

## Token provisioned and verified — the dispatch permission is live

New dedicated PAT placed at `<host-8>:/root/.opnsense-canary-dispatch-token`, `-rw------- root root`, 93 bytes. Written over ssh stdin so the value never appeared in process arguments on either host.

**Confirmed a genuinely separate credential**, not the release-please reuse found earlier:

```
md5 new canary dispatch token   <hash-2>
md5 RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN        <hash-1>
```

### Permission verification, from `<host-8>` itself

| probe | result | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `POST .../live-canary.yml/dispatches` (nonexistent ref) | **422** | **has `Actions: write`** — was 403 |
| `GET .../actions/workflows` | 200 | `Actions: read` |
| `POST /git/refs` (bad sha) | **403** | **no `Contents: write`** — least privilege holds |
| `GET .../actions/secrets` | 403 | no admin |

422 rather than 204 because the probe deliberately targets a ref that does not exist, so verifying the permission could not start a real canary run.

### Two factual notes on the token as issued

- **It is scoped to two repos, not one.** `opnsense2otel` and `meraki-dashboard-exporter` both return 200 (Actions read/write + contents read); `m7kni-net-site` returns 404, so it is a selected set rather than all-repos. That is broader than the "opnsense2otel only" recommendation but far narrower than what it replaces — worst case on leak is dispatching workflows on two repos, with no write to code anywhere. Flagging rather than treating it as a problem; trivial to narrow in the UI if unintended.
- **No expiry is set.** Same as the old token, so nothing got worse, but it means this one will not force its own rotation.

`RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` was left completely untouched: <host-1> still authenticates with it, and the repo secret is unchanged. The release pipeline and the canary are now separable, which they were not this morning.

### State, and the one criterion left

```
opnsense-testbed-up.timer      next Sat 2026-08-08 07:00 BST (06:00 UTC)
opnsense-testbed-canary.timer  next Sat 2026-08-08 07:05 BST (06:05 UTC)  [enabled]
lab power now                  all guests stopped, hold: none
```

The canary unit `Requires=`/`After=` the up unit, so it starts when the lab is genuinely ready rather than at a hoped-for time. **I deliberately did not fire a manual run**: the lab is powered down outside its window, so a dispatch now would fail at the pre-flight probe and produce a misleading red run. The permission is already proven by the 422.

The last criterion — one unattended 06:05 UTC run green end to end — resolves on its own in ~11 hours. That run is also what closes #656, whose finding is already fixed in `99b78147`.

## Closing — the last criterion is satisfied

`- [ ] One unattended 06:05 UTC run completes green end-to-end` is met. Seven consecutive green runs, all `workflow_dispatch` (which is `<host-8>`'s timer, not a manual trigger), all at 06:05:16Z:

| date | event | conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-14 | workflow_dispatch | success |
| 2026-08-13 | workflow_dispatch | success |
| 2026-08-12 | workflow_dispatch | success |
| 2026-08-11 | workflow_dispatch | success |
| 2026-08-10 | workflow_dispatch | success |
| 2026-08-09 | workflow_dispatch | success |
| 2026-08-08 | workflow_dispatch | success |

The first of those is the run this issue was waiting on — it fired the morning after the dedicated PAT landed. The inverted trigger works: `<host-8>` starts the run when the lab is genuinely up rather than at a time GitHub then delays by 2-3.5h, and the six scheduled runs before the change all failed at the pre-flight probe.

All six acceptance criteria are now checked. Not migrated to the new tracker, since it is finished work rather than open work.

---

Issue tracking for this project has moved in-repo to [`backlog/`](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense2otel/tree/main/backlog), managed by the `backlog` CLI. GitHub Issues stays enabled — external bug reports are still welcome here.

title: live-canary never runs inside the testbed power window — GitHub delays the cron by 2-3.5h

body:
## What

`go.opentelemetry.io/otel` v1.45.0 changed `WithEndpointURL`: a URL with an empty path
now has `URLPath` written out as an explicit `"/"` instead of being left empty.

```go
cfg.Metrics.URLPath = u.Path
if cfg.Metrics.URLPath == "" {
    // For HTTP exporters, a URL without a path targets the root path. Set it explicitly so the default signal
    // path is not appended by cleanPath. (URLPath is ignored by gRPC exporters.)
    cfg.Metrics.URLPath = "/"
}
```

`cleanPath` only substitutes the signal default (`/v1/metrics`, `/v1/logs`) for an
**empty** path, so the explicit `/` suppresses it.

## Why it matters here

Both of our endpoint helpers deliberately returned a pathless endpoint unchanged and
relied on that SDK default:

- `internal/telemetry/exporter.go` — `metricsEndpointURL`
- `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go` — `logsEndpointURL`

So on v1.45.0 an operator configuring a bare host (`--otlp.endpoint=https://collector:4318`,
the shape our docs show for a self-hosted collector) POSTs every metric and every log to
`/` instead of `/v1/metrics` and `/v1/logs`. The collector 404s and the exporter delivers
nothing — the same silent-zero-delivery failure mode as #80, from the opposite direction.

Only the metrics side had an end-to-end guard (`TestHTTPExporterPostsToSignalPath`), which
is what caught it on #635. The logs side had no equivalent and would have shipped broken.

## Fix

Set the signal path ourselves whenever the endpoint does not already target it, instead of
leaving a pathless URL for the SDK. That makes the behaviour independent of which side owns
the default, so a future SDK flip in either direction cannot move it again.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `metricsEndpointURL` returns an explicit `/v1/metrics` for pathless and root endpoints
- [ ] `logsEndpointURL` returns an explicit `/v1/logs` for pathless and root endpoints
- [ ] Both unit-test tables pin the explicit path, with the reason recorded
- [ ] `TestHTTPExporterPostsToSignalPath` passes on otel v1.45.0
title: otel v1.45.0: pathless OTLP endpoints silently POST to the server root

body:
Split out of #649 item 11, and **reframed**: the fix is not to derive a per-panel min interval from the collector's poll tier. The exporter exports on `--otlp.export-interval` (60s by default) regardless of which tier a collector polls on, so a 15m-tier collector still produces a sample every 60s — the poll tier is not the resolution of the data, and pinning panels to it would have been wrong. There is one correct figure for the whole dashboard and it belongs to the datasource, not to 815 panels.

## What was actually wrong

A panel's `queryOptions.interval` does not ask for data more often. It **overrides** the datasource's scrape interval, and it is the figure Grafana computes `$__interval` and `$__rate_interval` from.

The census before this change:

| datasource | ranged | pinned interval | panels |
|---|---|---|---|
| prometheus | yes | `30s` | 554 |
| prometheus | no (instant) | `30s` | 225 |
| prometheus | yes | `1m` | 42 |
| loki | yes | `30s` | 16 |
| loki | no (instant) | `5m` | 20 |

Verified live against the m7kni stack:

* `--otlp.export-interval` defaults to **60s** (`internal/options/otlp.go`), and `count_over_time(opnsense_up[10m])` returns exactly **10** — samples land 60s apart, as configured.
* The `grafanacloud-prom` datasource already declares `jsonData.timeInterval: "60s"` — the right answer, already configured, and every panel was overriding it down to 30s.

So the pin halved the figure the interval variables derive from:

* **Step.** A 30s step against 60s data returns every sample twice. Measured: the same 1h window returns **121 points at a 30s step and 61 at 60s**, for the 61 samples that exist. Pure oversampling — double the payload for zero extra information, on 779 panels.
* **`$__rate_interval`.** Grafana computes `max($__interval + scrape, 4 × scrape)`. At the pinned 30s that is **120s** — exactly two 60s samples, with no tolerance for a single late export, since `rate()` needs two points in the window. At the datasource's own 60s it is **240s**, or four samples.

**Nothing was visibly broken, and the issue should not claim otherwise.** 24h of `count_over_time(opnsense_up[120s]) < 2` returns zero starved buckets — exports have been perfectly regular, so the 120s window has been sufficient in practice. This is a configuration-correctness and query-cost fix, not a repair of an observed fault. The margin it restores is real but latent.

## The rule

**Prometheus panels pin nothing.** The datasource owns the figure; a panel that pins one has forked from it and will not follow when it changes.

**Loki range panels keep a `30s` floor.** This is a genuine exception, not an inconsistency: the `grafanacloud-logs` datasource declares no interval at all, so an unpinned Loki range query takes its step from panel width alone and a narrow time range collapses `[$__auto]` to a couple of seconds. Log arrival is continuous rather than tied to the export tick, so the floor is a rendering guard, not a claim about data rate.

**Instant queries pin nothing, either datasource.** An instant query has no step for a min interval to raise.

Derived in `_panel` from the queries themselves rather than passed by each helper, so the rule cannot be forgotten at a call site and a new helper inherits it.

## Incidental finding

The 20 Loki top-N tables carried `interval="5m"`, documented in `loki_table`'s docstring as "a cardinality guard on wide time ranges". It was **inert**: #471 converted those panels from range queries to instant ones, and an instant query has no step. Their window has been `[$__range]` ever since — which is what `test_no_loki_table_uses_the_step_derived_auto_interval` pins — so the guard the comment described was already doing the work. Removed, and the docstring corrected rather than left asserting a live control that was not one.

## Acceptance

- [x] No Prometheus panel emits `queryOptions.interval`; Loki range panels keep `LOKI_MIN_STEP`; instant panels emit none
- [x] Guard test pins all three, and fails when either half is reverted
- [x] `make grafana-check` passes; suite green

comments.body:
Shipped in `ffa93356`, pushed to `main`.

Generated output verified — main dashboard: 779 Prometheus panels with no `interval`, 16 Loki range panels at `30s`, 20 Loki instant panels with none. Health dashboard: all 104 Prometheus panels unpinned.

Both halves of the guard were checked against their own regression rather than only asserted: re-pinning `interval="1m"` on `statushistory()` fails `test_no_prometheus_panel_pins_a_min_step` (naming `Health History` and `Scrape Success`), and disabling the Loki branch of `_min_step` fails `test_loki_range_panels_keep_their_floor`. `make grafana-check` passes (1200 Prometheus targets validated, 79 manifests); suite is 415 tests green, up from 412.

Worth noting for whoever deploys: this changes only how Grafana derives the step, so nothing needs re-scraping — but the dashboard does not self-update, so it needs pushing to `gc-gitsync-m7kni` like any other change.

Correction to my previous comment: the line about needing a hand-push to `gc-gitsync-m7kni` is **wrong** — I was going off a stale note. `grafana-sync.yml` triggers on push to `main` under `paths: grafana/**`, so this deployed itself.

Both runs succeeded (`ffa93356` and `1100c10a`), and the live stack confirms it rather than just the green tick: fetching the deployed dashboard back shows 779 Prometheus panels with no `interval`, 16 Loki range panels at `30s`, 20 Loki instant panels with none, zero unbounded percent gauges, the `$opnsense_instance` description present, and `OpenVPN Sessions` / `OpenVPN Session Details` at one panel each.

No manual step is needed for either #649 or #650.

title: grafana: panel min interval belongs to the datasource, not to 815 panels

body:
An external Grafana-assistant review of the generated dashboard (815 panels, 6 domains, 45 leaf tabs) produced 12 findings. Each was checked against the generated `dashboard.json`, the tab sources, the existing guard tests and — for the two "broken panel" claims — against the live m7kni stack. This issue records the verdict on every one, and tracks the four that are real.

## Verdicts

| # | Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Health History` and `PF States Used %` return no data | **REJECTED — false positive** |
| 2 | 20 Prometheus table panels missing `format: "table"` | **REJECTED — all 20 are Loki** |
| 3 | 4 percent-unit gauges have no `max` | **ACCEPTED** |
| 4 | `NVMe Life Used` / `SATA SSD Endurance Used` use `max: 120` — copy-paste artefact? | **REJECTED — deliberate, documented** |
| 5 | `Domain, Talkers & Source Delta` row is missing a conditional gate | **ACCEPTED — for a different reason than stated** |
| 6 | 25 panels have no `description` | **REJECTED — deliberate, allowlisted (#423)** |
| 7 | 153 stat/gauge/bargauge panels have decorative flat thresholds | **REJECTED — deliberate policy (#415/#467)** |
| 8 | Duplicate panel titles across sub-tabs | **PARTIALLY ACCEPTED — 1 of 10** |
| 9 | `service_instance_id` ↔ `opnsense_instance` coupling is undocumented | **ACCEPTED** |
| 10 | Confirm tabs lazy-render | **REJECTED — already measured and budget-gated (#422)** |
| 11 | 753 panels at a 30s min interval; raise it for slow-moving data | **DEFERRED — see below** |
| 12 | Oversized rows (Kea 19 panels, Firmware 15, DNSBL 11) should be split | **REJECTED — no defect** |

## Why the rejections are rejections

**1 — the two "broken" panels are not broken.** The reviewer read `hasNoData: true` off Grafana's render status. All five metrics behind those two panels are live on the production instance right now, and both panels' exact generated PromQL returns a value:

```
max without (job, service_instance_id, service_name, service_version)
  (100 * opnsense_firewall_pf_states_current{opnsense_instance=~"opnsense"}
   / clamp_min(opnsense_firewall_pf_states_limit{opnsense_instance=~"opnsense"}, 1))
  => 0.4754

max without (job, service_instance_id, service_name, service_version)
  (opnsense_crash_reporter_status{opnsense_instance=~"opnsense"})
  => 1
```

`opnsense_up`, `opnsense_firewall_status`, `opnsense_crash_reporter_status`, `opnsense_firewall_pf_states_current` and `_limit` all return a vector. The reviewer also placed `PF States Used %` on Overview; it is on Network → Firewall (Overview carries a differently-titled stat tile, `PF states`). Their own report says only the two open tabs executed queries — so the Firewall tab never rendered, and `hasNoData` was the lazy-load state, not a query result. The suggested remedy (verify the metric names against the catalogue) is in any case already a CI gate: `panel_metric_gaps()` exists precisely because #591 shipped a panel querying a metric that never existed.

**2 — none of the 20 panels are Prometheus-backed.** All 20 named panels resolve to `group: "loki"` queries. `format: "table"` is a Prometheus query-model field; Loki has no such option, and these are already `queryType: instant` — which is what makes a Loki metric query render with label columns. Every one of the 145 Prometheus table panels already sets `format: "table"`; there are zero exceptions. The claim's premise ("188 Prometheus-backed table panels, 168 correct") counts Loki panels as Prometheus ones.

**4 — `max: 120` is deliberate** and the panel descriptions say why: *"100% is the rating, not a failure; drives usually run past it."* Both wear gauges deliberately leave headroom above the rated endurance so a drive at 104% is legible rather than pinned.

**6 — the empty descriptions are a recorded decision, not an omission.** `tests/test_panel_descriptions.py` fails the build on any undescribed panel unless its title is in `NO_DESCRIPTION_NEEDED` with a stated reason. #423's brief was explicitly the opposite of a blanket fill: filler text on a self-evident panel costs tooltip space and trains operators to ignore descriptions on the panels that carry a real warning. The reviewer's list of 25 is that allowlist.

**7 — flat thresholds are the designed default.** #415 and #467 removed an injected green/yellow(70)/red(90) triple from `bargauge()` and `gauge()` for exactly this reason: spending red/yellow on a version number or an inventory count manufactures false incidents. A neutral single step is now what an omitted `thresholds=` means, and a panel that genuinely owns a boundary must be added to an allowlist in `tests/test_threshold_defaults.py` as a reviewed decision. The named examples are already handled — `Table Utilization` and `PF States Used %` both carry real 70/90 boundaries today.

**10 — already measured.** #422 enumerated and executed every cold-load query against the live stack and set budgets; #619 then cut load-scoped variables 105 → 16 by moving each presence sentinel to the grouping level that consumes it. Deferred tab rendering is the property those budgets exist to protect, and `tests/test_cold_load_budget.py` fails if it regresses.

**12 — panel count per row is not a defect.** Rows are auto-grid; a 19-panel Kea row reflows. Splitting would add navigation depth without removing anything.

## Accepted work

- [ ] **3 — `max: 100` on the four unbounded percent gauges.** `NVMe Available Spare`, `SATA SSD Spare Available`, `Shared Memory Utilization`, `Table Utilization`. All four are 0–100 by construction (two are raw SMART percentages, two are `100 * used / limit`) and all four carry severity thresholds. Without a `max` the radial arc auto-scales to the observed value, so a drive at 4% spare and one at 96% can paint identical arcs and the 10/50 threshold markers land in the wrong place. This is a rendering defect, not a style point.
- [ ] **3b — make it structural.** `Builder.gauge()` raises when `unit` is `percent`/`percentunit` and no `mx` is passed, in the same style as `statetimeline()` failing the build on an unmapped timeline. A `max` on a bounded-unit gauge is not a fabricated severity boundary (which is what #467 removed) — it is the unit's own domain, and omitting it is always a bug.
- [ ] **5 — gate the two opt-in panels in `Domain, Talkers & Source Delta`.** The reviewer's stated reason is wrong: the row sits inside a tab already gated `present="has_flow_volume"`, so it cannot render on a box without flow volume. The real gap is that the row mixes three different availability conditions. `Top Talkers by Bytes (host, direction)` is opt-in behind `--flow.top-talkers` and `Source Byte-Delta Ratio` needs `--flow.log-mode=per_flow`, while `DNS Answer Cache` and `Unique Destinations` ship with the flow lane. On a default flow box two of the four panels are permanently empty. Its siblings `has_flow_country` and `has_flow_logs` exist for precisely this reason — the tab's own comment says an ungated row *"would render one flat 'unknown' line on every box that has not opted in"*. Sentinels are tab-scoped since #619, so this costs nothing at cold load.
- [ ] **8 — rename the `OpenVPN Sessions` table.** Two panels share that title *on the same tab*: a timeseries of the session count and a table of per-session detail. The other nine duplicates are cross-tab and unambiguous in place (`Uptime` on Overview / System / Unbound; the Tailscale ↔ NetBird `Node Info` / `Peers Known` / `Last Handshake` / `Plugin Service` pairs), and alert deep-links already resolve duplicates by requiring a tab qualifier — `tests/test_panel_links.py` raises on an unqualified ambiguous title, and one of its tests needs a duplicate to exist to stay meaningful. Renaming all ten is churn; renaming the same-tab collision is a fix.
- [ ] **9 — describe the `opnsense_instance` variable.** The six Loki panels filter on `service_instance_id=~"$opnsense_instance"` while the variable is populated from the Prometheus label `opnsense_instance`. That the OTel `service.instance.id` resource attribute and the Prometheus label always carry the same value is true by construction, but nothing on the dashboard says so, and renaming one without the other would silently empty every log panel. `zenarmor_client` is the only variable carrying a description today; this one earns the second.

## Deferred

**11 — min-interval tuning.** Confirmed: 753 panels at `30s`, 42 at `1m`, 20 at `5m`, against a 1m auto-refresh. The reviewer is right that a certificate-expiry or firmware panel has no business being stepped at 30s. The principled fix is not a hand-picked list but deriving the panel min-interval from the owning collector's poll tier — the exporter already classifies every collector `fast`/`medium`/`slow`/`cold` in `internal/collector/interval_tiers.go`, and a cold-tier collector polled every 15m cannot produce a meaningful 30s step. That is a materially larger change than the rest of this issue and is not bundled with it.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `make dashboard` regenerates cleanly and `make grafana-check` passes
- [ ] `python3 -m unittest discover grafana/tests` passes, including the new gauge guard

comments.body:
Shipped in `1100c10a`, pushed to `main`.

All four accepted items landed together plus the structural guard. Verified in the generated `dashboard.json`: zero unbounded percent gauges remain, `OpenVPN Sessions` is unique again, `$opnsense_instance` carries its description on both dashboards, and the Flow Volume tab now has `has_flow_top_talkers` / `has_flow_delta_ratio` gating a `Talkers & Source Delta` row split off from `Domain & Destinations`.

The guard was checked against the real defect rather than only asserted: reverting `Table Utilization`'s `mx=100` fails the build with the intended message. `make grafana-check` passes (1200 Prometheus targets, 121 variable queries, 79 manifests) and the suite is 412 tests green, up from 408.

Item 11 (min-interval tuning) stays deferred and is not tracked here — if it is picked up it wants its own issue, since the useful version of it is deriving the panel min-interval from `internal/collector/interval_tiers.go` rather than hand-picking panels.

## Second review pass — re-verified, no further changes

The reviewer re-ran against the deployed dashboard and confirmed 5 of the accepted items fixed. It re-raised three of the **rejected** items as "not applied yet" and flagged three new no-data panels. All six re-checked; nothing needs changing.

### The three new no-data observations are all fine — two are false positives

Checked against the live stack with each panel's exact generated query:

| Panel | Live result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `Disk Usage % by Mountpoint` | **14 series** | False positive — renders fine |
| `Jumbo Pool Utilization %` | returns **0**, both `jumbo9` and `jumbo16` pools exist (max 301879 / 169807, current 0) | False positive — 0% utilisation is the correct answer, not an empty panel |
| `Subsystem Status` | genuinely 0 series | **Correct by design** |
| `PF States Used %` (re-check requested) | **0.416** | Confirmed with data, second pass running |

`Subsystem Status` is the box-state verdict from this repo's own canary-triage doctrine: `opnsense_system_subsystem_status_code` is emitted **only while a subsystem is unhealthy**, so an empty panel means every subsystem is OK. Its description already says so.

**Deliberately NOT "fixing" that with a reassuring `noValue`.** A "All subsystems OK" placeholder would read as *checked, nothing found* when the exporter simply could not reach the firewall — which is precisely the failure `tests/test_empty_state_contract.py` exists to prevent: *"a blank panel prompts a question, a green zero ends the conversation."* The blank-plus-description design is the doctrine-compliant one.

### The three re-raised items remain rejected

**`format: "table"` — re-verified against the LIVE deployed dashboard this time**, not the repo. All 20 named panels resolve to `group: "loki"`, `queryType: "instant"`. The reviewer now calls them "instant Prometheus" — the *instant* half is right, the *Prometheus* half is not. `format` is a Prometheus query-model field with no Loki equivalent. Live count of Prometheus tables missing `format: "table"`: **0 of 145**. There is nothing to apply.

**25 descriptions** — an allowlist with a stated reason per entry, enforced by `tests/test_panel_descriptions.py`. Filling them is the change #423 explicitly decided against.

**Duplicate titles** — the one same-tab collision was fixed. The remaining nine are cross-tab, the tab disambiguates them, and alert deep-linking already refuses an unqualified ambiguous title.

**Kea 19-panel row** — auto-grid reflows; no defect.

### Note for a third pass

Every no-data finding across both reviews has been either lazy-render state or correct box-state; none has been a query defect. The render-status field is not evidence on its own — the panel's query has to be run. Both passes also mislocated `PF States Used %` on Overview when it is on Network → Firewall.

title: grafana: triage the external dashboard review — 4 real findings, 8 rejected

body:
Found verifying #639/#643 against the live box on `671098d`. **Not a #639 regression** — the private-address guard is working. This is a distinct defect in the correlator's merge step, and #639's guard is what made it visible.

## Symptom

Merged flow records with a **private `dst_ip`**, `dst_scope="local"`, still carrying geo:

| dst_ip | dst_scope | dst_geo_country | dst_geo_city | city_source | country_source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <lan-ip-19> | local | US | Mountain View | zenarmor | **maxmind** |
| <lan-ip-20> | local | GB | Bromley | maxmind | **maxmind** |
| <lan-ip-12> | local | US | Toronto | zenarmor | **maxmind** |
| <lan-ip-1> | local | GB | City of London | maxmind | **maxmind** |

4 records in a ~2h post-deploy window against 5000+ sampled private-`dst_ip` merged records. Source side is clean: **0 of 5000+** private `src_ip` records carry geo, and the public-but-local regression case (`<pub-ip-4>1055`, `src_scope="local"`) correctly keeps its geo. So the guard added in #639 works — this arrives by another route.

## `country_source="maxmind"` on RFC1918 is the tell

MaxMind declines private space (`geoip_lookups_total{database="skipped"}`), so `GeoEnricher.endpoint` can never resolve a maxmind-sourced country for `<lan-ip-12>`. That geo was resolved against a **different address** and then attached to this record.

## Root cause: positional merge of a reversed record

`mergeGeoEndpoint` (`internal/flow/geo.go`) pairs `dst.Src <- zen.Src` and `dst.Dst <- zen.Dst` **by position**, never checking that the two records name the same address at that position. A Zenarmor conn document records a connection from the initiator's side (`private -> public`); the NetFlow fragment being merged here is the **return** direction (`public -> private`). Positional pairing then attaches each end's geo to the opposite address.

Live proof, record 3 — `<pub-ip-10>:443 -> <lan-ip-12>:34210`:

```
src_ip <pub-ip-10>  (Cloudflare, public)   src_geo_zen_country GB
dst_ip <lan-ip-12>      (RFC1918, private)     dst_geo_zen_country CA
                                             dst_geo_city Toronto (zenarmor)
                                             dst_geo_country US (maxmind)
```

Two facts that only fit the reversed-orientation explanation:

- **`GB` is what Zenarmor fabricates for the private host** (#639/#643 evidence), yet it appears on the *public* Cloudflare address. That is `zen.Src` (the private end) merged onto `netflow.Src` (the public end).
- **`CA` / `Toronto` is Zenarmor's known anycast-wrong answer for Cloudflare** (#643 recorded exactly this: Montreal/Canada, lat/lon 45.5019/-73.5674). It appears on the *private* address. That is `zen.Dst` (the public end) merged onto `netflow.Dst` (the private end).

If the two records were aligned, one address could not carry the other's Zenarmor answer.

**Both ends are mismatched; only the dst end is visible.** The NetFlow src is public, so `endpoint()` resolves it correctly and the resolved fields overwrite the bad merge. The NetFlow dst is private, has no lookup of its own, and nothing overwrites what the merge put there.

All four are `flow_direction` `inbound` or `internal`, consistent with return-direction fragments.

## This predates #639, which changed the symptom rather than causing it

Before #639, `mergeGeoEndpoint` re-derived from the raw `Zen*` fields, so the same mismatch produced `dst_geo_country_source="zenarmor"` — also fabricated, also wrong, just differently attributed. #639 changed the merge to read the Zenarmor record's **resolved** fields (necessary, because the raw-field path bypassed the private-address guard entirely). That fix is correct and should stay; it inherits the misalignment underneath it, and it makes the provenance actively misleading — the record now claims `maxmind` for an address MaxMind never looked at.

## Proposed fix

Match endpoints by **address**, not by position. `MergeGeo` should take the two records' addresses and fold `zen`'s endpoint onto the endpoint naming the *same* address, merging nothing when neither matches. A positional fallback should not be kept as a silent default — a mismatch means the two records disagree about the connection, which is worth counting rather than papering over.

Worth checking while in there whether the same positional assumption affects anything else the correlator folds across the two records (L7, verdict, enrichment), since geo is only the field where a wrong answer is externally visible.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `MergeGeo` folds by address match, not endpoint position
- [ ] A reversed-orientation Zenarmor record merges each end onto the address it actually describes
- [ ] A record whose addresses match neither endpoint merges nothing, and the mismatch is counted
- [ ] No merged record with a private `dst_ip` carries `dst_geo_*` after deploy
- [ ] Regression guard: the aligned case still merges exactly as it does today
- [ ] Regression guard: public-but-local (`2001:8b0:1f05::/48`) keeps its geo on both ends
- [ ] Check whether the positional assumption affects other merged fields

Related: #639 (the guard, working), #643 (Zenarmor anycast-wrong city, the fingerprint used above), #346 (the correlator).
title: flow: MergeGeo pairs endpoints positionally, so a reversed-orientation Zenarmor record attaches each end's geo to the wrong address

body:
## Summary

The `goroutine_leak` Pyroscope profile type does not appear in Grafana Cloud over a 5-day window, while
the other profile types do. Filed as **suspected**, not confirmed — there is a benign explanation that
could not be ruled out read-only.

## What was verified

The build carries the runtime experiment:

```
opnsense_exporter_build_info{goversion="go1.26.5-X:goroutineleakprofile",version="77bdd8a"} 1
```

Startup log confirms the type is registered — `goroutine_leak=true` among all 11 profile types. Zero
pyroscope upload errors in the current run.

The pipeline itself is demonstrably healthy: `process_cpu` (3.6T samples/24h) and `goroutines`
(856k samples/24h) are both queryable in Grafana Cloud with real data.

## What could not be confirmed

`goroutine_leak` did not appear in `list-profile-types` org-wide over either a 1h or a 5d window. No
error anywhere points at a delivery fault.

## The benign explanation

A healthy process leaks no goroutines, so the profile may be uploading zero samples every cycle and
Grafana may not surface a profile type that has never carried a sample. That would make this a non-issue.

This is consistent with the rest of the evidence — `go_goroutines` was flat at 147-170 across 5 days with
no leak, so there genuinely should be nothing to report.

## Why it is still worth resolving

If the type is silently not uploading, the goroutine-leak detection this build was specially compiled for
is not actually working, and we would not find out until we needed it. The whole point of carrying a
non-default `GOEXPERIMENT` through every build path is to have this signal available.

Right now we cannot distinguish "working correctly and reporting nothing" from "not working" — and those
look identical from outside.

## How to settle it

A test build that deliberately leaks a goroutine, run long enough for one upload cycle, then check
whether the type appears. That distinguishes the two cases definitively. Does not need to run on prod.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Determined whether `goroutine_leak` uploads at all on a healthy process
- [ ] If it does not upload when empty: confirmed it does upload when a leak exists (deliberate-leak build)
- [ ] If it never uploads: root-caused and fixed, or the `GOEXPERIMENT` build flag dropped as dead weight
      across every build path rather than carried for a signal that does not arrive
- [ ] Outcome documented so the next person does not have to re-derive that "absent" is expected

Related: the `GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile` build-flag wiring, which is carried through every build
path specifically for this profile type.

comments.body:
## Settled: (a) — benign. Confirmed by controlled experiment, not inference.

`goroutine_leak` uploads on **every** cycle whether or not anything is leaked. On a healthy process the
uploaded profile is well-formed and carries zero samples. Absence from Grafana Cloud's profile-type
listing is the expected state for a signal that has genuinely never had anything to report. The
`GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile` build flag stays justified.

### Source reading first

- `vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/session.go:287-309` (`uploadData`) — for the goroutine-leak type:
  look up `pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak")`, if non-nil `p.WriteTo(buf, 0)`, then **unconditionally**
  `ps.upstream.Upload(...)`. There is no sample-count or buffer-length check anywhere before the upload.
- `vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/upstream/remote/remote.go:128-142` and `:152-241` — the job is
  enqueued and POSTed regardless of profile content. Only a full internal queue suppresses an upload, and
  that is logged as an error.
- `internal/profiling/profiling.go:32-39` — the runtime guard. `GoroutineLeakAvailable()` is
  `pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak") != nil`, gating whether the type is added to the list at `:65-67`. It
  reflects only whether the binary carries the experiment, not whether anything is currently leaked.

That already rules out "the client skips the upload when empty".

### Live experiment — decisive

Harness built against `github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go v1.4.1` (the version pinned in this repo's
`go.mod`), compiled `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile go build`, pointed at a local
`httptest` sink decoding every multipart `/ingest` POST. Nothing touched prod or <host-1>.

`pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak") != nil` → `true` at startup, matching production.

**Phase 1 — 25s, no leak.** Every ~3s cycle POSTed a `goroutineleak` profile, consistently 220 bytes
compressed / 192 decompressed. `go tool pprof -raw`:

```
PeriodType: goroutineleak count
Period: 1
Samples:
goroutineleak/count
Locations
```

A valid profile with `Samples:` and nothing under it. Zero samples, zero errors, still uploaded.

**Phase 2 — deliberate leak** (`<-leakForever`, unbuffered channel nobody sends to). The **very next**
cycle jumped to 424-427 bytes compressed / 625 decompressed and held exactly there for all 13 remaining
cycles over 40s:

```
Samples:
goroutineleak/count
          1: 1 2 3 4
Locations
     1: ... runtime.gopark proc.go:462
     2: ... runtime.chanrecv chan.go:667
     3: ... runtime.chanrecv1 chan.go:509
     4: ... main.main.func2 main.go:118
```

One sample, stack correctly pointing at the channel receive that leaked. Detection latency was one upload
cycle. Every upload in both phases returned 200 OK.

Both halves of the acceptance criteria are met: it uploads on a healthy process (empty) **and** it uploads
correctly when a leak exists (populated, accurate stack).

### What remains unknown, and why it is not ours

Why Grafana Cloud's `list-profile-types` does not surface a type that has only ever received zero-sample
payloads is backend behaviour. Not inspectable from this codebase and not affectable by a change here.
Given the zero-sample profiles are accepted (200 OK, no ingest errors) and the mechanism is proven, this is
the shape of "nothing to report", not a fault.

### Change

`docs/architecture.md` — documented the finding and the verification method beside the existing
goroutine-leak-profiling paragraph, so this does not get re-derived. Outside the docgen marker regions;
`make docs-check` passes.

title: pyroscope: goroutine_leak profile type never appears in Grafana Cloud - cannot distinguish healthy-and-empty from not-uploading

body:
## Summary

`opnsense_interfaces_line_rate_bits{pppoe0}` reports **64000** — 64 kbit/s for a ~1 Gb/s AAISP FTTP link.
The read is faithful (it is `ng_pppoe`'s default kernel baudrate) but the value is meaningless on this
device class and would silently break any utilisation-vs-line-rate calculation.

`tailscale0` and `zen0` report 0 for the same reason.

## Why it is not a decode bug

The kernel genuinely reports 64000 for a netgraph PPPoE pseudo-device; the number is a placeholder from
the netgraph layer, not a negotiated line rate. Nothing is being misread. The problem is that the series
is published as though it means something.

## Impact

Any panel or rule computing `rate(bytes) / line_rate_bits` on the primary WAN produces a utilisation
figure roughly 15,000x too high. Silent, and plausible-looking if you do not know the link speed.

## Proposed fix

Two reasonable options:

1. **Suppress the series** for carrier-less pseudo-devices (PPPoE, tunnel and overlay devices), the same
   way `input_queue_drops_total{ixl1}` is suppressed rather than published as a fabricated 0 when the
   kernel counter is garbage. That precedent is already in the codebase and is the right instinct.
2. **Keep it and document it** with a HELP caveat, matching how `link_state` already documents its
   `2 = unknown` value for `pppoe0`.

Option 1 is safer: a suppressed series cannot be divided by, whereas a documented one still can. But it
loses the ability to see the value at all, so it is a judgement call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decision recorded between suppression and documentation, with reasoning
- [ ] `line_rate_bits` on `pppoe0` / `tailscale0` / `zen0` no longer usable as a real line rate without
      the operator noticing
- [ ] Ethernet devices unaffected (`ixl0`, `ixl1` etc. keep reporting their real negotiated rate)
- [ ] If suppressing: the suppression keys on device class or on an implausible value, not on a device
      name allowlist that will rot

comments.body:
## Decision: suppress the series on carrier-less pseudo-devices

Owner decision, 2026-08-04.

Suppress `line_rate_bits` rather than publishing it with a HELP-text caveat.

**Reasoning:** a suppressed series cannot be divided by; a documented one still can. The failure mode here
is silent and plausible-looking — a utilisation panel reading ~15,000x high on the primary WAN — and a
HELP string does not protect anyone who is reading a dashboard rather than the metric metadata. This also
matches the precedent already in the codebase: `input_queue_drops_total{ixl1}` is suppressed rather than
published as a fabricated 0 when the kernel counter is garbage.

**Implementation constraints:**

- Suppression keys on device class or on an implausible value, **not** a device-name allowlist — an
  allowlist rots the moment a tunnel interface is renamed.
- Ethernet devices are unaffected and keep their real negotiated rate. Pinned as a regression test.

title: interfaces: line_rate_bits{pppoe0}=64000 is the netgraph placeholder, not a line rate

body:
## Summary

`internal/flow/geo.go:176-183` resolves the city field **Zenarmor-wins-else-MaxMind**, on the premise
that Zenarmor ships a commercial GeoIP2-City build. On this box that premise does not hold: Zenarmor's
city data is anycast-wrong for remote destinations and subdivision-level for local ones, and it wins the
field for ~72% of remote destinations.

Filed as suspected rather than confirmed because "which city DB is better" is a judgement call — but the
evidence below all points one way.

## Evidence

**Anycast addresses resolve to the wrong continent.** Zenarmor returns city `Montreal`, country `Canada`
for `chatgpt.com` (Cloudflare anycast `<pub-ip-11>ac40:9bd1`) and for `spclient.wg.spotify.com` —
from a London AAISP line. Its raw payload pins lat/lon 45.5019/-73.5674 for both.

**Local endpoints get a subdivision, not a city.** Every local endpoint comes back as city `England`
with lat/lon 51.5072/-0.1276. `England` is a subdivision. (This overlaps #639, which covers the separate
bug that private addresses get geo at all.)

**The two sources disagree on country 17.85% of the time:**

```
opnsense_flow_geoip_country_comparisons_total{result="agree"}     1,164,469
opnsense_flow_geoip_country_comparisons_total{result="disagree"}    253,077
```

Sampled disagreement: `<pub-ip-12>` -> MaxMind `CY`, Zenarmor `GB`.

**Zenarmor wins the city field for most remote traffic.** 30-minute window, remote-destination city
attribution: zenarmor 17,871 (**72%**) vs maxmind 6,866.

## What is already right - do not change it

The **country** field is safe: MaxMind wins by design, and `dst_geo_zen_country` preserves Zenarmor's
answer alongside it so the comparison is auditable. That is good design and the 17.85% disagreement rate
is exactly the kind of thing it exists to surface.

Only `*_geo_city` and `*_geo_region` inherit the weaker source.

## Proposed fix

Either:

1. **Flip the precedence** so MaxMind wins city the same way it wins country, with Zenarmor as fallback
   when MaxMind has no city; or
2. **Gate the Zenarmor arm** on it returning an actual city rather than a subdivision or a
   datacentre-of-record.

Option 1 is more consistent with how country is already handled and is the smaller conceptual change.
Given the deployment runs `GeoLite2-City` specifically (compose sets
`OPN2OTEL_GEOIP_DOWNLOAD_EDITIONS: "GeoLite2-City,GeoLite2-ASN"` and comments that City was chosen over
Country to get city/region **without** Zenarmor), the intent already appears to be MaxMind-first for city.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decision recorded on precedence, with the reasoning, since this reverses a deliberate earlier call
- [ ] MaxMind city wins where present (or Zenarmor gated on returning a real city)
- [ ] Country precedence and `dst_geo_zen_country` preservation unchanged
- [ ] Anycast spot-check: `chatgpt.com` from this box no longer reports Montreal/Canada
- [ ] `*_geo_region` follows whatever rule `*_geo_city` gets — they should not diverge

Related: #639 (private addresses getting geo at all).

comments.body:
## Decision: flip the precedence — MaxMind wins city and region

Owner decision, 2026-08-04. Recorded here because this reverses a deliberate earlier call and the
code comment at `geo.go:175-177` currently argues the opposite.

**Resolved:** MaxMind wins `*_geo_city` and `*_geo_region`, with Zenarmor as the fallback where
MaxMind has no answer. Mirrors how country already resolves.

**Reasoning:**

- The premise the original call rested on — that Zenarmor ships a better commercial GeoIP2-City build —
  does not hold on this box. Its city data is anycast-wrong for remote destinations (Montreal/Canada for
  Cloudflare anycast from a London line) and subdivision-level for local ones ("England").
- It was winning the field for 72% of remote destinations, so the defect is the common path, not an edge.
- The deployment already encodes MaxMind-first as the operator intent: compose sets
  `OPN2OTEL_GEOIP_DOWNLOAD_EDITIONS: "GeoLite2-City,GeoLite2-ASN"` and comments that the City edition was
  chosen over Country specifically to get city/region **without** Zenarmor.
- Option 2 (gate the Zenarmor arm on it returning a "real" city) was rejected: it needs a
  subdivision-vs-city / datacentre-of-record heuristic that would be fragile and would rot silently.

**Explicitly unchanged:** country precedence, the `Zen*` raw-value preservation, and the
agreement/disagreement counters. Those are working as designed — the 17.85% disagreement rate is exactly
the signal that counter exists to surface, and it is what made this diagnosable.

`*_geo_region` follows `*_geo_city`; they resolve from the same record and must not diverge.

title: flow: Zenarmor wins the city field but its city data is anycast-wrong and subdivision-level
