## Summary

`ixl2` is the physical SFP+ port carrying 100% of WAN1 traffic (it is the parent of `pppoe0`), and the
exporter emits no traffic, error or drop counters for it. Physical-layer errors on the primary WAN port
are invisible.

Box-side, `ixl2` currently shows 391 GB in / 532 GB out and 3,030 input drops. The exporter emits only:

- `admin_up`
- `admin_enabled`
- `output_queue_drops_total`

No bytes, packets, input errors, output errors or input drops.

## Root cause

The traffic API covers only **assigned** interfaces, and `ixl2` is an "Unassigned Interface" — the
assignment is on the `pppoe0` logical device layered over it. The logical `pppoe0` interface cannot show
physical-layer errors, so they have nowhere to surface.

## Why it matters

This is the one interface on the box where a physical fault would be both most consequential and least
visible. `pppoe0` carries ~91% of WAN volume and its error counters describe the PPPoE session, not the
SFP+ port underneath it. A dirty fibre or a flapping SFP shows up in `ixl2`'s Ierrs/Idrop and nowhere
else.

Same shape applies to any box where a WAN runs PPPoE over a physical port.

## Caveat for whoever implements this

`ixl2`'s `Ipkts` on the box currently reads **281,475,474,155,049** (approximately 2^48) — a corrupt or
wrapped kernel counter. Any work here should assume that field is unusable on this device.

Note the existing int32-wrap suppression already works correctly on `ixl1` (where `Idrop` reads
4,294,960,465 = int32 -6,831, and the exporter correctly emits **no series** rather than publishing a
fabricated 0 — that behaviour is right and should be preserved). But a 48-bit value would not be caught
by an int32-wrap check, so the guard needs widening if these counters are exposed.

## Proposed approach

Source physical-port counters from an endpoint that covers unassigned interfaces (or from the interface
inventory rather than the traffic API), and extend the wrap-suppression guard to catch implausible
values beyond the int32 case.

Worth deciding explicitly whether unassigned interfaces get the full counter set or a reduced
"physical health" subset — exposing all of them for every unassigned device has a cardinality cost for
data that is mostly zero.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ixl2` reports input/output bytes, packets, errors and drops
- [ ] Wrap/implausible-value suppression widened beyond int32 and covers the 2^48 `Ipkts` case
- [ ] `ixl1`'s existing int32 `Idrop` suppression still suppresses (regression guard)
- [ ] Decision recorded on scope: all unassigned interfaces vs only those parenting an assigned device

comments.body:
## Decision: uniform coverage — every device the statistics endpoint returns

Owner decision, 2026-08-04, plus recon that changes the shape of the fix.

### The fix is cheaper than the body assumed — no new endpoint

`api/diagnostics/interface/get_interface_statistics` is **already fetched every poll** by
`FetchInterfaceStatistics` (`opnsense/interface_index.go:125-193`), and its AF_LINK rows already carry the
full counter set for all 17 devices, assigned or not. Verified live:

```
"[ixl2] / <mac-1>": {
  "name": "ixl2", "network": "<Link#3>", "address": "<mac-1>",
  "received-packets": 281475478389769, "received-errors": 0,
  "dropped-packets": 0, "received-bytes": 393185547668,
  "sent-packets": 561408322, "send-errors": 0, "sent-bytes": 537868820722,
  "collisions": 0 }
```

The parser discards it: the AF_LINK branch (`interface_index.go:149-160`) takes only `DroppedPackets` and
`continue`s, dropping `ReceivedPackets`/`ReceivedBytes`/`SentPackets`/`SentBytes` that
`interfaceStatisticsRow` already decodes. `received-errors` / `send-errors` / `collisions` are on the wire
but have no struct fields at all.

Confirmed why ixl2 is missing today: the current source, `api/diagnostics/traffic/interface`, is restricted
by **OPNsense itself** to interfaces with a config identifier — live key set
`[opt7 opt4 opt2 lan opt3 opt8 opt6 opt1 opt5]`, 9 assigned only. Not an exporter filter.

### Scope: every device the endpoint returns

Chosen over "physical unassigned ports only" and over "only ixl2". A uniform rule has no classification to
maintain and none to rot; the alternative ("only ports parenting an assigned device") stops covering a port
at exactly the moment its child is removed, which is when you would most want to see it. Cost is a handful
of permanently-zero series on pseudo-devices, and cardinality is not scarce here.

Unassigned inventory on this box: `ixl2` (parent of `pppoe0`/WAN1), `ixl3`, `igb0`, `igb1` (physical, no
carrier, idle), `enc0`, `pflog0` (pseudo). `pfsync0` is a seventh that `interfaces_info` omits entirely but
`get_interface_statistics` returns.

### Two constraints on the implementation

**No double-sourcing.** The 9 assigned interfaces already get counters from the traffic endpoint. Two
independent sources for one series would drift and produce nonsense on `rate()`. The statistics-sourced
path fills the gap only — every device covered exactly once, and a regression that starts emitting both
must fail a test.

**The wrap guard widens on a plausibility check, not a magnitude ceiling.** ixl2 `received-packets` reads
281,475,478,389,769 = `0x100001de95031` — exactly 2^48 plus a plausible count, with bit 48 stuck high; the
low bits increment correctly (+150,568 over a minute, consistent with real traffic). The existing
`parseQueueDropCounter` guard (`opnsense/interfaces.go:193-199`) only catches an int32 sign-wrap and misses
this. A bare 2^48 ceiling would rot — it is theoretically reachable on a fast enough link over a long
enough uptime. So the predicate is physical: a packet count is implausible when the bytes on the same row
imply fewer than 20 bytes per packet, below the minimum Ethernet frame. For ixl2 that is 0.0014
bytes/packet. Applies only when the packet count is non-zero, or every idle device gets wrongly suppressed.

`ixl1`s existing int32 `Idrop` suppression (4,294,960,465 = 2^32 - 6,831) is pinned as a regression test.

### Caveat carried into the work: input drops may not exist here

netstat shows ixl2 `Idrop=3081`, but the APIs `dropped-packets` reads 0 for the same interface, and this
code already documents that `dropped-packets` lands on **output** queue drops via a libxo double-key /
PHP last-wins quirk. If no true input-drop counter is available from this endpoint, we emit nothing for it
and say so — output-queue drops must not be relabelled as input drops.

### Unrelated defect found and folded in

`internal/collector/interfaces.go:386-391` and `opnsense/interfaces.go:331-338` both assert the `enabled`
field is "always-populated ... on every row unconditionally" with "no legitimate absent state". Live data
contradicts this: the key is **entirely absent** for every unassigned row. Behaviour is harmless (Go
zero-values it to false, which is semantically correct for "no config to enable") but the comment is false.
Being corrected in place; no behaviour change.

title: interfaces: ixl2 carries all WAN1 traffic but has no traffic or error counters (unassigned parent of pppoe0)

body:
## Summary

Four syslog shapes on the prod box fall through to generic records because no registered parser matches
them. Each is backed by a real captured line cross-checked against the parser source. Separate from #638
(the cron regex bug), which is a different failure mode — that one has a parser that fails to match, these
have no matching branch at all.

## 1. dpinger `delay` alarm state

`internal/logship/syslog/dpinger.go:30-31` models only the `none` <-> `down` transition. The box also
emits a `delay` alarm state (latency threshold breached without the gateway going down), which is not in
the pattern. Gateway latency alarms are therefore invisible to the parsed stream.

## 2. unbound cached SERVFAIL

`internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go:60-61` models two SERVFAIL shapes. The box emits a third:
`SERVFAIL ... in cache`, i.e. a cached negative answer being served rather than a fresh resolution
failure. Worth distinguishing — a cached SERVFAIL is a different operational signal from a live one.

## 3. WebGUI login / session events

Security-relevant authentication events arrive under the `audit` and `configd.py` programs and match none
of the five current regexes. Successful and failed WebGUI logins are currently unparsed.

This is the highest-value of the four: it is the only one that carries a security signal, and "who logged
into the firewall" is exactly the kind of line that wants structured attributes rather than a generic
record.

## 4. DHCP message types

Several Kea and dnsmasq message types are unmodelled:

- `DHCP6_LEASE_ADVERT`
- `DHCP6_RELEASE_NA` / `DHCP6_RELEASE_NA_EXP`
- `DHCPDECLINE`
- `DHCPINFORM`
- dnsmasq "abandoning lease"

`DHCPDECLINE` and "abandoning lease" both indicate address conflicts, which is worth surfacing.

## Correctly declined, not gaps - do not "fix" these

Recorded so a future pass does not add parsers for noise:

- **Kea lease-file-cleanup housekeeping** (`DhcpLFC` program, 420 captures — the single largest bucket —
  plus `DHCPSRV_MEMFILE_LFC_*`)
- **dnsmasq daemon lifecycle chatter**
- **syslog-ng's own internal stats**
- Low-volume operational programs: `rule-updater.py`, `root`, `config`/`configctl`, `devd`, `php`, `sudo`

All of these fall through to generic records by the parsers' own documented design, which is correct.

## Impact

Lines still ship — nothing is lost. The cost is that queries on the structured attributes under-report,
and item 3 means WebGUI auth events cannot be queried structurally.

Visible as `opnsense_exporter_logs_debug_captured_total{receiver="syslog",kind="unparsed"}`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] dpinger `delay` alarm state parsed and distinguishable from `down`
- [ ] unbound cached-SERVFAIL parsed as distinct from live SERVFAIL
- [ ] WebGUI login success/failure parsed with user and outcome attributes
- [ ] The five DHCP message types above parsed
- [ ] Fixtures derived from the real captured lines, not synthesised — and any deliberately synthetic
      case says so in its comment
- [ ] The "correctly declined" list above left alone

comments.body:
## Recon corrections — three things in the body are wrong, verified against the live box

Read before implementing. All captured read-only from the production firewall, 2026-08-04.

**1. `DHCP6_RELEASE_NA_EXP` does not exist.** The real message id is **`DHCP6_RELEASE_NA_EXPIRED`**. It
fires as a pair with `DHCP6_RELEASE_NA`, same tid, back to back:

```
DHCP6_RELEASE_NA duid=[00:02:...], [no hwaddr info], tid=0x3cfc48: binding for address <pub-ip-4>102a and iaid=3394439514 was released properly
DHCP6_RELEASE_NA_EXPIRED duid=[00:02:...], [no hwaddr info], tid=0x3cfc48: binding for address <pub-ip-4>102a and iaid=3394439514 expired on release
```

Structurally like the existing `DHCP6_ALLOC_ENGINE_V6_ALLOC_FAIL*` burst handling — count once per burst,
not twice per event.

**2. WebGUI auth arrives under `audit` ONLY, not `configd.py`.** `configd.py`'s only login-adjacent lines
are periodic captive-portal RPCs like `[uuid] captive login logout enrich` — an RPC *command name* that
happens to contain the words, already matched by the existing `configdRPC` regex. Not an auth event. No
`configd.py` auth branch should be written.

**3. `DHCPDECLINE` / `DHCPINFORM` already match the regex.** Both fit the existing `dnsmasqLineRE`
(`^(DHCP[A-Z]+)\(([^)]*)\)\s*(.*)$`) and fall through at the `iscActions` allowlist lookup
(`dhcp.go:42-50`) instead. Adding two map entries is likely the whole fix for that half.

## Captured shapes

**dpinger `delay`** — both directions, structurally identical to the modelled none<->down pair:

```
MONITOR: WAN_DHCP (Addr: <pub-ip-9> Alarm: none -> delay RTT: 201.2 ms RTTd: 29.6 ms Loss: 0.0 %)
MONITOR: WAN_DHCP (Addr: <pub-ip-9> Alarm: delay -> none RTT: 199.9 ms RTTd: 63.2 ms Loss: 0.0 %)
```

**unbound cached SERVFAIL** — note the trailer is SHORTER than the two modelled shapes. `reUnboundServfail`
requires `at zone <z> from <upstream>`, which this lacks, so it correctly falls through today. Needs a new
branch, not a loosened existing regex — blurring them would merge two distinct signals:

```
[9284:5] error: SERVFAIL <<tailnet-1>. A IN>: SERVFAIL in cache
```

**DHCP6_LEASE_ADVERT** — highest volume of the four gaps, 41-125/day:

```
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.leases.0x3fa9c347e810] DHCP6_LEASE_ADVERT duid=[<duid-1>:d6:84], [no hwaddr info], tid=0xb9c201: lease for address <pub-ip-4>10ad and iaid=0 will be advertised
```

**dnsmasq conflict pair** — same event 2s apart, same MAC and IP, same pid:

```
DHCPDECLINE(ixl0) <lan-ip-21> <mac-2>
abandoning lease to <mac-2> of <lan-ip-21>
DHCPINFORM(ixl0_vlan50) <lan-ip-5> <mac-3>
```

## WebGUI auth — the owner generated real failures so nothing here is synthetic

Six deliberate failed logins, 2026-08-04: two as `root`, two as `rob`, two as `nouserlol` (nonexistent).

Success is TWO lines; failure is THREE, at three different syslog priorities (`<39>` auth.debug,
`<36>` auth.warning, `<35>` auth.err):

```
user root authenticated successfully for WebGui [using OPNsense\Auth\Services\WebGui + OPNsense\Auth\Local]
/index.php: Successful login for user 'root' from: <lan-ip-22>

user root failed authentication for WebGui on OPNsense\Auth\Services\WebGui via OPNsense\Auth\Local
user root could not authenticate for WebGui. [using OPNsense\Auth\Services\WebGui + OPNsense\Auth\Local]
/index.php: Web GUI authentication error for 'root' from <pub-ip-4>10be
```

**Finding: OPNsense does not distinguish a wrong password from a nonexistent user.** All three users
produced byte-identical shapes apart from the username. No user enumeration. A parser must never infer
that distinction, and a future reader should not go hunting for an "unknown user" branch.

**Two traps in the `/index.php:` lines, both biting the same regex:**

- the preposition differs — success is `from:` WITH a colon, failure is `from` WITHOUT
- the address can be IPv6 and therefore contains colons (`<pub-ip-4>10be` is a real captured value),
  so any split on `:` corrupts it

**Not captured, deliberately not modelled:** no logout or session-close line exists anywhere in four days
of audit logs — the WebGUI session appears to time out silently. Writing that branch from documentation is
the #284 failure mode and is not being done.

Also captured, a related but distinct shape:
`no active session, user not found (called "/ui/diagnostics/log/core/gateways" @ <lan-ip-22>)`

## Volume, 5-day window

| Shape | per day | note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DHCP6_LEASE_ADVERT | 41-125 | highest by far |
| unbound cached SERVFAIL | 3-12 | vs ~929 total SERVFAIL/day |
| DHCP6_RELEASE_NA(_EXPIRED) | 0-6 pairs | |
| DHCPINFORM | 0-2 | |
| dpinger delay | 0-10 | bursty, one WAN latency episode |
| WebGUI login | 1-2 | rare, highest operational value |
| DHCPDECLINE / abandoning lease | 0-1 | conflict event, pairs |

**Not verified, not modelled:** no ISC dhcpd (`dhcpd` program) DHCPDECLINE/DHCPINFORM was captured — this
box runs Kea plus dnsmasq-dhcp. The ISC wire format for those two actions stays unverified.

title: logship: four unmodelled syslog shapes (dpinger delay, cached SERVFAIL, WebGUI auth, DHCP message types)

## Summary

`opnsense_firmware_info` publishes `undefined` for all four identity labels on a box that has never run a
firmware update check, even though three of them are returned by the API unconditionally.

Live on prod:

```
opnsense_firmware_info{os_version="undefined",product_abi="undefined",
                       product_id="undefined",product_version="undefined"} 1
```

## The API actually returns the identity

`GET /api/core/firmware/status` on the prod box (OPNsense 26.7.1_1) returns exactly three top-level keys:

```
ALL top-level keys: ['product', 'status', 'status_msg']
last_check: None
status: 'none'
product.* identity: {'product_id': 'opnsense', 'product_version': '26.7.1_1', 'product_abi': '26.7',
                     'product_series': '26.7', 'product_arch': 'amd64'}
product_check: None
```

There is no `last_check` key at all, and no top-level `product_id` / `product_version` / `product_abi` /
`os_version`. The identity is present, nested under `product`, unconditionally.

## Root cause

`opnsense/firmware.go:11-16` reads identity from the **top level**:

```go
type firmwareStatusResponse struct {
    LastCheck      string `json:"last_check"`
    NeedsReboot    string `json:"needs_reboot"`
    OsVersion      string `json:"os_version"`
    ProductID      string `json:"product_id"`
    ProductVersion string `json:"product_version"`
    ProductAbi     string `json:"product_abi"`
```

and `opnsense/firmware.go:341-352` gates the whole population branch on a key that does not exist here:

```go
if resp.LastCheck != "" {
    data.CheckPresent = true
    data.OsVersion = resp.OsVersion
    data.ProductABI = resp.ProductAbi
    data.ProductId = resp.ProductID
    data.ProductVersion = resp.ProductVersion
    ...
```

Those top-level keys only appear once `core/firmware/check` has run. The struct already declares a nested
`Product` sub-object at `firmware.go:88-90` but reads only `product.product_check.upgrade_needs_reboot`
from it.

## What is and is not wrong

- **Wrong**: the three identity labels `product_id`, `product_version`, `product_abi`. All recoverable
  from `product.*` on every box, checked or not.
- **Not recoverable from this endpoint**: `os_version` (the FreeBSD version). Not present under `product`.
  `opnsense_system_info` already carries it correctly as `freebsd_version="15.1-RELEASE-p1"`.
- **Correct and faithful, leave alone**: `firmware_last_check_timestamp_seconds=0` and the zeroed
  `firmware_*_packages_count` series. No check has run, so there genuinely is no answer.

## Impact

`firmware_info` is useless as an inventory series on any box that has not run an API update check —
which is the default state after a reboot. Mitigated in practice because `opnsense_system_info` carries
the same identity correctly, so this is a duplicate-source inconsistency rather than lost data.

Note this interacts with the canary: #626 flags `firmware` `product.product_check.upgrade_needs_reboot`
as unverified-but-required for the same underlying reason (the box has not run a check).

## Proposed fix

Tolerant reader, matching the `chase` pattern in CLAUDE.md's Canary Drift Triage and the template at
`opnsense/health_check.go`: add `product_id` / `product_version` / `product_abi` to the nested `Product`
struct, and resolve identity top-level-wins-else-nested in an accessor. Populate identity **outside** the
`LastCheck` gate; leave the check-dependent fields inside it.

Decide deliberately what `os_version` should carry when absent — keeping `undefined` is defensible, but
it should be a decision, not a leftover.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `product_id`, `product_version`, `product_abi` populated on a box that has never run a firmware check
- [ ] Identity resolution is top-level-wins-else-`product.*`, so a checked box is unchanged
- [ ] Fixture covering the bare three-key envelope (`product` / `status` / `status_msg`, no `last_check`)
- [ ] `last_check_timestamp_seconds` and the package counts still read 0 on an unchecked box
- [ ] `os_version` behaviour on an unchecked box decided and documented

comments.body:
## Decision: populate `os_version` too, via the existing shared-result seam — zero extra API calls

Owner decision, 2026-08-04. The owner asked for `os_version` to be populated rather than left `undefined`,
with one constraint: **no duplicate calls to the OPNsense API.**

That constraint is satisfiable without compromise, because the mechanism already exists.

**Design (frozen):**

1. Identity (`product_id` / `product_version` / `product_abi`) comes from the tolerant reader described in
   the body — top-level-wins-else-`product.*`, populated outside the `LastCheck` gate. Zero new calls; the
   data is already in the response we decode today.
2. `os_version` comes from `internal/fetchshare`, the shared-result seam added in #571. `fetchSystemInfo`
   already decodes the FreeBSD version from `systemInformation` (`opnsense/system_resources.go:459`) on the
   60s medium tier. It publishes that result to the seam; the firmware fetch reads it with a generous
   `maxAge` instead of asking the box again.

The reason this is clean rather than a workaround: publisher and reader are **both methods on the same
`opnsense.Client`** (`c.results`), so it needs no new wiring into `internal/collector` or `main.go`. A seam
miss degrades to the current `undefined` rather than erroring.

Note the seam doc says an endpoint belongs there "only when a SECOND consumer in this process already
fetches it independently". The intent of that line is to stop the seam becoming an ambient result cache,
and this use is squarely within it — the alternative is the firmware collector fetching `systemInformation`
itself, which is exactly the duplicate request the seam exists to remove. `seamPublishedKeys` is
hand-maintained and `TestSeamPublishedKeysMatchCallSites` enforces it.

**Explicitly unchanged:** `firmware_last_check_timestamp_seconds=0` and the zeroed
`firmware_*_packages_count` series on an unchecked box. No check has run, so there genuinely is no answer,
and inventing one would be worse than the bug being fixed here.

title: firmware: opnsense_firmware_info publishes all-undefined identity labels - the data is available unconditionally under product.*

## Summary

Zenarmor-sourced geo is applied verbatim to RFC1918 addresses, so internal hosts get a country and a
"city" on flow log records. Roughly **921k records/day** on the prod box carry a fabricated country on a
private address.

Real records from Loki:

```
src_ip <lan-ip-23>  src_scope local  src_geo_country GB  src_geo_country_source zenarmor  src_geo_city England
src_ip <lan-ip-1>     src_scope local  src_geo_country GB  src_geo_country_source zenarmor  src_geo_city England
src_ip <lan-ip-7>   src_scope local  src_geo_country GB  src_geo_country_source zenarmor  src_geo_city England
```

30-minute window, `opnsense_source="merged"`:

| `src_scope` | `src_geo_country_source` | records / 30 min |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| local | **zenarmor** | **19,189** |
| local | maxmind | 8,207 |
| remote | maxmind | 619 |
| self | maxmind | 420 |
| self | zenarmor | 107 |
| remote | zenarmor | 12 |

## Root cause

`internal/flow/geo.go:147-198` (`GeoEnricher.endpoint`) has no private-address guard on the Zenarmor
fallback arm. MaxMind correctly declines to look up private space —
`geoip_lookups_total{database="skipped"} = 10,886,113`, 58.6% of all lookups — and then the
`case g.ZenCountry != ""` arm fills the field anyway.

So the guard exists on the MaxMind path and is missing on the fallback.

## Not a defect, checked

The 8,207 `local` + `maxmind` rows are correct: they are the AAISP routed IPv6 prefix
(`<pub-ip-4>100e`), which is public, legitimately GB, and correctly scoped `local`. Only the
`zenarmor`-sourced rows on RFC1918 space are wrong.

## Impact

"Traffic by source country/city" breakdowns attribute internal hosts to GB/England. Byte volumes are
unaffected — this is an attribution defect, not a volume one.

## Proposed fix

Apply the same private/reserved-address guard to the Zenarmor arm that MaxMind already honours. An
address in RFC1918/RFC4193/loopback/link-local space should get no geo from any source.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GeoEnricher.endpoint` skips the Zenarmor arm for private/reserved addresses
- [ ] Test covering RFC1918 v4, ULA v6, loopback and link-local with a populated `ZenCountry`
- [ ] No record with `src_scope="local"` on a private address carries `*_geo_country` after deploy
- [ ] Public-but-local addresses (the AAISP v6 prefix case above) still get geo — do not over-correct by
      keying the guard on `scope` instead of on the address itself
title: flow: Zenarmor geo is applied to RFC1918 addresses - no private-address guard on the fallback arm

body:
## Summary

`reCron` fails to match any cron MAIL line whose detail contains an embedded newline, which on the prod
box is **234 of 239 captured `/usr/sbin/cron` misses (97%)**. Those lines fall through to a generic
record with no `cron.user` / `cron.action` / `cron.command` attributes.

## Root cause

`internal/logship/syslog/cron.go:32`:

```go
var reCron = regexp.MustCompile(`^\((\S+)\)\s+(CMD|MAIL)\s+\((.*)$`)
```

Go's RE2 `.` does not match `\n`, and `$` without `(?m)` anchors at end of text. The real line on the box
carries a literal newline before the closing paren:

```
(nobody) MAIL (mailed 37 bytes of output but got status 0x0001\n)
```

`.*` stops at the `\n`, `$` then fails because `\n)` remains. No match.

The comment at `cron.go:25-31` reasons carefully about unbalanced parens and cron truncating the detail
mid-sentence — but not about cron embedding a newline, which is what actually happens here.

## Reproduction

```go
var reCron  = regexp.MustCompile(`^\((\S+)\)\s+(CMD|MAIL)\s+\((.*)$`)     // current
var reFixed = regexp.MustCompile(`(?s)^\((\S+)\)\s+(CMD|MAIL)\s+\((.*)$`) // candidate
```

| input | current | with `(?s)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(nobody) MAIL (mailed 37 bytes of output but got status 0x0001\n)` | **false** | true |
| `(root) MAIL (mailed 12 bytes of output)` | true | true |
| `(root) CMD (/usr/bin/foo -x)` | true | true |

`(?s)` fixes the failing case and leaves both existing shapes matching.

## Impact

Every cron MAIL line on a box whose cron jobs produce output lands as an unparsed generic record. Not a
data-loss bug — the line still ships — but the structured attributes the parser exists to produce are
absent, so any query on `cron.user` or `cron.action` under-reports.

Visible as `opnsense_exporter_logs_debug_captured_total{receiver="syslog",kind="unparsed"}`.

## Proposed fix

Add `(?s)` to the pattern, and trim the trailing `)` after allowing for the newline. Worth confirming the
trailing-paren trim still behaves for the newline case (`...0x0001\n)` should yield detail
`mailed 37 bytes of output but got status 0x0001` with both the `\n` and the `)` gone, or the newline
preserved — pick one deliberately and pin it in the test).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Failing test first, using the verbatim box line including the embedded `\n`
- [ ] `(?s)` (or equivalent) applied; all three shapes in the table above match
- [ ] Trailing-paren/newline trim behaviour pinned explicitly in the test
- [ ] `logs_debug_captured_total{receiver="syslog",kind="unparsed"}` drops materially on the prod box
      after deploy
title: logship: cron parser drops 97% of cron lines - RE2 '.' does not match the embedded newline in MAIL details

## Summary

A single Suricata ruleset sync fans out into **62 separate annotation candidates**, all stamped with the
same instant. That saturates the per-cycle cap and rate-limits the exporter against Grafana's annotation
API on every ruleset update.

Live on the prod box, 2026-08-04:

```
opnsense_exporter_annotations_written_total       64
opnsense_exporter_annotations_failed_total       162
opnsense_exporter_annotations_rate_limited_total 162
opnsense_exporter_annotations_skipped_total      183
opnsense_exporter_annotations_undeliverable_total  0
```

12 logged 429s, every one of them `kind=ids-ruleset-update`:

```
time=2026-08-04T03:15:42.973Z level=WARN source=watcher.go:236 msg="annotation post failed" kind=ids-ruleset-update err="grafana returned 429: Too Many Requests"
time=2026-08-04T03:16:42.848Z level=WARN source=watcher.go:236 msg="annotation post failed" kind=ids-ruleset-update err="grafana returned 429: Too Many Requests"
time=2026-08-04T03:17:42.637Z level=WARN source=watcher.go:236 msg="annotation post failed" kind=ids-ruleset-update err="grafana returned 429: Too Many Requests"
```

Episode ran 03:15-03:26 UTC, ~11 minutes.

## Root cause

`internal/annotations/catalog.go:133-138` keys the watch per ruleset file:

```go
{
    Metric:    "opnsense_ids_ruleset_last_updated_timestamp_seconds",
    Kind:      "ids-ruleset-update",
    Text:      "IDS ruleset %s updated",
    LabelKeys: []string{"ruleset"},
},
```

On this box that metric has 62 series, and a sync updates all of them at once — verified directly:

```
$ grep -c '^opnsense_ids_ruleset_last_updated_timestamp_seconds{' metrics
62
$ grep '^opnsense_ids_ruleset_last_updated_timestamp_seconds{' metrics | awk '{print $2}' | sort -u | wc -l
1
$ ... | sort | uniq -c
     62 1.7858136e+09
```

**62 series, one distinct timestamp.** One logical event, 62 annotation candidates, against a
`MaxPerCycle` of 20.

## This shape was known and only half-addressed

`internal/annotations/watcher_test.go:458-460` already documents it:

```go
// rulesetBacklog builds n distinct events, one per ruleset, all inside the
// lookback. This is the shape that produced #519 live: a fresh deployment with a
// 24h lookback found dozens of ids-ruleset-update events at once.
```

The #519/#524 work bounded the *storm* (attempt-counting cap, exponential backoff) and that part is
working correctly — `undeliverable_total=0`, all 64 real events eventually landed, cross-checked against
64 records fetched from Grafana's annotation store via `gcx api /api/annotations`. But the **fan-out
itself was never addressed**, so the box still self-inflicts a 429 storm on every ruleset sync and burns
183 skipped events getting through it.

## Proposed fix

Coalesce per-sync rather than per-file. Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. Emit one annotation per distinct timestamp for this kind — "IDS rulesets updated (62 files)" — since
   the per-file detail has no diagnostic value when they all move together.
2. Add a `Coalesce` field to the catalog entry that groups candidates sharing a `(kind, timestamp)` and
   renders a count.

Option 1 is a strictly smaller change and matches what the annotation is actually for (overlaying "the
ruleset changed here" on a dashboard). The per-ruleset breakdown is already available as a metric.

Note `threat-feed-update` (`catalog.go:139-148`) is the same per-entity shape and is `DefaultOff: true`
with a comment about volume — same class of problem, already mitigated by being off. Whatever lands here
should probably let that one be turned on safely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A single ruleset sync produces one annotation, not 62
- [ ] `annotations_rate_limited_total` stops climbing on ruleset syncs
- [ ] `annotations_skipped_total` stops climbing from this kind
- [ ] Test covering the "N series, one timestamp" shape (extend `rulesetBacklog`, which already builds it)
- [ ] `threat-feed-update` reassessed now that the fan-out is handled

## Also

`/opt/opnsense2otel/docker-compose.yml` on <host-1> still carries
`# TEMPORARILY OFF: unbounded retry storm on 429, see #519. Re-enable once fixed.` directly above
`OPN2OTEL_ANNOTATIONS_ENABLED: "true"`. Deployment-side, cosmetic, but the comment now says the opposite
of the setting.

Related: #519, #524.

comments.body:
## Decision: coalesce per sync; `threat-feed-update` stays default-off

Owner decision, 2026-08-04.

**Approach — option 2 from the body, in the shape of option 1.** A `Coalesce bool` on the `Watch` struct,
set on `ids-ruleset-update`. When set, candidates sharing `(kind, timestamp)` collapse into one annotation
whose text carries a count ("IDS rulesets updated (62 files)"). A coalesced annotation gets the base tag
and the `kind` tag only — the 62 per-ruleset label values must not become 62 tags. `LabelKeys` stays
declared, since it is still what identifies the series; it simply stops feeding text and tags when
coalescing. Singular case must read correctly.

The generic field rather than a hardcoded special-case, because the same per-entity shape recurs in the
catalogue and the next one should not need the watcher touched again.

**`threat-feed-update` stays `DefaultOff: true`.** Coalescing fixes the 429 storm but not the reason that
kind was turned off: a Q-Feeds refresh every ~20 minutes buries the annotation timeline on every dashboard,
in Explore and beside every alert. That is a cadence problem, not a fan-out problem, and it is unchanged.
Leaving it off also avoids a paired `grafana/annotations.py` edit — `grafana/tests/test_annotations.py`
asserts the push set and the dashboard layer set agree, so flipping one side alone reds CI.

Closes the "reassessed" acceptance item: reassessed, deliberately unchanged.

title: annotations: one IDS ruleset sync fans out to 62 annotations, self-inflicting a 429 storm

body:
## Summary

VIRGIN (WAN2, `ixl1`) outbound bytes read **~1.8x the kernel's own counter** in production. This is a
regression of #623: the NAT-pair dedupe that shipped to fix exactly this has gone effectively idle.

#623 was closed 2026-08-01 with a measured ratio of **0.989**. The same acceptance query today:

```promql
sum by (interface) (increase(opnsense_flow_bytes_total{source="netflow",direction="outbound",interface="VIRGIN"}[W]))
  / on (interface)
sum by (interface) (increase(opnsense_interfaces_transmitted_bytes_total{interface="VIRGIN"}[W]))
```

| window | ratio | kernel TX in window |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1h | **1.794** | 48.08 GB |
| 6h | **1.755** | 254.94 GB |
| 21h | **1.850** | 882.67 GB |

AAISP over the same 21h reads 0.987 out / 0.974 in — unaffected, and only because
`netflow_pppoe0` captures nothing ([[pppoe-netflow-capture-is-dead-upstream]]), so no post-NAT copy
exists on that WAN.

## Both of #623's measurement traps are excluded

#623's closing comment records two traps that produced confident-looking wrong numbers. Neither applies:

- **Not small-flow noise.** 48.08 GB of kernel TX in the 1h window is ~107 Mbit/s sustained. #623's
  bad reading was taken at 8 kbit/s on 2.31 MB.
- **No counter reset in window.** Container start `1785747701` (2026-08-03T09:01:41Z), measured at
  `1785828943`. Uptime 22.6h, so the 21h window sits entirely inside one run.

## The mechanism is idle — this is the tell

`increase(opnsense_flow_nat_pair_deduped_total[...])`:

| | at #623 closure (2026-08-01) | now (2026-08-04) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `{outcome="suppressed"}` per 5m | **39** | **0** |
| `{outcome="suppressed"}` per 21h | — | **27** |
| `{outcome="late_pre_nat"}` per 21h | — | 6 |

27 suppressions in 21 hours against millions of records, while 48 GB/h flows through VIRGIN at a
1.79 ratio. At fix time it fired 39 times every 5 minutes.

The NAT table itself is still being built and looks normal — `nat_pair_entries{translations}` 4200-6128,
`{identities}` 3320, `{carried}` 3496, `{conflict}` 14 (inside the 6-14 band #623 recorded), `{skipped}` 0.
So the table is populated; the suppression branch is simply not being reached.

## Record-level proof that both copies are emitted

Conversation `<lan-ip-8> -> <pub-ip-13>:23` egressing VIRGIN. pf's own state:

```
all tcp <pub-ip-14>:7694 (<lan-ip-8>:39216) -> <pub-ip-13>:23  ESTABLISHED:ESTABLISHED
```

Loki, 90-minute window, pre-NAT (`src_ip=<lan-ip-8>:39216`) vs post-NAT (`src_ip=<pub-ip-14>:7694`):

| flow window | pre-NAT `nf_bytes` / `nf_packets` | post-NAT `nf_bytes` / `nf_packets` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 06:17:26 -> 06:22:49 | 4294902944 / 2890603 | 4294902944 / 2890603 |
| 06:28 -> 06:33 | 4294901928 / 2890555 | 4294901928 / 2890555 |
| 06:33 -> 06:39 | 4294902420 / 2890329 | 4294902420 / 2890329 |
| 06:44 -> 06:49 | 4294902256 / 2890923 | 4294902256 / 2890923 |
| 06:49:53 -> 06:55:22 | 4294902776 / 2891052 | 4294902776 / 2891052 |
| 06:55 -> 07:00 | 4294901776 / 2890736 | 4294901776 / 2890736 |
| 07:00:46 -> 07:06:11 | 4294902860 / 2890475 | 4294902860 / 2890475 |
| 07:06:11 -> 07:11:39 | 4294901880 / 2890964 | 4294901880 / 2890964 |

Identical to the byte, both counted. The ~4.2949 GB values are `2^32 - ~65k`, ng_netflow counter-saturation
expiry, not a decode error — packet counts differ per record, so these are genuine distinct 5-minute slices.

## Three-way cross-check at the source (441 s, 07:21:56 -> 07:29:17 UTC)

```
ngctl netflow_ixl1 IPv4 bytes delta :  5879.31 MB
kernel ixl1 TX delta                :  5931.31 MB   (the node sees 99.1% of TX - the node is fine)
ngctl netflow_ixl0 IPv4+IPv6 delta  :  7109.96 MB
exporter flow VIRGIN outbound delta : 12885.04 MB   <-- 2.172x kernel ixl1 TX
```

12,885 MB is approximately 5,879 (the `ixl1` node's view) + ~6,000 (the `ixl0` node's view of the same
bytes). The exporter is summing both nodes' views of one conversation.

`src_scope` split of outbound flow-log records, 3h — 41% of VIRGIN outbound records are duplicate
post-NAT copies:

| interface | `src_scope="local"` (pre-NAT) | `src_scope="self"` (post-NAT dup) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| AAISP | 183,054 | **0** |
| VIRGIN | 132 | **91** |

## Eliminated by measurement - do not re-chase

- **Byte/packet mismatch between copies.** `natKey{canon,bytes,pkts}` needs exact equality and the table
  above shows exact equality. The key's design assumption holds.
- **Late-pre-NAT arrival path.** That path increments `{outcome="late_pre_nat"}`, which sat frozen at 7.
- **TTL expiry between copies.** Paired records land ~1s apart (epoch 1785825220 vs 1785825221);
  `dedupeTTL` is 2 min.
- **`src_addr`/`nat_addr` inverted in `BuildNATTable`.** Checked against OPNsense's own parser,
  `/usr/local/opnsense/scripts/filter/lib/states.py:216-245`: for a `->` (`direction=out`) row it sets
  `nat_addr` from the parenthesised field (pre-NAT) and `src_addr` from `parts[2]` (post-NAT).
  `opnsense/firewall_states.go:66` documents exactly that and `internal/flow/nattable.go:152-156` builds
  `post=(SrcAddr->Dst)`, `pre=(NatAddr->Dst)`. **The orientation is correct - do not "fix" it.**
- **Truncated state fetch.** `opnsense/firewall_states.go:88` posts `{"current":1,"rowCount":-1,...}`
  (bootgrid no-limit). Exporter sees 5,970 states vs `pfctl -si`'s 6,149 (97%, polling skew).

## Prime suspect (not confirmed)

`NATTable.Canonical(post)` returns `isPost=false` for these tuples, so `natAdmit` never reaches the
suppression branch. When that lookup misses, the post-NAT record also fails `couldBeTranslated()` — both
`<pub-ip-14>` and `<pub-ip-13>` are public, so "exactly one endpoint private" is false — so it is
emitted *and not even remembered*. **Both counters flat rather than one climbing is the tell**, and it
points at the map lookup rather than the pairing logic.

Likely candidates: a `netip.Addr` 4-byte-vs-v4-mapped-v6 key mismatch between `parseTuple`'s
`netip.ParseAddr` and the decoder's `AddrFrom4`, or the row not being present in the fetched snapshot.
Confirming needs instrumentation that could not be added read-only.

## Blast radius

Every per-WAN byte/rate panel, every WAN2 alert threshold, and the WAN-split of top-talkers read ~1.8x
high on VIRGIN. AAISP and all LAN/VLAN interfaces are unaffected.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root cause identified for why `Canonical(post)` misses on these tuples (add a temporary counter or
      a replay test against a captured export rather than guessing)
- [ ] Regression test pinning the exact production tuple shape (public->public post-NAT, v4)
- [ ] `nat_pair_deduped_total{outcome="suppressed"}` climbs in proportion to VIRGIN NAT'd traffic again
- [ ] VIRGIN outbound ratio back to ~1.0, measured over a window with real VIRGIN traffic and no
      container restart inside it
- [ ] A guard so this cannot silently regress again — the failure mode here is a metric that stays
      plausible while the mechanism does nothing

## Retest traps

- Read the **byte ratio**, not the correction count. Never compare correction counts across windows.
- Locate the traffic first, then measure over it.
- Check for a container restart inside any `increase()` window.

Regression of #623 (closed 2026-08-01 as verified). Related: #624.

comments.body:
## Measurement note before anyone re-measures this: the exporter restarted today

Not a change to the diagnosis — a trap for the next session, since every figure in this
issue is counter-derived.

The production exporter on <host-1> was redeployed **2026-08-04 ~08:45 UTC** (`671098d`), and
again shortly after (`787dde35`, then `cb5829d9`). Watchtower pulls `:main` hourly, so
expect further restarts.

Consequences for re-measuring:

- **`increase()` / `rate()` across any of those instants is meaningless.** This issue already
  records that trap from #623 ("reading byte ratios needs real WAN traffic AND no recent
  container restart"); it now applies to today specifically.
- **`nat_pair_deduped_total` restarted from zero.** The decisive evidence in this issue is
  that `increase(nat_pair_deduped_total{outcome="suppressed"}[5m])` reads **0** where it read
  **39** at #623's closure. Re-establish that against a window entirely inside one container
  lifetime, and confirm uptime with `process_start_time_seconds` before trusting it.
- Check the volume in the window rather than assuming: VIRGIN is no longer idle (882 GB in
  21h on 2026-08-04, ~107 Mbit/s sustained), so a Proxmox backup no longer has to be arranged
  to generate traffic — but a quiet window will still give a ratio dominated by small-flow
  noise, which is how a 2.002 ratio on 0.8 MB once looked like a real result.

Nothing in the shipped code touched the NAT-pair path. The releases since this issue was
filed cover annotations, syslog parsers, flow geo precedence and the private-address guard,
firmware identity, interface counters, and the geo merge orientation fix (#647) — none of
them the dedupe.

One adjacent thing worth knowing, because it was found in the same area and could confuse a
reader of merged flow records: #647 fixed `MergeGeo` pairing endpoints by POSITION rather
than by address, which meant a Zenarmor conn document describing a connection from the
initiator's side attached each end's geo to the opposite address. That is a **geo attribution**
defect only — it never touched bytes, packets or the NAT-pair logic, so it neither explains
nor affects the over-count here.

## Root cause: the pairing window was sized under the one condition that hides the failure

Fixed in `07e72429`. The prime suspect in the body — `NATTable.Canonical(post)` missing — was
**wrong**. The lookup hits. The pf row is present, the tuples match, the volumes match exactly.
What fails is the two-minute window.

### The mechanism, measured at the socket

`tcpdump` on <host-1>'s udp/2055 for 16 minutes, v9 decoded, pairs matched on exact bytes **and**
packets:

| node | export cadence |
| --- | ---: |
| LAN `ixl0` | one record every **324 s**, promptly at each window's close |
| WAN `ixl1` | **batches ~609 s apart**, two windows at a time |

Real pre→post arrival gaps: **266.4 s** and **590.9 s**. 4 of 4 pairs past the 120 s
`dedupeTTL`. The identity is expired and swept before its twin lands, so `Canonical` hits, the
`natSeen` lookup misses, the copy is remembered as `natRolePost` and emitted — and the pre-NAT
copy is long gone, so `late_pre_nat` never fires either. **Both counters flat is exactly what
that path produces**, which is why the tell in the body pointed the right way at the wrong cause.

The pf state was present throughout, confirmed against a live `query_states` pull:

```
{"direction":"out","proto":"tcp","src_addr":"<pub-ip-14>","src_port":"7694",
 "dst_addr":"<pub-ip-13>","dst_port":"23","nat_addr":"<lan-ip-8>","nat_port":"39216",
 "route-to":"<pub-ip-5>@ixl1"}
```

### Why #623 verified green at 0.989

Its capture was taken *with the 100 Mbit/s backup running over the policy-routed WAN*. The backup
is what put enough flows on the WAN-side `ng_netflow` node to keep its export datagrams filling —
p99 60 s. The measurement generated the traffic that made the mechanism work. Off that load the
WAN node carries a handful of flows, its datagram never fills, and it holds records until its own
flush. **The batching interval is set by the WAN node's flow rate, which rises as the box gets
quieter**, so no fixed window is safe and widening this one only moves the failure.

Only 1,501 of 2,745 `direction="out"` rows are translated, and **1,494 of those route via
`pppoe0`** — AAISP, which exports nothing, so it cannot double-count. Just **4** route via `ixl1`.
The population that can double-count on this box is tiny and long-lived, which is precisely the
shape whose exports batch worst.

### The fix — two proofs (Rob chose the failsafe both-ways option)

| outcome | proof |
| --- | --- |
| `suppressed` | the pre-NAT copy of this **exact export** was emitted (unchanged, #623) |
| `suppressed_by_conversation` | a pre-NAT record for this **conversation** was seen within `natConversationTTL` (15 min), so its LAN side is demonstrably captured |

The second is weaker on purpose: it infers this export's twin from the conversation's other
copies, and is wrong only if the pre-NAT copy of one window never arrives — which under-counts
that window instead of doubling it. It is gated on `NATTable.IsTranslatedPre`, so it holds one
entry per **translated conversation** rather than one per record — smaller than the exact table
despite the far longer TTL — and a live conversation refreshes its own entry.

### The guard

`opnsense_flow_nat_pair_deduped_total{outcome="unpaired"}` counts post-NAT copies pf **calls a
translation** that were emitted anyway because neither proof was available:

```promql
sum(rate(opnsense_flow_nat_pair_deduped_total{outcome="unpaired"}[15m]))
  /
sum(rate(opnsense_flow_nat_pair_deduped_total{outcome=~"unpaired|suppressed|suppressed_by_conversation"}[15m]))
```

It goes to **1** when the mechanism breaks, instead of everything reading zero. That is the
acceptance criterion "a metric that stays plausible while the mechanism does nothing" — with this
series present, three days of 1.79x would have been a one-glance diagnosis. It has its own panel
on the health dashboard (`NAT-Pair Unpaired Share`), and `kind="conversations"` joins
`kind="identities"` on the entries gauge.

### Corrections to this issue's own body

- **"Prime suspect: `Canonical(post)` returns `isPost=false`" — WRONG.** It returns true. Nothing
  is wrong with the map lookup, the key types, or `BuildNATTable`'s orientation.
- **"The mechanism is idle" understates it.** It is not idle, it is *structurally unable to
  close*: `natSeen` is populated (2,922 identities), it is simply never populated with the right
  entry at the right time.
- The "27 suppressions in 21 h" and "39 per 5 m" comparison is the count-across-windows trap this
  issue warns about in its own retest notes. The traffic mix changed completely — #623's
  population was a backup's many concurrent flows, today's is one long-lived 100 Mbit/s
  conversation whose records expire on 2^32 counter saturation. The *byte ratio* was the real
  evidence; the count difference was mostly the mix.

### Still open

Acceptance criterion 4 — "VIRGIN outbound ratio back to ~1.0" — cannot be ticked until watchtower
pulls `:main` and a measurement window elapses entirely inside one container lifetime. Re-measure
with the 21 h query from the body once uptime allows, and check `unpaired`'s share is small.

## Verified on the production box

`07e72429` deployed to <host-1> at 12:17 BST (manual pull + relaunch). Measured over windows
sitting entirely inside single container lifetimes, same 30-minute length either side so the
pipeline-lag bias is comparable:

| 30 min window | VIRGIN | AAISP |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| before (`cb5829d9`) | **1.974** | 0.944 |
| after (`07e72429`) | **0.936** | 0.874 |

Both post-fix figures sit below 1 because a 30-minute window loses the ~3 minutes of records
still inside the correlator at the far end — about 10%, which is why the before/after pair
above is the comparison that means something and neither absolute number is. A longer window
follows once uptime allows.

### The record-level proof

45 minutes of VIRGIN NetFlow records after the fix, grouped as the issue body grouped them:

| records | bytes | shape |
| ---: | ---: | --- |
| 7 | **30.064 GB** | `outbound` `src_scope="local"` — pre-NAT, policy-route corrected |
| 18 | **0.000 GB** | `outbound` `src_scope="self"` — post-NAT |

Against the issue body's 3-hour split of 132 local / 91 self, and the 60-minute sample taken
while diagnosing, which read **11 self copies carrying 38.654 GB alongside 9 local copies
carrying the identical 38.654 GB**. The large post-NAT copies are gone; what remains on the
`self` side is the firewall's own ICMP and DNS, which was never duplicated.

`nat_pair_deduped_total` over 15 minutes: `suppressed_by_conversation` **13.2**, `suppressed`
**0**, `late_pre_nat` **0**, `unpaired` **16.3**. The new proof is carrying the whole box, as
predicted — the exact-export window still cannot close against this WAN node's batching.

### Two claims in my previous comment were wrong, corrected in `eaab369e`

- **"Conversations is normally the smaller of the two."** It is not. 4,039 conversations
  against 3,026 identities at 40 minutes. The `IsTranslatedPre` gate makes the table scale
  with how much the box NATs rather than with its record rate — that is the property worth
  having — but the 7.5x longer TTL makes it larger in absolute terms. Both sit against the
  same `maxEntries` bound.
- **`unpaired` near 1 does not mean the bytes are double.** It is a share of RECORDS. This box
  reads **55% unpaired at a byte ratio of 0.94**, because the unpaired remainder is small
  firewall-originated flows while every duplicated gigabyte is paired. As originally worded
  the panel would have read as a live double count on a healthy box. It now says to read it
  *with* the interface-counter ratio: `unpaired` says whether the mechanism is alive, the
  ratio says whether the bytes are right.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] Root cause identified — the pairing window, not `Canonical`; measured at the socket
- [x] Regression test pinning the production tuple shape and the measured 266 s gap
- [x] Suppression climbing again in proportion to VIRGIN NAT'd traffic
- [x] VIRGIN ratio back from 1.974 to 0.936 on matched windows; the duplicate 4.29 GB copies
      are gone from the record stream
- [x] Guard against silent regression — `outcome="unpaired"` plus its own health panel

One thing worth watching rather than closing over: AAISP moved 0.944 -> 0.874 across the same
two windows. AAISP has no post-NAT copy to suppress (`pppoe0` exports nothing), and I could
not find a mechanism by which the new proof could touch it, so this reads as window variance
in a 30-minute sample rather than a regression — but it is a 7-point move and it deserves a
longer-window re-read before anyone treats it as noise.

## Do not reopen this on a quiet-WAN ratio

Rob paused the Proxmox backup that was driving VIRGIN at ~105 Mbit/s, so the next person to run
the acceptance query will see a small denominator and possibly a ratio near 2. **That is not a
regression of this issue.** Written down here and in `docs/flow.md` (`c9a5b9dc`) so it is not
re-litigated.

### The traffic level did not skew the before/after comparison

Worth stating plainly, because it was the obvious worry. VIRGIN kernel TX over the four hours
around the fix, sampled every 8 minutes, never left **104-107 Mbit/s** except one 86.8 dip:

| window (UTC) | VIRGIN TX | ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 09:54-10:24, pre-fix `cb5829d9` | ~105 Mbit/s | **1.974** |
| 10:50-11:20, post-fix `07e72429` | ~105 Mbit/s | **0.936** |

Same backup running on both sides. And this issue's original 1.794 / 1.755 / 1.850 were measured
on 48.08 GB / 254.94 GB / 882.67 GB of kernel TX — the body says so explicitly, because #624 had
already been burned once by small-flow noise. **The over-count was never a low-traffic artefact.**

### Three ways this ratio lies

Now in `docs/flow.md` under the acceptance query, since that is where someone will be standing
when they need it:

1. **A quiet WAN's ratio is noise.** It is a ratio of two sums, so an idle WAN has nothing large
   enough to dominate it and a doubled 3 MB of synthetic-monitoring pings still reads 2.0. With
   the backup off, VIRGIN is monitoring pings and bittorrent background. In that regime the
   answerable question is whether `outcome="suppressed"` and `outcome="suppressed_by_conversation"`
   are still moving — not what the ratio says.
2. **A short window under-reads by roughly (pipeline lag / window).** ~3 minutes of records sit in
   the correlator while the kernel counter is instantaneous, so 30 minutes reads **~0.9 when it is
   correct**; over 21 h the same lag is 0.2%. Both post-fix figures above sit below 1 for this
   reason, which is why the equal-length before/after pair is the comparison that means something
   and neither absolute number is.
3. **`increase()` across a container restart is meaningless.** Confirm `process_start_time_seconds`
   and keep the window inside one lifetime. Watchtower pulls `:main` hourly.

Plus the substitution that keeps recurring: **never compare a correction COUNT across two traffic
windows** (#624). The counters weight a 4 GB flow and a one-packet ping equally, so a count that
halves usually means the mix moved. Counts say a mechanism is alive; bytes say the totals are right.

### One genuine open edge

The fix is verified at ~105 Mbit/s. It is **not** verified on a near-idle VIRGIN, and that is the
harder case by this issue's own mechanism: the WAN node batches because its datagram does not fill,
so the gap grows as the WAN gets quieter. The measured gaps were 266 s and 591 s against a
15-minute `natConversationTTL`. If a quiet VIRGIN pushes them past 15 minutes the pairing lapses
and the over-count returns — on trivial byte volumes, but it would be real.

Rob's pause is the natural experiment for it. I am measuring whether
`suppressed_by_conversation` still fires with VIRGIN near zero, and will report here. **If it
stops, the answer is a larger `natConversationTTL`, not a new mechanism** — the two-proof
structure is unaffected either way.

title: Declare the GoReleaser v2 configuration schema

body:
## What

The v4 rename changes user-queryable telemetry identities from `opnsense-exporter` to `opnsense2otel`, but the v4 upgrade guide and generated release notes do not identify those changes. The guide currently says existing PromQL/LogQL queries keep working unmodified and that only image/environment/chart/docs references need updating.

The affected defaults and tags are:

- OTLP metric and log resource `service.name`: `opnsense-exporter` -> `opnsense2otel`
- Pyroscope application name: `opnsense-exporter` -> `opnsense2otel`
- Grafana annotation base tag: `opnsense-exporter` -> `opnsense2otel`

## Why

Operators with custom Loki selectors, OTLP-derived Prometheus selectors, profile queries, or annotation queries pinned to the old identity will see those views go empty after upgrading. This is an intentional v4 break, but it must be explicit in the migration contract before release.

This was independently reproduced during the v4 release-candidate audit in #632:

- `v3.0.0` documents `opnsense-exporter` as the default for both `--otlp.service-name` and `--pyroscope.application-name`.
- Current `main` documents `opnsense2otel` for both defaults and defines `annotations.BaseTag = "opnsense2otel"`.
- The <host-1> deployment emits `service_name=opnsense2otel` in m7kni metrics and Loki, and publishes profiles under `opnsense2otel`.
- `docs/upgrading.md` lists the project rename but does not mention these three query identities; it instead says existing LogQL queries remain unmodified.
- PR #358's breaking-change section also omits these identity migrations.

## Scope

Documentation and release-note contract only. The v4 runtime values are intentional and should not be reverted. Preserve the explicitly stable `opnsense_exporter_*` metric names and dashboard UIDs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `docs/upgrading.md` explicitly lists all three identity changes and their affected consumers.
- [x] The guide includes concrete old/new selector examples for Loki, OTLP-derived Prometheus labels, Pyroscope, and annotations where applicable.
- [x] The statement that existing queries remain unmodified is narrowed so it is true (metric names/dashboard UIDs), without implying identity-based queries are unchanged.
- [x] PR #358's v4 breaking-change notes include the telemetry identity migration, either through the completing commit's release note or an equivalent Release Please update.
- [x] Documentation validation gates pass.

Parent: #632

comments.body: Implementation checkpoint: `docs/upgrading.md` now names all three migrated identities, gives old/new Loki, OTLP-derived Prometheus, Pyroscope and annotation selectors, documents continuity overrides, and narrows the stability claim to metric names/dashboard UIDs. `make docs-check` passes. The Release Please acceptance item remains open until the issue-closing breaking-change commit is pushed and PR #358 is independently read back.

Completed by `bded064b6097bd7099634d73398acc627a1a253b` on `main`.

The upgrade guide now documents all three renamed identities, old/new selectors, continuity overrides, and the narrower stable-name contract. The completing commit carries the v4 `BREAKING CHANGE` note so Release Please can regenerate #358. Local build, lint, test, race, docs, deployment, testbed, canary, Grafana and public-IP gates passed before push. Waiting on exact-SHA CI and PR #358 read-back is tracked in #632.

title: v4.0.0 release-candidate audit and launch tracker

body:
## Problem

The `unparsed` debug capture on the live box has been running since 24 Jul 2026 and holds 12,622
shape-deduped entries. Several high-value programs land there with no parser, or with a parser that
does not match the shapes the box actually emits.

## Evidence

Source: `/opt/opnsense2otel/capture/syslog/*.ndjson` on <host-1>, 24 Jul – 1 Aug 2026. Entries are
shape-deduped per rotation window (#362), so the counts below are windows-with-that-shape, not raw
line volume. Shapes re-normalised independently to confirm `capture.NormaliseShape` is collapsing
correctly — it is; hex thread-ids and digit runs are handled.

| Program | Entries | Shapes | State |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `unbound` | 1839 | 69 | parser exists; 3 dnsbl shapes carry 1524 entries (83% of its unparsed volume) |
| `kea-dhcp6` | 1625 | 119 | parser registered for the program but does not match ALLOC_FAIL |
| `kernel` | 322 | 171 | parser exists; netmap + link-state shapes unmatched |
| `ppp` (mpd5) | 100 | 100 | **no parser at all** — every line a distinct shape |
| `devd` | 223 | 46 | no parser |

### Ranked candidates

1. **`ppp` (mpd5)** — no parser exists. The PPPoE link state machine:
   `[opt7_link0] LCP: state change Opened --> Stopping`, `[opt7_link0] LCP: rec'd Terminate Request`,
   `[opt7] Bundle: Status update: up 0 links, total bandwidth 9600 bps`, `[opt7] IPCP: LayerDown`.
   This is WAN flap detection on any PPPoE line. Best single win; 100/100 shapes distinct means the
   whole state machine is currently opaque.

2. **`kea-dhcp6` ALLOC_FAIL** — ~1000 entries across 119 shapes:
   `WARN [kea-dhcp6.alloc-engine.0x...] ALLOC_ENGINE_V6_ALLOC_FAIL_SUBNET duid=[...] tid=...: failed
   to allocate an IPv6 lease`, plus `_NO_POOLS` and `_CLASSES` variants. DHCPv6 pool exhaustion,
   happening continuously on the live box. `dhcp.go:35` registers `kea-dhcp6` but no branch matches
   these.

3. **`kernel` netmap ring overflow** — `[#] #.# [#] netmap_transmit ixl0 full hwcur # hwtail # qlen #`
   in 53 windows. This is the Zenarmor netmap ring overflowing, i.e. **dropped packets in the
   inspection path** — a real loss signal currently invisible. Also `<#>[#] ixl#: link state changed
   to DOWN` (7 windows) and `ixl0: Link is up, 10 Gbps Full Duplex ...`.

4. **`unbound` dnsbl** — 3 shapes, 1524 entries: `info: dnsbl_module: updating blocklist.`,
   `info: dnsbl_module: blocklist loaded. length is #`, `blocklist parsing done in #.# seconds
   (# records)`. Two cheap gauges (blocklist size, parse duration) and it clears 83% of unbound's
   unparsed volume.

5. **`devd`** — `Processing event '!system=IFNET subsystem=ixl0 type=LINK_DOWN'`,
   `... type=ADDR_ADD address=#.#.#.#`. Interface state stream. Overlaps with the kernel link
   events in (3); pick one source rather than double-counting.

### Deliberately out of scope — noise, better handled by `--logs.syslog.filter` guidance in docs

`DhcpLFC` (1127 entries, 7 shapes, lease-file housekeeping), `syslog-ng` reconnect chatter (891),
`/usr/sbin/cron` MAIL (714), `ntpd` startup banner (the copyright block is 8 of its 32 shapes),
`acme.sh` (35), `rule-updater.py` (128), `configd.py` (486), `opnsense`/AcmeClient (369).

## Scope

- [ ] `ppp` parser (`internal/logship/syslog/ppp.go`) — link/bundle/LCP/IPCP state, derived flap counter
- [ ] `kea-dhcp6` ALLOC_FAIL branches in the existing DHCP parser, derived allocation-failure counter
- [ ] `kernel` netmap-drop + link-state shapes, derived counters
- [ ] `unbound` dnsbl shapes, blocklist size + parse duration
- [ ] Derived-metric coverage: dashboard panels (`make dashboard` gate), `make docs`, full gate green

Each parser gets table-driven tests built from the **captured** lines above — per the standing rule
from #249–#257, formats asserted from memory have been wrong on the real box before.

## Acceptance

- Each listed program's dominant shapes produce structured attributes, not a raw body.
- A re-run of the unparsed capture on the live box no longer shows these shapes.
- Derived counters exist for: PPPoE link transitions, DHCPv6 allocation failures, netmap drops.

comments.body:
## Correction: the candidate list in the body is partly stale

It was derived from the whole 24 Jul – 1 Aug capture window, which mixes already-fixed and
transient conditions into the current picture. Re-derived from entries **since 2026-07-31** only:

| program | entries | shapes | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unbound` | 445 | 24 | steady — but see below |
| `firewall` | 441 | 13 | **new #1, was not on the list at all** |
| `DhcpLFC` | 280 | 7 | noise |
| `syslog-ng` | 222 | 9 | noise |
| `kea-dhcp6` | 218 | 55 | now LEASE_ADVERT + LFC housekeeping, not ALLOC_FAIL |
| `kernel` | 161 | 150 | netmap gone — see below |
| `ppp` | **0** | 0 | quiet since the 27 Jul flap; still unparsed |

**Dropped — `kernel` netmap is already handled.** `b04cd2c3` (2026-07-30) shipped the
`netmap_transmit` grammar in `kernel.go`, and the last netmap entry in the unparsed capture is
2026-07-30T15:11. Every one of the 53 entries predates the parser. Reading them as current state
was the error.

**Dropped — `kea-dhcp6` ALLOC_FAIL was transient.** The ~1000 entries were one client repeatedly
failing to get a v6 lease; that has resolved and the shape no longer appears. Not worth a parser
on the strength of a burst that is over.

**Added — `firewall` alias resolution.** Steady 441 entries over 13 clean shapes, and genuinely
operational:

```
resolving 24 hostnames (60 addresses) for overaaisp took 0.03 seconds
fetch alias url https://allowlists.grafana.com/synthetics (bytes: 12345)
processing alias url https://allowlists.grafana.com/synthetics took 1.2s
```

A slow or failing alias URL fetch is a real firewall problem and is currently invisible.
Resolution duration, address count and fetch size are all directly derivable.

**`ppp` still stands** despite reading zero this window — that is the point. The 100 shapes came
from a single 27 Jul PPPoE flap, and a WAN flap is exactly the rare-but-important event you want
parsed *before* it happens again. Real captured formats are in the body.

**`unbound` dnsbl needs a decision, not a parser.** `unbound.go` already states that the
dnsbl/blocklist chatter deliberately falls through to a generic record, and `unbound` is pinned in
`nonDerivedPrograms`. Extracting blocklist size and parse duration as gauges is a different
proposition from structuring the chatter, but it reverses a documented choice, so it should be
decided explicitly rather than folded into this issue.

## Revised scope

- [ ] `firewall` alias-resolution parser + derived counters (duration, addresses, fetch bytes)
- [ ] `ppp` parser — link/bundle/LCP/IPCP state, derived flap counter
- [ ] ~~kernel netmap~~ — already shipped in b04cd2c3
- [ ] ~~kea-dhcp6 ALLOC_FAIL~~ — transient, no longer occurring
- [ ] `unbound` dnsbl — awaiting a decision on reversing the deliberate fall-through

capture is an 8-day archive, not a snapshot, and it will keep offering fixed problems as current
ones.
