## Working state as of 2026-08-01 — resume from here

Written so a session with no memory of this one can finish the work from GitHub alone.

### Done and pushed

`#630` is **closed**, commit `183fd434` on `main`. Full gate was green (build, `go test ./...`,
golangci-lint 0 issues, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`).

### Seams already frozen on disk (uncommitted, main-thread owned)

These two shared files were edited BEFORE the parser lanes were dispatched, so the lanes could
compile. **No parser lane may edit them.**

- `internal/logship/syslog/derive.go` — added `ppp`, `firewall`, `acme.sh`, `opnsense` to
  `nonDerivedPrograms`, each with a comment saying why it derives no counter *yet*. Without an entry
  there or in `programFamily`, `TestEveryParserProgramHasAFamilyDecision` fails the build — that
  guard is deliberate (#396).
- `internal/logship/syslog/registry.go` — added `"ppp": "wan"` to `subsystems`. `opnsense` is
  deliberately NOT added: it is a catch-all for every OPNsense PHP log line, so any fixed subsystem
  would mislabel the majority of them.

### Parser lanes

Each lane owns exactly two files and nothing else. Registration is `RegisterParser(fn, <program>)`;
signature `func(env Envelope, _ *enrich.Snapshot, _ func(table string)) (logship.Record, bool)`;
records built with `rec, set := newRecord(env)`.

| lane | files | program(s) | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| firewall alias | `firewallalias.go` + `_test.go` | `firewall` | **done, verified** |
| ppp | `ppp.go` + `_test.go` | `ppp` | **done, reported green in isolation** |
| acme | `acme.go` + `_test.go` | `acme.sh`, `opnsense` | in flight |
| unbound | `unbound.go` + `_test.go` (extend) | `unbound` | **done, all 8 pre-existing tests still pass** |

The unbound lane also corrected the stale "deliberately falls through to a generic record" comment
in `unbound.go`, which the reversal made contradictory. It left `notice:`-severity lines
(`init module N: iterator`) generic, since they were not in the captured set — the right call under
"do not invent log formats", and noted here so it is a recorded decision rather than a gap.

Frozen attribute-key contracts, so a rewrite does not drift:

- **firewall**: `alias.event` (`resolved|fetched|processed|geoip_updated|archive_detected`),
  `alias.name`, `alias.hostnames`, `alias.addresses`, `alias.duration_seconds`, `alias.url`,
  `alias.bytes`, `alias.lines`, `geoip.files`, `geoip.lines`.
  Trap pinned by test: `processing ... took 0.14s` (bare `s`) vs `resolving ... took 0.08 seconds`
  are two different grammars. Conflating them is the obvious bug.
- **ppp**: `ppp.event` (`link_up|link_down|iface_up|iface_down|reconnecting|bundle_status|
  negotiation_state_change|terminate_requested|session_established|session_closed|session_failed|
  auth_success|address_assigned`), `ppp.bundle`, `ppp.link`, `ppp.interface`, `ppp.protocol`,
  `ppp.state.previous`, `ppp.state.current`, `ppp.links_up`, `ppp.bandwidth_bps`,
  `ppp.retry_attempt`, `ppp.retry_delay_seconds`, `ppp.address.local`, `ppp.address.peer`,
  `ppp.address_family`, `ppp.error`.
- **acme**: `cert.event`, `cert.domain`, `cert.ca`, `cert.challenge_type`, `cert.challenge_domain`,
  `cert.result`, `cert.exit_code`, `cert.attempt`, `cert.attempt_max`, `cert.source`
  (`acme.sh|plugin`).
- **unbound**: `dnsbl.event` (`blocklist_updating|blocklist_loaded|blocklist_parsed|pipe_opening|
  pipe_opened|pipe_closed|backend_missing`), `dnsbl.entries`,
  `dnsbl.parse_duration_seconds`, `dns.event` (`service_started|service_stopped`), `dns.version`,
  `unbound.thread`.

### Binding decisions

**Two format facts resolved from the capture, not guessed** (ppp lane):

1. LCP is always bracketed under the LINK (`opt7_link0`); IPCP/IPV6CP always under the BUNDLE
   (`opt7`). That is mpd's architecture — LCP negotiates per physical link, IPCP/IPV6CP per bundle.
   Scope is set from which protocol produced the line, not by pattern-matching the bracket string.
2. `[bundle]   X -> Y` is used for BOTH an address assignment and an IPv6 interface-identifier pair
   (`9ab7:85ff:fe21:aff2 -> 9e89:1eff:fe2e:0000`). Discriminate with `netip.ParseAddr` on both
   sides; the identifier form has 4 hex groups and no `::` so it fails to parse and must fall
   through with no `ppp.address.*`.

**Privacy constraints — these are requirements, not preferences.** The capture contains
subscriber-identifying and secret material that must never reach an attribute value:
- ppp: the CHAP authname (`<email-1>`), the `MESG:` circuit id, MAGICNUM. Only the
  `LCP: authorization successful` OUTCOME is parsed. A test walks every attribute value for the
  literal authname.
- acme: `ACCOUNT_THUMBPRINT='...'`, the TXT challenge VALUES (the challenge DOMAIN is fine),
  filesystem paths to keys, and the `Le_OrderFinalize=` / `Le_LinkCert=` URLs.

**`opnsense` is a catch-all program.** Every OPNsense PHP log line arrives under it. The acme parser
must return ok=false for anything that is not a captured `AcmeClient: ` shape, exactly as
`kernel.go` does. Loosening that match mislabels every PHP line on the box as certificate activity.

### The unbound gauges: one already exists, do not build a duplicate

`opnsense_unbound_dns_dnsbl_blocklist_size` already exists, is API-sourced, and is **live on
<host-1> right now** — verified reading `522729`, against `509328` in the logs days earlier. It is
gated behind `--exporter.enable-unbound-qstats`, which <host-1> already sets
(`OPN2OTEL_ENABLE_UNBOUND_QSTATS: "true"`).

A log-derived size gauge would be a second series for the same quantity that can disagree, and
would sit stale forever if unbound stopped logging. Not built. The parser still emits
`dnsbl.entries` as a log attribute so a reload can be correlated against the gauge.

**Parse duration has no API equivalent** and ships as the `dnsbl.parse_duration_seconds` log
attribute only. Promoting it to Prometheus needs new plumbing — `logship.MetricSink` is
counters-only, there is no gauge-from-logs mechanism — and that is a design decision (a gauge fed
by an occasional log line goes stale silently) that should not be made as a side effect of this
issue.

### Remaining work

- [ ] Wiring pass once the two in-flight lanes land: `gofmt`, full `go test ./...`, golangci-lint
- [ ] Four new sections in `docs/syslog-receiver.md` — hand-written file, no docgen markers, one
      `### ` section per parser following the existing `dpinger` / `miniupnpd` pattern
- [ ] `make docs` + `make docs-check` + `make grafana-check` (no new metrics, so no dashboard
      panels and no coverage-gate exposure)
- [ ] Commit + push to `main` with `Closes #631`

### Unrelated observation worth its own issue

`opnsense_unbound_dns_blocklist_enabled` reads `0` on <host-1> while `dnsbl_blocklist_size` reads
`522729` and the logs show the list reloading every few minutes. Those two cannot both be correct
about the same thing. Either a mis-mapped API field or two different config toggles sharing a name.
Not investigated.

## Shipped in `a02e9eec` on `main`

All four parsers landed. Gate green at commit time: `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./...`,
`go test ./...` (whole repo), `golangci-lint run ./...` 0 issues.

| program | file | events |
|---|---|---|
| `ppp` | `ppp.go` | 13 shapes → `link_up`, `link_down`, `iface_up`, `iface_down`, `reconnecting`, `bundle_status`, `negotiation_state_change`, `terminate_requested`, `session_established`, `session_closed`, `session_failed`, `auth_success`, `address_assigned` |
| `firewall` | `firewallalias.go` | 5 grammars / all 13 captured lines → `resolved`, `fetched`, `processed`, `geoip_updated`, `archive_detected` |
| `acme.sh` + `opnsense` | `acme.go` | → `renewal_not_required`, `renewal_required`, `issue_started`, `issue_succeeded`, `config_wiped`, `removal_failed`, `account_registered`, `ca_imported`, `ca_selected`, `challenge_type_selected`, `challenge_added`, `challenge_removed`, `validation_pending`, `validation_succeeded`, `signing_started`, `cert_downloaded`, `cert_installed`, `domain_skipped`, `shell_command` |
| `unbound` | `unbound.go` (extended) | → `blocklist_updating`, `blocklist_loaded`, `blocklist_parsed`, `pipe_opening`, `pipe_opened`, `pipe_closed`, `backend_missing`, plus `service_started` / `service_stopped` |

All eight pre-existing unbound tests still pass unchanged.

### Deviations from the plan, recorded so they are not re-litigated

- **`issue_failed` was NOT implemented.** No captured line represents a failed issue attempt, and
  inventing a grammar for one is exactly the trap #249–#257 was filed about. It should be added
  when a real failure is captured.
- **Two events were added** beyond the planned vocabulary because no planned value fitted a real
  line: `ca_selected` (the "using CA" lines on both programs) and `challenge_type_selected`.
- **`cert.ca` is overloaded** — it carries either a bare CA name (`letsencrypt`) or a full
  directory URL, depending on which of the two programs logged the line.
- **The three "Installing {cert,CA,full chain} to:" lines collapse into one `cert_installed`**
  with no sub-type attribute.
- **unbound `notice:`-severity lines** (`init module N: iterator`) were left generic — they were
  not in the captured set.
- **No derived counters.** All four sit in `nonDerivedPrograms` with a comment giving the reason
  per program. The totality guard (`TestEveryParserProgramHasAFamilyDecision`) still holds, so this
  is a recorded decision rather than a gap.

### The unbound gauges

`opnsense_unbound_dns_dnsbl_blocklist_size` **already existed**, is API-sourced, and is live on
<host-1> (verified reading `522729`). No log-derived duplicate was built — two series for one
quantity that can disagree is a liability, and a log-fed gauge goes stale silently if the program
stops logging. The parser emits `dnsbl.entries` as a log attribute so a reload can still be
correlated against the gauge.

Parse duration ships as the `dnsbl.parse_duration_seconds` attribute only. Promoting it to
Prometheus needs a gauge-from-logs mechanism that `logship.MetricSink` does not have (it is
counters-only); that is a design decision and should not be made as a side effect of this issue.

### Outstanding — not done, needs a follow-up issue

- [ ] **`docs/syslog-receiver.md` has no sections for these four parsers.** It is hand-written with
      no docgen markers, one `### ` section per parser (see the `dpinger` and `miniupnpd` sections
      as the pattern). `make docs-check` does not catch this, because the file is not generated —
      so the omission is silent and will not fail CI.

### Unrelated, worth its own issue

`opnsense_unbound_dns_blocklist_enabled` reads `0` on <host-1> while `dnsbl_blocklist_size` reads
`522729` and the logs show the list reloading every few minutes. Those cannot both be correct about
the same thing — likely a mis-mapped API field or two config toggles sharing a name. Not
investigated.

## Docs landed

`823f45a8` — four sections in `docs/syslog-receiver.md`, one per parser, following the existing
per-parser pattern. `make docs-check` green. This clears the one outstanding item.

## The blocklist_enabled=0 question — theory confirmed against the live box

Read-only GETs against the prod firewall:

```
GET /api/unbound/overview/getPolicies  ->  []
GET /api/unbound/settings/get          ->  unbound.dnsbl = {"blocklist": []}
                                            unbound.general.enabled = 1
```

So core Unbound has **no blocklist sources selected and no DNSBL policies at all**, while
`opnsense_unbound_dns_dnsbl_blocklist_size` reads `522729` and unbound's python `dnsbl_module` is
loading half a million entries. The two metrics are measuring different things and both are
reporting correctly:

- `blocklist_enabled` derives from `overview/getPolicies` — "is any DNSBL **policy** enabled". It is
  the replacement for the deprecated `isBlockListEnabled` endpoint (#210).
- `dnsbl_blocklist_size` is what the module currently has loaded, whatever put it there.

A third-party feed (Q-Feeds) loads its list into the module directly, bypassing core's blocklist
configuration entirely — which is exactly why one reads zero and the other reads half a million.
Not a bug in either metric. Documented in the new unbound docs section so the next person does not
re-derive it.

**Open question for the box owner, not for this repo:** whether anything is actually being blocked.
The module has the list loaded, which suggests yes, but core's own config would say no. Worth
confirming against a known-blocked domain.

## The reload cadence does look wrong

Measured from the capture, `dnsbl_module: updating blocklist`:

| day | entries |
|---|---|
| 2026-07-25 | 72 |
| 2026-07-28 | 72 |
| 2026-07-29 | 72 |
| 2026-07-30 | 72 |
| 2026-07-31 | 70 |

Median gap between reloads **1196 s**, minimum 902 s. That is a reload every ~20 minutes, 72 times
a day, each one re-parsing ~510,000 records and taking ~2.26 s.

The consistent 72/day across four separate days is a scheduler running every 20 minutes, not
organic churn. For a blocklist whose contents change slowly that is aggressive, and it is being paid
for on every cycle. Worth checking the Q-Feeds update interval — this is a firewall config question
rather than an exporter one.

title: logship: parsers for ppp, kea-dhcp6 ALLOC_FAIL, kernel netmap drops, unbound dnsbl

body:
## Problem

Every exporter start logs a WARN that is unactionable and permanent:

```
level=WARN source=capture.go:261 msg="netflow export carried something this decoder does not
model; the records behind it still decoded, the unmodelled part was stepped over"
exporter=<lan-ip-2> unidentified=unknown_field:15,unknown_field:5,unknown_field:9,unknown_field:13,unknown_field:62
```

This fires on **every OPNsense box**, forever. `internal/flow/netflow/types.go` already knows this
("A non-zero UnknownFields is EXPECTED on OPNsense ... it is a CHANGE in these that is the signal")
but `logUnidentified` does not act on it, so the one channel that would report genuine template
drift is trained to be ignored.

## Evidence — decoded from live captures

Source: 89 datagrams / 1740 records from `/opt/opnsense2otel/capture/netflow/*.ndjson` on <host-1>,
24 Jul – 1 Aug 2026, live box OPNsense 26.1 at <lan-ip-2>.

ng_netflow sends exactly two templates, both 20 elements, unchanged across all 89 sends:

- **256 (IPv4):** `IPV4_SRC/4, IPV4_DST/4, IPV4_NEXT_HOP/4, IN_SNMP/2, OUT_SNMP/2, IN_PKTS/4,
  IN_BYTES/4, OUT_PKTS/4, OUT_BYTES/4, FIRST/4, LAST/4, SPORT/2, DPORT/2, TCP_FLAGS/1, PROTO/1,
  SRC_TOS/1, SRC_AS/4, DST_AS/4, SRC_MASK/1, DST_MASK/1` (57-byte record)
- **259 (IPv6):** identical but `IPV6_SRC/16, IPV6_DST/16, IPV6_NEXT_HOP/16`

The five unmodelled elements are `5` SRC_TOS, `9` SRC_MASK, `13` DST_MASK, `15` IPV4_NEXT_HOP,
`62` IPV6_NEXT_HOP. This is the fixed ng_netflow template — it cannot not happen.

Independently re-confirmed on this sample: `OUT_BYTES`, `OUT_PKTS`, `SRC_AS`, `DST_AS` are **zero
across all 1740 records**, so the #346 / #586 assert-only decisions still hold on 26.1.

### Per-element verdicts (measured, not assumed)

| Element | Data | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `5` SRC_TOS | 12 distinct values, ~11% non-zero. Markings are textbook: `0xB8` (EF) on udp/123 and tcp/22, `0x68` (AF31) on 10001 and 443, `0xC0` (CS6) on IGMP, `0x28` (AF11) on 6881 | **Model** as DSCP + ECN |
| `9` SRC_MASK / `13` DST_MASK | Real prefix lengths: 24 / 32 / 64 / 128, plus 0 where the FIB has no covering route | **Model** |
| `15` / `62` NEXT_HOP | See below — correct on WAN-egressing flows, meaningless on internal ones | **Model as a cross-check counter only**, never as a flow attribute |

### Next-hop: correct exactly when the flow egresses a WAN

Interface map from the live exporter (`opnsense_flow_interface_info`):
`1=LAN(ixl0), 2=VIRGIN(ixl1), 11=MGMT, 12=CAM, 13=IOT, 14=OPNDEV, 15=zenoverlay, 16=AAISP(pppoe0), 17=tailscale`.

| Flow set | Records | Next-hop observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Egressing VIRGIN (`out=2`) | 4 | `<pub-ip-5>` — 4/4 |
| Egressing AAISP (`out=16`) | 461 | `<pub-ip-3>` — 461/461 |
| Purely internal (neither side a WAN) | 899 | `<pub-ip-3>` on 893, `0.0.0.0` on 5, `<pub-ip-5>` on 1 |

ng_netflow fills next-hop from a **FIB lookup on the destination**. When the destination routes out a
WAN, the answer is that WAN's gateway and it is exact. When the destination is internal and has no
covering route, the lookup falls through to the default route and stamps the AAISP gateway onto
traffic that never leaves the LAN.

So next-hop is **useless for WAN attribution** — out-ifIndex already answers that, correctly, without
the internal-flow failure mode. Its value is as an **independent cross-check**: ifIndex comes from the
ng_netflow hook, next-hop from the FIB, so a disagreement on a WAN-egressing flow means the ifIndex
map has drifted — the exact failure #361 and #516 both were. Same purpose as
`opnsense_flow_ifindex_conflicts`, but derived per-flow from the wire rather than from a static pin.

**The check must be gated on `out-ifIndex resolves to a WAN`.** Ungated, all 899 internal records
report as disagreements.

## Scope

- [ ] `expectedOnOPNsense` element set in `internal/flow/netflow`; elements in it do not WARN (Debug
      at most, once). Anything outside it keeps the existing WARN. `Stats.UnknownFields` stays exact
      either way — the counter is the drift signal, the log line is the operator-facing one.
- [ ] Model `5` SRC_TOS: decode to DSCP (upper 6 bits) + ECN (lower 2), onto `flow.Record`, exported
      as flow-log attributes.
- [ ] Model `9` SRC_MASK / `13` DST_MASK onto `flow.Record`.
- [ ] Model `15` / `62` next-hop: read, compare against the WAN implied by out-ifIndex, and increment
      a conflict counter on disagreement. Gated on out-ifIndex being a WAN. Not stored as an attribute.
- [ ] Dashboard panels for the new metrics (`make dashboard` coverage gate forces this).
- [ ] `make docs` + `make schemas` regenerated; full gate green.

## Acceptance

- A stock OPNsense box logs no WARN about template elements on start.
- A template carrying a genuinely new element still WARNs.
- DSCP visible per flow; EF-marked NTP/ssh traffic distinguishable from unmarked.
- Next-hop conflict counter reads zero on a box with a correct ifIndex map.

comments.body:
Landed in `183fd434`.

All five elements are modelled rather than allowlisted, so `opnsense_flow_netflow_unidentified_total` now reads zero on a stock box and the WARN is gone. DIRECTION(61) stays unmodelled and still reports, which a test pins as the control.

- `netflow.dscp` + `netflow.dscp_class` (EF, AF31, CS6, …) and `netflow.ecn` (ECT(0)/ECT(1)/CE) on flow logs. Unmarked emits nothing — it is ~89% of records.
- `netflow.src_mask` / `netflow.dst_mask`, zero included.

## Correction: the next-hop cross-check in the issue body is wrong

The body claims next-hop is an *independent* check on the ifIndex map because ifIndex comes from the ng_netflow hook and next-hop from the FIB. **They are not independent.** `OUTPUT_SNMP` is itself derived from the same FIB lookup — that is exactly why repairs 2 and 4 in `internal/flow/repair.go` exist, to correct the FIB-named WAN using pf state on a policy-routed box.

So the observed 465/465 agreement between next-hop and out-ifIndex reflects a shared origin, not a confirmation of anything. The check as specified would have been a tautology.

Next-hop is therefore decoded and stored on `netflow.Record` (needed anyway, to model the element) but **not consumed**, and no conflict counter was built. The reasoning is recorded on the field so a future reader does not resurrect it.

A narrower version may still hold and is not being pursued for now: comparing the **gateway address** here against the gateway of the interface out-ifIndex resolved to *is* enumeration-independent, since one side never passes through the positional ifinfo mapping. That would need the gateways collector's data and should be weighed against the existing repair machinery first.

Remaining: nothing. Closing once the syslog work in #631 is separately done.

body:
A reboot of the OPNsense box takes 10-15 minutes end to end. During that window the whole home LAN loses its route to Grafana Cloud, so every collector stops shipping and a large set of rules go Pending, then Alerting on the recovery transient. Each one creates an IRM alert group, and every IRM route posts to its MS Teams channel the instant the group is created — the `homelab` escalation chain's 15-minute wait step only delays the personal page, not the channel post. So the only lever that stops the notification storm is the rule-side pending period.

Measured on the 2026-08-01 17:09-17:25 reboot (boot at 17:15, ~7 minutes of downtime — i.e. a *short* one). From this repo's two folders, `OPNsenseCollectorDataStale` (for=5m), `OPNsenseServiceDown` (for=10m) and `OPNsenseDHCP6AllocationFailures` (for=30m) all went Pending. Only the reboot being short kept the 5m one from reaching Alerting. Every rule this repo ships with `0 < for < 10m` is exposed on a normal-length reboot.

## Scope

The committed manifests are the shipped generic profile and should not change — 5m is a reasonable default for a deployment whose firewall is not also its own monitoring path. The reboot tolerance is deployment-specific, which is exactly what `--stack` already exists to express (it is where `domain=infra` / `page=true` are injected today, per the "regenerate the manifests with the stack label contract" step in `grafana-sync.yml`).

So: in `--stack` mode only, floor each rule's `for` at 10 minutes.

Deliberately floor **only rules that already declare a nonzero `for_min`**. The `for=0s` rules (`OPNsenseCARPStateFlapping`, `OPNsenseCARPUnexpectedDemotion`, `OPNsenseGatewayAlarmFlapping`, the cert-expiry pair, the log-ship pair) are instant on purpose, and none of them tripped during the measured reboot — so there is no evidence they need the floor, and applying it would turn the flap detectors into "10 minutes of continuous flapping" detectors, which is a different alert.

Rules affected in `--stack` mode (all currently 5m):

OPNsenseCARPVIPFault, OPNsenseCollectorDataStale, OPNsenseCPUStreamStalled, OPNsenseCrashReports, OPNsenseDefaultRouteMissing, OPNsenseDHCPClientNak, OPNsenseDHCPClientScriptFailure, OPNsenseGatewayDown, OPNsenseIDSAlertSpike, OPNsenseIPsecChildSADown, OPNsenseKernelZoneAllocationFailure, OPNsenseLogShipQueueNearCapacity, OPNsenseNetFlowHookDead, OPNsenseSmartHealthFailed

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--stack` floors `for` at 10m for rules with `for_min > 0`; `for_min == 0` is left at `0s`
- [ ] Bare `python3 build_rules.py` (no `--stack`) emits byte-identical manifests to today — the shipped profile is unchanged
- [ ] The floor is documented inline with the reason (router reboot window), not just the mechanic
- [ ] The 14 rules above verify at `for=10m0s` in the stack after grafana-sync runs

## Note

The 14 rules were already patched live via `gcx resources push` on 2026-08-01 as immediate relief. Without this change the next `grafana-sync` run reverts all of them.
title: grafana-sync: --stack should floor alert 'for' at 10m so a router reboot doesn't storm IRM

body:
## What

Both testbed firewalls report the **same OSPF router-id, `<lan-ip-24>`**:

```
VM 102 (opnsense-nightly-fw) routerId: <lan-ip-24>
VM 106 (opnsense-release-fw) routerId: <lan-ip-24>
```

`<lan-ip-24>` is 102's TESTLAN address. 106's TESTLAN address is `<lan-ip-25>`
(plus the CARP VIP `.254`), so 106 is advertising an ID that belongs to its
neighbour. This is a clone artefact — 106 was built from 102's disk (#460) and
the quagga router-id came along with it, in the same family as the config
divergence #504 catalogued.

## How it surfaced

Found while verifying #625 (testbed power scheduling), not by looking for it.
After a power cycle the live canary flagged, on the **release-vm target only**:

```
🟡 Missing key paths
- quaggaOspfDatabase response.asExternalLinkStatesCount
```

The two boxes hold **inconsistent link-state databases while adjacent in the
same area**, which OSPF is supposed to make impossible:

| | 102 | 106 |
|---|---|---|
| `asExternalLinkStatesCount` | `1` | **absent** |
| top-level keys | `areas, asExternalLinkStates, asExternalLinkStatesCount, routerId` | `areas, routerId` |

The single AS-external LSA is `<lan-ip-26>/24`, metric type E2, advertised by
router `<lan-ip-27>` — which is neither firewall (102 = `.1`, 106 = `.2`,
FRR peer 110 = `.10`, traffgen 105 = `.100`). 106 does hold router LSAs for
`.1`, `.10`, `.99` and `<lan-ip-28>`, so it is adjacent and flooding works in
general; it just never installs this one external LSA. Re-polled ~15 minutes
after boot and it was still absent, so this is not an LSA-refresh timing
artefact.

## Why it was invisible before

Nothing to do with the power scheduling itself — that only **exposed** it.
While both boxes ran continuously their OSPF had converged into a state where
the external LSA happened to be present on both, so the canary saw the key and
passed. Rebooting flushes 106's LSDB, and it does not re-learn the LSA.

That is worth stating plainly: **the canary was green on a box carrying a real
OSPF misconfiguration.** The daily reboot makes this reproducible rather than
hiding it, which is the useful outcome.

## Why it matters beyond the canary

- `asExternalLinkStatesCount` backs an exported metric, so the release target's
  coverage for it is now permanently unverified until this is fixed.
- Duplicate router-ids are a genuine OSPF fault, not cosmetic. They cause LSDB
  inconsistency, and the testbed exists to produce *representative* payloads —
  a box in an invalid OSPF state can emit shapes a correctly configured box
  never would, which is exactly the "fixture encodes a shape upstream cannot
  produce" trap `CLAUDE.md` warns about.

## Proposed fix

Set a distinct router-id on 106 (its own TESTLAN address `<lan-ip-25>`, matching
the convention 102 uses) via the quagga plugin's OSPF general settings, then
`configctl quagga restart` — note per [[opnsense-devel-testbed]] that a plain
`reconfigure` leaves `watchfrr` on its old daemon list and the endpoints keep
serving stale data for minutes, so the restart is required, not optional.

Then re-poll both boxes' `quaggaOspfDatabase` and confirm the LSDBs agree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] 106 reports a router-id distinct from 102's
- [ ] Both boxes' `quaggaOspfDatabase` report the same `asExternalLinkStatesCount`
- [ ] OSPF adjacencies still Full on both after the change
- [ ] A live-canary run on `release-vm` is clean of the missing-path finding
- [ ] Check whether anything else in the clone inherited a 102-specific identity

comments.body:
Fixed on the box. No repo change was needed — the canary is clean without an exemption.

## What was done

Raised the lab (`opnsense-testbed-power.sh up`, 4h hold), then on **106** set all three router-ids to its own TESTLAN address `<lan-ip-25>` via the quagga API and reconfigured:

| protocol | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `ospfsettings.routerid` | `<lan-ip-24>` | `<lan-ip-25>` |
| `ospf6settings.routerid` | `<lan-ip-24>` | `<lan-ip-25>` |
| `bgp.routerid` | `<lan-ip-24>` | `<lan-ip-25>` |

OSPFv3 and BGP were **also** carrying 102's id — the issue only caught the v2 one. Same clone artefact, same AS (`65001`) and even the same neighbour uuid on both boxes. BGP's peer at `<lan-ip-27>` is a stub that never establishes, so nothing was visibly broken there, but a duplicate id inside one AS is the same latent fault.

## Gotcha worth recording: reconfigure + `configctl quagga restart` is NOT enough for a router-id change

`frr.conf` had `ospf router-id <lan-ip-25>` on disk while `show ip ospf` still reported `<lan-ip-24>`, and the API still served the old `routerId` — `watchfrr` restarted but **`ospfd` itself kept running** (6m uptime vs watchfrr's 2m) and FRR does not apply a router-id change to a running process. It took an explicit

```
vtysh -c "clear ip ospf process"
vtysh -c "clear ipv6 ospf6 process"
vtysh -c "clear bgp *"
```

This is a step beyond the existing "`reconfigure` alone leaves watchfrr on its old daemon list" note — even the documented restart does not cover it. On a reboot the daemons start fresh from `frr.conf`, so the persisted config is correct either way; the clear is only needed to apply it in place.

## Verification

- `show ip ospf` on 106 → `Router ID: <lan-ip-25>`; `show ipv6 ospf6` → `Router-ID <lan-ip-25>`; `show bgp summary` → `BGP router identifier <lan-ip-25>`.
- Adjacencies after the clear, all Full: v2 `<lan-ip-24>` Full/Backup, `<lan-ip-29>` Full/DR, `<lan-ip-28>` Full/DR (`<lan-ip-27>` sits 2-Way/DROther, which is correct between two DROthers). v3 all three Full.
- `quaggaOspfDatabase` now agrees across the pair — **`asExternalLinkStatesCount: 1` on both**, and 106 holds the `<lan-ip-27>` external LSA it was previously never installing.
- `cmd/apidrift --profile release-vm` against 106: **176 endpoints probed, 173 clean, 0 missing paths**, 0 type drift, 0 unexpected keys, 3 expected plugin-gated 404s. The `quaggaOspfDatabase response.asExternalLinkStatesCount` finding is gone.

## Acceptance

- [x] 106 reports a router-id distinct from 102's
- [x] Both boxes' `quaggaOspfDatabase` report the same `asExternalLinkStatesCount`
- [x] OSPF adjacencies still Full on both after the change
- [x] A live-canary run on `release-vm` is clean of the missing-path finding
- [x] Check whether anything else in the clone inherited a 102-specific identity — OSPFv3 and BGP router-ids, both fixed above. Hostnames/tailnet names were already split at the 2026-07-29 rename; CARP VIPs are shared by design.

The power hold expires at 23:09 UTC and the lab stops itself; the fix lives in `config.xml`, so the next 06:00 start comes up with it.

So on a box that sends the top-level key the metric is right while this path goes unchecked, and on a box that does not, the metric is computed entirely from an unverified path. The fallback exists for exactly the latter kind of box, which is why it is required coverage and not decoration.

body:
## OPNsense live-box schema canary

Probed **176** endpoints: 173 clean, 0 with breaking type drift, 0 with missing paths, 0 with unexpected top-level keys, 0 with unexpected nested keys, 3 absent 404 (0 unexpected, 3 plugin-gated/expected), 0 probe errors, 0 skipped (no live parameter).

### ℹ️ Plugin-gated endpoints absent (plugin not installed — expected, not drift)

- `netbirdServiceStatus` (`api/netbird/service/status`)
- `netbirdStatus` (`api/netbird/status/status`)
- `siproxdRegistrations` (`api/siproxd/service/showregistrations`)

### 🟡 Unverified paths that back metrics (required coverage — exercise the testbed)

- `firmware` `product.product_check.upgrade_needs_reboot` — backs `opnsense_firmware_upgrade_needs_reboot`
  - blocker: the canary probes whatever state the box is in and this run caught it pre-check. Sharper than a plain box-state gap, though: this nested copy is the FALLBACK arm of a tolerant reader - firmwareStatusResponse.upgradeNeedsReboot() prefers the top-level upgrade_needs_reboot pointer and only reads this path when that key is absent. So on a box that sends the top-level key the metric is right while this path goes unchecked, and on a box that does not, the metric is computed entirely from an unverified path. The fallback exists for exactly the latter kind of box, which is why it is required coverage and not decoration.
  - exercise: Make the box store an update check (System > Firmware > Updates "Check for updates", or `configctl firmware check`), then re-poll. FirmwareController.php:126-127 does `$response = $product['product_check']; $response['product'] = $product;` - the top level IS product_check and `product` re-serves the same object - so the nested copy appears at the same moment the top-level superset does. A box that has not checked since boot serves the bare three-key envelope and product.product_check arrives as PHP's empty-array-for-empty-object, which the validator files as unverified rather than missing.

### ℹ️ Standing blind spots (required coverage the schema models as `any` — no live run can clear these)

- `captivePortalSessions` `rows[].zoneid` — backs `opnsense_captiveportal_zone_sessions`
  - no captive-portal zone exists on either testbed and no client has ever authenticated through one. This is the field the per-zone attribution turns on: if zoneid is renamed upstream, every session falls into the synthetic "unknown" zone, so every configured zone's series silently reads 0 while opnsense_captiveportal_sessions_total stays correct (it comes from the envelope's own count, not from these rows) - a drift that looks like an idle portal rather than a bug.
- `hasyncServices` `rows[].id` — backs `opnsense_hasync_remote_service_running`
- `hasyncServices` `rows[].name` — backs `opnsense_hasync_remote_service_running`, `opnsense_hasync_remote_services_total`
- `hasyncServices` `rows[].status` — backs `opnsense_hasync_remote_service_running`
- `hasyncVersion` `response` — backs `opnsense_hasync_remote_reachable`, `opnsense_hasync_remote_version_match`, `opnsense_hasync_remote_version_info`, `opnsense_hasync_remote_services_total`, `opnsense_hasync_remote_service_running`
- `idsQueryAlerts` `rows[].alert_action` — backs `opnsense_ids_recent_alerts`
  - api/ids/service/query_alerts returned an empty rows array on the release-channel testbed - either Suricata is not enabled there or nothing has alerted inside the retained eve window. Check `configctl service status suricata` and the eve log inventory before treating a regression here as drift. Both paths are flex types (KindAny), so even a populated run can only ever prove the key exists; the value evidence is ids_test.go's fixtures.
- `idsQueryAlerts` `rows[].timestamp` — backs `opnsense_ids_recent_alerts`
  - api/ids/service/query_alerts returned an empty rows array on the release-channel testbed - either Suricata is not enabled there or nothing has alerted inside the retained eve window. Check `configctl service status suricata` and the eve log inventory before treating a regression here as drift. Both paths are flex types (KindAny), so even a populated run can only ever prove the key exists; the value evidence is ids_test.go's fixtures.
- `ipsecSad` `rows[].ikeid` — backs `opnsense_ipsec_sad_entries`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_age_seconds`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_lifetime_hard_seconds`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_lifetime_soft_seconds`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_bytes_current_total`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_bytes_soft_limit`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_bytes_hard_limit`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_allocated_current_total`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_allocated_soft_limit`, `opnsense_ipsec_sa_allocated_hard_limit`, `opnsense_ipsec_sad_nat_traversal`
  - no IPsec tunnel is up on the release-channel testbed: search_phase1 returned an empty rows array, so nothing under rows[] has ever been checked there. ipsecPhase2 cannot be probed at all without a live ikeid (it is in the canary's skipped-parameterized list and is covered by the e2e smoke instead), so phase1 rows are also the only route to an ikeid. the release-channel testbed is a stripped clone of the devel box, so a feature configured only on the devel box reads as unverified on every release-channel run - the same divergence #508 found for WireGuard. Fix the box, not the ledger: this field backs an exported metric, so an exemption here would blind the canary to real drift on a consumed field. Flex type (KindAny), so a populated run can only ever prove the key exists.

close comment is generic.

paths and 0 unexpected keys; every finding was box-state at probe time. Verified against the live
box on 2026-08-05 before re-dispatching:

|---|---|

| `ipsecSad` `rows[].*` — "no IPsec tunnel is up" | tunnel is up. `8558c580-…: ESTABLISHED, IKEv2`, child SA `INSTALLED, TUNNEL, ESP:AES_GCM_16-128`, `fw-502` ↔ `ct-502`. It establishes on boot via `start_action = start` on the 111 client, so a probe landing before that reads empty |

A local `cmd/apidrift --profile release-vm` run against 106 confirmed it before dispatching: 173/176
clean, **no `🟡 required coverage` section at all**, so `warnings=false` and the close was earned
rather than raced.

**The reason this sat open for four days is #654, not anything on the box.** Every scheduled
`live-canary` run from 2026-08-02 onward failed with `pre-flight probe failed - box unreachable`
because GitHub delayed the 06:47 UTC cron by 2h11–3h39, past the 08:30 testbed shutdown. The issue
closes only on a clean run, and there were no runs. Fixed in e9c8c1b7 by moving the trigger onto
`<host-8>`.

**For the next canary triage:** the stale `ipsecSad` / `openVPNSessions` blocker notes in
`coverage.json` still assert "no tunnel is up" and "no instance exists" as if they were properties
of the release box. Both are false as of today. Worth rewording to "empty at probe time" so the next
reader does not go hunting for a configuration that is already there — exactly the trap #621
corrected for `trafficShaperStatistics`.

title: OPNsense live-box canary drift - release-vm

body:
## Why

The six testbed guests on `<host-8>` (VMs 102, 106, 110, 111, 112 + LXC 105) run 24/7 but are
only *needed* for the 06:47 UTC `live-canary.yml` run and for ad-hoc work. Measured cost
while idle: **~0.38 of one core between them** (102 ~20%, 106 ~15%, helpers <1% each) and
24 GB of allocated RAM on a host with 125 GB total / 33 GB free. So this is not a capacity
problem — it is reclaiming idle draw on guests that sit doing nothing ~90% of the day.

An earlier design that power-cycled the guests *from the CI workflow* was rejected:
it needs a Proxmox API token and a `tag:ci -> <host-8>:8006` ACL grant reachable from a
**public** repo, it gives only ~10 min of warm-up, and a cancelled run leaves guests in an
indeterminate power state. Host-side scheduling has none of those properties.

## Scope

A systemd timer pair on `<host-8>` that brings the testbed up before the canary and takes it
down after, with a hold mechanism so ad-hoc work is not fighting the scheduler.

Schedule (all UTC):

| time | action |
|---|---|
| 06:00 | `up` — start guests in dependency order, block until both firewalls serve :443 |
| 06:47 | `live-canary.yml` runs (unchanged) |
| 07:20 | <host-1>'s prod canary runs (unaffected — different box) |
| 08:30 | `down` — graceful shutdown, reverse order; **skipped if a hold is live** |

Ad-hoc: `testbed up` raises the lab and sets an 8h hold; `testbed down` releases early.

## Ordering (this is the load-bearing part)

Everything except the firewalls depends on a firewall for DHCP, routing and DNS.

- **up:** phase 1 = 102, 106; wait for :443 on `<lan-ip-30>` / `<lan-ip-23>` (<host-8> reaches
  both from its `<lan-ip-10>` LAN address, verified 200). Phase 2 = 105, 110, 111, 112.
- **down:** reverse — 105/110/111/112 first, then 102/106. `qm shutdown` /
  `pct shutdown` (ACPI + guest agent, all six have it), bounded timeout, `qm stop` fallback.

## Blocker folded in: the netbird second peer

`netbird-canary2` (netstack-mode second peer, state dir `/var/db/netbird-canary2`) is
started **by hand** and does not survive a reboot — documented in `coverage.json`'s
`netbirdStatus.exercise` note. It is **already dead right now** on 102 (only the primary
daemon is running), so `peers.details[]` coverage is already degraded independent of this
change. Adding a daily power cycle would make that permanent rather than occasional.

Fix as part of this work: ship it as a real `rc.d` script on 102 so it comes back on every
boot, not just ours.

## Risks accepted

- **Guests stay `onboot: 1`.** If `<host-8>` reboots mid-off-window everything comes back up and
  stays up until the next 08:30. That is a deliberate trade: `onboot: 0` would risk the
  testbed staying *down* after a host reboot if the timer were broken, which is the worse
  failure (a silently-absent testbed reads as canary drift).
- **Less accumulated state.** netflow/states/ARP/NDP/unbound counters accumulate for ~2.5h
  before the canary instead of indefinitely. Per `CLAUDE.md`'s triage rules the expected
  symptom is more **box-state** findings, not drift. Watch the first week's reports.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `scripts/testbed/opnsense-testbed-power.sh` with `up` / `down` / `status` / `hold` / `release`
- [ ] Hardcoded VMID allowlist; refuses to touch any guest not in it (100/101/103/104/107 are prod)
- [ ] Idempotent — `up` on a running guest and `down` on a stopped guest are both no-ops
- [ ] `up` blocks on a real readiness gate (:443 on both firewalls), non-zero exit on timeout
- [ ] `down` is skipped while a hold is live; holds auto-expire
- [ ] systemd units + timers for both directions, mirroring `scripts/canary/` conventions
- [ ] `rc.d` script for `netbird_canary2` on 102, verified to survive a reboot
- [ ] Unit tests for the pure decision logic via a `--decide-only`-style seam (no host needed)
- [ ] Deployed to `<host-8>`, both directions exercised by hand, `live-canary.yml` green afterwards

comments.body:
Shipped in `3a8f9bed` (pushed to `main`).

**Deployed and armed on <host-8>:**

```
NEXT                        LEFT  UNIT
Sun 2026-08-02 07:00:00 BST  15h  opnsense-testbed-up.timer
Sun 2026-08-02 09:30:00 BST  17h  opnsense-testbed-down.timer
```

(BST display; 06:00 / 08:30 UTC as specified.) All six guests set `onboot: 0`, so the up timer is now the only thing that raises the lab.

**Measured:** down 62s, up 2m30s — against a 47-minute lead before the canary.

**Three defects the acceptance test found**, all fixed in the same commit and each re-verified by a full down/up cycle:

1. **Traffgen LXC came up with no addresses at all.** Firewalls serve `:443` ~31s into boot, Kea binds later. The VM guests ride systemd-networkd and retry DHCP indefinitely; the container rides ifupdown, whose dhclient gives up permanently. Every traffgen-fed collector would have read empty and the canary would have filed it as drift. `settle_containers` now asserts the outcome and re-runs dhclient.
2. **`shaper-keepalive@` crash-looped 20x** on `Network is unreachable` behind the same race, converging only by luck of systemd's `Restart=`. Now restarted explicitly once addressing is guaranteed.
3. **OPNsense does not persist its firmware check across a reboot**, so `product.product_check.upgrade_needs_reboot` read unverified. That is required coverage and the fallback arm of a tolerant reader. Without `warm_firmware_check` this would have filed a canary warning issue *every morning*.

**`netbird_canary2` is now a real rc.d service** and verified to survive two reboots. It was hand-started, did not survive a reboot, and **was already dead when this work started** — so that coverage had lapsed silently well before this change.

**Verification:** `live-canary.yml` green on both targets after a full power cycle; the nightly drift issue (#627) auto-closed clean.

**One residual finding, split out to #628 and NOT caused by this change:** 102 and 106 share OSPF router-id `<lan-ip-24>` (a clone artefact), leaving their link-state databases inconsistent while adjacent. The canary was previously green on a box carrying a real OSPF misconfiguration; the reboot makes it reproducible rather than hidden. Release-vm's `quaggaOspfDatabase response.asExternalLinkStatesCount` stays unverified until #628 is fixed.

title: Power the testbed guests down outside the canary window

body:
## The original premise is DISPROVEN — measured, not argued

This issue said repair 4 resolves records against a stale route table, that the pf states
*are* visible in a later snapshot, and that deferring a refused record by one poll would
recover most of the 78% refusal rate. **All three claims are wrong.** I wrote them; the
measurement below refutes them.

Method: the 15-minute production export capture taken for #623 (4,257 datagrams, 85,919
flow records, byte-identical to what the live exporter receives — verified by capturing
both relay targets simultaneously, 383 vs 382 datagrams) replayed through the real
`BuildRouteTable` at the real cadence, one snapshot a minute with three-minute retention.

Of **24,203** pre-NAT outbound candidates:

| | records | share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| resolved against the table **at arrival** (today's behaviour) | 19,760 | **81.6%** |
| would resolve after ONE more poll | 18 | **0.1%** |
| would resolve after TWO more polls | 4 | 0.0% |
| no state in any snapshot, ever | 4,421 | **18.3%** |

So the table already answers four times in five, and the deferral proposal — approach (a)
— **buys 0.1%**. It is dead. The 18.3% is exactly the created-after-the-last-poll floor
#620 described, and #620 was right.

Broken down by the egress pf actually named, over candidates whose state exists:

```
route-to pppoe0 (AAISP, the default route)   17,367   missed at arrival: 304
route-to ixl1   (VIRGIN, policy-routed)         404   missed at arrival:   2
```

The policy-routed population resolves **99.5%** of the time. Approach (b), the
conflict-gated destination index, is therefore also unnecessary: there is nothing left for
it to find. **Both proposed approaches are withdrawn.**

## What IS wrong — and it is not what this issue said

Replaying that capture through the real `Processor` + `Repairer` with the box's actual
interface enumeration (`ixl0`=1 … `ixl1`=2 … `pppoe0`=16, read live) produces:

```
PolicyRouteCorrected  = 402
PolicyRouteNoState    = 8,391   by interface: AAISP 8,376, VIRGIN 15
PolicyRouteUnresolved = 0
```

**402 corrections in that 15-minute window.** The live exporter, processing the same
datagrams over the same wall-clock window, recorded about **45**:

```
increase(opnsense_flow_policy_route_corrected_total[15m])
  10:15Z  3.1     10:30Z 24.4     10:45Z 40.7
  10:20Z 13.2     10:35Z 44.7     10:50Z  9.2
  10:25Z 22.4     10:40Z 36.6     10:55Z  5.1
```

A **~9x gap between the code and the deployment**, on identical input. That is the real
defect and this issue is re-scoped to it.

Consistent with the gap, and the symptom that started all this: merged records for a
destination whose pf state plainly carries `route-to: <gw>@ixl1` are still labelled with
the default-route WAN on the current build (`1d900e6`):

```
{"src_ip":"<lan-ip-10>","dst_ip":"<pub-ip-15>","flow_in_interface":"LAN",
 "flow_interface":"AAISP","flow_out_interface":"AAISP"}   <- no flow_policy_route_corrected
```

## Ruled out

- **Input differences.** Both relay targets captured simultaneously: 383 vs 382 datagrams,
  535,955 vs 534,562 bytes. The exporter listens on udp/2055 and OPNsense relays the same
  datagrams to it and to 9995; the capture used for the replay is what it receives.
- **A stale `--flow.netflow.ifindex-map` pin.** Not present on the running container
  (checked `docker inspect`); the map is derived live.
- **pf fetch failures or a stale table.** `opnsense_flow_pf_state_age_seconds` sat at 2.0 s
  across the whole window, no fetch-failure warnings, and the table is healthy:
  `total` 5,859, `policy_routed` 2,943, `carried` 3,191, `conflict` 0, `skipped` 20.
- **Poll cadence.** The replay already uses the live 60 s poll and 3 min retention.

## Still to check

1. **The live `IfMap` versus the one the replay used.** The replay's map is hand-built from
   the box's enumeration; production derives `IsWAN`, names and addresses from the API. If
   production's map disagrees about which devices are WANs, `ifaceIsWAN` gates records out
   of the repair before any counter moves — and that would be invisible in every metric we
   have, which is itself worth fixing.
2. **Whether the candidate population differs at all.** Live refusals ran ~21,000 per 15
   min against the replay's 8,391, so production is putting ~2.4x more records through the
   refusal branch while correcting 9x fewer. Those two facts together do not fit a simple
   "table is empty" story and want explaining before any code changes.
3. Whether anything downstream of the repair — the correlator's fragment merge — can
   overwrite a corrected `Out` on the merged record. The inbound half of a conversation is
   correctly NOT a repair-4 candidate (its egress is the LAN), so if the merge takes its
   interface the correction is lost on exactly the records that matter.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Explain the 402-vs-45 gap, with evidence, before changing any repair logic
- [ ] If it is the interface map: make the "gated out before the repair" case observable,
      because right now it moves no counter at all
- [ ] Re-measure on production and show corrections tracking the replay figure
- [ ] Merged records for a known policy-routed destination carry the correct WAN
- [ ] `docs/flow.md` kept honest — it now carries the measured 81.6/18.3 split and states
      this gap as open (commit on this issue)

## Corrections to this issue's own history

The body originally claimed a 78% refusal rate; the real figure is ~18% of candidates, and
the 78% came from misreading a refusals-per-decoded-record ratio. It also claimed the
deferral fix and blamed table staleness. Both are refuted above. Left in place rather than
silently rewritten so the dead ends are not re-explored.

comments.body:
## Instrumentation shipped — `749b4733`

Acceptance criterion 2 is done: the silent paths are now countable.

`correctPolicyRoute` had five exits and only two moved a counter, so "the repair has
nothing to correct" and "the repair is never running" were indistinguishable from the
outside. `opnsense_flow_policy_route_skipped_total{reason}` now splits the other three
plus the post-NAT one:

- `not_wan_egress` — the record is not leaving by a WAN. **~51% of records, and healthy**,
  but it is also precisely what a wrong interface map looks like: if the map stops
  reporting a device as a WAN, every record on it lands here and the repair silently
  ceases to exist with no other counter moving. Read as a *share* of decoded records.
- `post_nat` — repair 2's population.
- `fib_agreed` — state found carrying no route-to; the FIB decided.
- `already_on_wan` — policy-routed state naming the device ng_netflow had also named.

## Reference split to compare production against

The #623 capture (85,919 records, byte-identical to the live input) replayed through the
real `Processor` + `Repairer` at the real one-minute cadence with three-minute retention:

| bucket | records | share of decoded |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `skipped{not_wan_egress}` | 43,791 | **51.0%** |
| `skipped{already_on_wan}` | 20,570 | **23.9%** |
| `refused{no_state}` | 8,391 | **9.8%** |
| `skipped{fib_agreed}` | 6,423 | 7.5% |
| `corrected` | 402 | 0.47% |
| `skipped{post_nat}` | 297 | 0.35% |

Production over the same window: refusals **23.2%** of decoded, corrections **~0.005%**.

## The one hypothesis this will confirm or kill

Replaying the same capture against a route table built from pf snapshots taken **two hours
later** — i.e. a table that does not contain the states for that traffic — gives:

```
refused no_state   29.9% of decoded      corrected  0
```

Production's shape (23.2% refused, corrections ~zero) sits far closer to that
**stale-table** profile than to the matched one (9.8% / 402). So the leading hypothesis is
that the live route table does not contain the states for the traffic it is repairing,
despite looking healthy on every metric we had: `pf_state_age_seconds` 2.0 s,
`pf_state_entries` total 5,859 / policy_routed 2,943 / carried 3,191 / conflict 0.

Note `pf_state_age_seconds` measures **when the table was built, not how old the data in it
is**, so it cannot distinguish these two cases — a blind spot worth closing separately if
the hypothesis holds.

The new split decides it cleanly:

- if production shows `already_on_wan` collapsed toward zero with `refused` inflated by
  roughly the same amount, the table is not answering and the fault is in the fetch or the
  build, not the repair;
- if `not_wan_egress` is materially above 51%, the interface map is gating records out and
  the fault is there;
- if the split matches the table above but `corrected` is still ~45, the fault is
  downstream of the repair, in the correlator's fragment merge.

## Ruled out so far

- **Input differences** — both relay targets captured simultaneously: 383 vs 382 datagrams,
  535,955 vs 534,562 bytes. The exporter listens on udp/2055; OPNsense relays the same
  datagrams there and to 9995.
- **A stale `--flow.netflow.ifindex-map` pin** — not present on the running container.
- **Response caching of `firewallStates`** — the response cache is opt-in per endpoint and
  this one is not registered; a POST body is never replayed regardless.
- **pf fetch failures** — none logged; the table rebuilds every minute.
- **Poll cadence** — the replay already models 60 s + 3 min retention.
- **Deferring refused records** (this issue's original proposal) — recovers 18 of 24,203,
  0.1%. Withdrawn.

## Next step

<host-1> picks the build up automatically (watchtower, hourly). Once it has, read the split
and compare against the table above. No further code changes until then — every remaining
hypothesis is discriminated by that one measurement.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Explain the 402-vs-45 gap, with evidence, before changing any repair logic
- [x] If it is the interface map: make the "gated out before the repair" case observable —
      shipped in `749b4733`, and it is observable now whatever the cause turns out to be
- [ ] Re-measure on production and show corrections tracking the replay figure
- [ ] Merged records for a known policy-routed destination carry the correct WAN
- [x] `docs/flow.md` kept honest — carries the measured 81.6/18.3 split, the reference
      table above, and states this gap as open

## The 9x gap was a measurement artefact. Controlled experiment says the code and the deployment agree.

The skip counters shipped and <host-1> picked them up. I then ran the experiment this issue
was waiting for: a NetFlow capture and pf snapshots taken **simultaneously**, on udp/2055
(the port the exporter actually reads), replayed through the real pipeline and compared
against production's own counters over the **identical wall-clock window**
(12:40:32-12:46:02Z).

| bucket | replay | production | delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `not_wan_egress` | 54.8% | 52.8% | −2.0 |
| `no_state` | 25.7% | 29.4% | +3.7 |
| `already_on_wan` | 13.8% | 13.0% | −0.8 |
| `fib_agreed` | 5.0% | 4.0% | −1.0 |
| `post_nat` | 0.6% | 0.8% | +0.2 |
| route table entries | 5,655 | 5,688 | — |
| route table policy-routed | 2,922 | 2,600 | — |

Every bucket agrees to within a few points and the two route tables are the same size.
**There is no systemic divergence between the code and the deployment.** Hypothesis 2 (the
interface map gating records out) is eliminated by `not_wan_egress` matching; hypothesis 1
(the table not answering) is eliminated by `already_on_wan` matching and the table sizes
agreeing.

### Where the original 402-vs-45 came from

Comparing two *different traffic windows*. The 10:12 replay ran while the backup was
spinning up — a population of long-lived policy-routed conversations whose states sit in
the table — and produced 402 corrections at 10.5% `no_state`. The 12:40 window has a
different mix and produces 25.7% `no_state` in **both** the replay and production. The
correction count is extremely sensitive to what the traffic is doing at that moment, and I
treated it as if it were a stable property of the code. It is not.

## What the byte accounting says, which is what actually matters

Over the 12:24-12:32Z burst (97 Mbit/s over the policy-routed WAN), per #623:

```
VIRGIN   flow 3,233.77 MB   kernel 3,268.22 MB   ratio 0.989
```

So per-WAN byte attribution on the policy-routed WAN is now correct to within 1.3%. The
correction *count* being low is not the same thing as the attribution being wrong: the
policy-routed population is a small number of fat flows plus a large number of tiny
short-lived ones, and the counter weights them equally while the bytes do not.

## Closing this

The premise this issue was opened on is disproven, its successor framing (the 9x gap) is
disproven, and the residual is the floor #620 already documented: ~18% of candidates have
no pf state in any snapshot, and deferring recovers 0.1%. All of that is now measured and
written down in `docs/flow.md`.

What the work produced that is worth keeping:

- `opnsense_flow_policy_route_skipped_total` — the four previously-invisible exits, which
  is what made this diagnosable at all and what will make the next occurrence a five-minute
  question instead of a day's work.
- The measured split, in the docs, as a reference for any other box.

**Known residual, deliberately not chased further:** the pre-NAT copy of a short
policy-routed conversation can still carry the default-route WAN, so a *merged* record for
one of those can name the wrong WAN. It affects small flows, not byte totals. Worth a fresh
issue with its own evidence if it ever shows up in a real query — not worth speculative
work now.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Explain the 402-vs-45 gap, with evidence, before changing any repair logic — it was a
      cross-window comparison; the controlled same-window experiment shows agreement
- [x] Make the "gated out before the repair" case observable (`749b4733`)
- [x] Re-measure on production — the split matches the replay, and VIRGIN byte attribution
      is 0.989 against the kernel
- [~] Merged records for a known policy-routed destination carry the correct WAN — still
      false for short flows; noted above as the residual rather than left as a silent gap
- [x] `docs/flow.md` kept honest throughout, including correcting two claims of mine that
      measurement refuted

title: flow: repair 4 makes 9x fewer corrections in production than the same code makes on the same captured export

body:
## Summary

On a box where a WAN is captured in `egress_only` mode **and** the LAN side is also captured, a
NAT'd conversation is exported **twice** by ng_netflow — once pre-NAT on the LAN node, once
post-NAT on the WAN node. The exporter has no NAT-pair de-duplication, so whenever both copies
resolve to the same WAN, that WAN's byte total is counted twice.

Measured on the production box over 24 h:

| interface | flow `outbound` bytes | real `opnsense_interfaces_transmitted_bytes_total` | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VIRGIN (`ixl1`, ethernet) | **62.40 GB** | 45.05 GB | **+38.5%** |
| AAISP (`pppoe0`) | 226.50 GB | 213.33 GB | +6.2% |

62.32 GB of VIRGIN's 62.40 GB is a single population: TCP to Finland, i.e. the two hosts in the
`overvirgin` alias, which a policy-route rule sends out the Virgin WAN.

## Proof that it is a NAT-pair double count, not overhead

Splitting the same population in Loki by `src_scope` and by which repair fired returns **two
series of roughly equal volume**:

```
0.2 MB / 5m   {flow_egress_corrected="true",       src_scope="self"}    <- post-NAT copy  (ixl1 node)
0.2 MB / 5m   {flow_policy_route_corrected="true", src_scope="local"}   <- pre-NAT copy   (LAN node)
```

Both are labelled `flow_interface="VIRGIN"`, both carry the conversation's full byte count, and
they are the same conversation. Repair 2 (source-address) corrects the first; repair 4
(pf `route-to`) corrects the second. Each repair is individually right. Together they land two
copies of one conversation in one bucket.

## Why AAISP does not show it

`egress_only` is set on **both** WANs (`opt7,opt6`), so the asymmetry is not configuration. It is
[[pppoe-netflow-capture-is-dead-upstream]]: selecting a PPPoE interface for NetFlow captures
nothing, because `ng_netflow` attaches to mpd's framing node rather than the `ng_iface` node.
`netflow_pppoe0` exists in `ngctl list` and exports zero records.

So AAISP has **only** the pre-NAT copy and cannot double-count; its +6.2% is ordinary
header/timing overhead. VIRGIN is an ordinary ethernet device, its node works, and it gets both.

This also means the bug is **latent on any single-WAN box with an ethernet WAN** — it is not
multi-WAN-specific. It only became visible here because the policy-route repair is what pulls the
pre-NAT copy into the same bucket as the post-NAT one.

## The rest of the error is the same records in the wrong bucket

The pre-NAT copies that repair 4 does **not** correct stay labelled AAISP. So:

- VIRGIN is inflated by the pre-NAT copies that *were* corrected (+17.35 GB)
- AAISP is inflated by the pre-NAT copies that were *not* (+13.17 GB)
- total netflow outbound 288.90 GB vs 258.38 GB real, +11.8%

Making repair 4 more accurate **without** fixing this first would make VIRGIN's over-count worse,
not better, by moving more bytes from the second bucket into the doubled one. That ordering is
binding on #624.

## The fix is exact, and the data is already fetched

`api/diagnostics/firewall/query_states` — which the exporter already polls every 60 s for repair 4
— carries `nat_addr` and `nat_port` on the `direction="out"` row, holding the **pre-NAT** endpoint.
Live sample from the production box:

```
{"direction":"in",  "src_addr":"<lan-ip-10>",    "src_port":"36180", "dst_addr":"<pub-ip-15>","dst_port":"8007","nat_addr":null,      "nat_port":null,   "route-to":"<pub-ip-5>@ixl1"}
{"direction":"out", "src_addr":"<pub-ip-14>", "src_port":"42031", "dst_addr":"<pub-ip-15>","dst_port":"8007","nat_addr":"<lan-ip-10>","nat_port":"36180","route-to":"<pub-ip-5>@ixl1"}
```

So the NAT mapping is pf's own, verbatim — the same class of evidence repair 4 already relies on,
not an inference. No new endpoint, no extra API cost.

Sketch: extend `StateRow` with `NatAddr`/`NatPort`, build a second index on the `direction="out"`
tuple mapping post-NAT → pre-NAT, and where a post-NAT record's conversation has already been
emitted from its pre-NAT copy (or vice versa), drop one and count it.

Open design questions to settle before coding:

1. **Which copy wins?** The post-NAT copy is on the WAN and its byte count is what the interface
   counter measures. The pre-NAT copy is the only one that can correlate with Zenarmor (its
   5-tuple is what Zenarmor saw). Dropping the pre-NAT copy would silently reduce merged-record
   coverage. Preferred: keep the pre-NAT copy for correlation and emission, suppress the post-NAT
   copy's **bytes** for interface accounting, since repair 4 has already put the pre-NAT copy on
   the right WAN in the cases that matter.
2. **What happens when repair 4 refused?** Then the pre-NAT copy is on the wrong WAN and
   suppressing the post-NAT copy loses the only correct attribution. Suppression must be
   conditional on the pre-NAT copy having been resolved.
3. **Boxes with no post-NAT copy at all** (PPPoE WAN) must be unaffected — the mechanism can only
   ever subtract a copy it actually saw.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `nat_addr` / `nat_port` modelled on the `query_states` row; schema golden regenerated
      (`make schemas`)
- [ ] A NAT-pair index built from the same snapshot as the route table, conflict-counted the same
      way
- [ ] De-duplication decision documented in `internal/flow/` alongside the existing repair
      commentary, including which copy is kept and why
- [ ] A self-metric counting suppressed copies, so the mechanism is observable rather than silent
      (name TBD, e.g. `opnsense_flow_nat_pair_duplicates_total`)
- [ ] Grafana panel for it (coverage gate will force this)
- [ ] `docs/flow.md` states the double-count and its fix
- [ ] Re-measured on the production box: VIRGIN flow outbound within single-digit percent of
      `opnsense_interfaces_transmitted_bytes_total`, AAISP unchanged

comments.body:
## Live on <host-1> since 12:00:50Z — mechanism confirmed, byte re-measurement still outstanding

The repair is running and behaving as the capture predicted:

```
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="translations"}  4864
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="carried"}       2248
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="identities"}    4150
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="conflict"}        14
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="skipped"}          0

increase(opnsense_flow_nat_pair_deduped_total[45m])
  outcome="suppressed"    159
  outcome="late_pre_nat"    0
```

`conflict=14` lands exactly inside the 6-14 per build measured offline across 14
consecutive snapshots, which is the strongest available check that the index is being
built the same way in production as in the replay. `skipped=0` and a healthy
translations/carried ratio say the pf rows are parsing cleanly.

## The byte-ratio criterion is NOT met yet, and cannot be measured right now

The last acceptance box wants VIRGIN's flow-derived outbound within single digits of
`opnsense_interfaces_transmitted_bytes_total`. Two things make any number taken now
meaningless, and both would have produced a confident-looking wrong answer:

- **VIRGIN is idle** — 0.0077 Mbit/s. The +38.5% was measured over 24 h with a 100 Mbit/s
  backup running; at 8 kbit/s the ratio is dominated by small-flow overhead. A naive read
  right now gives 4.21 MB flow against 2.31 MB kernel, ratio 1.82, which means nothing.
- **The container restarted 19 minutes ago**, so any `increase()` window spanning 12:00:50Z
  crosses a counter reset.

Deferring the measurement rather than reporting that 1.82. It wants a window with real
VIRGIN traffic and a stable baseline — the next Proxmox backup to the `overvirgin` hosts
will provide both.

Leaving the issue closed since the fix is shipped and functionally verified; this comment
is the record of what is still unconfirmed. The check itself is one query:

```promql
sum by (interface) (increase(opnsense_flow_bytes_total{source="netflow",direction="outbound",interface="VIRGIN"}[1h]))
  / on (interface)
sum by (interface) (increase(opnsense_interfaces_transmitted_bytes_total{interface="VIRGIN"}[1h]))
```

Expect ~1.05. Before the fix it was 1.385.

## Acceptance criterion MET on production

The backup gave a 12:24-12:32Z burst peaking at 97 Mbit/s over the policy-routed WAN.
Measured over that window, exporter up since 12:22:45Z so no counter reset inside it:

| interface | flow-derived outbound | kernel `interfaces_transmitted_bytes_total` | ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **VIRGIN** | **3,233.77 MB** | **3,268.22 MB** | **0.989** |
| AAISP | 1,725.56 MB | 1,540.38 MB | 1.120 |

A second overlapping window agrees: VIRGIN 2,235.92 / 2,266.16 MB = **0.987**.

**Before the fix that ratio was 1.385.** It is now within 1.3% of the kernel's own counter,
on 3.2 GB of real policy-routed traffic. Ticking the last box.

## Two measurement traps worth recording

Both of these produced confident-looking wrong numbers before I caught them:

- **The burst was only eight minutes long.** A 14-minute window ending at 12:50 contained
  almost none of it and gave VIRGIN a ratio of 2.002 on 0.81 MB of traffic — pure
  small-flow noise. Always locate the traffic first (`rate(...[2m])` across the period)
  and measure over *that*, not over a round window.
- **A container restart inside the window makes `increase()` meaningless.** <host-1>
  restarted twice today; the first ratio I took spanned 12:00:50Z and was unusable.

## Mechanism health at steady state

```
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="translations"}  4864     {kind="carried"}  2248
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="identities"}    4150     {kind="conflict"}   14
opnsense_flow_nat_pair_entries{kind="skipped"}          0
increase(opnsense_flow_nat_pair_deduped_total[5m])   suppressed 39, late_pre_nat 0
```

## OPNsense live-box schema canary

Probed **176** endpoints: 175 clean, 0 with breaking type drift, 0 with missing paths, 0 with unexpected top-level keys, 0 with unexpected nested keys, 1 absent 404 (0 unexpected, 1 plugin-gated/expected), 0 probe errors, 0 skipped (no live parameter).

### ℹ️ Plugin-gated endpoints absent (plugin not installed — expected, not drift)

- `siproxdRegistrations` (`api/siproxd/service/showregistrations`)

### 🟡 Unverified paths that back metrics (required coverage — exercise the testbed)

- `trafficShaperStatistics` `items[].flows[].bytes` — backs `opnsense_trafficshaper_pipe_bytes`, `opnsense_trafficshaper_queue_bytes`
  - blocker: the traffic shaper is not configured on either testbed, so items[] is empty and NOTHING under it has ever been checked - this is the largest single unexercised surface in the ledger, 15 consumed paths behind one configuration step.
  - exercise: Configure the shaper and then put traffic through it: one pipe with a bandwidth limit, one queue on that pipe, and one shaper RULE attaching them to an interface (Firewall > Shaper > Pipes / Queues / Rules), apply, then generate traffic across that interface from the traffgen LXC on the isolated bridge is the only traffic source available (the Proxmox host is booted with ipv6.disable=1, so that LXC can never hold an IPv6 lease or terminate a v6 tunnel - only a VM can; see the keaLeases6 note). api/trafficshaper/service/statistics answers {status:ok,items:[]} when the shaper is unconfigured, which is the current state of both testbeds. Summed across the item's flow rows. TIMING MATTERS: dnctl reports LIVE flows, so an idle shaper serves its pipe and queue items with an empty flows array - active_flows reads a correct 0 and the four flow counters stay unexercised. Traffic has to be moving at the moment the canary polls.

## Fixed on the testbed, and the diagnosis was wrong in the ledger

Closed automatically by the canary at 08:54 — nightly clean, and the four
`trafficShaperStatistics items[].flows[].{pkt,bytes,drop_pkt,drop_bytes}` paths do not
appear anywhere in the report now. Both profiles came back with **no required-coverage
section at all**.

### The ledger note was wrong: the shaper HAS been configured all along

Every entry for these paths says *"the traffic shaper is not configured on either
testbed, so items[] is empty and NOTHING under it has ever been checked"*. That is not
what is on the boxes. Checked live on 2026-08-01:

- **nightly (102)**: pipe `10000` @ 200 Mbit/s (`testpipe`), queue `testqueue`, and rule
  `shape TESTLAN` on `opt1`/`vtnet2` — which had already passed **1,131,304 packets /
  151 MB**, last matched the minute I looked.
- **release-vm (106)**: the same pipe and rule.

So `items[]` was never empty. The failure was **`items[].flows[]`** being empty, which is
a completely different thing, and the note's own "TIMING MATTERS" paragraph is the actual
explanation: dnctl reports **live** flows, and this pipe has 0 ms delay, so a packet is
dequeued almost the instant it arrives and the row lapses between packets.

`traffgen.sh` runs **once a minute** from cron, so the row existed in bursts and the
canary usually polled between them. That is why this presented as intermittent rather
than permanent — and why nightly filed this issue while release-vm got lucky in the very
same run and closed #622 clean. It was a coin flip, not a gap.

### The fix, and why the numbers in it are measured

A systemd template unit on LXC 105 (`opnsense-nightly-traffgen`) holding a continuous
flow across TESTLAN:

```
/etc/systemd/system/shaper-keepalive@.service
ExecStart=/bin/ping -i 0.01 -s 500 -n -q %i
enabled: shaper-keepalive@<lan-ip-24>  (nightly)
         shaper-keepalive@<lan-ip-25>  (release-vm)
```

**One host covers both firewalls.** TESTLAN `<lan-ip-31>/24` is a shared segment — nightly
is `.1`, release-vm is `.2`, 105 is `.100` — so pinging both from 105 exercises both
shapers. Verified: a ping to `.2` populates 106's `flows[]` exactly as a ping to `.1`
populates 102's. No second generator needed on 111.

**Both the rate and the packet size are measured, not guessed.** Sampled against the live
API, 10–12 polls per interval:

| ping interval | populated |
| --- | --- |
| cron's once-a-minute burst | the status quo that filed this issue |
| `-i 2` | 3/5 |
| `-i 0.2` | 8/10 |
| `-i 0.05` | 9/10 |
| `-i 0.01` | 11/12 |
| `-i 0.01 -s 500` | **12/12** |

Size matters as well as rate, because a larger packet occupies the queue longer. ~434 kbps
per box against a 200 Mbit/s pipe — 0.2% of it, and negligible beside the 1.13M packets
the existing traffgen already puts through the same rule.

The obvious alternative — giving the pipe a non-zero delay so packets linger — would hold
the row at a far lower rate, but it edits the shaper config that the canary exists to
validate. Generating traffic changes no OPNsense config at all, which is why it was done
this way round.

### What this does not fix

The remaining `trafficShaperStatistics` entries in the report — `items[].description`,
`items[].id`, `items[].pipe`, `items[].template` — are under **standing blind spots**
(schema models them as `any`), not required coverage. No live run can clear those, by
construction, and they were not blocking.

`drop_pkt`/`drop_bytes` are now *validated* but still read 0: proving the keys exist does
not need the pipe saturated, and deliberately saturating a 200 Mbit/s pipe around the
clock is not worth it.

### Worth pruning from the ledger

`coverage.json`'s blocker text for these four paths should lose the "the traffic shaper is
not configured on either testbed" claim — it is false, and it sent me looking for a
missing configuration that was there the whole time. The real blocker was always the
sampling window, which the same note already described two sentences later.
