body:
## The policy-route repair's miss window is wider than #603 assumed, and the short VIRGIN flows fall in it

#603 shipped and works: the pf-state join is exact, `conflict=0` on a live 3,145-state table, and corrections fire on prod. This is about the one thing its verification measured that its costing did not predict.

## The finding

#603's comment says the flows the multi-WAN bug hurts are long:

> the ones this bug actually hurts (the 11.1 GB on VIRGIN) are long — sample state ages in the table run to 36 hours

Measured on prod 2026-07-31, the `ixl1` population is **19 states, and 18 of them are short**: `<lan-ip-10> -> <pub-ip-15>:8007` TCP connections, age under 90 seconds, a new one roughly every 10 seconds. Exactly one is long — a `<lan-ip-1>:32944` UDP flow.

That inverts which half of the population the mechanism reaches.

## Why the cadence cannot reach them

The miss window is **bidirectional**, and #603 only accounted for one side of it:

- a state that **expired** before its NetFlow record arrived (the side #603 documents), and
- a state **created after the last poll** — which #603 does not mention at all.

With a 300-second poll and a ~90-second state lifetime, one of those TCP connections can be created, used and closed entirely between two snapshots. It appears in no snapshot, so it is refused, correctly, every time. No cadence longer than the state lifetime reaches it.

Measured: `opnsense_flow_policy_route_refused_total{reason="no_state"}` runs at roughly **30% of decoded records**. The control that proves this is staleness rather than a broken join: 60 live flow records looked up against a table fetched **at the same moment** hit **58 of 60**.

## Why this is filed rather than fixed

Shortening the poll is a decision that was already made deliberately ("cold tier, 5 minutes, full table", with the full table measured at 3.3 MB / 645 ms), and re-litigating it silently would be the wrong move. The options, with what is known about each:

1. **Leave it.** Long policy-routed flows are corrected; short ones are refused and counted. `source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` stays empty, which is #603's one unmet acceptance item.
2. **Shorten the poll.** 60s would reach a ~90s state most of the time, at 5x the API cost — ~3.3 MB and ~650 ms per minute against a firewall where every request already costs two configd RPCs (see the api-request-cost note). It does not reach a 30-second state.
3. **Ask for less of the table.** `query_states` takes a `searchPhrase`; whether it can be filtered to route-to-carrying states server-side is unread. If it can, a much shorter cadence gets cheap.
4. **Hold a rolling union of snapshots** rather than replacing wholesale — a state seen in ANY recent snapshot stays answerable for a bounded time. Costs memory, not API calls, and reaches states that expired but not states created after the last poll. It fixes exactly half the window.

Recommendation: **3 if it works, else 4, else 1.** Not 2 on its own — it multiplies the cost of the thing it only partly fixes.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Establish whether `query_states` can be filtered server-side to states carrying a `route-to`, and what that costs
- [ ] Decide between the four options above, or state that option 1 is the answer and close
- [ ] If the cadence changes, `docs/flow.md`'s statement of the miss window changes with it — it currently describes only the expiry half
- [ ] Re-measure `policy_route_refused_total{reason="no_state"}` and `source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` on prod afterwards

## Related

- #603 — the mechanism this is about; shipped in `e5deddbd`, verified in the comment there

comments.body:
Closed by `8b0a506e` — **option 2+4**, both halves.

### Acceptance item 1: can `query_states` filter server-side? **No.**

Read against upstream source rather than probed, since the answer is structural. `FirewallController::queryStatesAction` passes `searchPhrase` to configd `filter list states` → `scripts/filter/list_states.py` → `lib/states.py:query_states()`. The filter is applied **after** `pfctl -vvs state` has dumped and Python has parsed every line into a record, as a substring match over `" ".join(record.values())`. Three consequences:

- **No field predicate.** You cannot ask for "states carrying a route-to". The `route-to` *value* is a device name, which collides with `iface` — a filter on the WAN device matches both.
- **Clauses AND, they do not OR.** N WAN devices would need N requests, which is worse than one.
- **It saves bytes, not work.** `pfctl`, the full parse and `fetch_rule_labels` (`pfctl -vvPsr`) all run first. The ~650 ms stays; only the 3.3 MB shrinks. And each request still costs two configd RPCs.

So the issue's "3 if it works, else 4, else 1" chain loses its first link.

### Acceptance item 2: the decision

Option 4 alone was rejected for this population, and it is worth writing down why since it was the fallback: the union only reaches states that **expired**, and at a 300 s poll against a ~90 s lifetime most refusals are states **created after the last poll**. It would have fixed the half that was not broken here. So both, as chosen:

- **Poll 5 min → 1 min.** Reaches a ~90 s state most of the time. Reaches a 30 s one never, and nothing would.
- **Rolling union, 3 min retention.** `BuildRouteTable` takes `Previous` and `Retain`. Fresh rows always win, so a failover corrects on the next poll instead of being pinned by history. Entries age from **last seen**, not from build time — otherwise a long-lived state would fall out of a union that exists to retain things, which has its own test.

Retention is sized as a bound on being *wrong*, not on memory: a carried entry is a claim about a dead state, and it goes bad on a WAN failover. Three intervals comfortably exceeds any export delay and keeps a mislabel to seconds. Raising it buys nothing and only widens that window — noted in the constant's comment so it does not get "tuned up" later.

Cost accepted explicitly: 5x request load, ~3.3 MB and ~650 ms per minute, plus the two configd RPCs per request.

### Acceptance item 3: docs

`docs/flow.md` now describes **both** halves, names which one the union closes and which one is a floor, and states why the 5-minute figure was wrong rather than silently editing the number. The `pf_state_age_seconds` help text no longer says "cold tier".

### Observability

`opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="carried"}` — an existing labelled gauge already on a `sum by (kind)` panel, so no new metric and no coverage-gate work. Persistently zero means the union is contributing nothing; dwarfing the fresh count means states are dying far faster than we poll.

Gate: `go test ./...` green, `golangci-lint run ./...` 0 issues, `make docs` + `make grafana-check` clean.

### Acceptance item 4 — still open, and it needs the deploy

Re-measuring `policy_route_refused_total{reason="no_state"}` and `source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` on prod needs the new build running. <host-1> pulls `:main` hourly via watchtower, so this lands on its own within the hour. **I have deliberately not hand-deployed.** Worth re-checking a few hours after it picks up:

- `refused_total{reason="no_state"}` should fall well below the ~30% baseline, but **not to zero** — the sub-30-second states are unreachable by design.
- `pf_state_entries{kind="carried"}` should be non-zero, which is what proves the union half is doing anything.
- `source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` should start populating. If it stays empty while refusals drop, the corrections are landing but something downstream of the repair is dropping them, and that is a separate bug.

Closing on the code; happy to reopen if the prod numbers do not move.

## Measured on prod — the remaining acceptance item

<host-1> picked up `81d14c0` this morning. Figures below are from Grafana Cloud, not the box.

### The union is doing real work

```
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="total"}          5531
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="carried"}        2942   <- 53% of the table
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="policy_routed"}  2609
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="conflict"}          0
opnsense_flow_pf_state_age_seconds                    ~32    (60s poll, sampled mid-cycle)
```

`carried` roughly equals the fresh count. By the metric's own help text that means states
are expiring about as fast as we poll — which is exactly the population this issue
measured (18 of 19 policy-routed states sub-90-second) and exactly the case the union was
added for. `conflict` stays 0, so the fresh-beats-carried rule is not producing key
collisions.

### Refusals are down, by less than hoped

`policy_route_refused_total{reason="no_state"}` as a share of decoded records:

| window | ratio |
| --- | --- |
| pre-deploy, 22h mean ending 2h before the cutover | **28%** |
| pre-deploy, individual 10m samples | 26–32% |
| post-deploy, latest 10m samples | **20–23%** |

So roughly a quarter of the refusals are gone, against a baseline that had been flat in a
26–31% band all day. Real and measurable, but not the collapse the issue's framing implied.

**I do not think the residue is a bug.** `Egress`'s contract has three ways to return
`ok == false`, and only two of them are staleness: the third is "this record is not a
pre-NAT egress copy at all", which no cadence or retention can ever resolve. The issue's
own control — 60 live records against a table fetched at the same instant hitting 58/60 —
was measured on *policy-routed* records specifically, not on the whole decoded stream, so
it never implied the whole 30% was recoverable. A floor in the high teens looks like the
honest shape of this.

Worth revisiting only if someone wants to split `refused_total` by whether the record even
looked like a pre-NAT egress copy. That would turn "23% refused" into two numbers that
mean different things, and only one of them would be a defect.

### The VIRGIN item — correcting the premise, not claiming a win

This issue and #603 both say `source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` "stays empty".
**That was already out of date before this change shipped.** The actual metric is
`opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_ratio_count`, and its VIRGIN series had been climbing for
the whole preceding 24 hours — 2 → 44 observations, at 0–16/hour.

So VIRGIN is populated, it is not new, and I cannot honestly attribute it to this work.
The new instance has produced observations at a comparable trickle in its first half hour.
Whether the *rate* improves needs a day of data against that 0–16/hour baseline; it is not
something this session can answer, and claiming it would be inventing a result.

Flagging rather than quietly ticking the box: the acceptance item as written ("re-measure
afterwards") is done, but the finding is that its premise had expired.

### Summary against the acceptance list

- [x] Establish whether `query_states` can be filtered server-side — **no**, and why is in
  the closing comment above.
- [x] Decide between the four options — 2+4, both shipped.
- [x] `docs/flow.md` describes both halves of the window.
- [x] Re-measured on prod: refusals 28% → 20–23%, `kind="carried"` at 2942, VIRGIN
  populated but not by this change.

title: Policy-route repair: the pf-state poll cannot reach a state that lives and dies between two snapshots

body:
Porting the structural wins from `rknightion/tailscale2otel#526`, which split one 437-panel v2
dashboard into a family and moved most of its variables off the dashboard. Every number below is
**measured from this repo's committed artifacts**, not estimated.

The two generators are close relatives — this repo's `coverage(*builders)` is where tailscale2otel's
came from, and its docstring is quoted in that issue. Several ideas went the other way and are worth
having back.

## TL;DR

| change | measured effect here |
| --- | --- |
| grouping-level variables | **104 dashboard-level variables → 18**; cold-load fan-out 105 → ~18 |
| a fourth grouping level (sub-tabs) | 7 leaves are over 35 panels; the worst is **95** |
| `AutoGridLayout` for uniform rows | rows reflow instead of clipping at narrow widths |
| an adhoc filter variable | folds several dropdowns into one, without losing the useful two |

Items 1 and 2 are the substantial ones. 3 and 4 are cheap. **Do not do 1 without also doing the two
gate fixes in "What breaks quietly" — they are not optional extras, they are what makes item 1 safe.**

## 1. Grouping-level variables: 104 → 18

`RowsLayoutRowSpec` and `TabsLayoutTabSpec` both accept a `variables: [...VariableKind]` list, so a
presence sentinel can live on the tab that consumes it rather than on the dashboard. Every one of
its queries then runs only when that tab is opened.

**This repo declares 104 dashboard-level variables — 6 visible and 98 hidden sentinels — and zero
grouping-level ones.** Walking `dashboard.json`'s layout for what each sentinel actually gates:

| sentinel population | count | can it move? |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| gate a **top-level** tab | 12 | **no** — must stay dashboard-level |
| gate only **nested leaves**, all under one domain | 27 | yes → onto that domain tab |
| consumed by rows in **exactly one leaf** | 59 | yes → onto that leaf |
| consumed by rows in 2+ leaves | 0 | — |
| referenced by nothing (dead) | 0 | — |

So the floor is **6 visible + 12 top-level gates = 18**, down from 104. Nothing is ambiguous: no
sentinel is used across more than one leaf, so there is no judgement call about where anything goes.

The 12 that cannot move are `has_haproxy`, `has_ipsec`, `has_netbird`, `has_nginx`, `has_openvpn`,
`has_relayd`, `has_siproxd`, `has_syslog`, `has_syslog_logs`, `has_tailscale`, `has_tor`,
`has_wireguard`. **A tab cannot gate itself on a variable scoped to itself** — the variable does not
exist until the tab renders, so the gate evaluates against nothing and the tab is permanently hidden.
That constraint is the whole reason the table above splits "gates a tab" from "used by rows in a tab".

`test_cold_load_budget.py` already measures the thing this improves: `MAX_LOAD_VARIABLES = 112 #
measured 105 (103 onDashboardLoad + 2 onTimeRangeChanged)`. That budget becomes ~18 and the comment
explaining why the number is large stops being needed.

### Seams

Small, and this repo's builder is already shaped for them:

- `Builder.row(title, names, present=, absent=, collapse=)` → add `variables=None`, emitted into the
  row spec only when non-empty.
- `Builder.tab(title, rows, present=, absent=)` and `tab_group(...)` → same.
- `Builder.sentinel(name, *, metric=, scope=, ...)` → take a **required** `scope` argument naming the
  grouping level that owns it. Required rather than defaulted: a default means a module can silently
  keep rebuilding the dashboard-level pile, and the migration then never finishes. That is exactly
  how tailscale2otel did it, and adding the argument to all 67 call sites regenerated a
  **byte-identical** artifact, which is what proved the migration was mechanical before any content
  moved.
- `_claim_sentinel_name` (`builder.py:928`) needs to key on `(scope, name)` rather than `name`, and
  keep raising on a same-scope duplicate. Duplicating a name across two *different* scopes has to
  stay legal — see below.

### The one thing worth verifying live before relying on it

Whether two tabs may each declare a variable of the **same name**. Persisting is not the question —
the failure that matters is Grafana resolving the name globally, last-declaration-wins, which
persists perfectly and then gates the wrong rows.

Tailscale2otel probed it by giving two tabs the same sentinel name over **opposite-truth** queries
(one matching live series, one matching a metric that does not exist), pushing, and rendering each
tab first. Each row gated on its own copy: **Grafana resolves tab-scoped variables per tab.** That
result should hold here, but it cost one push and two renders to establish and is worth re-checking
on your Grafana version rather than inherited on trust. This repo currently has 0 sentinels used in
more than one leaf, so nothing depends on it today — it only matters if that changes.

## 2. A fourth grouping level for the oversized leaves

`tab_group()` already nests one level (domain → leaf). Nesting a leaf's layout as another
`TabsLayout` gives domain → leaf → sub-tab, and **four grouping levels render correctly** — verified
live and in the static renderer during #526. Note Grafana's docs state a maximum of three; four
works, so that limit is enforced by the dashboard *editor*, not the API or the renderer. These
artifacts are generated and never hand-edited, so relying on it is acceptable — but it is beyond
documented support, so spend it only where a leaf is genuinely oversized. Collapsing a sub-tabbed
leaf back to sibling leaves is a mechanical change if a future Grafana starts enforcing it.

Seven leaves are over ~35 panels:

| leaf | panels | rows |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| System > System & Resources | **95** | 18 |
| Network > DHCP | 51 | 13 |
| Network > FRR Routing | 51 | 10 |
| Network > DNS - Unbound | 41 | 8 |
| Network > Protocol Stats | 41 | 16 |
| VPN & remote access > VPN | 39 | 10 |
| Security > Firewall & PF | 38 | 13 |

95 panels in one tab is a tab people scroll past rather than read. Derive the sub-tab groupings from
the **existing row titles** rather than inventing new ones — #526 did that for all three of its
splits and it kept the change reviewable, because every row lands somewhere obvious and the diff is a
move.

**Watch the PII/redaction gates while splitting.** In tailscale2otel three of five planned row merges
had to be abandoned: single-panel rows there existed *specifically* so a redaction gate covered one
table instead of nine aggregates, and merging would either have dropped the redaction or hidden
non-sensitive content. `test_empty_state_contract.py` and the `_cond` gates here play the same role —
if a row looks like a pointless one-panel row, check what its gate covers before folding it.

## 3. `AutoGridLayout` for uniform rows

`Builder._place()` (`builder.py:1067`) is a hand-rolled fixed 24-column packer and every row uses it.
`AutoGridLayout` reflows responsively — verified during #526, 3 panels wrapping to 2 columns at
1400px. Worth adding as `autogrid_row()` alongside `row()` and using it where a row is N same-size
panels; rows with deliberate asymmetry (a wide timeseries beside two stats) keep the explicit grid.

A helper that still took `(name, w, h)` triples would be `row()` with extra steps — the point is that
sizes are **not** stated.

## 4. One adhoc filter instead of several dropdowns

`AdhocVariable` with `baseFilters` pinned to a metric family replaces several label dropdowns with
one free-form filter whose key/value suggestions are scoped to that family. The six visible controls
here are `datasource`, `loki_datasource`, `opnsense_instance`, `interface`, `device`,
`zenarmor_client`.

The hybrid is probably right rather than folding everything: keep the two or three an operator picks
from constantly as explicit dropdowns (a short known option list beats free-form typing) and fold the
long tail into the adhoc. `zenarmor_client` looks like a fold candidate.

**Shape trap, and it is a nasty one.** `AdhocVariableKind` puts `datasource` and a **required**
`group` at the KIND level, as siblings of `spec` — unlike `QueryVariable`, which nests its datasource
inside the query. Getting it wrong produces a 422 whose CUE disjunction error names **`layout.kind`**
and never mentions the variable, so the real cause is completely masked. Bisect from a known-valid
fragment if a v2 push 422s. Verified by pushing and reading back: `group` and `datasource` at kind
level, `baseFilters` intact inside `spec`.

## What breaks quietly when variables move — do these WITH item 1, not after

#526 shipped four checkers that kept passing while covering less. Every one failed *silently*, which
is why they are listed as part of the work rather than as follow-ups. Three apply directly here:

**`tools/promqlcheck` resolves `$var` against `spec.variables[]` only.** The moment a variable moves
onto a tab, every panel referencing it reports as undeclared — and worse, the same blindness would
**accept** a panel borrowing a *sibling* tab's variable, which resolves to nothing at render time.
Fix: walk the layout and check each panel against the dashboard-level set unioned with the variables
declared by every grouping level enclosing it. Walk it **generically**, not against typed layout
kinds: a typed reader meeting an unknown kind deserialises it to an empty struct and drops every
panel underneath from the check while still reporting success. Negative-test the sibling-tab case
specifically — a walker that simply unioned every declaration in the document passes the obvious test
and accepts the bug.

**A "is this sentinel declared?" check must become "does it resolve *here*?".** Checking that a name
exists *somewhere on the dashboard* is too weak once scoping exists: a row gating on a sibling tab's
variable passes, then renders permanently hidden — on screen indistinguishable from a row correctly
hidden for want of data. In tailscale2otel that caught a real row that had been in that state.

**Any walker that reads panels out of rows must learn every layout kind it may meet** (relevant if
you take item 3). Tailscale2otel's empty-state contract accepted only `GridLayout`; the moment rows
became `AutoGridLayout` it returned an empty panel list for them and every per-panel assertion passed
*vacuously*. No failure, just less coverage. Worth adding a floor assertion — a row that reads as
having zero panels is a bug in the reader, since the generator cannot build one.

Fourth, for completeness: the tailscale2otel GitSync workflow's commit step used `git diff --quiet`,
which is blind to **untracked** files, so renaming its artifact made both new filenames invisible and
three consecutive green runs published nothing. **This repo is not exposed to that** — it copies to
stable pre-rename basenames, and `verify-gitsync.py` would catch it anyway. Mentioned only because
if the basenames ever change, that is the trap.

## Deliberately NOT recommended — checked, and this repo is already right

- **Splitting `coverage()`'s panel vs template-variable references.** tailscale2otel counted a
  sentinel's `label_values()` call as "visualized", so a signal could satisfy its every-signal-
  reaches-a-panel bar while appearing on no panel (`rknightion/tailscale2otel#527`). **This repo does
  not have that bug**: `sentinel()` appends to `self.variables` and never to `_exprs`, so
  `coverage()` already sees panel queries only. Worth a comment saying so on purpose, because it is
  one refactor away from being untrue.
- **`panel_metric_gaps()`** — this repo has it and tailscale2otel copied the idea.
- **Alert→panel links.** The `PANEL_LINKS` + `PANEL_LINK_EXEMPT` + ambiguity-check + string-`__panelId__`
  arrangement in `build_rules.py` is **better than tailscale2otel's** and needs nothing. Two findings
  from over there that it already prevents: a `panel=` pointing at a panel charting a *different*
  metric (three alerts were in that state, one linked to the very signal the alert exists because it
  cannot detect), and a title colliding across a two-dashboard family.

## Suggested order

1. Seams only: `variables=` on `row`/`tab`/`tab_group`, required `scope` on `sentinel()`, `(scope,
   name)` keying. Pass the dashboard scope everywhere. **Assert the regenerated artifact is
   byte-identical** — that is the proof the migration is mechanical.
2. The two gate fixes above, with the sibling-tab negative test, *before* moving any variable. They
   are what will tell you whether step 3 worked.
3. Move the 59 leaf-scoped sentinels, then the 27 domain-scoped ones. Re-measure `MAX_LOAD_VARIABLES`
   and lower the budget on purpose.
4. Sub-tab the seven oversized leaves, largest first.
5. `autogrid_row()` and the adhoc filter — independent of everything above, do them whenever.

Happy to be talked out of the fourth grouping level specifically; it is the one item here that trades
documented support for a real ergonomic win, and 95 panels in a tab may be tolerable if the rows are
well-ordered.

comments.body:
## Two corrections to the plan before starting, and a decision on step 1

**Measured this repo's committed artifact independently rather than taking the numbers on trust — they hold exactly.** 104 dashboard variables (98 hidden + 6 visible), and classifying each hidden sentinel by which grouping level consumes it reproduces the issue's table to the entry:

| population | count |
| --- | ---: |
| gates a **top-level** tab (immovable) | 12 |
| gates only a **leaf** tab → onto its domain | 27 |
| consumed by rows/panels in **exactly one leaf** | 59 |
| used across 2+ leaves | 0 |
| dead | 0 |

The 12 are exactly the ones named in the issue. Floor stays 6 + 12 = **18**.

**Correction 1 — the call-site count is 127, not 67** (`b.sentinel(` + `b.loki_sentinel(` across `grafana/`, both dashboards).

**Correction 2 — `scope=` is already taken, and it means something else.** `Builder.sentinel()` has a `scope=` parameter today for the **PromQL selector** scope (`collector` / `global` / `self_labeled` / `target_join`, validated against `SENTINEL_SCOPES`). Adding a second `scope=` meaning "grouping level" to the same signature would be a genuinely dangerous collision, so that name is not available.

## Decision: placement is DERIVED, not declared

Rob's call. Instead of a required per-call-site argument, the builder computes each sentinel's level at manifest time: walk the layout, find every reference, place the variable at the deepest grouping level that encloses all of them.

Reasoning, since this departs from the issue body:

- The analysis above **is** the derivation, and it already agrees with the hand-derived table — so the rule is known-correct on today's artifact before any code moves.
- It gets the self-gating rule right by construction. "A tab cannot gate itself on a variable scoped to itself" is the whole reason the table splits "gates a tab" from "used inside a tab", and it is the subtle one: 86 hand-written declarations are 86 chances to place a gate on the tab it gates, and the failure is **invisible** — a permanently hidden tab looks identical to a tab correctly hidden for want of data.
- It self-corrects. The day a module adds a second consumer in another leaf, the variable hoists automatically instead of resolving to nothing in the new place.
- The issue's argument for `required` was against a **default** ("a module can silently keep rebuilding the dashboard-level pile"). Derivation does not have that failure mode — there is no pile to persist, it is recomputed optimally every build.

The byte-identical check the issue proposes as proof of step 1 does not apply to a derived design, since the whole point is that output changes. The equivalent evidence is that the computed placement matches the independent classification above, and that is what will be asserted.

**Gate strictness: hard-fail on resolution only.** A build error if any panel or row references a variable that does not resolve at its position (the sibling-tab bug), and if any variable resolves nowhere. No committed placement-manifest artifact — Rob's call; placement is derived from references, so a placement change can only follow a reference change, which is already visible in the diff.

## Item 2: sibling leaves, not a fourth grouping level

Also Rob's call, against the issue's leaning. The seven oversized leaves get split into **sibling leaves at the existing third level** instead of gaining a fourth. Keeps the whole thing inside documented Grafana support, still fixes the 95-panel tab, and costs a wider leaf bar. Groupings still derived from existing row titles so the diff stays a move.

## Done — all five items, across `4da1b311`, `f5070ac4`, `81d14c03`

| change | predicted | measured after |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| dashboard-level variables | 104 → 18 | **104 → 18** |
| cold-load variable fan-out | 105 → ~18 | **105 → 16** |
| largest leaf | 95 panels | **34** |
| panels retained | — | **815 + 101, unchanged** |
| promqlcheck variable queries | — | **119** (was silently 21) |

### 1. Grouping-level variables — derived, not declared

The 18 that remain are exactly the 6 visible plus the 12 immovable top-level gates the issue named, name for name. `Builder.place_variables()` runs last in the build (after `organize_tabs`, or the domain level the 27 leaf-gates move onto does not exist yet) and puts each sentinel at the deepest grouping level enclosing every reference. Deviations from the plan and why are in the comment above.

Two things the derivation handles that a declaration would have had to remember: a variable referenced from outside the layout at all (another variable's query, an annotation, a link) pins to the dashboard, and a word-boundary match so `$has_dhcp` does not match `$has_dhcpv6_isc` and hoist both to their union.

### 2. Sibling leaves, not a fourth grouping level

Your call, and I think the right one — the splits fall on seams that already existed. Everything derived from existing row titles; no row split, merged, renamed or reordered within its group.

**The split introduced two bugs of its own, both quiet, both now fixed.** Worth recording because neither is obvious:

- `organize_tabs` gates a domain only when **every** leaf under it is optional. A new leaf missing from `OPTIONAL_TAB_PRESENCE` therefore silently un-gates its whole domain — "VPN & remote access" started rendering on a box with no VPN at all, empty, which is precisely what that table exists to prevent. The repo's own `test_fully_optional_domains_are_presence_gated` would have caught it; I hit it first by reading the output.
- Sibling leaves share their parent's sentinels, so the domain's OR condition listed `has_ipsec` twice. Deduped order-preservingly — the rendered condition must not depend on how many ways a feature has been split.

### 3 & 4. `autogrid_row()`, and no adhoc filter

`autogrid_row()` takes names only, as the issue insists. Applied to the 15 rows that are 3+ interchangeable small stat tiles — the worst clippers. Rows whose geometry means something keep the explicit grid, and so do the uniform 12-wide timeseries grids, where the arrangement is a deliberate reading layout rather than a packing accident. The v2 shape is copied verbatim from a live-deployed dashboard rather than derived, so the `columnWidthMode`/`rowHeightMode`/`fillScreen` trap you flagged never came up.

**No adhoc filter, and this is a finding rather than a skip.** Checked all six visible controls and there is nothing to fold: two are datasource pickers, `$opnsense_instance` is load-bearing for every sentinel's scoping, `$interface` and `$device` are the short known-option dropdowns the issue itself says to keep — and `$zenarmor_client`, the one named fold candidate, filters Loki **structured metadata** (`| device_name=~"$zenarmor_client"`). An adhoc variable emits stream-selector label matchers and `device_name` is not an indexed label, so folding it would break it, not simplify it. That is also why #435 made it a textbox and #474 a QueryVariable. Adding an adhoc that filters nothing would be pure cost.

### What breaks quietly — all three, done WITH item 1

- **`promqlcheck` resolved `$var` against `spec.variables` only.** Confirmed live: it went **119 → 21 variable queries with a green exit** the first time placement moved. Now walks the layout generically — dispatching on `kind`, never decoding typed layout kinds — and checks each reference against the dashboard set unioned with every **enclosing** level. Positional, not a document-wide union.
- **"Is it declared?" → "does it resolve here?"**, including the tab-cannot-gate-itself case.
- **Floor assertion** in both `promqlcheck` and `test_empty_state_contract`: a row read as having zero panels is a reader bug, since the generator cannot build one. `AutoGridLayoutItem` is understood, not merely tolerated.

**The sibling-tab negative test exists and was verified to work.** I mutated the walker to a naive document-wide union and confirmed all three of the sibling-row, sibling-panel and self-gating tests fail against it — a walker that unions everything passes the obvious tests, exactly as you warned.

### Also done

`MAX_LOAD_VARIABLES` lowered **112 → 22** on purpose, with the long comment explaining why the number was large deleted along with the number. A ceiling four times the real figure never fires, and creep back up is precisely the regression worth catching.

`Builder.all_variables()` is the new answer to "what does this dashboard declare?" and reads every level; the sentinel contract and scoping inventory go through it. The cold-load budget deliberately does not — which variables fire on load is its whole subject.

`coverage()` reading `_exprs` (panel queries only) is now stated **and tested** — three tests including a control, so the sibling project's #527 bug cannot arrive here by refactor.

One unrelated fix fell out: a GPS panel description said `$GPGGA`. Grafana interpolates descriptions, so that read as a variable resolving nowhere. The NMEA sigil is dropped.

### Gate

`go test ./...` green, `golangci-lint run ./...` 0 issues, 405 grafana unit tests green, `make grafana-check` and `make docs-check` clean.

### Not done, deliberately

~50 rows of 2–3 uniform 12-wide panels remain on the explicit grid. They are `autogrid_row()` candidates by the letter of item 3, but a 2-up or 3-up timeseries grid is a deliberate reading layout and already reflows acceptably, so converting them is churn for no clipping fixed. Flagging rather than leaving it to look undone — the rule if anyone wants them later is "uniform **and** interchangeable", not just uniform.

### Deploy

`grafana-sync.yml` publishes on push to `main`, so the dashboard family reaches m7kni on its own — no hand-push.

title: Adopt grouping-level variables and sub-tabs from tailscale2otel#526 (104 dashboard variables → 18)

body:
## Summary

`cmd/apidrift` validates `ipsecSad` key presence against the **synthetic placeholder row** that `setkey -D` produces on a box with no security associations, and that the API client already discards. The result is six permanent false "Missing" findings on every profile — prod, nightly and release-vm — for fields that are modelled and exported.

## The placeholder

`setkey -D` prints the literal line `No SAD entries.` when the SAD is empty. `list_sad.py` parses that line as a record:

```json
{"src":"No","dst":"SAD","nat":"ntries","satype":null,"spi":null,
 "ikeid":null,"phase1desc":null,"phase2desc":null,"id":"910a25ff..."}
```

(`nat="ntries"` is upstream's own bug: the guard is `keyparts[2].find("[")`, and `str.find` returns `-1` when absent, which is truthy, so it always slices.)

`opnsense/ipsec.go:327-330` documents this row verbatim and `FetchIPsecSAD` discards it — the client has been correct about this all along. The canary is the only consumer that treats it as data.

## What it costs

Six findings that can never be resolved and must never be exempted:

```
ipsecSad rows[].allocated, allocated_hard, allocated_soft,
         bytes_current, bytes_hard, bytes_soft
```

They are modelled and consumed — #578 exports them as `opnsense_ipsec_sa_bytes_*` and `_allocated_*` — so a `missingOK` would blind the canary to real drift on six live fields, which is exactly what the repo's triage rules say not to do (see the verdict recorded on #613). Leaving them as standing findings is no better: they are noise in every run's report and they are part of what stops prod reaching a clean canary (#531).

## Fix

Teach the probe to recognise the same placeholder the client does, and treat `ipsecSad` as **zero rows** rather than one row with six absent keys. `spi == null` is the more robust discriminator than matching `src=="No" && dst=="SAD"`, since a genuine SA always carries an SPI — but match whichever the client uses, and keep the two in step.

This fixes every profile at once and, unlike an exemption, keeps the six fields genuinely checked for the day a real SA exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The probe reports no findings for `ipsecSad` on a box with an empty SAD
- [ ] The six counters are still validated when a real SA is present — proven by a fixture with one real row plus one placeholder row
- [ ] No `missingOK` entry is added for any of the six
- [ ] The placeholder-detection rule lives next to (or is shared with) the client's, so the two cannot drift apart
- [ ] A clean run on prod for this endpoint
- [ ] Full gate green

## Related

- #613 — the ledger issue where this was diagnosed; the verdict there is "box-state, no exemption, fix the canary"
- #531 — prod's clean-run ledger, which this is one of the last items blocking
- #578 — modelled the six counters

body:
## Summary

A NetFlow record is strictly unidirectional and all of its volume lands in `Tx` — `processor.go:262-268` says so outright ("OUT_BYTES/OUT_PKTS are declared but always zero, so all volume is Tx and Rx stays zero"). The correlator then sums **both** unidirectional halves of a conversation into the same accumulator (`correlate.go`, `observeNetflowLocked`):

```go
e.nf.TxBytes += r.NF.TxBytes
e.nf.RxBytes += r.NF.RxBytes
```

So on a merged or multi-fragment record, `NF.TxBytes` is the conversation's total **in both directions** and `NF.RxBytes` is permanently zero. A record describing a 2 GB download reports 2 GB transmitted and nothing received.

## Why it is worth fixing now

Until #605 there was nothing to fix it *with*: a merged record's orientation was decided by whichever datagram arrived first, so "the forward direction" was not a well-defined thing to sum into. #605 makes orientation deterministic and keeps a representative of each half (`corrEntry.sample` and `corrEntry.mirror`), which is exactly the seam this needs — the forward half's bytes go to `Tx`, the mirror's to `Rx`, and `RxBytes` means something on a merged record for the first time.

## What needs deciding before implementing

- **`opnsense_flow_bytes_total` currently sums `Tx + Rx`** (`Counters.Bytes()`), so the total is unchanged by the split and no existing series moves. That should be confirmed rather than assumed — the whole point of splitting is that some consumer starts reading the two apart, and any consumer reading `Tx` alone as "the conversation's volume" would silently halve.
- **Zenarmor's `Zen` counters are a separate question.** They are never summed with `NF` (#346 decision 3) and a conn document reports its own directional split; whether the two sides' notion of "transmit" agrees needs checking against a real document before they are put on the same axis.
- **Fragments in neither orientation** cannot happen today (there are only two), but the code should refuse rather than guess if that changes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a merged record with both halves present, `NF.TxBytes` is the chosen orientation's volume and `NF.RxBytes` the mirror's
- [ ] `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` is unchanged for every existing consumer, verified against prod before and after
- [ ] A test proves the split is the same whichever half arrives first (the #605 property, extended to volume)
- [ ] The dashboard shows the two directions where it is useful to see them apart
- [ ] Docs state what `Tx`/`Rx` mean on a merged record versus a raw NetFlow one
- [ ] Full gate green

## Related

- #605 — establishes the deterministic orientation this depends on; split out of that issue deliberately, since it changes what a metric counts rather than what a label says
- #604 — `source_byte_delta_ratio` compares `NF` against `Zen`, so it reads these counters

comments.body:
## Shipped in `92d5256a`, verified on prod

The entry now accumulates the two halves separately and `finalize` assigns them once `orientation()` has chosen — the chosen half's volume to `Tx`, the mirror's to `Rx`. `orientation()` returns which half it picked so the assignment cannot be guessed.

### The decision the issue asked for, answered

> `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` currently sums `Tx + Rx`, so the total is unchanged by the split. That should be confirmed rather than assumed.

Confirmed by reading every consumer rather than by inspection of one: `volumeOf` (rollup.go:315) is the only path into the volume family and it calls `Counters.Bytes()`/`Packets()`, which sum both directions. `logemit` reports the same sums. Nothing in the tree reads `TxBytes` alone. A test pins `Bytes()` unchanged across the split.

Zenarmor's counters are deliberately **untouched**, per the issue's second question: whether the two sources agree on what "transmit" means has not been checked against a real conn document, and putting them on one axis before that is exactly the assumption this issue exists to remove.

### Live on prod

```
<lan-ip-6>:55677 -> <pub-ip-16>:3478 udp
  flow_nf_bytes=196   flow_nf_packets=3
  flow_nf_tx_bytes=136  flow_nf_tx_packets=2
  flow_nf_rx_bytes=60   flow_nf_rx_packets=1
```

136 + 60 = 196, so the total did not move. Before this, that record read 196 transmitted and nothing received.

### Scope call, stated rather than quietly taken

The split is emitted on the **flow log record** and not as a new metric dimension. Splitting `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` by direction-of-volume would double the largest flow family's series count for a distinction the log record already answers per flow, and the metric label set is deliberately closed at seven. The attributes are emitted on **merged records only** — on a raw NetFlow record they would restate `flow.nf.bytes` and say nothing.

### Acceptance

- [x] On a merged record with both halves present, `NF.TxBytes` is the chosen orientation's volume and `NF.RxBytes` the mirror's
- [x] `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` unchanged for every existing consumer, verified by reading the consumers and pinned by a test
- [x] A test proves the split is the same whichever half arrives first (#605's property, extended to volume)
- [x] Docs state what Tx/Rx mean on a merged record versus a raw NetFlow one
- [x] Full gate green
- [x] The two directions are visible where it is useful — on the flow log record, per the scope call above, rather than as a new metric dimension

body:
## Symptom

The `opnsense-exporter-health` dashboard in the m7kni stack has not been reconciled from GitSync since **2026-07-29T18:42:38Z**, despite `grafana-sync.yml` committing changed content to `rknightion/gc-gitsync-m7kni` six times on 2026-07-31 alone.

The live dashboard is **12 panels behind** the repository.

Found while verifying the opnsense2otel rename (7b7c984). It is **not caused by the rename** — the rename only added a title diff on top of an already-stale resource.

## Evidence

Live vs `gc-gitsync-m7kni@origin/main:networking/opnsense-exporter-health.json`:

| | title | elements |
|---|---|---|
| live (`gcx dashboards get opnsense-exporter-health`) | `OPNsense Exporter Health` | **88** |
| repo | `opnsense2otel Health` | **100** |

`metadata.annotations` on the live resource:

```
grafana.app/updatedBy:        access-policy:417a7d4d-b015-488f-ba9d-5b49351909cf
grafana.app/updatedTimestamp: 2026-07-29T18:42:38Z
```

Commits to `networking/opnsense-exporter-health.json` that never landed:

```
18d5703 2026-07-31 16:28:21   a301c81 2026-07-31 13:20:17
388a70e 2026-07-31 12:23:16   d02459f 2026-07-31 11:19:22
84ea473 2026-07-31 10:36:37   889fb59 2026-07-31 09:45:59
```

## Why this is worse than a stale dashboard

The **companion dashboard in the same commit reconciles fine.** `opnsense-exporter` (the operational dashboard) shows `updatedTimestamp: 2026-07-31T16:28:37Z` — 16 seconds after that same GitSync commit. So one of the two files in a single commit applies and the other does not, and `grafana-sync.yml` reports **success** either way: it only checks that the push to the GitSync repo succeeded, never that Grafana accepted it.

That makes this class of failure invisible. Self-observability panels added by a future change would appear in the repo, pass `make grafana-check`, pass CI, and simply not exist on the stack.

## Investigation notes

- Both resources carry the same `updatedBy` access policy, so it is not a credentials difference between the two.
- Worth checking whether the health dashboard was ever adopted into GitSync's managed set, or whether it retains a manager/provenance from how #431 first created it that makes GitSync decline to own it.
- `opnsense-exporter-health` was created against a **reserved** UID (frozen 2026-07-27, `exists=False` until #431 flipped it), so its creation path differs from the operational dashboard's.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root cause identified: why GitSync applies `opnsense-exporter.json` and skips `opnsense-exporter-health.json` from the same commit
- [ ] Live `opnsense-exporter-health` matches the generated `grafana/dashboard-health.json` (100 elements, title `opnsense2otel Health`)
- [ ] `grafana-sync.yml` gains a post-sync **verification** step that fails the workflow when a pushed dashboard's live spec does not match what was committed — a green sync must mean the stack actually changed
- [ ] The check covers both dashboards, so this cannot silently regress on either one

comments.body:
Fixed in `109e36e` and `bf13e4e`. Verified live: `opnsense-exporter-health` is now **100 elements**, titled `opnsense2otel Health`, `updatedTimestamp 2026-07-31T17:35:45Z` (was 88 / `OPNsense Exporter Health` / `2026-07-29T18:42:38Z`).

## Root cause

GitSync *was* pulling. It was **rejecting the write on schema validation** and skipping the file, which lands the repository in `CompletedWithWarnings` — a state nothing read.

There were **two** violations, not one, both the same mistake: a Python tuple used as shorthand, serialised as a JSON array where the v2 schema wants an object. GitSync reports only the first failure it hits and stops, so the second appeared on the very next pull after the first was fixed.

| # | Field | Offender |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `fieldConfig.overrides` | `grafana/tabs/flow_pipeline.py:321` — `("downloads/day .*", "unit", "short")` |
| 2 | `fieldConfig.defaults.thresholds.steps` | `grafana/build_dashboard.py:798` — `[(None, "green"), (1, "yellow")]` |

`Builder.ts()` forwarded overrides with a bare `overrides or []` and `_thresholds()` forwarded steps unchanged. Five other override call sites and every other threshold call site use the full object form, which is why only this one dashboard broke — and why its companion in the same commit kept applying, leaving no visible symptom.

Nothing caught it because the JSON is *well-formed*: `make dashboard`, `make grafana-check`, promqlcheck and CI all validate structure this repo defines, none validate against the schema Grafana enforces.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] **Root cause identified** — schema-validation rejection on two malformed fields, above.
- [x] **Live matches generated** — 100 elements, correct title, confirmed via `gcx dashboards get`.
- [x] **Post-sync verification that fails the workflow** — `scripts/verify-gitsync.py`, wired into `grafana-sync.yml`. Waits for GitSync to reach the pushed commit, then compares each live dashboard's title and element set against what was committed.
- [x] **Covers both dashboards** — both are passed as `--file` pairs; the run on `bf13e4e` printed `opnsense-exporter matches` and `opnsense-exporter-health matches`.

## Three traps worth keeping

**Fixing by field name is a losing game.** Each fix costs a CI round-trip plus a live pull to reveal the next one. `grafana/tests/test_field_overrides.py` now asserts the **shape**: nothing under a panel's `vizConfig` may be a list whose entries are themselves lists. That single invariant catches both bugs and the next one, before push. Confirmed to fail on the broken artifact and pass after regeneration.

**Repository sync status is ephemeral and actively misleading.** A failed pull still advances `lastRef`, so the next scheduled pull finds *"same commit as last time"*, does nothing, succeeds, and overwrites the status with `state=success` and an empty message list — reporting a clean sync over a resource it never wrote. Observed within ~10s. The verifier therefore treats the **live content comparison as the only verdict**; sync warnings are printed alongside a failure because they name the offending field, but cannot fail the job alone (the job history is persistent, so failing on it would wedge the gate on a long-fixed error).

**gcx has two output traps that produce confident wrong readings.** A response over ~1 MB is **spilled to a temp file** and gcx prints a `gcx.spill_reference` stub instead of the data — these dashboards are 1.4 MB, so parsing the stub reports a perfectly healthy dashboard as *"0 panels live"*. And gcx only emits JSON when it auto-detects an agent; on a bare CI runner it prints a **human table**. `-o json` fixes both.

title: GitSync silently stops reconciling dashboard-health: live stack 12 panels behind since 2026-07-29

body:
## Summary

`smartInfo`'s `output.endurance_used` and `output.spare_available` are modelled as `*float64` (`opnsense/smart.go:48-49`). smartctl serves them as **objects**. On the production firewall — the only target with a real disk — that decode failure costs **every per-device SMART metric**, not just the two wear gauges.

Same class and same blast-radius shape as #609 (`nginxVts` `overCounts`), found the same way: a live payload disagreeing with a struct that no fixture, gate or review had caught.

## The live payload

Probed read-only against the production firewall (OPNsense 26.7.1_1), `api/smart/service/list` then `api/smart/service/info` with `device=ada0&type=a&json=1`:

```
smartList -> {"devices":["ada0"]}

smartInfo output.endurance_used   -> {"current_percent": 84}
smartInfo output.spare_available  -> {"current_percent": 100, "threshold_percent": 10}
output.rotation_rate              -> 0        (an SSD, which is why these two exist at all)
```

Both are objects. Neither is a number, and neither is absent.

## Blast radius: all per-device SMART telemetry on prod

`c.doForm` → `unmarshalBody` turns any `json.Unmarshal` failure into an `APICallError` (`opnsense/client.go:816`), and `FetchSMART` handles a failed **info** call by appending the device with nothing but its name:

```go
var infoResp smartInfoResponse
if err := c.doForm(infoURL, form, &infoResp); err != nil {
    c.log.Debug("smart info call failed for device; skipping", ...)
    data.Devices = append(data.Devices, SMARTDevice{Device: deviceName})
    continue                              // opnsense/smart.go:226-233
}
```

So `ada0` is reported as a device with no health, no temperature, no power-on hours, no ATA attribute table, no rotation rate and no wear. Everything downstream of `infoResp.Output` (`smart.go:237-290`) is skipped.

Confirmed on the live m7kni stack — `opnsense_smart_devices_total` is the **only** `opnsense_smart_*` series that exists:

```
group by (__name__) ({__name__=~"opnsense_smart_.*"})  ->  ["opnsense_smart_devices_total"]
```

`devices_total` survives because it comes from `len(listResp.Devices)` before the per-device loop.

**It fails silently and reads as healthy.** The error is logged at `Debug`, and the collector still reports success:

```
opnsense_exporter_scrape_collector_success{collector="smart"}  ->  1
```

## Why no gate caught it

The two testbeds are virtio VMs. `smartList` returns no devices there, so the canary's `resolveParam` returns `""` and `smartInfo` is **skipped entirely** on both CI targets (`cmd/apidrift/probe.go:264-280`). Only the prod profile has a disk to probe with, and the prod canary's findings had not been triaged past the coverage warnings.

This also means the metrics #577 added — `opnsense_smart_device_endurance_used_percent` and `opnsense_smart_device_spare_available_percent` — have **never** worked on real hardware, which is the only hardware that can produce them.

## Two ledger claims this refutes

Both were about to be written into the ledger as part of #613, on the strength of the preliminary triage on #607/#608. Neither survives the live read:

1. **The verdict "box-state → `missingOK`, profile-scoped to `nightly` + `release-vm`" is wrong.** It rests on prod being able to report these. Prod *does* report them — as objects. This is a type mismodelling, not absent box state. A `missingOK` would have papered over a live decode failure on the one profile that exercises the endpoint.
2. **`smartInfo`'s existing note is wrong in a second way.** #613 already flagged that "the nightly virtio testbed cannot produce ANY smartInfo data at all (`api/smart/service/list` 404s on virtio disks)" is false. The live behaviour is neither a 404 nor data: `smartList` POSTs 200 with `{"devices":[]}`-shaped emptiness on a virtio box, so `smartInfo` is never probed there at all. (A GET returns `{"message":"Unable to run list action"}` — `smart.go:199-203` already documents that the plugin requires POST, and it cost me a wrong reading of prod before I noticed.)

## Fix

Model both as structs with optional members, derived from this capture and from smartmontools' own JSON emitter rather than from the two field names:

- `spare_available` → `current_percent`, `threshold_percent`
- `endurance_used` → `current_percent` (`threshold_percent` optional — do not assume its absence is guaranteed)

Keep the exported gauges reading `current_percent`, so no metric, label, dashboard or catalogue change is needed. `threshold_percent` is a candidate for a separate gauge, but that is an opportunity, not part of this fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test decodes the verbatim prod payload for both fields and fails before the fix — derived from the capture above, never a hand-written shape (the #609 rule)
- [ ] `FetchSMART` returns a fully populated `SMARTDevice` for a device whose payload carries object-shaped wear fields
- [ ] A regression test proves one bad field cannot cost the whole device: assert the health/temperature/attribute fields survive
- [ ] `opnsense_smart_device_endurance_used_percent` and `_spare_available_percent` accumulate on the prod box after deploy
- [ ] Every other per-device SMART family returns on prod (temperature, power-on hours, ATA attributes, health)
- [ ] Consider whether a failed per-device info decode should stop reporting `collector_success=1`, or at least count itself — it is currently a Debug log and nothing else
- [ ] `make schemas` regenerated; goldens stay structure-only
- [ ] Full gate green

## Related

- #609 — the same bug class, shipped and fixed the same day
- #613 — the ledger batch whose `smartInfo` verdict this refutes
- #577 — added the two wear metrics that have never worked
- #611 — per-profile coverage scoping, the other half of why prod's findings sat untriaged

comments.body:
Fix pushed as `d293332e`. **Not closing yet** — the acceptance list requires the per-device families to come back on the live stack, and that needs a CI build plus the hourly watchtower pull. I will verify and close (or reopen the question) after the redeploy.

## What the fix turned out to be

The verdict in the body holds, and upstream source confirms it is stronger than "these two happen to be objects on this drive". **Every** emission site in smartmontools writes an object keyed by `current_percent`:

| site | context |
| --- | --- |
| `ataprint.cpp:1206` | `spare_available`, guessed from the SATA attribute table |
| `ataprint.cpp:1208` | `spare_available.threshold_percent`, only when `0 < threshold < 50` |
| `ataprint.cpp:1217` | `endurance_used`, guessed from the SATA attribute table |
| `ataprint.cpp:1825` | `endurance_used`, Device Statistics page 7 — overrides the guess |
| `nvmeprint.cpp:505` | `spare_available`, both members, unconditionally |
| `nvmeprint.cpp:511` | `endurance_used` |

So a bare number is a shape upstream **cannot** produce, on any drive, on any transport. `threshold_percent` is emitted for `spare_available` only — no emitter writes it for `endurance_used`, which corrects the body's "do not assume its absence is guaranteed". It is modelled (so the canary does not read it as unmodelled drift) and deliberately not exported; a spare-threshold gauge is an opportunity, not part of this.

## The fixture

`opnsense/testdata/smart/info_ada0_prod_26_7.json` is the verbatim body prod returns for `ada0`, captured read-only, with `serial_number` and `wwn` redacted and every modelled field untouched. The pre-fix test failed on all eight assertions at once, which is the blast radius stated as a test:

```
expected EnduranceUsed to be non-nil (wire: {"current_percent":84})
expected SpareAvailable to be non-nil (wire: {"current_percent":100,...})
expected Model to survive, got ""
expected Health=true to survive, got <nil>
expected Temperature to survive
expected PowerOnHours to survive
expected all 14 ATA attribute rows to survive, got 0
expected RotationRate to survive as a present 0 (SSD)
```

The #577 fixture that hid this — `"spare_available": 100` written from the field *name* — is corrected in the same commit. It is the exact #609 failure: a fixture that agreed with the wrong code.

## Acceptance status

- [x] A test decodes the verbatim prod payload for both fields and fails before the fix
- [x] `FetchSMART` returns a fully populated `SMARTDevice` for object-shaped wear fields
- [x] A regression test proves one bad field cannot cost the whole device
- [ ] `_endurance_used_percent` / `_spare_available_percent` accumulate on prod — awaiting redeploy
- [ ] Every other per-device SMART family returns on prod — awaiting redeploy
- [x] Decode failures are no longer silent (see below)
- [x] `make schemas` regenerated; goldens structure-only
- [x] Full gate green

## On the last criterion — it was worth doing properly

Three things, because "a Debug log and nothing else" is what let this run for weeks:

1. **`APICallError.PartialDecode`.** `encoding/json` defers a type error and keeps decoding, so by the time `Unmarshal` returns, every field it understood is already written. `FetchSMARTDevices` now keeps that device instead of throwing it away over one bad field.

   One caveat found by the test rather than assumed: a mismatched field lands as a **present zero, not an absence** — json allocates the pointer before it discovers the mismatch. A drive with a shape-drifted `power_on_time` will export `power_on_hours 0`, which is wrong and looks plausible. That is the accepted cost of keeping the other fields, and it is why (2) is not optional.

2. **`opnsense_smart_device_info_errors{reason="failed"|"partial"}`**, always emitted, zero included. A series that only exists when something is wrong cannot be alerted on, and *absent* is exactly how this hid.

3. Its dashboard row is gated on a new `has_smart_plugin` sentinel (`devices_total`, which comes from the list call and survives this failure mode) rather than `has_smart` (`device_health`) — gating a decode-error panel on one of the series that goes missing would hide it precisely when it matters.

I did **not** make a per-device decode failure flip `collector_success` to 0. The device list still succeeded, other devices may be fine, and a collector-wide failure flag would misreport that; the gauge says what actually happened, at per-device granularity.

## Verified on the live production stack. Closing.

`d293332e` deployed at 19:01Z. Before the fix, `opnsense_smart_devices_total` was the **only** `opnsense_smart_*` series in existence. All twelve families are now present:

```
opnsense_smart_devices_total                    opnsense_smart_device_health
opnsense_smart_device_temperature_celsius       opnsense_smart_device_power_on_hours
opnsense_smart_device_rotation_rate_rpm         opnsense_smart_device_endurance_used_percent
opnsense_smart_device_spare_available_percent   opnsense_smart_device_info_errors
opnsense_smart_attribute_value                  opnsense_smart_attribute_worst
opnsense_smart_attribute_threshold              opnsense_smart_attribute_raw
```

Every value matches the captured payload:

| metric | live | captured payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `device_endurance_used_percent{device="ada0"}` | **84** | `{"current_percent": 84}` |
| `device_spare_available_percent` | **100** | `{"current_percent": 100, "threshold_percent": 10}` |
| `device_temperature_celsius` | **42** | `{"current": 42}` |
| `device_power_on_hours` | **39586** | `{"hours": 39585}` — advanced by one, as it should |
| `device_health` | **1** | `{"passed": true}` |
| `device_rotation_rate_rpm` | **0** | `0` (SSD) |
| `count(attribute_value)` | **14** | 14 ATA rows |
| `device_info_errors{reason="failed"}` | **0** | — |
| `device_info_errors{reason="partial"}` | **0** | — |

Both new error series are present and zero, which is the point of emitting them unconditionally: "healthy" is now a reading rather than an absence.

### Acceptance

- [x] A test decodes the verbatim prod payload for both fields and fails before the fix
- [x] `FetchSMART` returns a fully populated `SMARTDevice` for object-shaped wear fields
- [x] A regression test proves one bad field cannot cost the whole device
- [x] `_endurance_used_percent` / `_spare_available_percent` accumulate on prod
- [x] Every other per-device SMART family returns on prod
- [x] A failed per-device decode now counts itself instead of being a Debug log
- [x] `make schemas` regenerated; goldens structure-only
- [x] Full gate green

### One correction to this issue's own reasoning, since it went into the ledger

The body said no gate caught this because `smartList` returns no devices on the virtio testbeds, so `smartInfo` is "skipped entirely" on both CI targets. **That is wrong.** The live canary run reports `0 skipped (no live parameter)` and returns findings for `smartInfo` on both targets — it cannot do that without probing them. The testbeds do enumerate a virtio disk and `smartInfo` is probed there.

The real reason is sharper: a virtio disk carries none of the vendor-specific attributes smartctl regex-matches to derive these two percentages, so the only shape the testbeds can **ever** show for them is *absent* — and an absent key cannot reveal a type mismodelling. It took the one profile with a real SSD to serve an object where the struct said number.

The ledger now carries that, with the two paths exempted on `nightly` and `release-vm` only so prod keeps enforcing them (`16fbfd17`). A base-scoped exemption there would have hidden this permanently.

Closes #615.

body:
## What

`opnsense/testdata/schemas/exemptions.json` carries a base-scoped `missingOK` for `tailscaleStatus` `Self.KeyExpiry`. #593 asked for it to be retired by "enabling key expiry on the testbed Tailscale node". That framing is wrong in two ways, both established live on 2026-07-31, so the prune is parked here rather than left looking undone on a closed epic.

## Why it is not a one-step box change

**There are three nodes, not one.** The entry is base-scoped, so it applies to `nightly`, `release-vm` **and** `prod`, and each profile reads its own box's `tailscaled`. All three report `Self.KeyExpiry` absent (verified live). Pruning the base entry would immediately set `warnings=true` on all three runs — re-opening the two testbed issues that are currently clean and adding a permanent finding to the prod one.

**It is not a box-side setting at all.** All three nodes are tailnet-**tagged**, and Tailscale disables key expiry by default for tagged devices. Re-enabling is per-device from the admin console Machines page, or `POST /api/v2/device/{deviceId}/key` with `keyExpiryDisabled=false` — tailnet admin credentials, which exist on no box and in no repo (searched). No `tailscale` CLI flag sets it. Corroborated on prod: 7 of its 30 peers *do* carry `KeyExpiry`, which proves the tailnet permits expiry and that this is per-node state rather than a tailnet-wide policy.

**Do not enable it on the prod node.** An expired node key drops the production firewall off the tailnet, which is the transport for both <host-1>'s exporter polling and the prod canary. The canary would take itself offline to clear its own warning.

## The two-step

1. Enable key expiry on the **two testbed nodes** from the Tailscale admin console (or the device API), and confirm from a live canary run that `Self.KeyExpiry` is present on both.
2. **Move** the entry into `profiles.prod.missingOK` rather than deleting it — prod keeps the exemption, because its node must not expire.

Blocked on step 1, which needs tailnet admin access rather than box access.

## Why it matters

`Self.KeyExpiry` now backs an exported metric (#583), so a base-scoped exemption blinds the canary to real drift on a **consumed** field on all three profiles. That is the case the standing triage rule says to fix rather than exempt — hence a tracked parked item, not a permanent exemption.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Key expiry enabled on both testbed Tailscale nodes
- [ ] A live canary run shows `Self.KeyExpiry` present on `nightly` and `release-vm`
- [ ] The exemption moved to `profiles.prod.missingOK` with a reason, not deleted
- [ ] Prod's node left with expiry disabled, and the reason recorded where the next reader will look

comments.body:
Done in `d28029b0`. Both steps complete.

**Step 1 — verified live, not assumed.** You enabled key expiry on the two testbed nodes; I proved it the only way that counts: removed the base-scoped exemption first, pushed, and ran the canary against it (run [30689944562](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense2otel/actions/runs/30689944562)). With nothing suppressing the path:

```
release-vm  Probed 176 endpoints: 173 clean, 0 with missing paths, ...
nightly     Probed 176 endpoints: 175 clean, 0 with missing paths, ...
```

`Self.KeyExpiry` is present on both and is now genuinely enforced. Checking the log for the suppressed path would have proved nothing, which is why it was done this way round.

**Step 2 — moved, not deleted.** The entry now lives in `profiles.prod.missingOK` with the reason attached: prod's node keeps expiry disabled deliberately, because an expired node key drops the production firewall off the tailnet — the transport for both <host-1>'s polling and this canary. The note says so explicitly and marks it "do NOT promote back to base", since the next reader's instinct on seeing a lone prod exemption will be to prune it.

Acceptance:

- [x] Key expiry enabled on both testbed nodes
- [x] Live canary run shows `Self.KeyExpiry` present on `nightly` and `release-vm`

Net effect for #531: prod's warning stays (correctly, and now explained rather than inherited), while the two testbeds go from blind to enforcing on a field that backs `opnsense_tailscale_key_expiry_seconds` (#583).
