body:
## Summary

The Zenarmor flow lane emits **raw kernel device names** as the `interface` label for a small share of records, producing a second series for an interface that already has a friendly-name series. On prod, `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` carries both `interface="LAN"` and `interface="ixl0"`, both `interface="IOT"` and `interface="ixl0_vlan50"`, and so on — the same interface split across two label values, so any `sum by (interface)` under-reports each of them.

Found while diagnosing #602. Read-only investigation, no code changed.

## Evidence

`sum by (interface, source) (increase(opnsense_flow_bytes_total[3h]))`, Zenarmor lane only:

| interface label | bytes/3h |
|---|---|
| LAN | 88,900,160,205 |
| **ixl0** | **632,970,098** |
| IOT | 6,510,459,476 |
| **ixl0_vlan50** | **22,341** |
| MGMT | 25,775,061 |
| **ixl0_vlan100** | 0 |
| OPNDEV | 10,442,294 |
| **ixl0_vlan90** | 444 |

## Cause (high confidence, worth confirming before fixing)

`flowFromDoc` (`internal/logship/zenarmor/flowadapt.go:107`) resolves the friendly name only when the enrichment snapshot is present and the lookup hits:

```go
if snap != nil {
    if name, ok := snap.InterfaceName(r.In.Device); ok {
        r.In.Name = name
    }
    ...
}
```

`Iface.Label()` then falls back to `Device` when `Name` is empty (`record.go:129`) — deliberately, because "a wrong interface label is worse than a missing one". So any record processed before the interface map has loaded gets the raw device name.

The timing evidence fits a startup window rather than a persistent lookup failure:

- The raw-device series are active in only **1–4% of 5m windows** over 24h (`ixl0` 3.8%, `ixl0_vlan100` 2.3%, `ixl0_vlan50` 1.1%, `ixl0_vlan90` 0.9%, `ixl0_vlan25` 0%).
- `changes(process_start_time_seconds[24h])` = **14** — the exporter restarted 14 times in that window.
- 14 restarts × a few minutes of pre-snapshot ingest ≈ the 1–4% observed.

Discriminating check before implementing: after a restart, confirm the raw-device series stops increasing once `opnsense_flow_ifindex_entries` becomes non-zero. If it keeps increasing afterwards, the cause is a genuine map miss instead and this issue needs re-diagnosing.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than tolerating

`Label()`'s fallback is the right call for a record that must be emitted *now*. But the flow lane is push-based and the enrichment snapshot arrives on the exporter's own schedule, so the window is self-inflicted rather than inherent. Options to weigh:

- Hold Zenarmor flow records (as the VLAN repair already holds records, `vlanHoldWindow`) until the first interface map has loaded, with a bound and a counter for anything released early.
- Emit an explicit sentinel rather than the raw device, so the series is visibly "unresolved" instead of masquerading as a distinct interface.
- Leave the behaviour and document that raw-device labels are a startup artifact — the weakest option, since it leaves every `sum by (interface)` quietly wrong for that share.

Note this is separate from the deliberate VLAN handling: `vlanDevice` synthesising `ixl0_vlan50` from Zenarmor's parent-plus-tag report is correct and is what makes the lookup possible at all. The bug is only that the synthesised device name reaches the metric label when the lookup has not yet been possible.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Confirm or refute the startup-window diagnosis with the check above, and record the answer on this issue
- [ ] The `interface` label never carries a raw kernel device name for an interface the box has a description for
- [ ] Anything held or refused is counted as a self-metric, per the existing convention
- [ ] A test covers a flow record arriving before the first enrichment snapshot
- [ ] Re-measured on prod after a restart: no `ixl*` series accumulating on the Zenarmor lane
- [ ] Full gate green (`make test lint docs-check grafana-check`)

## Related

- #603 — multi-WAN egress misattribution
- #605 — merged records' interface dimensions decided by arrival order

comments.body:
## Discriminating check run — startup-window diagnosis **CONFIRMED**, and sharply

Read-only against live m7kni telemetry, 7-day window. The check in the body asked whether the raw-device series keep increasing after the map loads. They do not — not once.

```promql
count_over_time((sum(increase(opnsense_flow_bytes_total{interface=~"ixl.*",source="zenarmor"}[5m])) > 0)[7d:5m])
```

| condition on process uptime at the bucket | 5m buckets with a raw-device increase |
| --- | --- |
| (none — all buckets) | **48** |
| uptime > 120s | 46 |
| uptime > 180s | 30 |
| uptime > 240s | 3 |
| uptime > 300s | **0** |
| uptime > 600s | **0** |

`resets + changes(process_start_time_seconds[7d])` = **51 restarts** over the same window.

So: ~48 accumulating buckets against 51 restarts is **about one 5-minute bucket per restart**, and every byte ever attributed to a raw kernel device name lands with the process less than **300 seconds** old. Past five minutes of uptime the raw-device series are completely flat, across 7 days and 51 restarts.

That is not a lookup failure — a genuine map miss would be uptime-independent, and would have shown up somewhere in the 7 days of steady-state operation. It is a startup window, it closes on its own, and it closes at ~5 minutes.

Two notes for whoever implements the fix:

- **The window is wider than "a few seconds" and narrower than the body's "few minutes" guess.** 30 of the 48 buckets are past 180s. Any hold bound has to cover a ~4–5 minute cold start, not a ~30 second one; a `vlanHoldWindow`-sized bound would not have covered it.
- **`opnsense_flow_ifindex_entries == 0` is not a usable signal for this.** `count_over_time((sum(opnsense_flow_ifindex_entries) == 0)[7d:1m])` returns **nothing** over 7 days — the series is *absent* before it is populated, not zero. Anything gating on "ifindex_entries is zero" will never fire; it has to gate on the snapshot's presence, not on that value.

Also worth recording because it corrects a scale reading in the body: the raw-device volumes are per-process and reset on every restart, so the "632,970,098 bytes/3h for `ixl0`" figure is an accumulation across several restarts within that window, not a steady rate. The bug is real and the fix is still worth making — a `sum by (interface)` is genuinely wrong for the affected windows — but the ongoing leak rate is one cold start's worth of records per restart, not a continuous stream.

Acceptance item 1 (`Confirm or refute the startup-window diagnosis ... and record the answer`) is met by this comment. Remaining work is unchanged.

## Recommendation on the three options, given what the check measured

Not implementing this without a steer, because the three options in the body differ in what they do to `sum by (interface)` and that is a product call, not a mechanical one. What the measurement does settle:

**Option 1 (hold records until the map loads) is more expensive than the body assumed.** The window is up to **300 seconds**, not "a few minutes" loosely — 30 of the 48 accumulating buckets are past 180s of uptime. The Zenarmor flow lane runs at ~96,600 records/h, so a 5-minute hold is on the order of **8,000 buffered records** on a push lane, per restart. That is a real memory bound to size and defend, and `vlanHoldWindow` is nowhere near it.

**Option 2 (sentinel instead of the raw device) is cheap and honest, and it is what I would do.** It satisfies the acceptance item as written — the `interface` label never carries a raw kernel device name — and it converts a series that *masquerades as a real interface* into one that is visibly unresolved. It does not recover the bytes into `LAN`, so `sum by (interface)` is still short by one cold start's worth per restart; but those bytes become countable and attributable instead of silently splitting a real interface in two.

**Option 3 (document only) I would not take**, for the reason the body gives.

There is a fourth worth weighing before choosing, because it fixes the undercount rather than relabelling it: **resolve the name later**. The device name (`ixl0`, `ixl0_vlan50`) is already correct on the record — only the friendly name is missing — so if the rollup key retained the device and the friendly name were applied at emit time, a record ingested cold would land on the right series once the snapshot arrives. Whether that is possible depends on where the rollup keys by label, which I have not traced; if it keys at record time, this is off the table.

Either way, per the standing convention, whatever is held or refused gets a counter.

**Also worth correcting in the body before anyone sizes this**: the "632,970,098 bytes/3h for `ixl0`" figure reads as a rate but is not one. These counters reset with the process, and every byte lands within 300s of a start, so that number is an accumulation across several restarts in the window. The ongoing leak is one cold start's worth of records per restart — which is why this is correctly a P2, and why option 2's residual undercount is a smaller concession than it first looks.

## Shipped in `80d8f62b` — option 2, and the emit-time fix is off the table by the criterion you set

### The trace, first, because it was the condition

> Whether that is possible depends on where the rollup keys by label, which I have not traced; if it keys at record time, this is off the table.

**It keys at record time.** `Rollup.Observe` (rollup.go:157) calls `keyFor(rec)` (rollup.go:290), whose first field is `Interface: interfaceLabel(rec)` — the resolved LABEL STRING, not the device. The cell it lands in holds a **cumulative** counter, so the resolved name cannot be applied later without merging two cells' running totals into one emitted series mid-life.

The same is true of every other per-interface accumulator: `DistinctDests`, `LastSeen`, `TopTalkers` and `DeltaRatio` all key on `interfaceLabel(r)` at observe time. Retaining the device would mean a resolution-and-merge step in five snapshot paths, not one.

So option 4 is off the table on your own criterion, and option 1 was already ruled out by the measurement (300s window, ~96,600 records/h, ~8,000 buffered records per restart on a push lane).

### What shipped

`Iface.Unresolved` marks an interface whose device the source stated but whose description could not be looked up, and `Label()` returns `"unresolved"` for it. A **named** sentinel, not `""` — an empty label is *absent* to Prometheus, so the bytes would vanish from `sum by (interface)` entirely instead of showing up as a bucket that can be seen, alerted on and watched drain after a restart.

Two things it deliberately does not do:

- **The device is not discarded.** It still travels on the record and reaches the log as `flow.in_device` / `flow.out_device`, so a cold-window record can still be joined against the interface metrics by device. Nothing is lost; the raw name is only barred from the metric LABEL.
- **A populated interface table that simply does not name a device is left alone.** The sentinel is for "we could not ask", not "there is no answer" — otherwise it would swallow every real interface the box has no description for. Both cases have a test.

Counted by `opnsense_flow_interface_unresolved_total`, emitted from zero, with the 7-day/51-restart measurement written into its help text so a reader knows one burst per restart is the expected shape.

### Acceptance

- [x] Startup-window diagnosis confirmed and recorded (your comment above)
- [x] The `interface` label never carries a raw kernel device name for an interface the box has a description for
- [x] Anything refused is counted as a self-metric
- [x] A test covers a flow record arriving before the first enrichment snapshot, and its twin covers the populated-table-missing-one-device case
- [x] Full gate green
- [ ] Re-measured on prod after a restart: no `ixl*` series accumulating on the Zenarmor lane — deployed at `80d8f62b`, and the counter reads **31** for this process's own cold window, which is one restart's worth and exactly the predicted shape. Worth one more look after a few more restarts have accumulated.

Also, for the record: your correction of the body's "632,970,098 bytes/3h" figure is right and it changed the sizing — that number is an accumulation across restarts, not a rate, and the residual undercount option 2 leaves is one cold start's worth per restart.

title: Zenarmor flow lane emits raw kernel device names as the interface label, splitting each interface across two series

body:
## Summary

`fragmentDisagrees` (`internal/flow/correlate.go`) compares each NetFlow fragment's `In`, `Out`, `Direction`, `VLANID` and `Enrich` against the entry's sample and counts a mismatch as a disagreement about "the conversation's own identity" (#590). But the two **unidirectional halves** of one conversation share a `corrKey` by design, and their `In`/`Out`/`Direction` are necessarily mirror images — so the counter fires on ordinary bidirectional traffic by construction. That has two consequences: the counter cannot do the job it was added for, and `finalize()` emits whichever half arrived first, so a merged record's interface and direction are decided by arrival order.

Found while diagnosing #602. Read-only investigation against live m7kni telemetry, no code changed.

## Why the halves share a key

`corrKey` is `(community, bucket)`. `CommunityID` is computed from `CanonicalTuple`, which is deliberately direction-independent — `record.go:258` says so outright: *"across NetFlow's unidirectional halves, which report one conversation twice with the endpoints swapped"*. That is exactly the property that makes the correlator work. It also means the A→B and B→A records land on the same key with opposite ingress/egress interfaces and opposite directions, and `fragmentDisagrees` compares precisely those fields.

## Measured on prod

- `netflow_records_decoded_total` 431,190/h against `correlator_emitted_total` 134,733/h → **3.36 fragments per emitted record** (consistent with #346's measured 3.75).
- `correlator_fragment_disagreement_total` = **144,076/h**. Against non-first fragments (431,190 − 134,733 = 296,457), that is **48.6% of every fragment the counter can examine**.
- Merged flow logs, 90m sample, 1,304 merged records: `('LAN','AAISP')` 533 times and `('AAISP','LAN')` 117 times — the same conversation shape emitted with `In`/`Out` mirrored.
- 294 of 1,304 merged records (**22.5%**) have a public source address, i.e. the reverse half won the sample and the record is emitted describing the conversation backwards.

## Two problems, in order of impact

**1. `finalize()` emits arrival-order dimensions.** For a bidirectional conversation there is no single correct `In`/`Out`/`Direction` for the merged record, but the current behaviour picks one at random (whichever datagram landed first) rather than resolving it. 22.5% of merged records are labelled from the reverse half. This propagates into `interfaceLabel`, into `opnsense_flow_bytes_total{interface=...}`, and into the direction label. Worth deciding what a merged bidirectional record's interface and direction *should* mean before changing anything — that is a semantics question, not a bug fix.

**2. The counter is not actionable.** At 48.6% of examinable fragments it cannot distinguish "the fragments disagree about the conversation's identity" (the condition #590 wanted visible) from "this is a normal two-directional conversation". Either exclude the mirror-image case — compare the *canonical* orientation, or exclude `In`/`Out`/`Direction` for fragments whose endpoints are swapped relative to the sample — or split the counter so the expected case is counted separately from the genuinely anomalous one (a fragment disagreeing about VLAN or enrichment while pointing the same way).

The `TCPFlags` exclusion already in `fragmentDisagrees` is the precedent: a field that is merged by design is not a disagreement.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fragment_disagreement_total` counts only genuinely anomalous fragments; the mirror-image case is either excluded or counted separately under its own name
- [ ] A decision is recorded (issue comment is fine) on what `In`/`Out`/`Direction` mean on a merged bidirectional record, and `finalize()` implements it deterministically rather than by arrival order
- [ ] A test proves the two halves of one conversation do not register as a disagreement, and that the emitted dimensions are the same whichever half arrives first
- [ ] Re-measured on prod: the counter's rate is a small fraction of examinable fragments, or the issue documents why it legitimately is not
- [ ] Full gate green (`make test lint docs-check grafana-check`)

## Related

- #603 — multi-WAN egress misattribution (a separate cause of a wrong `Out`)
- #602 — the alert whose per-interface grouping this affects

comments.body:
## Read #603 alongside this one

These two are the same problem surface from two directions and fixing either in isolation will produce a wrong answer.

- **This issue (#605):** `In`/`Out`/`Direction` on a merged record are taken from whichever unidirectional half arrived first, so 22.5% of merged records describe the conversation backwards.
- **#603:** `Out` names the wrong WAN because the pre-NAT record — the only copy that can correlate with Zenarmor — inherits ng_netflow's FIB-derived `OUTPUT_SNMP`, which always points at the default-route WAN.

Both land on the same fields, and both feed `interfaceLabel` → `opnsense_flow_bytes_total{interface=...}` and every per-interface flow panel. The semantics question in this issue ("what should `In`/`Out`/`Direction` mean on a merged bidirectional record") is an **input** to #603's repair: a destination-matching mechanism cannot decide what "egress" means until the record's orientation is deterministic. Settle it here first, or at minimum in the same pass.

Do not treat them as sequential independent tickets.

## Decision: what `In`/`Out`/`Direction` mean on a merged bidirectional record

Recorded before any code, per the acceptance list and because #603's repair consumes it.

### The rule

**A merged record is described from ONE of its two unidirectional halves, chosen by evidence, never by arrival order. Every dimension on the emitted record comes from that one half — the tuple, `In`, `Out`, `Direction` and the scopes together.**

Precedence for choosing the half, strongest evidence first:

1. **Zenarmor's conn document, when the entry has one.** It is the only connection-oriented source in the pipeline — one document per connection, with an explicit `direction` — so it is the only thing here that knows who *initiated*. Prefer the NetFlow half whose `Direction` matches it.
2. **Otherwise, the half with the earliest `Start`** (FIRST_SWITCHED, firewall clock). The initiator's half starts first by definition, and the firewall clock is independent of the order datagrams reached us.
3. **Tie on `Start` → prefer the local→remote half** (`SrcScope != "remote"`). A tie means we cannot tell who initiated; describing the conversation from the local end is the more useful reading and is what the rest of the pipeline assumes.
4. **Still tied → canonical tuple order**, so the outcome is total and deterministic.

### Why "pick one whole half" rather than "compute merged dimensions"

Because there is no coherent merged answer, and splicing produces incoherent records.

`In`, `Out`, `Direction`, `SrcScope`, `DstScope` and the tuple are one **consistent set** on each half: `In=LAN, Out=WAN, Direction=outbound, src=local` on the forward half, and the exact mirror on the reverse. Taking `Out` from one and `Direction` from the other yields a record describing a conversation that never happened, and `interfaceLabel` (`processor.go:387`) reads `Direction` to decide *which* of `In`/`Out` to label by — so those two fields are not independently choosable even in principle.

I considered and rejected adopting Zenarmor's *tuple* on a merged record (using it for direction only, as above). Zenarmor carries no ifIndex, so its orientation cannot supply `In`/`Out`; splicing its tuple onto a NetFlow half's interfaces would recreate exactly the incoherence in the previous paragraph, and would leave `SrcScope`/`DstScope` describing the other orientation.

### What this does NOT decide

**It does not force every merged record to read "outbound".** Rule 3 is a tiebreak, not the primary rule — an inbound-initiated conversation (a port-forwarded service, say) is still identified as inbound by rules 1 and 2, which are initiation evidence rather than locality. That distinction was the main risk in the obvious "always orient local→remote" formulation, and it is why initiation evidence is ranked above locality rather than the other way round.

### The consequence #603 needs

Once this lands, a merged record's orientation is a fact rather than a coin flip, so "which interface did this conversation leave by" is a well-formed question and `Out` on the chosen half is the field a destination-match (or pf-state) mechanism has to correct. **#603 should be read as: repair `Out` on the orientation this issue establishes.** Doing it the other way round — correcting `Out` on a half chosen by arrival order — would correct the reverse half 22.5% of the time.

### Mechanism, and the counter

The correlator keeps the first fragment of **each** orientation (`sample` and its mirror; there are only ever two), decides between them in `finalize()`, and:

- `fragmentDisagrees` compares a fragment only against the sample **of its own orientation**. The mirror-image case stops being a disagreement by construction — the same reasoning as the existing `TCPFlags` exclusion: a field that differs by design is not a disagreement.
- Mirror fragments are counted separately as their own `CorrelatorStats` counter, so the expected case stays visible instead of being silently dropped from the numerator. Per the standing convention, what is excluded gets counted.

### Not in scope here, recorded so it is not lost

A NetFlow record is strictly unidirectional and all its volume lands in `Tx` (`processor.go:262-268`), so the correlator currently sums **both halves' bytes into `TxBytes`** and leaves `RxBytes` at zero. A merged record therefore reports the whole conversation as transmit. Once orientation is deterministic, the forward half's bytes could go to `Tx` and the mirror's to `Rx`, which would make `RxBytes` mean something on merged records for the first time — but that changes what `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` counts and deserves its own issue rather than riding along on this one. Filing separately.

## Re-measured on prod after deploy. Closing, with the residual documented rather than waved away.

`f88f7f91` deployed at 19:01Z. Measured over a 3-minute window on the live stack:

| | rate/3m |
| --- | --- |
| `netflow_records_decoded_total` | 14,204 |
| `correlator_emitted_total` | 2,944 |
| examinable fragments (decoded − emitted) | 11,260 |
| `correlator_fragment_disagreement_total` | **2,524 → 22.4%** of examinable |
| `correlator_fragment_mirrored_total` | **2,188 → 19.4%** of examinable |

Before the fix the disagreement counter read **48.6%**. The mirror split accounts for the difference almost exactly: ~19 points were the conversation's reverse half being counted as an anomaly, and they now sit in their own series where they belong.

### The last acceptance item, answered honestly

> Re-measured on prod: the counter's rate is a small fraction of examinable fragments, **or the issue documents why it legitimately is not**

It is not a small fraction. 22.4% is much better than 48.6% and it is now *meaningful* — every one of those is a genuine same-orientation disagreement, where two fragments pointing the same way reported different interfaces, direction, VLAN or enrichment — but it is not small, and I am not going to call it fixed.

The most likely dominant cause is already filed: **#603**. A pre-NAT record's `Out` comes from ng_netflow's FIB lookup, and the egress repair rewrites it only for records whose source is a WAN address — so across a long flow's fragments, `Out` can legitimately differ between the copies depending on which repair fired. That is exactly a same-orientation disagreement on the interface field, and it should shrink when #603's pf-state mechanism gives every fragment the same authoritative answer.

So: the counter now measures the thing it was built to measure (#590), and its remaining level is a real signal about `Out` instability rather than an artifact of bidirectional traffic. Re-measure after #603 lands; if it stays near 22% then something else is moving and it deserves its own issue.

### Acceptance

- [x] `fragment_disagreement_total` counts only genuinely anomalous fragments; the mirror case is counted separately as `correlator_fragment_mirrored_total`
- [x] A decision recorded on what `In`/`Out`/`Direction` mean on a merged bidirectional record, and `finalize()` implements it deterministically (see the decision comment above; `corrEntry.orientation()`)
- [x] A test proves the two halves do not register as a disagreement, and that the emitted dimensions are identical whichever half arrives first — plus one pinning that an inbound-initiated conversation stays inbound, which the naive "always orient local→remote" rule would have broken
- [x] Re-measured on prod; the rate is documented above, including why it is not yet small
- [x] Full gate green

### Split out deliberately

**#617** — a merged record still sums both halves' bytes into `NF.TxBytes` with `RxBytes` permanently zero. This issue makes the orientation deterministic, which is the prerequisite for splitting them, but that changes what `opnsense_flow_bytes_total` counts and belongs on its own issue rather than riding along here.

Closes #605.

title: Correlator: the two unidirectional halves of one conversation register as fragment disagreements, and finalize() emits arrival-order dimensions

body:
## Summary

`opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_ratio` is documented as "1.0 is agreement" between NetFlow and Zenarmor byte counts on a merged record. Measured against live prod data, the two sides are not measuring the same thing, in two independent ways — so the ratio's deviation from 1.0 is mostly measurement artifact rather than the "disagreement is the signal" the metric is built to expose (#346 decision 3).

Found while diagnosing #602. Read-only investigation, no code changed.

## Problem 1 — wire bytes against payload bytes on the majority of records

`zenBytes` (`internal/logship/zenarmor/flowadapt.go:243`) falls back to Zenarmor's **payload** bytes (`pbytes`) when `nbytes` is 0. That fallback is right on its own terms — the alternative is reporting "DNS: 311 flows, 0 bytes" — but the resulting figure is then compared against NetFlow's **wire** bytes.

Measured on prod:

- `payload_byte_fallback_total` = 49,028/h against 96,627 Zenarmor flow records/h → the fallback fires on roughly **half** of all Zenarmor flow records.
- 54% of merged records (486 of a 900-record sample) are 2–3 packet UDP flows, exactly the population where `nbytes` is 0.
- On that population the implied per-packet gap clusters at **26–28 bytes** (IPv4 IP+UDP header = 28) with a second cluster near 48 (IPv6). Mean 92.0 NetFlow bytes/pkt against 52.6 Zenarmor bytes/pkt.
- p90 of the ratio on that sub-population alone: **1.96**.

So on half the records the metric reports header overhead as "source disagreement". This is worst precisely where the metric is least useful and best where it agrees anyway: flows of ≥64 packets show mean Zenarmor 1092 packets against NetFlow 1121 and a ratio of 1.42; 16–64 packet flows sit at 1.09.

Whatever the fix, the two sides need to be comparable. Options to weigh: prefer `pbytes` on both sides when either side fell back; add packets to the comparison so header overhead is derivable; carry a "byte basis" marker on the record so the histogram can split wire-vs-wire from payload-vs-wire; or exclude fallback records from `DeltaRatio.Observe` entirely and count the exclusions.

## Problem 2 — a window-partial NetFlow total against a whole-connection Zenarmor total

`corrKey` buckets by `floor(End / window)` (`internal/flow/correlate.go:59`), so a connection longer than the window emits one record per window carrying **only that window's** NetFlow bytes. The single Zenarmor conn document carries the **whole connection's** counters and merges into whichever bucket its `End` falls in. The prod box has `activeTimeout=1800`, so long flows are re-reported by ng_netflow every 30 minutes and this is routinely triggered.

Measured on prod: 3.2% of merged records overall and **12.3% of AAISP records** have a ratio below 0.9. Examples:

```
ratio 0.013   nf=210    nfp=3    zen=15718  zenp=239
ratio 0.025   nf=1260   nfp=24   zen=50215  zenp=63
ratio 0.043   nf=887    nfp=16   zen=20489  zenp=41
```

These read as "Zenarmor counted 75× more bytes than crossed the wire", which is impossible. They are a partial total against a complete one. The metric's own doc comment ("a ratio below 1 … is rare but real on the short-UDP payload-fallback flows") accounts for a different and much smaller effect than what is actually there.

## Why this matters beyond the deleted alert

#602 removes the alert built on this series, but the histogram and its dashboard panel stay. As it stands the panel invites exactly the misreading the alert made: it looks like an inspection-coverage signal and is mostly an accounting-basis signal. Either the comparison is made like-for-like, or the metric's help text and the panel description need to say plainly what the deviation from 1.0 actually consists of.

If the underlying security question ("is traffic evading inspection") is still wanted, it needs a **byte-weighted** comparison — the ratio of summed bytes on merged records — not a percentile of per-flow ratios. Byte-weighted, prod currently reads 1.22–1.36, i.e. no blind spot.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The two sides of the ratio are on a comparable basis, or the record carries enough information for a consumer to tell which basis it is on
- [ ] Records whose NetFlow side is a window partial against a whole-connection Zenarmor side are either excluded, corrected, or counted so the sub-1.0 tail is explicable
- [ ] Whatever is excluded or refused is **counted** as a self-metric, per the existing convention in `RepairStats` and `CorrelatorStats`
- [ ] The metric help text and the dashboard panel description state what the deviation from 1.0 comprises
- [ ] A test pins the wire-vs-payload case and the window-partial case with fixtures derived from real captures, not synthesised shapes
- [ ] Full gate green (`make test lint docs-check grafana-check`)

## Related

- #602 — delete the alert built on this series
- #603 — multi-WAN egress misattribution

comments.body:
## Shipped in `2e3057ec`, verified on prod

Both halves, as decided: a byte-basis marker carried on the record, and window partials excluded from `DeltaRatio.Observe` with a counter. Not the byte-weighted rewrite, not docs-only.

**Problem 1 — the basis.** `finalize()` builds a merged record from a NetFlow half, so the Zenarmor lane's own `PayloadByteFallback` did not survive the merge at all: the basis was invisible on precisely the record the ratio is computed from. The merged record now carries `Repairs.ZenBytesArePayload`, emitted as `flow.zen_bytes_are_payload`. Those records stay IN the histogram — excluding half the data would be worse than labelling it.

**Problem 2 — the window partial.** Excluded and counted. The discriminator is the **Zenarmor side's own span crossing a window boundary**, using the same bucket arithmetic `corrKey` does. That is read from one clock, so it needs no agreement between the two sources' timestamps — which matters, because their disagreement is what the metric is for.

### Live on prod

A real merged record, 25 minutes after deploy, carrying both markers:

```
<lan-ip-6>:55677 -> <pub-ip-16>:3478 udp STUN pass
  flow_nf_bytes=196  flow_zen_bytes=114
  flow_zen_bytes_are_payload=true
  flow_window_partial=true
```

`196 - 114 = 82` across 3 packets — the payload-vs-wire gap this metric was reporting as source disagreement.

```
opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_excluded_total  1,452 in ~15 min
```

Non-zero and steady, which is what a box with a 1800-second active timeout should produce. It is emitted from zero, so "the histogram is complete" is a claim a reader can check rather than assume.

### Acceptance

- [x] The two sides are on a comparable basis, or the record carries enough for a consumer to tell which basis it is on
- [x] Window partials excluded and counted
- [x] The exclusion is a self-metric, per the `RepairStats` / `CorrelatorStats` convention
- [x] The metric help text and the dashboard panel description state what the deviation from 1.0 comprises — including the byte-weighted recommendation for the security question
- [x] Tests pin both cases; the window-partial fixture uses the live figures recorded on this issue (`nf=210 nfp=3 zen=15718 zenp=239`) and the payload case uses the measured 28-byte-per-packet IPv4 IP+UDP shape rather than an invented one
- [x] Full gate green

One thing worth knowing for whoever reads the panel next: a **short** flow can be marked `window_partial` when its Zenarmor span merely straddles a bucket boundary. That is not a false positive — the conn document still merged into one bucket while the NetFlow side split across two — but it does mean the exclusion rate is not a pure measure of long connections.

title: source_byte_delta_ratio is not a like-for-like comparison: wire bytes vs payload bytes, and a window partial vs a whole connection

body:
## Summary

On a multi-WAN box with pf policy routing, the exporter attributes **policy-routed egress traffic to the wrong WAN**. The pre-NAT NetFlow record — the only copy that can ever correlate with a Zenarmor conn document — inherits ng_netflow's `OUTPUT_SNMP`, which is a FIB lookup and therefore always names the *default-route* WAN. The existing egress repair (`correctEgress`, `internal/flow/repair.go:874`) cannot fix it because it keys on the record's **source address**, and a pre-NAT record's source is a private LAN address.

Consequence on prod: **every byte that Zenarmor inspected and that actually left via WAN2 is reported as WAN1**, and WAN2 gets zero correlated records — so `opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` is permanently empty while VIRGIN carries 11.1 GB/3h.

Diagnosed read-only against live m7kni telemetry and the prod firewall (OPNsense 26.7.1_1). No code changed.

## Topology (prod, read from `/conf/config.xml` and `workers.map`)

| role | key | device | descr |
|---|---|---|---|
| WAN1, default route | `opt7` | `pppoe0` | AAISP |
| WAN2, policy-routed | `opt6` | `ixl1` | VIRGIN |
| LAN trunk | `lan` | `ixl0` | LAN |
| VLAN children | `opt2/3/4/8` | `ixl0_vlan50/100/25/90` | IOT / MGMT / CAM / OPNDEV |

- NetFlow capture: `opt7,opt4,opt2,lan,opt3,opt8,opt6`, with `egress_only = opt7,opt6`. `activeTimeout=1800`, `inactiveTimeout=15`.
- Zenarmor: a **single** worker, `netmap@ixl0` / `netmap@ixl0^`, tags `lan;netmap;routedmode`. It inspects only the LAN trunk (and its VLAN children, which ride the same NIC). It sees neither WAN.
- pf has 16 active `route-to` rules; default gateway is `pppoe0`.

## The two copies of one outbound flow

For a LAN host going out via WAN2, ng_netflow exports two records with **different 5-tuples**:

1. **Pre-NAT**, captured on `lan`: `<lan-ip-10>:45794 → <pub-ip-15>:8007`. Same tuple Zenarmor saw on ixl0, so same community-id → **this is the copy that correlates**. Its `OUTPUT_SNMP` comes from the FIB.
2. **Post-NAT**, captured on `ixl1` (egress_only): `<pub-ip-14>:25012 → <pub-ip-15>:8007`. Source is VIRGIN's own WAN address, so `correctEgress` resolves it correctly to VIRGIN — but the tuple no longer matches anything Zenarmor saw, so it can **never** correlate.

## Confirmed on prod, same conversation, both copies

From the merged/netflow flow logs in Loki (90m window):

```
PRE  <lan-ip-10>     -> <pub-ip-15>:8007 tcp  lane=merged   out=AAISP   zen=11259  in=LAN
POST <pub-ip-14>  -> <pub-ip-15>:8007 tcp  lane=netflow  out=VIRGIN  egress_corrected=true
```

Independently confirmed on the box:

```
# pfctl -ss
all tcp <pub-ip-15>:8007 <- <lan-ip-10>:45794                          TIME_WAIT:TIME_WAIT
all tcp <pub-ip-14>:25012 (<lan-ip-10>:45794) -> <pub-ip-15>:8007      TIME_WAIT:TIME_WAIT

# route -n get <pub-ip-15>
   gateway: <pub-ip-3>
 interface: pppoe0            <-- what OUTPUT_SNMP reports
```

pf NATs the flow to `<pub-ip-14>` and sends it out `ixl1`. The FIB says `pppoe0`. The merged record carrying Zenarmor's 11,259 bytes is labelled **AAISP**.

## Consequence in the metrics

`sum by (interface, source) (increase(opnsense_flow_bytes_total[3h]))`:

| interface | netflow | zenarmor |
|---|---|---|
| AAISP | 128.8 GB | 0 |
| VIRGIN | **11.1 GB** | **0** |
| LAN | 6.9 GB | 88.9 GB |
| IOT | 571 MB | 6.5 GB |

VIRGIN's 11.1 GB is entirely post-NAT records (295 of a 300-record sample have source `<pub-ip-14>`, `egress_corrected=true` on 292). Not one carries Zenarmor data. VIRGIN is a live WAN — 119.9 GB out on the link — not an idle backup.

## Proposed direction

Rob's suggestion — match on the destination for locally-originated/pre-NAT records — verifies on real data: joining pre-NAT and post-NAT copies on `(dst addr, dst port, proto)` found 12 matched pairs in the 90m sample, all 12 of them merged records. NAT preserves the destination for outbound traffic, so it is a usable join key. Sketch, for discussion rather than a decided design:

- A short-lived table keyed on `(proto, dst addr, dst port)` populated by post-NAT WAN-egress records (which carry the true egress via the existing repair), consulted by pre-NAT records to override `Out` — a third mechanism alongside repairs 1–3, with its own counter so it is observable like the rest.
- Ambiguity is real and must be refused rather than guessed: two LAN hosts to the same `(dst, dport)` over different WANs cannot be separated on that key alone. Consider `(proto, dst addr, dst port, src port)` — pf preserves the source port in many of the states above (`<lan-ip-1>:32944 → <pub-ip-2>:32944`) but rewrites it in others (`<lan-ip-10>:45794 → <pub-ip-14>:25012`), so the source port is a tiebreaker, never a requirement.
- Alternative worth costing first: read the pf state table (or `pfctl -ss`) via the API and resolve egress from the NAT binding directly. That is authoritative rather than inferential — pf is where the routing decision actually happens — at the cost of a new polled endpoint and a per-flow lookup.
- Whatever is chosen, `ifaceIsWAN` currently treats `Iface.Corrected` as proof-of-WAN-by-construction (`internal/flow/repair.go:996`), so a new mechanism setting `Out` must not reuse that flag without re-reading how direction inference consumes it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pre-NAT NetFlow record for traffic policy-routed out a non-default WAN is labelled with the WAN it actually left by, verified against `pfctl -ss` on the prod box for a specific conversation
- [ ] `opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` accumulates observations, or the issue documents why VIRGIN legitimately cannot correlate and what the metric means instead
- [ ] The mechanism has its own counter in `RepairStats`, published as a self-metric, and refusals (ambiguous key) are counted separately from successes
- [ ] Ambiguous cases are refused, not guessed — with a test that proves two hosts to the same destination over different WANs do not get cross-attributed
- [ ] `docs/` states the multi-WAN attribution behaviour and its limits
- [ ] Full gate green (`make test lint docs-check grafana-check`)

## Related

- #602 — the alert that surfaced this (VIRGIN reading 0 is what prompted the investigation)
- #604 — `source_byte_delta_ratio` is not a like-for-like comparison
- #605 — the `interface` label on merged records names the egress WAN, not the interface Zenarmor inspected on

comments.body:
## Read #605 alongside this one

These two are the same problem surface from two directions and fixing either in isolation will produce a wrong answer.

- **This issue (#603):** `Out` names the wrong WAN because the pre-NAT record inherits the FIB default route.
- **#605:** `In`/`Out`/`Direction` on a merged record are taken from whichever unidirectional half arrived first, so 22.5% of merged records describe the conversation backwards.

Both land on the same fields, and both feed `interfaceLabel` → `opnsense_flow_bytes_total{interface=...}` and every per-interface flow panel. Concretely: a destination-matching repair for this issue has to know which orientation the record is in before it can decide what "egress" means, and #605's answer to "what should `Out` mean on a bidirectional merged record" is an input to that. Settle #605's semantics question first, or at minimum in the same pass.

Do not treat them as sequential independent tickets.

## Status 2026-07-31: not started. The session that was going to do this ran out of budget before reaching it.

Recording this so the next reader does not have to guess whether any of the flow cluster was attempted. It was not — no code, no probes, no decision recorded. Nothing in this issue or in #605, #604, #606 has been superseded; read them exactly as filed.

What that session did land, none of it touching `internal/flow/` or `internal/logship/zenarmor/`: #602, #610, #611, #612 (SHAs `fc8a370`, `34c1524`, `78d20f4`, `8148653`), plus #615 filed as a new P0. `main` is at `8148653`, tree clean, CI green.

The ordering constraint from the comment above still stands and is still the first thing to get right: **#605's semantics decision is an input to this issue's repair**, and #605/#603/#604/#606 contend on `internal/flow/correlate.go`, `repair.go`, `record.go` and `zenarmor/flowadapt.go`, so they are one sequential lane, not four parallel ones.

## The pf-state-table alternative was costed first, as the body asked. It wins outright — and it is not the join the body sketched

Probed read-only against the prod firewall (OPNsense 26.7.1_1) via <host-1>. **Recommendation: build the pf-state mechanism and do not build the `(proto, dst addr, dst port)` destination-match table.** The reasoning below is measurement, not preference.

### `api/diagnostics/firewall/query_states` carries the routing decision verbatim

The endpoint (POST, `{"current":1,"rowCount":-1,"searchPhrase":""}`) returns one row per state with these keys:

```
age bytes descr direction dst_addr dst_port expires flags gateway id iface interface
ipproto label nat_addr nat_port pkts proto rule src_addr src_port state
```

plus an optional **`route-to`** field, formatted `<gateway>@<device>` — for example `<pub-ip-5>@ixl1`. That is not an inference about where a packet went. It is the `route-to` pf applied, naming the egress device, straight from the state that made the decision.

Its presence is also an exact discriminator for the bug: `route-to` is set **only** when a policy-route rule fired. A state without it followed the FIB, which is precisely the case where `OUTPUT_SNMP` is already correct. So the mechanism is "override `Out` iff the state carries a `route-to`" — no heuristic about when to trust ng_netflow.

### The join is the pre-NAT tuple itself. No NAT-binding join, no ambiguity

The body assumed the pre-NAT copy would have to be joined to a post-NAT one. It does not. pf keeps **both** states, and the `direction: "in"` state is the pre-NAT view **and already carries `route-to`**. Here is the exact conversation from the body, live:

```json
{"proto":"tcp","direction":"in","src_addr":"<lan-ip-10>","src_port":"36104","nat_addr":null,
 "dst_addr":"<pub-ip-15>","dst_port":"8007","route-to":"<pub-ip-5>@ixl1",
 "descr":"Policy-route overvirgin hosts via VIRGIN"}
{"proto":"tcp","direction":"out","src_addr":"<pub-ip-14>","src_port":"32552","nat_addr":"<lan-ip-10>",
 "nat_port":"36104","dst_addr":"<pub-ip-15>","dst_port":"8007","route-to":"<pub-ip-5>@ixl1"}
```

The first row's `(proto, src_addr, src_port, dst_addr, dst_port)` **is** the pre-NAT NetFlow record's 5-tuple, verbatim. So the lookup is a full-5-tuple exact match against `direction:"in"` rows, not a partial-key match on the destination.

That removes the ambiguity the body flagged as needing refusal, measured on the live table:

| check over the live state table | result |
| --- | --- |
| `direction:"in"` rows | 2,844 |
| …of which carry `route-to` | 1,492 (`pppoe0` 1,473, **`ixl1` 19**) |
| duplicate 5-tuple keys among them | **0** |
| duplicate 5-tuple keys across all `direction:"in"` rows | **0** |
| keys mapping to more than one egress device | **0** |

Zero. The destination-match table the body sketched would have had to refuse the two-hosts-one-destination case; this key cannot produce it, because it is the same tuple pf itself keys states by. (Refusals still need counting — see below — but for "no state found", not for "ambiguous".)

`route-to` also proves VIRGIN is reachable through this mechanism: 19 `direction:"in"` states currently name `ixl1`, which is the population that today reports as AAISP.

### Cost, measured rather than estimated

| | |
| --- | --- |
| full table, `rowCount:-1` | **2.94 MB**, **642 ms**, 5,836 rows |
| current state count | 5,949 (`pf_states` says limit 1,000,000) |
| rows carrying `route-to` | 3,211 of 5,836 (55%) |
| rows carrying a NAT binding | 1,778 |

Not free, and not prohibitive. It belongs on the slow or cold poll tier with the table held as a lookup map, not fetched per flow. Note this is a **new endpoint** — the existing `opnsense/pf_states.go` hits `api/diagnostics/firewall/pf_states/1`, which returns `{"current","limit"}` counts only and is no use here.

### The real limitation, which is not ambiguity

**A short flow may have no live state left by the time its NetFlow record arrives.** The prod box runs `inactiveTimeout=15`, so a record can land ~15–30s after the conversation ended, by which point a short UDP state is gone. The long flows are safe — sample state ages in the table run to 36 hours — and the ones this bug actually hurts (the 11.1 GB on VIRGIN) are long. But it is a genuine miss window, it is **not** something a longer poll interval fixes, and it wants its own counter: a pre-NAT record with no matching state must be **refused and counted**, never guessed.

That is also why the destination-match table is not worth building as a fallback. It would be blind to exactly the same short flows (their post-NAT copy is equally gone), while adding an ambiguity class this mechanism does not have.

### Implementation sketch, for whoever picks this up

- New `Fetch*` for `api/diagnostics/firewall/query_states` (**POST**, so it needs `postEndpoints` in `contract.go`, a `captureRequests` entry, and the golden POST count bumped — per the CLAUDE.md checklist). It is a core route, so it must **not** go in `NegativeCacheable404Endpoints()`.
- Build a map from `direction:"in"` rows that carry `route-to`: `(proto, src, sport, dst, dport) -> egress device`. Ignore rows without `route-to` — their FIB answer is already what ng_netflow reported.
- A fourth repair alongside 1–3, consulted for records whose `Out` disagrees with the state's device. Two counters in `RepairStats`, kept apart because they call for opposite operator responses: corrections applied, and pre-NAT records with **no matching state** (the miss window above).
- **Do not set `Iface.Corrected` for this.** `ifaceIsWAN` (`repair.go:996`) short-circuits on that flag as proof-of-WAN-by-construction, with a comment stating only repair 2 sets it and only from the WAN table. A route-to device is a WAN in practice, but reusing the flag would silently widen a documented invariant that direction inference depends on. Give the new mechanism its own marker, or teach `ifaceIsWAN` about the device explicitly — `IfMap` already implements `IsWAN(device)` (`ifmap.go:495`), which the `wanKnower` assertion picks up, so the honest path is available.
- Acceptance still requires verifying one real conversation end-to-end against `pfctl -ss`. The conversation above (`<lan-ip-10> -> <pub-ip-15>:8007`) is a live, reproducible instance of the bug and is the one to use.

### Status

Costing done and recorded; **implementation not started**. #605's orientation decision — the input this issue was waiting on — is recorded there and shipped as `f88f7f91`, so that dependency is cleared.

## Shipped in `e5deddbd`, and verified on the production firewall

The pf-state mechanism, exactly as costed: a fourth repair keyed on the `direction:"in"` row's pre-NAT 5-tuple, `route-to` read as the routing decision itself, cold-tier poll of the whole table held as a lookup map. `Iface.Corrected` is not set — the marker is `Repairs.PolicyRouteCorrected` and the direction rules learn the device through `IfMap.IsWAN`, per the note on this issue.

### Live verification, prod (read-only), 2026-07-31

**The join, before writing any code.** Fetched the whole table from prod and re-derived every number in the costing comment against it:

| check | measured |
| --- | --- |
| rows / size / time | 6,602 · 3.3 MB · 645 ms |
| `direction:"in"` rows | 3,232 |
| …carrying `route-to` | 1,768 (`pppoe0` 1,747, **`ixl1` 21**) |
| duplicate 5-tuple keys among them | **0** |
| keys mapping to more than one egress device | **0** |

**The key the code actually uses, against real flow records.** Took 60 live flow records from Loki (outbound, private source) and looked each one up in a table fetched at the same moment, with the exporter's own key: **58 of 60 hit**, every hit resolving to a real egress device. The two misses are the expiry window.

**The mechanism running on prod.** After deploying `main` to <host-1>:

```
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="total"}          3,145
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="policy_routed"}  1,917
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="conflict"}           0
opnsense_flow_pf_state_entries{kind="skipped"}           14
opnsense_flow_pf_state_age_seconds                      272
opnsense_flow_policy_route_corrected_total                3
opnsense_flow_policy_route_refused_total{reason="unresolved_device"}  0
```

`conflict` is zero on a live 3,145-state table, which is the costing comment's ambiguity claim holding at runtime rather than in a sample.

### One thing the costing comment got wrong, and it is not academic

> the ones this bug actually hurts (the 11.1 GB on VIRGIN) are long

**They are not.** The `ixl1` population on prod is 19 states, and 18 of them are `<lan-ip-10> -> <pub-ip-15>:8007` TCP connections with an age under 90 seconds — a new one roughly every 10 seconds. Only one is long (a `<lan-ip-1>:32944` UDP flow, age 13m+).

That matters because the miss window is **wider in one direction than this issue assumed**. A state is missable not only because it EXPIRED before its record arrived, but because it was CREATED after the last poll. With a 300-second cadence and a ~90-second state lifetime, those short VIRGIN connections can live and die entirely between two snapshots, and no cadence short of their lifetime reaches them. `policy_route_refused_total{reason="no_state"}` runs at ~30% of decoded records for exactly this reason, and the 58/60 hit rate against a FRESH table is the control that separates "the join is wrong" from "the snapshot is old".

The long flow is what produced the three corrections above: it re-exports on the 1800-second active timeout, its state persists across polls, and it is corrected every time. So the mechanism is right and the cadence reaches the flows it was chosen for — it does not reach the short ones. Whether that is worth a shorter poll is a product call and is filed separately rather than decided here.

### A defect this verification turned up

The counter rose while **no flow log record carried `flow.policy_route_corrected`**. `finalize()` takes every non-volume dimension from one chosen orientation, and a conversation arrives as several NetFlow records, so a repair applied to any other fragment vanished at the merge — silently, and not only for this marker: `VLANSubnetAttributed` and `PayloadByteFallback` were lost the same way. Fixed in `b1a8c961` by unioning `Repairs` across fragments, the same treatment `TCPFlags` already gets.

### Acceptance

- [x] A pre-NAT record policy-routed out a non-default WAN is labelled with the WAN it actually left by, verified against the live pf state table for a specific conversation
- [x] The mechanism has its own counters, published as self-metrics, with refusals counted separately from successes — and split three ways, because "no state" and "unresolved device" have different fixes
- [x] Ambiguous cases refused, not guessed, with a test proving two hosts to one destination over different WANs do not cross-attribute — and `conflict=0` on the live table says the key cannot produce the ambiguity at all
- [x] `docs/flow.md` states the multi-WAN attribution behaviour and its limits
- [x] Full gate green
- [ ] `opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_ratio{interface="VIRGIN"}` accumulating — **not yet**, and the reason is the cadence finding above, not the mechanism

body:
## Summary

`OPNsenseFlowSourceDivergence` fires permanently in the m7kni stack. It is not detecting anything: the threshold (`p90 > 1.5` for 30m) sits **below the metric's normal operating range on every interface that produces data**, and the metric it reads cannot support the claim the rule makes. Delete the rule and everything generated from it.

Diagnosed against live m7kni Prometheus/Loki and a read-only session on the prod firewall (OPNsense 26.7.1_1). No code changed.

## Evidence: it is always true

Fraction of the last 24h each interface's p90 exceeds 1.5:

| interface | fraction of 24h breaching | observations/s |
|---|---|---|
| AAISP (WAN1) | **1.00** | 11.2 |
| Loopback | **1.00** | 1.8 |
| LAN | 0.96 | 3.4 |
| MGMT | 0.94 | 0.069 |
| CAM | 0.82 | 0.016 |
| tailscale | 0.77 | 0.070 |
| IOT | 0.55 | 0.14 |
| locally-originated | 0.13 | 0.010 |
| VIRGIN (WAN2) | 0.00 | 0 (no data — see #603) |

AAISP is decisive: ~40k observations/hour, so this is not a small-sample artifact. Its CDF over 1h — 83.3% of records ≤1.5, 97.0% ≤2 — puts p90 at ~1.7 in steady state, permanently.

## Evidence: there is nothing to detect

The alert's stated premise is "Zenarmor is inspecting far fewer bytes than are actually crossing the wire … a security-relevant blind spot". Byte-weighted, the two sources agree:

- `opnsense_flow_bytes_total`: netflow 36.7 GB/h vs zenarmor 30.2 GB/h → **1.22**
- byte-weighted over a 900-record merged-flow-log sample: **1.36**; packet-weighted **1.25**
- large flows agree closely: NetFlow packets 16–64 → mean ratio 1.09; ≥64 packets → mean Zenarmor packets 1092 against NetFlow 1121, ratio 1.42

## Root cause of the false positive

The threshold rationale in the rule's own runbook — "the 0.9–1.25 range that per-packet header overhead alone accounts for" — is calibrated for bulk traffic, where 48 bytes of L3/L4 header on a 1500-byte packet is 3%. It does not hold for the population that actually dominates merged records by count.

- 54% of merged records (486 of a 900-record sample) are 2–3 packet UDP flows.
- On those, `zenBytes` (`internal/logship/zenarmor/flowadapt.go:243`) falls back to Zenarmor's **payload** bytes because `nbytes` is 0 until Zenarmor has tracked the flow past its first packets. NetFlow counts **wire** bytes.
- Measured per-packet gap on that population clusters at 26–28 bytes (IPv4 IP+UDP = 28) with a second cluster near the IPv6 48-byte header. Mean 92.0 NetFlow bytes/pkt vs 52.6 Zenarmor bytes/pkt.
- p90 of that sub-population alone: **1.96**.
- Live fallback rate: `payload_byte_fallback_total` = 49,028/h against 96,627 Zenarmor flow records/h — roughly half of all merged comparisons are wire-against-payload.

So a 1.5 threshold on p90 is below the floor set by header overhead on small flows. See #604 for the metric-level problems (wire-vs-payload, window-partial-vs-whole-connection) that make the series unfit for this alert regardless of threshold.

## Why not just retune the threshold

A blind spot is a **volume** property. p90 of an *unweighted per-flow* ratio is set by thousands of tiny flows with high header ratios, while the bytes that matter sit in a handful of large flows at ≈1.0. No threshold on this series can express "X% of bytes went uninspected". Retuning would hide the false positive without making the series answer the question.

Two interfaces are also structurally not inspection paths at all, so they could never be meaningfully alerted on:

- **Loopback** — `interfaceLabel` (`internal/flow/processor.go:387`) picks `Out` for non-inbound records, and traffic whose destination is the firewall's own WAN address routes via lo0. Confirmed on the box: pf state `all udp <lan-ip-1>:32944 (<pub-ip-2>:32944) <- <pub-ip-15>:62191` — these are NAT-reflection / de-NAT bookkeeping artifacts, not real loopback traffic.
- **locally-originated** — the firewall's own traffic. Zenarmor does not inspect it.

Zenarmor monitors exactly one interface on this box (`/usr/local/zenarmor/etc/workers.map`: a single worker `netmap@ixl0`, tags `lan;netmap;routedmode`), so a "Zenarmor blind spot" alert keyed on egress-WAN interface labels is measuring the wrong axis by construction.

## Scope

- [ ] Remove the `opnsense-flow-source-divergence` entry from `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py` (~line 2163) and its title mapping (~line 2462)
- [ ] Remove `grafana/alerts/grafana-managed/opnsense-flow-source-divergence.json`
- [ ] Remove the `## OPNsenseFlowSourceDivergence` section from `grafana/runbooks.md` (~line 1921)
- [ ] Fix the runbook-count assertion in `grafana/tests/test_runbooks.py` (~line 119, currently pins 64 including this rule)
- [ ] `make rules` + `make grafana-check` green
- [ ] Delete the rule from the live m7kni stack (it is deployed via gcx push to the `opnsense-alerts` folder)

Keep the `opnsense_flow_source_byte_delta_ratio` histogram and its dashboard panel — the distribution is still informative to look at. It is only the alert that is wrong.

## Not in scope here

- #603 — multi-WAN egress misattribution (why VIRGIN has no data at all)
- #604 — the metric is not a like-for-like comparison

comments.body:
## Quantified: which interface labels can carry Zenarmor data at all

Zenarmor runs a single netmap worker on `ixl0` (the LAN trunk) — vendor best practice, confirmed against their docs. Measured over a 90m sample of the merged/netflow flow logs, that constrains which `interface` labels can ever carry a correlated observation:

- **Zero** merged records exist where neither `In` nor `Out` is a LAN-side interface (LAN / IOT / MGMT / CAM / OPNDEV). Every record Zenarmor contributed to has a LAN-side interface on one end.
- `in=locally-originated`: 308 merged records, **0 of which egress a WAN**. Firewall→LAN traffic crosses ixl0 so Zenarmor sees it; firewall→internet never touches ixl0 so it cannot. The netflow-only lane holds 21 such records in the same window.

So `locally-originated` traffic to the internet, `tailscale` traffic terminating on the firewall, and anything on `ixl1`/`ixl2` that does not traverse ixl0 are **structurally** outside Zenarmor's view — not a coverage failure, a consequence of where the inspection point correctly sits. An alert reading "Zenarmor inspected fewer bytes than crossed the wire" on those labels can only ever be a false positive.

Reinforces the decision to delete rather than retune: the metric's `interface` label and Zenarmor's inspection point are on different axes.

body:
## What

`internal/logship/syslog/registry.go` maps program `netbird` to `subsystem="vpn"`, but **a parser registered on that name can never fire**, so netbird lines ship as generic records and the dashboard's Tunnel lifecycle annotation layer stays silent on a NetBird box.

#596 registered parsers for `wireguard` and `tailscaled` and closed. netbird was deliberately not delivered, because #596's premise for it turned out to be wrong: the problem is not a missing parser, it is that **the app-name on the wire is not `netbird`**.

## Why it cannot be reached today (verified, not inferred)

1. **The app-name is `/usr/local/bin/netbird`.** netbird's syslog hook passes an empty tag — `lSyslog.NewSyslogHook("", "", syslog.LOG_INFO, "")` (`util/syslog_nonwindows.go:17`) — and Go's standard library substitutes argv[0]:

   ```go
   // $(go env GOROOT)/src/log/syslog/syslog.go:123-125
   if tag == "" {
       tag = os.Args[0]
   }
   ```

   The rc.d `command_args` invokes `%%PREFIX%%/bin/netbird`, so that is what lands in the app-name field. Neither an exact nor a prefix registration on `netbird` can reach it. Only the rc script's three `logger -s -t netbird` lines genuinely carry that app-name, and none of them is a tunnel transition.

   OPNsense *does* route it to syslog (`netbird_logfile="syslog"` in the plugin's rc template) and netbird does support it (`util/log.go:92-96` → `AddSyslogHookToLogger`) — the routing is fine, only the tag is wrong.

2. **There is no canonical Info-level lifecycle line.** `conn.Log.Infof("set ICE to active connection")` (`conn.go:429`) also fires on a relay→ICE **upgrade** mid-session, so it is not an establishment edge. Teardown is split across `close peer connection` and `peer connection closed`.

3. **Those open/close lines are idle churn, not lifecycle.** `client/internal/lazyconn/` closes and reopens idle peers on a `DefaultInactivityThreshold = 15 * time.Minute`, controlled by a **server-side management feature flag** (`lazyconn/env.go` — unset locally means "defer to management"). So the same line means different things on different deployments and the log alone cannot tell them apart. A parser that treated `peer connection closed` as `terminated` would emit a tunnel-down marker every 15 minutes on an idle-but-healthy peer.

4. **Version drift, #379's trap repeating.** freebsd-ports is at netbird 0.76.0; OPNsense 26.1's package repo ships 0.72.2. #379 already found one netbird field unreachable on the packaged build, so upstream source is necessary but not sufficient evidence here.

## What unblocks it

**A live capture of the forwarded app-name from an enrolled box.** One command answers it, because that file is written `flags(syslog-protocol)`:

```bash
head /var/log/netbird/netbird_$(date +%Y%m%d).log   # field 4 is the app-name
```

That settles whether the wire name is `/usr/local/bin/netbird`, a basename, or something the plugin rewrites. **Do not register the full path speculatively** — it would be guessing at both `PREFIX` and argv, and a wrong prefix registration is worse than none because it looks handled.

Then a decision is still needed on (3): whether any available line is a lifecycle edge at all, given the lazy-connection churn. If none is, the honest outcome is a documented won't-do for `vpn.event` on netbird plus a subsystem-only attribution — which is roughly where `tailscale` (no `d`) landed in #596.

## Prior art to respect

- `#379` — netbird `sessionExpiresAt` won't-do stands; that field is unreachable on OPNsense's packaged build.
- The standing boundary against this exporter owning peer-level VPN data (`tailscale2otel` owns the equivalent for Tailscale).
- The Tunnel lifecycle layer's `opnsense_subsystem=~"vpn|ipsec"` regex stays **deliberately wide**. Narrowing it to the covered programs would hide this gap in the query as well as in the data — the wide regex is what makes "this box has vpn records but no vpn_event" observable.

## Scope

1. Capture the real app-name from an enrolled box and record it here.
2. Decide whether any netbird line is a genuine lifecycle edge, given the lazy-connection churn. A documented "no" is an acceptable answer.
3. If yes: register a parser on the confirmed app-name setting `vpn.event`, and extend `TestTunnelLifecycleAnnotationMatchesEveryVPNLifecycleParser` (which already evaluates the real annotation filters against `buildRecord` output) to cover it.
4. If no: record the won't-do in `docs/syslog-receiver.md` and update `grafana/annotations.py`'s coverage note, which currently names netbird as the one remaining gap.
5. Either way, correct the `netbird` entry's comment in `registry.go` if the capture contradicts the app-name finding above.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Real forwarded app-name captured from a live enrolled box, recorded here
- [ ] Lifecycle-edge question decided explicitly, with the churn reasoning addressed
- [ ] Parser registered and covered by the annotation test, **or** a documented won't-do in `docs/syslog-receiver.md` + the annotations note updated
- [ ] `registry.go`'s netbird comment matches whatever the capture proved

comments.body:
## Settled by live capture: app-name confirmed, and the answer to scope item 2 is **YES** — at engine granularity

CLOSING. The app-name prediction in the body is correct to the character. The lifecycle-edge
analysis is correct about every candidate it evaluated and **incomplete**: all four candidates
were peer-level, and the edge that works is engine-level — the same granularity `wireguard` (the
tunnel instance) and `tailscaled` (the whole node) already settled on in #596. So this lands a
parser rather than a documented won't-do.

Captured from the enrolled **devel** testbed (VM 102, `nightly` profile) on 2026-07-31. Prod has
no netbird and was not touched.

### 1. The forwarded app-name — verified, not predicted

```
head /var/log/netbird/netbird_20260731.log
```

```
<6>1 2026-07-31T00:00:14+01:00 <host> /usr/local/bin/netbird 95047 - [meta sequenceId="1"] started new probe for STUN, TURN servers
<6>1 2026-07-31T00:01:14+01:00 <host> /usr/local/bin/netbird 95047 - [meta sequenceId="2"] started new probe for STUN, TURN servers
<6>1 2026-07-31T00:02:48+01:00 <host> /usr/local/bin/netbird 95047 - [meta sequenceId="4"] refreshed mgmt cache domain=turn.netbird.io type=A
```

Field 4 is **`/usr/local/bin/netbird`**. Census over all 19 retained daily files (4,888 lines):

| app-name (field 4) | lines | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/usr/local/bin/netbird` | 4,817 | the daemon, via logrus' syslog hook |
| `netbird` | 12 | the rc script's `logger -s -t netbird` — **all 12 are `Starting netbird.`** |
| other | 59 | continuation lines of multi-line messages (no envelope of their own) |

Three independent confirmations of the mechanism, so nothing here rests on inference:

- **On the box:** `/usr/local/etc/rc.d/netbird:40` has `command_args="… /usr/local/bin/netbird service run …"` with `%%PREFIX%%` already substituted. argv[0] is that literal.
- **Upstream:** `util/syslog_nonwindows.go:17` still passes the empty tag at the packaged **v0.74.4** and at ports' **v0.76.0**.
- **The PRI field agrees.** Daemon lines are `<6>` = facility 0 / severity 6, which is exactly `syslog.LOG_INFO` with no facility bits — the third argument of `NewSyslogHook`. The rc lines are `<13>` = user.notice, `logger(1)`'s default. Two producers, two priorities, both as the source predicts.
- Routing is confirmed live too: `/etc/rc.conf.d/netbird` contains `netbird_logfile="syslog"`.

### 2. A SECOND, WORSE FINDING: the daemon's lines were shipping with NO subsystem at all

`subsystems` held `netbird` only, so `subsystemFor("/usr/local/bin/netbird")` returned **empty** —
no prefix rule in `subsystemFor` reaches a path. All 4,817 daemon lines shipped unattributed, and
the `netbird` entry only ever reached one line in 18 days.

This invalidates a claim both #596 and this issue rely on. #596's body says the three unparsed VPN
programs "ship as generic records **with a subsystem label** and no structured attributes". True
for `wireguard` and `tailscaled`; **false for netbird**. The consequence is the one that matters:
the Tunnel lifecycle layer's deliberately wide `opnsense_subsystem=~"vpn|ipsec"` regex could not
select netbird records **even as a denominator**, so "this box has vpn records but no vpn_event"
was never observable for netbird. The wide-regex argument silently did not hold for the one program
it was being kept wide for. Same class of miss as `tailscale` (no `d`) in #596, worse blast radius.

### 3. The lifecycle-edge decision: engine-level, and the churn objection does not reach it

The churn objection in the body is **correct and now live-confirmed** — the box logs
`lazy connection manager is enabled by management feature flag` and
`inactivity threshold configured: 15m0s`, so on this very tenant lazyconn genuinely does close and
reopen an idle peer. It rules out the peer-level lines and nothing else. The engine pair is
untouched by it:

| line | `vpn.event` | source (v0.74.4 → v0.76.0) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Netbird engine started, the IP is: <addr>` | `established` | `client/internal/connect.go:418` → `:438` |
| `stopped NetBird client` | `terminated` | `client/internal/connect.go:444` → `:464` |

**Why the pair is balanced**, from the control flow rather than from counting matches. Both lines
are in ONE function — the closure `operation` that `connect.go` hands to `backoff.Retry`. The
established line sits immediately after `engine.Start()` returns nil and immediately before
`state.Set(StatusConnected)`; every earlier failure path (`no management client`, login refused,
relay token rejected, engine start error) does `return wrapErr(err)` before reaching it. The
terminated line is the closure's **last** statement, after `<-engineCtx.Done()`, `engine.Stop()`
and `statusRecorder.ClientTeardown()`. A `terminated` therefore cannot be minted without an
`established` earlier in the same iteration — the objection that kept OpenVPN's daemon shutdown out
of #406's vocabulary.

**The capture is the empirical half, and it is a stronger check than a match count:** 18 days hold
**5 establishments and 4 terminations**, the difference being the session still running when the log
was read. It also holds six earlier daemon start/stop cycles from before enrollment — 248
`failed to login to Management Service` lines and **not one engine start** — which is a live
demonstration that this pair tracks overlay connectivity rather than the service.

**Five families deliberately left generic**, each a line the capture actually contains:

- **`stopped Netbird Engine` DOUBLE-LOGS.** Two call sites reach `Engine.Stop()` on one teardown — `connect.go:437` after the engine context is cancelled, and the daemon server's down path at `client/server/server.go:999`, which upstream itself flags with `// TODO: consider calling connectClient.Stop() instead of engine.Stop().` Observed **twice per teardown on 4 of 4 teardowns**, same PID, same second. It is the obvious-looking teardown line and it is the wrong one.
- **`starting`/`stopped NetBird service`** are the daemon **process**, not the overlay. Six such pairs bracket periods with no tunnel at all; counting them would mint six false establishments in 18 days on one box. `Starting netbird.` under app-name `netbird` is the same event, excluded for the same reason.
- **Every peer-level line**: `set ICE to active connection` (which, as the body says, also fires on a relay→ICE upgrade mid-session), `close peer connection`, `peer connection closed`, `first wg handshake detected within`, and the lazyconn bookkeeping. Two sufficient reasons: the idle timer makes their meaning deployment-dependent and unknowable from the log, and per-peer VPN topology is out of scope by the standing boundary.
- **Control-plane reachability**: `connected to the Management Service stream`, `reconnected to Signal or Relay server`, the relay connect/close pair, `disconnected from the Management service but will retry silently`. The tunnel survives all of them — the last says so in the line itself.
- **Teardown steps**: `ensuring wg interface is removed, Netbird engine context cancelled`, `interface wt0 has been removed`. `stopped NetBird client` already marks the completion; counting both double-counts one event.

No failure case is modelled: nothing in this pair states an authentication, certificate or liveness
verdict. A refused login produces no engine start, so the **absence** of an `established` is the
signal, and the refusal itself is a control-plane fact the poll lane reports as `daemonStatus`.

### 4. Version — the body's version claim is wrong

The body says "OPNsense 26.1's package repo ships 0.72.2". The box runs **`netbird-0.74.4`**
(`os-netbird-1.3_3`, OPNsense 27.1.a_40), and #379 already established 0.74.4 as the ceiling
`pkg rquery` offers. The capture shows both generations —
`starting NetBird client version 0.72.2` ×245 and `0.74.4` ×6 — so 0.72.2 is history on this box,
not the current package. Support-window safety was checked rather than assumed: **both grammar
strings and the empty syslog tag are byte-identical at v0.74.4 and at ports' v0.76.0**, so a package
bump inside the window cannot silently break the parser.

### 5. What landed

| file | change |
| --- | --- |
| `internal/logship/syslog/netbird.go` | new. Parser registered on `/usr/local/bin/netbird` via `RegisterParserWithBodyEnrichment`; the full derivation above is the file comment |
| `internal/logship/syslog/netbird_test.go` | new. 8 tests: the two-app-name attribution, parser registered for the daemon name and **not** for `netbird`, both lifecycle ends, address-shape independence, 25 must-stay-generic lines drawn from the capture, the rc line staying generic through `buildRecord`, no-identity-extraction, body-enrichment opt-in |
| `internal/logship/syslog/registry.go` | added `"/usr/local/bin/netbird": "vpn"` (finding 2), and the netbird comment rewritten to what the capture proved |
| `internal/logship/syslog/derive.go` | `vpnBackendNetBird`; `nonDerivedPrograms` entry, matching wireguard/tailscaled |
| `internal/logship/syslog/vpn_annotation_test.go` | both netbird ends added to `TestTunnelLifecycleAnnotationMatchesEveryVPNLifecycleParser` |
| `docs/syslog-receiver.md` | the won't-do bullet replaced by two operator bullets (the app-name is a path; the markers are the engine and why the peer lines are not events); the lifecycle section, its table, its heading and the parser table updated |
| `grafana/annotations.py` | "STILL UNCOVERED: netbird" → all five backends covered, with the argv[0] and lazyconn caveats kept |

Not counted into `opnsense_log_events_vpn_total`, for #406's frozen-tuple reason — same disposition
as wireguard and tailscaled, so `sampleKeep` never drops these lines.

**The Tunnel lifecycle layer's `opnsense_subsystem=~"vpn|ipsec"` regex is unchanged and stays
wide.** Not narrowed even now that all five backends are covered: the wide form is what would make
a sixth backend's records visible as vpn traffic with no `vpn_event`, which is how this whole class
of gap was found.

**Fail-injected, not asserted.** Deleting the one new `subsystems` line fails
`TestNetbirdDaemonAppNameIsTheVPNSubsystem` *and* both new annotation rows with
`opnsense_subsystem = "", which the layer's ^(?:vpn|ipsec)$ does not select` — so the registry
entry, the parser and the dashboard query are pinned to each other in both directions.
`go test ./internal/logship/...` green, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `check_public_ips` OK.

### Acceptance

- [x] Real forwarded app-name captured from a live enrolled box, recorded here
- [x] Lifecycle-edge question decided explicitly, with the churn reasoning addressed
- [x] Parser registered and covered by the annotation test
- [x] `registry.go`'s netbird comment matches what the capture proved

### Corrections to this issue and to #596, for the record

1. **"the THREE lines the rc script emits with `logger -s -t netbird`"** — there are **four** (`:45`, `:50`, `:58`, `:60` of the installed rc script). Only `Starting netbird.` appeared in 18 days. Neither count changes the verdict; the number was simply wrong in the body, in #596's closing comment and in the old `registry.go` comment.
2. **"OPNsense 26.1's package repo ships 0.72.2"** — the ceiling is **0.74.4**, and it is what the box runs.
3. **#596's "their lines ship as generic records with a subsystem label"** — false for netbird. They shipped with **no** subsystem, which is finding 2 above and the more consequential half of this issue.
4. **The body's expectation that a documented won't-do was the likely outcome** — not upheld. The lazyconn objection is sound but scoped to peer-level lines, and the engine-level pair was never evaluated.
