body:
Spun out of #550. Speculative but plausibly valuable — filing so the idea is not lost, **not** proposing we build it yet.

## The opportunity

`api/diagnostics/activity/get_activity` returns `{"headers": [7], "details": [906]}`. We parse two header lines and **never read `details` at all** — `opnsense/activity.go:43` declares `Details []any` and nothing in the repo touches it. That is ~330 KB per poll fetched, JSON-unmarshalled into `interface{}`, and dropped on the floor.

Row shape (real capture, prod box 2026-07-30):

```json
{"C":"10","PID":"11","THR":"100013","USERNAME":"root","PRI":"199","NICE":"ki31",
 "SIZE":"0B","RES":"192K","STATE":"CPU10","TIME":"41.7H","WCPU":"98.27%",
 "COMMAND":"[idle{idle: cpu10}]"}
```

## The trap that makes the naive version useless

**These are threads, not processes.** 906 rows on a box running far fewer processes. Consequences that any implementation must handle:

- **Top-N by `WCPU` returns idle threads.** The three hottest rows on a healthy box are `[idle{idle: cpuN}]` at ~98%. A naive "top 10 processes by CPU" panel would show nothing but idle.
- **`PID`/`THR` are unusable as labels.** They churn continuously; a per-thread series is created and abandoned on a timescale of minutes. Raw cardinality is not the constraint here (the exporter uses ~4.6k of a 100k budget) — *churn* is. Abandoned series cost storage and make `rate()` meaningless.
- `COMMAND` for a thread carries the `{...}` thread-name suffix and needs normalising before it can be a label.

## What might actually work

Aggregate, never per-thread:

- **By `USERNAME`** — bounded (4 users on this box), stable, and answers "what is consuming CPU/memory by owner".
- **By normalised `COMMAND`** — strip the `{thread}` suffix and the `[]` kernel brackets, then sum `WCPU`/`RES` per command name. Bounded by the number of distinct binaries, which is stable. Must exclude `idle` explicitly or every panel is dominated by it.
- Possibly a **thread-count per command**, which is the one genuinely new signal — a process leaking threads is invisible in every other metric we export.

## Open questions before this is worth building

1. Is there a real question an operator has that this answers and `services`/`system` do not? "Which process is eating the CPU on my firewall" is plausible; it is not obviously *frequent*.
2. Aggregation must happen exporter-side, so the 330 KB parse cost stays regardless — this makes the payload *useful*, it does not make it *cheaper*. It therefore does not resolve #550's cost problem and must not be treated as if it does.
3. Interacts directly with #550's tier decision: if `activity` moves to 60s, this data arrives at 60s too, which is fine for aggregate CPU by command but weak for catching short-lived spikes.
4. Default-off almost certainly (`--exporter.enable-*`), per the opt-in convention for higher-cardinality collectors.

## Recommendation

Leave parked until #550 settles the tier and the ARC work (#551) lands. Revisit if a concrete "which process is eating my firewall" question actually comes up in practice.
title: idea: aggregate get_activity process table by COMMAND/USERNAME (payload we already fetch and discard)

body:
Spun out of #550. Free data we already pay for and discard.

## What is missing

`internal/collector/system.go:55` exports a single `memory_arc_bytes` total for ZFS ARC. The `get_activity` payload we already fetch on every `activity` poll carries the full composition in its headers:

```
ARC: 7603M Total, 2866M MFU, 4166M MRU, 32M Anon, 46M Header, 481M Other
     6571M Compressed, 11G Uncompressed, 1.71:1 Ratio
```

Two of the seven header lines, currently parsed and thrown away — `opnsense/activity.go` iterates `resp.Headers` and matches only the threads and CPU lines.

## Why it is worth having

MFU vs MRU split is the standard read on whether the ARC is serving a working set or thrashing, and the compression ratio is the honest measure of what ARC is actually buying on a ZFS box. On this hardware ARC is 7.6 GB of 12 GB wired — it is not a rounding error.

## Scope

- Parse the two `ARC:` header lines in `opnsense/activity.go` alongside the existing threads/CPU regexes.
- Export the components. Naming to be decided during implementation — either labelled (`opnsense_system_memory_arc_component_bytes{component="mfu|mru|anon|header|other"}`) or separate gauges. Labelled is probably right: the set is closed and code-defined.
- Compressed/uncompressed bytes plus the ratio (derive the ratio at query time from the two byte gauges rather than exporting a unitless ratio).
- Keep the existing `memory_arc_bytes` total exactly as-is — it comes from `systemResources` and must not start coming from here.

## Notes

- **Zero additional API cost.** Same payload, same poll, currently discarded.
- Must degrade cleanly on non-ZFS installs: UFS boxes emit no `ARC:` header at all, so absent must mean absent, not zero.
- The `system` collector owns the existing ARC total but `activity` owns this payload. Decide which collector emits these before writing code — splitting ARC series across two collectors with different poll tiers would be worse than either home.
- Dashboard panel required in the same commit per the coverage gate.

comments.body:
Implemented and closed by `e6427a6f`.

## The scope questions, answered

**Naming — labelled, as the issue guessed.** `opnsense_activity_arc_component_bytes{component="mfu|mru|anon|header|other"}`, plus `opnsense_activity_arc_compressed_bytes` and `_uncompressed_bytes`. The set is closed and code-defined, so labels beat five separate gauges. The ratio is derived at query time from the two byte gauges, not exported.

**Home — the `activity` collector.** The issue flagged split poll tiers as the reason that would be bad. #559 moved `activity` to the medium tier, so `activity` and `system` now both sit at 60s and that objection no longer applies. The alternative (having `system` fetch `get_activity`) would have added a 2.15 s call per poll for data already on the wire.

**`opnsense_system_memory_arc_bytes` is untouched** and still comes from `systemResources`, as the issue required. The `Total` field on the ARC line is matched by the parser only so it cannot be mistaken for a component, then discarded — one series with two differently-timed sources would disagree with itself.

## The issue's assumption about non-ZFS boxes was wrong

> Must degrade cleanly on non-ZFS installs: UFS boxes emit no `ARC:` header at all, so absent must mean absent, not zero.

The requirement is right; the mechanism is not. A live UFS box (**testbed 102, OPNsense 27.1.a, checked 2026-07-30**) emits the header **present but empty**:

```
'Mem: 402M Active, 5410M Inact, 1117M Wired, 682M Buf, 1284M Free'
'ARC: '
'Swap: 8192M Total, 8192M Free'
```

So "was there an `ARC:` line" is the wrong absence test. Keying on it would have parsed a bare prefix into zero-valued components and published a real, permanently empty cache on every UFS install — which is exactly the failure the acceptance criterion existed to prevent, arrived at by following the criterion's own suggested implementation.

Presence is therefore keyed on **parsed content**, and there is a regression test for all three shapes: empty header, missing header, and unparseable contents.

Both shapes are real captures rather than synthetic:

- ZFS, production box (26.7.1_1): `ARC: 7818M Total, 3034M MFU, 4222M MRU, 22M Anon, 46M Header, 483M Other` + `     6772M Compressed, 11G Uncompressed, 1.70:1 Ratio`
- UFS, testbed 102: `ARC: `

## One more absence case

Composition and compression are tracked independently. The compression figures live on a **separate** header entry (the continuation line, which carries no `ARC:` prefix), so it can arrive without them. If it does, composition still publishes and compression stays absent — a 1:1 ratio would read as "compression is doing nothing", which is a different and wrong statement.

## Dashboard

Two panels on the Memory & Swap row: **ZFS ARC Composition** (stacked, by component) and **ZFS ARC Compression** (in-memory versus logical, the gap being memory saved). Both absent on non-ZFS boxes, following the metrics. Coverage gate green.

title: feat(system): export ZFS ARC composition breakdown (MFU/MRU/Anon/Header/Other + compression) — free from get_activity

body:
Spun out of #535, but the scope is general: **we have never audited what belongs in the 15s fast tier**, and the tier table (`internal/collector/interval_tiers.go`) was assigned by judgement, not measurement. #535 established that every API request costs the firewall two extra configd RPCs, which makes request *count* a first-class cost for the first time and is the trigger for actually measuring this.

This issue is a **spike + decision**, not an implementation plan. The measurements below are done; what is needed is a set of calls on how to act on them.

## Two distinct costs

Tiering has been reasoned about as "how fresh does this data need to be". There are actually two independent costs, and they rank the endpoints differently:

1. **Per-request cost (fixed, payload-independent).** Every API request = 2 configd RPCs on the box, each exec'ing a script (#535). The fast tier is 13 endpoints × 5760 polls/day = **~75k requests/day → ~150k configd RPCs/day**, all by itself.
2. **Per-byte cost.** The box builds and serialises the payload; we parse it. This is where one endpoint dominates everything else.

An endpoint can be cheap on one axis and appalling on the other. `netflow/isEnabled` is 23 bytes but still pays the full per-request tax; `get_activity` is a rounding error on request count and 88% of all fast-tier bytes.

## Method

Live, read-only, against the prod box (OPNsense 26.7.1_1) on 2026-07-30. Per-endpoint request rate from `opnsense_exporter_api_requests_total` deltas on <host-1> over 120s; payload size and churn by fetching each fast-tier endpoint twice 60s apart and comparing bytes.

Measured total: **235 requests / 120s ≈ 1.96 req/s**, of which **104 (44%) are the 15s fast tier**.

## The data

| endpoint | collector | bytes | bytes/day @15s | changed in 60s | what it actually is |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| `diagnostics/activity/get_activity` | activity | 331,164 | **1.91 GB** | changed | full `top` output, 906 threads |
| `interfaces/overview/interfaces_info` | interfaces | 17,181 | 99 MB | changed | live counters + config |
| `diagnostics/interface/get_protocol_statistics` | protocol | 13,629 | 79 MB | changed | live counters |
| `diagnostics/traffic/interface` | interfaces | 6,598 | 38 MB | changed | live counters |
| `routing/settings/searchGateway` | gateways | 3,285 | 19 MB | changed | ~90% config, 4 live fields |
| `diagnostics/firewall/pf_statistics/info` | pfstats | 1,383 | 8 MB | changed | live counters |
| `diagnostics/netflow/cacheStats` | netflow | 1,340 | 7.7 MB | changed | live counters |
| `diagnostics/netflow/getconfig` | netflow | 1,080 | 6.2 MB | **IDENTICAL** | pure config (selected interfaces) |
| `diagnostics/firewall/pf_statistics/timeouts` | pfstats | 540 | 3.1 MB | **IDENTICAL** | pure config (pf timeout limits) |
| `diagnostics/interface/get_vip_status` | carp | 167 | 1.0 MB | **IDENTICAL** | CARP failover state |
| `diagnostics/firewall/pf_statistics/memory` | pfstats | 115 | 0.7 MB | **IDENTICAL** | pure config (pf limits) |
| `diagnostics/netflow/status` | netflow | 37 | 0.2 MB | **IDENTICAL** | service running state |
| `diagnostics/netflow/isEnabled` | netflow | 23 | 0.1 MB | **IDENTICAL** | pure config |

Fast tier total ≈ **2.17 GB/day**, of which `get_activity` alone is **88%**.

## Findings

**1. `get_activity` is the whole problem, and we throw away 99.8% of it.**
331 KB every 15s to extract ~500 bytes of `top` header. `opnsense/activity.go:43` declares `Details []any` and **nothing in the repo ever reads it** — confirmed by grep. So `encoding/json` fully unmarshals 900+ process rows into `interface{}` on every poll, purely to discard them. The exported metrics are thread counts and CPU percentages, parsed exclusively from `resp.Headers`.

`ActivityController::getActivityAction()` takes no parameters (it is a bare `configdRun('system diag activity json')`), so the payload cannot be narrowed server-side. The levers are: poll it less often, or source the same numbers from a cheaper endpoint.

**2. The body cache is structurally forbidden from helping here.**
`internal/collector/interval_tiers_test.go:113` fails the build if *any* endpoint owned by a fast-tier collector carries a body TTL, on the rationale that a 15s poll replaying a cached payload would flat-line the series. That rationale is correct for live data and wrong for config data, and it is enforced at **collector** granularity — precisely the mixed-collector case #344 already acknowledges ("the tier follows the LIVE half and the body cache handles the static endpoints"). For fast-tier collectors that promise is currently unavailable: netflow's three static endpoints cannot be cached at all while the netflow collector is fast.

**3. Churn is not cacheability — `get_vip_status` is the counter-example.**
It was byte-identical over 60s and must absolutely stay on the fast tier: it is CARP failover state, and "unchanged" is its normal condition right up until the moment the change is the single most important event the exporter can report. Any admission rule based on observed churn alone would get this exactly backwards. Same logic protects `netflow/status` (service running state) more weakly.

**4. Mixing happens at field level, not just endpoint level.**
`searchGateway` is 3,285 bytes of which only `status`, `delay`, `stddev`, `loss` changed between samples — roughly 40 config fields per gateway are re-sent every 15s. Nothing in the current design can exploit this, and I am *not* proposing we try; noting it because it means "cache the static endpoints" has a ceiling well short of the theoretical win.

**5. netflow is the cleanest available win.**
Three of its four endpoints (`getconfig`, `isEnabled`, `status`) were identical and are config/service-state. They are 23 of 104 fast-tier requests/120s (~22%) for 6.5 MB/day. Only `cacheStats` carries live counters.

## Decisions taken (2026-07-30)

The measurements above stand as the record. All open questions are now settled; the comment thread has the reasoning.

| # | decision |
|---|---|
| A | `get_activity` — **RESOLVED 2026-07-30.** Split by metric: CPU moves to `cpu_usage/stream` over SSE as cumulative counters (#553 authorised the pilot, built in #559); thread counts stay on `get_activity` with the `activity` collector demoted to medium. Measured driver: `get_activity` is 2.15 s/call = a **14% firewall duty cycle** at 15s, buying only 13% CPU timeline coverage. |
| B | Fast-tier body-cache ban — **relax** `interval_tiers_test.go:113`, allowing a body TTL on a fast-tier collector's endpoint when justified per-endpoint in `bodyCacheOwners`. |
| C | Fast-tier admission rule — **write one.** Churn is not the test: `get_vip_status` is byte-identical for days and must stay fast, because a change in CARP failover state *is* the alertable event. |
| D | Scope — netflow + `get_activity` first, full 63-collector re-audit as a separate issue. |
| Q1 | Prometheus-scrape mode — **unchanged.** The clamp and warning apply only when OTLP is a delivery path. No `--exporter.expected-scrape-interval`. |
| Q2 | Over-export of slow/cold tiers — **won't fix, deliberately.** Repeated identical samples are effectively free: DPM is set by the export interval whether or not the value moved. Cutting export frequency per tier would trade that for sparse series that read as dashboard gaps. Must be documented so it is not "fixed" later. |
| Q3 | Phase alignment (polls landing just before export) — **dropped entirely**, not deferred. Values stay on average half a lane-interval old; accepted. |

## Implementation scope, final

1. **Poll cadence follows the consuming lane** — `effective = max(declaredInterval, laneInterval)`, OTLP delivery paths only. `--collector.poll-interval-override` still wins outright.
2. **Startup warning** when a resolved poll interval is shorter than the lane consuming it (after 1, only reachable via an explicit override), plus a warning when `--otlp.fast-export-interval` is set with no fast-tier collectors enabled.
3. **Document the Q2 decision** — why the slow and cold tiers deliberately export unchanged values.

Out: phase alignment, per-tier export lanes, any Prometheus-mode behaviour change, and #535's syslog exclude (dropped there — fixing request volume fixes the log volume proportionally).

## Binding implementation constraint: do NOT clamp inside `resolveInterval`

Found while reading the wiring. This one is a trap and it fails silently, so it is recorded in the body rather than buried in a comment.

Fast **lane membership** is currently derived from the *effective* poll interval:

```go
// internal/collector/collector.go:1679
if c.resolveInterval(coll) <= IntervalFast {
```

That is deliberate (#390) — it is what lets an operator override move a collector between export lanes. If the new lane clamp writes back into `resolveInterval`, membership starts depending on the clamp that depends on membership:

| `--otlp.fast-export-interval` | clamped interval | `<= IntervalFast`? | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `15s` | `max(15s, 15s)` = 15s | yes | correct |
| unset | `max(15s, 60s)` = 60s | no | harmless — the lane is not built at all when the interval is 0 |
| **`30s`** | `max(15s, 30s)` = 30s | **no** | **fast lane configured but EMPTY — silent** |

Any intermediate fast-export-interval breaks it, and nothing fails loudly: the reader is constructed over an empty gatherer set and simply exports nothing on that lane.

**Required shape — split the two concepts, keep the dependency one-directional:**

- `resolveInterval(coll)` keeps its current meaning: the **declared** interval (code tier, or operator override). Lane membership continues to read *this*, so #390's semantics are unchanged.
- A **new** effective-poll-interval applies `max(declared, laneInterval)` and is what the scheduler ticks on, what `collector_poll_interval_seconds` reports, and what `StatusTracker.SetInterval` records.

Membership decides the lane → the lane clamps the cadence. Never the reverse.

Call sites to check when implementing — `resolveInterval` currently has four (`scheduler.go:58` definition, `scheduler.go:78` scheduler, `collector.go:1612`, `collector.go:1679` lane membership). Each needs an explicit decision about which of the two it wants; `collector.go:1679` must keep the declared one, `scheduler.go:78` must take the effective one.

**Test that would have caught this:** assert that with `fast-export-interval=30s` and at least one fast-tier collector enabled, `FastCollectorNames()` is non-empty.

## Explicitly not in scope

- Reducing the per-request configd cost — upstream OPNsense, #535.

comments.body:
## Decisions taken (Rob, 2026-07-30)

- **B — fast-tier body-cache ban:** relax `interval_tiers_test.go:113` to allow a body TTL on a fast-tier collector's endpoint when justified per-endpoint in `bodyCacheOwners`.
- **C — admission rule:** yes, write one.
- **D — scope:** netflow + `get_activity` now; full 63-collector re-audit as a separate issue.
- **A — `get_activity`:** not settled. Rob asked to investigate a cheaper source *and* whether we should be extracting more from the payload we already pay for. Results below.

## A — investigation results

### A1. Is there a cheaper source for CPU% and thread counts? **No.**

Negative result, recorded so it is not re-derived:

- The `system` collector already covers **load average, uptime, memory total/used, ZFS ARC total, swap, disk** — from `systemTime` / `systemResources` / `systemSwap` / `systemDisk`. None of those carry CPU utilisation or thread state counts.
- `api/diagnostics/cpu_usage/stream` is an **SSE stream** — already on the do-not-scrape list from the #226 audit.
- `api/diagnostics/cpu_usage/getCPUType` is topology only (`hw.model`, `kern.smp.cpus`, `kern.smp.cores`), and we already fetch it under a cache TTL.
- configd exposes a generic `system sysctl values %s` action, and **`kern.cp_time` would be a strictly better CPU source than `top`** — it is a cumulative per-state tick counter, so it would give a proper `rate()` instead of `top`'s instantaneous sample. But there is **no generic sysctl API controller**: `sysctl.values` is only reachable through controllers that hardcode their own sysctl list (`getCPUTypeAction`, `systemTimeAction`). Confirmed by `find /usr/local/opnsense/mvc/app/controllers -iname '*ysctl*'` → no results. Reaching `kern.cp_time` over the API needs an upstream change.

So `get_activity` is the only available source for CPU% and thread counts, and `ActivityController::getActivityAction()` takes no parameters. The only lever on the 331 KB is **how often we ask**.

### A2. Is there more worth extracting from the payload? **Mostly no — and that is the useful finding.**

The payload is `{"headers": [7 strings], "details": [906 rows]}`.

**Headers (7 lines, ~500 bytes) — we parse 2 of 7.** The other five carry load averages, uptime, `Mem:` breakdown, the `ARC:` breakdown and `Swap:`. Tempting, but **almost all of it duplicates what the `system` collector already exports** from cheaper endpoints — `load_average`, `swap_total_bytes`, `swap_used_bytes`, `memory_arc_bytes` all exist today. Adding them here would be a second, differently-timed source for series we already have.

The one genuine gap is the **ARC composition breakdown** — `MFU / MRU / Anon / Header / Other`, plus `Compressed / Uncompressed / Ratio`. `system.go:55` exports only a single `memory_arc_bytes` total. ARC hit composition is real signal on a ZFS box. Worth a separate issue; it does not justify a 331 KB poll on its own, but it is free if we are fetching this anyway.

**Details (906 rows, ~330 KB) — not worth exporting.** These are **threads, not processes** (`THR` field; rows look like `[idle{idle: cpu10}]`). Consequences:

- A naive top-N by `WCPU` returns idle threads — the three hottest rows on a healthy box are `[idle{idle: cpuN}]` at ~98%.
- Per-thread series are unusable as labels: `PID`/`THR` churn constantly. Cardinality itself is not the constraint (we use ~4.6k of a 100k budget) but **label churn is** — a per-thread metric creates and abandons series continuously.
- Anything genuinely useful would need aggregation by `COMMAND` or `USERNAME`, which is bounded and stable — but that is a new collector's worth of design, not a free extraction.

**Conclusion on A2:** the 330 KB is genuinely waste today, and making it non-waste is a bigger project than making it smaller. Recommend not blocking the tier decision on it.

### A3. Revised recommendation for A

Move `activity` to the **60s medium tier** and file the ARC-breakdown extraction separately. Rationale:

- No cheaper source exists, so frequency is the only lever.
- The metrics are thread counts and CPU percentages. `top`'s CPU figures are an instantaneous sample, not an average over the interval — sampling one every 15s versus every 60s changes how often we take a snapshot, not the quality of any individual snapshot. There is no `rate()` being computed off it that a longer interval would distort.
- Cuts ~1.43 GB/day (1.91 → 0.48) and removes 4,320 requests/day.

The honest cost: CPU and thread-count graphs go from 15s to 60s resolution, and a short CPU spike between samples can be missed. If sub-minute CPU visibility matters, the correct fix is upstream (`kern.cp_time` via a sysctl endpoint), not a 331 KB poll.

**Still needs a call from Rob**, since it is a visible dashboard fidelity change.

## Note

This spike also turned up a correction to #535's cost model — the configd actions already carry `cache_ttl:300`, so no scripts are re-executed per request and the per-request cost is log volume, not CPU. Details in that issue.

## The 15s fast tier is currently buying <host-1> almost nothing

Checked <host-1>'s compose: it sets **neither** `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_OTLP_EXPORT_INTERVAL` nor `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_OTLP_FAST_EXPORT_INTERVAL`, so both are at their defaults:

| knob | default | <host-1> |
|---|---|---|
| `--otlp.export-interval` | `60s` | 60s (default) |
| `--otlp.fast-export-interval` | `0s` (disabled) | disabled |
| `IntervalFast` (poll) | `15s` | 15s (code default, **not** a <host-1> setting) |

<host-1> is OTLP-push-only, so OTLP export is the sole delivery path. Fast-tier collectors therefore **poll the firewall every 15s into a snapshot that is only read every 60s.** Three of every four fast-tier polls are overwritten before anything reads them.

Two corrections to how this has been framed:

1. **DPM is already 1/min.** Data points per minute is set by the *export* interval, not the poll interval — so <host-1> is already at 1 DPM per series. There is no Grafana Cloud billing win available here, because the billing side is already correct. The waste is entirely on the firewall side.
2. **15s is the code default, not a <host-1> override.** Changing it changes behaviour for every user, including Prometheus-scrape deployments that may genuinely scrape at 15s.

The 15s poll is not *literally* worthless: at export time the value is at most 15s stale rather than at most 60s stale. That is a real but modest freshness gain, bought at 4× the API requests — and under #535, 4× the configd audit lines.

Note that `--otlp.fast-export-interval` (#390) exists precisely to make the fast tier pay off — export fast-tier series at 15s while everything else stays 60s. <host-1> does not use it. So today <host-1> pays the full cost of a fast tier and collects the smallest available share of the benefit.

## The trap in "just change IntervalFast to 60s"

If `IntervalFast` becomes 60s it equals `IntervalMedium`, and the fast tier stops existing as a distinct poll cadence. It would still route export-lane membership under #390, but a tier whose interval is identical to the default is a confusing thing to keep in the table.

## Proposal: make poll cadence follow the lane that consumes it

The coherent principle is **do not poll faster than the thing that reads the snapshot**. Concretely:

- If `--otlp.fast-export-interval` is set, fast-tier collectors poll at that interval. Set it to 15s and you get a genuine 15s lane, end to end.
- If it is unset and OTLP is the only delivery path, fast-tier collectors poll at `--otlp.export-interval` instead of 15s. <host-1>'s fast tier drops to 60s automatically, cutting ~78 requests/min to ~20 with no loss of exported data points.
- Prometheus-scrape deployments keep today's behaviour: the exporter cannot know the scrape interval, so 15s stays the default there.
- Emit a **startup warning** whenever a resolved poll interval is shorter than the interval that will consume it. That is the general fix — it catches this class of misconfiguration for any tier, not just fast.

This gets the outcome Rob wants (<host-1> stops polling at 15s) without hardcoding a 60s fast tier for users whose delivery path actually consumes it faster.

## Decision needed

Which of:

- **(a)** Implement the follow-the-consumer rule above + startup warning. Recommended.
- **(b)** Just change `IntervalFast` 15s → 60s globally. Simplest, one-line, but collapses fast into medium for everyone including Prometheus users scraping at 15s.
- **(c)** Leave the code alone and fix <host-1> only — set `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_OTLP_FAST_EXPORT_INTERVAL=15s` (use the data we already pay for) or override the fast collectors to 60s (stop paying).

(a) and (c) are not exclusive — (c) is the immediate mitigation, (a) is the durable fix.

## Scope change: this is now "realign poll cadence with export cadence" (Rob, 2026-07-30)

Decided: the poll/export decoupling is a **leftover from when Prometheus scrape drove collection**. #336 split them so a scrape stopped triggering a firewall fetch — correct at the time, but the two were left with no relationship at all, and nothing has re-established one since OTLP push became the primary delivery path. That is the actual defect; the 15s fast tier is a symptom.

Also decided: **#535's syslog exclude is dropped.** Fixing the request volume fixes the log volume, proportionally and with no new operator-facing knob.

## Current behaviour (as-built, verified)

| | |
|---|---|
| poll interval | tier table → `IntervalFast 15s` / `Medium 60s` / `Slow 5m` / `Cold 15m`, `--collector.poll-interval-override` wins (`scheduler.go:56`) |
| poll phase | startup + deterministic FNV-hash-of-name jitter in `[0, 5s)` (`sleepJitter`, `scheduler.go:412`) — **arbitrary relative to export** |
| poll deadline | `advanceDeadline` walks forward from the previous deadline, so poll *duration* does not accumulate drift (`scheduler.go:399`) |
| export | `sdkmetric.NewPeriodicReader(..., WithInterval(cfg.ExportInterval))`, `telemetry/provider.go:84` |
| fast lane | optional second `PeriodicReader` at `FastExportInterval` over a disjoint gatherer set, `provider.go:105` (#390) |
| export phase | reader construction time. The SDK exposes no phase control. |

Nothing anywhere compares a poll interval to the interval that consumes it.

## Design

### 1. Poll cadence follows the consuming lane

New resolution order, replacing `resolvePollInterval`'s current terminal step:

1. `--collector.poll-interval-override=<name>=<dur>` — explicit operator intent, **always wins, never clamped by this rule** (warned about, see §3).
2. Otherwise `effective = max(tierInterval, consumingLaneInterval)`.

Consuming lane per collector:

| collector | OTLP on, fast lane set | OTLP on, no fast lane | OTLP off (Prometheus scrape) |
|---|---|---|---|
| fast tier | `--otlp.fast-export-interval` | `--otlp.export-interval` | tier interval (15s), unchanged |
| every other tier | `--otlp.export-interval` | `--otlp.export-interval` | tier interval, unchanged |

`max()` not "replace": a cold collector must not start polling every 60s because the export lane is 60s. The rule only ever makes polling **slower**, never faster — so it cannot increase load on anyone's firewall, which matters for a change shipping to other people's boxes.

On <host-1> (`export-interval` 60s default, no fast lane) this takes the fast tier 15s → 60s: **~78 → ~20 requests/min**, with zero change in exported data points, and a 4× cut in this box's share of #535's audit volume.

`IntervalFast` stays in the table. It remains the Prometheus-mode default and, importantly, the **classifier** for fast-lane membership under #390 — so the tier keeps its meaning even where it no longer sets the cadence.

### 2. Phase alignment — polls land just before the export

Worth doing, and cheaper than it looks. Both sides are periodic with the same period once §1 lands, so a phase offset established once persists; Go tickers target absolute deadlines and do not accumulate drift.

- Capture a common `epoch` at startup, before constructing either the readers or the pollers.
- Construct the OTLP readers at `epoch`, so exports land at `epoch + n·P`.
- Schedule polls at `epoch + n·P − lead` (replacing the cold-start jitter for lane-aligned collectors), computed from the epoch rather than by accumulating, reusing the existing `advanceDeadline` shape.
- `lead` sized from observed poll duration — we already export `opnsense_exporter_api_request_duration_seconds` and per-collector poll duration, so this can be measured rather than guessed. Default a few seconds, operator-overridable.

**Keep the herd-spreading.** The current name-hash jitter exists to stop every collector dialing the firewall at once, and the poll-concurrency cap (8) exists for the same reason. Aligning every collector to the same instant would undo that. So spread collectors across the window `[epoch + n·P − lead − spread, epoch + n·P − lead]` — jitter *within the lead window* instead of jitter against an arbitrary phase.

Failure mode to accept explicitly: if a poll overruns `lead`, that collector's export carries the previous cycle's value. That is already what happens on average today, so it is a smaller-benefit case, not a regression.

### 3. Startup warning

Warn when a resolved poll interval is **shorter than the lane that consumes it** — which after §1 can only happen via an explicit `--collector.poll-interval-override`. Message should name the collector, both intervals, and the ratio of wasted polls, e.g.:

```
poll interval shorter than its export lane; N of every M polls will be overwritten unread
  collector=activity poll=15s lane=otlp.export-interval(60s)
```

Also warn on `--otlp.fast-export-interval` set with no fast-tier collectors enabled, which is silently a no-op today.

This is the general form of the bug and is worth having independently of §1 — it catches the whole class, not just this instance.

## Open questions — need decisions before implementation

**Q1. Does the rule apply to Prometheus-scrape deployments at all?**
The exporter cannot know the scrape interval. Options: (a) leave Prometheus mode exactly as today (recommended — no behaviour change for existing scrape users); (b) add `--exporter.expected-scrape-interval` purely to drive the clamp and the warning. (b) is more correct and more knobs.

**Q2. The reverse direction — are we over-*exporting* the slow tiers?**
This is the other half of "rethink the whole export interval", and it is a real DPM question. A cold-tier collector polls every 15m but exports every 60s, so **15 identical samples are billed per actual change**. Across the cold and slow tiers that is a large share of DPM spent on values that did not move.

Fixing it properly means an export lane per tier. Two constraints make that non-trivial: Grafana Cloud's OTLP gateway is HTTP/1.1-only, so concurrent exports need a TCP connection each and the default `MaxIdleConnsPerHost=2` throttles them — going from 2 lanes to 4 needs the transport tuned deliberately. And sparse series read as gaps in Grafana, which is exactly why `IntervalCeil` is 15m today.

Recommend **not** bundling this into #550. It is a bigger change with a billing upside and a real risk of making dashboards look broken. Its own issue, informed by measuring what share of DPM the slow/cold tiers actually represent.

**Q3. Is `lead` worth the complexity, or is §1 enough on its own?**
§1 alone removes the waste. §2 only improves *freshness at export time* — with §1, poll and export run at the same period but arbitrary phase, so an exported value is on average half an interval old and at worst a full interval. §2 makes it consistently `lead`-old. Worth it for a 60s lane; marginal for a 15s one.

## Not in scope

- Reducing the per-request configd cost — upstream OPNsense, #535.
- `get_activity`'s 331 KB payload — still open above, unaffected by this design.

## Decisions on the open questions (Rob, 2026-07-30)

**Q1 — Prometheus-scrape mode: unchanged.** The clamp and the warning apply only when OTLP is a delivery path. Scrape-only deployments keep today's tier intervals exactly, and no `--exporter.expected-scrape-interval` flag is added. Accepted cost: a scrape-only user scraping at 60s keeps over-polling the fast tier and we say nothing about it.

**Q2 — over-export of the slow/cold tiers: won't fix, but document it.** Repeated identical samples are effectively free: DPM is set by the export interval whether or not the value moved, so cold-tier collectors exporting an unchanged value every 60s costs nothing beyond what the lane already costs. Reducing export frequency per tier would cut DPM but produce sparse series that read as dashboard gaps, which is the same reason `IntervalCeil` is 15m. **Closed as a deliberate decision, not an oversight** — needs writing down somewhere durable so it stops being re-raised as a bug.

**Q3 — phase alignment: dropped entirely.** Not just deferred. §1 removes all the wasted polling; §2 only improved freshness-at-export, and it is not worth owning the epoch anchoring, reader-construction ordering and herd-spreading interaction for that. Exported values remain on average half a lane-interval old, which is accepted.

## Implementation scope, final

1. **Poll cadence follows the consuming lane** — `effective = max(tierInterval, laneInterval)`, OTLP delivery paths only. `--collector.poll-interval-override` still wins outright.
2. **Startup warning** when a resolved poll interval is shorter than the lane that consumes it (after 1, only reachable via an explicit override), plus a warning when `--otlp.fast-export-interval` is set with no fast-tier collectors enabled.
3. **Document the Q2 decision** — why the slow and cold tiers deliberately export unchanged values, so it is not "fixed" later.

Explicitly out: phase alignment, per-tier export lanes, any Prometheus-mode behaviour change, and #535's syslog exclude.

## Implementation trap: do not clamp inside `resolveInterval` (now in the body)

Recording this in the timeline too, since it was found after the design comment above and it invalidates the most obvious way to implement §1.

Fast **lane membership** reads the *effective* poll interval — `collector.go:1679`, `if c.resolveInterval(coll) <= IntervalFast`. That is deliberate under #390: it is what lets an operator override move a collector between export lanes. Clamping inside `resolveInterval` therefore makes membership depend on the clamp that depends on membership.

It survives both the values we happen to care about and fails on everything between them:

| `--otlp.fast-export-interval` | clamped | `<= IntervalFast`? | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `15s` | 15s | yes | correct |
| unset | 60s | no | harmless (lane not built when interval is 0) |
| **`30s`** | 30s | **no** | **lane configured but empty, silently** |

Fix is to split declared from effective: `resolveInterval` keeps the declared interval and keeps feeding lane membership; a new effective-poll-interval applies `max(declared, lane)` and feeds the scheduler, the reported `collector_poll_interval_seconds`, and `StatusTracker.SetInterval`. Membership → lane → cadence, one direction only.

Guard test: with `fast-export-interval=30s` and a fast-tier collector enabled, `FastCollectorNames()` must be non-empty.

## <host-1> will likely run a 15s fast lane — which puts decision A back in play

Noting the interaction, because it removes an accidental fix I referred to earlier.

If <host-1> sets `--otlp.fast-export-interval=15s` (the expected config, and the thing #390 was built for), then the lane clamp resolves fast-tier collectors to `max(15s, 15s)` = 15s. `activity` is a fast-tier collector, so it keeps polling every 15s and **the 1.9 GB/day stands**. The clamp only demoted it in the no-fast-lane case, which <host-1> is not expected to stay in.

So decision A has to be made on its own merits rather than falling out of §1. Three routes:

1. **Demote `activity` under rule C.** The admission rule as drafted is *fast tier is for data whose change is itself the alertable event, or which feeds a `rate()` alerted on at sub-minute resolution*. Thread counts and `top`'s instantaneous CPU percentages meet neither. Applying the rule demotes `activity` to medium — which is the tidiest outcome, because it makes A a consequence of C rather than a standing one-off exception.
2. **Consume `cpu_usage/stream` over SSE.** ~6 MB/day against 1.9 GB/day, authenticates once at connect so it also sidesteps #535's per-request tax. Gated on the SSE architecture decision in **#553**, and it only replaces the CPU half — the stream carries no thread counts, so `activity` would still need a slower poll for those.
3. **Accept it.** Keep 15s and the payload.

Recommend 1, with 2 revisited only if #553 concludes we want outbound SSE for other reasons anyway. 1 needs no new architecture and is decided by a rule we have already agreed to write.

Cross-reference: the SSE research is tracked in **#553** (sections 1–2, plus acceptance items for giving `cpu_usage/stream` an explicit verdict and for deciding whether outbound SSE consumption is an architecture we will adopt at all). That last one gates route 2 here.

## Decision A, measured properly: yes we want 15s CPU — and `get_activity` is a bad way to get it

Rob pushed back on demoting `activity`, on the grounds that we want the data at 15s. Checked it rather than argued it, and the answer splits cleanly by metric.

### `get_activity` costs 2.15 seconds of firewall work per call

Live from <host-1>'s own histogram:

```
api_request_duration_seconds_sum{endpoint="api/diagnostics/activity/get_activity"}   25.750862
api_request_duration_seconds_count{endpoint="api/diagnostics/activity/get_activity"}        12
```

**2.15 s/call average.** For scale, `pf_statistics/info` on the same box and same sample is 0.09 s.

It is inherent, not incidental. `activity.py:49` runs:

```python
subprocess.run(['/usr/bin/top','-aHSTn','-d2','999999'], ...)
```

`-d2` is *two displays*, and the script takes the second (`split('\n\n',2)[-1]`). top must wait out its inter-display delay to compute a CPU delta at all — the first display would be since-boot averages and therefore useless. So the ~2s is the price of the CPU numbers being real. It also runs `procstat -ath` (a full thread walk) first, at `activity.py:44`.

**At a 15s poll that is a 14% duty cycle, permanently** — the firewall is running `procstat` + `top` for 2.15 of every 15 seconds, forever. At 60s it is 3.6%.

### The CPU numbers are genuine, but the sampling is sparse

Because they come from top's second display, they are a real ~2-second CPU delta — not a lifetime average. Rob is right that this is legitimate data and that a firewall wants sub-minute CPU visibility.

But note what a 15s poll actually buys: **a 2-second sample every 15 seconds ≈ 13% timeline coverage.** Sustained saturation is caught; a 10-second spike between samples is invisible. We pay a 14% duty cycle to observe 13% of the timeline.

### `cpu_usage/stream` is strictly better data *and* ~300× cheaper

`iostat -w 1` behind SSE gives a **continuous 1-second series — 100% timeline coverage** — at ~70 bytes/sec and effectively no firewall CPU (iostat reads sysctls; no process-table walk, no PHP worker held open for 2s). It also authenticates once at connect, so it sidesteps #535 entirely.

This is not "cheaper but worse". For the CPU half it is **better resolution, complete coverage, and near-zero cost**. My earlier framing of SSE as merely a "partial win" understated this.

### Revised recommendation for A — split by metric, not by collector

| metric | source | cadence |
|---|---|---|
| CPU user/nice/sys/intr/idle | `cpu_usage/stream` (SSE) | continuous 1s |
| thread counts (total/running/sleeping/waiting) | `get_activity` | medium (60s) or slower |

Thread-state counts are instantaneous gauges with no sub-minute alerting story, so 60s loses nothing. They are also the *only* thing `get_activity` uniquely provides.

Outcome: keep — in fact substantially improve — the 15s CPU visibility Rob wants, while taking `get_activity` from a 14% duty cycle and 1.9 GB/day down to 3.6% and 480 MB/day.

**This makes #553's outbound-SSE architecture decision the gate on the good outcome for A**, rather than an optional nicety. If #553 concludes we will not consume SSE, A falls back to a straight choice between keeping the 14% duty cycle and accepting 60s CPU.

**Decision A is now resolved** — every open question on this issue is closed.

Rob authorised the SSE pilot in #553, so A splits by metric rather than demoting the whole collector:

- **CPU** → `cpu_usage/stream` over SSE, accumulated into `cpu_seconds_total{mode}`. 100% timeline coverage instead of 13%, ~0% firewall duty cycle instead of 14%. Built in **#559**.
- **Thread counts** → stay on `get_activity`, with the `activity` collector demoted to medium. They are instantaneous gauges with no sub-minute alerting story, and they are the only thing that endpoint uniquely provides.

Net on `get_activity`: 14% duty cycle → 3.6%, 1.91 GB/day → 480 MB/day.

This issue's own remaining scope is unchanged and unblocked: §1 poll-cadence-follows-lane, the startup warning, and documenting the Q2 over-export decision — with the `resolveInterval` split described in the body.

Implemented and closed by `286b3f50`. All three scoped items landed.

1. **Poll cadence follows the consuming lane** — `internal/collector/poll_lane.go`. `effective = max(declared, laneInterval)`, OTLP delivery paths only, override still wins outright, scrape-only untouched.
2. **Startup warning** — `PollLaneWarnings()`, logged from `StartPolling`. Both cases: an override polling faster than its lane, and `--otlp.fast-export-interval` set with no fast-tier collector enabled.
3. **Q2 documented** — `docs/configuration.md`, under "Why the slow and cold tiers export unchanged values", stating both halves of the reasoning (repeated identical samples are free because DPM follows the export interval; per-tier lanes would trade that for sparse series that read as dashboard gaps) so it is not re-raised as a bug.

## The trap held, and the guard test proves it

The body's warning was correct and the split is implemented exactly as specified: `resolveInterval` still returns the **declared** interval and still feeds `FastCollectorNames()`; the clamp lives one layer above in `effectiveInterval`, which feeds the scheduler, `collector_poll_interval_seconds` and `StatusTracker.SetInterval`.

`TestFastLaneMembershipSurvivesIntermediateFastExportInterval` pins `fast-export-interval=30s` with a fast-tier collector enabled and requires non-empty membership. I confirmed it actually catches the bug rather than merely passing: injecting the circular version (`FastCollectorNames` reading `effectiveInterval`) makes it fail with `fast lane membership = []`, while every other test in the package still passes. 15s and unset both survive the injected bug, exactly as the body predicted.

## Effect on <host-1>

`--otlp.export-interval` at its 60s default with no fast lane, so every fast-tier collector goes 15s -> 60s: ~78 -> ~20 requests/min, with zero change in exported data points.

Two things worth knowing about how this interacts with decision A, now that #559 has landed:

- If <host-1> later sets `--otlp.fast-export-interval=15s`, the fast tier returns to a 15s poll. That is the intended behaviour and is now much cheaper than it was, because `get_activity` is no longer fast-tier.
- The new `cpu` collector is fast-tier and makes **no API call**, so a 15s fast lane buys 15s CPU resolution for free. That is the case this design was worth building for.

Also corrected in passing: `docs/configuration.md` described fast-lane membership as following the "effective" poll interval. It follows the **declared** one, and after this change that distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic.

## Decisions B, C and D now have tracking issues

These three were taken here on 2026-07-30 but deliberately left out of this issue's implementation scope, and had no home until now.

| decision | issue | scope |
|---|---|---|
| **B** — relax the fast-tier body-cache ban | #567 | Change `TestBodyCachedEndpointsPollSlowerThanTheirTTL` from a blanket fast-tier ban to a per-endpoint recorded justification. Does **not** attach any TTL — it only removes the structural blocker, so #344's "tier follows the live half, body cache handles the static endpoints" arrangement stops being unavailable to the one tier that polls most often. |
| **C** — fast-tier admission rule | #568 | Write the criterion a new collector is held against, covering both cost axes and all three admission clauses. Carries the draft wording plus the requirement that it admit `carp` (zero churn, transition is the event) and `cpu` (no API call at all) without special-casing either. |
| **D** — full tier re-audit | #569 | Every collector, not just the fast tier. Depends on #568 landing first, since the audit applies that criterion rather than inventing one. |

Two things carried forward into #568 that were settled after this issue closed and are not in the body above:

- **Dashboard fidelity is an admission clause in its own right.** `interfaces` and `protocol` were demoted to 60s on the reference deployment on the grounds that no alert or recording rule samples them faster than a 5m window, and that was overruled: *"I care less about recording/alerting rules and more about dashboard fidelity and I think interfaces and protocol should be 15s but yeah netflow can stay 60."* Both are back at 15s. Any rule written without a fidelity clause would re-demote them, so #568 pins it.
- **The fast tier is 7 collectors, not 6** — `cpu` joined it in #559. It is the one member that costs the firewall nothing, which is a shape the rule has to accommodate rather than trip over.
