body:
Follow-up from #537. The residual finding there was that on a **stock deployment the `country` label is still empty**, because `--geoip.enabled` defaults off — it needs a MaxMind database the exporter does not ship. That is the thing worth fixing, and it is fixable.

## The licensing answer: GeoLite2 cannot be bundled

Checked against MaxMind's current terms rather than assumed.

Bundling GeoLite2 into a product you distribute requires a **[Commercial Redistribution License for GeoLite2](https://support.maxmind.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408928143643-Commercial-Redistribution-License-for-GeoLite2)** — a paid, signed agreement. It additionally requires that we hold every downstream user to a EULA restricting their use to "Internal Restricted Business Purposes", and grants end users only a personal, nontransferable, nonexclusive right.

That is incompatible with an Apache-2.0 public Docker image on two counts: we cannot impose those downstream restrictions, and we are not going to sign a commercial agreement to do it. **So the current download-it-yourself arrangement is correct for MaxMind and must stay.**

(For the record, GeoLite2 was CC BY-SA 4.0 until December 2019 and stopped being so — anything found online asserting otherwise is describing the old terms.)

## The alternative that does work: DB-IP Lite

**[DB-IP Lite](https://db-ip.com/db/lite.php)** publishes IP-to-Country and IP-to-ASN databases **in MMDB format** under a plain **[Creative Commons Attribution 4.0](https://db-ip.com/db/download/ip-to-country-lite)** licence, updated monthly, with no account or token required to download.

Why this fits particularly well here:

- **The reader is already generic.** `go.mod` uses `oschwald/maxminddb-golang/v2`, the raw MMDB reader — not `geoip2-golang`. Any MMDB file works provided the record schema matches.
- **The file split already matches.** DB-IP ships country and ASN as separate databases, which maps directly onto the existing `--geoip.country-database` and `--geoip.asn-database` flags. No config surgery.
- **CC BY, not CC BY-SA.** No ShareAlike clause to reason about against Apache-2.0.

**Runner-up: [IPinfo Lite](https://ipinfo.io/lite)** — also MMDB, also free, country + continent + ASN in a single file. Two drawbacks: it is **CC BY-SA 4.0** (a ShareAlike clause on bundled data is a question I would rather not have to answer), and downloading requires signup for a token, which complicates a reproducible CI build. Worth benchmarking for accuracy, but DB-IP is the better default.

## The one thing that must be verified first

**Schema compatibility is NOT confirmed.** DB-IP's download page documents the licence and formats but publishes no schema comparison against GeoLite2, and I would not assert it from memory. The exporter reads these exact paths (`internal/geoip/geoip.go:109-135`):

```
continent.code
country.iso_code
registered_country.iso_code
represented_country.iso_code
city.names          (City database only)
subdivisions.iso_code
autonomous_system_number
autonomous_system_organization
```

This is cheap to settle: download the Lite MMDB and read it with the existing reader. If the ASN field names differ, a small field-alias in the decode structs handles it — the reader is tag-driven.

## Why it is worth doing

- Makes `country` on the flow families actually work out of the box, which is what #537 was really about.
- Makes GeoIP enrichment on filterlog / sshd / Suricata log lines (#528) work without an operator sourcing a database first.
- Removes the MaxMind account, license key and `--geoip.download.*` machinery from the happy path — that stays for operators who want MaxMind's better accuracy.
- Lets `--geoip.enabled` plausibly default **on**, which is the real prize.

## Costs and open decisions

- **Image size.** Country + ASN MMDB is roughly 10-20 MB combined. Needs measuring before committing.
- **Staleness.** A database baked into an image goes stale between releases, where the download path refreshes independently. `OPNsenseFlowGeoIPDatabaseStale` already exists and would cover it, but the bundled copy's build date should be surfaced honestly rather than implying freshness.
- **Attribution is a real, ongoing obligation.** CC BY requires crediting DB-IP wherever results are displayed — so `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, the docs site, and arguably the webui console. This is not a one-line note; getting it wrong is the licence violation.
- **Accuracy is lower than GeoLite2.** DB-IP Lite is explicitly a reduced-coverage subset. Docs must say so and point at MaxMind for operators who need better.
- **Should `--geoip.enabled` flip to default-on?** Probably, but it is a separate behaviour change with its own log/flow byte cost (#528's upgrade note), so decide it deliberately rather than as a side effect.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Verify DB-IP Lite MMDB decodes against the existing structs; record the field-by-field result
- [ ] Measure the image size delta for country + ASN
- [ ] Decide bundle-vs-download precedence: an operator-supplied database must always win over the bundled one
- [ ] Wire the bundled paths as the defaults for `--geoip.country-database` / `--geoip.asn-database`
- [ ] Attribution in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, docs, and the webui where geo results are shown
- [ ] Surface the bundled database's build date honestly; confirm the staleness alert behaves
- [ ] Decide separately whether `--geoip.enabled` defaults on
- [ ] Document the accuracy trade-off and how to switch to MaxMind
- [ ] Refresh mechanism for the bundled copy — CI job or release-time fetch, since it updates monthly

comments.body:
## Provider decision: DB-IP Lite — and the licensing concern largely dissolves

Researched properly rather than asserted. Recording the reasoning because the obvious worry (ShareAlike infecting our Apache-2.0 code) turns out not to be the deciding factor.

### CC BY-SA does not threaten our licence, in either direction

From the [CC BY-SA 4.0 legal code](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/legalcode.en):

- **§1** defines *Adapted Material* as material "translated, altered, arranged, transformed, or otherwise modified". Shipping a vendor `.mmdb` byte-for-byte in an image is none of those — it is mere aggregation, and the Go code is not derived from the database.
- **§4(2)** is the only database-specific trigger, and it is narrow:

  > if You include all or a substantial portion of the database contents **in a database in which You have Sui Generis Database Rights**, then **the database** in which You have Sui Generis Database Rights (**but not its individual contents**) is Adapted Material

So ShareAlike bites **only if CI builds a derived database** — converting CSV→MMDB ourselves, merging country+ASN, or trimming the file to shrink the image. And even then it attaches to *that database*, never to the exporter.

**Conclusion: if CI downloads the vendor's MMDB and copies it in verbatim, CC BY and CC BY-SA are equivalent for our purposes.** The difference only surfaces if we ever repack or trim — which is plausible enough for image size that CC BY's freedom there stays a genuine, if secondary, advantage.

Attribution is required identically by both, so it does not discriminate.

### What actually decides it: integration, not licence

| | DB-IP Lite | IPinfo Lite |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | CC BY 4.0 | CC BY-SA 4.0 |
| Risk to Apache-2.0 code | none | none (per above) |
| Files | **2 — country + ASN** | 1 combined (`ipinfo_lite.mmdb`) |
| Maps onto existing `--geoip.country-database` / `--geoip.asn-database` | **directly** | no |
| MMDB record schema | GeoIP2-shaped (still to verify) | **flat and different**: `network`, `country`, `country_code`, `continent`, `continent_code`, `asn`, `as_name`, `as_domain` |
| Download | **anonymous direct** | token-in-URL (`?token=$TOKEN`) |
| Update cadence | monthly | **daily** |
| Vendor's own quality claim | "reduced coverage and accuracy" subset | same validation as premium |

**DB-IP wins on integration decisively.** Two files matching the two existing flags; likely no decode changes; and no token — which matters more than it looks, since a signup-gated download adds a CI secret to manage and rotate, and a vendor gating downloads can change terms behind the gate.

**IPinfo genuinely wins on data.** Daily vs monthly is a real gap for a database baked into an image, and DB-IP self-describes Lite as reduced-accuracy while IPinfo claims Lite receives premium validation. But this exporter labels metrics with **country only** — city and region are log attributes — and independent testing puts country-level accuracy above 95% for every provider. The delta lands almost entirely on data we do not label with. If that changes, switching is a swap of decode structs, not an architecture change.

IPinfo's schema being flat and non-GeoLite2 is worth noting as a hard fact rather than a preference: adopting it *requires* new decode structs regardless, whereas DB-IP may require none.

### Layering, as decided

1. **MaxMind** — if the operator supplies credentials or a database path, it wins outright. Best accuracy, unchanged behaviour, no bundled data involved.
2. **Operator-supplied path** — an explicit `--geoip.*-database` beats the bundled copy.
3. **Bundled DB-IP Lite** — the default value of those flags, refreshed by CI.

That ordering is what lets `--geoip.enabled` default on and closes #537's residual finding: the `country` label is empty on a stock deployment today purely because no database ships.

### Still unverified

DB-IP's schema compatibility. Their download page documents licence and format but publishes no schema comparison against GeoLite2, so it stays the first acceptance item — download the Lite MMDB, read it with the existing `oschwald/maxminddb-golang/v2` reader against the structs at `internal/geoip/geoip.go:109-135`, record the field-by-field result.

Not legal advice — this is a reading of the licence text, and the CC BY attribution obligation is the part where getting it wrong actually matters.

## Verdict: **drop-in** for Country and ASN. No struct changes needed for the two databases the acceptance item names.

Verified by downloading the current (2026-07) DB-IP Lite MMDB files and decoding them with `github.com/oschwald/maxminddb-golang/v2 v2.4.1` (the exact version pinned in `go.mod`) into unmodified copies of `countryRecord` and `asnRecord` from `internal/geoip/geoip.go:107-136`. Full scratch program, raw dumps and decoded output are below.

### Download

Pattern `https://download.db-ip.com/free/dbip-<product>-lite-YYYY-MM.mmdb.gz` worked first try, no account/token, plain `curl`:

```
curl -o dbip-country-lite-2026-07.mmdb.gz https://download.db-ip.com/free/dbip-country-lite-2026-07.mmdb.gz  → HTTP 200
curl -o dbip-asn-lite-2026-07.mmdb.gz     https://download.db-ip.com/free/dbip-asn-lite-2026-07.mmdb.gz      → HTTP 200
curl -o dbip-city-lite-2026-07.mmdb.gz    https://download.db-ip.com/free/dbip-city-lite-2026-07.mmdb.gz     → HTTP 200 (checked out of curiosity, not requested by acceptance — see below)
```

This is trivially automatable in CI: predictable filename, current year-month, no auth. The only wrinkle for a scheduled job is computing `YYYY-MM` and handling a 404 on the 1st of the month if DB-IP's publish lags UTC midnight (not observed here, not tested).

### File sizes and metadata

| File | Compressed (.gz) | Uncompressed (.mmdb) | `database_type` | Build time (metadata `build_epoch`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dbip-country-lite-2026-07.mmdb` | 4,046,283 B (3.86 MiB) | 8,182,135 B (7.80 MiB) | `DBIP-Country-Lite` | 1782869996 → 2026-07-01 01:39:56 UTC |
| `dbip-asn-lite-2026-07.mmdb` | 5,209,292 B (4.97 MiB) | 9,634,823 B (9.19 MiB) | `DBIP-ASN-Lite (compat=GeoLite2-ASN)` | 1782870319 → 2026-07-01 01:45:19 UTC |
| `dbip-city-lite-2026-07.mmdb` (not requested, checked anyway) | 62,244,938 B (59.4 MiB) | 131,263,181 B (125.2 MiB) | `DBIP-City-Lite` | 1782870305 → 2026-07-01 01:45:05 UTC |

Country + ASN combined uncompressed: **~17.0 MB**, comfortably inside the roadmap's 10-20 MB estimate. Both files self-report their build date in `Metadata.BuildEpoch`, which is exactly what the existing staleness-surfacing needs (acceptance item "surface the bundled database's build date honestly") — no separate mechanism required.

### Field-by-field verdict (Country + ASN Lite)

| Exporter path (`geoip.go` struct tag) | DB-IP Country/ASN Lite | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `continent.code` | present, e.g. `"NA"` | populates |
| `country.iso_code` | present, e.g. `"US"` | populates |
| `registered_country.iso_code` | **key absent from the schema entirely** (`registered_country` never appears anywhere in the file, confirmed via `strings` over all three files) | always decodes empty — inert, not broken |
| `represented_country.iso_code` | **key absent from the schema entirely**, same check | always decodes empty — inert, not broken |
| `city.names` | absent in Country/ASN Lite (expected — City-only field, see below) | empty, as designed |
| `subdivisions.iso_code` | absent in Country/ASN Lite (expected — City-only field) | empty, as designed |
| `autonomous_system_number` | present, e.g. `15169` | populates |
| `autonomous_system_organization` | present, e.g. `"Google LLC"` | populates |

All five test IPs (`<pub-ip-9>`, `<pub-ip-6>`, `<pub-ip-14>`, `<pub-ip-17>8888`, and unallocated `203.0.113.1`/TEST-NET-3) behaved as expected: real lookups populate country/continent/ASN, the unallocated address returns a nil lookup (`RAW: null`) and every field zero-values cleanly with no decode error.

**`countryFrom`'s three-way fallback (`geoip.go:142-150`) is dead code against DB-IP data** — not wrong, just inert, because DB-IP never omits `country` the way MaxMind does. The code comment at `geoip.go:104` cites `<pub-ip-6>` as the canonical case with no `country` object, only `registered_country` — I checked this specific claim against DB-IP and it does NOT hold there: DB-IP's `<pub-ip-6>` record carries `country.iso_code=AU` directly (raw dump below). So the fallback chain still exists as designed for MaxMind but simply never triggers with a DB-IP file loaded. Not a defect, just worth knowing before anyone "simplifies" that function.

### Raw decode evidence

Country Lite, `<pub-ip-9>`:
```json
{"continent":{"code":"NA","geoname_id":6255149,"names":{"en":"North America", ...}},
 "country":{"geoname_id":6252001,"is_in_european_union":false,"iso_code":"US","names":{"en":"United States", ...}}}
```
Decoded into `countryRecord`: `{"Continent":{"Code":"NA"},"Country":{"ISOCode":"US"},"RegisteredCountry":{"ISOCode":""},"RepresentedCountry":{"ISOCode":""},"City":{"Names":null},"Subdivisions":null}`

Country Lite, `<pub-ip-6>`:
```json
{"continent":{"code":"OC", ...},"country":{"iso_code":"AU", ...}}
```
Decoded: `{"Continent":{"Code":"OC"},"Country":{"ISOCode":"AU"}, ...}` — contradicts the geoip.go:104 comment's premise for this specific IP against DB-IP (see above).

Country Lite, `203.0.113.1` (TEST-NET-3, unallocated): `RAW: null`, decodes to an all-zero `countryRecord`, no error.

ASN Lite, `<pub-ip-9>`:
```json
{"autonomous_system_number":15169,"autonomous_system_organization":"Google LLC"}
```
Decoded into `asnRecord`: `{"Number":15169,"Org":"Google LLC"}`

ASN Lite, `<pub-ip-14>` (prod box's own WAN address):
```json
{"autonomous_system_number":5089,"autonomous_system_organization":"Virgin Media Limited"}
```
Decoded: `{"Number":5089,"Org":"Virgin Media Limited"}`

ASN Lite, `<pub-ip-17>8888` (IPv6, Google public DNS): `{"Number":15169,"Org":"Google LLC"}` — IPv6 lookups work identically, both files are `ip_version=6` (dual-stack tree) per metadata.

ASN Lite, `203.0.113.1`: `RAW: null`, decodes to `{"Number":0,"Org":""}`, no error.

Full output files (available if useful, not attached): `country-output.txt`, `asn-output.txt` — every one of the 5 IPs × both files, raw JSON + both struct decodes.

### ASN file structure

ASN is a **separate file** from Country, not merged — matches the exporter's existing `--geoip.country-database` / `--geoip.asn-database` two-flag split exactly, no config changes needed. `database_type` for the ASN file is literally `"DBIP-ASN-Lite (compat=GeoLite2-ASN)"`, i.e. DB-IP is asserting schema compatibility with GeoLite2-ASN in the metadata string itself, which matches what was measured here.

### Bonus finding: DB-IP City Lite, checked but not required by this acceptance item

Downloaded and decoded the City Lite file out of curiosity since `countryRecord` also carries City-only fields (`city.names`, `subdivisions.iso_code`). Two things worth flagging if City support is ever considered:

- `city.names.en` populates correctly (e.g. `"Mountain View"` for `<pub-ip-9>`, `"Totton"` for `<pub-ip-14>`) — this part is drop-in.
- **`subdivisions[].iso_code` does NOT populate.** DB-IP City Lite's subdivision entries carry only `names` (e.g. `{"names":{"en":"California"}}`) — there is no `iso_code` key in the subdivision object at all in the Lite tier. So `RegionISO` (`geoip.go:165-173`, which reads the *last* subdivision's `iso_code`) would always decode empty against DB-IP City Lite even though the city name itself works. This would need either a name-based alias (reading `subdivisions[].names.en` instead of `.iso_code`, changing the `Result.RegionISO` semantic from an ISO code to a free-text name) or accepting City name works but region code does not. Uncompressed size is also much larger: 125.2 MB, vs. the roadmap's country+ASN estimate — City was never part of this acceptance item's scope but is worth a separate line item if `--geoip.enabled` defaulting on ever gets extended to city-level data.

### Bottom line

**drop-in** for the two databases this acceptance item asks about (Country Lite + ASN Lite). No struct changes, no field aliases, no code changes required to decode either file with the existing `countryRecord`/`asnRecord` types and the pinned `maxminddb-golang/v2` version. `registered_country`/`represented_country` simply never populate with DB-IP data (schema doesn't model the concept) but that is inert, not a defect — the primary `country.iso_code` path DB-IP actually needs is populated on every test IP that has a record at all. City-tier subdivision ISO codes are the one real gap, and out of scope for this item's two named databases.

## Scope extended: city names in, with a size decision attached

City-level data is now in scope for this issue. The verification above already covered the relevant facts, so recording the trade-off here rather than leaving it to be rediscovered mid-implementation.

**DB-IP City Lite is 125 MB uncompressed, against Country Lite's 8.18 MB.**

It is not additive. `--geoip.country-database` already accepts "a MaxMind Country OR City database... a City database is a strict superset", so bundling City *replaces* Country. The image delta is therefore:

| bundle | size |
|---|---|
| Country + ASN | 8.18 + 9.63 = **~17.8 MB** |
| City + ASN | 125 + 9.63 = **~135 MB** |

That is roughly +117 MB for city names, and the exporter is a static Go binary — this would very likely be the largest single thing in the image.

**What city data actually buys, precisely.** City and region are *log attributes only*. They are never metric labels at any setting — `--flow.geoip.metric-dims` gates the `country` label alone, and the flow rollup help text states ASN and city never become labels. So this enriches shipped flow and filterlog/sshd/Suricata log records in Loki, and changes no metric.

**And one thing it does NOT buy, verified:** DB-IP City Lite's `subdivisions[]` entries carry only `names`, never `iso_code`. So `RegionISO` (`internal/geoip/geoip.go`) decodes empty against DB-IP City data even where a city name is present. City names work; region ISO codes do not. Anyone reading a "region" field and finding it blank should find that documented rather than filing a bug.

### The decision this phase must make

1. **Bundle Country + ASN (~17.8 MB) and support City as operator-supplied.** City works today via `--geoip.country-database` pointing at any City MMDB; document the DB-IP City Lite URL so an operator who wants it can fetch it. Keeps the image small, keeps city available. *This is the recommendation unless image size is genuinely not a concern.*
2. **Bundle City + ASN (~135 MB).** City names out of the box, no operator action. Costs ~117 MB on every pull, forever, for data that touches no metric.
3. **Bundle Country + ASN, and have CI publish the City file as a release artifact** so it is a documented one-line download rather than a hunt, without carrying it in the image.

Option 3 is the compromise if city-out-of-the-box matters but 135 MB does not appeal.

Whichever is chosen, the accuracy caveat stands: DB-IP Lite is explicitly a reduced-coverage subset, and city-level accuracy is where free databases diverge most from paid ones — independent testing puts free-tier city accuracy at roughly 70-78% in North America and Western Europe, against country accuracy above 95% everywhere. Docs must not imply city is as trustworthy as country.

### Updated acceptance

- [x] Verify DB-IP Lite MMDB decodes against the existing structs — **drop-in, no code changes** (see report above)
- [x] Measure image size delta — Country+ASN ~17.8 MB, City+ASN ~135 MB
- [ ] **Decide bundle composition** — options 1/2/3 above
- [ ] Bundle-vs-operator precedence: MaxMind creds win outright, then an explicit `--geoip.*-database`, then the bundled copy as the flags' default
- [ ] Wire the bundled paths as flag defaults
- [ ] CI refresh job — `dbip-{country,asn,city}-lite-YYYY-MM.mmdb.gz`, anonymous, predictable
- [ ] Surface the bundled build date from `Metadata.BuildEpoch` (already available, no extra work)
- [ ] CC BY attribution: `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, docs, and the webui where geo results are shown
- [ ] Document that `RegionISO` is always empty against DB-IP City data
- [ ] Document the accuracy trade-off, city especially, and how to switch to MaxMind
- [ ] Decide separately whether `--geoip.enabled` defaults on

Closed by `21b97af`.

**Bundle composition decided: option 1, Country + ASN only (~17.8 MB).** City stays operator-supplied — the URL and a paragraph are in the docs — and no release artifact is published. ~117 MB on every pull forever for data that only ever lands on log attributes and never on a metric label did not justify itself.

**`--geoip.enabled` defaults on**, which is what closes #537's residual finding.

**The files are NOT committed.** They are fetched at image build time on a dedicated stage: 17.8 MB of binary per month is exactly the cost being avoided, and an image cannot lie about its own data the way a second copy in git can drift. Each file is verified on fetch — gunzip CRC, size floor, MMDB magic, and the expected `database_type` — so a renamed or re-typed upstream product fails the build rather than shipping. Previous-month fallback handles a publish lag on the 1st; `--build-arg DBIP_MONTH` pins it.

Refresh is a monthly rebuild of `:main`, gated on both files actually being present so a run cannot republish last month's data and look like it worked.

**Consequence worth stating plainly:** builds now depend on `download.db-ip.com`, and a fetch failure is fatal. That is deliberate — a silently geo-less release is worse than a loud failure — but it does put a third party in the release path.

Verified in the built image: both databases load (`DBIP-Country-Lite`, `DBIP-ASN-Lite (compat=GeoLite2-ASN)`) and lookups resolve through the repo's own `Open`/`Lookup`. Verified on a non-Docker build that nothing exists at the bundled path, the exporter starts fail-open with a warning, and enrichment is simply absent — pinned by a test.

**CC BY attribution** lands in four places: `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, a licences file beside the data in the image, the docs, and the console footer (unconditional — the console cannot know which database answered, and a sometimes-credit is a sometimes-missing credit).

### One thing the implementation surfaced that was not in the plan

`OPNsenseFlowGeoIPDatabaseStale` fired at **14 days**, sized for GeoLite2's twice-weekly rebuild. DB-IP republishes **monthly**, so on a stock deployment it would have sat firing for roughly half of every month while describing a working updater. Retuned to **45 days**, with the reasoning recorded in the rule so nobody puts it back.

The cost is real and accepted: a dead MaxMind updater now takes 45d to page instead of 14d. Tolerable because this is a warning about data *drift*, not an outage, and `opnsense_flow_geoip_downloads_total` / `_reloads_total` catch a broken updater immediately for anyone watching. A per-provider threshold was considered and rejected — the gauge carries no provider label, and splitting a warning-severity drift alert into two rules is more machinery than the difference is worth.

Also documented, both verified during the spike: `RegionISO` always decodes empty against DB-IP City data (its `subdivisions[]` carry `names` but never `iso_code`), and `countryFrom`'s three-way fallback is inert against DB-IP — it exists for MaxMind and must not be 'simplified' away.

Full gate green: `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`, `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint run ./...`.

title: geoip: ship a redistributable GeoIP database in the image — GeoLite2 cannot be bundled, DB-IP Lite can

body:
Found while implementing #544 item 4. Not part of that work — separate bug.

## What

Prod `ixl1` reports:

```
input queue drops = 4294958080
```

That is `2^32 - 9216` — a **negative value that has wrapped through an unsigned 32-bit field**. The real figure is `-9216`, which is itself nonsense for a drop count and points at the driver or the netstat plumbing rather than at us.

`opnsense_interfaces_input_queue_drops_total` publishes it **verbatim, as a counter**. Consequences:

- Any `rate()` or `increase()` over a window containing the wrap is garbage.
- If the underlying value later moves back toward zero the counter appears to reset, so `rate()` treats the drop from ~4.29e9 to a small number as a counter reset and produces an enormous spike.
- A dashboard panel showing "4.29 billion input queue drops" reads as a catastrophic fault on a healthy interface.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than documenting

This is not a case where the box is telling the truth in an awkward unit. The value is not a real count at any scale — no interface has dropped 4.29 billion packets on an input queue on a box with this uptime, and the arithmetic identifies it precisely as a small negative.

## Options, in rough order of preference

1. **Reject implausible values at parse time**: treat a value above some threshold (or, more precisely, one that decodes as a small negative when reinterpreted as `int32`) as absent rather than as data. Absent is honest; a fabricated 0 is not, because it claims the interface reported no drops.
2. Clamp to 0 and count the rejection on a self-metric so the suppression is visible rather than silent.
3. Document it and leave it — rejected, because the failure mode is a false catastrophic reading rather than a missing one.

Worth checking the same treatment for `output queue drops` and any sibling counter decoded from the same payload, rather than fixing this one field in isolation.

## Scope

- [ ] Confirm the value's provenance — driver, `netstat`, or the API layer — against the live box
- [ ] Decide reject-vs-clamp and apply it consistently across the queue-drop counters from this payload
- [ ] Unit test with the real captured value `4294958080`
- [ ] Note the behaviour in the metric help text
- [ ] Check whether any shipped alert or dashboard panel currently reads this series

comments.body:
Fixed in `12abef6`.

**Provenance confirmed against the live box, and it is not us:** `netstat -i -d -W -n -I ixl1` reports `4294958080` in the Idrop column itself, so the wrap happens in the driver or the netstat plumbing below the API. `ixl0` on the same box reports a plausible 24494, so it is not a blanket `ixl` fault either — worth knowing before anyone chases it as one.

**Reject, not clamp** — option 1. Any value that reinterprets as a negative `int32` is treated as absent and no series is emitted for that interface. Absent is honest; 0 asserts the interface reported no drops.

Took the whole 32-bit negative half rather than guessing at how small the negative should be: no interface has genuinely dropped 2.1 billion packets on a queue, so nothing real is suppressed.

Missing and malformed values deliberately keep the tolerant `safeAtoi` convention (#102) every other counter on this struct uses. This narrows only the implausible-value case — widening it to absence would drop series on boxes that merely omit the column.

Applied to `send queue drops` from the same payload too, per the issue's last line.

Consumers checked: one dashboard panel reads `input_queue_drops_total` and **no alert does**, so nothing shipped needs retuning. Help text on both counters now states the behaviour.

Tests pin the real captured `4294958080` at both layers — the parse, and the collector emitting nothing for `ixl1` while `ixl0` beside it still reports 7.

title: collector(interfaces): input_queue_drops publishes a wrapped negative as a counter on prod ixl1

body:
Found during the netisr per-CPU work (#538/#539), worked around locally rather than fixed, because the helper is shared and three lanes were editing the tree concurrently.

## The bug

`internal/collector/testhelpers_test.go:92` drains a collector's `Update()` through a **fixed 500-slot buffered channel** with a **synchronous** call:

- `Update()` writes metrics into the channel
- nothing reads until `Update()` returns
- so a collector emitting more than 500 metrics blocks forever on write

The netisr prod fixture emits **776**. The result is not an assertion failure — it is a 120s test timeout with no indication of the cause.

## Why it matters now

Nothing hit this before because no collector emitted that many metrics in one `Update()` from a single fixture. That has changed: the per-CPU netisr series alone are ~672 on a 12-workstream box, and the cardinality budget (100k global, ~4.6k used) means there is no reason for future collectors to stay small. The next high-volume collector will hit exactly this wall and will see a timeout rather than a diagnosis.

## Fix

Drain concurrently instead of relying on buffer size — start a goroutine reading the channel before calling `Update()`, close and collect after. That removes the cap entirely and makes the helper independent of how many metrics a collector emits. `internal/collector/network_diag_test.go` already does this locally and can be the model; the local copy should be deleted once the shared helper is fixed.

A capacity assertion is not sufficient: it would turn a hang into a clearer failure, but every new high-volume collector would still have to bump a magic number.

## Scope

- [ ] Rewrite the shared helper to drain concurrently
- [ ] Remove the local workaround in `network_diag_test.go` and any other lane that grew one
- [ ] Confirm the netisr prod fixture (776 metrics) passes through the shared helper
- [ ] `go test ./internal/collector/...` green

comments.body:
Fixed in `8cdc140` (pushed as `faaaab3`).

The shared `collectMetrics` helper now drains concurrently with `Update` rather than relying on a 500-slot buffer, so it no longer cares how many metrics a collector emits. The local workaround in `network_diag_test.go` is removed.

Rejected the capacity-assertion alternative for the reason the issue gave: it converts the hang into a clearer failure but leaves the magic number for the next high-volume collector to bump.

`TestCollectMetricsHandlesMoreThan500Metrics` enforces its own 10s deadline, so a reintroduction fails naming the cause instead of timing out the whole package at 120s. It emits 776 — the real netisr prod figure, not a round number picked to be safely large. Verified red against the old helper before the fix, then green.

`go test ./internal/collector/` green.

title: test: shared collectMetrics helper deadlocks above 500 metrics — silently, as a timeout

body:
From the #536 Part C sweep, deliberately deferred out of that wave because the metric names were not frozen and inventing them mid-lane would have been guesswork.

## The gap

`dhcp6c` ships **1,444 lines unparsed** in the capture window — the largest single unparsed program on the box. It is the exact IPv6 counterpart of the `dhclient` work that landed in #541, and none of it is covered:

- Renew/Reply lifecycle on the WAN (`Sending Renew on pppoe0`, `Received REPLY for RENEW`)
- Prefix delegation state, including `pltime` and `vltime` — the v6 equivalent of the lease countdown that #541 established as the single most useful signal
- Failure to renew, which on a PD setup takes down every downstream v6 prefix, not just the WAN address

`kea-dhcp6` (1,356 lines) is a **partial** gap rather than a total one — it has a parser, but two grammars are unmodelled. `ALLOC_ENGINE_V6_ALLOC_FAIL_*` is the one worth catching: it means v6 clients were refused a lease.

## Why this is not just "do #541 again"

`#541`'s countdown lesson applies directly: export absolute `*_timestamp_seconds` gauges, not a countdown computed in the exporter, or a dead `dhcp6c` looks identical to a healthy one. But v6 has a second dimension v4 does not — a delegated **prefix** has its own lifetimes independent of the WAN address, so the label set is not simply `{interface}`.

## Hard constraint

`ALLOC_ENGINE_V6_ALLOC_FAIL_*` lines carry a raw **DUID**. That must never become a label — it is unbounded and client-identifying. It stays on the log record, exactly as the MetricSink contract requires.

## Scope

- [ ] Capture real `dhcp6c` lines first — #541 found two asserted formats were wrong on the real box, and prior parser work found the same
- [ ] `dhcp6c` parser + registry/subsystem mapping
- [ ] Lease and prefix-delegation lifetime gauges, `*_timestamp_seconds` form
- [ ] Renew/reply/failure counters
- [ ] `kea-dhcp6` `ALLOC_ENGINE_V6_ALLOC_FAIL_*`, DUID off every label
- [ ] Explicit decision on `kea-dhcp6`'s LFC lines (leaning exclude, same as `DhcpLFC`)
- [ ] Alerts mirroring #541's four, adapted for PD
- [ ] Dashboard panels (coverage gate), `make docs` + `make grafana-check` green

comments.body:
Closed by `b15d78f`.

**Captured the real grammar from the box first.** A healthy box emits only **six** distinct `dhcp6c` shapes over 24h. The issue's asserted formats held up this time, but everything beyond the capture is read off the format string that produced a captured line — `dhcp6c`'s own `client6_send`/`update_prefix`/`ifaddrconf`, OPNsense's `dhcp6c_script.sh`, kea's `alloc_engine.cc` — rather than invented, and those fixtures are labelled as such in the test names.

### Metrics

Counters: `dhcp6c_message_total{interface,direction,type}`, `dhcp6c_event_total{interface,event,reason}`, `dhcp6_alloc_fail_total{reason}`. All vocabularies closed and code-defined.

Gauges, all absolute `*_timestamp_seconds` with `{interface, prefix_length}`: `dhcp6c_prefix_updated`, `dhcp6c_prefix_preferred_expiry`, `dhcp6c_prefix_valid_expiry`.

**Two lifetime gauges, not one.** An ISP deprecating a prefix ahead of withdrawal shortens `pltime` first; collapsing them would hide exactly that warning. Absolute rather than a countdown for #541's reason — a countdown computed in the exporter keeps counting down from a stale value, so a dead `dhcp6c` would look identical to a healthy one.

### The label set

`{interface, prefix_length}`. The prefix itself is **never** a label: it changes on re-delegation, which is the very event these metrics watch. `prefix_length` survives that test — a /48 stays a /48 — and it distinguishes a second, differently-sized delegation on the same WAN. Two same-size delegations on one interface collapse last-write-wins, documented in the help; no home/SMB WAN produces that.

DUID, prefix and every configured address stay as record attributes. A test walks every sink call argument asserting none of them leaks into a label.

Note `interface` on `dhcp6c_event_total` means the WAN for prefix/script events and the **downstream** device for `address_added`/`address_removed` — that is the honest reading of each line, and `address_*` is exactly the self-describing subset.

### The triple-count

kea emits up to three `ALLOC_ENGINE_V6_ALLOC_FAIL_*` lines per failed allocation sharing a `tid`. Resolved from `alloc_engine.cc` structure rather than with a dedupe table: exactly one *scope* line and one *cause* line per failure, plus an optional `CLASSES`. **Only the cause line is counted** — one-per-failure like the scope line, and unlike it, it carries the actionable reason. No state, no ordering dependence. Pinned by feeding the captured three-line burst and asserting exactly one sink call.

### Verdicts

- **LFC lines excluded**, matching the existing precedent — now pinned by a test rather than left as an accident of omission.
- **`COMMAND_RECEIVED`: no metric.** It is ~48% of `kea-dhcp6` volume and it is the control channel answering our own lease polling, so a metric on it would measure the exporter.
- **New family, not `familyDHCPClient`.** A v4 and a v6 uplink fail independently and the vocabularies do not overlap; folding them would hide a v6-only outage behind a healthy v4 rate.
- **Only `Sending … on <iface>` teaches the PID→interface table.** The `add an address … on ixl0` line comes from the same daemon PID but names a LAN device, so letting it write would file the next reply and prefix update under the wrong interface. Dedicated test for that trap.

### Deliberately not modelled

`addrconf.c`'s IA_NA lease lifetimes — the literal v6 twin of the v4 lease. A real upstream shape, but this box is PD-only and never emits it, and standing up a three-gauge family on no capture is how #284's phantom generation happened. **A box taking a v6 WAN address by DHCPv6 has no lease gauge today** — filed as a follow-up if anyone's setup needs it.

### Alerts and dashboard

Three rules (in `21b97af`'s `build_rules.py` edit — shared file): `OPNsenseDHCP6PrefixExpiring` (critical, the only one that pages — valid lifetime gone means every downstream address is removed), `OPNsenseDHCP6PrefixNotRefreshing` (warning, 2h ≈ 2× the observed `pltime`, the leading indicator), `OPNsenseDHCP6AllocationFailures` (warning).

Four panels on the DHCP tab under 'WAN DHCPv6 Client & Prefix Delegation'. Coverage 953/953.

Full gate green: `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`, `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint run ./...`.

title: logship(syslog): dhcp6c / kea-dhcp6 have no IPv6 WAN lease coverage — the v6 twin of #541

body:
From the #539 spike (Lane B), which explicitly scoped this out as too large for its pass and flagged it as the cheapest follow-up.

## What

`api/diagnostics/interface/get_protocol_statistics` is already called every scrape. Several whole sections never reach `ProtocolStatistics` (`opnsense/protocol_statistics.go:209-234,567-755`):

- `sack` — SACK recovery behaviour. **`sack.byte-retransmits` = 56.9M live on prod.**
- `hostcache` — TCP host cache hits/misses/evictions
- `tw` — TIME_WAIT recycling
- `pmtud` — path-MTU-discovery blackhole detection
- `tcp-signature` — TCP-MD5

Roughly 60 untouched sub-fields with real nonzero values, at **zero extra API cost** — the payload is already fetched and decoded.

## Why it matters

`pmtud` blackhole counters in particular are a classic cause of "some sites load, some hang" that is otherwise invisible and very hard to diagnose from the outside. `sack` retransmit volume is a direct TCP-health signal for a box that is fundamentally a packet forwarder. `hostcache` evictions indicate churn pressure.

## Scope

Audit all five sections against the live payload on prod plus both dev boxes, decide per sub-field, and expose what has operational meaning. Expect some to be genuinely uninteresting — the deliverable is a reasoned selection, not all 60 mechanically.

Cardinality is not a constraint here (global limit 100k, exporter uses ~4,622) — judge on usefulness.

## Acceptance

- [ ] All five sections audited against live payloads on all three boxes
- [ ] Per-sub-field verdict recorded, with reasons for exclusions
- [ ] Selected fields exposed as metrics
- [ ] `pmtud` blackhole counters included unless there is a stated reason not to
- [ ] Dashboard panels (coverage gate)
- [ ] `make docs` + `make grafana-check` green

comments.body:
Shipped in `b04cd2c`. 13 metric families, 24 series, zero extra API cost.

**Two corrections to the issue body, both from reading the live payloads:**

1. **"~60 sub-fields" is wrong — the five sections hold 21 fields total.** The estimate was high by roughly 3x.
2. **The hostcache description is wrong on the box.** It claims hits/misses/evictions; live, the `hostcache` section has exactly two keys, `entries-added` and `buffer-overflows`. The actual **hit** counters exist but live at top level as `statistics.tcp.connections-hostcache-{rtt,rttvar,ssthresh}` — already decoded since forever and exported by nothing, the same unmarshalled-but-unread shape as #542. They are included, as `opnsense_protocol_tcp_hostcache_hits_total{metric}`, because that is what the issue actually asked for even though they sit outside the five named sections.

**Verdicts: 21 audited, 21 included, 0 excluded.** The issue expected exclusions and I pushed back on their absence, but having read the full field list the honest answer is that these sections are small and each field names a distinct fault or recovery mode. The weakest is `tw_responds`, which is mostly ordinary retransmitted-FIN handling — kept as the baseline the other two TIME_WAIT counters spike against, and that reason is recorded rather than a manufactured exclusion. All three `pmtud` fields are in, per the acceptance criterion.

Two fields beyond the original five sections were added after a stop-and-ask: `sack.lost-retransmissions` (a retransmission that was itself lost has no equivalent signal anywhere else) and `sack.tso-chunk-retransmits`. These are the only ones that touched the golden schema — two structure-only `numeric` paths, regenerated with `make schemas`.

**Release compatibility: zero differences.** All 21 keys present with identical spelling on prod 26.1, dev release 26.7.1 and dev nightly 27.1.a. So they are emitted unconditionally with no presence-gating, unlike the #237 ECN/syncookies group in the same file, and the compat ledger is untouched.

**Panel caveat, in the help text as well as here:** the SACK retransmit counters are a *subset* of `tcp_retransmitted_{packets,bytes}_total`, which also count plain RTO retransmission. They overlap — never sum them on one panel. `lost_retransmissions` names all three families it is a subset of.

Panels live in a new **TCP Recovery, Host Cache & Path MTU** row on Protocol Stats.

title: collector: get_protocol_statistics drops ~60 sub-fields including sack, hostcache, tw and pmtud

body:
From the #539 spike. Filing as one issue because it is one recurring mistake, not five unrelated gaps — the fix is partly a review habit.

## The pattern

A rich per-row payload is reduced to a same-class aggregate with the **identifying dimension thrown away rather than summed**. Five independent instances found:

| # | Where | Dimension discarded | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | netisr (`opnsense/network_diagnostics.go:99-116`) | per-workstream/CPU — 96 rows → 8 series | Hid the prod diagnosis entirely (see #538/#539) |
| 2 | `get_routes` (`network_diagnostics.go:65-72`) | whole table → 2 numbers; `flags`, `netif`, `destination`, `gateway` discarded | No default-route-loss or per-interface route signal |
| 3 | `get_bpf_statistics` (`bpf_statistics.go:16-24,120-140`) | `direction` (input/output/bidirectional) summed into the aggregation key | 3-value dimension silently gone |
| 4 | `get_interface_statistics` (`interface_index.go:48-51`) | per-address rows; only `Name`/`Network` decoded | Only obtainable IPv4-vs-IPv6 traffic split per device, already fetched |
| 5 | ARP/NDP (`arp_table.go:12`, `ndp.go:6`) | raw `intf` device, distinct from `intf_description` | On VLAN/bridge these diverge; #534 covers `manufacturer`, this is separate |

Item 1 is the one that proved the cost: the collapsed view said "ip6 is dropping, raise the queue limit" while the per-CPU view said "8 of 12 CPUs are idle and cpu0 is overloaded" — opposite remedies. #539 has the numbers.

## Why one issue

Fixing these individually leaves the habit intact. The generalisable rule:

> When a payload has one row per entity and the collector aggregates, the entity identifier belongs on a label unless there is a stated reason it cannot — and "cardinality" is only that reason when it approaches the actual budget. Summing a counter across entities is fine; discarding the dimension that says *which* entity is not.

Worth considering whether this can be caught mechanically — a check that flags a struct field unmarshalled but never read (which is exactly how #542's `references` and ARP's `manufacturer` were found), or a review-checklist line in the add-a-collector docs.

## Note on cardinality

Do not gate any of these opt-in on cardinality grounds. Global series limit is 100k; the exporter uses ~4,622. Item 4 is ~30 series, item 3 ~3x current, item 2 ~76 rows, item 5 free. Only item 1 is material (~680 on a 12-core box) and Rob has already chosen default-ON with an opt-out for it.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Items 2-5 exposed (item 1 is #539's own spec)
- [ ] Each keeps the existing aggregate so no dashboard breaks
- [ ] Decision recorded on catching this mechanically vs by checklist
- [ ] Add-a-collector docs updated with the rule if no mechanical check is viable
- [ ] `make docs` + `make grafana-check` green

comments.body:
Items 2-5 shipped in `49913c9`. **This issue stays OPEN** for the mechanical check, which is the part that stops the habit rather than the instances.

## Items done

| # | What it now exposes |
|---|---|
| 1 | netisr per-CPU — shipped earlier in `b04cd2c` |
| 2 | `network_diag_interface_routes{proto,device,interface}`, `routes_by_flags{proto,flags}`, `default_route_present{proto}`, `default_route_info{proto,device,interface,gateway}` |
| 3 | `bpf_direction_{listeners,received_packets_total,dropped_packets_total,matched_packets_total}{process,interface,direction}` |
| 4 | `interfaces_address_family_{received,sent}_{packets,bytes}_total{device,family}`, `interfaces_output_queue_drops_total{device}` |
| 5 | `device` label on `arp_table_entries` and `ndp_entries` (with `manufacturer` from #534) |

Every existing metric keeps its name, type and label set — a regression assertion fails if `direction` ever leaks onto the aggregate BPF families.

**`destination` is a label nowhere.** 76 routes on prod, 52 of them transient `UHS` host routes plus 36 tailscale peer routes; an interface count answers the same question without the churn. **`gateway` is a label on `default_route_info` only** — one or two series ever, and a default gateway changing is itself the event worth seeing. `default_route_present` is emitted for a fixed `{ipv4,ipv6}` set every scrape so the alertable case is a `0` rather than an absent series; `OPNsenseDefaultRouteMissing` fires on it.

**Item 4's framing in the body is misleading and the help text now says so.** The family split covers *locally addressed* traffic only — prod `ixl0` reports 419.9M received packets at device level against 24.5M summed across its address rows, about **6%**. Forwarded transit is attributed to no local address. It answers "how much v6 does this box itself speak", not "how much of my traffic is v6". Item 4 also costs **+1 GET per interfaces poll** on the fast 15s tier (2 calls → 3); left there because `netstat -i -n -W -b -d` is cheap, but flagging it.

## Input to the mechanical check — the design is now decided by evidence

A crude textual scan returns 160 hits, and **its failure modes are the useful result**: ~30 false positives (`RowCount`/`Total` envelope fields) and it *misses* genuine ones — `ndpEntry.Expire` (`opnsense/ndp.go:9`) is parsed and dropped but invisible to text matching. **So the check must be type-aware (`go/types`), not textual.** That is the decision this issue's "worth considering whether this can be caught mechanically" was asking for.

Highest-value genuine hits found by hand, as seed cases:

- `hostdiscovery.go:23-25` **`OrganizationName`** — the same OUI signal as #534, on a *persistent* inventory rather than a volatile table, currently rejected in a code comment on cardinality grounds that contradict the 100k budget.
- ~50 unused TCP counters in `protocol_statistics.go` (beyond the five sections #545 took).
- `interfaces.go` **`Driver`** and `HWOffloadCapabilities` — `Driver` is precisely what tells you whether the oqdrops override caveat applies to a given device, which item 4 above had to document in prose instead.
- `ndpEntry.Expire`, plus `ndpEntry.Type` which is published as an always-empty label because 26.1 sends no such key.

## Unrelated bug found on the way

Prod `ixl1` reports `input queue drops = 4294958080` — that is 2^32 − 9216, a wrapped negative — and `opnsense_interfaces_input_queue_drops_total` publishes it verbatim as a counter. Any `rate()` on that series is nonsense. Filed separately.

Closed by `6ff859d`.

`cmd/fieldaudit` is the mechanical check this issue stayed open for. Type-aware (`go/types`), wired as a unit test so it rides `make test` and CI with no workflow change; `make fieldaudit` gives the readable report.

The type-awareness earns its keep beyond `ndpEntry.Expire`: it separates `dnsmasqLeaseRow.MacInfo` (dead) from `keaLeaseRow.MacInfo` (read), and `interfaceConfigEntry.IsPhysical` (dead) from `interfaceOverviewRow.IsPhysical` (read). No name-based approach can do that. Both pairs are regression-pinned.

No new module dependency — `go list -deps -export -json` plus `go/importer` is the ~80 lines `go/packages` would have cost in vendor. ~0.6s per audit.

**Exemptions are exact keys with a written reason, minimum 20 characters**, mirroring `NOT_ANNOTATED`. Glob patterns were rejected deliberately: a `Type.*` glob over the 77 protocol-statistics counters would silently absorb *future* dead fields on the same struct, which is the exact rot the gate exists to prevent. The ledger also fails on an entry whose field is gone or is now read, so neither side can drift. Verified in both directions by breaking it on purpose.

**Result: 345 of 1,765 json-tagged fields are dead — 20%.** Bulk is 77 protocol-statistics counters, 59 bootgrid envelope fields (the ones a textual scan false-positived on, cleared by the ledger rather than a special case in the checker), and 43 unbound extended statistics.

One analysis fix rather than papering over with exemptions: a whole-struct *conversion* carries every field into another type and now counts as a read, which removed 7 false positives.

**14 fields marked SHOULD BE EXPORTED, now tracked:** #555 (interface `Driver` / `HWOffloadCapabilities`), #556 (the raw lease-grid interface id — this issue's item-5 pattern found in three more places, plus dnsmasq `mac_info`), #557 (hostdiscovery vendor, Kea pool stats, mbuf ceiling, syslog target state), #558 (firewall rule protocol).

The `hostdiscovery.go` comment rejecting `organization_name` on unbounded-cardinality grounds **was wrong** and is corrected in place — bounded OUI vendor set, 100k budget against ~4.6k in use. It was unread because nobody exported it.

`make test` + `golangci-lint run ./...` green.

title: collector: five payloads are collapsed to aggregates with the identifying dimension discarded

body:
From the #539 spike (Lanes C and D), verified live by the dispatcher.

## What

`api/diagnostics/system/memory` (`SystemController::memoryAction`, backed by `vmstat -m -z --libxo json`) is **not in `defaultEndpoints()`** and has never been called. Verified live on prod: **258 malloc types + 242 UMA zones**.

Every zone carries `name, size, limit, used, free, requests, fail, sleep, xdomain`. **`fail` is FreeBSD's canonical "the kernel could not allocate X" counter** — a generic silent-drop detector covering the resources a firewall actually exhausts.

## Scope correction — the mbuf slice is already covered

Both lanes framed this as wholly-new kernel telemetry. It is not: `opnsense_mbuf_failures_total{type=...}` and `opnsense_mbuf_sleeps_total` already exist from `systemMbuf`. **Do not duplicate them.**

What is genuinely uncovered is pf and socket exhaustion (live prod):

```
pf states        limit=3258600  used=12780  free=10590  fail=0
pf state keys    limit=      0  used=16275  free=10727  fail=0
pf source nodes  limit=3258600  used=    0  free=    0  fail=0
socket           limit=1042770  used=  462  free= 3350  fail=0
tcp_inpcb        limit=      0  used=  263  free= 1126  fail=0
udp_inpcb        limit=      0  used=   70  free= 1091  fail=0
tcpreass         limit= 127355  used=    0  free= 1092  fail=0
```

`pf source nodes` is worth noting: Lane B independently found source-tracking unexposed from `pf_statistics/info`. Two lanes hit the same blind spot from different endpoints, which is a decent signal it matters.

`limit` is also useful in its own right — it surfaces ceilings not otherwise exposed.

## Cardinality — NOT the deciding factor

Both lanes recommended `enable-*` opt-in gating on cardinality grounds. **Overturned:** the global series limit is 100k and the exporter uses ~4,622. ~500 series does not justify hiding a `fail` counter.

There is still a legitimate **signal-to-noise** argument for curating — 258 malloc types includes entries like `CAM I/O Scheduler` that no firewall operator will query. But that must be argued on usefulness, not on cardinality, and the default should lean toward including rather than excluding.

Suggested shape: a named allowlist of network/pf/socket-relevant zones emitting `{used, free, limit, fail, sleep}`, PLUS a `zone_failures_total` summed across ALL zones so nothing is silently invisible. Malloc types are probably noise — but check before dropping them wholesale.

## Alerting

- `increase(zone_fail_total[5m]) > 0` on any zone — hard page. This is the point of the issue.
- `used / limit > 0.8` for `pf states`, `socket`, `pf table entries` — saturation warning.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Endpoint registered in `defaultEndpoints()`, endpoint count bumped in `client_test.go`
- [ ] Response struct added to `schemaRegistry`, `make schemas` run
- [ ] Zone metrics emitted; mbuf zones NOT duplicated against the existing mbuf collector
- [ ] Catch-all `zone_failures_total` across all zones
- [ ] Curation decision recorded, argued on usefulness not cardinality
- [ ] Alert rules for `fail > 0` and `used/limit > 0.8`
- [ ] Dashboard panels (coverage gate)
- [ ] `make docs` + `make grafana-check` green

comments.body:
Shipped in `49913c9`. 12 metric families, ~2,599 series on prod, `--exporter.disable-kernel-memory` (default ON), slow 5m tier, own **Kernel Memory** dashboard tab.

**Emitting everything, no curation** — all 228 zones and 258 malloc types. The body's suggested allowlist is superseded: which exhaustion matters is not knowable before it happens, and 2,599 series is 2.6% of a 100k budget.

## Three things the box taught us

**1. Zone names are NOT unique on the wire — this would have 500'd every scrape.** UMA emits one row per NUMA domain and per instance. Prod sends `NetFlow IPv4 cache` and `NetFlow IPv6 cache` **seven times each**, `vm pgcache` and `buffer arena-40` twice, and both dev boxes send malloc `dummynet` twice. Emitted naively that is a duplicate series under an identical label set, which makes `Gather()` error — a 500 on `/metrics` on every box, not a subtle bug. Rows are merged by name (counters summed, `item_size_bytes` maxed because the two `buffer arena-40` rows genuinely differ at 4096 vs 40960), with `assertNoDuplicateSeries` guarding it. The `{zone}` label set in the spec survives unchanged.

**2. `limit == 0` means NO CEILING CONFIGURED, not a ceiling of zero.** Proof needing no source reading: prod's `pf state keys` reports `limit=0` with `used=17452`. **113 of 242 prod rows** are `limit==0 && used>0`, so an unguarded `used/limit` returns `+Inf` on nearly half the box. Every panel and rule guards it. Also exclude `pf anchors` / `pf Ethernet anchors` from saturation views — their limit is `2147483647` (INT_MAX), so they read as permanently 0%.

**3. The proposed `increase(zone_fail_total[5m]) > 0` hard page is unshippable as written.** Prod has **158,488 failures right now on a healthy box**, and every one is in `256 Bucket` (144,270), the other `N Bucket` zones, `vm pgcache` and `vmem btag`. UMA's per-CPU bucket allocator is *designed* to fail and fall back to the slow path. An unscoped rule pages continuously from the moment it deploys.

`OPNsenseKernelZoneAllocationFailure` is therefore scoped to `pf states|pf state keys|pf source nodes|socket|tcp_inpcb|udp_inpcb|tcpreass` — all reading `fail=0` on prod, dev release and dev nightly, so any line there is real. Plus `OPNsenseKernelZoneNearLimit` at `used/limit > 0.8` with the divide guard. **Sleeps are zero on every zone on all three boxes.**

## Live inventory

| box | release | distinct zones | malloc types |
|---|---|---|---|
| prod 26.1 | 26.1 | 228 | 258 |
| dev release | 26.7.1 | 219 | 248 |
| dev nightly | 27.1.a | 219 | 251 |

**The zone set tracks loaded kernel modules, not the release** — both dev boxes are identical across 26.7.1 and 27.1.a; prod differs only because it runs NetFlow. The one genuinely release-driven difference is the malloc type `inotify`, on 27.1.a only (newer FreeBSD base). Recorded in the collector doc comment so the canary does not read it as drift.

## mbuf overlap — resolved in help text, not by dropping zones

Six zones overlap the existing mbuf collector: `mbuf`, `mbuf_packet`↔`packet`, `mbuf_cluster`↔`cluster`, `mbuf_jumbo_page`↔`jumbop`, `mbuf_jumbo_9k`↔`jumbo9`, `mbuf_jumbo_16k`↔`jumbo16`. (`type=sfbufs` has no UMA zone — it comes from `netstat -m`'s sendfile section.) Two independent readings of the same kernel state from two endpoints at two moments is useful, and a hole in an all-zones family is worse than an overlap, so nothing is excluded and the help text names the mapping and says never to sum them.

## Notes

- `opnsense/acl.go` needed a row (`TestEndpointACLCoversEveryEndpoint`). Classified against upstream rather than guessed: Core's ACL lists the seven `api/diagnostics/system/system_*` URLs individually with no wildcard and nothing covers `.../memory`, on both `stable/26.7` and `master`, so `ACLStatusUnknown` + Note.
- **Upstream's own transform in `memoryAction` is dead code.** It renames malloc `type`→`name` and adds `totals`, guarded on `!empty($data['malloc-statistics'])` — but libxo nests everything under `vmstat`, so the guard never passes. Confirmed on `stable/26.7`, `master` and all three boxes. Only the wire shape is modelled; modelling the renamed form would repeat the #284 phantom-generation mistake exactly.
- `malloc-statistics.memory[].size` is an **array** (power-of-two size classes) with no honest scalar reduction, so it is modelled for the canary and not emitted.
- `pf source nodes` exists on prod but reads `used=0 free=0` — source tracking is not in use there. Not a fault.

title: collector: add api/diagnostics/system/memory — UMA zone fail/sleep is the generic kernel-exhaustion signal

body:
From the #539 spike (Lane B), verified by the dispatcher.

## Verified

`References` appears at **exactly one line** in the whole non-vendor, non-test tree:

```
opnsense/firewall.go:7:	References    int    `json:"references"`
```

It is unmarshalled on every scrape and read by nothing. `internal/collector/firewall.go`'s `Update()` never touches it.

## Live values on prod (<lan-ip-2>)

```
pppoe0        486        ixl0          187        lo0 (skip)     28
ixl0_vlan50   264        ixl1           84        all            42
ixl0_vlan100  263        ixl0_vlan90    44        (zeros: enc0, igb0/1, ixl2/3, pflog0, pfsync0)
```

This is the per-interface PF state-table reference count. Today the exporter has exactly one global `pf_states_current` — **this is the only per-interface breakdown of PF state usage obtainable anywhere**, and it is already being fetched.

## Proposed

`opnsense_firewall_pf_interface_references{interface}` gauge. ~15 series, zero extra API cost, one line to emit.

Worth a panel: per-interface PF state share makes "which interface is consuming the state table" answerable, which today requires shelling into the box.

Note the API returns two keys with a literal `" (skip)"` suffix (`lo0 (skip)`, `pfsync0 (skip)`) and an aggregate `all` key — decide explicitly whether to emit, strip the suffix, or filter, rather than letting them through as odd label values.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `opnsense_firewall_pf_interface_references{interface}` emitted
- [ ] `(skip)` suffix and the `all` aggregate key handled deliberately, with the choice noted in the metric help
- [ ] Unit test covering a populated and a zero interface
- [ ] Dashboard panel (coverage gate)
- [ ] `make docs` + `make grafana-check` green

comments.body:
Shipped in `b04cd2c`.

`opnsense_firewall_pf_interface_references{interface, skipped}` — gauge, ~15 series, zero extra API cost.

**The odd keys, handled as decided:**

- The `" (skip)"` suffix is **stripped into a `skipped="true"` label** rather than discarded. Discarding it would have repeated the exact mistake #544 is about — pf not filtering an interface at all is real information. (Half of this was already in place from #105: the suffix was stripped and `all` filtered. What was missing was the skip *state*, which was being thrown away. Now carried as a derived `Skipped bool`, tagged `json:"-"` so it adds no phantom golden-schema path.)
- The aggregate `all` key stays **excluded**, and the help text says why: emitting a sum beside its parts double-counts every `sum()` panel. Asserted absent in both tests.
- Zero-valued interfaces are emitted.

Help text carries the gauge-not-counter warning (plot it, never `rate()` it), the meaning of `skipped`, and "use `sum()` in PromQL instead — do not add it back".

Panel: **PF State References by Interface**, on Firewall & PF beside the state-table gauges. This is the panel that answers "which interface is eating the state table", which previously needed a shell on the box.

title: collector: expose pf_statistics/interfaces references — parsed every scrape, read by nothing

body:
From the #539 spike (Lane D). Structural gap verified; incident magnitude needs confirming.

## The gap (verified)

The DHCP WAN is `ixl1` / VIRGIN (`opnsense_interfaces_info{device="ixl1",link_type="dhcp"}`). **`dhclient` has zero matches in `internal/logship/syslog/registry.go`** — the DHCP parser claims `dnsmasq-dhcp`, `kea-dhcp4`, `kea-dhcp6`, `kea-ctrl-agent`, `kea-dhcp-ddns`, `dhcrelay` and `dhcp6c`, but not `dhclient`. Its lines therefore arrive as untyped generic records with a blank subsystem.

Consequence: **nothing in the exporter reports WAN lease state, time-to-expiry, or renewal failure.** A DHCP WAN that stops renewing loses its address at lease expiry, and a retransmit storm is a leading indicator hours ahead of the outage. Neither is visible today.

## The incident — NEEDS CONFIRMING before acting on the numbers

Lane D reported, from Loki:

```
07-23..07-29 baseline   ~250 per 6h   (~42/hr)
07-30 02:00-09:00       4474-4570 per HOUR   <-- ~100x, sustained 8+ hours
07-30 10:00             3170          (ends ~10:20 UTC)
07-30 11:00-14:00       47 / 29 / 48 / 54    (back to baseline)
```

Sample: `DHCPREQUEST on ixl1 to <pub-ip-18> port 67` repeating, then `DHCPACK from <pub-ip-18>`, `bound to <pub-ip-14> -- renewal in 213071 seconds`.

**I could not re-verify this.** The Grafana OAuth token expired at `2026-07-30T12:18:35Z` mid-session. Re-run the query before treating the magnitude as fact:

```
sum(count_over_time({service_name="opnsense-exporter", opnsense_source="syslog"} |= "DHCPREQUEST" [1h]))
```

If it holds, an 8-hour retransmit storm on the production WAN self-resolved with zero telemetry and no alert. That is the case for this issue.

## Proposed

Parser + subsystem mapping for `dhclient`, then:

- **`opnsense_dhcp_client_lease_expiry_seconds{interface}`** — gauge, parsed from `bound to X -- renewal in N seconds`. The single most useful signal here: a countdown that stops counting down is the outage, hours early.
- **`opnsense_dhcp_client_requests_total{interface, type}`** — `DHCPDISCOVER`/`DHCPREQUEST`/`DHCPACK`/`DHCPNAK`.
- **`opnsense_dhcp_client_script_events_total{interface, reason}`** — from `dhclient-script: Reason RENEW|BOUND|EXPIRE|FAIL on <if>`.

Cardinality ~5-10 series. No API cost — these lines already arrive.

Alerts: request rate above baseline for 15m; any `DHCPNAK`; `Reason EXPIRE|FAIL` as an immediate page; lease-expiry gauge below a threshold without a renewal.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Storm confirmed or refuted against Loki, result recorded here
- [ ] `dhclient` added to the subsystem map and a parser registered
- [ ] The three metrics above, with the expiry gauge as the priority
- [ ] Alert rules + runbook entries
- [ ] Table-driven tests from real captured lines (capture first — prior parser work found asserted formats were wrong on the real box)
- [ ] `make docs` + `make grafana-check` green

comments.body: Confirmed - there was a 11-12 hour issue here

Shipped in `b04cd2c`. Storm confirmed by you independently (11-12 hours), so the magnitude is settled and the acceptance box for it is met.

**Metrics — one deliberate deviation from the proposal:**

| metric | type | labels |
|---|---|---|
| `opnsense_log_events_dhcp_client_total` | counter | `interface`, `type` |
| `opnsense_log_events_dhcp_client_script_total` | counter | `interface`, `reason` |
| `opnsense_log_events_dhcp_client_lease_bound_timestamp_seconds` | **gauge** | `interface` |
| `opnsense_log_events_dhcp_client_lease_renewal_timestamp_seconds` | **gauge** | `interface` |

**`dhcp_client_lease_expiry_seconds` was NOT built.** A countdown computed in the exporter has to be recomputed against wall-clock at scrape time, which means **a stale countdown is indistinguishable from a fresh one** — precisely the failure this metric exists to catch. Two absolute `*_timestamp_seconds` gauges instead; the countdown is derived in the panel as `renewal_timestamp - time()`, and the line crossing zero *is* the fault. Precedent: the GeoIP build-time gauge in `flow.go`.

Second correction to the issue text: this is the **renewal (T1) deadline** dhclient reports, not absolute lease expiry. dhclient never logs the latter, so there is more headroom than the metric implies, not less. Stated in the help text and the runbook.

**Alerts (4):** `OPNsenseDHCPClientRequestStorm` (>0.1/s for 30m — calibrated against your incident: ~42/hr baseline, ~4,500/hr storm, so ~8x above normal and ~12x below what was observed), `OPNsenseDHCPClientNak`, `OPNsenseDHCPClientLeaseRenewalOverdue` (critical), `OPNsenseDHCPClientScriptFailure` on `reason=~"expire|fail|timeout"` (critical).

**Captured formats, verbatim from the box** — two differ from what was assumed:

```
DHCPREQUEST on ixl1 to <pub-ip-18> port 67
DHCPACK from <pub-ip-18>
bound to <pub-ip-14> -- renewal in 302400 seconds.
dhclient-script: Reason RENEW on ixl1 executing
```

`bound to` has a **trailing full stop**. `dhclient-script: Reason` lines arrive under program **`dhclient`**, not `dhclient-script` — so the script counter was built rather than skipped.

`DHCPNAK` could not be captured: a working WAN never NAKs. Its grammar comes from ISC/OpenBSD dhclient source and rides a captured line shape. Flagged rather than presented as verified.

**DHCPACK carries no interface**, unlike DHCPREQUEST. Resolved by correlating on syslog **PID** — the captured renewal shows PID 97927 emitting REQUEST → ACK → `bound to` in sequence. Bounded insertion-ordered map, max 64, oldest evicted, mutex-guarded; an unknown PID resolves to **empty, never a guess**. The script's Reason line uses the script's own PID (7351 vs 97927) so it deliberately does not teach the table.

**One behaviour change worth knowing:** `observeDHCPClient` is the only deriver that emits more than one observation per record, so `bound to` lines are now sampling-eligible under `--logs.syslog.sample` (default off) where they previously were not. Correct — they are counted before sampling — but it is a change.

Both lease gauges are in the `NOT_ANNOTATED` ledger with reasons. `bound_timestamp` is a fair future annotation candidate (a WAN rebind can change the public address) and is excluded only because adding an annotation kind was outside this issue's scope — the reason says so rather than implying it was rejected.

title: logship: no coverage of dhclient / WAN DHCP lease state — a renewal storm on prod went unseen

body:
## Symptom

On the live m7kni dashboard, `Threat feed malware_ip updated` markers render every ~20 minutes even though the **Threat feed updated** annotation toggle is off in the controls menu.

## What is actually happening

Two separate copies of every event exist, and only one of them has per-kind control.

1. The **derived** layer (`grafana/annotations.py:241`, `Threat feed updated`) queries Prometheus and is `enable=False` by design (#523). Verified `enable: false` on the live dashboard too — the picker is honest.
2. The exporter also **pushes** the same event into Grafana's own annotation store (`internal/annotations/catalog.go:111`, kind `threat-feed-update`). The dashboard surfaces those through **Exporter-pushed events**, a catch-all query on the single tag `opnsense-exporter` (`grafana/annotations.py:354`). That layer matches all ten pushed kinds, so the per-kind toggle governs the derived copy only.

Verified against the live store:

- `GET /api/annotations?tags=opnsense-exporter` returns the exact annotations in the report (ids 2012/2013, service account `sa-1-opnsense-exporter-annotations`, tags `opnsense-exporter, threat-feed-update, instance:opnsense, feed:malware_ip`), one per 20 min.
- `GET /api/annotations?tags=n8n-change&tags=dashboard:opnsense-exporter` (the **External change events** layer) returns `[]` over the same window, so that layer cannot be the source despite appearing to be the one that hides them. The two Grafana-store layers are adjacent in the menu and identical in colour.

Not related to OTLP-vs-scrape: `opnsense_qfeeds_feed_last_update_timestamp_seconds`, `opnsense_ids_ruleset_last_updated_timestamp_seconds` and `opnsense_system_config_last_change` are all present in `grafanacloud-prom` under their normal names, so the derived layers would work if enabled.

## Decision

Fix it exporter-side (owner call): the push catalogue and the dashboard default set must agree. Q-Feeds refreshes every ~20 min, so pushing `threat-feed-update` writes ~72 org-wide annotations a day that every dashboard, Explore session and alert annotation then carries — the same noise argument that made the derived layer default-off.

## Scope

- [ ] `Watch.DefaultOff` in `internal/annotations/catalog.go`, set on `threat-feed-update`
- [ ] `KnownKinds()` / `DefaultKinds()` helpers
- [ ] `--annotations.kinds` (repeatable, env `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_ANNOTATIONS_KINDS`): when set it is the exact push set, overriding the defaults in both directions; validated against `KnownKinds()` at startup
- [ ] `Config.Kinds` honoured in `Watcher.detect`
- [ ] Parity test in `grafana/tests/test_annotations.py`: a Go watch with `DefaultOff` ⇔ its dashboard layer `enable=False`, so this class of divergence cannot come back silently
- [ ] `make docs` (flag tables) and any annotation docs page
- [ ] Note in `grafana/README.md` that `Exporter-pushed events` is a catch-all over every pushed kind, not per-kind

## Not in scope

Splitting the catch-all into per-kind store layers (would take the toggle count from 16 to ~26) and cleaning up the ~72/day of `threat-feed-update` annotations already in the m7kni store — that is a separate operational decision.

comments.body:
Fixed in a53bba9 (pushed to main).

- `Watch.DefaultOff` on `threat-feed-update`; `KnownKinds()` / `DefaultKinds()` / `DefaultOffKinds()`
- `--annotations.kinds` (env `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_ANNOTATIONS_KINDS`, comma-separated) — exact set once given, validated against `KnownKinds()` in `AnnotationsConfig.Validate`, so a typo fails startup instead of silently writing nothing. The startup log line now names the resolved set.
- `Watcher.detect` skips a disabled kind; the resolved set is computed once in `New`.
- Parity guard `test_the_push_default_matches_the_dashboards_own_default` reads `DefaultOff` out of the Go source and asserts it against the layer's `enable`. Mutation-checked: deleting the `DefaultOff` line fails it with the qfeeds metric named.
- Docs: both the `grafana/README.md` and `docs/integration-dashboards.md` default-on/off lists were still the pre-#523 set (IDS ruleset, Config change detail and Tunnel lifecycle all listed as off); corrected, and both now state that `Exporter-pushed events` is a catch-all the per-kind toggles do not govern.

Gate: `make test`, `golangci-lint run ./...` (0 issues), `grafana` pytest (349 passed), `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check` — all green.

Deployment note: <host-1> picks this up on the next watchtower pull of `:main`. The ~72/day of `threat-feed-update` annotations already in the m7kni store are not touched by this — deleting them is the separate operational call noted as out of scope.

title: annotations: threat-feed events reach the dashboard despite the per-kind toggle being off

body:
Timeboxed investigation. Prompted by finding that the netisr payload carries a per-CPU dimension we collapse, and that netmap drops are visible only in syslog.

## Confirmed already — the anchor case

`api/diagnostics/interface/get_netisr_statistics` returns **12 workstreams x 8 protocols = 96 work rows**. We aggregate to **8 series** keyed on `protocol` alone (`opnsense/network_diagnostics.go:100-113`). The aggregation itself is correct (counters summed, watermark/length maxed) but the per-CPU dimension is gone.

On the prod box that collapse hides the diagnosis outright:

```
ip6:  cpu0 wmark=1000 drops=683   <-- at limit
      cpu1 wmark= 564 drops=0
      cpu2 wmark= 656 drops=0
      cpu3 wmark= 632 drops=0
      cpu4-11 entirely idle
```

Collapsed, that reads "ip6 is dropping, raise the queue limit". Per-CPU, it reads "8 of 12 CPUs are unused and cpu0 is overloaded" — a completely different remedy. See #538.

We also drop, from the `protocol` array: `policy` (hybrid/direct/default), `policy-type` (cpu/source), `flags`, and `protocol` (the numeric id). `policy`/`policy-type` in particular explain *why* a queue behaves as it does and belong on an info metric.

## Scope of the spike

**1. netisr — decide the cardinality question.** Per-CPU is 96 series instead of 8 on a 12-core box, and scales with core count. Options: expose per-CPU behind an `--exporter.enable-*` opt-in (consistent with how other high-cardinality detail collectors are gated); or keep the aggregate and add a small number of derived series (e.g. per-protocol max-CPU-watermark, count-of-active-CPUs, imbalance ratio) that capture the signal without the full fan-out. Recommend the latter as default plus the former as opt-in, but that is the spike's call. Also add the `policy`/`policy-type`/`flags` info metric.

**2. Kernel endpoints we already call — audit for dropped fields.** Same class of loss may exist elsewhere. Registered today:

```
get_netisr_statistics      get_socket_statistics      get_protocol_statistics
get_memory_statistics      get_bpf_statistics         get_interface_statistics
get_interface_config       get_pfsync_nodes           get_routes
pf_statistics/{info,memory,timeouts,interfaces}       activity/get_activity
```

For each: diff the live payload against the struct and list fields parsed-but-unexposed or not parsed at all. The ARP `manufacturer` case (#534) shows this is a recurring pattern, not a one-off.

**3. Kernel endpoints we do NOT call.** Sweep the OPNsense API surface for anything exposing sysctl, vmstat, netstat -m/-Q, interrupt counts, per-CPU stats, mbuf zones beyond what the `mbuf` collector covers. Cross-check against the do-not-scrape landmine list from the #227 audit so we do not re-litigate confirmed-empty modules.

**4. netmap — what is actually obtainable.** Beyond the `netmap_transmit ... full` syslog line in #536, establish whether any netmap ring state is reachable via API at all (Zenarmor/Sensei status endpoints, `ifconfig` output, sysctl `dev.netmap.*`). If nothing is reachable, the syslog parser in #536 is the whole answer and this closes that thread definitively rather than leaving it open.

## Deliverable

A comment on this issue listing, per finding: the data, where it comes from, its cardinality cost, whether it is alertable, and a recommended verdict (implement / opt-in / skip). Anything worth doing gets split into its own issue. No code changes in this issue.

## Acceptance

- [ ] netisr per-CPU exposure decided and written up, with the cardinality tradeoff stated
- [ ] netisr `policy`/`policy-type`/`flags` info metric decided
- [ ] Dropped-field audit complete for all currently-registered kernel/diagnostics endpoints
- [ ] Sweep for unused kernel endpoints complete, cross-checked against the #227 landmine list
- [ ] netmap reachability question answered definitively yes or no
- [x] Follow-up issues filed for everything with a positive verdict — #541 #542 #543 #544 #545, plus design constraints added to #536 and #538
