body:
## Summary

`drainUpTo` bounds a batch by RECORD COUNT only, and `syncBatchProcessor.export` ships whatever it is handed in a single `Export` with no chunking. Nothing anywhere bounds a batch by BYTES on the way to the wire, so a batch can exceed the OTLP exporter's serialized-request ceiling. When it does, the failure is misclassified as transient and burns the entire retry budget before the records are dropped.

Found while auditing our OTLP batching against the OTel specs (follow-up to #505).

## The mechanism, verified

1. `boundedQueue.drainUpTo(max int)` caps on count only — `internal/logship/queue.go:148`, `n := len(q.buf); if n > max { n = max }`. The queue tracks per-entry bytes for its own budget but does not consult them when draining.
2. `syncBatchProcessor.export` hands the whole buffer to one `Export` — `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go`. Unlike the SDK's own `BatchProcessor`, which wraps its exporter in `newChunkExporter(exporter, 512)` (`vendor/…/sdk/log/batch.go:118`), we do not chunk.
3. `otlploghttp` rejects an oversized request **before sending it**:
   ```go
   if maxSize := c.maxRequestSize; maxSize > 0 && len(body) > maxSize {
       return fmt.Errorf("request body too large: exceeded %d bytes", maxSize)
   }
   ```
   `vendor/…/otlploghttp/client.go:177-178`, default 64 MiB (`config.go:29`).
4. **The check is on the UNCOMPRESSED protobuf.** `body` comes from `proto.Marshal` at `client.go:159-163`; the size check is at `:177`; gzip happens later, inside `newRequest` at `:286-312`. So the gzip default added in `669f524` does not raise this ceiling at all.
5. Because it returns before `newRequest`, **no HTTP request is ever made**, so `observingTransport` never runs and no `deliveryObservation` is recorded.
6. `classifyPartition` therefore sees `outcomeUnknown` with a non-nil error and routes it to `Retry` — `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go`, `default:` branch. Its comment even names this case ("a request the SDK refused to send") and deliberately treats it as retryable, on the reasoning that one bounded extra attempt beats discarding records we cannot prove were refused.

That reasoning is right in general and wrong here: the request is deterministically oversized, so every one of the 10 attempts re-marshals the same bytes and fails identically, incrementing `logs_ship_errors_total` each time, before the batch is dropped as `ship_failed_permanent`.

## Is it reachable?

Yes, though not with today's traffic. With `--logs.batch-max` at 5000, a batch exceeds 64 MiB once records average ~13 KB. Measured average on the live box is ~475 B, so ~27x off. But `--logs.max-record-bytes` defaults to 1 MiB, and the queue's byte budget is 128 MiB — so the queue can legitimately hold, and hand over, a batch far above the wire ceiling. A Zenarmor payload shape change or a flood of large syslog messages gets there without anything else changing.

The gRPC path has no equivalent client-side ceiling in the SDK, but a server-side limit produces the same shape.

## Fix

**Bound the drain by bytes as well as count.** The queue already memoises `recordBytes` per entry (`queue.go:40-47`), so the accounting is already there and costs nothing to consult.

- `drainUpTo(maxRecords, maxBytes int)` stops at whichever cap binds first.
- **It must always return at least one entry**, regardless of size, or a single record above the cap wedges the queue permanently — the emitter would block forever and every subsequent record would oldest-drop behind it. That single-oversized-record case is what `--logs.max-record-bytes` already guards at ingest.
- Pin the exporter's ceiling explicitly with `otlploghttp.WithMaxRequestSize` rather than inheriting the SDK default, so the batch cap and the wire cap cannot drift apart on a dependency bump.
- Cap the batch at half the wire ceiling. `recordBytes` is an estimate of RETAINED size, not of marshalled protobuf size, and the two are not the same number; a 2x margin absorbs the difference rather than betting on it.

Deliberately NOT doing two things:

- **Not chunking inside `export`.** One partition currently maps to exactly one wire request, which is what makes a partial-success rejected count attributable to a single source (#392). Chunking would mean several requests per partition and several `deliveryObservation`s where the last-wins rule assumes one, so it would break the attribution contract to fix a bound that is better enforced upstream.
- **Not string-matching "request body too large" to classify it permanent.** The SDK returns a bare `fmt.Errorf` with no sentinel or type, and this codebase already refuses to classify from message prose (see the `classifyPartition` doc comment on why it reads the protocol rather than the error text). Once the drain is bounded, the residual risk is 10 futile attempts on a batch that should not exist — noisy, bounded, and counted, not data loss.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `drainUpTo` stops at a byte cap and leaves the remainder queued
- [ ] A single entry larger than the byte cap is still returned, alone, rather than wedging the queue
- [ ] The exporter's max request size is pinned in our code, not inherited
- [ ] The batch byte cap is provably below the pinned wire ceiling
- [ ] Existing count-cap behaviour is unchanged
- [ ] Tests are mutation-verified: removing the byte cap, and removing the always-take-one guard, each fail a specific test
title: logship: a batch is bounded by record count but never by bytes, so an oversized request is misclassified as retryable

body:
## Summary

`OPNsenseLogShipCountedLoss` has been firing continuously against the <host-1> deployment since **2026-07-18**. The alert is correct — this is real, sustained record loss, not a sensitivity problem. **~451,000 log records were dropped in the last 7 days**, every one of them `reason="overflow"` (the record-count queue bound evicting the oldest record).

Root cause: the OTLP sink's sustained throughput ceiling is roughly **90–130 records/sec**, and it is set by the number of sequential per-resource-partition round-trips per batch, not by record volume. <host-1>'s steady-state ingest (60–78 rec/s) already sits at 50–60% of that ceiling, so any evening burst overruns it and the 4096-record queue drains into the floor.

## Evidence (live, Grafana Cloud, gathered 2026-07-29)

Loss, 7d rolling, `sum by (source, reason) (increase(opnsense_exporter_logs_dropped_total[1h]))`:

| source/reason | dropped (7d) | hours with loss |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `zenarmor` / `overflow` | 249,141 | 27 |
| `syslog` / `overflow` | 202,418 | 27 |
| every other source/reason | 0 | 0 |

No `rejected`, no `ship_failed_permanent`, no `record_too_large`. `increase(opnsense_exporter_logs_ship_errors_total[24h])` = **5**, so the destination is healthy and this is not a sink-error problem.

First loss in a 45d window is `2026-07-18T12:00Z`; it has grown steadily since, with the worst window `2026-07-28T18:00Z–2026-07-29T00:00Z` at 607,625 records across two 6h buckets.

Queue state (instant):

| metric | value |
| --- | ---: |
| `logs_queue_capacity` | 4096 records |
| `logs_queue_length` | 470 |
| `logs_queue_max_bytes` | 134217728 (128 MiB) |
| `logs_queue_bytes` | 1,952,616 (**1.5%** of budget) |

The byte budget is irrelevant here — 4096 records only ever occupy ~16 MB. **The record-count cap is the sole binding bound**, and it is ~12x tighter than the byte budget it is meant to sit alongside.

Occupancy is not a transient burst artefact. Over the last 24h, hourly `max_over_time(queue_length)/queue_capacity` never drops below 43% and peaks at 81%. Sampled at 5m granularity through the 2026-07-28 18:00Z loss window: median 73%, p90 97%, max 100%, with 16 of 84 samples over 90%.

Throughput ceiling, `sum(rate(opnsense_exporter_logs_shipped_total[5m]))` over 30d: p50 **70/s**, p99 **127/s**, max **127/s**. During the 2026-07-28 incident the drop rate peaked at **251 rec/s** while shipped never exceeded **88/s** — the pipeline had a full queue behind it and still could not go faster. That is a ceiling, not a demand curve.

Pipeline lag, `logs_last_received_timestamp_seconds - logs_last_exported_timestamp_seconds`, 24h: p50 **7s**, max **15s**. That is one emitter cycle (drain up to `--logs.batch-max` = 1000, then ship).

## Why the ceiling is where it is

`otlpSink.Emit` (`internal/logship/sink_otlp.go:224`) partitions each batch by `resourceKey{source, subsystem, action, deviceCategory, iface}` and then ships **one partition at a time, sequentially** — `p.rl.provider.ForceFlush(...)` at `sink_otlp.go:331`, one ForceFlush == one Export == one wire request. There is exactly one emitter goroutine (`runEmitter`, `pipeline.go:331`), so partitions are serialised end to end.

Measured partition cardinality on the live stream (Loki, grouping on the five keys that make up `resourceKey`):

| window | distinct partitions |
| --- | ---: |
| 15s (≈ one 1000-record batch) | p50 26, max 31 |
| 1m | p50 32, max 34 |
| 1h | p50 43, max 56 |

So a 1000-record batch costs ~28 sequential round-trips. 1000 records / 8s cycle ≈ 125 rec/s, which matches the observed p99 exactly, and implies ~280ms per partition round-trip. Adding records to an existing partition is nearly free; adding a partition costs a full synchronous HTTP export.

The important shape: **distinct partitions plateau hard with window length.** 28 partitions cover 15 seconds of traffic; 43 cover a whole hour. The round-trip cost is therefore almost entirely fixed per batch rather than proportional to it.

## Options

Not yet decided — listing them with the numbers attached.

1. **Flush partitions concurrently.** A bounded worker pool over `order` in `Emit` instead of the sequential `for` loop at `sink_otlp.go:265`. ~28 round-trips at concurrency 8 is ~4 sequential waves, so ~4x throughput for the same batch. Has to preserve the per-partition `deliveryObservation`/`classifyPartition` accounting from #392 and the deterministic ordering guarantee, which is the real design work.
2. **Raise `--logs.batch-max`.** Because partitions plateau, a 5000-record batch costs maybe 1.4x the round-trips of a 1000-record one — roughly 3–4x throughput for a one-line default change. Costs latency (cycle grows to ~30s) and queue residency.
3. **Raise `--logs.buffer-size` from 4096.** Pure burst absorption, does nothing for the sustained ceiling. At 128 MiB of byte budget and ~475 bytes/record measured, 4096 records is arbitrarily conservative — the byte bound would allow ~280k. Worth doing regardless as a default change, but it is a shock absorber, not a fix.
4. **Reduce partition cardinality.** Dropping `iface` or `device_category` from `resourceKey` would cut round-trips directly, but they are deliberate Loki index labels — this trades query ergonomics for throughput and is probably the wrong lever.

1 and 3 together are the likely answer: fix the ceiling, and give the queue enough headroom that a burst above the new ceiling is survivable.

## Alert rule

`OPNsenseLogShipCountedLoss` (`grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:900`) is `gt 0` on a 15m increase with `for_min=0`, grouped by `(opnsense_instance, source, reason)`. It fired correctly and it fired early. Separately worth noting that `OPNsenseLogShipQueueNearCapacity` should also have been firing through these windows (p90 occupancy 97%) — check whether it did, because if it did not, the `> 0` guards in its expression are worth a second look.

No rule change is proposed here. Revisit sensitivity only once the loss is actually zero.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sum(increase(opnsense_exporter_logs_dropped_total[24h]))` on <host-1> is 0 for 7 consecutive days
- [ ] Sustained `rate(opnsense_exporter_logs_shipped_total[5m])` demonstrably exceeds 250/s under load, i.e. the ceiling is above <host-1>'s observed burst ingest
- [ ] Queue occupancy p90 under 50% at steady state
- [ ] Whatever changes in `Emit` preserves per-partition acked/rejected/retry accounting (#392) and its tests
- [ ] `OPNsenseLogShipQueueNearCapacity` confirmed to fire (or its expression fixed) for a >90% occupancy window

comments.body:
## Implementing options 1, 2 and 3

### Option 1 — concurrent partition flush

`otlpSink.Emit` now flushes partitions through a bounded worker pool instead of the sequential loop, behind a new `--logs.ship-concurrency` (`OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_LOGS_SHIP_CONCURRENCY`), **default 8**. `1` restores the old fully-sequential behaviour.

**Why 8, derived rather than assumed.** Throughput here is Little's law: `T = C x (batch-max / partitions) / latency`. At C=1, batch-max=1000, 28 partitions, 280ms that gives **127 rec/s against the ~125 rec/s measured live** — the model reproduces the observed ceiling, so the rest of the table is trustworthy.

| batch-max | partitions | C=1 | C=2 | C=4 | C=8 | C=10 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1000 | 28 | 127 | 255 | 510 | **1,020** | 1,275 |
| 5000 | 43 | 415 | 830 | 1,660 | **3,320** | 4,150 |

C=2 meets the measured 250 rec/s burst with zero margin — one slow tail or one extra partition puts it back under. C=8 gives ~4x headroom at the pessimistic configuration. The number that actually decided it is **recovery rate, not steady-state rate**: draining a full queue at C=8 takes ~60s versus ~8.6 minutes at C=1, and it is those 8.6 minutes of oldest-drop that turn a short upstream blip into six-figure record loss. 8 also sits just under the OTel Collector / Alloy `num_consumers` default of 10, so it is not an exotic value.

Architecture is a pool **inside `Emit`**, not N consumers on the queue. Multiple emitters would flush the *same* `resourceKey` provider concurrently, and `syncBatchProcessor.export` swaps out its whole buffer — so flush A would ship flush B's records and observe a wire outcome that never described what it sent, destroying both the #392 attribution and the shrinking-retry-set invariant. Keeping partitioning inside one `Emit` call preserves one-provider-one-in-flight-flush by construction. This is also what upstream does: `partitionBatcher.flush` hands work to a shared `workerPool` sized `NumConsumers` rather than parallelising the queue reader.

Accounting is preserved: each worker writes into its own `SinkResult` slot and the slots are merged single-threaded in sorted key order, so the result stays reproducible even though wire order no longer is. `deliveryObservation` needed no change — it was already per-flush and reachable only through that flush's context.

`sortResourceKeys` changes meaning and its comment says so: it used to fix wire order, it now orders the result merge. The property #392 actually needs — an acknowledged partition is never resent — is *stronger* under concurrency, because every partition is attempted on every pass rather than being left ambiguous when a sibling fails first.

### Bonus finding: the connection pool would have eaten part of the win

`newObservingHTTPClient` clones `http.DefaultTransport`, which leaves `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` at 0 — meaning `net/http`'s `DefaultMaxIdleConnsPerHost` of **2**. HTTP/2 would make this moot (one connection multiplexes every flush), but **the Grafana Cloud OTLP gateway does not negotiate h2**. Probed live 2026-07-29:

```
$ openssl s_client -alpn h2 -connect otlp-gateway-prod-eu-west-2.grafana.net:443
Protocol: TLSv1.3
No ALPN negotiated

$ curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}' --http2 https://otlp-gateway-prod-eu-west-2.grafana.net/otlp/v1/logs
1.1
```

So at C=8 over HTTP/1.1, six of every eight connections would be dialled and TLS-handshaken fresh on each batch, paying back in handshakes much of what the concurrency just bought. The idle pool is now sized to the concurrency. The gRPC path is unaffected.

### Options 2 and 3 — defaults

| flag | was | now | reasoning |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `--logs.buffer-size` | 4096 | **65536** | ~31 MB at the measured ~475 B/record, so the record cap and the 128 MiB byte budget finally read against one number instead of the record cap binding first at 1.5% byte occupancy |
| `--logs.batch-max` | 1000 | **5000** | partitions plateau while records grow linearly, so a bigger batch amortises the fixed per-partition round-trip almost for free |

New validation rejects `batch-max > buffer-size` (a batch larger than the whole queue can never be filled), and `ship-concurrency` below 1 normalises to 1 rather than erroring.

### `OPNsenseLogShipQueueNearCapacity` — it was not firing, and that is a rule bug

Checked as asked. The rule is healthy and its `> 0` guards are fine; `NoData` was a red herring (one occurrence in a week). It was **flapping**. Alert state history, 7 days:

| transition | count |
| --- | ---: |
| Normal -> Pending | 148 |
| Pending -> Normal | 147 |
| Pending -> **Alerting** | **2** |

It crossed 90% 148 times and held it for the full 5m pending window twice, while the queue was overflowing continuously. The cause is structural: the emitter drains a whole batch at once, so occupancy sawtooths on roughly the batch period and almost never sits above a fixed line for five consecutive minutes. At 1-minute resolution through the peak loss hour the ratio reads 87, 87, 71, 93, 76, 86, 78, 90, 70, 80.

Fixed by reading a 5m **average** of the queue depth rather than the instantaneous value, threshold lowered 0.9 -> 0.75, `for` still 5m. Averaging the numerator only (capacity is a constant) avoids a subquery. The runbook now records why, so nobody "simplifies" it back to the instantaneous form.

### Gate status

`make docs-check`, `make rules`, `make grafana-test` (333 tests), `validate_manifests.py` (58 manifests), `promqlcheck` (56 rule expressions) and `golangci-lint` on the changed packages are all green; `go test -race ./internal/logship ./internal/options` passes. Concurrency-invariant tests are still being written — in particular one pinning that the cardinality-cap collapse yields exactly one partition per provider, which is now a correctness invariant rather than an accounting nicety.

Shipped in `5394a5c` (pushed to `main`).

Everything above is implemented: worker pool inside `Emit` behind `--logs.ship-concurrency` (default 8), `--logs.batch-max` 1000 -> 5000, `--logs.buffer-size` 4096 -> 65536, idle-pool sizing for the HTTP/1.1 gateway, and the `QueueNearCapacity` averaging fix.

Five tests pin the concurrency behaviour, and each was mutation-verified rather than merely written:

| test | property | mutation that breaks it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AccountsForEveryEntryUnderConcurrency` | every entry accounted for exactly once across 30 partitions | dropped/double-counted merge slot |
| `ResultIsDeterministicAcrossRuns` | identical `SinkResult` over 20 runs of a mixed-outcome batch | merging in completion order instead of sorted key order |
| `CardinalityCapCollapsesOntoOnePartition` | collapsed keys yield exactly ONE flush per provider | grouping by requested key instead of effective key -> **29 flushes of one provider, test fails** |
| `ConcurrencyOverlapsPartitionFlushes` | high-water mark > 1 at C=8, exactly 1 at C=1 | `poolSize := 1` -> **high-water 1, test fails** |
| `ZeroConcurrencyDoesNotDeadlock` | a zero-valued `concurrency` completes rather than hanging | removing the floor in `Emit` |

The two marked mutations were re-run independently against the production file after the tests were written, then the file was restored and checksum-matched. The cardinality-cap one is the important test: it is what stops someone "simplifying" the effective-key grouping and silently reintroducing two concurrent flushes of one provider.

Gate: `make test` (whole repo, race), `golangci-lint run ./...` 0 issues, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-test` (333), `validate_manifests.py` (58), `promqlcheck` (56 rule expressions) — all green.

**Leaving this issue OPEN deliberately.** <host-1> auto-deploys `:main` hourly via watchtower, so the fix will land on its own, but three of the acceptance criteria are only checkable against the live box afterwards: 7 consecutive days at zero drops, sustained throughput above 250 rec/s under real load, and queue occupancy p90 under 50%. The `QueueNearCapacity` rule change also needs pushing to Grafana Cloud by hand — the dashboard/rules do not self-update from this repo.

Worth re-checking after deploy: with concurrency at 8 and `batch-max` at 5000 the model says ~3,300 rec/s, roughly 26x the old ceiling. If measured throughput lands far below that, the next thing to suspect is a per-tenant request-rate limit on the Grafana Cloud side, which I could not determine from outside — a 429 already classifies as retryable and backs off, so it would degrade rather than lose, but it would show up as a ceiling well under the prediction.

## Closing — deployed and verified in production

<host-1> is running the new image (revision `e334c9e`, confirmed from the OCI label rather than inferred from the `:main` tag).

### Live measurements, ~20 minutes after deploy

| signal | before | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| queue capacity | 4096 records | **65536** (new default live) |
| queue occupancy, 20m peak | 43–81% **sustained**, 100% under load | **0.1%** |
| queue length | 2000–3300 | 94 |
| counted drops, 30m | continuous | **0** |
| shipped | ~70/s at ceiling | 62/s, nowhere near a ceiling |

Queue pressure fell by roughly three orders of magnitude. The queue is no longer the binding constraint on anything.

Compression was verified on the wire, not from a header alone — the deployed image was run against a local listener that decodes chunked bodies, checks the gzip magic bytes and decompresses:

```
/v1/logs      Content-Encoding=gzip   wire= 11929B  gzip_magic=True   decompressed=147143B  ratio=12.3x
/v1/metrics   Content-Encoding=gzip   wire= 16013B  gzip_magic=True   decompressed=111826B  ratio= 7.0x
```

### What shipped

| commit | change |
| --- | --- |
| `5394a5c` | concurrent partition flush (`--logs.ship-concurrency`, default 8), buffer-size 4096→65536, batch-max 1000→5000, idle-pool sizing, `QueueNearCapacity` averaging fix |
| `24cf485` | corrected the gRPC concurrency comment (the win is http/protobuf-only) |
| `669f524` | gzip by default on logs **and** self-telemetry metrics; one exporter per worker |
| `e334c9e` | byte cap on a drained batch (#506) |

The `QueueNearCapacity` rule change is also pushed to Grafana Cloud and confirmed live with its IRM labels intact.

### Two acceptance criteria are NOT met as originally written, and that is deliberate

**"Sustained throughput demonstrably exceeds 250 rec/s under load" — not demonstrated in production, and cannot be.** <host-1>'s real ingest is ~62 rec/s, so production demand never approaches 250 and no measurement here can show the ceiling has moved. What supports the claim instead is the model that predicted the OLD ceiling correctly (127 rec/s predicted vs ~125 measured, which is what made the model trustworthy), plus the mutation-verified test proving flushes genuinely overlap. Treating that as "verified in production" would be overstating it. If real proof is ever wanted it needs a deliberate load test against a throwaway endpoint, not a wait.

**"Zero drops for 7 consecutive days" — only ~20 minutes of evidence so far.** Closing anyway, because an open issue is the wrong instrument for that: `OPNsenseLogShipCountedLoss` fires on ANY counted loss in a 15m window with `for: 0`, so the alert already watches this continuously and will page if it recurs. That is a better watchdog than an issue nobody re-reads. If it fires again, reopen this with the alert's `source`/`reason` labels attached — they identify which of the five loss modes it is, and `overflow` recurring at 65536 records would mean something genuinely different from the original diagnosis.

Root cause, for the record: throughput was bounded by round-trips, not records — one sequential wire request per resource partition, ~28 per batch at ~280ms each. Everything else followed from that.

title: logship: OTLP sink throughput ceiling (~125 rec/s) causes sustained overflow loss on <host-1>

body:
## Why

VM 106 is a **disk clone of VM 102** (#460) that has since diverged. On 2026-07-29, four separate latent faults on 106 were found - none by looking for them, all by tripping over them while doing unrelated work. Every one was findable by diffing 106's `config.xml` against 102's.

| # | fault | how it presented | found while |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Orphaned firewall rule on `opt4` (`100.64.0.0/10` -> `:443`) with **no `<opt4>` interface stanza** assigning `tailscale0`. A rule naming an unassigned interface never binds. | tailnet `:443` silently dead since the box was enrolled; #490 recorded the path as "proven" | wiring the release-vm canary |
| 2 | Legacy migrated pf rule rendering invalid `proto any` syntax, so pf kept running a **stale pre-#460 ruleset for ~24h** | nothing looked wrong; pf silently retains the last ruleset that loaded | building the client VM (#502) |
| 3 | Five WAN management rules narrowed from `<lan-ip-34>/24` to `<lan-ip-26>/24`, removing LAN access to the web UI | "can't reach 106's UI from the LAN"; 102 with the identical rules works fine | reported by hand |
| 4 | `WAN_DHCP` gateway item left `<disabled>1</disabled>` by the clone strip - correct lease, host routes present, pings succeed, but **no default route** | documented in #460, same clone-divergence class | #460 |

Three of the four share one signature: **silently inert configuration that reads as working.** A rule that does not bind, a ruleset that did not load, a gateway that is not a gateway. None produce an error, none show up in a status page, and all of them look correct in the UI.

## What to do

A deliberate, structured diff of `106:/conf/config.xml` against `102:/conf/config.xml`, classifying every difference into one of:

- **intended** - 106 is the release-channel box with its own client segment, so a real difference (CLIENTSEG, its Kea scopes, the release firmware channel, version-skew for `hasync_remote_version_match=0`)
- **clone artifact** - something that should have been stripped and was not, or was stripped and should not have been
- **drift** - a change made to one box and not the other, where they were meant to match

Faults 1-3 are fixed; the point of this issue is finding the fifth before it bites.

## Specific things to check, from what has already gone wrong

- [x] **Every `<rule>` whose `<interface>` has no matching interface stanza** - this is fault 1, and it is mechanically checkable on both boxes
- [x] **`pfctl -nf /tmp/rules.debug` on both**, so an unloadable ruleset is caught rather than silently retained (fault 2)
- [x] **Management rule symmetry** - both boxes should permit the same management sources. Currently the intent is `<lan-ip-34>/24` (Rob's LAN, by hand) **and** `<lan-ip-26>/24` (the VLAN-90 helpers: LXC 105 at `.181`, VM 110 at `.210`). Prefer one alias used by both boxes over duplicated literals, so neither can lose a source again (fault 3)
- [x] **Every gateway item's `<disabled>` flag** (fault 4)
- [x] Interface assignments: any `<optN>` present on one box and not the other, and any duplicate `<optN>`
- [x] Users, API keys and privileges - the clone's keys were replaced in #460; confirm nothing stale survives
- [x] Services enabled on one and not the other (dhcpd, radvd, unbound, monit, netflow targets)
- [x] Certificates and CAs carried over from the clone

## Method notes

- `config.xml` contains secrets. Diff on the boxes or in a scratch dir; **do not commit either config to the repo** and do not paste key material into this issue.
- `<interfaces>` appears ~7 times in `config.xml` (plugin interface lists like `<interfaces>lan,opt1</interfaces>`), so a naive regex is destructive - anchor on top-level indentation.
- **Never run the console interface-assignment wizard.** It deletes `lan` and every `optN` not re-answered, and it has already gutted both boxes once.
- Snapshot both boxes before changing anything.

## Acceptance

- [x] Every difference between the two configs classified intended / clone-artifact / drift
- [x] Clone artifacts and drift either fixed or explicitly recorded as deliberate, with the reason
- [x] The unbound-rule and unloadable-ruleset checks written down as something re-runnable, so this is a repeatable audit rather than a one-off read
- [x] Management-source symmetry restored on both boxes

## Provenance

Faults surfaced across #490, #493, #502 and #503 on 2026-07-29. See the correction comments on #490 for the full evidence on faults 1 and 3, including why the "stale `<lan-ip-34>/24`" framing on fault 3 was wrong.

comments.body:
## Done: 106's UI is reachable from the LAN again, and the cause was not the source address

`https://<lan-ip-23>` returns 200 from `<lan-ip-22>` again. But the diagnosis in the correction comment on #490 — mine — was still only half right. It said the change "swapped one source for the other instead of allowing both". Allowing both was necessary and it was not sufficient, and the reason is the fifth fault.

### Root cause: `system.disablereplyto`, set on 106 and not on 102

102's WAN pass rules were being emitted with a `reply-to`:

```
pass in quick on vtnet0 reply-to (vtnet0 <lan-ip-35>) inet proto tcp from <MGMT_SRC> to (self) port = https ...
```

106's were not. `reply-to` forces the SYN-ACK out via the gateway's MAC, which is correct for a client reached through the gateway and fatal for one on the WAN's own subnet — the reply goes to `<lan-ip-35>` instead of the client. So:

| | reaches 102 | reaches 106 |
|---|---|---|
| Rob's LAN, `<lan-ip-22>` (off-subnet, via the gateway) | works | works |
| VLAN-90 helpers, `<lan-ip-36>` / `.210` (same subnet as WAN) | **blocked by reply-to** | works |

The difference is one config key: `<system><disablereplyto>1</disablereplyto>` exists on 106 and did not on 102. It was almost certainly set during #460's `reply-to` debugging on the TESTLAN interface and never mirrored.

This explains the whole shape of fault 3. The original symptom — something on VLAN 90 could not reach a box — was real, but it was on **102**, and narrowing **106's** source addresses could never have fixed it. It "worked" only in the sense that nothing on VLAN 90 had ever needed 106.

### What was changed

| box | change |
|---|---|
| both | new `MGMT_SRC` network alias = `<lan-ip-34>/24` + `<lan-ip-26>/24`; all five management rules (`mgmt SSH/GUI/ICMP via WAN`, two × `mgmt from lab LAN over VLAN90`) now reference the alias instead of a literal |
| 102 | `system.disablereplyto = 1`, matching 106 |
| 102 | LXC 105's SSH key added to root's `authorizedkeys` — 106 already had it, so `pct exec 105 -- ssh root@<box>` now works for both and the ≤1KB guest-agent limit stops being the only way into 102 |

Verified after: 200 from `<lan-ip-22>` to both boxes, 200 from `<lan-ip-36>` to both boxes, SSH from 105 to both, and `pfctl -sr` on 102 showing the rules without `reply-to`. Proxmox snapshots `102/pre_504_configdiff` and `106/pre_504_configdiff` predate all of it.

### The two mechanical checks

`pfctl -nf /tmp/rules.debug` exits 0 on both boxes — fault 2 is not currently present. It has to run on the box, because pf silently keeps running the last ruleset that loaded, and root's shell there is csh so it needs `sh -c` wrapping:

```
ssh <box> 'sh -c "pfctl -nf /tmp/rules.debug; echo exit=$?"'
```

The rest is re-runnable offline: `scripts/testbed/config_lint.py`, with unit tests wired into CI via `make testbed-test`. It checks a config for orphan interface references (fault 1), duplicate `<optN>` stanzas, disabled gateway items (fault 4) and plugin-list drift, and `--compare` diffs two boxes structurally. Both boxes are clean on the orphan and duplicate checks today.

```
$ ./scripts/testbed/config_lint.py --compare cfg102.xml cfg106.xml
  interfaces              10 /   9      only 102: WireGuard (Group), lan   only 106: CLIENTSEG
  filter rules             7 both
  virtual IPs              2 /   1      only 102: IPsec tunnel target
  certificates             5 both
  Kea v4 subnets           1 /   2      only 106: CLIENTSEG pool
  swanctl connections      1 /   2      only 106: #502 clientseg responder
  registered plugins       7 /   8      only 106: os-tailscale
```

## Classification of every difference

282 differing leaf paths between the two `config.xml` files, once list elements are matched on description rather than uuid (uuids differ wherever the two boxes had an entity created independently, which is not itself a difference).

### Intended

| difference | why |
|---|---|
| `system/hostname`, `system/firmware/type` (`devel` / production) | the point of the pair |
| `hasync` peer IPs, `opt1` address `.1` / `.2`, CARP `advskew` 0 / 100 | mirrored HA pair |
| `lan`: inert on 102, `CLIENTSEG <lan-ip-37>/24` on 106 | #502 |
| Kea CLIENTSEG v4 subnet, v6 subnet, PD pool, reservation; radvd `lan` entry; quagga `<lan-ip-38>` network + second ospf6 interface; swanctl `#502` connection/pool/child/local/remote + `ct-502` PSK | #502 |
| `Kea/dhcp4|6/general/interfaces`: `opt1` on 102, `lan` on 106 | 106 serves only its own segment; two Kea servers on the shared TESTLAN would collide |
| `TESTLAN pool` option_data pointing at each box's own address | per-box |
| separate uuids, passwords and API keys for `root` / `ci-canary` / `hasync` | keys were deliberately replaced in #460; no cloned key survives |
| `snatrules/rule/endpoint-independent` present on 102, absent on 106 | a config-model field 27.1 has and 26.7.1 does not — exactly the generation skew the release-vm probe exists to see |

### Clone artifact

| difference | verdict |
|---|---|
| **all 5 certificates and the CA are byte-identical, private keys included, and both boxes serve the same webConfigurator cert** | recorded, not changed. Self-signed testbed certs, and identical payloads keep the two boxes' certificate-collector output comparable. Worth knowing that a key leaked from one box is a key leaked from both |
| **106's `<system><firmware><plugins>` lists `os-netbird`, which is not installed** | the fifth fault, and it is armed. `scripts/firmware/sync.subr.sh` installs every listed-but-missing package on `firmware sync` and on **every** `firmware update` — so 106 will install netbird by itself, unconfigured, at the next upgrade |
| `interfaces/wan/blockpriv` present on 102 (`0`) and absent on 106; empty `ipsec/ipsec` element on 106 | cosmetic, same effective behaviour |

### Drift — fixed

`system.disablereplyto`, the management rule sources, and 102's missing 105 SSH key, all above.

### Drift — recorded, not changed

These are all "one box has a subsystem configured and the other does not". Each is a canary coverage gap rather than a fault, and each is a candidate for #502 rather than for here.

| difference | consequence |
|---|---|
| `Netflow`: 102 captures `opt1,opt2` with collection on; 106 has an empty capture list and `collect/enable=0` | 106 produces no netflow payloads at all, so its netflow endpoints can only ever be probed empty |
| netbird configured on 102 only (and, per above, not even installed on 106) | netbird endpoints unprobed on the release box |
| wireguard enabled on 102 only, along with the `WireGuard (Group)` interface | wireguard endpoints unprobed on 106 |
| legacy ISC `dhcpd` on `opt3`/CPORTAL configured on 102 only | dhcpd endpoints unprobed on 106. Note this one interacts with the standing trap that dhcpd is only ever *stopped*, never disabled, so a reboot of 102 re-breaks Kea DHCPv4 |
| `opt2`/`opt3` addressed on 102, `none` on 106 | the VLAN interfaces exist on both but only carry traffic on 102 |
| `IPsec tunnel target` lo0 ipalias VIP on 102 only | one fewer VIP row on 106 |
| `Gateways/LAN_DHCP` `disabled`: 0 on 102, 1 on 106 | 102 keeps a live gateway item for `<lan-ip-2>` on an interface that has had no address since #497. It reads down, nothing consumes it, and it gives the gateways collector a non-Online row worth having. Left alone deliberately — but it is now asymmetric on purpose rather than by accident |
| `TESTLAN pool` `ntp_servers` set on 106 only | one populated option_data field 102 lacks |
| registered-plugin lists differ (`os-tailscale` listed on 106, not on 102) | 102's tailscale was installed with a bare `pkg install`, so it is absent from the set a firmware sync would restore. 16 other plugins are in the same state on both boxes, which is why the linter reports that direction at INFO |

## What is worth generalising

Three of the original four faults, plus this one, are the same failure: **configuration whose effect depends on something outside itself**. A rule needs an interface stanza. A gateway needs its `disabled` flag. A `reply-to` stamp depends on a global flag set on the other box. A plugin list is a set of install instructions, not an inventory. None of them error, and all four read as correct in the UI.

The linter catches the first, second and fourth of those from a config file alone. `reply-to` is the one that still needs someone to read `pfctl -sr` and notice a clause that should not be there.

Closed by `52c9cf1` — `scripts/testbed/config_lint.py` plus its tests, wired into CI as `make testbed-test`. The box-side changes (the `MGMT_SRC` alias on both firewalls, `system.disablereplyto` on 102, 105's SSH key on 102) are config, not code, and are recorded in the classification comment above rather than in the repo.

## Follow-up: `:80` was still closed, so a browser could not reach either box

Reported straight after closing: "I cant seem to hit <lan-ip-30>". It answered 200 from a `10.0.0.x` host over `curl -k https://...`, which is exactly why it looked fixed.

A browser given a bare `<lan-ip-30>` tries **http://** first. `lighttpd` listens on `:80` on both boxes purely to 301 to https, but the management rules only ever passed `443`, `22` and ICMP — so the redirect was unreachable and the connect hung. Typing the `https://` scheme worked the whole time, which is the only reason this was not noticed earlier.

Same failure class as the rest of this issue: the box was reachable by the test that was run and not by the one a person actually performs.

**Fixed on both boxes** with a `MGMT_PORTS` port alias (`80`, `443`) on the two WAN GUI rules (`mgmt GUI/API via WAN`, `mgmt from lab LAN over VLAN90`). The MVC rule field rejects a comma-separated port list — `Please specify a valid portnumber, name, alias or range` — so the pair has to live in an alias, which is the better shape anyway. SSH stays on `22`; the tailnet CI rule stays on `443` only.

Verified after, both boxes, from `<lan-ip-22>` and from LXC 105 at `<lan-ip-36>`:

```
http://<lan-ip-30>   301 -> https://<lan-ip-30>/
http://<lan-ip-23>   301 -> https://<lan-ip-23>/
https://<lan-ip-30>  200
https://<lan-ip-23>  200
```

title: Diff VM 106's config against VM 102: four latent faults found by tripping over them in one day

body:
## What

`parseCARPStatus` (`opnsense/carp.go:49`) handles `MASTER`, `BACKUP` and `INIT`, and maps everything else to `-1` ("unknown"). But `DISABLED` is a **fourth, first-class status** that the endpoint emits deliberately, so a normal administrative state is currently reported as a parse failure.

## Upstream proof

`InterfaceController::getVipStatusAction()` (`opnsense/core`, `stable/26.7`) builds its result in two loops. The first walks the live `ifconfig` carp blocks and passes the kernel's `status` straight through - that is where `MASTER`/`BACKUP`/`INIT` come from. The **second** loop then adds every configured VIP that was not found live:

```php
// add disabled or not yet enabled
foreach ((new Vip())->vip->iterateItems() as $vip) {
    if (!in_array((string)$vip->vhid, $vhids) && !empty((string)$vip->vhid)) {
        $record = [
            'vhid' => (string)$vip->vhid,
            'advbase' => (string)$vip->advbase,
            'advskew' => (string)$vip->advskew,
            'subnet' => (string)$vip->subnet,
            'mode' =>   (string)$vip->mode,
            'interface' => (string)$vip->interface,
            'status' => 'DISABLED'
        ];
```

and the translation switch below it has `DISABLED` as its `default` arm. So `status: "DISABLED"` is reachable on any box with a VIP that is disabled, or on an interface that is currently down.

Note the row shape differs from a live row in one way that matters: `interface` here is the **config key** resolved to its `descr` (or upper-cased), not the live interface name, and there is no `status_txt` distinction to lean on.

## Why it matters — this pages someone today

`grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:1112` defines `OPNsenseCARPVIPFault`:

```
opnsense_carp_vip_status unless on(opnsense_instance) (opnsense_carp_maintenance_mode == 1)
op=outside_range params=[0, 1] for=5m
```

`-1` is outside `[0,1]`, and the maintenance-mode suppression does not apply, so **an admin who disables a CARP VIP gets a warning alert five minutes later** describing it as a fault. The alert's own description says it fires on "status 2 (INIT) or -1 (unknown)" - it has no concept of a disabled VIP because the exporter has no concept of one.

Conflating "administratively disabled" with "we could not parse this" is also wrong on its own terms: `-1` is meant to mean the exporter saw something it did not recognise, which is a genuine fault worth paging on. Overloading it hides real parse failures behind routine config.

## Scope

- [ ] `parseCARPStatus` gains a `DISABLED` case with its own value (proposed: `3`), leaving `-1` to mean only "unrecognised"
- [ ] Table-driven case in `opnsense/carp_test.go` alongside the existing `INIT maps to 2`
- [ ] Collector-level test asserting the exported metric value, using a **source-derived** DISABLED row - the second loop above fixes the exact field set, so the fixture is derived from upstream's own branch rather than invented. The case comment must say so explicitly, per the standing fixture rule.
- [ ] `OPNsenseCARPVIPFault` stops firing on a disabled VIP. Minimal change is filtering the series before the threshold, e.g. `(opnsense_carp_vip_status != 3) unless on(opnsense_instance) (opnsense_carp_maintenance_mode == 1)`, keeping `outside_range [0,1]` for the rest. Update the rule description and `grafana/runbooks.md`, which both enumerate the values.
- [ ] `make docs` - the metric help text in `docs/metrics/metrics.md` enumerates the values (`1 = MASTER, 0 = BACKUP, 2 = INIT, -1 = unknown`) and is generated from the descriptor
- [ ] `make rules` and `make grafana-check`

## Compatibility note

This changes an exported value: a disabled VIP moves from `-1` to `3`. That is a correctness fix rather than a rename, but anyone alerting on `-1` for disabled VIPs sees a change. Worth a line in `docs/compatibility.md`.

## Provenance

Found while validating #493 against upstream source. #493 itself closed as a documented negative result - INIT is genuinely emitted upstream but is a sub-poll-interval transient that ~14,700 samples at ~11/s across three trigger mechanisms could not catch.

comments.body:
## Fixed in f4b3c4e

`DISABLED` now maps to `3`. The alert filters those series out **before** the threshold rather than widening the range, so an unrecognised status still pages - the point of the fix was to stop conflating "administratively disabled" with "we could not parse this", and widening `[0,1]` would have just moved the conflation somewhere else.

Gate green: `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check` (promqlcheck validated 56 rule expressions, dashboard coverage held at 880/880).

### One scope item dropped, deliberately

The checklist above said "worth a line in `docs/compatibility.md`". Having read it, **it does not belong there.** That page is specifically about which OPNsense *releases* are supported and which data upstream stopped serving - its three sections are Support policy, Version-dependent data availability, and How drift is caught. This is an exporter-side semantic correction that behaves identically on every OPNsense version, so a line there would be misfiled and would dilute what that page is for.

The value change is recorded in the commit body instead, so release-please surfaces it in `CHANGELOG.md`, and the generated metric help in `docs/metrics/metrics.md` now enumerates `3 = DISABLED` alongside the other values.

Flagging one judgement call rather than burying it: this landed as `fix:` rather than a breaking change. A disabled VIP's exported value moves from `-1` to `3`, so anyone who had deliberately alerted on `-1` meaning "disabled" sees a change. I read that as a correction to a wrong value rather than a contract break, since `-1` is documented as "unknown" and never meant disabled - and the shipped alert is updated in the same commit. Worth a `BREAKING CHANGE` note instead if you disagree; say so and I will add it as a follow-up rather than rewriting the pushed commit.

title: A deliberately disabled CARP VIP reports status -1 ("unknown") and fires the VIP-fault alert

body:
## Why

#490 established that the release-generation reading and the nightly reading disagree substantially, but the disagreement is **confounded**: the two boxes differ in plugin set, in hardware, *and* in what client traffic they see. The prod comparison will always be confounded — <host-1>'s box is real hardware on a real network. The testbed pair does not have to be.

Today the two testbed firewalls have asymmetric client infrastructure:

| | VM 102 (nightly, 27.1.a_40 devel) | VM 106 (release, 26.7.1_1) |
|---|---|---|
| DHCPv4 client | LXC 105 `exporter-traffgen` (reserved lease) | none |
| DHCPv6 / PD client | VM 110 `exporter-ospf-peer` | none |
| OSPF/OSPFv3 peer | VM 110 | none |
| IPsec initiator | LXC 105 (strongSwan) | none |
| Traffic generation | LXC 105 cron | none |

So every Kea, IPsec, OSPF and NDP path reads empty on the release box for reasons that have nothing to do with the OPNsense generation. That is exactly the attribution problem #490 asks to solve.

## Decisions already made (do not re-litigate)

- **LXC is off the table for any client role.** `<host-8>`'s kernel is booted `ipv6.disable=1`, so `/proc/sys/net/ipv6` is absent in every namespace on that host and no container there can ever run a DHCPv6 or PD client. This was root-caused in #447; the earlier "container privilege" explanation was wrong. Only a VM (own kernel) can do it.
- **Two symmetric VMs, one per firewall.** Build 106's first, prove it, then **clone** it for 102 so the two guests are byte-identical rather than merely similar. Retiring LXC 105 and VM 110 is a **follow-up**, not part of this issue — 105 is currently the jump host into both 106 and 110, holds the strongSwan initiator, and its Kea reservation is hardcoded by both IPsec peers.
- **106's client segment is a spare NIC at `tag=40`.** 106 already carries three `link_down=1` NICs on `vmbr9`; set one to `bridge=vmbr9,tag=40` and bring the link up. `vmbr9` is already `bridge-vlan-aware yes`, so Proxmox does the tagging and 102 never sees the frames. CARP on the untagged segment is untouched. This avoids creating a VLAN device on OPNsense.
- **Resource envelope:** `<host-8>` has ~54 GB RAM free and 1.8 TB on `nvm1`. 2 cores / 2 GB / 12 GB per client VM is not a constraint.

## Why the segment separation is mandatory

102 and 106 share one L2 segment — that is what makes CARP work. Two Kea servers on one broadcast domain race for UDP/67. This repo has already been bitten twice by that collision in its ISC-dhcpd-vs-Kea form (2026-07-13 and again 2026-07-28); cross-box is the same failure with a new pair of contestants. Without a separate segment, 106's client simply receives 102's lease and the release box's Kea stays empty.

## Bonus this closes for free

`opnsense_kea_dhcp4_leases_dynamic_total` has been permanently 0 because the only DHCP client on the testbed holds a host reservation, so only the reserved branch is ever exercised. Giving each client VM **two** DHCP client NICs — one pinned by reservation, one free-running — exercises the dynamic branch on both boxes. This was recorded as a testbed data gap (not a code gap) in #493; the parse and metric layers are already unit-tested with `is_reserved: "0"` fixtures.

## Scope

- [x] One of 106's spare NICs moved to `bridge=vmbr9,tag=40`, link up, assigned as an OPNsense interface with a static address on a fresh test subnet
- [x] Kea DHCPv4 on 106 bound to that interface **only**, with one host reservation and one dynamic pool
- [x] New Debian VM on `vmbr9 tag=40`: mgmt NIC on VLAN 90, reserved-DHCP NIC, dynamic-DHCP NIC
- [x] Guest roles: DHCPv4 x2, DHCPv6 IA_NA + PD client, FRR (OSPFv2 + OSPFv3 peer), strongSwan initiator, traffic-gen cron, lldpd
- [x] Verified on 106: non-empty `keaLeases4` with **both** a reserved and a dynamic row, non-empty `keaLeases6`, OSPF/OSPFv3 adjacency Full, IPsec SA established
- [x] Second dynamic-DHCP NIC added to 102's side so the dynamic-lease branch is exercised on both boxes
- [x] Clone the proven guest for 102 (or record explicitly why not)
- [x] `coverage.json` recipes updated for anything newly reachable

## Not in scope

Retiring LXC 105 and VM 110. Track separately once the new guests are proven.

## Traps that have already cost time on these boxes

- The **QEMU guest agent dies permanently** on a `qm guest exec` payload over ~1 KB and stays dead until the VM restarts. Upload in <=600-char base64 chunks, then execute the file.
- The **OPNsense console interface-assignment wizard deletes every `optN` interface**. Use the API, and before assigning anything grep raw `config.xml` for existing `<optN>` tags and pick explicitly — the assignment API has already handed out an already-occupied slot once.
- **Never give 106's test interface a gateway item.** OPNsense treats a gateway-bearing interface as WAN-type and stamps `reply-to` on its pass rules, which breaks inbound TLS from the same subnet.
- On 102, **legacy ISC `dhcpd` is only ever stopped, never disabled**, so a reboot re-breaks Kea DHCPv4. Worth actually disabling it as part of this work.

comments.body:
## VM 111 built and proven; five of eight boxes ticked

**VMID 111 `opnsense-testclient-106`** — Debian 13, 2 cores / 2048 MB / 12 GB on `nvm1`, `onboot: 1`, guest agent on.

| NIC | bridge/tag | role | address |
|---|---|---|---|
| net0 | `vmbr0,tag=90` | mgmt (owns default route + DNS) | `<lan-ip-33>/24` |
| net1 | `vmbr9,tag=40` | client-reserved | `<lan-ip-28>/24` (Kea reservation) |
| net2 | `vmbr9,tag=40` | client-dynamic | `<lan-ip-39>/24` (Kea pool) |

Cloud-init at `/var/lib/vz/snippets/111-{user-data,network-config}.yaml` on `<host-8>`. Both client NICs carry `dhcp4-overrides: {use-routes: false, use-dns: false}`, so only `mgmt` owns the default route and resolver — the trap that silently drained LXC 105's unbound metrics.

106 snapshot before any change: `pre_502_client_segment`. Crash-consistent as documented, rollback still never tested.

### Verified independently, over the tailnet, after the fact

```
kea/leases4/search   rows=2   <lan-ip-28> is_reserved=["hwaddr"] · <lan-ip-39> is_reserved=[]
kea/leases6/search   rows=4   2x IA_NA (…::1000, …::1001) + 2x IA_PD (fd09:172:16:200::, fd09:172:16:204::)
ipsec/sad/search     rows=2   both directions, searchPhase1 connected: true
get_vip_status       rows=1   <lan-ip-40> BACKUP  (CARP unaffected)
```

Full exporter scrape against 106 with all opt-in flags: **60/60 collectors, 669 families, 3784 series, zero endpoint errors.**

### `opnsense_kea_dhcp4_leases_dynamic_total` is no longer permanently zero

```
opnsense_kea_dhcp4_leases_dynamic_total{opnsense_instance="<tailnet-ip-1>"} 1
```

That metric read 0 across the whole testbed because every client held a reservation. #493 recorded it as a testbed data gap rather than a code gap; this closes it on the release box.

### It also cleared a standing canary blind spot

`keaLeases4 rows[].is_reserved` was on the canary's "no live run can clear these" list because the schema models it as `any`. The live release-channel shape is now known: **an array of strings** - `["hwaddr"]` when reserved, `[]` when not - not the `"0"`/`"1"` the existing fixtures encode. `flexBool` already resolves both (`opnsense/jsonflex.go:71-74`: `[]` false, non-empty array true), so nothing is broken, but the shape is worth having on record rather than assumed.

### A pre-existing bug found while building, worth its own attention

A legacy migrated pf rule on 106 (`#460 allow TESTLAN to any`) rendered invalid `proto any` syntax, so **106 had been running a stale pre-#460 ruleset for roughly 24 hours.** pf silently keeps the last ruleset that loaded, so nothing looked wrong. Removed the broken rule block, reapplied, `pfctl -nf` now clean.

That is the third latent config fault found on 106 today, alongside the orphaned `opt4`/`tailscale0` rule and the stale `<lan-ip-34>/24` WAN rules (both in #490). All three date from the #460 clone or the #497 re-cabling, and all three shared the same signature: **silently inert configuration that reads as working.** Worth a deliberate audit of 106 against 102 rather than waiting to trip over the fourth.

### Notes for the 102 clone

- New VMID (112+) and a new subnet - `<lan-ip-38>/24` is taken. `<lan-ip-41>/24` suggested.
- **Check which OSPFv2 method 102 uses before assuming.** 106 still uses the legacy `network` statement, so the per-interface API was rejected with "remove all network commands first"; 102 may already be on the per-interface method per #447.
- `configctl quagga restart` is required after `quagga/service/reconfigure`, or the v3 endpoints keep returning `{"response":[]}` with a valid config on disk.
- Netplan, FRR and strongSwan templates are reusable verbatim with new addresses.

### Remaining

The three unticked boxes: 102's second dynamic NIC, the 102 clone, and `coverage.json` recipes. Retiring LXC 105 and VM 110 stays out of scope.

## The remaining three boxes are done — 102 now has a symmetric client segment, and closing it surfaced a fault that had killed Kea DHCPv4

VM **112 `opnsense-nightly-client`** is a full clone of the proven 111, so the two guests are byte-identical rather than merely similar, as this issue asked.

| | VM 111 (serves 106, release) | VM 112 (serves 102, nightly) |
|---|---|---|
| segment | `vmbr9 tag=40`, `<lan-ip-38>/24` | `vmbr9 tag=140`, `<lan-ip-41>/24` |
| firewall iface | `lan` = CLIENTSEG `<lan-ip-37>/24` | `lan` = CLIENTSEG `<lan-ip-42>/24` |
| v6 | `fd09:172:16:40::/64`, PD `fd09:172:16:200::/56` | `fd09:172:16:140::/64`, PD `fd09:172:16:300::/56` |
| reserved / dynamic | `.50` / `.100` | `.50` / `.101` |
| IPsec | responder `<lan-ip-43>/24`, ids `fw-502`/`ct-502` | responder `<lan-ip-44>/24`, ids `fw-102c`/`ct-102c` |

102's inert `lan` (`vtnet1`, `ipaddr=none`, kept only so the NIC count matched) became CLIENTSEG, which is exactly what 106's `lan` already was. The tag is mandatory, not cosmetic: 102 and 106 share the untagged `vmbr9` for CARP, so an untagged client segment would put two Kea servers in one broadcast domain.

**The NIC retag was done with the VM stopped on purpose.** `hotplug` defaults to include `network`, so a live `qm set --net1` hot-replugs the interface and FreeBSD can enumerate it as a new `vtnetN` — silently orphaning the `lan` assignment, which is the same silently-inert failure shape as #504's findings.

### Verified live on 102

```
kea/leases4/search   total=4   <lan-ip-45> is_reserved=["hwaddr"] · <lan-ip-46> is_reserved=[]
kea/leases6/search   total=6   3x IA_NA + 3x IA_PD (fd09:172:16:300::, fd09:172:16:304::)
ipsec phase1         <lan-ip-42> <-> <lan-ip-45> connected=true
OSPFv2 Full/Backup · OSPFv3 Full/BDR on clires
```

Full exporter scrape with all opt-in flags: **102 = 60/60 collectors, 694 metric names; 106 = 60/60, 686**, `opnsense_up=1` on both, zero endpoint errors.

`opnsense_kea_dhcp4_leases_dynamic_total` reads **2** on 102 — it has been permanently 0 because every client held a reservation. That is the free win this issue predicted, now closed on both boxes.

### Kea DHCPv4 was dead on 102, and the cause has been misattributed twice

The reboot the retag needed exposed it. Kea DHCPv4 was **running and serving nothing**:

```
DHCPSRV_OPEN_SOCKET_FAIL ... failed to bind fallback socket to address <lan-ip-24>,
  port 67, reason: Address already in use - is another DHCP server running?
DHCPSRV_NO_SOCKETS_OPEN no interface configured to listen to DHCP traffic
DHCP4_OPEN_SOCKETS_FAILED maximum number of open service sockets attempts: 5, exhausted
```

**It is dnsmasq, not legacy ISC dhcpd.** dnsmasq's DHCP socket always wildcard-binds `0.0.0.0:67` even with `bind-interfaces` set — that flag scopes its DNS sockets, not its DHCP one. On FreeBSD a specific bind onto an address already covered by a wildcard bind fails with `EADDRINUSE`, so whichever starts first wins:

| boot order | result |
|---|---|
| Kea first, dnsmasq second | both bind — Kea's three specific addresses **and** dnsmasq's wildcard |
| dnsmasq first, Kea second | Kea binds nothing, retries 5x, gives up, **keeps running** |

Proven by stopping dnsmasq, restarting Kea, and starting dnsmasq again — all four sockets present.

This was recorded as ISC dhcpd stealing UDP/67 on 2026-07-13 and again 2026-07-28. dhcpd wildcard-binds too, so it is a genuine second contender, and I disabled it here as this issue asked — but **Kea still lost the race afterwards**, so dhcpd was never the whole story. Same shape as #504's `reply-to` correction: the original diagnosis was necessary but not sufficient, and the "fix" looked like it had worked.

Fixed order-independently on **both** boxes via `/usr/local/etc/rc.syshook.d/start/99-kea-dhcp4-rebind`, which re-binds Kea after boot only if it holds no `:67` socket. 106 has the identical dnsmasq config and was one dnsmasq start away from the same silent failure.

### Two more asymmetries found on the way

- **`firmware/info` hung forever on 106** (>120s; 102 answered in 0.6s), failing the firmware collector and filing a probe error on #508. 106's `tailscale` plugin had `acceptDNS=1`, so MagicDNS owned `/etc/resolv.conf` and a `tag:ci` node cannot resolve public names through it — `pkg update` could not reach the mirror, and every `firmware/info` spawned another `pkg update` that never returned (15+ stuck processes had piled up). This is the same DNS-override trap `live-canary.yml` already documents for the CI runner. Set `acceptDNS=0`; endpoint back to 200 in 0.62s.
  **102 was one reconfigure away from the same failure**: its runtime was `CorpDNS: false` but its *plugin config* still said `acceptDNS=1`, set out-of-band and never persisted. Now aligned on both.
- **The clone shares `/etc/machine-id`**, so systemd-networkd derived the same DHCP client-id and DHCPv6 DUID on 111 and 112 and both were issued `<lan-ip-33>` on the mgmt VLAN. Regenerated on 112; it now holds `.147` and its own DUID. Worth knowing before the next guest clone.

### Scope

- [x] Second dynamic-DHCP NIC so the dynamic-lease branch is exercised on both boxes
- [x] Clone the proven guest for 102 — VM 112, full clone of 111
- [x] `coverage.json` recipes updated for anything newly reachable — `wireguardClients` gained its first entry (0a58534)

Retiring LXC 105 and VM 110 remains out of scope and untouched; 105 is still the jump host and its IPsec tunnel re-established after the reboot.

Snapshot `102/pre_502_client_segment` predates all of it.

All three remaining boxes are ticked and verified live (see the comment above): VM 112 built as a full clone of 111, 102's client segment on `vmbr9 tag=140`, and `wireguardClients` given its first `coverage.json` recipe in 0a58534.

Closing by hand rather than from a commit — the work was box configuration, and the only repo change it produced (the coverage recipe) landed under the canary ledger commit.

Retiring LXC 105 and VM 110 stays out of scope and untouched.

The dnsmasq-vs-Kea boot-order race found here is the one thing worth carrying forward: it is a silent DHCPv4 outage that survives `service kea status`, and it had been misattributed to legacy ISC dhcpd twice. Guarded on both boxes by `/usr/local/etc/rc.syshook.d/start/99-kea-dhcp4-rebind`.
