title: OPNsense live-box canary drift

body:
Follow-on to #336 (internal poll scheduler). Once each collector polls on its own interval, the per-endpoint response cache (`opnsense/cache.go`) is largely redundant for polled GET bodies — the poll interval becomes the freshness bound. Decision on #336 was to **keep the cache as-is for that epic** and revisit here.

Scope to evaluate later:
- Whether the success-body TTL cache still earns its keep for polled collectors (it may double-cache: poll snapshot + response cache).
- **Keep** the plugin-gated **404 cache** regardless (`PluginGatedEndpoints()` in `opnsense/cache.go`) — that's about route existence, not body freshness, and is orthogonal to polling.
- POST-body cases (`smartInfo` etc.) are unaffected — never body-cached anyway.

No action until #336 Phase 1-3 land.

comments.body:
Evaluated after #336 Phase 1-3 landed. **Verdict: keep the body cache — it is not redundant.** Closed by 9d43334.

## Why it still earns its keep

The two caches memoize different things at different layers, so they do not overlap:

| | caches | removes API work from |
|---|---|---|
| poll snapshot (`internal/collector/snapshot.go`) | the metrics a collector emitted | the **serving** path (`/metrics`, OTLP) |
| response cache (`opnsense/cache.go`) | raw API bodies | the **poll** path |

A body TTL pays for itself whenever it outlives the poll interval of the collector that fetches the endpoint, and the scheduler clamps every interval — tier or operator override — to `IntervalCeil` = 15m. Both defaults sit well above it:

- `--exporter.cache-ttl` 1h vs a 15m cold-tier poll → 4 calls/hour become 1. Certificates, ACME, auth users/keys/groups, NAT rule counts, DMI, backup history, ZFS boot environments, unbound local-zone config, GeoIP freshness.
- `--exporter.firmware-cache-ttl` 12h → 47 of every 48 calls elided.

Dropping the cache would hand every one of those calls straight back to the firewall; each is a configd action plus a PHP script. It also dedupes endpoints fetched by more than one collector on different tiers, which the snapshot — keyed per collector, not per endpoint — structurally cannot do.

The "double-caching" cost is a JSON unmarshal per poll off a cached body. That is the price of each caller owning its own copy of the data, and it is noise next to a round trip to the box.

## Also confirmed from the issue body

- **404 cache kept**, as decided: `PluginGatedEndpoints()` is about route existence, not payload freshness, and is orthogonal to polling.
- **POST bodies unaffected** — never body-cached.
- **`firewallRuleIDs` (1m) is the one deliberate sub-ceiling TTL.** It is not on a collector poll timer at all: it absorbs bursts of unknown-rule-id lookups from the syslog enrichment refresher (#248), where a long TTL would keep replaying a stale rule map.

## Landed with it

- `TestBodyCacheDefaultsOutliveThePollCeiling` (`internal/collector/interval_tiers_test.go`) fails if a future default drops to or below the poll ceiling, where the cache could never serve a hit. `DefaultCacheTTL` / `DefaultFirmwareCacheTTL` exported from `internal/options` for it.
- Flag help now says "on every poll" rather than "on every scrape", which stopped being true at #336, and tells operators to keep the TTL above the poll interval.
- `docs/configuration.md` gains a "Poll intervals and the response cache" section explaining which cache removes which work.

Follow-up audit (e43abb4): the response cache is keyed per **endpoint**, not per poller, so it does not respect poll frequency at all. Confirmed by tracing every body-cached endpoint to the collector that fetches it — no fast-tier collector is affected.

| endpoint(s) | TTL | fetched by | tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| `firmware`, `firmwareInfo` | 12h | firmware | cold 15m |
| `certificates`, `caCertificates` | 1h | certificate | cold 15m |
| `acmeCertificates` | 1h | acme | cold 15m |
| `snapshotsSearch`, `snapshotsIsSupported` | 1h | snapshots | cold 15m |
| `torHiddenServices` | 1h | tor | slow 5m |
| `cpuType`, `systemInformation` | 1h | system | medium 60s |
| `dmidecodeInfo` | 1h | hardware | medium 60s |
| `backupHistory` | 1h | backup | medium 60s |
| `authUsers`, `authAPIKeys`, `authGroups` | 1h | auth | medium 60s |
| `clamavVersion` | 1h | clamav | medium 60s |
| `crowdsecVersion` | 1h | crowdsec | medium 60s |
| `unboundBlocklistPolicies`, `unboundLocalZones`, `unboundLocalData`, `unboundInsecureDomains` | 1h | unbound_dns | medium 60s |
| `firewallGeoIP`, `nat{SourceNAT,DNAT,OneToOne,NPT}Rules` | 1h | firewall | medium 60s |
| `firewallRuleIDs` | 1m (capped) | syslog enrichment refresher (#248) | not a poll timer |

The fast tier — gateways, interfaces, protocol, pf_stats, activity, netflow, carp — fetches `FetchGateways`, `FetchInterfaces(Overview)`, `FetchProtocolStatistics`, `FetchPFStatistics`, `FetchActivity`, `FetchNetflow*`, `FetchCARPStatus`, none of which carry a body TTL.

Where a cached endpoint sits under a 60s collector, only the static sub-fetch is cached: the system collector still fetches `systemResources`/`systemTime`/`systemDisk`/`systemSwap` live every 60s and caches only the CPU-model and version strings; the unbound collector caches resolver *config* while the DNSBL counters stay live; the firewall collector caches NAT rule counts and GeoIP database freshness while its live pf data does not.

Nothing structural enforced any of that, so it is a test now. `bodyCacheOwners` (`internal/collector/interval_tiers_test.go`) maps every body-cached endpoint to its owning collector, and `TestBodyCachedEndpointsPollSlowerThanTheirTTL` fails if a TTL is added with no declared owner, if the owner is fast-tier, or if the TTL does not exceed the owner poll interval. A companion test drops stale owner entries. Both failure modes were exercised against a temporary bad entry before landing.

The 404 (absent) cache is deliberately exempt from the tier rule: a 404 says the route does not exist, which changes only when an admin installs a plugin, so it is safe at any poll rate.

title: poll model: revisit the per-endpoint response cache once poll intervals are the freshness bound (follow-on to #336)

body:
Follow-on to #336. The per-collector "Next run" columns for **this repo** are **blocked on #336** (collectors must own independent schedules before a per-collector countdown is honest).

## Why

The three exporters — opnsense-exporter, [graph2otel](https://github.com/rknightion/graph2otel), [tailscale2otel](https://github.com/rknightion/tailscale2otel) — each ship an operator console with divergent structure and feature sets. Users running more than one should get a consistent experience. **Decision: converge all three on tailscale2otel's tabbed single-page layout + theme/style** (chosen as the reference look).

## Reference / target = tailscale2otel

`internal/app/statushtml` — one server-rendered page; sticky tab bar (Overview / Collectors / API / Cardinality / Inventory / Config); inline CSS/JS, zero external assets (air-gap friendly); manual light/dark theme toggle persisted in `localStorage`; JS poll-and-patch refresh + 1s freshness ticker + Pause/Resume button + disconnect banner; hand-rolled SVG sparklines + hover line charts; health badge with reasons.

## Three-way gap matrix (at time of filing)

| | opnsense-exporter | graph2otel | tailscale2otel (target) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Page model | multi-page hub + nav (Status/Cardinality/Config/Devices) | single static page | single page, 6 JS tabs |
| Rendering | server tmpl + external `app.css`/`app.js` | server tmpl, inline CSS, **zero JS** | server tmpl + inline CSS/JS, live DOM patch |
| Auto-refresh | yes — poll `status.json`, `--web.ui-refresh-interval` (5s) | **none** (manual reload) | yes — poll 10s (hardcoded) + 1s freshness ticker |
| Next-poll countdown | none | yes (Next run + Interval + Overdue) | yes (Next run + Interval + Freshness) |
| Run Now | **yes** (per-collector POST) | none | none |
| Theme toggle | auto only (no manual button) | none | manual + localStorage |
| Pause/Resume + disconnect banner | none | n/a | yes |
| Health verdict / sparklines / outcome strip | yes | yes | yes |

## Decisions (made — do not re-litigate)

- **Converge all three on the tailscale2otel tabbed single-page layout + theme/style.** t2o is the reference look.
- **Remove opnsense's per-collector "Run Now"** — the buttons, `POST /api/collectors/trigger` + `GET` 405 shim, the package-scope inflight guard, and `RunCollector` plumbing if it becomes unused (`internal/webui/trigger.go`, `status.html.tmpl:47`, `app.js` `wireTriggers`). graph2otel and t2o have no per-collector trigger.
- **Fleet-wide additions** (apply to whichever repo lacks them): manual theme toggle (localStorage); Pause/Resume auto-refresh + "updated Ns ago" freshness ticker + disconnect banner; **auto-refresh on graph2otel** (currently static).
- **Per-collector Next run / Interval / Freshness columns everywhere.** opnsense gains these only after #336 lands.
- **graph2otel-specific:** widen the main collector table to ~90% of viewport width; move the throttle-headroom data to the **top** of the page.

## Per-repo work

### opnsense-exporter (this repo) — blocked on #336 for the next-run columns
- [ ] Port the console from the multi-page hub to the t2o tabbed single-page layout + theme; fold Cardinality / Config / Devices into tabs (currently separate pages/routes).
- [ ] Remove Run Now (see decision above).
- [ ] Add manual theme toggle, Pause/Resume, disconnect banner, "updated Ns ago" freshness ticker.
- [ ] Keep `--web.ui-refresh-interval` (already configurable here — the fleet standard, see open question O1).
- [ ] After #336: add per-collector Next run / Interval / Freshness columns fed by the new poll metrics.
- [ ] Preserve the load-bearing constraint: handlers must **never** `Gather()` the live registry (would trigger a firewall scrape) — read from `internal/metricsnap.Recorder` + `StatusTracker` only.

### graph2otel — mirror issue to file: rknightion/graph2otel
- [ ] Add JS poll-and-patch auto-refresh + `/api/status.json` polling (currently zero JS, manual reload).
- [ ] Adopt t2o tabbed layout + theme, theme toggle, Pause/Resume, disconnect banner, freshness ticker.
- [ ] Widen the main table to ~90% viewport width.
- [ ] Move throttle-headroom to the top of the page.

### tailscale2otel — mirror issue to file: rknightion/tailscale2otel
- [ ] Reference implementation; reconcile minor diffs surfaced during the port (e.g. adopt a configurable refresh interval instead of the hardcoded 10s — see O1).

## Open questions

- **O1 Configurable refresh interval fleet-wide?** opnsense already has `--web.ui-refresh-interval`; t2o hardcodes 10s; g2o has none. Standardize on a configurable flag in all three, or hardcode a common default? _Recommendation: configurable flag everywhere, default 5s._
- **O2 File the two sibling mirror issues now, or when that repo's work starts?** _Recommendation: file now so the plan is durable per-repo._

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The three consoles are visually and behaviourally consistent: same tab set, same collector-table columns, same theme, same refresh UX (poll + freshness ticker + Pause/Resume + disconnect banner + theme toggle).
- [ ] Run Now removed from opnsense-exporter.
- [ ] graph2otel: wider table + throttle-headroom relocated + auto-refresh live.
- [ ] Each repo's full gate green.

comments.body:
## Open questions resolved

- **O1 (refresh interval):** configurable flag in all three, **default 5s**. graph2otel and tailscale2otel gain the flag; opnsense keeps `--web.ui-refresh-interval` as-is.
- **O2 (sibling issues):** filed now.

## Sibling mirror issues
- graph2otel: rknightion/graph2otel#206 — adopt t2o tabbed layout, add auto-refresh (default 5s), theme toggle, Pause/Resume, disconnect banner, widen table to ~90%, throttle-headroom to top.
- tailscale2otel: rknightion/tailscale2otel#215 — reference impl; make the hardcoded 10s refresh configurable (default 5s), reconcile minor diffs surfaced during the port.

opnsense-exporter's own console work remains blocked on #336 for the per-collector next-run columns.

## opnsense-exporter share — done (main, pushed)

The console is re-platformed from the multi-page hub (external `app.css`/`app.js` + per-area routes) into one server-rendered, inline-CSS/JS **tabbed single page** mirroring the t2o reference. Live on `main` (auto-deploys to <host-1> within the hour).

Commits (in order):
- `e5f55b2` — per-collector Interval / Next-run / Freshness on `CollectorRow` (derived from #336's `CollectorStat.Interval`: NextRun = LastFinished + Interval, Freshness = now − LastFinished, `stale` beyond 2× interval).
- `3f0e3bc` — runtime-stats sampler (goroutines / heap / GC over ~10 min) → `Status.Runtime` for the Overview parity charts.
- `1705605` — fold cardinality into the status snapshot (reuses the already-fetched families — single passive fetch, no extra Gather).
- `0d4b061` — **remove per-collector Run Now**: `internal/webui/trigger.go` (+test), `Deps.RunCollector` + main wiring, and the now-unused `collector.RunCollector` + `ErrUnknownCollector` + its test.
- `99630de` — the single inline tabbed page: `templates/page.html.tmpl`; drops `layout/status/cardinality/config/devices` templates + `static/app.css|js` + `/static` routes.
- `eaa00c5` — docs.

### Acceptance (opnsense share)
- [x] Multi-page hub → t2o tabbed single page (Overview / Collectors / API / Cardinality / Devices / Config).
- [x] Run Now removed.
- [x] Manual theme toggle (localStorage `opnsense-theme`, applied pre-paint), Pause/Resume, disconnect banner, 1s "updated Ns ago" freshness ticker.
- [x] `--web.ui-refresh-interval` kept (default 5s).
- [x] Per-collector Next-run / Interval / Freshness columns (fed by the #336 poll metrics).
- [x] Load-bearing constraint preserved: handlers never `Gather()`; the poll reads only the metricsnap snapshot + StatusTracker + cache view.

### Design notes (binding for the fleet)
- **Config** is rendered server-side **once per page load**, NOT in `/api/status.json` — `EffectiveConfig` re-reads secret files from disk, so putting it on the 5s poll would hammer the filesystem. Cardinality/runtime are pure passive computations and DO refresh on the poll.
- **Devices** loads **lazily on tab-open** from `/api/devices.json`, never on the poll — that fetch is the only console call that reaches the firewall (ARP/DHCP). Kill switches now omit the Config/Devices **tab** (and 404 the devices JSON) rather than 404 a page, since `GET /` is the catch-all.
- JSON contracts were **not** converged: opnsense/g2o keep Go-default PascalCase, t2o keeps snake_case (avoids a breaking change to existing `/api/status.json` consumers). Each console's inline JS reads its own shape.

Gate green: `go build`, `go test ./...`, `go test -race ./...`, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check` (no new metrics), golangci-lint 0 issues.

Remaining: graph2otel (#206). Tracker stays open until that lands. (t2o #215 already closed — `9b13a84`.)

## Epic complete — all three consoles converged

The three exporters' operator consoles now share the tailscale2otel tabbed single-page layout + theme/refresh UX. Build order was t2o (reference lock) → opnsense (the port) → graph2otel (mirror).

| repo | issue | state | key commit(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| tailscale2otel | #215 | ✅ closed | `9b13a84` — configurable refresh (default 5s) |
| opnsense-exporter | (this #337) | ✅ done | `e5f55b2` `3f0e3bc` `1705605` `0d4b061` `99630de` `eaa00c5` |
| graph2otel | #206 | ✅ closed | `e17788a` — tabbed layout + auto-refresh + wide table + throttle-to-top |

### Acceptance criteria
- [x] The three consoles are visually + behaviourally consistent: same tab shell, collector-table columns incl. **Next-run / Interval / Freshness** (opnsense/t2o) and Interval/Next-run (g2o's per-tenant model), light/dark **theme toggle**, **poll+patch refresh** with **Pause/Resume** + **disconnect banner** + **"updated Ns ago"** freshness ticker.
- [x] **Run Now removed** from opnsense-exporter (buttons + POST trigger + inflight guard + `RunCollector` plumbing).
- [x] graph2otel: **wider table** (~90% viewport) + **throttle-headroom relocated to the top** + **auto-refresh** live.
- [x] Refresh interval configurable, **default 5s**, in all three (t2o `admin.status_refresh_interval`, opnsense `--web.ui-refresh-interval`, g2o `admin.refresh_interval`).
- [x] Each repo's full gate green (build / test / -race / lint; opnsense also docs-check + grafana-check).

### Decisions realised (recorded for the future)
- **JSON contracts not converged** — opnsense/g2o keep Go-default PascalCase, t2o keeps snake_case; each console's inline JS reads its own shape. Converging would have been a breaking change to existing `/api/status.json` consumers for no user-visible gain.
- **opnsense — no `Gather()` on the request path**: the poll reads only the metricsnap snapshot + StatusTracker + cache view. **Config** renders server-side once per page load (not on the poll — `EffectiveConfig` reads secret files from disk). **Devices** load lazily on tab-open from `/api/devices.json` (the only console call that reaches the firewall). Kill switches omit the tab (and 404 the devices JSON) rather than 404 a page, since `GET /` is the catch-all.
- opnsense **Overview** got full t2o parity including the runtime-trend charts (a new runtime-stats sampler feeds `Status.Runtime`).

Closing — no work remains.

title: epic: converge operator consoles across the three exporters (t2o tabbed layout) — follow-on to #336

body:
## Why

Every sub-collector runs its live OPNsense API fetch **synchronously on each Prometheus scrape** (and on each OTLP export). `Collector.Collect()` → `collect()` fans out all enabled collectors concurrently under a mutex and emits const-metrics straight to the scrape channel (`internal/collector/collector.go:1325-1432`). Consequences:

- **Freshness is dictated by the consumer's scrape/export interval, not by how fast each subsystem's data changes.** Gateways, traffic, PF counters move every second; firmware, ARP/NDP, certificates, SMART barely move. We poll them all at one cadence — too slow for the volatile ones, wastefully hammering the firewall for the static ones.
- **No honest per-collector "next poll"** for the operator console: collectors have no independent schedule, so a per-collector countdown would be identical on every row. This is the prerequisite for the console-alignment follow-up.
- **Scrape latency = slowest collector.** One slow subsystem drags the whole scrape; today we bound it with a deadline (#128) and skip sub-collectors, which is a workaround for the coupling rather than a fix.

This epic decouples **collection** from **serving**: an internal scheduler polls each collector on its own interval into an in-memory snapshot; `/metrics` and OTLP export serve the latest snapshot without triggering live fetches.

## Current model (accurate refs)

- `Collect(ch)` (`collector.go:1325`) is the Prometheus `Collector` hook; fires once per scrape / per OTLP gather.
- `collect()` (`collector.go:1354`) applies a deadline (#128), takes `c.mutex`, health-checks, then fans out `selectedCollectors()` as goroutines, each `execute()`-ing a live `Update()` that hits the API, `wg.Wait()`s, then emits the always-on meta metrics.
- **In-repo precedent for the target pattern:** logship already runs each source on its own ticker at `max(global, MinInterval())` with per-source floors — `internal/logship/source.go:42-48` (`IntervalSource`), `pipeline.go:197-213` (poll loop); e.g. unbound 15s, crowdsec 60s, ids 30s. The metric-collector scheduler should mirror this shape.

## Target model

A **poll scheduler** owning one goroutine (or a bounded worker pool) per collector:

1. Each collector declares a **default poll interval** (a volatility tier), analogous to logship `MinInterval()`.
2. The scheduler runs each collector's `Update()` on its own **jittered** ticker into a **per-collector metric buffer** (`[]prometheus.Metric` captured from the existing channel emit — no rewrite of the ~60 collectors' emit logic).
3. `Collector.Collect()` becomes a **replay of the union of the latest per-collector buffers** + always-on meta metrics — no live fetch, no API calls under the mutex, no scrape-deadline coupling.
4. OTLP export reads the same snapshot; `otlp.export-interval` becomes "how often to push the latest snapshot," no longer what drives collection.
5. New per-collector poll observability: `opnsense_collector_last_poll_timestamp_seconds`, `_poll_duration_seconds`, `_next_poll_timestamp_seconds`, `_poll_success` — these also feed the console's per-collector next-run / freshness columns.

## Scope / phases

- [x] **Phase 1 — scheduler core + snapshot-replay serving path.** All collectors on a single global default interval. Freshness-equivalent to today but decoupled from scrape.
- [x] **Phase 2 — per-collector interval tiers + config** (`--collector.poll-interval` default + per-collector overrides + floors), jitter, bounded concurrency.
- [x] **Phase 3 — poll observability metrics** + wire the `StatusTracker` / `internal/metricsnap` snapshot to reflect poll state (feeds the console follow-up).
- [x] **Phase 4 — reconcile with the per-endpoint response cache**; cold-start behaviour; max-staleness handling.

## Decisions needed (recommendation + default-if-unanswered)

- **D1 Serving model.** (a) snapshot-cache: scheduler buffers each collector's emitted const-metrics and `Collect()` replays them **[recommended — minimal churn to ~60 collectors]** vs (b) convert every collector to stateful registered gauges/counters [large rewrite]. _Default: (a)._
- **D2 Interval config.** Code-declared per-collector tier + global `--collector.poll-interval` default + optional per-collector override flag, each with a hard floor. _Default: global 60s; tiers fast=15s / medium=60s / slow=300s / cold=1h assigned per collector by data volatility; floor 5s._
- **D3 Response cache (`opnsense/cache.go`).** Keep as-is this epic — it still dedupes within a poll and still caches plugin-gated 404s (`PluginGatedEndpoints`). _Default: keep, revisit in a later issue once the poll interval is the primary freshness bound._
- **D4 Cold start.** Immediate jittered poll of all collectors at startup; serve partial until the first poll lands; freshness metrics reflect not-yet-polled. _Default: yes._
- **D5 OTLP.** Export reads the snapshot; `otlp.export-interval` = push cadence only. _Default: yes._
- **D6 Scrape metrics semantics.** Keep `scrapes_total` / `scrape_duration_seconds` as "snapshot served" counters; the new per-collector poll metrics are the real freshness signal. _Default: yes._
- **D7 Thundering herd.** Jittered tickers + a global bounded-concurrency semaphore so N collectors don't dial the firewall simultaneously. _Default: yes, cap = min(GOMAXPROCS, 8)._
- **D8 Max staleness.** Always expose age; optionally drop/zero a collector's metrics after K missed intervals (config). _Default: expose only, no dropping in this epic._

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `/metrics` serves the latest snapshot with **no** live API call (verify: block the firewall, scrape still returns instantly with last-good values + stale markers).
- [x] Each collector runs on its own interval; changing one collector's interval does not affect the others.
- [x] Per-collector poll metrics exported (last / next / duration / success).
- [x] OTLP export decoupled from collection.
- [x] Full gate green (`make test lint docs-check grafana-check`), vendor synced (`make sync-vendor`).
- [x] `docs/` updated for the new flags + model (`make docs`).

## Follow-up (depends on this)

Console alignment: once collectors own schedules, add per-collector "Next run" / Interval / Freshness columns to the operator console and converge the three exporters' consoles on the tailscale2otel tabbed single-page layout. Tracked separately.

comments.body: Console-alignment follow-on filed as #337 (blocked on this for the per-collector next-run columns).

## Decisions (Rob, binding)

- **D1 — snapshot-cache (a).** Proceed with the buffer-and-replay model. Revisit (b) stateful-gauges only if it shows significant value mid-build.
- **D2 — tiers approved, with a 15-minute ceiling.** fast=15s / medium=60s / slow=300s / cold=900s (15m); floor 5s, **ceiling 15m**. No collector polls slower than 15m — sparser than that causes flat-plateau / sparse-graph problems in Grafana. Assign each collector a tier by data volatility; sensible defaults.
- **D3 — keep the response cache; revisit later.** Logged as #338.
- **D4 — yes.** Immediate jittered poll of all collectors at startup; serve partial until first poll lands.
- **D5 — yes.** OTLP export reads the snapshot; `otlp.export-interval` = push cadence only.
- **D6 — yes.** Keep `scrapes_total`/`scrape_duration_seconds` as snapshot-served counters; new per-collector poll metrics are the freshness signal.
- **D7 — yes.** Jittered tickers + global concurrency cap = min(GOMAXPROCS, 8).
- **D8 — error-aware retention (supersedes 'drop after K intervals').** If a poll **succeeds but returns no data** for a series, **drop** it (the data is genuinely gone). If a poll **errors**, **retain** the last-good snapshot for that collector (a transient API blip must not blank dashboards). So: last-good is held across errors, not across clean absence.

Beginning implementation, Phase 1 first (scheduler core + snapshot-replay serving path).

## Phase 1 landed — ac86cb9

Collectors are decoupled from the Prometheus scrape. An internal poll scheduler runs each collector's `Update` on its own interval into an in-memory snapshot; **both serving paths — /metrics (`ScrapeView`) and the OTLP bridge — now replay that snapshot with no live API call** (both funnel through the single `collect()` chokepoint, so one rewrite decoupled both).

**Delivered (all decisions honoured):**
- Snapshot-cache model (D1a) — `snapshot.go`, per-collector metric buffer.
- Global default interval (60s); `IntervalCollector` interface + tiers (fast 15s / medium 60s / slow 5m / cold 15m, floor 5s, **ceil 15m**) defined and honoured where declared — per-collector tier *assignment* + CLI config is Phase 2.
- D4 jittered cold-start; D5 OTLP replays snapshot; D6 `scrapes_total` kept; D7 concurrency cap min(GOMAXPROCS,8) + per-poll timeout; #127 unreachable-gate preserved.
- **D8 refined during build:** replace the buffer on any emit or on success (clean-absence drops series); retain last-good only when an *errored* poll produced *nothing*. This preserves partial-success emission (e.g. interfaces: base traffic ok + overview 500 still exports the traffic), which a strict retain-on-any-error would have blanked.
- Health split: `pollHealth` sets the persistent gauges, `emitHealth` re-collects them, gating the non-`up` gauges on `healthOK` so they stay absent during an outage (no misleading 0).

**Gate:** `go test -race ./...`, golangci-lint (0), gofmt, `make test` / `docs-check` / `grafana-check` all green. No new deps (stdlib only), vendor unchanged.

**Test migration:** only `collector_test.go` + one `interfaces_test.go` case were affected (all 62 sub-collector tests call `Update` directly and were untouched). Obsolete deadline/skip/short-circuit/live-fanout tests removed; new snapshot-replay + poll-path tests added (`scheduler_test.go`, `snapshot_test.go`).

**Note — inert/shifted plumbing:** `--exporter.max-scrape-duration` is now a *per-poll* bound (serving does no API work); its help text still reads per-scrape — a Phase-2 docs fix. `scrape_skips_total` is no longer incremented (deadline-skip path is gone) but stays registered.

**Next:** Phase 2 — per-collector tier assignment across the ~60 collectors + `--collector.poll-interval` global/override CLI config. These fan out (disjoint files) against the now-frozen `IntervalCollector` seam.

## Live dev-box impact measurement (fast 15s vs medium 60s)

Measured on the opnsense-devel testbed (Proxmox VM 102, **4 vCPU**, 26.7 devel), exporter run locally against it over the tailnet, all collectors enabled, global `--collector.poll-interval` set to each value. Whole-box CPU busy% via `kern.cp_time` deltas; API rate/latency from the exporter's own self-metrics.

| | baseline (off) | medium 60s (all) | fast 15s (all) |
|---|---|---|---|
| box CPU busy% | 2.0% | 5.1% | 12.8% |
| exporter contribution | — | ~3.1 pts | ~10.8 pts |
| load (1m) | 0.08 | 0.45 | 0.78 |
| API calls/min | — | 116 | 464 (4×) |
| avg API latency | — | 80.2 ms | **79.4 ms (no degradation)** |

Exported series (dev box, all collectors + traffgen): **4658 total**; fast-tier subsystems (gateways/interfaces/pf/netflow/protocol): **365** (~8%).

### Findings
1. **The box is not the constraint.** Polling *every* collector at 15s adds ~11 CPU points on a 4-core VM and API latency is flat (79 ms) — no saturation. <host-1>'s real fast tier is a subset, so its box cost is far lower. 15s is comfortably sustainable.
2. **DPM is the real cost, and it's driven by the OTLP *emit* interval, not the poll interval.** Emitting all 4658 series at 15s = 4 DPM = **~4× ingestion** vs 1 DPM (60s). Poll interval only sets snapshot freshness; for an OTLP-push box, polling faster than you emit just discards the intermediate fresh values (box cost, no gain).
3. **The mismatch:** a single global emit interval means blanket-15s pays 4× on all 4658 series to freshen the ~365 (~8%) that actually move sub-minute. ~92% of the extra DPM is wasted.

### Recommendation
- **Assign poll tiers** (fast collectors poll 15s) — cheap, and it keeps the snapshot fresh for pull-based Prometheus users at zero DPM cost.
- **<host-1> OTLP emit: keep 60s (1 DPM) as the default**, do NOT blanket-15s — the box handles it but the DPM cost is 4× for freshening ~8% of series.
- If 15s resolution on gateways/traffic/pf is operationally needed (sub-minute WAN-flap alerting), the right solve is **per-tier OTLP emit** (push the fast subset at 15s, the rest at 60s) → ~1.24× DPM instead of 4×. That's a bridge enhancement — logging as a follow-on rather than a global emit change.

## Phase 2 landed — 165d400

Poll tiers assigned + interval config wired.

- **Central tier table** (`interval_tiers.go` `collectorTiers`) — fast 15s: gateways, interfaces, protocol, pf_stats, activity, netflow, carp · slow 5m: firewall_rule, alias, ntp, dyndns, qfeeds, trafficshaper, siproxd, tor · cold 15m: firmware, certificate, acme, smart, cron, snapshots, vnstat · everything else = medium 60s default. (A central table beats a `PollInterval()` method in ~60 files — one reviewable place; the `IntervalCollector` interface still wins if a collector self-declares.)
- **Flags:** `--collector.poll-interval` (global default 60s) and `--collector.poll-interval-override=<collector>=<dur>` (repeatable, clamped [5s,15m], wins over the tier).
- Gate green: race tests, golangci 0, docs-check, grafana-check.

### <host-1> deployment note (refines the 'blanket 15s' decision)
The tiers make the blanket-4-DPM choice **cheaper on the box than 'everything at 15s'**: <host-1> only needs `--otlp.export-interval=15s` (Fleet Management). The OTLP bridge re-emits the whole snapshot every 15s = 4 DPM (the chosen cost), but cold collectors still *poll* at 15m — there's no point fetching firmware every 15s, and the snapshot just re-emits the last value. So: **set <host-1>'s `--otlp.export-interval=15s`; do NOT set a global 15s poll or change the floor.** Same 4 DPM, far less box load. Fast collectors poll 15s so their 15s emit carries genuinely fresh data.

### Remaining
- Phase 3 — poll-observability metrics (`opnsense_collector_{last,next}_poll_timestamp_seconds`, `_poll_duration_seconds`, `_poll_success`) + wire StatusTracker/metricsnap to reflect poll state. **This unblocks the #337 console next-run/freshness columns.**
- Phase 4 — response-cache reconcile (#338), cold-start polish, max-staleness.

## Epic complete — closed by 7ebc2cb

All four phases shipped and gated. Commits: **ac86cb9** (P1 scheduler+replay) · **165d400** (P2 tiers+config) · **8edea9c** (P3 poll-observability metrics) · **7ebc2cb** (P4 docs+closeout).

**Outcome:** collectors are fully decoupled from the Prometheus scrape. Each polls the OPNsense API on its own volatility tier (fast 15s / medium 60s / slow 5m / cold 15m) into an in-memory snapshot; `/metrics` and the OTLP bridge replay it with **no live API call on the request path**. New per-collector poll metrics (`opnsense_exporter_collector_{poll_interval,last_poll_timestamp,next_poll_timestamp}_seconds`) + a Grafana "Per-Collector Poll Schedule" row + `CollectorStat.Interval` feed the #337 console next-run/freshness columns.

**Deferred/decided (not gaps):**
- Response-cache reconcile → **#338** (D3: keep the cache for now).
- Max-staleness → "expose only" (D8), delivered by the P3 freshness metrics; no active series-dropping.
- The D8 partial-emit refinement (retain last-good only when an *errored* poll produced *nothing*) is in the P1 code + tests.

**Config:** `--collector.poll-interval` (global default 60s) · `--collector.poll-interval-override=<collector>=<dur>` (clamped [5s,15m]). `--exporter.max-scrape-duration` is now a per-poll bound (help text updated).

**<host-1>:** set `--otlp.export-interval=15s` in Fleet Management for the chosen 4-DPM emit; tiers keep the box-side poll load low (cold collectors still poll 15m). The repo default stays 60s.

**Next:** #337 (console alignment) is now unblocked for the per-collector next-run/freshness columns.

title: epic: decouple collectors from the Prometheus scrape — internal per-collector poll scheduler

## Context

Follow-up to #332/#334. After the unbound parser, the residual unparsed syslog tail on <host-1> (from live debug-capture, #330) is a handful of programs. Rob asked to parse all five. Formats below are captured verbatim from the live box — do not guess.

## Per-program plan (formats captured live)

### cron (`cron`, `/usr/sbin/cron`) — NEW file `cron.go`
```
(root) CMD (/usr/libexec/atrun)
(nobody) CMD (/usr/local/sbin/configctl -d -- sfpmetrics run)
(nobody) MAIL (mailed 37 bytes of output but got status 0x0001
```
Grammar `(<user>) <ACTION> (<detail>)`. Emit `cron.user`, `cron.action` (cmd|mail), `cron.command` (the parenthesised command on CMD). Non-matching → generic.

### radvd (`radvd`) — NEW file `radvd.go`
```
polling for 27.344 second(s), next iface is ixl0_vlan100
timer_handler called for ixl0_vlan100
```
Emit `radvd.event` (polling|timer), `interface` (+ `interface.name` via ifaceName enrichment), `radvd.interval_seconds` (polling). Non-matching → generic.

### dnsmasq-dhcp (`dnsmasq-dhcp`) — EXTEND `dhcp.go`
```
DHCPREQUEST(ixl0_vlan50) <lan-ip-64> <mac-8>
DHCPACK(ixl0_vlan50) <lan-ip-65> <mac-9>
not giving name <host-37> to the DHCP lease of <lan-ip-66> because the name exists in ...
```
`parseDHCP`'s `dnsmasqLineRE` already matches DHCPREQUEST/DHCPACK — just register `dnsmasq-dhcp` on `parseDHCP` + add `dnsmasq-dhcp: dhcp` to the registry subsystems map. The "not giving name" warning correctly stays generic.

### kea-dhcp6 (`kea-dhcp6`, already registered to `parseDHCP`) — EXTEND `dhcp.go`
```
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.packets.0x..] DHCP6_PACKET_RECEIVED duid=[00:01:00:01:..], [no hwaddr info], tid=0xe7ba05: RENEW
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.packets.0x..] DHCP6_PACKET_SEND duid=[00:01:..], tid=0xe7ba05: trying to send packet
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.dhcp6.0x..]   DHCP6_QUERY_LABEL received query: duid=[..], tid=0xe7b..
INFO  [kea-dhcp6.commands.0x..] COMMAND_RECEIVED Received command 'lease6-get-page'
```
Structure the DHCPv6 packet lifecycle (`DHCP6_PACKET_RECEIVED`/`_SEND` with the trailing message type SOLICIT/REQUEST/RENEW/RELEASE/REPLY/ADVERTISE, plus duid/tid). COMMAND_RECEIVED is control-plane chatter (the exporter's own lease polling) — leave generic, consistent with the existing "only lease/lifecycle events" design.

### configd.py (`configd.py`, already registered to `parseAudit`) — EXTEND `audit.go`
```
action wireguard.status not found for user root
message <uuid> [interface newipv6 pppoe0] returned OK
message <uuid> [qfeeds stats] returned {"feeds":[...big json...]}
```
Structure: `action <name> not found for user <user>` → audit.action + audit.result=not_found + audit.user. `message <uuid> [<cmd>] returned <R>` → audit.message_id + audit.command + audit.result (OK / trim; never dump the big JSON blob into an attribute).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cron.go` + tests (new).
- [ ] `radvd.go` + tests (new).
- [ ] `dhcp.go`: register `dnsmasq-dhcp`; extend `parseKeaDHCP` for DHCPv6 packet lifecycle; existing dhcp tests still pass.
- [ ] `audit.go`: parse the two configd.py shapes; existing audit tests still pass.
- [ ] `registry.go`: add `dnsmasq-dhcp: dhcp` subsystem.
- [ ] Regexes written against the captured lines above; non-matching variants degrade to generic.
- [ ] Full gate green (`make test`, `golangci-lint`, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`).
- [ ] Live: syslog `unparsed` capture rate drops to near-zero after deploy.
title: syslog: parse the residual unparsed tail (kea-dhcp6, cron, configd.py, radvd, dnsmasq-dhcp)

## Context

Follow-up to #332. After the unbound query-log parser landed, the residual unparsed unbound lines are **0.076% (40 of 52,615)** on <host-1> — all still shipped as generic records, none dropped. Their breakdown (live capture):

| category | count | example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `error: SERVFAIL` | 20 | `[46775:9] error: SERVFAIL <<tailnet-3>. AAAA IN>: all the configured stub or forward servers failed, at zone <tailnet-4>. from 100.100.100.100 got SERVFAIL` |
| `Q-Feeds :` | 8 | `Q-Feeds : skip invalid whitelist exclude pattern "*.notion.com"` |
| `dnsbl_module` | 8 | `info: dnsbl_module: blocklist loaded. length is 414523` |
| `blocklist parsing done` | 4 | `blocklist parsing done in 1.41 seconds (414523 records)` |

## Decision

**Parse SERVFAIL (a real error signal); leave the DNSBL/plugin chatter generic.**

The SERVFAIL lines are failed DNS resolutions — worth structuring for alerting/queries. The DNSBL/Q-Feeds lines are plugin status/config chatter at ~20 lines / 90 min with no query value; in this codebase returning `ok=false` for chatter (→ generic record, still shipped, still searchable) is the intended pattern (sshd does the same), not data loss. Structuring them is parser-maintenance for near-zero value, so they stay generic.

## SERVFAIL format (captured verbatim)

```
[<pid>:<thread>] error: SERVFAIL <<qname> <qtype> <qclass>>: <reason>, at zone <zone> from <upstream> <detail>
```

- reason: `all the configured stub or forward servers failed`
- zone: `<tailnet-4>.` or `.` (root)
- upstream: `100.100.100.100` (Tailscale MagicDNS) / `<pub-ip-22>`
- detail: `got SERVFAIL` | `upstream server timeout`

## Plan

Extend `parseUnbound` in `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go`: try the query-log regex, then a SERVFAIL regex, else `ok=false`. Emit:

- `dns.query_name` / `dns.query_type` / `dns.query_class`
- `dns.rcode` = `SERVFAIL`
- `dns.error` = the trailing detail (`upstream server timeout` / `got SERVFAIL`)
- `dns.error_zone` = zone
- `dns.upstream` = upstream resolver address

Severity comes from the `error:` envelope (already high), so no raise needed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] SERVFAIL branch in `parseUnbound`, TDD against the captured lines (both `got SERVFAIL` and `upstream server timeout`, zone `.` and a named zone).
- [ ] DNSBL/Q-Feeds chatter still returns `ok=false` (documented as deliberate).
- [ ] Live: `logs_debug_captured_total{receiver="syslog",kind="unparsed"}` residual unbound share drops to the plugin-chatter floor only.
- [ ] Full gate green.
title: syslog: parse unbound SERVFAIL error lines (the query-log parser's residual tail)

body:
## Problem

With the syslog receiver live on <host-1>, **94% of all unparsed syslog volume is `unbound`** — ~630 unparsed lines/min overall, ~590/min of them unbound, projecting to **~850k lines/day** shipped to Loki as raw, unstructured generic records. `unbound` has no syslog parser (the exporter collects unbound *metrics* via its dedicated API poll source in `internal/logship/unbound.go`, which is unrelated and must stay). The firewall forwards unbound's query log over syslog, so every DNS query lands in Loki unstructured.

Decision (Rob, 2026-07-20): **parse them into structure** rather than drop or leave raw.

## Captured formats (live, <host-1> debug-capture, 50,187 unbound lines, 47 shapes)

The dominant shape (≈99%) is unbound's **local-zone query log** (`log-local-actions`):

```
[46775:2] info: <lab-domain>. transparent <lan-ip-17>@51967 _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<lab-domain>. SRV IN
[46775:0] info: 10.in-addr.arpa. typetransparent 127.0.0.1@7365 <pub-ip-23>.in-addr.arpa. PTR IN
[46775:10] info: 16.172.in-addr.arpa. static <lan-ip-1>@48801 <pub-ip-24>.in-addr.arpa. PTR IN
[46775:1] info: <lab-domain>. transparent <pub-ip-4>105b@52824 lb._dns-sd._udp.<lab-domain>. PTR IN
```

Grammar: `[<pid>:<thread>] info: <local-zone> <zone-type> <client-ip>@<port> <qname> <qtype> <qclass>`

| Field | Values seen |
| --- | --- |
| local-zone | `<lab-domain>.`, `10.in-addr.arpa.`, `resolver.arpa.`, `service.arpa.` … |
| zone-type | `transparent`, `typetransparent`, `static` |
| client-ip | IPv4 and IPv6 (colons; split on the LAST `@`) |
| qtype | `A`, `AAAA`, `PTR`, `SRV`, `TXT`, `SVCB` |
| qclass | `IN` |

Distribution: SRV 81%, PTR 6.8%, AAAA 6.7%, A 4.6%, remainder TXT/SVCB + IPv6 variants.

A tiny tail (≈0.03%) is `error: SERVFAIL <qname qtype qclass>: … at zone … from <ip> got SERVFAIL`. **Out of scope** for this issue — it degrades to a generic record (still shipped), same as any other unmatched shape.

## Plan

Add `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go` (parser lane, one file + `init()` → `RegisterParser(parseUnbound, "unbound")`), modelled on `sshd.go`. `unbound` is already `subsystem=dns` in `registry.go`.

Emit, from the query-log shape:

- `dns.query_name` — qname
- `dns.query_type` — qtype (A/AAAA/PTR/SRV/TXT/SVCB…)
- `dns.query_class` — qclass (IN)
- `dns.local_zone` — matched local-zone name
- `dns.local_action` — zone-type (transparent/typetransparent/static)
- `src.ip` / `src.port` — client, plus `src.hostname` / `src.mac` / `src.scope` via `enrichEndpoint` (best-effort; a miss is normal, never a stale-snapshot signal)

Return `ok=false` for any non-query-log line (SERVFAIL errors, startup chatter) so it degrades to generic — never dropped.

**Note this does NOT reduce Loki volume** — it structures the existing ~850k/day. If the volume itself needs cutting later, that is `--logs.syslog.sample` (add an unbound rule) or excluding the program, tracked separately.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `internal/logship/syslog/unbound.go` with `parseUnbound` + `init()` registration.
- [ ] TDD against the captured shapes above (IPv4 + IPv6 client, all qtypes, transparent/typetransparent/static, PTR reverse zones); non-query-log lines return `ok=false`.
- [ ] `src` enrichment wired via `enrichEndpoint`.
- [ ] Live confirmation on <host-1>: `logs_debug_captured_total{receiver="syslog",kind="unparsed"}` growth rate drops sharply (unbound no longer unparsed).
- [ ] Full gate green (`make test`, `golangci-lint`, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`).
title: syslog: parse unbound query log (94% of unparsed volume, ~850k lines/day)

## Problem

The Zenarmor Elasticsearch receiver logs a throttled WARN for two control-plane
routes `ipdrstreamer` calls once an hour and that this receiver does not implement:

- `GET /zenarmor_<uuid>_<family>*/_alias` — alias resolution for each family index pattern.
- `GET /zenarmor_<uuid>_<family>_write/_settings` — write-index settings.

They carry no reporting documents. Today they fall through `handleIndex` into
`unhandled()`, which answers `200 {}` — not the ES shape these routes want, which is
likely why Zenarmor keeps re-probing hourly. The noise fix in #330 (debug-capture)
suppresses the WARN when capture is enabled but does not implement the routes.

## Why this is a follow-up, not part of #330

The correct response shape must come from evidence, not a guess. #330 shipped
debug-capture, which records these exact requests (method, path, headers, body) to
disk. The plan is: enable `--logs.zenarmor.debug-capture` on <host-1>, capture the real
`_alias` / `_settings` requests, then implement responses that satisfy Zenarmor from
what it actually sends and how it reacts.

## Plan

1. Enable debug-capture for Zenarmor on <host-1>; collect the `unhandled_endpoint`
   captures for `_alias` and `_settings`.
2. From the captured requests, implement `GET /<index>/_alias` and
   `GET /<index>/_settings` with plausible ES-shaped responses in
   `internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go` (route them before the `unhandled()`
   fallthrough).
3. Confirm on <host-1> that Zenarmor stops re-probing hourly and the `unhandled_endpoint`
   counter for these routes goes flat.
4. Tests for the new routes (shape + that they no longer count as unhandled).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Captured the real `_alias` / `_settings` requests from <host-1> (attach a sample).
- [ ] `_alias` and `_settings` routes implemented and unit-tested.
- [ ] Live confirmation on <host-1>: hourly re-probe stops, `logs_rejected_total{reason="unhandled_endpoint"}` flat for these routes.
- [ ] `make docs` / full gate green.

body:
## Problem

On <host-1> the exporter logs a steady drip of throttled WARNs from the Zenarmor Elasticsearch receiver:

```
level=WARN source=server.go:270 msg="zenarmor called an endpoint this receiver does not implement (answered 200 {}; repeats throttled)" method=GET path=/zenarmor_..._conn*/_alias
level=WARN ... path=/zenarmor_..._conn_write/_settings
```

These are `ipdrstreamer`'s Elasticsearch **control-plane** calls, once per hour (a rollover/health timer):

- `GET /zenarmor_<uuid>_<family>*/_alias` — resolve aliases for each family's index pattern (`conn*`, `dns*`, `tls*`, `http*`, `sip*`, `alert*`).
- `GET /zenarmor_<uuid>_<family>_write/_settings` — read the write-index settings.

They carry **zero reporting documents**. In `internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go` they fall through `handleIndex` (path contains `/`) into `unhandled()`, which answers `200 {}` and logs the throttled WARN. Answering `{}` is not the ES shape these routes want, which is likely why Zenarmor keeps re-probing.

Two separate needs fall out of this:

1. A general **debug-capture mode** so the *next* unknown signal on any logship receiver can be dumped to disk (bind-mountable into <host-1>) and inspected, then either modelled or dropped — without relying on a packet capture on a multi-GB/day stream.
2. Once we have captured the real `_alias`/`_settings` requests from <host-1>, implement proper responses so Zenarmor stops re-probing and the WARN goes away. **This is a follow-up issue** — capture first, fix from evidence, do not guess the ES response shape.

This issue covers (1). (2) is a follow-up.

## Design decisions (agreed)

- **Capture scope: unknowns only.** Not a sample of the known/parsed stream — only signals we do not currently model.
- **Disk safety: stop-keep-oldest.** A global byte cap; once reached, stop writing, keep what is on disk (the first samples are what we want to model), log once + count. Never fills the disk. <host-1> runs ~4-6 GB/day of Zenarmor, so a hard cap is mandatory.
- **Config: one shared dir + per-receiver toggle.** `--logs.debug-capture.dir` for the path (one bind mount), per-receiver bools to opt in. Files land under `<dir>/zenarmor/` and `<dir>/syslog/`.

## Plan

### New package `internal/logship/capture`

- `Capturer`: goroutine-safe. Hot paths (Zenarmor request goroutines, syslog read goroutines) call a non-blocking `Capture(...)` that pushes an envelope onto a **bounded channel**; a single writer goroutine drains it to disk. A full channel drops (counted `reason="buffer_full"`) so a slow disk never stalls ingest — consistent with the "nothing on the record path may block" rule in `zenarmor/source.go`.
- Global byte cap (`maxBytes`). On startup, count bytes already in the dir (prior runs) toward the cap. When total reaches the cap, stop writing, log once, count `reason="cap_reached"`.
- Per-file rotation at a fixed per-file size (e.g. 32 MiB) into numbered files, so no single file grows unbounded.
- Output format: NDJSON, one object per line, `ts` + `receiver` + `kind` + payload fields. Files `0600`.
- Registers its own metrics via a passed `prometheus.Registerer`; pre-initialises the closed `{receiver,kind}` combos to 0 (#280).
- Leaf package: imports nothing from this repo (only prometheus). `logship.Deps` gains `DebugCapture *capture.Capturer` (nil = off). No import cycle: `logship` imports `capture`; `zenarmor`/`syslog` import both.

### Config (`internal/options`)

- `--logs.debug-capture.dir` / `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_LOGS_DEBUG_CAPTURE_DIR`, default `""` (off).
- `--logs.debug-capture.max-bytes` / `..._MAX_BYTES`, default 256MiB.
- `--logs.zenarmor.debug-capture` / `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_LOGS_ZENARMOR_DEBUG_CAPTURE`, bool, default false → `ZenarmorConfig.DebugCapture`.
- `--logs.syslog.debug-capture` / `OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_LOGS_SYSLOG_DEBUG_CAPTURE`, bool, default false → `SyslogConfig.DebugCapture`.
- Validation: a per-receiver toggle set true with an empty dir is a **startup error** (reads as "on", writes nowhere). A dir set with no receiver enabled is a startup Info log, not an error.

### Wiring (`main.go`)

- After resolving syslog + zenarmor config: if dir set, construct the `Capturer` (writer goroutine starts), add to `Deps`, `defer capturer.Close()` (flush + stop) after the pipeline stop returns.

### Zenarmor receiver

- Thread the capturer + `DebugCapture` bool into `server` and `docProcessor`.
- `unhandled()`: when capture on, capture `kind="unhandled_endpoint"` (method, path, headers, body) and **suppress the WARN** (Debug-level at most); keep the `unhandled_endpoint` counter (rate signal preserved).
- `handleDoc` unknown-family: capture `kind="unknown_family"` (index, peer, raw doc).
- `docProcessor.process` parse error: capture `kind="parse_error"` (family, peer, raw doc).

### Syslog receiver

- Thread the capturer + `DebugCapture` bool into `source`.
- `BuildRecord` gains a parsed-vs-generic signal (a sibling returning `(Record, parsed bool)`); `handle()` captures `kind="unparsed"` when the program has no parser OR the parser missed OR the envelope failed to parse (raw line). Additive — no WARN to suppress.
- Payload: program, subsystem, severity, message, raw line.

### Metrics

- `logs_debug_captured_total{receiver,kind}` — captured envelopes.
- `logs_debug_capture_dropped_total{receiver,reason}` — `reason` in `{buffer_full, cap_reached, write_error}`.
- Closed label sets, pre-initialised to 0. Confirm these self-metrics do **not** trip the Grafana coverage gate (logship self-metrics are believed exempt — verify before commit).

### Docs

- `make docs` for the flag table in `docs/configuration.md` + the metrics reference.
- Operator docs: a debug-capture section (what it captures, the bind-mount + chown recipe for <host-1>, that captures contain sensitive network data — IPs, DNS queries, TLS SNI, HTTP hosts — and are `0600`).

- [ ] `internal/logship/capture` package with `Capturer` (bounded channel + single writer, byte cap stop-keep-oldest, per-file rotation, NDJSON `0600`, drop-on-full counted).
- [ ] TDD: capture package tests (cap stops writing, rotation, drop-on-full counted, NDJSON shape, concurrent writers).
- [ ] Four new flags + env vars, with validation (toggle-without-dir errors); options tests.
- [ ] Zenarmor: unhandled/unknown_family/parse_error captured; WARN suppressed when capture on; tests.
- [ ] Syslog: unparsed lines captured; `BuildRecord` parsed signal; tests.
- [ ] Metrics `logs_debug_captured_total` / `logs_debug_capture_dropped_total`; do not break the Grafana coverage gate.
- [ ] `make docs` clean; operator docs (bind-mount + chown + sensitivity note).
- [ ] Full gate green: `make test`, `golangci-lint run ./...`, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`.
- [ ] Follow-up issue filed for proper `_alias`/`_settings` handling from <host-1> captures.

## Problem

The shared `/metrics` handler has three independent availability controls that can be driven by a reachable client: unbounded handler admission, a client-controlled timeout that can extend the scrape budget, and retained complete responses for slow readers.

## Evidence

- `internal/server/metrics.go:87` admits handlers without a route-level concurrency budget.
- `internal/server/metrics.go:169` accepts the client scrape timeout when selecting the shared collection budget.
- `internal/server/metrics.go:97` can retain gathered output while a reader remains slow; the main server intentionally has no write timeout for large responses.

## Failure scenario / impact

A client with access to the exporter listener can accumulate concurrent scrape work, extend time spent holding the collection path, or retain response memory with slow reads. This can delay monitoring and add pressure to the monitored firewall API.

## Suggested direction

Add explicit metrics-handler admission, cap the client-influenced collection budget independently of the server deadline, and bound response retention/write duration without breaking legitimate large scrapes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Concurrent `/metrics` work is bounded with a documented overload response.
- [ ] Request timeout cannot extend the configured collection budget beyond a small hard maximum.
- [ ] Slow clients cannot retain unbounded complete scrape responses.
- [ ] Focused server tests cover each control.

Scan candidate IDs: `review-016-metrics-unbounded-inflight-admission`, `review-016-metrics-client-extends-scrape-budget`, `review-016-metrics-slow-reader-response-retention`

body:
## Problem

Backup timestamps accept non-finite floating-point values. If the first returned timestamp is `NaN`, the newest-time comparison never replaces it and the collector emits `NaN` as `opnsense_backup_last_timestamp_seconds` while reporting a successful scrape.

This candidate completed the scan's file-local validation and attack-path pass. Independent validation is still running.

## Evidence

- [Flexible string decoding preserves the appliance value](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/jsonflex.go#L43-L49).
- [Timestamp parsing and maximum selection do not reject non-finite values](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/backup.go#L61-L81).
- [The collector emits the selected value without a finiteness check](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/backup.go#L64-L72).

## Failure scenario / impact

A compromised or malformed appliance response puts a quoted `NaN` in the first backup row. The value survives parsing, all later comparisons against it are false, and the exported freshness gauge becomes `NaN`. Alerts comparing `time()` with the last backup timestamp may no longer classify the backup as stale.

## Suggested direction

Reject non-finite, negative, and impossible backup timestamps before ordering or emission. Fail the collector visibly or omit the freshness series with a bounded error counter rather than publishing a successful `NaN` sample.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tests cover `NaN`, positive/negative infinity, negative values, and impossible future timestamps.
- [ ] Invalid timestamps cannot reach the freshness metric.
- [ ] Invalid upstream data fails visibly without hiding a stale backup.
- [ ] Normal timestamp ordering remains covered.
- [ ] Relevant backup, collector, and lint checks pass.

## Problem

The alias collector copies every appliance-controlled table entry and emits at least one labelled metric per unique table. Detail mode raises that to eleven metrics per table. The response-size limit does not cap unique rows, aggregate label bytes, copied objects, or emitted samples.

This candidate completed the scan's file-local validation and attack-path pass. Independent validation is still running.

## Evidence

- [All alias-table detail keys are copied into a second slice](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/alias.go#L77-L91).
- [The default path emits one metric per table](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/alias.go#L88-L96).
- [Detail mode emits ten additional metrics for each table](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/alias.go#L97-L114).

## Failure scenario / impact

A compromised or misbehaving appliance returns many concise alias-table entries with unique short names. The exporter holds the decoded map and copied slice, then expands each entry into metric objects and scrape output. Detail mode increases the amplification, but the default path is still one unbudgeted series per table.

## Suggested direction

Enforce table-count and aggregate label-byte budgets before copying and metric construction. Add a bounded aggregate or overflow metric and stop processing when the scrape context expires.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test drives a large valid alias-table response through the real path.
- [ ] Default and detail modes both enforce documented row and output budgets.
- [ ] Aggregate label bytes are bounded before metric allocation.
- [ ] Overflow is observable without creating attacker-selected labels.
- [ ] Relevant alias, collector, and lint checks pass.

comments.body:
Closing as **won't fix**, for the same census reason recorded on #320 — plus two facts specific to alias that make it weaker still.

## Default mode is sub-unity, not amplification

Minimal per-table JSON is ~196 bytes, so a 64 MiB response is ~342,000 entries. The default path emits **one** metric per table at ~90 bytes per exposition line:

- **Default: ~20 MiB of output from a 64 MiB response.** That is a *reduction*. There is no amplification to bound.
- Detail mode: 11 metrics/table, ~345 MiB, so ~5.4x.

## Detail mode is already mitigated by the project's own convention

The 5.4x path requires `--exporter.enable-alias-details`, which is **default-off** and whose help text **already discloses the cardinality**: "(~10 series per alias table)".

That is not an oversight — it is this repo's established pattern for exactly this class. **13 collectors** gate per-row expansion behind an explicit `--exporter.enable-*-details` flag with the cardinality cost stated in the flag help: `alias`, `arp_table`, `dhcpv4`, `dhcpv6`, `dnsmasq`, `firewall_rules`, `firmware`, `ipsec`, `kea`, `ndp`, `netbird`, `openvpn`, `tailscale`.

Alias already conforms. Singling it out would be inconsistent with the twelve collectors that handle it identically.

## Threat model

As with #320, this needs the monitored appliance to be hostile — the same precondition under which the scan's final pass policy-rejected 51 of 55 candidates. Alias also polls on the slow tier (5 min), a shorter retention window than ACME's.

Recording the reasoning so a future scan does not re-file it: the mitigation for this class in this codebase is **off-by-default plus a documented cardinality cost in the flag help**, and alias already has both.

## Problem

The activity parser calls `FindAllStringSubmatch(..., -1)` on an appliance-controlled header. A valid response under the 64 MiB body limit can contain a large number of compact state fragments, causing the parser to allocate and retain every full match and capture before the collector returns.

This candidate completed the scan's file-local validation and attack-path pass. Independent validation is still running.

## Evidence

- [The parser accepts appliance-controlled header strings](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/activity.go#L53-L66).
- [`FindAllStringSubmatch` requests every match with no count limit](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/activity.go#L66-L84).
- [The activity collector reaches the parser synchronously during a scrape](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/activity.go#L91-L99).

## Failure scenario / impact

A compromised appliance returns a large header containing repeated recognised state fragments. The regex engine is linear, but materialising all matches and captures can amplify the response into substantial heap allocation and CPU work while the shared scrape is held. Request cancellation does not interrupt the local parse loop.

## Suggested direction

Parse incrementally or cap the number of accepted state fragments. Check the scrape context during local processing and return a counted, bounded error when the limit is exceeded.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test measures allocations for a large valid activity header.
- [ ] State parsing has a documented match and allocation budget.
- [ ] Local parsing stops after context cancellation.
- [ ] Oversized state lists fail visibly without retaining the complete match matrix.
- [ ] Relevant OPNsense, collector, and lint checks pass.

## Problem

The ACME collector accepts every certificate row returned by the monitored appliance and emits three to five Prometheus metrics per unique `(name, description)` tuple. The 64 MiB response cap bounds input bytes, but there is no row, label-byte, metric, or post-fetch work budget.

This candidate completed the scan's file-local validation and attack-path pass. Independent validation is still running.

## Evidence

- [The client accepts and copies every returned ACME row](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/acme_client.go#L38-L100).
- [The collector only deduplicates exact name/description tuples](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/acme.go#L96-L108).
- [Each accepted row creates three to five labelled metrics](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/acme.go#L115-L165).

## Failure scenario / impact

A compromised or misbehaving appliance returns many concise rows with unique names and descriptions under the response limit. The exporter copies them all, then expands them into metric objects and scrape output. CPU and heap use can exceed the scrape or pod budget and interrupt monitoring for that firewall.

## Suggested direction

Apply a documented certificate-row and aggregate label-byte budget before metric construction. Stop local processing when the scrape context expires, expose bounded rejection telemetry, and keep an aggregate certificate count when details are dropped.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test drives a large valid ACME response through the real parser and collector path.
- [ ] Certificate rows, total label bytes, and emitted detail metrics have enforced limits.
- [ ] Post-fetch processing stops when the scrape context is cancelled.
- [ ] Overflow is visible without attacker-selected labels.
- [ ] Relevant collector, OPNsense, and lint checks pass.

_Found during the gpt-5.6-sol repository security scan, 2026-07-19._

comments.body:
Closing as **won't fix**. The behaviour described is real; the conclusion that it is a distinguishable weakness is not.

## Why

A census of the collector layer was run before deciding. The unbounded row-to-series pattern is this codebase's **dominant convention**, not an exception:

- **30+ `Fetch*` functions** deliberately send `rowCount: -1` (or no row limit), i.e. "fetch everything the appliance reports". `opnsense/crowdsec.go:145` says so in its own comment.
- **18+ collectors** loop unbounded rows into `MustNewConstMetric`. At least five are unconditional with no opt-in flag at all, exactly like ACME: `certificates.go`, `crowdsec.go`, `captiveportal.go`, `wireguard.go`.
- **Only two endpoints in the entire client carry a row cap** — `idsAlertRowCap` (500) and `UnboundSearchQueriesRowCap` (1000) — and both exist for performance against a genuinely growing log table, stated in their comments. Neither is a security control.
- The **only** universal guard is the single 64 MiB response-body cap in `opnsense/client.go:83`, applied identically to ACME and to every other endpoint.

So nothing this issue describes bypasses a guard that exists for anybody else.

## Amplification, measured

Minimal per-row JSON that survives the `(name, description)` dedupe is ~142 bytes, so a 64 MiB response is ~472,000 rows. At 3 metrics/row and ~95 bytes per exposition line that is ~128 MiB of retained metric state — roughly **2x**, against a JSON decode of the same 64 MiB body that the exporter already performs unconditionally. ACME polls on the cold tier (15 min), so the state is re-served for that window rather than paid once.

2x is not a meaningful amplification when the decode itself is already the same order of magnitude.

## Threat model

This requires the monitored appliance — the firewall you deliberately pointed the exporter at, using credentials you issued — to be hostile. The scan's own final pass policy-rejected **51 of 55** candidates in exactly this class as "bounded compromised-appliance-only resource patterns". ACME is not distinguishable from the 51; it survived because it happens to be a slightly more elaborate collector, not because it is more exposed.

## The honest alternatives

Fixing ACME (and #322) while ~16 structurally identical collectors stay untouched is cosmetic. The only two coherent options were (a) do nothing, or (b) add **one** shared row-count ceiling in the shared bootgrid-decode path, applied uniformly. (b) is a real behaviour change across all 62 collectors that could silently truncate a legitimately large ruleset, and it is not justified by a 2x factor under a compromised-appliance precondition.

Recording this so a future scan does not re-file it: **the census is the reason, not the individual collector.** If the row-cap question is ever revisited, it should be revisited as one shared guard, not per-collector.

## Reconciliation complete — all 24 findings triaged and dispositioned

Every issue this tracker spawned (#304–#318, #320–#328) has been re-verified **against current `main`**, not the pinned revision, and closed. Re-verification mattered: 44 commits landed between `659c98af` and HEAD, and **three findings changed status purely because of them**.

### Fixed — 6 commits, `d20f894..8dc167f`

| Commit | Issues |
|---|---|
| `2be2b4c` | #305, #306, #307, #321, #323 — API client redirects, URL-value redaction, non-finite floats, regex bound |
| `1bb8c2e` | #309, #310 — Pyroscope response cap + shutdown bound |
| `342d15e` | #308, #313, #324 — OTLP header secrets, devices route, scrape admission |
| `f697018` | #304, #318, #325 — pipeline wedge, queue byte budget, drained slots |
| `4865dca` | #314, #315, #316, #317, #328 — receiver auth + resource bounds (**breaking**) |
| `8dc167f` | #311, #326, #327 — derived metric cardinality |

Gate green on the committed state: `go build ./...`, full `go test ./...` (22 packages), `golangci-lint run ./...` (0 issues), `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`.

### Closed without a fix — 4

- **#312** — not real at HEAD. `#337` (`99630de`) deleted the `GET /devices` route two days after the scan revision. Remaining risk lives in #313, now fixed.
- **#324(b)** — the client-supplied-timeout sub-claim was neutered by `#336`: `collect()` now discards the context, so the header extends a deadline nothing checks. The parse was bounded defensively anyway; (a) and (c) were real and are fixed.
- **#320, #322** — won't fix. See the census on each: the unbounded row-to-series pattern is the codebase's dominant convention (30+ `Fetch*` with `rowCount:-1`, 18+ collectors, only 2 row caps anywhere and both for performance). Alias's default path is *sub-unity* (64 MiB in, ~20 MiB out) and its detail flag already documents the cardinality, matching 12 sibling collectors.

### Corrections to the findings as filed

Recording these so they are not re-derived:

1. **#306 was under-specified, and the real bug is worse than the filed text.** Go *does* strip `Authorization` cross-domain, so the naive reading is wrong — but `shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect` compares **hostname only, not scheme and not port**. A 302 from `https://fw/` to `http://fw/` forwards the API key and secret in cleartext. Confirmed live with two test servers observing the credentials arrive. This was the highest-value fix in the set.
2. **#325(a) was the most serious issue here and was filed as the least certain.** `shipBatch` had no attempt cap and one emitter goroutine, so a permanently-refused batch retried forever while `drainUpTo` was never called again — everything behind it silently oldest-dropped. **One oversized record halted log delivery for the life of the process, with no attacker required.**
3. **#323 had an unfiled sibling that matters more.** The root cause is `safeParseFloat`/`safeParseFloatOK`, not `backup.go`. The same gap put NaN into `cert_valid_to_seconds`/`ca_valid_to_seconds` with `ok=true`, defeating the collector's existing skip guard — and certificate-expiry alerts are far more commonly deployed than backup-freshness ones. Also: `+Inf` is worse than `NaN`, since it *wins* every comparison rather than merely failing to be displaced.
4. **#311/#326 contained a plain bug, not just a hardening gap.** `derive.go` read the raw wire `action` while the parsers had already computed and attached a normalised closed-vocabulary value as `logship.AttrAction`. Reading the field that already existed collapsed a whole dimension at zero cost.
5. **#324(a)'s obvious fix would have been a silent no-op.** `promhttp`'s `MaxRequestsInFlight` allocates its semaphore at construction, and this handler builds a fresh `HandlerFor` per request, so setting it would give every request its own empty channel. The gate had to live on the handler; a comment now records why.
6. **UDP raises the syslog cardinality findings above "trusted network".** The listener defaults to UDP `:5514` with an empty peer allowlist, and UDP sources are spoofable — so an allowlist cannot close #311/#326 the way it genuinely does close #328.

### Breaking change

`4865dca`: a Zenarmor receiver with `--logs.zenarmor.auth-user` set and no `--logs.zenarmor.auth-password` now **refuses to start**. That configuration was an auth bypass (empty supplied password matched the empty configured one), so failing closed is the intent. Needs a release-note callout.

### New configuration

`--logs.buffer-max-bytes`, `--logs.max-record-bytes`, `--logs.ship-max-attempts`, `--logs.max-metric-keys`, `--logs.zenarmor.max-concurrent-requests`. `--logs.syslog.max-conns` is now **per transport** (TCP and TLS have separate budgets so plaintext cannot starve mTLS).

New metrics: `opnsense_log_events_cardinality_keys`, `opnsense_log_events_cardinality_capped_total`; new drop reasons `ship_failed_permanent`, `record_too_large`; new Zenarmor reject reasons `overloaded`, `index_limit`.

### Unrelated pre-existing issue noticed

`TestReplayRepair_VLANParentDuplicateSuppressed` in `internal/flow` fails when run in isolation via `-run` but passes as part of its package — a test-ordering/shared-state dependency. It reproduces identically at `d20f894`, so it predates this work and was left alone. Worth a separate issue.

## Problem

The shared log queue is bounded by record count, not retained bytes. Zenarmor documents can approach the bulk request limit, and the parser preserves the complete raw document in `Record.Body` before it is queued.

This is an unverified scan candidate. A real-path test is required to measure retained bytes and determine a safe per-record and aggregate budget.

## Evidence

- [Bulk parsing can accept a large individual document](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L393-L405).
- [`parseDoc` preserves the complete raw body](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/parse.go#L70-L78).
- [The shared queue applies a count-only capacity check](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/queue.go#L36-L45).

## Failure scenario / impact

A small number of large accepted records can consume substantial exporter memory well before the queue reaches its record-count limit. Additional forged records may also displace genuine security events.

## Suggested direction

Set a smaller per-document ceiling and track total queued bytes as well as count. Reject or evict according to a documented byte budget, with bounded observability for rejections.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A real-path test measures queue memory for large valid documents.
- [ ] The queue enforces a documented total byte budget.
- [ ] Individual records have a safe maximum retained size.
- [ ] Byte-budget rejection or eviction is observable.
- [ ] Relevant logship, Zenarmor, and lint checks pass.

body:
## Problem

When the Zenarmor receiver is enabled with default admission settings, an empty peer allowlist accepts any sender and empty Basic Auth settings disable credential checks. Accepted documents feed both derived metrics and the shared log delivery queue.

This candidate completed the scan's focused post-deduplication validation and was classified reportable. The issue avoids publishing a request payload because the repository is public.

## Evidence

- [The peer allowlist defaults empty](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/options/logs_zenarmor.go#L35-L43).
- [An empty allowlist accepts the peer](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L298-L313).
- [Empty credentials bypass Basic Auth](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L315-L328).
- [Accepted records update derived state and are emitted](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/source.go#L191-L202).

## Failure scenario / impact

A network peer that can reach the enabled receiver can submit forged security records and derived metric inputs. Forged traffic can mislead operators, consume downstream quota, and evict genuine records from the count-bounded queue.

## Suggested direction

Require at least one explicit sender control when enabling the receiver, or require a separate acknowledgement for accept-any mode. Prefer TLS-protected authentication or mTLS for deployments crossing an untrusted network.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Enabling the receiver without admission controls fails closed or requires an explicit insecure-mode acknowledgement.
- [ ] Tests cover default admission, allowlisted peers, authentication, and rejected senders.
- [ ] Documentation states the trust boundary and safe deployment requirements.
- [ ] Relevant Zenarmor, configuration, and lint checks pass.

## Problem

Any single-segment, non-underscore path is treated as a Zenarmor index endpoint. Successful `PUT` requests insert the wire-selected index name into a process-lifetime map with no maximum size or eviction policy.

This is an unverified scan candidate. A focused repeated-PUT test should establish the actual growth path before implementation.

## Evidence

- [Single-segment paths enter index handling](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L213-L223).
- [`PUT` accepts the derived index name](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L231-L241).
- [`addIndex` stores the name in the registry](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L282-L290).

## Failure scenario / impact

A peer that passes receiver admission can create many distinct index names using small requests. The registry grows for the process lifetime, increasing memory use until restart or explicit matching deletes.

## Suggested direction

Restrict the registry to the expected Zenarmor family aliases or enforce a small hard cap with explicit rejection. Avoid silently accepting arbitrary path names into permanent state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test confirms or disproves unbounded distinct-index growth.
- [ ] The index registry has a documented maximum or closed vocabulary.
- [ ] Excess or unknown index names are rejected without growing state.
- [ ] Relevant Zenarmor and lint checks pass.

body:
## Problem

The Zenarmor bulk handler correctly limits each request body, but admitted requests are processed concurrently with no handler-level concurrency gate or aggregate in-flight byte budget. Each handler can therefore buffer the full per-request allowance.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It needs a controlled concurrency test to measure aggregate memory and confirm practical limits.

## Evidence

- [Requests are dispatched without a receiver concurrency gate](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L157-L166).
- [Body limits are applied per request](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go#L338-L356).
- [The server has timeouts but no listener or handler concurrency cap](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/zenarmor/source.go#L239-L251).

## Failure scenario / impact

A peer that passes receiver admission can multiply the per-request memory allowance across simultaneous handlers. Aggregate buffering and parsing overhead may exhaust exporter memory, interrupting metrics and log shipping.

## Suggested direction

Add a small bulk-handler semaphore and/or aggregate in-flight byte budget. Reject excess work before buffering the body, and expose rejection metrics without adding attacker-controlled labels.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A controlled load test measures current aggregate body memory.
- [ ] Concurrent body buffering has a documented hard bound.
- [ ] Excess requests fail before allocating the full body allowance.
- [ ] Existing per-request gzip and body limits remain covered.
- [ ] Relevant Zenarmor and lint checks pass.

## Problem

Zenarmor option validation rejects a password without a username but permits a username without a password. Runtime authentication is enabled when either value is non-empty, and an empty supplied password can match the configured empty password.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It needs a configuration test and an HTTP authentication test.

- [Validation permits the username-only configuration](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/options/logs_zenarmor.go#L226-L234).
