## Failure scenario / impact

An operator can believe receiver authentication is enabled after setting a username, while clients only need that public identifier and an empty password. This weakens protection against log injection and receiver resource abuse.

Require username and password to be configured together, reject half-configured authentication during startup, and test both mismatch directions.

- [ ] No half-configured credential pair can authenticate over HTTP.
- [ ] Fully configured and fully disabled authentication retain their intended behaviour.

## Problem

The default-enabled `GET /api/devices.json` route independently triggers live device retrieval for every request. It has no route-local admission control, timeout, single-flight guard, or cached snapshot before three sequential OPNsense API operations.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It is tracked separately from the HTML route because callers can invoke the JSON endpoint directly.

## Evidence

- [The JSON handler calls `devicesReport` directly](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/webui/devices.go#L41-L50).

Automated callers can accumulate waiting JSON requests, consume the shared upstream concurrency budget, and add sustained work to the firewall API. Normal scrape latency and monitoring availability may suffer.

## Problem

The default-enabled `GET /devices` handler performs live device retrieval for every request. It has no route-local timeout, request cap, single-flight guard, or cached snapshot before calling three sequential OPNsense API operations.

This is an unverified scan candidate. A focused concurrency test is needed to measure queueing and interference with ordinary scrapes.

## Evidence

- [The HTML handler calls `devicesReport` with the request context](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/webui/devices.go#L28-L37).
- [Each request reaches the live device accessor](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/webui/devices.go#L61-L68).

## Failure scenario / impact

Repeated page requests can accumulate waiting handlers, consume the shared OPNsense client concurrency budget, and add sustained work to the firewall API. This can delay normal scrapes and degrade monitoring or firewall responsiveness.

## Suggested direction

Use a cached snapshot or single-flight request, a small route semaphore, and a fixed route deadline. Excess requests should be coalesced or rejected without entering the shared scrape budget.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A concurrency test demonstrates current queueing and scrape interference.
- [ ] Excess `GET /devices` work is bounded or coalesced.

## Problem

Accepted `filterlog` messages retain wire-selected action, interface, and rule identifiers. Those raw values become keys in the process-lifetime firewall metrics map, which has no enforced series limit, eviction policy, or overflow bucket.

This is an unverified scan candidate. Existing tests support the source-to-sink trace, but an end-to-end cardinality test is still required.

## Evidence

- [The parser retains raw filterlog fields](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/syslog/filterlog.go#L84-L125).
- [Derived observations are dispatched before queue insertion](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/syslog/source.go#L209-L216).
- [Unique tuples enter an uncapped map and are copied during collection](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/collector/logevents.go#L68-L70).

## Failure scenario / impact

A sender that can reach an enabled syslog listener can create many distinct firewall label tuples. Heap use, scrape allocation, response size, and CPU then grow with attacker-controlled cardinality, while injected tuples also distort security-event totals.

## Suggested direction

Normalize action to a closed vocabulary, constrain interface and rule identity where possible, and enforce a hard key budget with a counted overflow bucket before inserting into the metrics map.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test drives many unique accepted filterlog tuples through the real path.
- [ ] The derived firewall metrics store has an enforced maximum cardinality.
- [ ] Overflow is observable without creating new attacker-selected labels.
- [ ] Relevant syslog, collector, and lint checks pass.

## Problem

The final Pyroscope flush is raced against a ten-second timer, but the timeout branch still calls `profiler.Stop()` synchronously. The vendored uploader's `Stop` waits for uploader goroutines without a context, so the exporter can remain blocked after reporting a flush timeout.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It is distinct from #121, which added the final flush; this ticket covers whether its timeout actually bounds shutdown.

## Evidence

- [The flush is raced against a ten-second timer](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/profiling/profiling.go#L120-L138).
- [`profiler.Stop()` is called synchronously after the timeout branch](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/profiling/profiling.go#L140-L147).
- [The vendored remote stop waits for uploader workers](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/upstream/remote/remote.go#L120-L127).

## Failure scenario / impact

An unresponsive profiling backend can keep exporter shutdown beyond the intended limit. Service managers may delay restart or force-kill the process, losing final state and extending monitoring gaps.

## Suggested direction

Make the complete profiling shutdown path obey one explicit deadline, including uploader worker termination. If the vendored API cannot be cancelled safely, isolate the stop path or update the dependency to a cancellable implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A blocking-backend test measures total shutdown time at the pinned revision.
- [ ] The complete profiling stop path returns within the documented bound.
- [ ] Normal final-profile delivery still works.
- [ ] Relevant profiling tests and lint pass.

## Problem

The vendored Pyroscope uploader reads the backend response body with `io.ReadAll` and no size limit. An enabled, reachable backend controls that response.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It needs a focused uploader test with a bounded synthetic response before remediation is chosen.

## Evidence

- [The operator-selected endpoint is passed to Pyroscope](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/profiling/profiling.go#L78-L88).
- [The vendored uploader reads the complete response body](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/upstream/remote/remote.go#L226-L233).

## Failure scenario / impact

A misbehaving or compromised profiling backend can return an unexpectedly large body and cause substantial transient heap growth in the exporter, potentially interrupting metrics and log delivery.

## Suggested direction

Cap response-body reads to the small amount needed for diagnostics, close the body promptly, and surface a clear error when the cap is exceeded. Prefer an upstream dependency fix if available, then update the vendored copy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test reproduces or disproves unbounded response buffering.
- [ ] Backend response reads have a documented hard byte limit.
- [ ] Oversized responses fail cleanly without retaining the complete body.
- [ ] Relevant profiling tests and lint pass.

body:
## Problem

The OPNsense HTTP client follows redirects without constraining the destination host, scheme, or port. A redirect response can therefore make the exporter send a follow-up request from its own network position.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It needs a focused two-server redirect test before the impact is treated as proven.

## Evidence

- [The shared client has no `CheckRedirect` restriction](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/client.go#L417-L431).
- [All API requests use that client](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/client.go#L624-L631).

## Failure scenario / impact

A hostile or compromised monitored appliance, reverse proxy, or TLS endpoint could redirect requests toward HTTP services reachable from the exporter. Depending on method-preserving redirect behaviour, this may create blind reads or state-changing requests to internal services.

## Suggested direction

Reject redirects by default, or constrain them to the exact configured origin and scheme. If redirect support is required, validate the resolved destination and make the accepted policy explicit in tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test confirms whether a second local server receives redirected requests.
- [ ] Cross-origin, alternate-port, and downgrade redirects are rejected.
- [ ] Allowed redirect behaviour is documented and regression-tested.
- [ ] Relevant client tests and lint pass.

## Problem

The shared OPNsense HTTP client uses Go's default redirect policy. Requests receive Basic Auth before `Do`, but there is no repository-level `CheckRedirect` policy to pin the destination or reject HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects.

This is an unverified scan candidate. The exact redirect matrix still needs focused tests against the repository's configured Go toolchain.

## Evidence

- [The shared client is built without a redirect policy](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/client.go#L417-L431).
- [Basic Auth is attached before the request is sent](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/client.go#L597-L606).
- [The request is handed to the redirect-following client](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/opnsense/client.go#L624-L631).

## Failure scenario / impact

A qualifying redirect from the configured appliance or reverse proxy may forward the OPNsense API credential to another service, alternate port, or plaintext hop. Compromise of that credential could expose any API permissions granted to it.

## Suggested direction

Reject redirects or pin them to the exact configured HTTPS origin. Add explicit tests for same host, alternate port, subdomain, unrelated host, and HTTPS downgrade, with assertions that `Authorization` never reaches an unapproved destination.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Focused tests establish current credential-forwarding behaviour.
- [ ] Redirects cannot forward OPNsense credentials outside the approved origin.
- [ ] HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects are rejected.
- [ ] Relevant client tests and lint pass.

## Problem

`drainUpTo` advances the queue slice without clearing the drained `Entry` values. Those entries contain pointer-bearing record fields, so large bodies and attribute maps can remain reachable through the queue's backing array after delivery.

This is an unverified scan candidate. It should be reproduced with a focused heap-retention test before the implementation direction is treated as final.

## Evidence

- [`drainUpTo` copies and reslices without clearing drained slots](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/queue.go#L73-L78).
- [Accepted records enter the long-lived queue](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/push.go#L86-L92).
- [The queue remains attached to the pipeline](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/659c98afd38a130bf3c1f4d99e909a4170367b49/internal/logship/pipeline.go#L108-L115).

## Failure scenario / impact

A stream of large accepted records can leave previously delivered data resident until the backing array is replaced or the pipeline stops. That can increase GC pressure and exporter memory use even when the sink keeps pace.

## Suggested direction

Clear drained slots before reslicing, and ensure a fully drained queue cannot retain stale record pointers. Add a regression test or benchmark that measures retained heap after repeated push-and-drain cycles.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A focused test reproduces or disproves retention at the pinned revision.
- [ ] Drained queue slots no longer retain record bodies or attribute maps.
- [ ] Queue ordering, capacity, and drop-oldest behaviour remain unchanged.
- [ ] Relevant tests and lint pass.

body:
The public dashboard currently covers most exporter features, but it is hard to navigate and several panels are misleading in a long-running Grafana Cloud stack. The flat 39-tab layout overflows, current-value panels render historical deployment identities as duplicate cards, gateway history carries the same unstable labels, and some state mappings make healthy or known sentinel values look broken.

The recording rules need fixing in the same cycle. Eight deployed recording rules are currently in an error state and none of the expected `instance:opnsense_*` series are being written, even where their source metrics exist. The dashboard also does not expose the derived series.

This issue tracks a full overhaul while keeping the dashboard useful as the general-purpose public dashboard for every feature the exporter supports. Installations should still hide unsupported sections dynamically.

## Plan

- Rework navigation into a layered hierarchy with a small set of top-level domains and nested feature tabs.
- Keep conditional rendering for optional collectors and make it apply cleanly to nested sections.
- Normalise away scrape/deployment identity labels where they create duplicate logical devices.
- Use instant queries for current state and range queries only for history/trends.
- Improve panel titles, descriptions, units, legends, thresholds, value mappings, table fields, and empty/error states.
- Add useful overview signals from the exporter and recording rules without turning the landing page into another exhaustive tab.

- Regenerate the dashboard JSON and statistics from source.

## What & why

Replace the stock Prometheus landing page (title + 3 links) with a rich, hub-and-spoke, server-rendered **operator console**, matching the comprehensiveness of `meraki-dashboard-exporter` and the Go `internal/admin` pattern of `graph2otel`. Everything the console needs already exists internally (62 self-registering collectors, per-collector scrape timing/success, self-metrics, the per-endpoint response cache, ARP/DHCP data) but is unsurfaced.

## Scope

New self-contained `internal/webui` package (Go `html/template` + `go:embed` + vanilla-JS live polling; no framework, no CDN, static-binary friendly). Hub-and-spoke: a rich landing dashboard linking to standalone sub-pages.

**Pages:**
- **`/` status/overview** — global health badge + "why not healthy", exporter stat tiles, per-collector table (state, success rate, runs/failures, last-scrape duration, inline SVG **sparkline** + outcome strip, staleness, last error, **Run Now** button), skipped-collectors, a **cache/data-freshness card** (per-endpoint TTL/remaining), an **API/auth card** (auth state, request count, avg duration, top endpoints by error).
- **`/cardinality`** hub + drill-downs (`all-metrics`, `all-labels`, `label-values/{metric}`), growth-rate, threshold recommendations, active alerts, `export.json`.
- **`/config`** — effective config as a readable table, **all secrets redacted** (presence-only; the secret string never reaches the view layer).
- **`/devices`** — ARP + DHCPv4/v6 merged (IP, MAC, hostname, interface, expiry, manufacturer via embedded OUI table).

**Behaviour:** always-on (replaces the landing page), no auth, live JS polling of JSON twins. Per-page kill switches `--web.ui-disable-config` / `--web.ui-disable-devices` (default off). `--web.ui-enabled` (default true) / `--web.ui-refresh-interval` (default 5s).

## Key architectural decisions (from design + adversarial review)

- **The console must never trigger a firewall scrape.** Gathering the live `collectorRegistry` runs every sub-collector's `Update()`. A new passive `internal/metricsnap.Recorder` captures metric families from the **real** scrape paths (both `/metrics` and the OTLP bridge); the UI reads the last-scrape snapshot. Zero extra scrape load.
- New in-memory `collector.StatusTracker` (updated in `execute()`) retains per-collector run history for the status table.
- `Collector.RunCollector` runs one collector out-of-band via a `WithContext` clone (scrape-safe); Run Now has a per-collector in-flight guard.
- The `/` mount keeps the existing `MetricsPath != "/"` guard (else `ServeMux` double-registers `/`).

Full design + implementation plan live in the repo's gitignored `docs/superpowers/` (not committed).

- [ ] `internal/options`: `--web.ui-*` flags + redacted `EffectiveConfig` (secrets presence-only), TDD
- [ ] `internal/webui`: status page + `/api/status.json` (passive, no `Gather()`), TDD
- [ ] Cardinality suite (hub, all-metrics, all-labels, label-values, growth, export), TDD
- [ ] `/config` redacted page + kill switch; a test proves no secret leaks
- [ ] `/devices` page + embedded OUI lookup; ARP-only expiry / v6-no-hostname handled
- [ ] Run Now endpoint (405/404/409/200) + live-polling/filter/sort `app.js`
- [ ] Wired into `main.go`; `/` guard preserved; `--web.ui-enabled=false` falls back to the stock landing
- [ ] `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./...`, `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint run ./...` all green
- [ ] `make docs` run (new flags enter the flag tables); `make docs-check` green; short console docs page added
- [ ] Manual smoke: all four pages render, Run Now works, live polling updates, `/config` leaks nothing, opening the UI does not bump `exporter_scrapes_total`

body:
## Summary

`drop-self-traffic` over the syslog transport matches only the **first** bound syslog listen port. `syslogProcessor.Process` (`internal/logship/zenarmor/syslog.go`) passes `ports[0]` into `docProcessor.process`, and `ports` is built in the syslog `newSource` in UDP→TCP→TLS order.

## Impact

If more than one syslog listener is enabled (say UDP and TCP) and Zenarmor streams to a **non-first** one, the box→exporter self-traffic connection Zenarmor reports won't match `ports[0]`, so `drop-self-traffic` silently won't drop it. **No data loss** — the self-record just ships instead of being dropped, adding a little noise (the same artefact-of-measuring record the filter exists to remove). Single-listener setups (the common case) are unaffected.

## Fix sketch

`Process` already receives the full `ports []int`. Teach `isSelfTraffic` (`internal/logship/zenarmor/self.go`) to match the record's dst port against **any** bound port, or thread all ports through and test each. Small, self-contained.

Surfaced by the final review of #298. Minor; no rush.
title: fix(zenarmor): self-traffic over syslog only matches the first bound listen port

body:
## Mission

Let the Zenarmor receiver ingest reporting data over **syslog** (a Zenarmor business-tier transport) through the shared syslog receiver, at full feature parity with the existing Elasticsearch mirror path.

Proven from a live capture (2026-07-18, prod box → local listener, 33,743 records, both UDP and TCP). Wire format is one syslog line per record:

```
<PRI>TIMESTAMP HOSTNAME zenarmor[PID]: daemon=zenarmor, index=<family>, data=<JSON>
```

The `data=` JSON is the **same schema** as the ES mirror, so the existing `zenDoc` decoder, `index→family` map, enrichment and exclude logic are all reusable. Five families seen, blocks in each: `conn` (17810), `dns` (5655), `http` (3818), `tls` (3383), `alert` (3073).

## Decisions already made (do not re-litigate)

- **Full parity** — `--logs.zenarmor.families`, `exclude`, `enrich`, `drop-self-traffic` all apply over syslog too. Achieved by extracting the ES receiver's per-record core (`handleDoc`) into a shared `docProcessor` that both transports drive.
- **Transport selector** — one `--logs.zenarmor.transport=elasticsearch|syslog` flag (default `elasticsearch`, no breaking change). Only one transport ingests at a time, so **double-shipping is structurally impossible** — no runtime conflict-check needed; `transport=syslog` is a startup-validated requirement for `--logs.syslog.enabled`.
- **Bridge shape** — the syslog receiver gains an optional `ProgramProcessor` delegation hook; `zenarmor` imports `syslog` (never the reverse) and registers the processor when `transport=syslog`. It runs no independent listener.
- **Records stay `source="zenarmor"`** regardless of transport, so dashboards/alerts are transport-agnostic. The syslog copy does not go through the generic syslog derive/sample path.

## Prerequisite

- [ ] #297 — fix the `alertinfo` decode bug (arrays/number/string sid). On the critical path: `alert` is 100% of blocked records and currently ships raw. Fixes the ES path too.

## Phases

- [ ] **Extract shared `docProcessor`** from `zenarmor.handleDoc` — pure refactor, ES behaviour unchanged (existing tests are the guard).
- [ ] **Parse the syslog envelope** (`daemon=zenarmor, index=, data=`) — pure function, tested against real captured lines (data JSON must not be tokenised).
- [ ] **`ProgramProcessor` hook** in the syslog receiver — interface + `RegisterProgramProcessor` + `source.handle` delegation read lazily at `Run()`.
- [ ] **Syslog→zenarmor adapter + factory branch** — `transport=syslog` builds the processor, registers it, returns no push source; self-traffic matched on the syslog listen port.
- [ ] **`--logs.zenarmor.transport` flag** (`elasticsearch` default) + validation; ES-only checks (listen-http, es-TLS) gated to the ES transport.
- [ ] **Cross-validation + main wiring** — `transport=syslog` requires `--logs.syslog.enabled`; enrichment refresh covered by `LogsZenarmorEnrichWanted()`.
- [ ] **Docs** — transport section in `docs/zenarmor-receiver.md` (house register); `make docs`.
- [ ] **Dashboard + full gate + end-to-end smoke** against the real capture (no new metrics ⇒ coverage gate should pass; verify).

## Notes / open verification

- Receiver-vocabulary test stays valid: the ES-only reject reasons (`peer`/`auth`/`unhandled_endpoint`/`body`) remain compiled call-sites in `server.go`, so the closed vocab is unchanged under `transport=syslog`.
- Confirm `self_traffic` actually fires over syslog (the box→exporter:syslog-port flow Zenarmor reports, the analogue of the ES `_bulk` link) — keep the filter regardless; note the finding in docs.
- Implementation plan (scratch, gitignored): `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-18-zenarmor-syslog-transport.md`.

comments.body:
Shipped — all phases complete, pushed to `main` (10 commits, `9b2a0fb..cf5f150`), full gate green (`go test ./...`, `-race` on logship, `golangci-lint`, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`), and a final whole-branch review (opus) returned READY TO MERGE with no Critical/Important findings.

**Commits**
- `9b2a0fb` fix(zenarmor): decode alertinfo arrays/number/string sid (also closes #297 — the ES path was dropping every alert)
- `6e8e988` refactor(zenarmor): extract shared docProcessor from handleDoc
- `f2e1fba` feat(zenarmor): parse the daemon=zenarmor syslog envelope
- `4d27493` feat(syslog): add optional ProgramProcessor delegation hook
- `cf87f79` feat(options): add --logs.zenarmor.transport selector (elasticsearch|syslog)
- `142575f` feat(zenarmor): drive the shared processor from the syslog receiver
- `f6610a5` feat(options): require the syslog receiver for transport=syslog
- `47c4476` feat(logship): per-record Record.Source override (transport-agnostic source label)
- `410b0f0` docs(zenarmor): transport section
- `20ca1b7` + `cf5f150` test: end-to-end across all five families + factory-branch coverage

**How it works**
`--logs.zenarmor.transport=elasticsearch|syslog` (default elasticsearch — no behaviour change). `transport=syslog` rides the shared syslog receiver via a `ProgramProcessor` delegation hook (no second listener) and requires `--logs.syslog.enabled`. Both transports run through one shared `docProcessor`, so families/exclude/enrich/drop-self-traffic and the derived counters are identical, and records ship `source="zenarmor"` in Loki regardless of transport (via the new per-record source override). Only one transport ingests at a time, so double-shipping is impossible by construction.

**Scope change during the build:** the "records stay source=zenarmor regardless of transport" promise wasn't free — the syslog receiver names its records `source="syslog"` — so it needed the `Record.Source` override in `47c4476`. Chosen deliberately (true parity) over accepting `source=syslog`+`subsystem=<family>`.

**Deferred as follow-ups (both Minor, neither blocks):**
- self-traffic over syslog matches only the first bound listen port (`ports[0]`); a multi-listener box streaming to a non-first port silently won't drop self-traffic — no data loss, records just ship. Would need an `isSelfTraffic` multi-port check.
- `programProcessor` is a package global with panic-on-dup; the pipeline isn't safely re-buildable in one process (production builds once, so inert today).

Verified against the live capture: five families (conn/dns/tls/http/alert), blocks in each, both UDP and TCP framing.

body:
## Summary

The `zenAlertInfo` struct in `internal/logship/zenarmor/parse.go` is typed against a shape OPNsense/Zenarmor never sends. All four fields mismatch the real payload, so `json.Unmarshal` fails the entire `alert` document and every alert record ships as a raw body with a counted ParseError. This affects the **Elasticsearch receiver path today**, independent of the in-flight syslog work.

## Evidence

Live capture 2026-07-18 from the prod box (`<lan-ip-2>`). Real `alertinfo`:

```json
"alertinfo": {
  "match": { "dst_hostname": "239.255.255.250" },
  "action": "reject",
  "category": ["Application Category"],
  "signature": ["Network Management"],
  "severity": 0,
  "sid": "appcategories.689585a5-37ba-41f9-86e4-160e8a0de793",
  "gid": 0,
  "rev": 0
}
```

Current struct vs reality:

| field | struct type | real type |
|-------|-------------|-----------|
| `category` | `string` | array of strings |
| `signature` | `string` | array of strings |
| `severity` | `string` | number |
| `sid` | `int` | string |

Any one mismatch fails the whole-document unmarshal.

## Impact

`alert` was 100% of blocked records in the capture (3073/3073 `is_blocked=1`). Every one currently ships without its structured `alertinfo.*` attributes — the block reason, category and signature are all lost to Loki, and `logs_parse_errors_total{stage="document"}` is inflated. This looks like another source-derived phantom shape that passed CI without ever meeting a real payload (cf #284).

## Fix

- Add flex decoders: string-or-array → joined string; string-or-number → string.
- Retype `zenAlertInfo` (`category`/`signature` flex-strings, `severity`/`sid` flex-scalar); add `alertinfo.action`.
- Correct the phantom-shape fixtures/assertions in `parse_test.go` / `fixtures_test.go` to the real shape above.
- `make schemas` (goldens stay structure-only).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A decode test using the verbatim captured `alertinfo` passes (`parsed=true`, all `alertinfo.*` attributes populated).
- [ ] `alertinfo.sid` carries the string id; `alertinfo.severity` carries the numeric value as text.
- [ ] Fixtures no longer encode the string/int phantom shape.
- [ ] `make test` + `make schemas` green; schema diff is structure-only.
title: fix(zenarmor): alertinfo decode fails on real payload shape — every alert ships as raw body

comments.body:
## Triage — both findings box-state, no code change

Verified against upstream source and the live testbed (2026-07-18). Neither is drift.

### `ipsecSad` — `rows[].reqid` / `state` / `addtime_diff` / `addtime_hard` / `addtime_soft`

**Verdict: box-state.** The testbed IPsec tunnel was down at probe time, so `api/ipsec/sad/search` returned the synthetic `No SAD entries.` placeholder row — `{"src":"No","dst":"SAD","satype":null,"spi":null,"nat":"ntries"}` — which carries none of the real-SA fields. `list_sad.py` emits `reqid`/`state` only when setkey prints them as `key=value`, and `addtime_*` only from the `created`/`diff` lines, so an empty SAD legitimately omits all five. `FetchIPsecSAD` already discards the placeholder (null `spi`/`satype`), so there was never a metric impact — this was purely a canary-shape artefact of an empty SAD.

Root cause: the traffic-gen LXC (the tunnel initiator) had lost its `<lan-ip-56>` TESTLAN address — Kea stopped leasing on that segment — so IKE could not source from `<lan-ip-56>` and no kernel SA existed.

**Fixed at source rather than exempted** (these fields back exported metrics — an exemption would blind the canary to real drift on them). Pinned the initiator's `eth0` to its reserved static `<lan-ip-56>/24` and re-initiated the child. `api/ipsec/sad/search` now returns two real `esp`/`mature` SA rows carrying `reqid=1`, `state=mature`, `addtime_diff/hard/soft`, and the tunnel is stable (DPD `restart`, `start_action=start`), so the daily canary will validate these fields going forward.

### `unboundInfra` — `data`

**Verdict: box-state (transient).** `data` is the infra cache; the resolver's cache was momentarily empty at probe time and the key was absent. Re-checked live minutes later — `data` carries two hosts (`<lan-ip-2>`, `<pub-ip-4>1`) with the RTT/RTO fields the collector reads. The traffic-gen drives per-minute lookups, so the cache stays warm; not exempted (masking the whole payload would blind the endpoint), and the next run clears on its own.

### `siproxdRegistrations` (plugin-gated absent)

Expected — siproxd is not installed. Not drift.

No repo change. Closing.

body:
## Problem

The repository does not run the Go race detector in CI, and the full race-enabled test suite cannot currently be added as a clean gate because `TestEnrichMessageAllocations` asserts zero allocations under instrumentation that itself adds allocations.

On the audited tree, `go test -race ./...` fails only that allocation assertion. Running the same race suite while excluding `TestEnrichMessageAllocations` passes across all packages. The production code is therefore not known to have a race from this run, but the project has no repeatable gate that will keep it that way.

## Evidence

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:41-42` runs `go test -v ./...` without `-race`.
- `internal/logship/syslog/enrichgeneric_bench_test.go:93-109` requires `testing.AllocsPerRun(...) == 0` in a normal unit test.
- Fresh audit results:
  - `go test -race ./...` fails `TestEnrichMessageAllocations` because race instrumentation adds allocations.
  - `go test -race ./... -skip '^TestEnrichMessageAllocations$'` passes all packages.

The zero-allocation invariant is valuable and should remain enforced in normal CI. The issue is that a performance assertion and a concurrency-safety gate currently cannot coexist in the same invocation.

## Suggested direction

Keep the allocation assertion in the normal test job and exclude it only from race builds, for example with a race build constraint and a small non-race test file. Add a dedicated race job that runs the complete applicable suite without a hand-maintained command-line skip.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Normal `go test ./...` still runs `TestEnrichMessageAllocations` and enforces the zero-allocation invariant.
- [ ] `go test -race ./...` passes without a command-line `-skip` exception.
- [ ] CI contains a race-detector job covering all applicable Go packages.
- [ ] The exclusion mechanism is local to the allocation test and documented, so new tests are included in race coverage automatically.
- [ ] The race job has an appropriate timeout and caching strategy without weakening failures or using `continue-on-error`.
- [ ] The release checklist treats a race failure as a blocking failure.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17.

A dedicated `race` job runs `go test -race -timeout 15m ./...` (no `continue-on-error`) and is wired into `ci-success` as a blocking gate.

body:
## Problem

A default scrape launches every selected sub-collector in its own goroutine. The generated catalogue currently contains 61 collectors, and several collector `Fetch` implementations perform additional concurrent sub-endpoint requests.

The shared HTTP transport sets `MaxIdleConnsPerHost`, which controls only how many completed connections can remain available for reuse. It does not cap active requests or active connections. There is no exporter-level semaphore limiting concurrent OPNsense API work.

This is not yet a confirmed live failure: the audit did not benchmark a real low-end firewall under a default scrape. It is an architectural risk that should be measured and bounded before increasing the major version's feature surface further.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/collector.go:1334-1345` starts one goroutine for every selected collector and waits for all of them.
- `opnsense/client.go:410` sets `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` but not `MaxConnsPerHost` or an equivalent request semaphore.
- Multiple API client methods use `runConcurrentFetches`, creating nested fan-out inside the top-level collector fan-out.
- `make docs-check` reports 61 collectors in the current default catalogue.

## Failure scenario / impact

Prometheus scrapes a low-power or busy OPNsense appliance. The exporter emits a burst of dozens of simultaneous PHP/configd API calls, with some collectors adding nested calls. The appliance spends significant CPU/memory on monitoring traffic, API latency increases, requests hit scrape deadlines, and the next scrape can overlap before the previous load has fully cleared. The exporter can become a source of instability for the firewall it is meant to observe.

## Suggested direction

Measure peak in-flight requests and end-to-end scrape duration against representative OPNsense hardware, then introduce an explicit per-instance concurrency budget. An API-call semaphore is likely easier to reason about than relying only on transport connection settings, especially with nested fan-out and HTTP/2.

Choose a default from measurements, allow an operator override if justified, and preserve prompt context cancellation while requests wait for capacity.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A deterministic test server records peak concurrent OPNsense API requests during a default/all-collector scrape.
- [ ] The exporter enforces a documented maximum number of in-flight upstream requests, including nested `runConcurrentFetches` calls.
- [ ] Requests waiting for capacity respect scrape cancellation/deadlines and cannot deadlock nested collectors.
- [ ] Benchmarks compare representative limits and record both peak concurrency and total scrape duration.
- [ ] The selected default is validated against at least one representative low-resource OPNsense deployment, or the absence of live validation is explicitly recorded before merge.
- [ ] If configurable, the flag/env documentation explains the load-versus-latency trade-off and rejects invalid values.
- [ ] Existing collector correctness and scrape-deadline tests remain green.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17.

comments.body: Fixed in 8847e3f. Added a shared per-client semaphore around every request round-trip (bounds nested `runConcurrentFetches` too), configured by `--opnsense.max-concurrent-requests` (default **16**, must be ≥ 1). A slot is held for one round-trip and released before retry backoff, so no goroutine holds a slot while waiting for another — nested fan-out cannot deadlock — and a waiting acquire respects scrape cancellation. A deterministic test records peak concurrency across limits 1/4/16 and proves the cap holds. **No low-end-hardware benchmark was run**; 16 keeps scrape latency low on capable boxes while giving small deployments an opt-down.

body:
## Problem

The maintained Kubernetes manifest and the inline manifest in the deployment guide both hard-code `ghcr.io/rknightion/opnsense-exporter:v1.0.1`. The repository's current release is 2.2.1, and a new major release would make the copy-paste example older still.

#147 correctly replaced mutable `:latest` with an immutable release tag, but the selected tag became a second version source with no release automation. The comments tell operators to substitute their deployed version, yet a copied manifest is valid as written and silently deploys the old v1 release.

## Evidence

- `deploy/k8s/deployment.yaml:21-24` recommends an immutable tag but sets it to `v1.0.1`.
- `docs/deployment/kubernetes.md:60-64` repeats the same hard-coded version.
- `version.txt` currently contains `2.2.1`.
- The release process updates `version.txt` and release artifacts, but neither Kubernetes example is derived from that version or checked for drift.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator copies the maintained manifest from the current branch or documentation and deploys it without noticing the substitution comment. They receive an obsolete exporter lacking current collectors, security fixes, flags, and dashboard compatibility. The manifest appears intentionally pinned and current, so the version skew is easy to miss.

## Suggested direction

Keep immutable pinning, but remove the silently stale hard-coded example. Options include release automation that updates the tag from `version.txt`, generating the published manifest per release, or using an unmistakable placeholder that must be substituted before `kubectl apply`.

Whichever approach is chosen, establish one source of truth and make CI fail when maintained deployment artifacts drift from it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Neither maintained Kubernetes example silently defaults to `v1.0.1`.
- [ ] The image remains pinned to an immutable release tag or digest; this must not regress to mutable `:latest`.
- [ ] The manifest and documentation share one version source or are checked against each other automatically.
- [ ] A release-version change updates the published Kubernetes example automatically or causes CI to fail with an actionable message.
- [ ] The approach is compatible with release-please and does not require hand-editing the same version in multiple files.
- [ ] The hardened fields added by #147 remain unchanged.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17. Follow-up to #147.

comments.body: Fixed in 6e70c1f. Both the maintained manifest and the guide keep an immutable pin (never `:latest`) but now carry an inline `x-release-please-version` marker and are listed as `generic` `extra-files` in `release-please-config.json`, so every release rewrites the tag from `version.txt` — one source of truth, no hand-editing. Set to the current `2.2.1` (image tags carry no leading `v`, matching the published tags). The #147 hardened fields are untouched.

body:
## Problem

The security guide's recommended Docker configuration for a self-signed/private OPNsense CA does not work with the official container image.

`docs/security.md` tells users to mount one certificate at `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/opnsense-ca.crt`. The official runtime image is distroless, so it has no `update-ca-certificates` command and does not automatically merge files from that directory into Go's trust roots. Merely mounting the file there leaves the certificate untrusted.

The Docker deployment guide already contains the correct approach: mount the CA bundle at an arbitrary path and set `SSL_CERT_FILE` to that path. The two maintained guides therefore contradict each other on a security-sensitive setup.

## Evidence

- `docs/security.md:60-71` recommends mounting only `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates/opnsense-ca.crt`.
- `docs/deployment/docker.md:178-188` documents that the official runtime is distroless and has no `update-ca-certificates`.
- `docs/deployment/docker.md:184-201` correctly sets `SSL_CERT_FILE` to the mounted CA bundle.
- `opnsense/client.go:366-405` uses Go's system certificate pool unless `--opnsense.insecure` is selected; it does not read `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates` itself.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator follows the security guide exactly and the exporter still fails TLS verification against OPNsense. Because the next documented option on that page is `--opnsense.insecure`, the broken recommended path creates pressure to disable certificate verification entirely, exposing API credentials and monitoring data to interception.

## Suggested direction

Replace the security guide's Docker snippet with the verified `SSL_CERT_FILE` configuration from the Docker guide and link to the detailed deployment section. Keep host-level trust-store instructions distinct from distroless-container instructions.

A dedicated `--opnsense.tls-ca-file` option may improve usability later, but correcting the unsafe documentation does not need to depend on that feature.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/security.md` no longer claims that mounting a certificate under `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates` is sufficient in the official image.
- [ ] The security guide shows `SSL_CERT_FILE` and a mounted CA bundle, consistent with `docs/deployment/docker.md`.
- [ ] Host installation and container installation instructions are clearly distinguished.
- [ ] The documented container configuration is verified against the official distroless image using a test CA/server or an equivalent automated TLS test.
- [ ] `--opnsense.insecure` remains explicitly discouraged outside testing.
- [ ] A docs check or link/reference test prevents the two CA recipes from drifting apart again.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17.

comments.body: Fixed in ea9b864. `docs/security.md` now separates the **host** recipe (`cp` + `update-ca-certificates`, explicitly host-only) from the **distroless container** recipe (`SSL_CERT_FILE` + a mounted bundle, matching `docs/deployment/docker.md`) and links to the canonical Docker section; `--opnsense.insecure` stays discouraged. A new `scripts/docgen` guard test fails if either guide drops `SSL_CERT_FILE` or if the broken `/usr/local/share/ca-certificates` bind mount reappears, so the two recipes cannot drift.

body:
## Problem

The validation added by #108 prevents empty and non-slash-prefixed telemetry paths, but still accepts paths reserved by the exporter itself. Setting `--web.telemetry-path=/-/healthy` or `--web.telemetry-path=/-/ready` registers the metrics handler under that pattern and then registers the fixed health/readiness handler under the same pattern.

`net/http.ServeMux` treats duplicate patterns as a programmer error and panics. A syntactically valid configuration therefore produces a raw startup panic and crash loop instead of the normal configuration-error path.

## Evidence

- `internal/options/exporter.go:55-66` validates only non-empty and leading `/`.
- `main.go:694` registers the configured metrics path on the default mux.
- `main.go:696-697` subsequently registers the fixed `/-/healthy` and `/-/ready` routes.

Reproduced against the audited tree with:

```text
go run . --opnsense.protocol=http --opnsense.address=127.0.0.1 \
  --opnsense.api-key=audit-key --opnsense.api-secret=audit-secret \
  --web.telemetry-path=/-/healthy --web.listen-address=127.0.0.1:0
```

The process panics from `net/http.(*ServeMux).register` when `main.go` registers `/-/healthy` the second time and exits with status 2.

## Failure scenario / impact

A Helm value, environment variable, or operator configuration reuses a conventional health path for metrics. The exporter immediately crash-loops with a Go stack trace rather than logging which flag conflicts. This is a narrow configuration trigger, but it is deterministic and prevents the process from starting.

## Suggested direction

Reject `/-/healthy` and `/-/ready` as reserved telemetry paths during configuration validation. Prefer constructing and validating all handlers on a private `http.ServeMux` rather than the package-global mux, so future fixed routes cannot introduce another unvalidated collision.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--web.telemetry-path=/-/healthy` exits through the normal logged configuration-error path and does not panic.
- [ ] `--web.telemetry-path=/-/ready` behaves the same way.
- [ ] Unit tests cover both reserved paths alongside the empty and non-slash-prefixed cases from #108.
- [ ] The default `/metrics`, a custom path such as `/prometheus`, and the existing `/` behavior remain valid.
- [ ] Route registration uses a private mux or another mechanism that makes all exporter-owned path conflicts explicit and testable.
- [ ] `go test ./...` and `make lint` pass.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17. Follow-up to #108.

comments.body: Fixed in f3a96b1. `ValidateMetricsPath` now also rejects reserved paths (`server.HealthyPath`/`ReadyPath`, one source of truth, no options→server import), so `--web.telemetry-path=/-/healthy` or `/-/ready` exits via the normal logged config-error path instead of panicking on a duplicate `ServeMux` pattern. Registration also moved off `http.DefaultServeMux` onto a private mux. Unit tests cover both reserved paths alongside the empty/non-slash cases and confirm `/metrics`, `/prometheus`, and `/` stay valid.

body:
## Problem

The log-shipping pipeline reports records as shipped when they have only been handed to the OpenTelemetry SDK's asynchronous batch queue. That queue can drop records silently, and export failures happen after the call that the pipeline treats as success.

`otlpSink.Emit` calls `Logger.Emit`, which has no error result, and then returns `nil`. The pipeline consequently increments `opnsense_exporter_logs_shipped_total` for every record in the batch. The sink itself acknowledges in a comment that the SDK batch queue drops silently.

The problem is amplified by resource partitioning: up to 64 resource keys each receive a separate `LoggerProvider` and `BatchProcessor`, so the pipeline's one counted bounded queue feeds multiple additional uncounted queues.

Stateful source cursors are periodically persisted while those records may still be queued, and final cursors are persisted before `sink.Shutdown` confirms the providers were flushed. A queue overflow, extended exporter outage, shutdown timeout, or restart can therefore produce permanent loss while the self-metrics and documentation imply successful or at-least-once delivery.

## Evidence

- `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go:38-41` explicitly notes that the SDK batch queue drops silently.
- `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go:158-160` calls `lg.Emit(ctx, r)` and returns `nil` because delivery cannot be observed there.
- `internal/logship/sink_otlp.go:215-225` creates a separate SDK batch processor for every resource key, up to `maxLogResources = 64`.
- `internal/logship/pipeline.go:245-254` increments `logs_shipped_total` whenever the sink's synchronous `Emit` returns nil.
- `internal/logship/pipeline.go:274-282` persists final cursors before calling `sink.Shutdown`.
- `docs/log-shipping.md:296-307` promises at-least-once delivery within a run.
- `docs/log-shipping.md:328-334` describes records handed to the sink and cursor lag as shipped.

## Failure scenario / impact

Grafana Cloud or another OTLP endpoint becomes unavailable while sources continue producing logs. The pipeline's counted queue drains successfully into SDK queues, so `logs_shipped_total` continues rising and `logs_ship_errors_total` need not change. When the SDK queues fill, records are silently dropped. Cursors continue to advance and are persisted. After connectivity returns or the exporter restarts, those records are neither retried nor reported as lost.

An operator looking at exporter self-metrics sees apparent successful shipping during the data-loss window.

## Suggested direction

First decide and document the delivery contract. If the intended contract is at-least-once, cursor advancement and persistence need to be tied to an observable export acknowledgement, with a bounded retry/spool strategy. If the intended contract is best-effort, the metrics and documentation must say that plainly and all queue/export drops must be observable.

Avoid the current double-buffering arrangement, or use a processor/export path with observable enqueue rejection and export failures. Distinguish records accepted for delivery from records confirmed exported instead of calling both "shipped".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A deterministic test fills or blocks the downstream OTLP path and proves that every dropped record is observable through a counter and/or returned error.
- [ ] `logs_shipped_total` counts only the delivery stage its help text and documentation claim; if it means enqueue acceptance, it is renamed or documented accordingly.
- [ ] Asynchronous exporter failures are surfaced through exporter self-observability rather than only internal SDK handling.
- [ ] Cursor persistence semantics match the chosen delivery guarantee; an unacknowledged record is not permanently skipped when at-least-once is promised.
- [ ] Shutdown failure/timeout cannot be reported as a clean flush while cursors claim the buffered records were delivered.
- [ ] The effect of one batch processor per resource key is removed, bounded with observable accounting, or explicitly justified and tested under endpoint outage.
- [ ] `docs/log-shipping.md`, metric help text, and tests all describe the same delivery semantics.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17. Related foundation: #228.

comments.body: Fixed in 736289b. Delivery contract: **in-memory at-least-once**. The per-resource-key async `BatchProcessor` is replaced by a synchronous processor whose `Export` error propagates back through `Emit`; the emitter retries a failed batch in memory until acknowledged, so a transient outage is ridden out. Loss now happens only via counted queue overflow or a shutdown-abandoned batch (`logs_dropped_total{reason="ship_failed"}`). `logs_shipped_total` means confirmed export; shutdown drain is context-bounded and returns an error rather than faking a clean flush. Does not survive a process restart mid-outage — documented tier boundary. Docs, help text and tests updated.

body:
## Problem

The optional Zenarmor receiver configures only `ReadHeaderTimeout` on its `http.Server`. There is no deadline covering request-body reads, no idle timeout, and no connection-level bound.

`ReadHeaderTimeout` stops a client from trickling the headers, but it stops applying once the headers are complete. The bulk handler then reads the request body synchronously. A client can therefore send valid headers and trickle the body indefinitely, retaining a connection and goroutine for as long as it keeps making progress.

The feature is opt-in, but once enabled its default listener is `:9200`; the default peer allowlist is empty and authentication is optional. Network policy may mitigate the risk, but the receiver itself currently has no bound.

## Evidence

- `internal/logship/zenarmor/source.go:149-153` constructs `http.Server` with `Handler`, `TLSConfig`, and `ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second` only.
- `internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go:326-337` reads the full request body before handling the bulk payload.
- `internal/options/logs_zenarmor.go:34-46` documents the all-interface listener and accept-any-peer defaults once the receiver is enabled.

This is a standard HTTP slow-body resource-exhaustion path and is independently testable with a local TCP client; no live OPNsense box is required.

## Failure scenario / impact

One or more reachable clients open connections, send complete HTTP headers, and then send request-body bytes slowly enough to avoid disconnecting. Each connection occupies server resources indefinitely. With enough connections the exporter exhausts file descriptors, memory, or goroutine capacity, preventing legitimate Zenarmor batches and potentially affecting the metrics HTTP server in the same process.

## Suggested direction

Give complete requests a bounded lifetime, not just their headers. This could be an `http.Server.ReadTimeout`, a per-request body deadline derived from configuration, or another explicit deadline that covers decompression and parsing. Add an `IdleTimeout`, and consider a bounded connection listener if timeouts alone do not provide an acceptable upper bound.

Choose defaults large enough for the documented 64 MiB maximum bulk request on the slowest supported deployment, and document the trade-off if the values are configurable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A client that completes headers but stalls or trickles the request body is disconnected within a documented upper bound.
- [ ] Idle keep-alive connections are also bounded.
- [ ] Normal Zenarmor bulk requests, including realistically large requests, complete under the default limits.
- [ ] A regression test uses a slow or stalled client and proves the handler does not remain blocked indefinitely.
- [ ] Shutdown still drains legitimate in-flight requests within its existing bounded shutdown context.
- [ ] The receiver documentation identifies the timeout behaviour and continues to recommend an allowlist and/or authentication on shared networks.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17. Related receiver feature: #276.

comments.body: Fixed in 1605294 (same change as #288). The Zenarmor `http.Server` now sets `ReadTimeout: 120s` (covers the whole request body + gzip decode, generous enough for the 64 MiB ceiling on a ~0.5 MB/s link) and `IdleTimeout: 120s`, so a slowloris body-trickle can no longer pin a goroutine after headers land. Graceful shutdown drain is unchanged.

body:
## Problem

The optional Zenarmor HTTP receiver caps the number of compressed bytes it reads, but does not cap the number of bytes produced by gzip decompression. `readBody` wraps `r.Body` with `http.MaxBytesReader(..., maxBodyBytes)`, creates a `gzip.Reader`, and then calls `io.ReadAll` on the decompressed stream.

`maxBodyBytes` is 64 MiB. That limits the wire payload, not its expansion. A much smaller highly-compressible request can expand to many gigabytes and drive the exporter into memory exhaustion before `io.ReadAll` returns.

The feature is opt-in, but once enabled its default listener is `:9200`; the default peer allowlist is empty and authentication is optional. Anything that can reach that port can exercise this path unless the operator has added network or application-level restrictions.

## Evidence

- `internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go:52-55` — `maxBodyBytes = 64 << 20`.
- `internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go:327` — `http.MaxBytesReader` is applied to the compressed request body.
- `internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go:329-337` — the gzip reader is passed directly to unbounded `io.ReadAll`.
- `internal/options/logs_zenarmor.go:34-46` — the enabled receiver defaults to `:9200`, accepts any peer when the allowlist is empty, and does not require authentication.

This is a code-path finding; it does not require a live OPNsense box. A regression test can reproduce it using a small gzip stream whose decompressed output exceeds the configured body ceiling.

## Failure scenario / impact

An unauthenticated client sends a small gzip-compressed request containing highly repetitive data. The request stays under the 64 MiB compressed-input limit, but decompression continues without a ceiling. The exporter allocates until the body finishes or the process/container is killed for exceeding its memory limit. Metrics and log ingestion from that exporter stop, and a restart loop remains exploitable while the receiver is reachable.

## Suggested direction

Apply a second limit to the reader after content decoding. Read at most `maxBodyBytes + 1` decompressed bytes, reject the request when the extra byte is present, and avoid retaining an oversized buffer. Keep the compressed-input limit as a separate defence.

It may be useful to name the two limits independently if realistic compressed and decompressed bulk sizes need different ceilings, but that is an implementation choice rather than a requirement.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A gzip request whose decompressed body is at or below the configured ceiling is accepted and parsed normally.
- [ ] A small gzip request whose decompressed body exceeds the ceiling is rejected with a stable non-2xx response without allocating the complete expanded body.
- [ ] An uncompressed body over the existing ceiling remains rejected.
- [ ] A truncated or invalid gzip stream remains an error and is never parsed as raw NDJSON.
- [ ] A regression test covers a high-compression-ratio payload and demonstrates that the decompressed limit, rather than only the wire-size limit, is enforced.
- [ ] The rejection is observable through an existing or new bounded-vocabulary receiver metric/log signal.

Found during the pre-major-version codebase audit on 2026-07-17. Related receiver feature: #276.

comments.body: Fixed in 1605294. \`readBody\` now caps the **decompressed** gzip stream via \`io.LimitReader(maxBodyBytes+1)\` and rejects an over-ceiling body through the existing 400 + \`reject("body")\` path without ever fully buffering it. Regression tests cover a zip bomb (compressed body under the wire limit, decompressed over it), an under-ceiling gzip that still parses, an oversized uncompressed body, and a truncated stream that stays an error.

body:
## Summary

#250 shipped universal IP/interface enrichment and listed seven acceptance criteria. Six landed. The seventh never did and nothing recorded why:

> - [ ] Benchmark: enrichment stays on the receiver goroutine's nanosecond budget

There is no `func Benchmark` anywhere in `internal/logship` (`rg "func Benchmark" internal/logship/` → zero hits). The closing commit `310dd28` does not mention it, the issue has no comments, and the parent tracker #261 ticks #250 as fully done. So it was silently dropped rather than deliberately descoped.

Found by an audit of every issue closed in the last six weeks, checking each against the code rather than its closing comment.

## Why it is worth doing rather than just un-ticking the box

The budget is not a nice-to-have — it is the design constraint the whole path rests on. `enrichMessage` runs **on the receiver goroutine**, synchronously, before the record reaches the queue. `Deps.Miss` is documented in `internal/logship/source.go:84-88` as MUST NOT block and MUST NOT do I/O for exactly this reason: a slow enrichment path stalls the socket read loop and **silently drops datagrams**. UDP syslog gives no backpressure signal, so the failure mode is invisible — no error, no counter, just missing lines.

<host-1> is a live example of the load this sits under: ~5M lines/day across the receiver.

The path already carries deliberate bounds that a benchmark would guard (`internal/logship/syslog/enrichgeneric.go:23-30`):

- `maxEnrichedIPs = 3` — bounds addresses resolved per line
- `maxEnrichedDevices = 2` — bounds interface-name resolution per line

and a regex (`ipRe`) that runs against **every** non-filterlog line. A regression there — a wider pattern, an unbounded scan, a lookup that starts allocating — is precisely what silently eats the budget, and nothing currently detects it.

## Scope

- Add `BenchmarkEnrichMessage` (or similar) in `internal/logship/syslog`, covering the realistic shapes: a line with no IP, a line with one IP, and a pathological line the caps exist for (a traceroute / routing-table dump with many addresses).
- Benchmark against a warm `enrich.Snapshot` — a cold cache misses every lookup and would measure the wrong thing.
- Assert nothing about wall-clock in CI (machine-dependent, flaky). The value is the committed baseline + `benchstat`-able number, not a gate. If a gate is wanted later, `testing.AllocsPerRun` on the no-IP path is the stable thing to pin, since zero-allocation on the common path is the property that actually protects the goroutine.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `go test -bench=. ./internal/logship/syslog/` reports a benchmark for the enrichment path
- [ ] Cases cover: no IP, one resolvable IP, and a many-address line that exercises `maxEnrichedIPs`
- [ ] Uses a populated snapshot, not a cold cache
- [ ] The measured baseline is recorded in the closing comment so a future regression has something to compare against
- [ ] #250's seventh checkbox is ticked, or explicitly closed out with a reason

Low priority — no user-visible bug is known. This closes a stated commitment and guards a path whose failure mode is silent.

## Summary

`logs_rejected_total{source="zenarmor", reason="unhandled_endpoint"}` read **60** on the live box after ~1 day. Zenarmor is calling an Elasticsearch route the receiver does not implement, and **there is no way to find out which one**, because the handler throws the evidence away.

`internal/logship/zenarmor/server.go`:

```go
// unhandled answers anything outside the observed endpoint set permissively, so a
// change in Zenarmor's client surface degrades into a counted signal rather than a
// silent outage. The counter is the point: logs_rejected_total{reason=
// "unhandled_endpoint"} is what tells an operator to come and look.
func (s *server) unhandled(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request, _ string) {
	s.m.reject("unhandled_endpoint")
	writeJSON(w, http.StatusOK, map[string]any{})
}
```

Both the request and the path are discarded. So the counter tells the operator to come and look, and when they come there is nothing to look at — confirmed on <host-1>: `docker logs opensense-exporter | grep -iE "unhandled|unknown endpoint|not found"` returns nothing at all.

The permissive `200 {}` is right and should stay: a receiver that 404s an unrecognised call could break Zenarmor's client. This is only about the diagnostics.

## Why it matters

The counter is doing exactly half its job. It proves something changed in Zenarmor's client surface but names nothing, so the next step is packet capture on a 4-6 GB/day stream — the expensive path this counter exists to avoid. 60 in a day is low-rate and steady rather than a flood, which is the shape of a periodic probe (a health check, a template/ILM/settings call) rather than a one-off.

Note the receiver's index bookkeeping is real: `PUT`/`HEAD`/`DELETE` on an index are handled and mutate `s.indices`, so an unhandled call is one **outside** that set — worth knowing which, since it may be something we should model rather than swallow.

## Change

Log the method and path, rate-limited, at WARN or INFO:

- The pipeline already has `logLimiter` (`internal/logship/pipeline.go`) for exactly this — rate-limiting repeated error logging so a flapping endpoint cannot flood the log. Reuse that pattern rather than logging all 60.
- Key the limiter on method+path so a new unhandled route is reported promptly even if another is already being suppressed.
- The receiver has no logger today (`server` holds `cfg`, `onBulk`, `m`); `Deps.Logger` is available at the factory, so it needs threading through `newServer`.

Optional, decide during implementation: a `path` label on the counter. **Recommend against** — the path contains index names (`zenarmor_0000000000_<uuid>_<family>_write`), so it is attacker-influenceable, wire-sourced cardinality, which #280 explicitly forbids pre-initialising or labelling by. A log line is the right surface for an unbounded value; the counter should stay `{source, reason}`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An unhandled endpoint logs its method and path at least once, rate-limited so a repeating caller cannot flood
- [ ] The response stays a permissive `200 {}` — Zenarmor's client must not break
- [ ] No wire-sourced value becomes a metric label
- [ ] A test asserts the log fires for an unhandled route and that repeats are suppressed
- [ ] `logs_rejected_total{reason="unhandled_endpoint"}` still counts every occurrence, suppressed or not

Found while auditing the <host-1> deployment (#279/#280 follow-up). Live evidence: 60 rejections, image `version=98b3166`, ~1 day uptime.

comments.body:
Done in bc800b0.

## What changed

`unhandled()` now logs the method and path it was called with, throttled per `method+path`:

```
level=WARN msg="zenarmor called an endpoint this receiver does not implement (answered 200 {}; repeats throttled)" method=PUT path=/_ilm/policy/zenarmor source=zenarmor
```

(that is real output, captured from `TestUnhandledEndpointLogsMethodAndPath`, not a mock-up)

Throttle is 15m per distinct `method+path`. The interval is long deliberately: the counter carries the **rate**, so the log only has to carry the **identity** — one line per route is enough to act on, and the shape observed on <host-1> (60/day, steady) is a periodic probe that would otherwise re-report a fact the operator already has.

Took the recommendation against a `path` label. The path is logged, never labelled.

## The one thing the issue did not cover

The issue says to key the limiter on method+path. Doing that literally is a bug: `logLimiter.last` is a `map[string]time.Time` with **no cap**, so keying it on a wire-sourced path lets a peer walking `/x-1`, `/x-2`, … grow it without bound. That is the same hazard #280 forbids for metric labels, merely relocated from a label into a map — and `--logs.zenarmor.allowed-peers` is optional (empty = allow all), so the allowlist cannot be relied on to close it.

The limiter was safe until now only because every key was code-defined and bounded (`"poll:"+name`, `"ship"`).

So rather than duplicate it into the receiver, `logLimiter` was **promoted to the exported, bounded `logship.LogLimiter`**:

- holds at most `maxKeys` keys, purging expired entries before refusing, so the cap bounds keys held **per interval** rather than silencing new keys for the life of the process
- zenarmor: `unhandledLogMaxKeys = 64` — generous next to Zenarmor's real surface (a handful of routes)
- pipeline: `errorLogMaxKeys = 64` — a backstop its bounded key set never reaches; behaviour there is unchanged

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] An unhandled endpoint logs its method and path at least once, rate-limited so a repeating caller cannot flood
- [x] The response stays a permissive `200 {}` — asserted by the pre-existing `TestUnhandledEndpointIsCountedNotFatal`
- [x] No wire-sourced value becomes a metric label — counter stays `{source, reason}`
- [x] A test asserts the log fires for an unhandled route and that repeats are suppressed
- [x] `logs_rejected_total{reason="unhandled_endpoint"}` still counts every occurrence, suppressed or not

## Tests

New, in `internal/logship/zenarmor/server_test.go`:

| test | pins |
| --- | --- |
| `TestUnhandledEndpointLogsMethodAndPath` | the route reaches the log at all |
| `TestUnhandledEndpointLogSuppressesRepeatsButCountsEvery` | 5 calls → 1 log line, counter = 5 |
| `TestUnhandledEndpointLogsEachDistinctRoute` | a new route is not suppressed by another's throttle |
| `TestUnhandledEndpointLogsEachDistinctMethod` | GET and PUT on one path are distinct keys |

New, in `internal/logship/loglimiter_test.go`: `TestLogLimiter{SuppressesRepeatsPerKey,AllowsAgainAfterInterval,BoundsItsKeySet,PurgesExpiredKeysWhenFull}`.

Mutation-tested — every one of these fails when the behaviour it pins is removed, so none is vacuous:

| mutation | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| no log at all (the bug as filed) | all 4 unhandled tests |
| no throttle | `...SuppressesRepeatsButCountsEvery` |
| keyed on a constant, not method+path | `...EachDistinctRoute`, `...EachDistinctMethod` |
| counter moved inside the throttle | `...SuppressesRepeatsButCountsEvery` |
| limiter cap removed | `...BoundsItsKeySet`, `...PurgesExpiredKeysWhenFull` |

Gate green: `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint run` (0 issues), `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check`, plus `-race` on the new tests. No metric added or changed, so no docs/dashboard regeneration.

## Follow-up

The route Zenarmor is actually calling is still unknown — this change is what makes it knowable. It will name itself in the exporter's logs within ~a day of the next <host-1> deploy; `/_ilm/policy/...` and `/_index_template/...` are the guesses the shape suggests, but nothing here assumes that.

title: unhandled_endpoint counter names nothing, so it cannot be acted on

## Summary

The `metadata.subsystems` health model added in `0bda657` ("read per-subsystem health detail from metadata.subsystems", Refs #236) rests on a premise that is **not true of any OPNsense release**. Upstream never populates `metadata.subsystems`. It is initialised to `[]` and never written to again.

Found while triaging #271, where the canary flagged `healthCheck` → `subsystems` as a missing path.

## Evidence

`src/opnsense/mvc/app/controllers/OPNsense/Core/Api/SystemController.php`, `statusAction()`:

```php
$response['metadata'] = [
    'system' => [...],
    'translations' => [...],
    'subsystems' => []          // line 79 — initialised empty
];

$statuses = json_decode(trim($backend->configdpRun('system status', [...])), true);
if ($statuses) {
    ...
    $response['subsystems'] = $statuses;   // line 174 — TOP-LEVEL, inside the if
    unset($response['status']);
}
```

`metadata.subsystems` is assigned once, at line 79, to `[]`. Grepping every `subsystems` / `$response[` occurrence in the file (lines 68, 79, 106, 174, 175) shows **no other write**. The only per-subsystem map upstream ever emits is the **top-level** one at line 174.

The blob is **identical on `master`, `stable/26.1` and `stable/25.7`** (sha `ea83f28ac81c223d86bd9c530a329244a1b2cf9d`), last touched by `2862db60b` on 2025-01-21. There is no 26.1 vs 26.1.11 divergence to model — the endpoint has not changed in ~18 months.

## What the two shapes actually are

What `0bda657` modelled as two **generations** are two **box states** of one unchanged generation:

| box state | payload |
| --- | --- |
| healthy (`$statuses` falsy) | metadata only; **no** top-level `subsystems`; `metadata.system.status` = `2` (int, the enum `->value`) |
| ≥1 subsystem reporting | **+ top-level `subsystems`** map; `metadata.system.status` = `"OK"`/`"ERROR"` (string, via `toValueNameArray()`) |

This also explains the int-or-string tolerance in `GetMetadataSystemStatus`: correct behaviour, wrong stated reason. It is state-dependent, not version-dependent.

## Consequences

None of these is a live bug — `AllSubsystems()` merges both maps and the top-level one wins — but the model is wrong and it actively misleads triage:

- **`opnsense/testdata/health/v26_1_11_metadata_subsystems_error.json` and `v26_1_11_multi_subsystem.json` are fabricated.** They place a populated map under `metadata.subsystems`, a shape no OPNsense build emits. Confirmed: they are the only two fixtures whose `metadata.subsystems` is a non-empty object.
- **`HealthCheckResponse.Metadata.Subsystems` (`opnsense/health_check.go:89`) can only ever decode `[]`.** Its three readers (`health_check.go:175`, `:227`, `:231`) are permanent no-ops.
- **The field's doc comment states the false claim as fact** (`health_check.go:80-94`: "the per-subsystem map as served by OPNsense 26.1.11 and later"), as did the `healthCheck` note in `exemptions.json` (corrected in #271's commit).
- `v26_1_ok.json` is mildly synthetic too: it carries a top-level `"subsystems": []`, which upstream cannot emit — the `if` block that creates the key is the same one that fills it.

## Also worth checking (separate, lower priority)

The `System.*` / `CrashReporter.*` / `Firewall.*` legacy exemptions look **pre-25.1**, killed by the 2024-12-12 refactor `1fc5a6335`. By the "current + previous stable" support-window rule they are already outside the window and prunable. Their old note's stated trigger ("when 26.1.10 and older leave the support window") was wrong; the note is corrected in #271's commit but the entries are left in place pending a decision here.

## Change

- [ ] Delete the two fabricated fixtures, or rebuild them as what they were meant to represent — a **reporting** box, which means a populated **top-level** `subsystems` map
- [ ] Decide `Metadata.Subsystems`: delete the field and its three readers, or keep it as defensive tolerance with a comment that says plainly it is unpopulated on every known release and why it is retained
- [ ] Fix the doc comments at `opnsense/health_check.go:80-94` to describe box state, not generations
- [ ] Re-point `GetMetadataSystemStatus`' int-vs-string comment at the real cause (`->value` vs `toValueNameArray()`, i.e. box state)
- [ ] Regenerate `v26_1_ok.json` from a real healthy capture, or drop its impossible top-level `"subsystems": []`
- [ ] Decide whether to prune the pre-25.1 `System.*`/`CrashReporter.*`/`Firewall.*` exemptions

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No fixture encodes a payload shape upstream cannot produce
- [ ] No comment or ledger note claims `metadata.subsystems` is populated on any release
- [ ] The health tests still cover both real box states (healthy, and ≥1 subsystem reporting)
- [ ] `go test ./...` green

Verified 2026-07-17 against upstream source directly (not inferred): the `subsystems` handling is byte-identical across `master`, `stable/26.1` and `stable/25.7`.

comments.body:
Done in 80649b1. The premise held up under independent verification, but one claim in the issue body was wrong — details below.

### Verified, not inferred

Re-read the upstream controller directly rather than trusting the original triage. `metadata.subsystems` is initialised to `[]` in the `$response['metadata']` literal and **never assigned again**; the only per-subsystem map upstream emits is the top-level one, set inside `if ($statuses)`. The blob is byte-identical on `master`, `stable/26.1` and `stable/25.7` (`ea83f28a`) and untouched since 2025-01-21 — so there was never a 26.1 → 26.1.11 divergence to model.

### Correction to this issue: `v26_1_ok.json` was NOT synthetic

The body called it "mildly synthetic" for carrying a top-level `"subsystems": []`, on the reasoning that the `if` block which creates the key is the same one that fills it. **That reasoning was wrong, and I only caught it by reading the block line by line instead of trusting the summary.** The ACL filter *inside* that block can `unset()` every entry it just built:

```php
if ($statuses) {
    foreach ($statuses as $subsystem => $status) {
        ...
        if (!$acl->isPageAccessible($this->getUserName(), $status['location'])) {
            unset($statuses[$subsystem]);   // can empty it completely
            continue;
        }
    }
    $statusCodes = array_column($filteredStatuses, 'statusCode');
    $response['metadata']['system']['status'] = $order[$statusCodes[0] ?? 2];   // -> "OK"
    $response['subsystems'] = $statuses;                                        // -> []
}
```

Empty `$statusCodes` → the `?? 2` default → the **name** `"OK"`, alongside an empty array. So `"OK"` alongside `[]` is a real payload for a user whose ACL hides every reporting subsystem's page. That fixture is now `v26_1_acl_filtered.json` with the mechanism documented, rather than deleted. The genuinely impossible one is `v26_1_empty_map.json` (`{}` — PHP never encodes an empty array as an object); it's kept as an explicitly-labelled parser-tolerance fixture rather than a claimed capture.

### Changes

- **Field and readers gone.** `Metadata.Subsystems` plus its three no-op readers. `AllSubsystems` loses the union, the precedence rule and the "never observed on a real box" caveat — there is no second map to prefer.
- **Fabricated fixtures deleted**: `v26_1_11_metadata_subsystems_error.json`, `v26_1_11_multi_subsystem.json`.
- **Fixtures renamed by BOX STATE**, since 26.1 and 26.1.11 are one generation: `v26_1_quiet` (real capture — int status, no map), `v26_1_acl_filtered`, `v26_1_empty_map`.
- **Comments corrected**, including `GetMetadataSystemStatus`: the int-vs-string split is box state (`->value` seed vs the enum name stamped in the `if`), not versions. The tolerance was right for the wrong stated reason.
- **Golden schema regenerated** (`make schemas` drops `metadata.subsystems`).

### The pre-25.1 exemptions: keeping them

Decided **not** to prune. They're already outside the current+previous window, but this isn't a ledger edit — the exemptions exist because the structs do, and deleting the structs drops support for pre-25.1 boxes. That's a product decision, not canary hygiene. The note now says exactly that instead of naming a trigger that has already fired. Open an issue if that support should end.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] No fixture encodes a payload shape upstream cannot produce (the one that can't is labelled synthetic on purpose)
- [x] No comment or ledger note claims `metadata.subsystems` is populated on any release — only `CHANGELOG.md` still contains the old claim, as the historical record of 0bda657, which is not rewritten
- [x] Health tests still cover both real box states (quiet, and ≥1 subsystem reporting)
- [x] `go test ./...` green

Gate: `go test ./...`, `golangci-lint run`, `make docs-check`, `make grafana-check` all green.

The taxonomy gap from #271 is closed in 7f380d5: **box-state** is now the fifth verdict, listed first, with "did upstream actually change?" as the opening question. It also carries the two rules this post-mortem earned — verify against upstream source before assigning a verdict, and never let a fixture encode a shape upstream cannot produce.
