body:
## Problem

The `release-please` job in the release workflow authenticates with `token: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN }}` and has no fallback to `github.token`. This fine-grained PAT is what lets the release PR run CI unattended (it's authored as a trusted PAT identity instead of `github-actions[bot]`, avoiding the "action_required" approval gate on reusable workflows). Fine-grained PATs expire (at most one year), and there is no code path that degrades gracefully if the secret is missing, revoked, or expired.

Because the `binaries`, `publish`, and `edge` jobs all declare `needs: release-please`, and a GitHub Actions `if:` condition that doesn't itself call a status function (`success()`/`failure()`/`always()`/`cancelled()`) is implicitly ANDed with `success()`, a failed `release-please` job (e.g. due to an auth failure from an expired PAT) causes all three downstream jobs to be skipped — not just release-PR management, but also the `:main` edge image publish that normally happens on every ordinary push to main.

## Evidence

`.github/workflows/release-please.yml:28` — the release-please step's token input, no fallback:
```yaml
token: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN }}
```

`.github/workflows/release-please.yml:64-75` — the `edge` job, gated behind `needs: release-please`:
```yaml
edge:
  needs: release-please
  if: needs.release-please.outputs.release_created != 'true'
  ...
```

`binaries` (lines 33-44) and `publish` (lines 48-59) similarly declare `needs: release-please` and gate on `needs.release-please.outputs.release_created`.

Not livebox-validated (this is a CI/workflow-configuration finding, not something exercisable against a live OPNsense box).

## Failure scenario / impact

The `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` PAT expires or is revoked (it is a fine-grained PAT with a maximum one-year lifetime). From the next push to `main` onward, the `release-please` job fails authentication on every run. Because `binaries`, `publish`, and `edge` all have `needs: release-please`, GitHub Actions' implicit `success()` gate skips all three jobs on every subsequent push — so no `:main` edge container image is published (any deployment tracking `:main` silently stops receiving updates), and no release can be cut until someone notices and rotates the token. The only visible signal is a workflow-run failure notification, which is easy to miss.

## Suggested direction

Fall back to the default token when the PAT is unset, e.g. `token: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN || github.token }}`, so an expired/missing PAT degrades to bot-authored release PRs (with the known stuck-CI-approval annoyance) rather than hard-failing edge image publishing entirely. Optionally add a scheduled canary/expiry check that fails loudly well before the PAT lapses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `release-please` step's `token:` input falls back to `github.token` (or equivalent) when `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` is unset/empty, so the job can still authenticate and produce a release PR without the PAT.
- [ ] A missing/expired `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` no longer causes `binaries`, `publish`, and `edge` to be skipped on ordinary pushes to `main` — `edge` image publishing continues to function even if the PAT is absent.
- [ ] Document (in the workflow file or repo docs) that the fallback path means bot-authored release PRs may need manual "Approve and run" for reusable-workflow CI checks, so the tradeoff is understood.
- [ ] (Optional/stretch) A scheduled job or check warns before the PAT's expiry date so rotation happens proactively instead of reactively after a failure.

Part of the production-readiness bug bash — tracker: #72
_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body: Fixed in `7aa5d42`. The release-please step's `token:` is now `${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN || github.token }}` (#1). With the fallback, an expired/missing PAT no longer fails the `release-please` job, so the `needs: release-please` downstream jobs (`binaries`/`publish`/`edge`) keep running — `:main` edge publishing continues (#2). The tradeoff (bot-authored release PRs may need a manual "Approve and run" for reusable-workflow CI) is documented in an inline comment on the token line (#3). #4 (proactive PAT-expiry canary) left as the noted optional stretch. `actionlint` passes.

body:
## Problem

The `api-contract` CI job clones the `opnsense/docs` repository at the mutable `master` branch and then imports Python modules directly out of that clone, and separately installs `phply`, `jinja2`, and `pydantic` via pip with no version or hash pinning. Every other `uses:` reference in this repository's workflows is SHA-pinned (the repo runs OpenSSF Scorecard specifically to catch this class of issue), but this job's supply chain is not: it executes whatever code currently sits on `opnsense/docs@master` and whatever the latest PyPI releases of those three packages happen to be, on every scheduled/dispatch/PR run.

The job runs with `issues: write` (and `contents: read`) permissions. `extract.py` does `sys.path.insert(0, args.docs)` and then `from lib.utils import collect_api_modules`, which is a direct import — i.e. execution — of code sourced from the unpinned clone, not just a data read.

## Evidence

- `.github/workflows/api-contract.yml:26` — `OPNSENSE_DOCS_REF: master` (comment above frames this only as a reproducibility concern, not a security one)
- `.github/workflows/api-contract.yml:49` — `python -m pip install --quiet phply jinja2 pydantic` (no versions, no hashes)
- `.github/workflows/api-contract.yml:52` — `git clone --depth 1 --branch "$OPNSENSE_DOCS_REF" https://github.com/opnsense/docs upstream/docs`
- `tools/opnsense_api_contract/extract.py:22-24`:
  ```python
  sys.path.insert(0, args.docs)
  ...
  from lib.utils import collect_api_modules
  ```
  This imports and executes Python sourced from the unpinned `opnsense/docs` clone.

Not livebox-validated (this is a CI/supply-chain finding, not a runtime exporter behavior).

## Failure scenario / impact

A compromised `opnsense/docs` master branch, or a malicious release of `phply`/`jinja2`/`pydantic` pushed to PyPI, gets executed in the runner on the next scheduled/dispatch run of `api-contract.yml`. The job's `issues: write` token (contents:read + issues:write, ephemeral, read-only on fork PRs) could be exfiltrated or used to spam/edit/close issues, and the job's own output (`out/report.md`) could be manipulated to fabricate a plausible-looking "OPNsense API contract drift" issue.

Downstream impact is meaningfully mitigated: `api-contract-enrich.yml` is workflow_dispatch-only (human-gated), re-verifies the triggering issue was canary-created (author/title/state/label/body-marker), explicitly treats issue content as untrusted input, and requires independent per-endpoint confirmation against upstream OPNsense source before opening any mechanical-only PR. So the realistic residual impact is issue spam / a fabricated drift report that the hardened downstream path is designed to catch — not an unmitigated path to a malicious PR against `opnsense/client.go`.

## Suggested direction

Pin `OPNSENSE_DOCS_REF` to a specific commit SHA (Renovate can bump it via a `customManager`) instead of `master`, and pin the `pip install` line to exact package versions, ideally with `--require-hashes`. This closes the unpinned/arbitrary-code channel while keeping the parser deliberately updatable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `OPNSENSE_DOCS_REF` in `.github/workflows/api-contract.yml` is pinned to a specific commit SHA rather than `master`
- [ ] A Renovate custom manager (or equivalent) is configured to track and bump `OPNSENSE_DOCS_REF` so the pin doesn't silently go stale
- [ ] The `pip install phply jinja2 pydantic` step pins exact versions for all three packages (and ideally uses `--require-hashes` with a lockfile/requirements file)
- [ ] `make lint`/CI passes with the pinned versions, confirming `extract.py` still works against the pinned `opnsense/docs` commit
- [ ] No other unpinned `git clone`+import or unpinned `pip install` calls remain elsewhere in `.github/workflows/`

_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

Fixed in `b2cf72e`.

- **`OPNSENSE_DOCS_REF`** pinned from `master` → commit `343a092eb04ea5eed0094afd6b60435ecffb1393` (#1). The clone step now `git init` + `git fetch --depth 1 origin <sha>` + `checkout FETCH_HEAD` (shallow-fetch by SHA, since `--branch` can't take a SHA).
- **Renovate customManager** (`git-refs` datasource) added in `renovate.json` to bump the pinned SHA via a `# renovate:` annotation, so it doesn't go stale (#2).
- **pip deps** moved to a pinned `tools/opnsense_api_contract/requirements.txt` (`phply==1.2.6`, `jinja2==3.1.6`, `pydantic==2.13.4`), installed with `pip install -r`; Renovate's pip_requirements manager bumps them (#3). (`--require-hashes` not used — it needs a full transitive lockfile; exact top-level pins close the arbitrary-version channel.)

The remaining `opnsense/core`/`opnsense/plugins` clones are parsed as **data** — the canary's subject-under-test that must track upstream branches — not imported/executed, so pinning them would defeat the drift check.

body:
## Problem

Several `Fetch*` functions in `opnsense/` issue multiple independent HTTP GETs to distinct OPNsense API endpoints one after another, even though the sub-calls write to disjoint fields of the same result struct and have no dependency on each other. Because each sub-collector already runs concurrently with the other ~30 sub-collectors (via a goroutine + WaitGroup in `internal/collector/collector.go`), the wall-clock cost of any one sub-collector is the *sum* of its own endpoint latencies, not the max — and a slow multi-call collector can become the long pole that determines total scrape duration.

The clearest case is `FetchSystemResources`, which builds a slice literal from six separate fetch calls (`fetchSystemMemory`, `fetchSystemTime`, `fetchSystemDisk`, `fetchSystemSwap`, `fetchSystemInfo`, `fetchCPUType`). Go evaluates slice-literal elements left-to-right before the slice exists, so these six GETs execute strictly sequentially. The same sequential-fan-out pattern exists in the chrony (3 calls), netflow (3 calls), pf_statistics (3 calls), and haproxy (2 calls) fetchers.

## Evidence

- `opnsense/system_resources.go:399-437` — `FetchSystemResources` sequentially calls `fetchSystemMemory`, `fetchSystemTime`, `fetchSystemDisk`, `fetchSystemSwap`, `fetchSystemInfo`, `fetchCPUType` inside one slice literal before checking accumulated errors.
- `opnsense/chrony.go:255-283` — three sequential `c.do` calls.
- `opnsense/netflow.go:63-115` — three sequential GETs.
- `opnsense/pf_statistics.go:67-127` — three sequential GETs.
- `opnsense/haproxy.go:167-231` — two sequential GETs.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:890-899` — confirms sub-collectors already run in their own goroutines under a `sync.WaitGroup`, so overall scrape time is ≈ max over collectors; a collector whose internal cost is a sum of latencies becomes the binding constraint.

Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box: measured per-endpoint timings for the system-resources group were systemResources 0.347s, systemTime 0.234s, systemDisk 0.122s, systemSwap 0.121s, system_information 0.191s, cpuType 0.098s — summing to ~1.11s sequential versus ~0.35s if fanned out concurrently (i.e., bounded by the slowest single call).

## Failure scenario / impact

On a slower or more loaded OPNsense box where each diagnostics endpoint takes roughly 1s to respond, `FetchSystemResources` alone takes ~6s per scrape because its six calls are serialized, when parallelizing them would bound it to ~1s (the slowest single call). This directly erodes headroom against the Prometheus `scrape_timeout`, and the same effect compounds across chrony, netflow, pf_statistics, and haproxy, each paying the sum instead of the max of their respective endpoint latencies.

## Suggested direction

Fan the independent sub-calls out with an `errgroup`/`sync.WaitGroup` inside `FetchSystemResources`; each sub-fetch already writes to a disjoint field of the shared result struct (Memory/Time/Disks/Swap/Info/CPUType), so concurrent execution introduces no data race, and the existing partial-failure tolerance (accumulate/report per-call errors) should be preserved. Apply the same fan-out pattern to the chrony, netflow, pf_statistics, and haproxy fetchers where their sub-calls are similarly independent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `FetchSystemResources`'s six sub-fetches (memory, time, disk, swap, info, CPU type) execute concurrently rather than sequentially, and a test (e.g. using a mock HTTP server with per-endpoint artificial delay) asserts total call duration is closer to the slowest single call than to the sum of all calls.
- [ ] Existing partial-failure behavior is preserved: if one sub-fetch errors, the others still complete and the aggregated result/error reflects only the failing endpoint(s), verified by a unit test that fails one mocked endpoint and asserts the rest still populate.
- [ ] No data race is introduced: `go test -race ./opnsense/...` passes for the modified fetchers.
- [ ] The same concurrent fan-out is applied to `FetchChrony`, `FetchNetflow` (or equivalent pf_statistics/netflow fetch entrypoint), `FetchPFStatistics`, and `FetchHAProxy...` (haproxy fetcher), each covered by an analogous timing/partial-failure test.
- [ ] `make test` and `make lint` remain green after the change.

_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body:
Fixed in `baa4964`.

Added `runConcurrentFetches(fns...)` (WaitGroup + indexed error slice — race-free since each fn writes disjoint fields and `errs[i]` is single-writer) and applied it to all five:
- **FetchSystemResources** (6 calls). Found via `-race` that `fetchSystemInfo` and `fetchCPUType` both lazily allocate+write `data.Info` → **pre-allocate `data.Info` single-threaded** before the fan-out so they write disjoint *fields*.
- **FetchPFStatistics** (3 calls) — same clean pattern.
- **FetchChronyStatus** — the gating `tracking` call stays first; `sources` + `sourcestats` (disjoint, both failure-tolerant) run concurrently.
- **FetchHAProxyStats** — `counters` + `info` fetched into separate locals concurrently, processed single-threaded after the join; counters still gates plugin-presence.
- **netflow collector Update** — the 3 separate public fetches run in a WaitGroup; emission + fail-fast ordering (is-enabled→status→cache) unchanged.

**Tests:** timing tests (`opnsense/concurrency_test.go` + `TestNetflowCollector_ConcurrentFetch`) with per-endpoint 60ms delays assert total ≈ max, not sum (#1, #4); partial-failure is already covered by the existing `_PartialFailure`/`_SubFetchFailure`/plugin-absent tests, which stayed green (#2); `go test -race ./opnsense/...` passes (#3). Gate: `make test`, `make lint` (0 issues), `make docs-check`.

body:
## Problem

`Collector.Collect()` invokes `c.collect(context.Background(), ch, nil)` (`internal/collector/collector.go:853-855`) with a bare background context — no deadline whatsoever. This is the path used for every gather that doesn't attach a per-request timeout: notably every OTLP-bridge periodic export (the OTLP `PeriodicReader` gathers `collectorRegistry`, wired in `main.go:377-396`, and the prometheus-bridge producer's `Collect()` ignores the reader's export-timeout context), and any Prometheus scrape whose HTTP client doesn't send the `X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds` header (`internal/server/metrics.go:55-59` only derives a deadline when that header is present).

All gathers — deadline-bound or not — funnel through the same `collect()` function, which takes the single shared `c.mutex.Lock()` at `collector.go:862`. Because the OPNsense API client retries each call up to 3 times with a 15s HTTP timeout (`opnsense/client.go:26`, `:212`) and only aborts early on `ctx.Err()` (which never fires for a background context), a single blackholed/packet-dropping firewall turns each API call into ~45s, and a multi-call fetcher like `FetchSystemResources` (6 sequential calls, `opnsense/system_resources.go:407-414`) into ~270s. A deadline-less collect holds the shared mutex for that entire window, so every concurrent, properly deadline-bound Prometheus scrape queues behind it, times out waiting for the lock, and falls into the `ctx.Err()` guard at `collector.go:870-877` — which returns *before* `collectHealthMetrics` runs, so scrapes during the outage emit only `scrapes_total`, `endpoint_errors_total`, and exporter build-info: no `up`/health metrics and no firewall metrics at all.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/collector.go:853-855` — `Collect()` calls `c.collect(context.Background(), ch, nil)` with the comment "scrape everything with no deadline".
- `internal/collector/collector.go:862` — `collect()` takes the shared `c.mutex.Lock()`, serializing every gather (OTLP and Prometheus) through one lock.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:870-877` — the `ctx.Err()` guard that a deadline-bound scrape hits after queuing behind a stuck lock holder; it returns early, before `collectHealthMetrics`, so `up`/health and all firewall metrics are dropped for that scrape.
- `internal/server/metrics.go:55-59` — a request deadline is derived only when `X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds` is present on the incoming scrape request; header-less scrapers get no deadline.
- `main.go:377-396` — the collector is registered on `collectorRegistry`, which the OTLP bridge's periodic reader gathers on its own interval, independent of any per-scrape HTTP deadline.
- `opnsense/client.go:26` (`MaxRetries=3`) and `:212` (`httpClient.Timeout=15s`); `opnsense/client.go:288-329` — the retry loop only short-circuits on `ctx.Err()`, which a background context never sets.
- `opnsense/system_resources.go:407-414` — `FetchSystemResources` issues 6 sequential `c.do()` calls, so worst case is ~6 × 45s ≈ 270s held under a single lock.

This is a concurrency/timeout defect confirmed by code-path analysis, not an API-shape claim, so no live-box validation is applicable (`livebox_validated: false`).

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator enables `--otlp.enabled` (or scrapes `/metrics` with a client that doesn't send the Prometheus scrape-timeout header, e.g. plain `curl` or a non-Prometheus collector) while the target OPNsense firewall starts silently dropping packets (blackhole/network fault). The next OTLP gather (or header-less scrape) calls `collect()` with no deadline, retries every stalled API call for ~45s each, and can hold the shared collector mutex for minutes. Every concurrent, correctly-configured Prometheus scrape queues behind that lock, times out, and returns early via the `ctx.Err()` guard — emitting only `scrapes_total`/`endpoint_errors_total`/build-info, with no `up`/health signal and no firewall metrics at all. The outage-handling design (per-scrape deadlines, ctx.Err() guard) is defeated by the one deadline-less caller, turning a single stalled subsystem into a multi-minute total metrics blackout for all consumers of the exporter.

## Suggested direction

Apply a default collection deadline inside `collect()` whenever the incoming context carries none — e.g. a new `--exporter.max-scrape-duration` flag (default around 50s) — so no gather can hold the mutex unbounded, and derive the OTLP gather's deadline from the configured OTLP export interval rather than leaving it as `context.Background()`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test asserts that calling `Collector.Collect()` (or the internal `collect()`) with a background/no-deadline context results in an effective deadline being applied (e.g. via a context with `Done()` firing within the configured max-scrape-duration), not an unbounded call.
- [ ] A unit test simulates a slow/blocked API client call under the default-deadline path and asserts `collect()` returns (releasing the mutex) at or before the configured `--exporter.max-scrape-duration`, rather than running to completion of all retries.
- [ ] A unit test or integration test asserts the OTLP-bridge gather path no longer calls `collect()` with `context.Background()` directly, and instead derives a deadline from the OTLP export interval.
- [ ] `internal/options` gains the new flag/env var (documented via `make docs`), with a sensible default (~50s) and coverage in the existing collectors/options flag tests.
- [ ] A regression test verifies that when the default-deadline gather times out, subsequent queued Prometheus scrapes acquire the mutex promptly (bounded wait) rather than queuing behind an unbounded hold.
- [ ] `make docs-check` passes with the new flag documented in `docs/configuration.md`.

Part of the production-readiness bug bash — tracker: #72

_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body:
Fixed in `4baabb8`.

- **New flag `--exporter.max-scrape-duration`** (`OPNSENSE_EXPORTER_MAX_SCRAPE_DURATION`, default **50s**) in `internal/options/exporter.go`, documented via `make docs` (#4, #6).
- **`collect()`** applies `context.WithTimeout(ctx, maxScrapeDuration)` whenever the incoming context has no deadline (`ctx.Deadline()` → `!ok`). A caller-supplied deadline (Prometheus `X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds`) still wins. Falls back to a 50s package default when the flag isn't wired (direct-construction tests).
- **`Collector.Collect()`** (the OTLP/registry entry point) now derives its deadline from `otlpGatherTimeout` — wired in `main.go` to `min(otlp export interval, max-scrape-duration)` — instead of `context.Background()` (#3). New `WithMaxScrapeDuration`/`WithOTLPGatherTimeout` options; `main.go` assembles the OTLP config before building the collector so the interval is available.

**Tests** (`collector_test.go`): `TestCollectAppliesDefaultDeadline` — background collect → sub-collector sees a deadline (#1); `TestCollectBoundedByMaxScrapeDuration` — a sub-collector blocking on `ctx.Done()` with a 150ms bound returns \<1s AND a second collect acquires the mutex promptly (#2, #5); `TestOTLPCollectDerivesDeadlineFromInterval` — `Collect()` with `otlpGatherTimeout` set applies that deadline (#3). Gate: `make test`, `make lint` (0 issues), `make docs-check`.

body:
## Problem

When the OPNsense firewall is unreachable, the exporter still runs its full ~49-collector fan-out on every scrape instead of short-circuiting, and the underlying HTTP retry policy makes each failed call as noisy and slow as possible. `Collector.Collect()` first calls `collectHealthMetrics` to determine `opnsense_up` (internal/collector/collector.go:782-802), and when that health check fails it logs "failed to fetch system health status; continuing with sub-collectors" (collector.go:881-886) — but the result is discarded rather than used to skip the rest of the scrape, unlike the existing context-expired early-return guard a few lines above (collector.go:870-877). Every enabled sub-collector then still dials the firewall.

Compounding this, `opnsense/client.go`'s retry loop (client.go:283-334) has no backoff or jitter: on a transport error it sleeps a fixed `time.Sleep(25 * time.Millisecond)` (client.go:324) and retries up to `MaxRetries = 3` times, logging an Error-level "failed to send request; retrying" line on every attempt. It never retries on 5xx responses (client.go:328 returns immediately via `readResponse`), and when all retries are exhausted it returns a generic `APICallError{Message: "max retries of %d times reached", StatusCode: 0}` (client.go:330-334) that discards the actual underlying transport error (DNS failure, connection refused, timeout are all indistinguishable to the caller/metrics, even though the real error is visible in the per-attempt log line at client.go:321).

Together these mean a down or flapping firewall produces a large burst of doomed dials and error-level log lines every single scrape interval, and short transient blips (e.g. a firmware-check restart of lighttpd/configd) cause full scrape failures with an unhelpful generic error, rather than being absorbed by sane backoff.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/collector.go:881-886` — health-check failure is logged but not used to short-circuit the fan-out:
  ```go
  if err != nil {
      c.log.Error(...) // "failed to fetch system health status; continuing with sub-collectors"
  }
  ```
- `internal/collector/collector.go:888-899` — fan-out to all enabled sub-collectors runs unconditionally, regardless of the health-check outcome above.
- `opnsense/client.go:312-329` — retry loop: fixed 25ms sleep, no backoff/jitter, no retry on 5xx:
  ```go
  time.Sleep(25 * time.Millisecond)
  ...
  return c.readResponse(path, resp, responseStruct)
  ```
- `opnsense/client.go:330-334` — final error discards the underlying cause:
  ```go
  return APICallError{
      Message:    fmt.Sprintf("max retries of %d times reached", MaxRetries),
      StatusCode: 0,
  }
  ```
- Empirical repro (exporter built at HEAD, pointed at a dead address `127.0.0.1:9`, one `/metrics` scrape): 240 total log lines, 223 at `level=ERROR`, of which 174 are "failed to send request; retrying" (58 endpoint calls x 3 attempts each) and the remainder are per-collector "failed to update" errors. Not livebox-validated (both findings' `livebox_validated` is `false`); this reproduction is against a synthetic dead address, not the real OPNsense box.

## Failure scenario / impact

1. Firewall reboots or loses network for 10 minutes with a 15s scrape interval: roughly 40 scrapes x ~223 error lines each ≈ 9,000 error log lines and ~10,000 wasted TCP dial attempts against a box that may already be struggling, drowning out the one useful signal (`opnsense_up=0`). This worst case requires the connection to be actively refused (host up, API/web service down); under pure packet loss the request-scoped scrape deadline trips a different code path (client.go:314-320) that does not retry-log, so volume there is lower.
2. A nightly firmware check restarts lighttpd/configd for ~1-2s exactly as a scrape lands: with only a fixed 25ms x 3 retry budget (~75ms total), the scrape fails outright, `scrape_collector_success=0` and `endpoint_errors_total` increment, producing a recurring false "firewall degraded" blip on dashboards for what was actually a sub-second, self-healing hiccup — and the operator diagnosing it only sees "max retries of 3 times reached" with no indication of whether it was DNS, refused, or timeout.

## Suggested direction

When the health check fails with a transport-level error (`StatusCode==0`), consider skipping the sub-collector fan-out for that scrape (still emitting `opnsense_up=0` and the always-on exporter metrics), or adding a simple trip-after-N circuit breaker. Separately, consider jittered exponential backoff (e.g. 100ms/400ms) honoring context cancellation, retrying idempotent GETs on 502/503/504, demoting per-attempt retry logs to Warn/Debug, and wrapping the last attempt's real error into the final `APICallError` message.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test simulates a health-check transport failure (`StatusCode==0`) and asserts the sub-collector fan-out is skipped (or bounded by a circuit breaker) for that scrape, while `opnsense_up` is still reported as `0`.
- [ ] A unit test asserts the retry loop in `opnsense/client.go` waits increasing (non-fixed) intervals between attempts rather than a constant 25ms, for repeated transport errors.
- [ ] A unit test asserts a GET request receiving a 502/503/504 response is retried at least once, whereas today it returns immediately without retry.
- [ ] A unit test asserts that when all retries are exhausted, the returned `APICallError` includes the underlying transport error (not just the generic "max retries of %d times reached" string with `StatusCode: 0`).
- [ ] A log-volume regression test (or documented manual repro) confirms that pointing the exporter at an unreachable address for one scrape produces materially fewer than ~223 ERROR-level log lines.
- [ ] `make lint` and `make test` pass with the change.

Part of the production-readiness bug bash — tracker: #72
_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body:
Fixed in `d228260`.

**Collector short-circuit (`collect`):** when `collectHealthMetrics` returns a transport-level `*opnsense.APICallError` (`StatusCode==0` — DNS/refused/timeout/context-abort), the sub-collector fan-out is skipped for that scrape; `opnsense_up=0` (already emitted by `collectHealthMetrics`) plus the always-on meta metrics are surfaced via a new `collectAlwaysOn` helper. A reachable box returning an HTTP error still falls through (`StatusCode != 0`), so it doesn't mask real per-collector failures.

**Client retry loop:**
- Jittered exponential backoff — `retryBackoff(n) = 100ms << (n-1)` (100/200/400ms) with full jitter over [base/2, base], via a `select` on `ctx.Done()` so a cancelled scrape doesn't sleep pointlessly (replaces the fixed 25ms).
- Idempotent **GET**s retried on **502/503/504** (`retryableStatus`); non-GET and other codes unchanged.
- Per-attempt retry logs demoted **Error→Warn** (the log-storm source); `opnsense_up=0` is the real signal.
- Exhausted-retries `APICallError` now embeds the underlying cause: `max retries of 3 times reached: <transport error>`.

**Tests:** `opnsense/retry_test.go` — backoff strictly increasing (#2), GET retried on 503 / POST not (#3), exhausted-retries error includes the dial cause (#4). `internal/collector` `TestCollectShortCircuitsWhenFirewallUnreachable` — unreachable client → fan-out skipped (fake sub-collector `calls==0`), `opnsense_up=0`, and **0** ERROR log lines (#1, #5; was ~223). Gate: `make test`, `make lint` (0 issues), `make docs-check`.

body:
## Problem

The exporter's only self-metric for API calls is `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total`, a bare counter incremented solely on error. It has no denominator, so operators cannot compute an error *rate* for any endpoint, and there is no per-endpoint latency metric at all. The only timing self-metric that exists is `opnsense_exporter_scrape_collector_duration_seconds`, which is per-*collector*, not per-endpoint. Several collectors (e.g. `system`) call multiple OPNsense API endpoints inside a single `Update()`, so when a collector's total duration spikes there is no way from `/metrics` alone to tell which underlying endpoint call is responsible.

All outbound API traffic funnels through a single choke point, `Client.doWithContentType`, which `do()` and `doForm()` both call. This is the natural place to record request counts and durations, but it currently records neither.

## Evidence

- `opnsense/client.go:262-335` — `doWithContentType` is the single choke point for every API call (`do`/`doForm` both route through it) and records no counters or histograms.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:716-720` (also referenced at lines 825, 845) — the only per-endpoint self-metric, `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total`, is incremented only on error, keyed by `endpoint`+`instance`.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:640-667` and `812+` — `opnsense_exporter_scrape_collector_duration_seconds` / `opnsense_exporter_scrape_collector_success` are set around each sub-collector's `Update()` call — per-collector granularity only, not per-endpoint.
- Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box: within the single `system` collector, sub-calls ranged from 0.098s (`cpuType`) to 0.347s (`systemResources`), and `diagnostics/activity/get_activity` took 2.575s — none of these are individually observable in `/metrics` today; only the aggregate `system` collector duration is exposed.

## Failure scenario / impact

A scrape starts timing out on a busy firewall: `opnsense_exporter_scrape_collector_duration_seconds{collector="system"}` reports 8s, but nothing in `/metrics` indicates which of the collector's ~6 underlying endpoint calls regressed. The operator has no rate metric either — `endpoint_errors_total` shows raw error counts with no request volume to divide by, so a spike from 1/100 to 1/2 failing requests looks identical to one from 1/10000 to 1/20. Diagnosing either problem currently requires SSHing to the firewall and curling endpoints by hand instead of reading one histogram from Prometheus.

## Suggested direction

In `doWithContentType`, record an `opnsense_exporter_api_requests_total{endpoint,code}` counter and an `opnsense_exporter_api_request_duration_seconds` histogram (endpoint label only — roughly 107 endpoints, so bounded cardinality), wired into the always-on emit path alongside the existing `endpointErrors` counter increment.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A new counter (e.g. `opnsense_exporter_api_requests_total`) is incremented for every call that passes through `doWithContentType`, labeled by endpoint and response code, regardless of success/failure.
- [ ] A new histogram (e.g. `opnsense_exporter_api_request_duration_seconds`) records call duration for every request through `doWithContentType`, labeled by endpoint.
- [ ] A unit test in `opnsense/` asserts that both the counter and histogram are updated after a successful `do()`/`doForm()` call, and that the counter is still updated (with an appropriate `code` label) after a failed call.
- [ ] `make docs` picks up the two new metrics in the generated metrics reference without manual edits, and `make docs-check` passes.

body:
## Problem

The ARP-table and NDP collectors each emit one Prometheus time series per neighbor entry — `opnsense_arp_table_entries{ip,mac,hostname,interface_description,type,expired,permanent}` (`internal/collector/arp_table.go:35-65`) and the NDP equivalent `{ip,mac,interface_description,type}` (`internal/collector/ndp.go:34-61`) — and both collectors are **default-on** (`exporter.disable-arp-table`, `exporter.disable-ndp`, `internal/options/collectors.go:6-9,114-117`, both `Default("false")`).

This contradicts a convention the repo enforces everywhere else. `CLAUDE.md` states explicitly: "Use `exporter.disable-*` (default-on) for low-cardinality collectors; reserve `exporter.enable-*` (default-off) for collectors with extra per-scrape API cost or high cardinality." Every other collector emitting one series per host/lease/peer — dnsmasq, kea, dhcpv4, dhcpv6, tailscale, openvpn, unbound, firewall-rules — gates that per-item detail behind an opt-in `enable-*-details` flag and defaults to a cheap aggregate (see `docs/configuration.md:239-260`, "High-cardinality detail options"). ARP and NDP are the two per-host collectors that were never brought into this pattern: they have no aggregate fallback at all and no default-off detail switch, so every install gets the unbounded per-entry series whether it wants them or not. `opnsense/arp_table.go` even fetches a `TotalEntries` field (used at `arp_table.go:74`) that the collector never emits — the aggregate data is already available and simply isn't surfaced.

Cardinality growth is not just proportional to network size — it churns. IP/MAC/hostname label sets change as DHCP leases move, devices roam between wifi APs, and IPv6 privacy-address rotation constantly mints new NDP entries, so even a stable small network keeps generating fresh series over time.

## Evidence

Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box (85 ARP entries, 66 NDP entries on a small home network — already ~150 default-on per-host series with no aggregate option).

- `internal/collector/arp_table.go:35-38` — per-entry `GaugeValue` with 7 labels:
  ```go
  prometheus.NewDesc(
      prometheus.BuildFQName(namespace, subsystem, "entries"),
      "ARP table entries",
      []string{"ip", "mac", "hostname", "interface_description", "type", "expired", "permanent"},
      nil,
  )
  ```
- `internal/collector/ndp.go:36` — per-entry labels `{"ip", "mac", "interface_description", "type"}`, same one-series-per-row pattern.
- `internal/options/collectors.go:6-9` and `:114-117` — both flags are `exporter.disable-arp-table` / `exporter.disable-ndp`, `Default("false")` (i.e. collector runs unless explicitly disabled); no matching `enable-arp-details` / `enable-ndp-details` entry exists in `CollectorFlags` (`internal/options/collectors.go:357-412`).
- `opnsense/arp_table.go` — `TotalEntries` is fetched but never read by the collector (dead aggregate data).
- Contrast: `internal/options/collectors.go` dhcpv4 details flag comment explicitly says "high cardinality on large networks," and `docs/configuration.md:239-260` documents dnsmasq/kea/dhcpv4/dhcpv6/tailscale/openvpn/unbound detail metrics as opt-in high-cardinality options — ARP/NDP are absent from that list despite the identical per-host shape.
- `CLAUDE.md:48` (repo's own stated policy): "Use `exporter.disable-*` (default-on) for low-cardinality collectors; reserve `exporter.enable-*` (default-off) for collectors with extra per-scrape API cost or high cardinality."

## Failure scenario / impact

On any network larger than a handful of hosts — a few thousand clients on guest wifi, VLANs, or a campus network — a default install of the exporter emits thousands of high-churn `opnsense_arp_table_entries` / NDP series per scrape without the operator ever opting in, inflating Prometheus/Mimir ingest and head-cardinality cost. Even on a small home network, IPv6 privacy-address rotation and DHCP lease churn continuously mint new series (an ARP entry flipping `expired=false→true` alone creates a brand-new labelset), so the cost grows over time even without network growth. This is the exact problem the `enable-*-details` convention exists to prevent everywhere else in the exporter, but ARP/NDP fall outside it.

## Suggested direction

Split ARP and NDP like the DHCP collectors: keep a cheap default-on aggregate (entries total, and/or grouped by interface/type — `TotalEntries` is already fetched and unused) and move the per-entry `ip`/`mac`/`hostname` series behind new default-off `exporter.enable-arp-details` / `exporter.enable-ndp-details` flags. This is a breaking change for anyone dashboarding on the current per-entry metric, so it needs a migration note in the changelog/docs and a corresponding Grafana dashboard update.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A default `opnsense-exporter` run (no `enable-*-details` flags set) no longer emits per-entry `ip`/`mac`/`hostname`-labeled ARP or NDP series; it emits a low-cardinality aggregate instead (e.g. total entries, optionally by interface/type).
- [ ] New `exporter.enable-arp-details` and `exporter.enable-ndp-details` flags (default off) exist, gate the existing per-entry metrics, and are wired the same way as the existing dhcpv4/dhcpv6 `enable-*-details` flags in `internal/options/collectors.go`.
- [ ] A unit test asserts that with details disabled, the ARP/NDP collectors' `Update()` does not register any per-entry series but does register the aggregate; with details enabled, per-entry series are registered as before.
- [ ] `docs/configuration.md`'s "High-cardinality detail options" table includes ARP and NDP alongside dnsmasq/kea/dhcpv4/dhcpv6/tailscale/openvpn/unbound (regenerated via `make docs`, verified by `make docs-check`).
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md`/release notes call out the default-metric-shape change as breaking, and the Grafana dashboard (`grafana/`) is updated so the ARP/NDP panels still resolve after `make dashboard`.

body:
## Problem

`scrapeTimeout` in `internal/server/metrics.go` derives the per-scrape collection budget from the incoming `X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds` request header. Its docstring promises that "missing, malformed or non-positive headers yield ok=false (no deadline beyond the request context)", and the guard that is supposed to enforce this is `if err != nil || seconds <= 0 { return 0, false }`.

`strconv.ParseFloat` happily parses the strings `"NaN"`, `"+Inf"`, `"-Inf"`, and large-magnitude values like `"1e300"` into `float64` NaN/Inf without an error. Because IEEE-754 defines every comparison against `NaN` (including `NaN <= 0`) as `false`, a header value of `"NaN"` slips past the "non-positive" check entirely. The function then computes `timeout := time.Duration(NaN * float64(time.Second))`, which converts to `0`, and returns `(0, true)` — i.e. it reports a *valid* timeout of zero. The caller (`ServeHTTP`) then does `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 0)`, producing a context that is already expired before any sub-collector runs. Separately, `"+Inf"` or huge finite values like `"1e300"` pass the guard as well and produce an effectively infinite timeout (~292 years), silently defeating the timeout mechanism instead of erroring.

## Evidence

`internal/server/metrics.go:120-138`:
```go
// scrapeTimeout derives the collection budget from Prometheus' scrape-timeout
// header. The offset is subtracted so the exporter serializes its response
// before Prometheus gives up; if the offset would consume the entire budget,
// the raw header value is used. Missing, malformed or non-positive headers
// yield ok=false (no deadline beyond the request context).
func scrapeTimeout(header string, offset time.Duration) (time.Duration, bool) {
	if header == "" {
		return 0, false
	}
	seconds, err := strconv.ParseFloat(header, 64)
	if err != nil || seconds <= 0 {
		return 0, false
	}
	timeout := time.Duration(seconds * float64(time.Second))
	if timeout > offset {
		return timeout - offset, true
	}
	return timeout, true
}
```

Reproduced independently with the exact logic above:
- header `"NaN"` → `timeout=0s, ok=true`; `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 0)` then reports `context deadline exceeded` immediately.
- header `"+Inf"` / `"1e300"` → `timeout≈2562047h` (~292 years), effectively no deadline.
- header `"-Inf"` / `""` → correctly `ok=false`.

Not livebox-validated (real Prometheus never sends these header values); confirmed via standalone reproduction of the function's logic.

## Failure scenario / impact

Any client that can reach the unauthenticated `/metrics` endpoint (this includes the real Prometheus scraper as well as anyone else who can hit the port, since the header is attacker-controlled) sends `X-Prometheus-Scrape-Timeout-Seconds: NaN`. `scrapeTimeout` returns a "valid" zero-duration timeout, `ServeHTTP` wraps the request context in an already-expired deadline, and every sub-collector observes a cancelled context before it can query OPNsense — the scrape response contains only exporter self-metrics, silently dropping all OPNsense data for that single request. Sending `+Inf` or a very large numeric string instead disables the scrape-timeout budget entirely for that request. Impact is confined to the single crafted request (no crash, no cross-request state, no data leak), and real Prometheus never emits these values, so likelihood in normal operation is very low — this is a robustness/input-validation gap rather than an exploitable vulnerability.

## Suggested direction

Tighten the sanity guard to reject non-finite values, e.g. add `|| math.IsNaN(seconds) || math.IsInf(seconds, 0)`, or equivalently invert the check to `!(seconds > 0)` (which is `true` for `NaN` since all comparisons against `NaN` are false, correctly falling through to `ok=false`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test with header `"NaN"` asserts `scrapeTimeout` returns `ok=false` (not a zero-duration `ok=true`).
- [ ] A unit test with header `"+Inf"` asserts `scrapeTimeout` returns `ok=false`.
- [ ] A unit test with header `"-Inf"` asserts `scrapeTimeout` returns `ok=false` (already correct behavior — guards against regression).
- [ ] A unit test with a large finite value (e.g. `"1e300"`) that would overflow to an unreasonable `time.Duration` either is rejected or clamped, and the test documents the chosen behavior.
- [ ] Existing valid-header test cases (e.g. `"5"`, `"0.5"`) still return `ok=true` with the correct computed timeout, confirming no regression.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/server/...` passes with the new guard in place.

- `NaN` → `ok=false` (previously `(0, true)` — an immediately-expired deadline).
- `+Inf`/`Inf` → `ok=false` (previously ~292-year budget).
- `-Inf`, `""` → `ok=false` (already correct; regression-guarded).
- `1e300`/`1e309` → `ok=false` (acceptance #4: **rejected** via the 24h cap rather than overflowing `time.Duration`; documented in the const comment).

body:
## Problem

The `interfaces` collector fetches interface overview data (`FetchInterfacesOverview()`) as a secondary call alongside its base `FetchInterfaces()` call. When the overview fetch fails, the collector logs a `Warn`-level message and returns `nil` from `Update()` instead of returning the error. Because the exporter's error-surfacing machinery (`execute()` in `internal/collector/collector.go`) only increments `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total` and sets `scrape_collector_success{collector="interfaces"}=0` inside the `if err := coll.Update(...); err != nil` branch, a `nil` return produces zero machine-readable signal for the failure.

This means a persistent failure of the overview endpoint silently drops `opnsense_interfaces_info` and `opnsense_interfaces_admin_up` from `/metrics` on every scrape, while every health signal the exporter itself emits (`scrape_collector_success`, `endpoint_errors_total`) continues to read healthy. Other multi-endpoint collectors in this codebase do not have this gap: `kea.go`'s `Update()` accumulates a `firstErr` across its multiple `Fetch*` calls and returns it at the end, correctly surfacing partial multi-endpoint failures while still emitting whatever metrics it could gather. `interfaces.go` is the only collector in `internal/collector/` that uses this silent-swallow-and-return-nil pattern for a secondary endpoint failure.

## Evidence

`internal/collector/interfaces.go:180-186`:
```go
overview, oerr := client.FetchInterfacesOverview()
if oerr != nil {
    c.log.Warn(...)
    return nil
}
```

`internal/collector/collector.go:838-847` — `execute()` only touches `endpointErrors`/`success` inside the `err != nil` branch of `coll.Update(...)`, so a `nil` return here means neither the counter nor the gauge reflects the failure.

Contrast: `internal/collector/kea.go` (`Update()`, roughly lines 130-201) accumulates a `firstErr` across multiple `Fetch*` calls and returns it, so partial failures are surfaced via the standard collector error path while still emitting whatever data succeeded.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator tightens the API user's privileges (or an OPNsense upgrade/plugin change alters the `api/interfaces/overview/interfaces_info` endpoint) and the overview endpoint starts failing while the base interfaces endpoint keeps succeeding. `opnsense_interfaces_info` and `opnsense_interfaces_admin_up` — used for dashboard joins and link-state-vs-admin-state alerting — silently go stale on every scrape. `scrape_collector_success{collector="interfaces"}` stays at `1` and `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total` never increments for this endpoint, so any meta-alerting built on the exporter's own instrumentation sees nothing wrong. The only trace is a `Warn`-level log line, and the problem is discovered only when someone notices a dashboard join is broken.

## Suggested direction

Keep the current partial-tolerance behavior (still emit traffic metrics when the overview fetch fails), but make the failure observable through the exporter's own instrumentation — e.g. surface the overview fetch error through the same error path `kea.go` uses (an accumulated error returned from `Update()`) so `scrape_collector_success` and `endpoint_errors_total` reflect it, rather than only logging a `Warn`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test simulates `FetchInterfacesOverview()` returning an error while the base `FetchInterfaces()` call succeeds, and asserts that `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total{endpoint="api/interfaces/overview/interfaces_info"}` increments.
- [ ] The same test asserts `scrape_collector_success{collector="interfaces"}` is set to `0` for that scrape, instead of remaining `1`.
- [ ] The test also asserts that traffic-related metrics still available from the base fetch (e.g. interface traffic counters) continue to be emitted despite the overview failure, preserving today's partial-tolerance behavior.
- [ ] The fix follows the same error-accumulation pattern already used in `internal/collector/kea.go`'s `Update()` (or an equivalent mechanism), rather than introducing a third distinct error-surfacing pattern.
- [ ] `make lint` and `make test` pass with the change.

Test `TestInterfacesCollector_OverviewFailureSurfaced` drives the real collector through `execute()` with a mux where `/api/diagnostics/traffic/interface` succeeds and `/api/interfaces/overview/interfaces_info` returns 500, and asserts all three: base traffic metric (`opnsense_interfaces_received_bytes_total`) still emitted, `scrape_collector_success=0`, and `endpoint_errors_total{endpoint="api/interfaces/overview/interfaces_info"}=1`. body:
## Problem

When a scrape's context deadline expires before it can acquire the collector's global scrape mutex, `Collector.Collect()` takes an early bail-out path that emits only a handful of meta-metrics (`scrapes_total`, `endpoint_errors_total`, exporter info) and returns without running `collectHealthMetrics()`. That function is the only place `opnsense_up`, `firewallHealthStatus`, `crashReporterStatus` and `systemStatusCode` are set and collected, and it is also the gate before `execute()` runs the per-collector `scrape_collector_duration_seconds` / `scrape_collector_success` series. The result: the HTTP handler still returns a normal 200 with a valid (if sparse) metrics payload, Prometheus records the scrape as a success (`up==1` on the exporter target), and `opnsense_up` — the documented "is the firewall reachable" signal — is silently absent rather than 0.

Because `c.scrapes` is incremented on this bail path identically to a full, successful scrape, there is also no counter that distinguishes a skipped/deadline-expired scrape from a real one — the only trace is a `Warn`-level log line. A mutex pile-up in front of a slow firewall therefore degrades observability precisely when it matters most, and any alert built on `opnsense_up == 0` cannot fire for the affected scrape interval, because the series doesn't exist rather than reading 0.

## Evidence

`internal/collector/collector.go:868-878` — the deadline-expired bail path:

```go
if ctx.Err() != nil {
    // ... logs a Warn ...
    c.scrapes.Collect(ch)
    c.endpointErrors.Collect(ch)
    c.collectExporterInfo(ch)
    return
}
```

- `collectHealthMetrics()` (around `internal/collector/collector.go:782-800`) is the sole place `c.isUp` (`opnsense_up`), `firewallHealthStatus`, `crashReporterStatus`, and `systemStatusCode` are populated and collected — it is skipped entirely on the bail path.
- `execute()` (which emits `scrape_collector_duration_seconds` / `scrape_collector_success`) never runs on this path either.
- `c.scrapes` is incremented on both the bail path (`collector.go:872`) and the full path (`collector.go:900`), so `scrapes_total` cannot distinguish a skipped scrape from a completed one.
- `internal/server/metrics.go:68-71` — the HTTP handler serves whatever the gather produces as a normal 200 regardless of which path fired.
- The exporter's internal deadline is `scrape_timeout` minus a ~500ms default offset (`internal/options/exporter.go:29`, wired in `internal/server/metrics.go:126-138`), so there is a narrow (~500ms, or deterministic if the scrape-timeout header is NaN/Inf) window where the exporter's own derived context has expired while Prometheus's request is still live — this is the case where the 200-with-absent-`opnsense_up` response actually reaches and is accepted by Prometheus as a successful scrape. This finding was not livebox-validated.

## Failure scenario / impact

Two Prometheus scrapes (an HA pair, or Prometheus plus an OTLP-bridge tick) hit an exporter sitting in front of a slow-responding firewall. Scrape A acquires the global scrape mutex and holds it for an extended period; scrape B queues behind it and its internal deadline expires before it can acquire the lock. If B's own HTTP request is still open when it bails (the ~500ms offset window, or always when the timeout header is malformed), it returns a 200 containing only exporter meta-metrics. Prometheus counts this as a successful scrape (target `up==1`) and writes staleness markers for the missing `opnsense_*` series. The consuming Prometheus server sees dashboards flapping between real data and no-data, `scrapes_total` silently over-counts relative to what Prometheus actually observed, and any "firewall down" alert keyed on `opnsense_up == 0` never fires during the degradation because the series is absent rather than 0.

## Suggested direction

On the deadline-expired bail path, emit a dedicated signal distinguishing it from a normal scrape — e.g. a separate `opnsense_exporter_scrape_skipped_total` counter and/or explicit `scrape_collector_success=0` for the collectors that were skipped — rather than folding it into `scrapes_total` unchanged. This is a non-binding direction; the exact metric shape is an implementation decision.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test drives `Collector.Collect()` with a context that is already expired at mutex-acquisition time and asserts the resulting metric set does NOT silently look identical to a successful scrape (i.e., some counter/gauge distinguishes a skipped scrape from a completed one).
- [ ] A unit test asserts `scrapes_total` (or a new dedicated counter) allows an operator to detect the number of deadline-expired/skipped scrapes distinctly from completed scrapes.
- [ ] A unit test confirms that on the bail path, `opnsense_up` is either emitted as 0 or that an equivalent explicit "skipped" signal is present — not simply absent with no other indicator.
- [ ] `make docs` / `make docs-check` pass with any new metric documented in the generated metrics reference.
- [ ] A regression test covers the NaN/Inf scrape-timeout-header trigger path (already deterministic) to confirm the new signal fires reliably, not just in the narrow timing window.

comments.body:
Fixed in `6664350`.

New counter **`opnsense_exporter_scrape_skips_total`** (labels: `opnsense_instance`), pre-initialised to 0 and collected on both paths so it is always present.

- On the deadline-expired bail path (`collector.go`), increment `scrape_skips_total` **instead of** `scrapes_total`. `scrapes_total` is still Collected (unincremented) so it stays present at its completed-scrape count, and its help now says it counts *completed* scrapes only. This resolves both the over-count and the "indistinguishable from a real scrape" problems.
- `opnsense_up` stays **absent** on the bail path (I deliberately did not emit a misleading `opnsense_up=0`, which would falsely page "firewall down" during exporter mutex contention); `scrape_skips_total` is the explicit skip signal per acceptance #3's "OR equivalent explicit signal" clause.

**Tests:**
- `TestCollectDeadlineExpiredEmitsSkipSignal` (collector): expired context → `scrape_skips_total==1`, `scrapes_total==0`, `opnsense_up` absent. Covers #1/#2/#3.
- `TestCollectSkipSignalOnZeroDeadline` (collector): a 0-duration deadline (exactly what a NaN header yields) → skip signal fires deterministically. Covers #5.
- `TestScrapeTimeoutNaNYieldsExpiredDeadline` (server): documents that `scrapeTimeout("NaN") == (0s, true)`, so the handler builds `context.WithTimeout(reqCtx, 0)` — an already-expired deadline — which is the deterministic bail trigger (not the ~500ms window). Together these cover the full NaN-header → skip-signal chain across the package boundary.

**Docs/dashboard (#4):** `make docs` documents the new metric (556→557); added to the Diagnostics **"Scrape & Skip Rate"** panel. Gate green: `make test`, `make lint` (0 issues), `make docs-check`, dashboard coverage 557/557.

body:
## Problem

When the exporter shuts down with Pyroscope profiling enabled (`--pyroscope.server-address`), the code claims it flushes a final profile, but the actual shutdown path silently drops the in-progress profiling window for every non-CPU profile type (heap/alloc/inuse, and mutex/block/goroutine when enabled).

`Profiler.Stop()` in the vendored Pyroscope SDK just closes the session's `session.go` `stopCh` and stops the CPU collector; it never calls `reset()`/`uploadData()` for the current delta window, which is the only code path that uploads heap/alloc/mutex/block/goroutine profiles. The real flush primitive in the SDK is `Flush(true)`, which resets the window, uploads it, and waits for the upload — but the exporter never calls it. Compounding this, `Profiler.Stop()` unconditionally returns `nil`, so the exporter's own error-handling branch for a failed final flush is dead code that can never execute, and the doc comment above `profiling.go`'s `Stop()` wrapper is factually wrong for anything but the CPU profile.

There's also a secondary, lower-confidence race: the one job that IS enqueued on shutdown (the final CPU profile) can be dropped too, because the uploader's worker-shutdown select randomly chooses between the "done" and "jobs" channels, so all workers can exit before draining a still-queued final CPU job.

## Evidence

- `internal/profiling/profiling.go:63-64` — comment states "Callers should Stop() it on shutdown to flush the final profile" (false for non-CPU profile types).
- `main.go:357-360` — `stopProfiling` wraps `profiler.Stop()` with an error branch logging `"failed to flush final pyroscope profile"`; this branch is unreachable.
- `vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/api.go:101-107` — `Profiler.Stop()` is `p.session.Stop(); p.uploader.Stop(); return nil` — always returns `nil`.
- `vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/session.go:149-154` — the `<-ps.stopCh` case in `takeSnapshots` only calls `ps.cpu.Stop()`; it never calls `ps.reset()`/`ps.uploadData()`.
- `vendor/github.com/grafana/pyroscope-go/session.go:143-147` — the `flushCh` case is the real flush primitive (reset + upload + wait), only reachable via `Flush(true)`, which the exporter never calls.
- `internal/profiling/collector.go:122-131` — the final CPU profile job that IS enqueued on shutdown.
- `internal/profiling/remote.go:244-256` — `handleJobs`'s worker-shutdown `select` picks randomly between `<-r.done` and `<-r.jobs`, so a queued final CPU job can be lost across all 5 workers (~(1/2)^5 chance per queued job).

Verified in a throwaway worktree at HEAD (not on a live OPNsense box — this is a Go-SDK-level repro): starting `pyroscope.Start` with `UploadRate=1h` against an `httptest` server, allocating, then calling `Stop()` produces 0 uploads received; the identical run calling `Flush(true)` before `Stop()` produces heap (godeltaprof) + CPU uploads received. `livebox_validated: false` — no live-box confirmation was performed or claimed for this finding.

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator runs the exporter with `--pyroscope.server-address` set (optionally with `--pyroscope.enable-mutex-block`) and the process is restarted or SIGTERM'd, as happens on every deploy or crash-loop restart. Up to the configured upload window (default 15s) of heap/alloc data — and, when enabled, the mutex/block/goroutine data that is often the most useful signal for diagnosing what was happening right before shutdown — is silently dropped on every restart, even though the code and its log message claim a final flush occurs. During an incident investigated via Pyroscope, the profiles covering the moments leading up to a crash-loop restart are exactly the ones missing. Additionally, because the "flush failed" error branch is unreachable dead code, an operator can never be alerted that this loss occurred.

## Suggested direction

In `stopProfiling` (`main.go:357-361`) or a `Stop` helper in `internal/profiling`, call `profiler.Flush(true)` before `profiler.Stop()`; this is safe as long as CPU profiling stays in the profile set (`profiling.go:31-37`) since the SDK deadlocks in `Flush` if CPU profiling is disabled. Consider bounding the flush with a timeout, since a dead Pyroscope server would otherwise hold `Flush` for up to the SDK's upload timeout (~30s). Also correct the false doc comment at `profiling.go:63-64` and remove or repurpose the dead error branch in `main.go` since `Profiler.Stop()` always returns `nil`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test (or documented manual repro against the vendored SDK) demonstrates that after the fix, stopping the profiler with an in-progress heap/alloc window results in that window being uploaded before the process exits.
- [ ] The shutdown path in `main.go`/`internal/profiling` calls the SDK's real flush primitive (`Flush(true)` or equivalent) before `Stop()`, guarded so it cannot deadlock if CPU profiling is ever made optional.
- [ ] The final-flush call is bounded by a timeout so a dead/unreachable Pyroscope server cannot hang exporter shutdown indefinitely.
- [ ] The doc comment at `internal/profiling/profiling.go:63-64` accurately describes what `Stop()` does (and does not do) for each profile type.
- [ ] The dead/unreachable error-handling branch around `profiler.Stop()` in `main.go` is either removed or replaced with error handling that can actually fire (e.g. from the new flush call).
- [ ] `make test` and `make lint` pass with the change.

Part of the production-readiness bug bash — tracker: #72

_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body:
Fixed in `962bead`.

- **New `profiling.Stop(profiler, logger)`** calls `profiler.Flush(true)` — the SDK's only reset+upload+wait path for the non-CPU delta window — **before** `profiler.Stop()`. The flush runs in a goroutine bounded by a 10s `stopFlushTimeout`; on timeout it logs a warning and proceeds, so an unreachable Pyroscope server can't hang shutdown (SDK's own upload timeout is ~30s). Guarded by the invariant that `profileTypes` always includes `ProfileCPU` (the SDK deadlocks in `Flush` if CPU profiling is off).
- **`main.go`** `stopProfiling` now calls `profiling.Stop(...)`; the unreachable `if err := profiler.Stop(); err != nil` branch (`Profiler.Stop()` always returns nil) is removed.
- **`profiling.go` Start doc comment** corrected — no longer claims `Stop()` flushes the final profile.

**Test (acceptance #1):** `TestStop_FlushesFinalWindow` starts the real SDK with `UploadRate=1h` (so no periodic upload fires) against an `httptest` server, allocates to fill the heap delta, then calls `profiling.Stop` and asserts the server received an upload it otherwise wouldn't have. This is exactly the adversarial repro (`Stop()` alone → 0 uploads; `Flush(true)`+`Stop()` → uploads). Gate green: `make test`, `make lint` (0 issues), `make docs-check`.

body:
## Problem

`opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total` is documented (`docs/metrics/metrics.md`: "Total number of errors by endpoint") as always carrying an API path in its `endpoint` label — e.g. `api/wireguard/service/show`. That contract holds for the two normal error paths, but breaks on the recovered-panic path: when a sub-collector goroutine panics, the counter is incremented with the collector's bare subsystem slug (e.g. `wireguard`) instead of an API endpoint path. The same label on the same metric therefore carries two disjoint value domains depending on which failure mode fired, and the panic-created series is never pre-initialised to 0 like the real endpoint series are, so it only appears in the metric after the first panic ever occurs.

This is a metric-contract/label-hygiene defect, not a data-loss bug: the `OPNsenseEndpointErrors` alert rule groups by `endpoint` and interpolates its value into the alert summary/description, so on a panic it still fires — it just renders the collector's subsystem name ("wireguard") instead of a real API path in the alert text, which is misleading and inconsistent with every other value the label ever takes.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/collector.go:730-731` — pre-initialisation walks known API paths only:
  ```go
  for _, path := range c.Client.Endpoints() {
      c.endpointErrors.WithLabelValues(string(path), c.instanceLabel).Add(0)
  }
  ```
- `internal/collector/collector.go:845` — the normal Update-error path uses the real API path:
  ```go
  c.endpointErrors.WithLabelValues(err.Endpoint, c.instanceLabel).Inc()
  ```
  where `err` is `*opnsense.APICallError` and `Endpoint` is set to `string(path)` at every construction site in `opnsense/client.go` (e.g. lines 272, 296, 316, 331, 350, 362, 369, 377, 385).
- `internal/collector/collector.go:825` — the recovered-panic path uses the collector's subsystem slug instead:
  ```go
  c.endpointErrors.WithLabelValues(coll.Name(), c.instanceLabel).Inc()
  ```
  `coll.Name()` returns a bare subsystem slug (e.g. `wireguard.go`'s `Name()` returns `WireguardSubsystem`, i.e. `"wireguard"`), not an API path.
- `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:52-57` — `OPNsenseEndpointErrors` groups `by (opnsense_instance, endpoint)` and renders `{{ $labels.endpoint }}` into the alert summary/description, assuming that value is always an API path.
- This behavior is currently locked in by `collector_test.go`'s `TestExecuteRecordsScrapeMetrics`, which asserts the panic case increments `endpointErrors` with label = the collector's `Name()`.

Not livebox-validated (code-only finding; no live-box behavior to reproduce beyond the source).

## Failure scenario / impact

A sub-collector panics (e.g. an unexpected API response shape triggers an index-out-of-range). The recovered-panic handler increments `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total{endpoint="wireguard", ...}` instead of any real API endpoint value. Because this series is never pre-initialised to 0, it appears in the metric for the first time only once a panic has already occurred. The `OPNsenseEndpointErrors` alert still fires (so the error isn't silently lost), but its rendered summary/description reads something like "The wireguard API endpoint has returned errors..." — a subsystem slug presented as if it were an API endpoint path — which is confusing to on-call responders and breaks any per-endpoint error breakdown or dashboard that expects `endpoint` to always be an `api/*`-style path.

## Suggested direction

Either record panics in a separate counter (or rely solely on the existing `scrape_collector_success=0` signal that `execute` already emits) or, if the shared counter is kept, label the panic increment with an explicit sentinel value (e.g. `panic:<collector>`) and document it in `docs/metrics/metrics.md`. Panic isolation/recovery itself is correct and already covered by `collector_test.go:428` — only the label value used on that path needs to change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test asserts that on a recovered sub-collector panic, `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total` is either incremented on a distinct panic-specific counter, or incremented with a label value that is never equal to any value produced by `Client.Endpoints()` / `APICallError.Endpoint` (e.g. asserting it matches a `panic:` prefix or similar sentinel, not a bare subsystem slug).
- [ ] `docs/metrics/metrics.md` is updated (via `make docs`) to accurately describe the panic-path label behavior for `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total` (or the new panic counter, if one is added).
- [ ] `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py`'s `OPNsenseEndpointErrors` rule (or a new panic-specific rule) is verified to render a sensible, non-misleading summary/description when the panic path fires.
- [ ] Existing `collector_test.go` `TestExecuteRecordsScrapeMetrics` panic-case assertion is updated to match the new label/counter behavior rather than continuing to lock in the subsystem-slug value.
- [ ] `make test` and `make docs-check` pass after the change.

Part of the production-readiness bug bash — tracker: #72

_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body:
Fixed in `86326fc`.

- **`collector.go:825`** — the recovered-panic path now increments `opnsense_exporter_endpoint_errors_total` with `"panic:"+coll.Name()` (e.g. `panic:wireguard`) instead of the bare subsystem slug. The `panic:` prefix can never equal a `Client.Endpoints()`/`APICallError.Endpoint` value (those are `api/*` paths), so the label's two failure modes are now distinguishable.
- **Metric help + `docs/metrics/metrics.md`** (regenerated via `make docs`) now state: "a recovered collector panic uses a 'panic:<collector>' sentinel value instead."
- **`TestExecuteRecordsScrapeMetrics`** panic case updated to assert the `panic:fake_panic` sentinel rather than locking in the slug.
- **`OPNsenseEndpointErrors` alert** (acceptance #3): left as the shared counter+rule per the issue's "keep the shared counter with a sentinel + document" option. It now renders `OPNsense exporter endpoint errors (panic:wireguard)` — the `panic:` prefix makes it unambiguous that a collector panicked rather than presenting a slug as an API path, so it is no longer misleading. `sum by (endpoint)` grouping and the `increase(...[2m])` window are unaffected.

body:
## Problem

The docs-generation verification gate does not fully check top-level `Collector` metrics — metrics created directly in `internal/collector/collector.go`'s `New()` (e.g. `opnsense_up`, `exporter_scrapes_total`) rather than by a sub-collector. `verifyMetricsAgainstRegistry` in `scripts/docgen/verify.go` only iterates `collector.AllCollectors()`, which is the sub-collector registry (`collectorInstances`, populated by each sub-collector's `init()`). The top-level `Collector` produced by `New()` is never a member of that slice, so its own metric descriptors are never `Register()`'d/`Describe()`'d by the gate and have zero runtime cross-check.

Separately, documentation for these top-level metrics is generated purely by static AST parsing in `parseTopLevelMetrics` (`scripts/docgen/main.go`), whose constructor switch only recognizes `NewGauge`, `NewCounterVec`, and `NewDesc`. Any top-level metric declared with `NewGaugeVec`, `NewCounter`, `NewHistogram`, `promauto`, or with a `Help` string built from a non-literal identifier falls through this switch silently. Because both the runtime gate and the static parser miss these shapes, a metric added this way vanishes entirely from the generated docs and pinned metric counts while `make docs-check` still exits 0 — a silent regression in something the project advertises as an enforced gate. The identical mistake made inside a sub-collector file, by contrast, is a hard fatal in `verify.go`.

## Evidence

- `scripts/docgen/verify.go:42` — `verifyMetricsAgainstRegistry` walks only `collector.AllCollectors()`.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:131-133` — `AllCollectors()` returns `collectorInstances`, the sub-collector registry populated via `init()`; the top-level `Collector` from `New()` is not a member.
- `scripts/docgen/main.go:309-331` — `parseTopLevelMetrics`'s constructor switch handles only `NewGauge`, `NewCounterVec`, and `NewDesc`.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:642-720` — existing top-level metrics happen to use only the three recognized constructor shapes, which is why the gap has stayed latent until now.

Reproduction (performed in a throwaway worktree, since removed): added
```go
c.newThing = prometheus.NewGaugeVec(prometheus.GaugeOpts{Name: "exporter_new_thing", ...})
```
to `New()` in `internal/collector/collector.go` plus its struct field.
- `go build ./...` — exit 0
- `make docs` — exit 0; `git status` showed only the collector.go edit, every generated doc file unchanged; the metric is absent from `docs/metrics/metrics.md` and README, and the pinned metric count stayed at 556
- `make docs-check` — exit 0, printing "docgen: registry verification passed" and "check passed — all generated docs current"

Not livebox-related — this is pure docgen tooling, no live OPNsense interaction involved.

## Failure scenario / impact

A maintainer adds a new top-level per-scrape metric (e.g. a timeout counter sibling to `exporter_scrapes_total`) using `NewGaugeVec`, `NewCounter`, or `NewHistogram` instead of one of the three recognized shapes, wires it into `Describe`/`Collect`, and ships it live on `/metrics`. The "Complete Metrics Reference" docs and the "all 556 metrics" claims across the site/README never mention the new metric, and CI (`make docs-check`) never flags the discrepancy — silently diverging from the advertised guarantee that all generated docs are cross-checked against the live collector registry. Users relying on the generated docs as the authoritative metric list get an incomplete picture, and the same class of omission in a sub-collector file would instead be caught as a hard build failure, creating an inconsistent and surprising trust boundary.

## Suggested direction

Have `verify.go` also `Describe()` a constructed top-level `Collector` (via `New()` with a fake/mock client) and require those fully-qualified metric names to appear in the AST-derived set, closing the asymmetry with sub-collector verification. Secondarily, extend `parseTopLevelMetrics` to recognize `NewGaugeVec`, `NewCounter`, `NewHistogram`, and `promauto`-wrapped constructors, and make it fatal (rather than silently skip) when it encounters a constructor shape or non-literal `Help` value it cannot parse inside `New()`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test asserts that `verifyMetricsAgainstRegistry` (or an equivalent runtime check) covers metrics registered by the top-level `Collector.Describe()`, not just `collector.AllCollectors()`.
- [ ] A top-level metric added to `New()` via `NewGaugeVec`, `NewCounter`, or `NewHistogram` is either correctly reflected in the generated docs and pinned metric count, or causes `make docs-check` to fail with a clear error naming the unparsed constructor.
- [ ] `parseTopLevelMetrics` fatals (non-zero exit) rather than silently skipping when it encounters a top-level metric constructor shape it does not recognize, or a `Help`/`Name` value that is not a string literal.
- [ ] Reproducing the throwaway-worktree scenario from this issue (adding an unhandled top-level constructor) causes `make docs-check` to exit non-zero.
- [ ] Existing top-level metrics (`opnsense_up`, `exporter_scrapes_total`, etc.) continue to generate correctly after the fix, with no change to the pinned metric count for unrelated code.

Part of the production-readiness bug bash — tracker: #72
_Found by automated bug bash, 2026-07-03. Verified adversarially._

comments.body:
Fixed in `02a90a2` (straight to main).

- **Runtime coverage (acceptance #1):** `verifyMetricsAgainstRegistry` now constructs the top-level `Collector` (via a throwaway `opnsense.NewClient` — no network I/O) and `Describe()`s it, requiring every described fqName to be in the combined AST doc set (sub-collectors + top-level). `TestVerifyCoversTopLevelCollector` drops `opnsense_up` from the documented set and asserts the top-level pass flags it missing.
- **Parser (acceptance #2/#3):** `parseTopLevelMetrics` now parses `NewCounter` and `NewGaugeVec`, and **FATALs** with a naming error on any recognised-but-unparsed metric constructor (`NewHistogram`/`NewSummary`/`*Vec`/`*Func`/…). `parsePrometheusOpts` FATALs on a missing/non-literal `Name` or `Help`.
- **Reproduction (acceptance #4):** adding a `prometheus.NewHistogram(...)` to `New()` makes `make docs-check` exit non-zero: `FATAL: parseTopLevelMetrics: unhandled top-level metric constructor "prometheus.NewHistogram" in New() — teach the parser…`. Reverted after confirming.
- **Acceptance #5:** existing top-level metrics still generate correctly; total metric count unchanged at 556.

Gate: `make docs`/`docs-check` green, `make test` green (incl. new test), `make lint` 0 issues.
