body:
## Problem

Every sub-collector builds Prometheus const metrics keyed purely on config- or data-derived label values (schedule/description/command/origin for cron jobs, description/service/hostnames for dyndns accounts, description/commonname/cert_type/in_use for certificates, name/description for ACME certs) and drops the OPNsense row UUID that would otherwise guarantee uniqueness. OPNsense itself enforces no uniqueness on these fields, so two config rows can legitimately collapse onto the same label tuple.

When that happens, `prometheus.Registry.Gather()` (a checked registry, `internal/server/metrics.go:61`) returns a "collected metric ... was collected before with the same name and label values" error. The HTTP handler is built with `promhttp.HandlerFor(prometheus.Gatherers{h.self, reg}, promhttp.HandlerOpts{})` (`internal/server/metrics.go:68-71`), and the zero-value `HandlerOpts{}` selects `ErrorHandling: HTTPErrorOnError` (the vendored `promhttp` default) with `ErrorLog: nil`. Under `HTTPErrorOnError`, any Gather error aborts the whole HTTP response with a 500 and serves zero metric families — including the unrelated `h.self` gatherer's own process/go metrics — and because `ErrorLog` is nil, nothing is logged to explain why. The panic-recovery shield in `internal/collector/collector.go` only covers goroutine panics; a duplicate-label collision surfaces later, at `Gather()` time, outside that shield, so it is not caught there either.

## Evidence

- `internal/server/metrics.go:61` — per-request registry is `prometheus.NewRegistry()` (checked, errors on duplicate name+label-value series).
- `internal/server/metrics.go:68-71` — `promhttp.HandlerFor(prometheus.Gatherers{h.self, reg}, promhttp.HandlerOpts{})`; zero-value `HandlerOpts` = `ErrorHandling: HTTPErrorOnError`, `ErrorLog: nil`.
- `internal/collector/cron.go:34-37` (labels built at `internal/collector/cron.go:49-58`) — cron `job_status` metric keyed on `(schedule, description, command, origin)` with `enabled` as the metric *value*, not a label; two cron rows identical in those four fields collide regardless of enabled state (`opnsense/cron.go` fetches `Cron.UUID` but it is never used as a label).
- `internal/collector/dyndns.go:47-50` vs `:43-46` — `account_last_update_timestamp_seconds` is labeled `(description, service, hostnames)`, omitting `interface`, while the sibling `account_enabled` metric includes `interface`; two dyndns accounts sharing description+service+hostnames but differing only by interface (normal dual-WAN failover setup) collide on the timestamp metric.
- `internal/collector/certificates.go:100-129` (registration at `certificates.go:42`) — leaf-cert labels are `(description, commonname, cert_type, in_use, instance)` with no uniqueness guarantee (e.g. an old cert left behind with the same description after ACME renewal).
- `internal/collector/acme.go:40,64` — ACME certificate metrics keyed only on `(name, description)`.
- `internal/collector/collector.go:814-848` — the concurrent-collection panic shield only `recover()`s goroutine panics; it does not run at `Gather()` time and does not catch this class of error.

The verifier independently reproduced this with a standalone program using the exporter's exact pattern (`MustNewConstMetric` + `promhttp.HandlerFor(reg, promhttp.HandlerOpts{})`) and two identical label tuples: the response was `status: 500` with body `collected metric "opnsense_..." {...} was collected before with the same name and label values`. Not livebox-validated (both findings state `livebox_validated: false`); the live box currently has only 3 certificates with no active duplicates, so this is a proven-by-repro latent condition rather than an actively firing one today.

## Failure scenario / impact

A user clones a cron job to edit it and disables the original, leaving two rows identical in `(schedule, description, command, origin)` — a common workflow. Or a dual-WAN setup configures the same dyndns hostname+description+service on two interfaces. Or a certificate gets re-imported/re-issued keeping the same description. From that moment, every single `/metrics` scrape returns HTTP 500 with zero metrics served — not just the offending subsystem's series, but ALL ~50 collectors' output plus process/go runtime metrics, because the checked registry's `Gather()` fails atomically and `HTTPErrorOnError` discards the entire response. Prometheus marks the whole target down. Nothing is logged (`ErrorLog: nil`), so there is no diagnostic trail pointing at the duplicate config row — the outage looks like a total exporter/target failure and persists until someone finds and removes the duplicate.

## Suggested direction

Two complementary changes: (1) make label sets unique by including a stable per-row identifier (e.g. the UUID already fetched from OPNsense but currently discarded) or by deduplicating/aggregating rows that share a label tuple before emitting metrics; and (2) set `promhttp.HandlerOpts{ErrorHandling: promhttp.ContinueOnError, ErrorLog: <slog adapter>}` in `internal/server/metrics.go` so a single bad series degrades to a logged warning and a partial scrape instead of a total outage, matching node_exporter's behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test constructs two cron rows identical in `(schedule, description, command, origin)` (differing only in `enabled` or UUID) and asserts the cron collector's registered metrics no longer collide (e.g. by including a unique label) OR that `/metrics` still returns 200 with the other collectors' series intact.
- [ ] A unit test constructs two dyndns accounts sharing `description`+`service`+`hostnames` but differing `interface` and asserts `account_last_update_timestamp_seconds` does not produce a duplicate label tuple.
- [ ] A test exercising `internal/server/metrics.go`'s handler with a deliberately duplicate-emitting fake collector asserts the HTTP response is not a blanket 500 that drops all metric families (i.e. `ErrorHandling` is no longer the zero-value `HTTPErrorOnError`), and that the duplicate/error condition is logged.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/collector/... ./internal/server/...` passes with the above tests included.
- [ ] `make docs-check` remains green (no generated-doc drift introduced by any label changes).

body:
## Problem

The Grafana Cloud OTLP shortcut (`--otlp.grafana-cloud-endpoint`), and more generally any `--otlp.endpoint`/`--otlp.grafana-cloud-endpoint` value that includes a URL path, silently posts metrics to the wrong path and delivers zero data.

`internal/telemetry/exporter.go` passes the configured endpoint straight into the OTel SDK's `WithEndpointURL` option for both the HTTP (`otlpmetrichttp`) and gRPC (`otlpmetricgrpc`) exporters. The vendored SDK's `WithEndpointURL` uses the URL's path **verbatim** as the request path, only substituting the default `/v1/metrics` signal path when the supplied path is empty. This is different from the `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` environment-variable code path in the same SDK, which does `path.Join(u.Path, "/v1/metrics")` — i.e. it appends the signal path rather than replacing it. Grafana Cloud's published OTLP gateway URL is a base URL of the form `https://otlp-gateway-<zone>.grafana.net/otlp`, and the exporter's own docs tell users to configure exactly that base URL. Because the SDK keeps the path as-is instead of appending `/v1/metrics`, every export request goes to `.../otlp` instead of `.../otlp/v1/metrics`, which the gateway does not serve.

Export failures from this misconfiguration are deliberately non-fatal (metrics export must never crash the exporter), so the only visible symptom is a rate-limited `slog.Warn` line — nothing forces the operator to notice that the documented, first-class Grafana Cloud integration is completely non-functional.

## Evidence

- `internal/telemetry/exporter.go:67` and `:82` — pass `cfg.Endpoint` into `otlpmetricgrpc.WithEndpointURL` / `otlpmetrichttp.WithEndpointURL` respectively.
- `vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlpmetric/otlpmetrichttp/internal/oconf/options.go:288-302` — `WithEndpointURL` sets `cfg.Metrics.URLPath = u.Path` verbatim.
- `vendor/.../oconf/options.go:113-124` (`cleanPath`) — only substitutes the default `/v1/metrics` path when the given path is empty/`.`; a non-empty path like `/otlp` is kept as-is.
- `vendor/.../oconf/envconfig.go:60` — by contrast, the `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` env-var path does `path.Join(u.Path, "/v1/metrics")`, i.e. it appends rather than replaces.
- `docs/configuration.md:136,154-158` — instructs users to set `--otlp.grafana-cloud-endpoint` to the gateway **base URL** (e.g. `https://otlp-gateway-prod-eu-west-2.grafana.net/otlp`), which is exactly the value Grafana Cloud publishes.
- `internal/options/otlp_test.go:88` — codifies this base-URL usage as the expected/correct input.
- `internal/options/otlp.go:178-189` (`assembleOTLP`) — feeds the Grafana Cloud base URL straight into `cfg.Endpoint` with no path adjustment.

An overlay-injected test that started `telemetry.Start` against a local HTTP server with `Endpoint=<srv>/otlp` observed every export POST hitting path `/otlp`, never `/otlp/v1/metrics`. Not livebox-validated (`livebox_validated: false`).

## Failure scenario / impact

An operator follows `docs/configuration.md`'s documented Grafana Cloud shortcut exactly as written: `--otlp.enabled --otlp.grafana-cloud-instance-id=... --otlp.grafana-cloud-token=... --otlp.grafana-cloud-endpoint=https://otlp-gateway-prod-eu-west-2.grafana.net/otlp`. The exporter starts and logs "otlp metrics export enabled", giving every appearance of working. Every export tick (60s) then 404s against `/otlp` on the gateway, and zero metric series ever arrive in Grafana Cloud. The only symptom is a rate-limited `slog.Warn` roughly once every 30s — easy to miss in normal log volume, especially since the exporter deliberately treats export failures as non-fatal. An operator who instead sets the identical URL via `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (which the flag help implies is just a fallback for the same value) would have it work correctly, since that SDK code path appends the signal path.

## Suggested direction

In `newExporter`/`assembleOTLP`, when the configured endpoint URL has a non-empty path that doesn't already end in the signal-specific suffix (`/v1/metrics` for HTTP), join it onto the path rather than passing it straight to `WithEndpointURL` — mirroring the SDK's own env-var semantics (e.g. `WithEndpoint(u.Host)` + `WithURLPath(path.Join(u.Path, "/v1/metrics"))` for the HTTP exporter). Add a unit test that starts a local HTTP server and asserts the actual request path received, for both a bare base URL (Grafana Cloud shortcut) and a full signal URL (should not get double-suffixed).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test starts a local HTTP test server, configures the exporter with `--otlp.grafana-cloud-endpoint=<server>/otlp` (or the programmatic equivalent), and asserts the received request path is `/otlp/v1/metrics`, not `/otlp`.
- [ ] A unit test confirms that an endpoint already ending in `/v1/metrics` is not double-suffixed (e.g. `<server>/v1/metrics` still resolves to `/v1/metrics`).
- [ ] A unit test confirms an endpoint with no path (e.g. `<server>`) still defaults to `/v1/metrics`, preserving current behavior for that case.
- [ ] `docs/configuration.md`'s Grafana Cloud OTLP example is verified (by the above tests, or a doc-linked example test) to actually reach the signal path documented by Grafana Cloud.
- [ ] Existing `internal/options/otlp_test.go` assertions about the "gateway base URL" form continue to pass unchanged, confirming no regression to the documented input format.
- [ ] `make test` and `make lint` pass with the fix applied.

body:
## Problem

Every published container image (`ghcr.io/rknightion/opnsense-exporter:latest`, versioned release tags, and `:main`/edge builds) embeds an empty binary version, because the Dockerfile's build ARG name and the value the publish pipeline supplies for it differ in case.

The Dockerfile declares `ARG Version` (capital V) and interpolates it into the Go build's `-ldflags "-X main.version=${Version}"` and into an OCI `LABEL`. The shared reusable workflow `rknightion/.github/.github/workflows/container-publish.yml` (invoked by `.github/workflows/publish.yml`), which actually publishes images, passes the build arg as `VERSION=${{ env.COMPUTED_VERSION }}` (all caps). Docker build-arg names are case-sensitive, so `VERSION` from the caller never binds to the Dockerfile's `Version` ARG. The ARG stays unset, `${Version}` expands to the empty string, and `main.version` gets compiled in as `""`.

This regression is invisible in CI: `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `docker-build-verify` job happens to pass `Version=ci-test` (matching the Dockerfile's case), so the CI build path works correctly while the real publish path is broken. GoReleaser-built binaries (non-container release artifacts) are unaffected, since GoReleaser sets `-X main.version={{ .Version }}` directly and doesn't go through this Docker ARG at all.

## Evidence

- `Dockerfile:7` — `ARG Version`
- `Dockerfile:18` — `-ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=${Version}"` (and a corresponding `LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version=${Version}` later in the file)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:82-83` — passes `Version=ci-test` (case matches the Dockerfile, masking the bug in CI)
- `.github/workflows/publish.yml:19-21` — invokes the shared `rknightion/.github` container-publish reusable workflow with no `build-args` of its own
- The reusable workflow at pinned SHA `f31690684f4292d1fe8e528618f7c8306fe27d9a` (`rknightion/.github/.github/workflows/container-publish.yml`, v1.3.1) supplies `build-args: |\n  ${{ inputs.build-args }}\n  VERSION=${{ env.COMPUTED_VERSION }}` (all caps)

Reproduced directly against a real published image:
```
$ docker run ghcr.io/rknightion/opnsense-exporter:1.0.1 ...
msg="starting opnsense-exporter" version=""
```
Same result for `:latest` and edge `:main`. An older, pre-reusable-workflow cached image correctly showed `version=1.0.0`, confirming this regressed when publishing moved onto the shared workflow.

`internal/collector/collector.go:642-645,756-757` wires this same `main.version` variable into the `opnsense_exporter_build_info` metric, so the metric also carries an empty `version` label on every container deployment.

Note: the `org.opencontainers.image.version` OCI label showing `"main"` on some tags is a separate mechanism (docker/metadata-action supplies its own version label via `docker-build-push-action`'s `labels:` input, independent of the Dockerfile's own `LABEL`) — it is not additional proof of this same root cause and shouldn't be conflated with it, but the Dockerfile-authored label is still empty/wrong for the same case-mismatch reason.

## Failure scenario / impact

Trigger: any image published through the current pipeline — a tagged release, `:latest`, or an edge `:main` build.

Consequence: the running exporter reports `version=""` at startup in logs, and every scrape of `opnsense_exporter_build_info` carries an empty `version` label. Anyone relying on this for fleet version tracking, dashboards/alerts keyed on running version, or bug triage against a reported version gets no signal at all — it's indistinguishable across releases. This affects 100% of container-image consumers of the project; binary releases via GoReleaser are unaffected.

## Suggested direction

Rename the Dockerfile ARG (both build stages, the ldflags interpolation, and the version `LABEL`) to `VERSION` so it matches what the reusable workflow actually supplies, rather than trying to change the shared reusable workflow. Add a release/publish smoke check that pulls the just-published image and asserts the reported version is non-empty and matches the expected tag, so this class of regression can't silently reoccur.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docker build` invoked with `--build-arg VERSION=<x>` (matching the real publish pipeline's casing) produces a binary/image whose `main.version` is `<x>`, not empty
- [ ] Running `ghcr.io/rknightion/opnsense-exporter:<newly published tag>` and checking its startup log shows a non-empty `version=` field matching the published tag
- [ ] The `opnsense_exporter_build_info` metric exposed by a freshly published container image carries a non-empty, correct `version` label
- [ ] `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `docker-build-verify` job is updated/kept consistent so it continues to pass the same build-arg name and case actually used by the real publish workflow (so this discrepancy can't mask a future regression)
- [ ] A CI or release-time smoke check runs the published image and fails the pipeline if the reported version is empty

body:
## Problem

All 14 timestamp panels/columns in the Grafana dashboard that use Grafana's `dateTimeAsIso` unit render as dates around 1970-01-21 instead of the real timestamp. Grafana's `dateTimeAsIso` (and sibling `dateTime*`) value formats interpret the raw numeric field as epoch **milliseconds**. Every metric fed into these panels is an epoch-**seconds** gauge (named `*_timestamp_seconds` / `*_seconds` or documented as Unix seconds), and none of the panel query expressions multiply the value by 1000 before display. A value like `1.78e9` (seconds since epoch, i.e. mid-2026) is instead interpreted as `1.78e9` milliseconds since epoch, which lands on 1970-01-21.

This affects every panel/column built with `unit="dateTimeAsIso"` across the dashboard-building code in `grafana/tabs/`, with zero exceptions found (`rg -c dateTimeAsIso grafana/dashboard.json` = 14, and `grep '* 1000'` across `grafana/*.py` = 0 hits).

## Evidence

- `grafana/tabs/system.py:86` — `opnsense_system_config_last_change` set to `unit="dateTimeAsIso"` with no scaling.
- `grafana/tabs/system.py:284` — `opnsense_firmware_last_check_timestamp_seconds` same issue.
- `grafana/tabs/vpn.py:122` — WireGuard "Last Handshake" column, via `unit_overrides`.
- `grafana/tabs/tailscale.py:56` — Tailscale peer last-handshake column.
- `grafana/tabs/certificates.py:69`, `:126`, `:162`, `:195` — ACME/CA cert validity/renewal timestamps.
- `grafana/tabs/dhcp.py:116`, `:225`, `:247` — DHCP/Kea lease-expiry and dnsmasq columns.
- `grafana/tabs/services_cron.py:170` — cron/service last-run timestamp.
- `grafana/tabs/qfeeds.py:51` — Q-Feeds update-schedule column.
- Committed artifact: `rg -c dateTimeAsIso grafana/dashboard.json` = 14 (matches count above).
- Collector-side confirmation that these are epoch seconds, not milliseconds: `internal/collector/wireguard.go:113-118` computes `age := now.Unix() - int64(instance.LatestHandshake)`, which only makes sense if `LatestHandshake` is Unix seconds; `internal/collector/tailscale.go:83` names its metric `peer_last_handshake_timestamp_seconds`; `internal/collector/system.go:66` and `:168-172` emit `config_last_change` straight from the raw Unix-seconds API field.

Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box: `opnsense_system_config_last_change` scraped as `1.781894023e9` (epoch seconds), which the affected panel renders as a January 1970 date.

## Failure scenario / impact

Any user opening the Grafana dashboard shipped with this exporter sees "Config Last Changed", "Last Firmware Check", WireGuard/Tailscale "Last Handshake", ACME "Last Renewal"/"Last Run", CA "Validity Start", dnsmasq/Kea lease-expiry columns, dyndns "Last Update", and Q-Feeds update-schedule columns all displaying dates around 1970-01-21 instead of the actual event time — on every deployment, with no configuration needed to trigger it. This makes 14 distinct panels/columns of the reference dashboard show definitively wrong, useless data out of the box.

## Suggested direction

Scale each affected expression by 1000 before it reaches a `dateTimeAsIso`-formatted field (e.g. append `* 1000` to the PromQL expression), or introduce a shared builder helper (e.g. `ts_epoch()`) that wraps any epoch-seconds expr with the `*1000` conversion so future panels can't regress this. Regenerate `grafana/dashboard.json` via `make dashboard` after the fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every panel/column in `grafana/tabs/*.py` using `unit="dateTimeAsIso"` (or `unit_overrides` setting it) multiplies its underlying epoch-seconds expression by 1000 before formatting.
- [ ] `grafana/dashboard.json` is regenerated via `make dashboard` and the diff shows the `* 1000` scaling applied to all 14 previously-affected panels/columns.
- [ ] A regression test (or dashboard-build assertion) fails if a panel sets `dateTimeAsIso` on a query expression that does not include a `* 1000` (or equivalent millisecond-conversion) scaling factor.
- [ ] Manual verification against a live OPNsense box (or a fixture value) confirms `opnsense_system_config_last_change` and at least one other affected metric (e.g. WireGuard last handshake) now render the correct real-world date/time in the dashboard, not a 1970 date.
- [ ] `make dashboard` continues to pass its "all catalogue metrics on the dashboard" coverage gate after the change.

body:
## Problem

The `OPNsenseGatewayDown` alert cannot detect an outage on a default gateway that has OPNsense monitoring administratively disabled, because the collector never emits `opnsense_gateways_status` (or rtt/rttd/loss) for such a gateway in the first place, and neither the portable Prometheus rule nor the Grafana-managed rule has a fallback for the resulting missing-series case.

In `internal/collector/gateways.go` the status/rtt/loss metrics are emitted only inside a nested guard: `if v.Enabled { if v.MonitorEnabled { ... c.status.Set(...) ... } }`. `MonitorEnabled` is derived from the gateway's `monitor_disable` API field (`opnsense/gateways.go`), but OPNsense's API separately reports a real `status` field (e.g. "Online"/"Down") regardless of whether monitoring is enabled — the collector simply discards that value when monitoring is off instead of exporting it. The result is that for any default gateway with monitoring disabled, no `opnsense_gateways_status{default_gateway="true", ...}` series exists at all, at any time — not even a "1" (healthy) value.

`grafana/alerts/build_rules.py` builds `OPNsenseGatewayDown` as `opnsense_gateways_status{default_gateway="true"} < 1`, with no `absent()`/coverage clause to catch the "no series" case. The Grafana-managed rule variant additionally defaults `noDataState` to `"OK"` (only the `opnsense-exporter-down` rule overrides this to `"Alerting"`), so a permanently-missing series is treated as healthy rather than unknown. This is not a hypothetical corner case: it is the exact configuration of the live reference OPNsense box's IPv6 default gateway (a DHCPv6-PD/PPPoE-style setup where monitoring the volatile next-hop is commonly disabled), so the shipped, marquee critical alert has a real, reproducible pager blind spot.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/gateways.go:267-283` — status/rtt/rttd/loss metrics are nested inside `if v.Enabled { if v.MonitorEnabled { ... } }`; nothing is emitted when `MonitorEnabled` is false.
- `opnsense/gateways.go:190-251` — `MonitorEnabled = !parseStringToBool(v.MonitorDisable)` (line 226); `g.Status` is parsed unconditionally from the API's `status` field via `parseGatewayStatus(v.Status, ...)` (line 249), i.e. the API supplies a usable status independent of monitor state, which the collector discards.
- `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:62-65` — `OPNsenseGatewayDown` expression: `opnsense_gateways_status{default_gateway="true"} < 1`, no `absent()`/coverage clause.
- `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:262` and `grafana-managed/opnsense-gateway-down.json:15` — default `noDataState` is `"OK"`; only `opnsense-exporter-down.json` overrides it to `"Alerting"`.
- `internal/collector/gateways_test.go:157-225` (`TestGatewaysCollector_Update_EnabledWithoutMonitor`) currently pins this behavior: exactly 6 metrics emitted for an enabled/monitor-disabled gateway, with no status metric — confirming this is intentional/tested code, not an accidental slip, but the resulting alert-coverage gap is still a defect.
- Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box: its `gatewaysStatus.json` shows a gateway with `"defaultgw": true`, `"monitor_disable": "1"`, `"status": "Online"` — a real default gateway for which no `opnsense_gateways_status` series is ever produced.

## Failure scenario / impact

On the live box's configuration, the IPv6 default gateway has `defaultgw=true` and `monitor_disable=1`. If that gateway's connectivity dies, no `opnsense_gateways_status` series exists for it (there never was one), so `OPNsenseGatewayDown` never activates — its selector matches zero series, and with `noDataState: OK` on the Grafana-managed rule there is no secondary "unknown" signal either. An operator who read the alert as "all default gateways are paged on down" instead learns about the v6 outage only when dependent services start failing. This is a shipped, bundled critical alert silently covering less than its documented/assumed scope for a realistic default-gateway topology (monitoring disabled on a volatile PPPoE/DHCPv6-PD next-hop is a common real-world pattern, not an edge case).

## Suggested direction

Either (a) emit the API-reported status/rtt/loss for gateways with monitoring disabled instead of discarding them, (b) add a coverage/absence alert such as `opnsense_gateways_info{default_gateway="true"} unless on(name) opnsense_gateways_status` to flag default gateways with no status series, or (c) at minimum document in the alert description/README that `OPNsenseGatewayDown` only covers monitor-enabled gateways. Any of these should also revisit `noDataState` for gateway-related Grafana-managed rules.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test asserts that a default gateway with `monitor_disable=1` but a valid API `status` field results in `opnsense_gateways_status` being emitted (or, if direction (b)/(c) is chosen instead, a test asserts a coverage alert/absence check exists and fires for this configuration).
- [ ] `TestGatewaysCollector_Update_EnabledWithoutMonitor` is updated to reflect the new expected metric count/behavior rather than continuing to pin the current gap.
- [ ] `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py` includes either an updated `OPNsenseGatewayDown` expression or a new coverage rule that fires (or is proven not to fire) when a `default_gateway="true"` gateway has no corresponding `opnsense_gateways_status` series, with a test in the alerts test suite covering it.
- [ ] If `noDataState` remains `OK` for gateway-related Grafana-managed rules, the docs/README explicitly call out this limitation so operators aren't misled about alert coverage.
- [ ] `make test` and `make docs-check` (or the equivalent alerts build/test target) pass with the change.

body:
## Problem

The shipped Prometheus rules file `grafana/alerts/opnsense.rules.yaml` fails `promtool check rules` and is rejected outright by Prometheus, Mimir, and the Grafana Cloud ruler — the three targets `grafana/README.md` explicitly recommends loading it into. The file is generated by `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py`, which builds a single `description` string per alert and reuses it verbatim for both the Grafana-managed-alerting output and the plain Prometheus/`rulefmt` output. One alert's description, `OPNsenseGatewayHighLoss`, uses `{{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.1f" }}%` — `$values` is a Grafana classic/unified-alerting template variable that does not exist in Prometheus's rule-template context (which only defines `$labels`, `$value`, `$externalLabels`, `$externalURL`). Prometheus's template parser fails on the undefined variable, and because rule files are validated/loaded as a whole, this single bad template makes the **entire file** unloadable — all 19 alert rules and all 8 recording rules, not just the one broken alert.

This has been broken since the rules file was first added (commit `81d36dd`) and is not caught by any existing CI check.

## Evidence

- `grafana/alerts/opnsense.rules.yaml:67` — the generated `description:` annotation for `OPNsenseGatewayHighLoss` contains `{{ $values.A.Value | printf "%.1f" }}%`.
- `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:74` — the `RULES` dict entry for `opnsense-gateway-high-loss` defines this description string.
- `grafana/alerts/build_rules.py:193-220` — `emit_prometheus()` reuses the same `description` string verbatim for the Prometheus/`rulefmt` YAML emission with no stripping/translation of Grafana-only template syntax.
- `grafana/README.md:81-83` — labels this file "recommended for most users" and instructs loading it into "Prometheus, Mimir, or the Grafana Cloud ruler".

Reproduction:
```
$ promtool check rules grafana/alerts/opnsense.rules.yaml
FAILED: group "opnsense-exporter-alerts", rule 7, "OPNsenseGatewayHighLoss": annotation "description": template: __alert_OPNsenseGatewayHighLoss:1: undefined variable "$values"
```
Removing that one template fragment and re-running yields `SUCCESS: 27 rules found` (19 alert rules + 8 recording rules), confirming this single template bug is the sole cause of the whole-file failure. Independently reproduced via `promtool` 3.5.0 (`docker run --entrypoint promtool prom/prometheus:latest check rules`) against HEAD `eb025ae`, matching the finder's result exactly.

## Failure scenario / impact

A user follows `grafana/README.md` and adds `opnsense.rules.yaml` to their `prometheus.yml` `rule_files:` list: Prometheus refuses to load the file (fatal rule-file load error, or a rejected `/-/reload`). The same file rejected by `mimirtool rules load` or an upload to the Grafana Cloud ruler. As a result none of the 19 alerts — including the critical `OPNsenseExporterDown` and `OPNsenseGatewayDown` pager alerts — nor any of the 8 recording rules ever actually load, silently leaving the user with zero alerting coverage despite having followed the documented, recommended setup path.

## Suggested direction

In `build_rules.py`, stop sharing one `description` string across both emission formats — keep per-format descriptions (or strip/translate Grafana-only template constructs, e.g. rewriting `{{ $values.A.Value }}` to the Prometheus equivalent `{{ $value }}`, specifically for `emit_prometheus()`), then regenerate `opnsense.rules.yaml`. Also add `promtool check rules` (or equivalent) to CI/`make rules` so this class of bug cannot ship again.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `promtool check rules grafana/alerts/opnsense.rules.yaml` exits 0 and reports all 27 rules (19 alerts + 8 recording rules) loaded successfully.
- [ ] The `OPNsenseGatewayHighLoss` alert's Prometheus-emitted `description` annotation contains no Grafana-only template variables (`$values`, `$values.A.Value`, etc.) — only Prometheus template context variables (`$labels`, `$value`, etc.).
- [ ] A unit/regression test in `grafana/alerts/` (or a `make rules`-invoked check) fails if any future `RULES` entry's Prometheus-emitted description contains `$values` or other non-Prometheus template syntax.
- [ ] CI (or `make rules`) runs `promtool check rules` (or equivalent programmatic validation) against the generated `opnsense.rules.yaml` and fails the build on any validation error.
- [ ] The Grafana-managed-alerting emission path (if a separate output exists) still renders `$values.A.Value` correctly, i.e. the fix does not regress the Grafana-native format.

comments.body:
Scope clarification after review with Rob: the repo ships the same rules in two formats, and this finding applies **only to the portable `opnsense.rules.yaml`** — the `grafana-managed/*.json` manifests are a separate rendering where `{{ $values.A.Value }}` is valid Grafana templating and are unaffected.

The portable yaml cannot be re-scoped as "Grafana-managed only": `grafana/README.md:11` documents it as portable **Prometheus rule groups** ("load it into Prometheus, Mimir, or the Grafana Cloud ruler") and `build_rules.py`'s header calls it "THIS is the artifact most users want". In that documented engine the $values syntax is rejected/renders literally, so the defect stands as filed. If the portable format is ever dropped as a product decision, close this then.

Resolved by dropping the portable Prometheus rules format entirely (product decision, 2026-07-03): `grafana/alerts/opnsense.rules.yaml` and the `emit_prometheus()` path are removed in 2af458a. The `$values` template that promtool rejected only existed in that portable artifact — the Grafana-managed manifests under `grafana/alerts/grafana-managed/` render `{{ $values.A.Value }}` correctly and are now the only supported format. No promtool gate needed since there's no Prometheus rule-group file to validate.

body:
## Problem

When `--exporter.instance-label` is left unset, the exporter decides the value of the `opnsense_instance` label (and the equivalent OTLP `service.instance.id` resource attribute and Pyroscope profiling tag) via a one-shot 5-second race at startup, not a deterministic rule. `instanceLabel` is initialized to the configured `opnsConfig.Host` (address/host:port), then a background goroutine calls `FetchSystemHostname()` against the live OPNsense API; if that call returns before a 5-second timer fires, the label is "upgraded" to the box's real hostname, otherwise the address value is kept permanently for the life of the process. There is no retry — whichever side of the `select` wins is final, and the loser's result is silently discarded.

Because this value is baked once into every metric's `opnsense_instance` label, into the OTLP resource identity, and into Pyroscope tags, the exact same deployment can emit two entirely different sets of series identities across restarts, purely based on how fast the box happened to answer the hostname API call that particular time. The underlying API client itself can legitimately take up to ~45s to fail over (HTTP timeout 15s × up to 3 retries), so a 5s bound is easily exceeded by ordinary conditions — not just catastrophic ones — and is most likely to be exceeded exactly when a firewall and its exporter restart together (power event, maintenance window), which is a common real-world pattern for this audience.

## Evidence

`main.go:26-29` — the timeout constant:
```go
// instanceLabelLookupTimeout bounds the best-effort startup hostname lookup used
...
const instanceLabelLookupTimeout = 5 * time.Second
```

`main.go:303-339` — the race itself:
```go
instanceLabel := *options.InstanceLabel
if instanceLabel == "" {
    instanceLabel = opnsConfig.Host
    ...
    hostname, hErr := opnsenseClient.FetchSystemHostname()
    ...
    case <-time.After(instanceLabelLookupTimeout):
        // falls back to opnsConfig.Host, logs a WARN only
```

The resolved `instanceLabel` is then threaded into:
- `internal/collector/collector.go` — `instanceLabelName = "opnsense_instance"` applied via `c.instanceLabel` to every metric (build_info, scrape counters, endpoint errors, all generic gauges)
- `main.go:353` — Pyroscope profiling tag
- `main.go:396` (area) — OTLP resource `service.instance.id` via `telemetry.Start(...)`

The API client's own retry/timeout budget (`opnsense/client.go`) is up to ~45s (15s HTTP timeout × up to 3 retries), far exceeding the 5s bound — confirmed via the commit message of `258205c`, which introduced this exact 5s mitigation and explicitly documents the ~45s worst case it is trying to bound.

Not livebox-validated for the specific race (timing-dependent), but the systemInformation hostname format (e.g. `opnsense.example.com`) vs a typical configured address/IP is confirmed structurally distinct from client behavior.

## Failure scenario / impact

A power event restarts the exporter host and the firewall together. The exporter's process comes up first (or the firewall is still booting its API), the 5s hostname lookup times out, and every `opnsense_*` series is labelled `opnsense_instance=<configured address>` (e.g. `<lan-ip-68>`) for the life of that process. Weeks later, a routine exporter restart happens while the firewall is fully healthy and answers within 5s — now every series relabels to `opnsense_instance=<hostname>` (e.g. `opnsense.example.com`). PromQL queries, alert rules, and Grafana dashboard variables pinned to the old label value go silent or return empty, and the metric history for that instance splits into two disjoint, non-contiguous series sets. The only trace of what happened is a single startup WARN log line — there is no error and nothing to alert on.

## Suggested direction

Make the default deterministic rather than race-based: either always default to the configured address (only use the API hostname when explicitly requested via a flag), or keep retrying the hostname lookup in the background with a flag-controlled timeout that fails startup (refusing to serve `/metrics`) rather than silently falling back and switching identity later.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test asserts that with `--exporter.instance-label` unset, the resolved instance label is deterministic and does not depend on the timing of `FetchSystemHostname()` (e.g. by mocking a slow/failing API client and asserting the label choice is consistent across repeated runs, or asserting the fallback-to-hostname path is opt-in only).
- [ ] A unit or integration test simulates `FetchSystemHostname()` taking longer than the current 5s bound (e.g. via a fake client with configurable delay) and asserts the exporter behaves per the chosen fix (either always uses the address, or blocks/fails startup rather than silently switching identity mid-life).
- [ ] The chosen behavior is documented in `docs/configuration.md` (regenerated via `make docs`), explicitly describing what determines `opnsense_instance` when the flag is unset and any startup-blocking behavior, so operators do not need to read the source to predict the label.
- [ ] No code path exists where the same running exporter, or two consecutive process restarts against an unchanged configuration, can produce two different `opnsense_instance` (or OTLP `service.instance.id` / Pyroscope tag) values without an explicit config change.
- [ ] `go test ./...` and `make lint` pass.

body:
## Problem

`opnsense_firewall_interface_hits_total` is emitted as a Prometheus `CounterValue` with the help text "Total number of firewall rule matches per interface", but the underlying OPNsense endpoint (`api/diagnostics/firewall/stats`) does not return anything counter-shaped. On the live box, `FirewallController::statsAction` runs `filter read log` over only the most recent 5000 firewall log records (default `$limit`), counts occurrences grouped by interface, sorts descending, and returns just the top 10 interfaces plus a synthetic `"other"` bucket for everything beyond the top 10. That value rises and falls as old log lines age out of the fixed-size window — it is not monotonic, it does not count all rule matches (only logged ones), and the label is the interface *description* (e.g. `IOT`, `LAN`) rather than the OS device name (e.g. `igb0`, `ixl0`) that every other firewall metric in this exporter uses.

Because the collector labels this a `CounterValue`, Prometheus treats any decrease as a counter reset. The shipped Grafana dashboard panel then applies `rate()` to it, so a normal, expected decrease (traffic mix shifting, old log lines rolling out of the window) is misread as a full-window counter reset and renders a spurious spike. Series also appear and disappear as the top-10 ranking churns, and a fake `other` "interface" shows up once more than 10 interfaces are logged.

## Evidence

- `internal/collector/firewall.go:147-150` — sets metric help text "Total number of firewall rule matches per interface".
- `internal/collector/firewall.go:237-245` — emits the value via `prometheus.CounterValue` for metric `interface_hits_total`.
- `opnsense/firewall.go:74-95` — `FetchFirewallStats` calls the `firewallStats` endpoint.
- `opnsense/client.go:100` — `firewallStats` maps to `api/diagnostics/firewall/stats`.
- `grafana/tabs/firewall.py:127` — shipped "Interface Rule Hits/s" panel applies `rate(opnsense_firewall_interface_hits_total...[RATE])` to this series.

Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box. `FirewallController.php::statsAction` (lines ~105-155) defaults `$limit=5000`, reads the most recent firewall log records, counts and groups by interface, `arsort`s, keeps only the top 10 plus a synthetic `gettext("other")` bucket (`value = count(records) - top_cnt`), and labels each entry with `$label_map[$n->if]` — the interface **description**, not the OS device name. Sample live payload:

```json
[{"label":"IOT","value":3126},{"label":"AAISP","value":913},{"label":"LAN", "...":"..."}]
```

For comparison, every other firewall metric in this exporter (e.g. `pfStatisticsByInterface`-derived metrics) labels by OS device (`igb0`, `ixl0`, `pppoe0`, `all`, `enc`, ...), so a PromQL join on the `interface` label between `interface_hits_total` and any other firewall metric silently fails to match. Git history (commit `499eb01`, "per-interface hit counters") shows a genuine counter was intended here, confirming this is a defect rather than a deliberate gauge-as-counter design choice.

## Failure scenario / impact

Traffic mix shifts on the firewall (e.g. a previously-busy interface goes quiet and its log lines age out of the fixed 5000-record window) → the reported value for that interface decreases → because the metric type is `CounterValue`, Prometheus's `rate()`/`increase()` interpret the decrease as a counter reset and compute a spurious spike equal to roughly the whole window count → the shipped "Interface Rule Hits/s" dashboard panel shows a fake traffic spike, and any alert rule built on `increase(opnsense_firewall_interface_hits_total[...])` fires falsely. Separately, once more than 10 interfaces have logged traffic, interfaces that drop out of the top-10 ranking go stale mid-series while a synthetic `other` "interface" appears with no stable identity, and any attempt to join this metric to other firewall metrics on `interface` fails because the label vocabularies (description vs. OS device) don't match.

## Suggested direction

Re-emit this as a `GaugeValue` with an honest name and help text (e.g. `firewall_log_entries_recent{interface=...}`, "entries per interface in the most recent 5000 firewall log records"), decide explicitly how to handle/label the synthetic `other` bucket, and update the shipped dashboard panel to plot the gauge directly rather than applying `rate()`/`increase()` to it. Non-binding — do not treat this as the fix spec.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `opnsense_firewall_interface_hits_total` (or its renamed replacement) is registered and emitted as a `prometheus.GaugeValue`, not `CounterValue`, with help text that accurately describes a sliding-window log count rather than "total rule matches".
- [ ] A unit test in `internal/collector` feeds a decreasing sample sequence (simulating log lines aging out of the window) and asserts the metric type is `GaugeValue` so a regression back to `CounterValue` is caught.
- [ ] The synthetic `"other"` bucket returned by the API is either explicitly labeled/documented as an aggregate (not a real interface) or dropped, with a test asserting the chosen behavior.
- [ ] `grafana/tabs/firewall.py`'s "Interface Rule Hits/s" (or equivalently renamed) panel no longer wraps this metric in `rate()`/`increase()`, and `make dashboard` regenerates without diff drift once the panel query is fixed.
- [ ] `make docs` is run so the metrics reference and collector docs reflect the corrected metric name/type/help text, and `make docs-check` passes.

body:
## Problem

`FetchCaptivePortalSessions` decodes the captive portal zones map (`api/captiveportal/session/zones`) into a `flexStringMap` (`opnsense/jsonflex.go`). `flexStringMap.UnmarshalJSON` was written to handle a known OPNsense quirk where PHP serializes an *empty* associative array as a JSON array (`[]`) instead of `{}` — so it treats any JSON array as an empty map.

The problem is that OPNsense's `SessionController::zonesAction` builds the zones response as `$response[(string)$zone->zoneid] = $zone->description`, keyed by zoneid. When zoneids are sequential starting at 0 — which is exactly what happens for the first configured zone(s), the common/default case — PHP's `json_encode` re-integerizes those numeric string keys and serializes the result as a JSON *list*, e.g. `["test"]`, not an object. `flexStringMap.UnmarshalJSON` cannot distinguish this populated-but-array-shaped case from the genuinely-empty-map case, so it silently discards a non-empty, real zone list and returns an empty map.

Downstream, `internal/collector/captiveportal.go` reports `zones_total` from the (wrongly empty) map, and any active session's zoneid fails the zone-name join, falling through to a synthetic `zone_id="unknown"` series instead of its real zone label.

## Evidence

Confirmed against a live OPNsense 26.1.8 box: with 1 configured captive portal zone, `GET api/captiveportal/session/zones` returned the JSON array `["test"]`, and the exporter emitted `opnsense_captiveportal_zones_total{...} 0` with no per-zone `opnsense_captiveportal_zone_sessions` series for that zone.

- `opnsense/jsonflex.go:119-131` — `flexStringMap.UnmarshalJSON` treats any input starting with `[` as an empty map:
```go
func (m *flexStringMap) UnmarshalJSON(data []byte) error {
    trimmed := bytes.TrimSpace(data)
    if len(trimmed) > 0 && trimmed[0] == '[' {
        *m = flexStringMap{}
        return nil
    }
    ...
```
- `opnsense/captiveportal.go:77-84` — zones are decoded via this type and iterated to build `data.Zones`; with an empty map, zero zones are produced.
- `opnsense/captiveportal.go:104-111` — session-to-zone join looks up the session's zoneid in the (empty) zones map and falls back to the synthetic `unknown` zone on miss.
- `internal/collector/captiveportal.go:67-83` — emits `opnsense_captiveportal_zones_total` and per-zone series directly from `data.Zones`.
- `opnsense/captiveportal_test.go:10` — the existing unit fixture hardcodes the zones payload as a JSON **object**, `{"0":"Guest WiFi","1":"Lab"}`, which is a shape the real PHP endpoint cannot produce for zoneids 0 and 1 (it would emit `["Guest WiFi","Lab"]`, an array) — which is why this defect was never caught by tests.

## Failure scenario / impact

Any OPNsense box with captive portal zones whose zoneids are sequential starting from 0 — the default numbering for the first zone(s) configured, and the case on the validated live box — causes the exporter to report `opnsense_captiveportal_zones_total == 0` even though zones are configured, and to attribute all active captive portal sessions to a synthetic `zone_id="unknown"` label instead of their real zone. An operator alerting on `zones_total == 0` as a health signal, or graphing sessions per zone, gets silently wrong data on every scrape of an otherwise-healthy, correctly configured box.

## Suggested direction

In `FetchCaptivePortalSessions`, decode the zones payload as `json.RawMessage` first and branch on its shape: if it's a JSON object, keep the existing map-decode path; if it's a non-empty JSON array, treat each element's index as the zoneid (`"0"`, `"1"`, …) with the element value as the description. Alternatively, source the zone list from the `settings/searchZones` bootgrid endpoint, which always returns rows regardless of key numbering.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A unit test feeding the zones payload `["test"]` (array shape, zoneid 0) asserts the decoded zone map contains `{"0": "test"}`, not an empty map.
- [ ] A unit test feeding a payload with zoneids that are not sequential-from-0 (e.g. `{"3":"Lab"}`, still object-shaped) continues to decode correctly, confirming no regression on the non-array case.
- [ ] A unit test feeding a genuinely empty zones payload (`[]`) still decodes to an empty map, confirming the original empty-map quirk handling is preserved.
- [ ] With the array-shaped fixture above, the captive portal collector unit test asserts `opnsense_captiveportal_zones_total` reflects the real zone count (not 0) and that a session with zoneid `0` is attributed to its real zone label, not `zone_id="unknown"`.
- [ ] `opnsense/captiveportal_test.go`'s existing fixture is corrected (or a new fixture added) to reflect a shape the real OPNsense PHP endpoint can actually produce for sequential-from-0 zoneids.

## Mission

Work **every issue in milestones [M1](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/milestone/1) and [M2](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/milestone/2)** — the output of the 2026-07-03 production-readiness bug bash — and bring this exporter to a hardened production posture. All 96 issues live on the [opnsense-exporter roadmap project](https://github.com/users/rknightion/projects/5) with Status/Priority/Effort/Area/Type set. M1 = provable bugs, correctness defects, operational/security risks. M2 = improvements with a concrete stated payoff. Priority labels (`P1`>`P2`>`P3`) + phases below express ordering; there are **no due dates**.

**This issue is the parent tracker.** Progress lives here and on the individual issues, so any future session can resume from GitHub alone. This issue deliberately sits in no milestone and no project.

## How these issues were produced (trust level)

Three adversarial discovery rounds (77 → 39 → 7 confirmed findings) over the whole repo, each candidate independently re-verified by a separate agent instructed to refute it; 8 candidates were killed. 123 confirmed findings were merged into 96 issues (same root cause = one issue). ~40% carry evidence validated against a **live OPNsense 26.1.8_5 box** — issue bodies say so explicitly. Every issue is self-contained: Problem / Evidence (file:line at eb025ae) / Failure scenario / Suggested direction / Acceptance criteria.

## Operating rules (binding)

1. **Read each issue IN FULL before working it — body AND comments.** Comments may carry dedupe verdicts and scope changes that override the body.
2. **Validate before implementing.** Line numbers reference commit `eb025ae`; re-confirm the mechanism in current code first. If a premise no longer holds, say so on the issue and close it with a note — never force a fix.
3. **TDD per issue:** failing test reproducing the defect → minimal fix → green. Run the full gate (`make test`, `make lint`, `make docs-check`, and `make dashboard`/`make rules` when grafana/ or metrics change) with evidence before closing.
4. **Never hand-edit generated artifacts** (docgen-marked docs, dashboard.json, rule JSONs) — change the source/builder and regenerate (`make docs`, `make dashboard`, `make rules`).
5. **One commit per issue** (tightly-coupled issues in one file may share a commit with multiple `Closes #N` trailers), conventional-commit message, `Closes #N` in the body, **committed straight to `main` and pushed immediately** — the push closes the issue. Post a short closing comment with the SHA.
6. **Metric renames/removals are breaking** for existing dashboards/alerts: when an issue requires one (e.g. the firewall hits-counter fix), update the shipped dashboard + rules in the same commit and call the break out in the commit body for release notes.
7. **Live-box validation** is available for API-shape questions: SSH + API credential *location* is documented in `~/repos/chat-personal/opnsense/CLAUDE.md` ("API Access") — read-only use only, never paste credentials anywhere.
8. **Keep this tracker current:** tick each phase checkbox as its issues close and post a phase-completion comment (issues closed + SHAs, anything re-scoped/closed-stale, anything parked). Parked issues get a comment stating exactly what blocks them.
9. **Project hygiene:** move each issue's project Status → In Progress / Done as you go.

### Decisions already made — do not re-litigate
- Milestone routing, priorities, areas and effort estimates were set at triage; challenge only with new evidence, on the issue.
- The duplicate-label blast-radius fix (#81) lands `promhttp.ContinueOnError` **and** per-collector label-uniqueness fixes both — they are complementary, not alternatives.
- Plugin-absent behaviour follows the existing convention: 404 ⇒ collector emits nothing (no zero-valued series).
- **Alerting format: Grafana-managed only.** The portable Prometheus rule-group file (`opnsense.rules.yaml`) was dropped 2026-07-03 (2af458a); ship only `grafana/alerts/grafana-managed/*.json`. This closed #76 and #95 and re-scoped #84's promtool criteria to Grafana-managed manifest validation.

body:
Part of the fleet-wide docs effort tracked in **rknightion/m7kni-net-site#28** (Phase 2). This repo's doc site is served under the m7kni.io hub at `/opnsense-exporter/`, so its own Zensical build + theme overrides determine what search engines and LLMs see for these pages.

Two things are bundled here because they touch the same files:

1. **Redesign & rebrand alignment** — adopt the new m7kni.io brand and colour scheme (light-first, the shared wordmark / palette / type tokens) so the whole fleet reads as one product family. **Tune it for documentation, not marketing:** unlike the vibrant hub *landing* page, these are end-user **product documentation** sites — prioritise a clean, professional, highly readable, documentation-friendly presentation (sensible density, strong nav/TOC/search, scannable reference content) while staying on-brand in palette, type, and logo. Brand-consistent, docs-first. The exact spec follows from the hub redesign — treat the visual details as **pending finalization in rknightion/m7kni-net-site#28** and don't front-run them.
2. **SEO / LLM discoverability** — the metadata improvements below, fully specified now and able to proceed independently of the visual spec.

## Why (SEO/LLM part)

Like the hub, this site's `docs/overrides/main.html` is an empty passthrough, so OpenGraph/Twitter/JSON-LD/robots meta are either absent or (if copied from the hub) injected client-side and invisible to non-JS crawlers and LLMs (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, CCBot, social unfurlers). Render them server-side.

## Tasks

- [ ] **Redesign & rebrand alignment** — apply the finalized hub brand/scheme in a professional, documentation-friendly way (spec via rknightion/m7kni-net-site#28). Brand-consistent palette/type/logo; docs-first layout, density, and navigation.
- [ ] **Server-render head tags** — `main.html` `extrahead` override emitting canonical, `theme-color`, OpenGraph, Twitter (`summary_large_image`), and `robots` meta server-side, reading `config.extra.*` + `page.meta.*`. Mirror the hub's implementation once #29 lands (reuse the same override pattern). ⚠️ MiniJinja — no Python string methods.
- [ ] **JSON-LD** — per-page `Article` (not `TechArticle`) + a repo-level `SoftwareSourceCode`/`SoftwareApplication` node (name, description, `programmingLanguage`, `codeRepository` → this GitHub repo). `Organization` site-wide.
- [ ] **Remove any client-side `seo.js`** if this repo carries a copy; server-side supersedes it.
- [ ] **GEO content-shape pass** on the docs prose (biggest evidence-backed LLM-citation win): definition-first sentences (lead a config option with what it does), self-contained/chunkable `##`/`###` sections (restate the subject, don't rely on "it"/"this"), config/flag/env reference as **tables** not prose, language-tagged code fences (```yaml/```bash), strict one-H1-per-page hierarchy.
- [ ] **robots.txt** — ensure this repo's `docs/robots.txt` allows the current AI UAs (`GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `OAI-SearchBot`, `PerplexityBot`, `CCBot`, `Applebot-Extended`, `Meta-ExternalAgent`, plus user-action bots). (Note: the hub regenerates per-site `robots.txt` at merge time — keep the source consistent with the hub's policy.)
- [ ] **Align zensical version** — match the fleet's pinned zensical version and Renovate handling as decided in Phase 1 (rknightion/m7kni-net-site#29). Depending on that decision this repo may drop zensical from its own CI entirely (if the hub build is the only consumer) or keep it pinned + Renovate-grouped for local/preview builds — follow the fleet approach from #29, don't invent a per-repo variant.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Site is on-brand with the new m7kni.io scheme while reading as a clean, professional product-documentation site.
- [ ] `curl` of a deployed page under m7kni.io/opnsense-exporter/ (no JS) shows server-rendered OG/Twitter/canonical/JSON-LD/robots meta.
- [ ] Docs pages follow the GEO content-shape checklist above.
- [ ] zensical version handling matches the fleet decision in #29.
- [ ] Site build green; renders correctly under the hub.

## Notes

- llms.txt / llms-full.txt / sitemaps for this site are generated centrally by the hub's scripts over this repo's Markdown — **not** per-repo work here.
- Do the SEO/LLM + version tasks whenever useful; gate only the visual-redesign task on the hub spec.

comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed report — both errors are now fixed in main (commit 0e6b9bc).

## Root cause
Newer OPNsense releases (you're on 25.7.11) serialize some API values in ways the exporter's strict JSON parsing rejected:

- **`protocol` collector** — `api/diagnostics/interface/get_protocol_statistics` can return network counters at max-uint64 in scientific notation (`1.8446744073709552e+19`), which doesn't fit a Go `int`. The protocol response now parses those counters as `json.Number` and degrades over-range/garbage values to `0` instead of failing the whole collector.
- **`dnsmasq` collector** — `api/dnsmasq/leases/search` returns `"interfaces": []` (array) instead of `{}` when there are no interface entries, and `"is_reserved": []` instead of `"0"`/`"1"` on some rows. Both are now handled by tolerant JSON types.

While investigating I also fixed the same class of issue in two more collectors that fail on 25.7:
- **`kea`** — `is_reserved` returned as `[]`.
- **`unbound`** — an empty `up` uptime string was hard-failing the entire collector.

All four are covered by new tests.

## What you need to do
The fix is on `main` but not yet in a tagged release. Once a new `latest` image is published it'll carry these fixes — since your deployment uses `image: ghcr.io/rknightion/opnsense-exporter:latest` with `imagePullPolicy: Always`, a pod restart after the next build will pick it up. I'll comment again when a release is tagged.

## One note on your logs
If you also see intermittent `failed status code: 0; max retries` or `404 Not Found` entries across various collectors, those are transient — they happen when the OPNsense box is briefly unreachable or mid-reboot (the web server returns 404 before plugins finish loading) — and are not caused by the exporter.

Import Grafana Dashboard error

https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/main/deploy/grafana/dashboard.json

[Grafana v12.4.0 (d1729c53a7]

> Validation failed
> Dashboard.dashboard.grafana.app "" is invalid: [DashboardSpec.variables: Invalid value: incompatible list lengths (0 and 4), DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "AdhocVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "ConstantVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "CustomVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "DatasourceVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "GroupByVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "QueryVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "SwitchVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.kind: Invalid value: conflicting values "TextVariable" and "IntervalVariable", DashboardSpec.variables.3.spec.refresh: Invalid value: conflicting values "onTimeRangeChanged" and ""]

The Grafana 12.4 import report is now tracked in #420. The audited current dashboard moved from the referenced `deploy/grafana/dashboard.json` path to `grafana/dashboard.json` and the canonical artifact now targets Grafana 13 schema v2. #420 owns reproduction of the 12.4 CRD validation failure and a generated/tested Grafana 11/12 compatibility path without weakening the Grafana 13 artifact.

@ehnwebmaster — this is fixed, and there is now a supported dashboard for Grafana 12. Sorry it sat for a while; the report was buried in a comment on the Renovate dashboard issue rather than filed on its own, so it was easy to lose. It has been tracked as #420 since, and that issue is now closed.

**Your error reproduced exactly.** The file you imported (`deploy/grafana/dashboard.json`, since deleted) was v2beta1 with an `IntervalVariable`, and posting it to a pinned `grafana/grafana:12.4.0` container returns your 422 word for word — `conflicting values "AdhocVariable" and "IntervalVariable"`. It was a real schema defect, not anything about your setup.

**What to use now.** Import **`grafana/dashboard-compat.json`**. It is classic schema and imports cleanly on Grafana 11.5.0 and 12.4.0 — CI starts a container of each version on every commit, imports the file, and reads it back to check the panels and variables survived, so the support claim is tested rather than asserted.

`grafana/dashboard.json` is the canonical dashboard and needs **Grafana 13+**. Worth knowing before you try it on 12: Grafana 12.4 accepts it with **HTTP 200** and then shows an **empty dashboard** — no error anywhere, the schema is simply stored and ignored. Grafana 11.5 at least refuses, though its message (`Dashboard title cannot be empty`) points at the wrong thing.

**The one difference in the compatibility build**, so it is not a surprise: classic schema cannot show and hide panels, and the canonical dashboard leans on that heavily — a tab whose metrics your firewall does not emit is hidden on Grafana 13. Since that is impossible in classic, plugin-gated tabs are left out rather than shipped permanently empty, because an empty CrowdSec tab on a box without CrowdSec looks exactly like a broken exporter. The compatibility build carries the 187 panels that are present on every OPNsense box: Overview, System & Resources, Services/Cron/DynDNS, Certificates, Interfaces, Gateways & WAN, Routing & Neighbors, Protocol Stats, Firewall & PF, and Diagnostics.

If you need a tab that is missing there — IDS, HAProxy, VPN, DHCP and so on — Grafana 13 is the answer; a hand-edited copy will stop tracking the generated one and rot.

Details, including the full failure matrix and the degradation list, are in [`docs/integration-dashboards.md`](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/main/docs/integration-dashboards.md#grafana-11-and-12-use-the-compatibility-dashboard) and [`grafana/README.md`](https://github.com/rknightion/opnsense-exporter/blob/main/grafana/README.md). If the compatibility dashboard misbehaves on your 12.4, please open a fresh issue and tag it — a report against a tested artifact is much easier to act on.

@ehnwebmaster — correction to my reply above, before you act on it: **the compatibility dashboard has been withdrawn**, so please ignore the `dashboard-compat.json` recommendation. The decision is that this project supports **Grafana 13+ only**, because the show/hide-by-plugin behaviour is the point of the dashboard and classic schema cannot express it. Building the compatibility version made that concrete rather than theoretical: 31 of the 41 tabs and 154 rows are gated on which metrics your firewall emits, so the classic build had to drop them, and it shipped without IDS, HAProxy, VPN or DHCP. Better to say "Grafana 13" plainly than to hand you a file that quietly lacks three quarters of it.

What still stands from that reply, and it is the part that affects you:

- **Your original 422 was a real bug**, reproduced word for word from the file you imported. Not your setup.
- **`grafana/dashboard.json` needs Grafana 13+.** On Grafana 12.4 it imports with **HTTP 200** and then renders an **empty dashboard with no error anywhere** — so if you try it and get nothing, that is the version, not a broken export. Grafana 11.5 at least refuses, though its message (`Dashboard title cannot be empty`) points at the wrong thing. Both now documented in the README and on the docs site so nobody else loses an afternoon to it.

Sorry for the double reply — the first was accurate when I posted it and stopped being accurate an hour later.
